Acheron.text: river of the infernal regions, app. supposed by S. to be a lake Tit. IV. iii. 44 .

Achitophel.text: Absalom's counsellor (2 Samuel xv.), 2H4 I. ii. 39 .

Adam.text: (2 ‘buff’ was used for ‘the naked skin’) 1. “the offending Adam,” the Old Adam, H5 I. i. 29 .

Agenor.text: father of Europa Shr. I. i. 172 .

Ajax.text: son of Telamon ( 2H6 V. i. 26 ), one of the Greek heroes in the Trojan war, taken as the type of the dull-witted warrior ( Lr. II. ii. 132 ; cf. Troil. II. i. 1 -59); with pun on ‘a jakes’ LLL. V. ii. 578 .

Alecto.text: one of the Furies 2H4 V. v. 40 “fell A's snake.”

All.text: sb. “all our,” of us all John IV. ii. 102 , Cor. IV. vi. 34 .—adj. any whatever Mac. III. ii. 11 “Things without all remedy.” —adv. only, exclusively All'sW. III. ii. 71 , Lr. I. i. 102 , Sonn. lxxvi. 5 .—“all too,” altogether too 2H4 V. ii. 24 .—conj. although R3 IV. iv. 226 “Thy head, all indirectly, gave direction.”

Amazonian.text: resembling an Amazon or female warrior 3H6 I. iv. 114 , Cor. II. ii. 96 “his Amazonian chin” (‘beardless’).

Anthropophaginian.text: Wiv. IV. v. 10 , one of the “Anthropophagi” ( Oth. I. iii. 144 ) or cannibals.

Antipodes.text: those who dwell on the opposite side of the globe Mer.V. V. i. 127 , R2 III. ii. 49 “wandering with the Antipodes.”

Ariachne.text: incorrect for ‘Arachne’, who challenged Athene to a weaving match; the goddess tore up A.'s web, and A. hanged herself, but Athene changed her into a spider Troil. V. ii. 152 .

Arthur.text: (2 perhaps suggested by place-names such as ‘Arthur's Head’, ‘Arthur's Seat’) 1. “Arthur's show,” exhibition of archery by the ‘Order of Knights of Prince Arthur's Round Table’, or ‘the fellowship of Prince Arthur's Knights’, a society of archers which met on Mile-end Green 2H4 III. ii. 303 .

Atalanta.text: famous for her swiftness of foot AYL. III. ii. 156 “Atalanta's better part” * , 295

Ate.text: goddess of mischief John II. i. 63 “An Ate, stirring him to . . . strife” ; (hence) pl. incitements to mischief LLL. V. ii. 692 “More Ates, more Ates! stir them on!”

Atlas.text: giant supposed to support the universe 3H6 V. i. 36 .

Atropos.text: one of the Fates 2H4 II. iv. 212 .

Ave.text: shout of welcome Meas. I. i. 70 “A-s vehement.”

Bacchanal.text: (from Bacchus, the name of the Greek and Roman god of wine) 1. priest, priestess, or devotee of Bacchus MND. V. i. 48 .

Barbary.text: (country on the north coast of Africa) 1. short for ‘Barbary horse’ R2 V. v. 78 .

Basan.text: Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 127; cf. Psalms xxii. 12 (‘bulls of Basan’).

Basimecu.text: contemptuous term for a Frenchman 2H6 IV. vii. 31 “Mounsieur Basimecu, the dauphin of France.” ∥ Still applied to Italian organgrinders, with the pronunciation ‘boz imacu’, in some parts of Warwickshire.

Bedlam.text: (earlier ‘Bedlem’, ‘Bethlem’, ‘Bethlehem’) 1. the Hospital of St. Mary of Bethlehem in London used as an asylum for the mentally deranged 2H6 V. I. 131 “To Bedlam with him; Tom o' Bedlam,” madman Lr. I. ii. 152 .

Bergomask.text: dance after the manner of the people of Bergamo (a province in the state of Venice), who were noted for the rusticity of their manners and speech MND. V. i. 361 , 370

Bermoothes.text: Bermudas Tp. I. ii. 229 “the stillvex'd Bermoothes.”

Bevis.text: of Hampton (i.e. Earl of Southampton), the hero of a mediaeval romance, of whom incredible stories were told H8 I. i. 38 .

Bezonian.text: needy beggar, rascal 2H4 V. iii. 115 , 2H6 IV. i. 134 .

Boreas.text: the north wind Troil. I. iii. 38 “the ruffian ”

Briareus.text: a hundred-handed giant in Greek mythology Troil. I. ii. 30 “a gouty Briareus, many hands and no use.”

Brownist.text: adherent of the sect founded in Elizabeth's reign by Robert Brown, an English Puritan Tw.N. III. ii. 36 .

Bucklersbury.text: street of London off Cheapside, inhabited by herbalists Wiv. III. iii. 79 “smell like Bucklersbury in simple-time.”

Bull.text: the sign Taurus of the zodiac Tit. IV. iii. 70 .

Burgundy.text: old edd. also “Burgonie, -ony, -uny” ( H5 V. ii. 68 , Lr. I. i. 250 ), “Burgo(i)gne” ( H5 V. ii. 7 ).

Cadmus.text: founder of Thebes MND. IV. i. 118 .

Calydon.text: “the prince of Calydon” ( 2H6 I. i. 236 ) = Meleager (son of Œneus of Calydon and Althæa), whom the Fates decreed to die when a certain log on the hearth was burnt.

Cambyses.text: 1H4 II. iv. 430 “in King Cambyses' vein,” in the ranting style of ‘King Cambyses, a lamentable Tragedy, mixed ful of pleasant mirth’ by Thomas Preston, 1569 - 70

Camelot.text: Lr. II. ii. 89 “Goose . . . I'd drive ye cackling home to Camelot” * ; not yet satisfactorily explained: see the commentators.

Cancer.text: the fourth of the signs of the zodiac, which the sun enters at the summer solstice, June 21 Troil. II. iii. 208 “add more coals to Cancer.”

Capet.text: = Hugh Capet, the first French king of the Capetian dynasty (A.D. 987-996) H5 I. ii. 78 .

Capitol.text: the great national temple of Rome, dedicated to Jupiter Optimus Maximus, on the Saturnian or Tarpeian (afterwards Capitoline) Hill Cor. I. i. 50 , &c., Cæs. I. i. 67 , &c.

Cassibelan.text: Cassivelaunus, king of the Britons in Cæsar's time Cym. I. i. 30 , &c.

Cataian.text: for ‘Cathaian,’ man or woman of Cathay, i.e. China, (hence) sharper, scoundrel Wiv. II. i. 147 , Tw.N. II. iii. 83 .

Cerberus.text: three-headed watch-dog of the infernal regions in ancient mythology LLL. V. ii. 590 .

Ceres.text: goddess of agriculture Tp. IV. i. 60 , 2H6 I. ii. 2 .

Cham.text: obs. form of ‘Khan’, formerly applied to rulers of the Tartars and Mongols, esp. the emperor of China Ado II. i. 279 “the Great Cham's beard.”

Charon.text: ferryman who conveyed the shades of the departed across the Styx; allusively in Troil. III. ii. 10 “be thou my Charon.”

Chartreux.text: the Charterhouse or Carthusian monastery in Smithfield, London H8 I. i. 221 “A monk o' the Chartreux,” I. ii. 148 “a Chartreux friar.”

Cimmerian.text: applied to Aaron, the Moor, in Tit. II. iii. 72 .

Circe.text: enchantress of the island of Aea, who transformed all who drank of her cup into swine Err. V. i. 271 , 1H6 V. iii. 35 .

Clare.text: “votarists of Saint Clare,” order of nuns, called Poor Clares and Minoresses, instituted by St. Clare at Assisi in the 13th cent., Meas. I. iv. 5 .

Cocytus.text: river of the infernal regions Tit. II. iii. 236 .

Colbrand.text: Danish giant in ancient legend John I. i. 225 , H8 V. iv. 23 .

Colossus.text: bronze statue of Apollo of enormous size, one of the seven wonders of the world, reputed to have stood astride the entrance to the harbour of Rhodes, Cæs. I. ii. 135 “he doth bestride the narrow world Like a Colossus” ; hence colossuswise Troil. V. v. 9 .

Commentaries.text: the Commentarii or memoirs of Cæsar 2H6 IV. vii. 65 .

Cytherea.text: Venus, Shr. Ind. ii. 53 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 122

Damascus.text: referred to as the place where Cain slew Abel, 1H6 I. iii. 39 .

Dansker.text: Dane, Ham. II. i. 7 . ∥ The Danish form.

Daphne.text: nymph pursued by her lover Apollo and changed into a laurel tree MND. II. i. 231 , Shr. Ind. ii. 59 .

Delphos.text: Delphi, the oracle of Apollo Wint. II. i. 182 .

Destinies.text: the three goddesses, the Parcae or Fates, believed to determine the course of human life R2 I. ii. 15 , Ven. 733 .

Deucalion.text: the Greek Noah, Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 444

Dick.text: used like ‘Jack’=fellow, lad LLL. V. ii. 465 “some Dick, That smiles his cheek in years.”

Dictynna.text: a title of Diana LLL. IV. ii. 37 .

Dido.text: ‘queen of Carthage’ ( Shr. I. i. 158 ), in love with æneas Tp. II. i. 80 , Rom. II. iv. 44 , Ham. II. ii. 477 [ 468 ].

Dis.text: god of the infernal regions Tp. IV. i. 89 .

Downs.text: the part of the sea within the Goodwin Sands off the east coast of Kent, a famous rendezvous for ships 2H6 IV. i. 9 “whilst our pinnace anchors in the Downs.”

Ebrew.text: 1H4 II. iv. 201 “a Jew else, an Ebrew Jew.”

Echo.text: Echo personified (in Greek mythology, an oread or mountain nymph) Rom. II. ii. 161 .

Egyptian.text: (?) gypsy Oth. III. iv. 57 ; “ thief,” a robber in the Greek romance of ‘Theagenes and Chariclea’, who attempted to kill Chariclea, whom he loved Tw.N. V. i. 122 .

Elue.text: in old edd. = Elbe, H5 I. ii. 45 , 52

Elysium.text: in Greek mythology, the abode of the blessed after death Gent. II. vii. 38 ; state of perfect happiness H5 IV. i. 294 .

Emmanuel.text: formerly written at the head of deeds, letters, &c. 2H6 IV. ii. 110 .

Enceladus.text: giant of ancient story Tit. IV. ii. 94 .

Englished.text: put into plain English, described in plain terms Wiv. I. iii. 50 .

Ephesian.text: boon companion Wiv. IV. v. 19 , 2H4 II. ii. 164 .

Epicurean.text: luxurious, sensual Wiv. II. ii. 304 “ rascal” ; suited to the taste of an epicure (S.) Ant. II. i. 24 “Epicu'rean cooks.”

Epicurus.text: an Athenian philosopher (about 300 B.C.) Cæs. V. i. 77 .

Erebus.text: place of darkness, hell Mer.V. V. i. 87 .

Ethiop.text: blackamoor Ado V. iv. 38 ;—adj. black AYL. IV. iii. 36 “ words, blacker in their effect.”

Faustus.text: the famous German magician made familiar in England by Marlowe, Wiv. IV. v. 71 .

Finsbury.text: ‘Finsbury Fields outside Moorgate were the archery ground of the Londoners, and a favourite resort of citizens and their wives’ 1H4 III. i. 256 .

Flibbertigibbet.text: Lr. III. iv. 118 , IV. i. 62 one of the names of fiends taken from Harsnet's ‘Declaration of egregious Popish Impostures’, 1603

French.text: LLL. III. i. 9 “ brawl” (see BRAWL sb.); Wiv. I. iii. 91 “ thrift . . . myself and skirted page” ; ‘French pages were the fashion at this period, and the discarding of the excess of serving-men is commonly alluded to’ (H. C. Hart).

Galen.text: celebrated physician of the 2nd cent. A.D., All'sW. II. iii. 12 . Cor. II. i. 130 “the most sovereign prescription in ” ; (hence gen.) a physician Wiv. II. iii. 29 “What says my Æsculapius? my Galen?.”

Gallia.text: Gaul, France H5 V. i. 94 “in the wars,” 1H6 IV. vii. 48 .

Gallian.text: French 1H6 V. iv. 139 , Cym. I. vi. 66 .

Ganymede.text: cup-bearer to Zeus (Jupiter) AYL. I. iii. 128 .

Gargantua.text: the large-mouthed voracious giant in Rabelais AYL. III. ii. 239 .

George.text: the jewel, on which is a figure of St. George, forming part of the insignia of the order of the garter 2H6 IV. i. 29 , R3 IV. iv. 367 , 370

Gog.text: perversion of GOD Shr. III. ii. 163 “by g-s-wouns.”

Golias.text: form of “Goliath” Wiv. V. i. 24 (Ff Q3 “Goliah”), found also in Chaucer and app. used in mediaeval Latin 1H6 I. ii. 33 “Samsons and Goliasses.”

Gorgon.text: any of three mythical women, having snakes for hair, whose look turned the beholder to stone Mac. II. iii. 79 “destroy your sight With a new Gorgon,” Ant. II. v. 116 .

Greece.text: Shr. Ind. ii. 95 “John Naps of ,” ? read “Greete”†, the name of a hamlet near Winchcomb in Gloucestershire and of a village on the Warwick road near Birmingham; Troil. II. i. 13 “The plague of ” ‘alluding, perhaps, to the plague sent by Apollo on the Grecian army’ (J.).

Greek.text: “merry ,” Troil. I. ii. 116 , IV. iv. 56 ; a common phr. in 16-17th cent. for ‘merry fellow, roysterer, boon companion’; so “foolish Greek” addressed to the clown in Tw.N. IV. i. 19 .

Grizel.text: later form of the proper name ‘Grisilde’ borne by the heroine of Chaucer's Clerk's Tale (adapted from a story of Petrarch's), who is the proverbial type of a meek, patient wife Shr. II. i. 289 [ 297 ].

Guy.text: Guy of Warwick, who slew the giant COLBRAND (q.v.) H8 V. iv. 23 “not Samson, nor Sir Guy.”

H.text: Ado III. iv. 55 , quibble on ACHE sb. (q.v.).

Hallowmass.text: the feast of All Hallows, All Saints' Day, Nov. 1st, Gent. II. i. 28 “to speak puling, like a beggar at ,” Meas. II. i. 133 , R2 V. i. 80 (old edd. “Hollowmass”; ‘Hallowmass . . . was, in S. 's time, ten days nearer the winter solstice than now,’ Clark and Wright). ∥ Cf. ALL-HALLOWMASS.

Harry.text: ten-shilling pieces coined in the reign of Henry VIII, 2H4 III. ii. 239 .

Hebrew.text: reading of F1 in Gent. II. v. 58 , Mer.V. I. iii. 58 , 179 ; cf. EBREW.

Hecate.text: (usu. 2 syll.; 3 syll. in 1H6 III. ii. 64 , as also once in Milton, Comus 535); goddess of Greek mythology supposed to preside over witchcraft and magical rites MND. V. ii. 14 [ i. 391 ] (F1 “Hecates”), Mac. III. v. 1 (F1 “Hecat”), Lr. I. i. 112 (F1 Qq “Heccat”; used abusively=hag, witch 1H6 III. ii. 64 “that railing Hecate” (viz. Joan of Arc).

Hector.text: transf. in allusion to the Trojan hero =valiant warrior Wiv. I. iii. 11 , II. iii. 35 .

Henry.text: 3 syll. in R3 II. iii. 16 and elsewhere.

Herod.text: represented in the old mystery plays as a blustering tyrant Wiv. II. i. 20 “What a of Jewry is this!,” Ham III. ii. 16 (see OUT-HEROD), Ant. III. iii. 3 “ of Jewry dare not look upon you But when you are well pleas'”

Hesperides.text: nymphs who were fabled to guard, with the aid of a dragon, the garden in which golden apples grew in the Islands of the Blest; used allusively and as sing. Per. I. i. 27 “this fair , With golden fruit, but dangerous to be touch'd” ; transf. applied to the garden LLL. IV. iii. 341 (ref. to the 11th Labour of Hercules).

Hesperus.text: the evening star All'sW. II. i. 167 .

Hibbocrates.text: i.e. Hippocrates, Greek physician (4th cent. B.C.) Wiv. III. i. 66 .

Hiems.text: winter personified LLL. V. ii. 899 , MND. II. i. 109 .

Hiren.text: name of a female character in Peele's play of ‘The Turkish Mahamet and Hyrin the fair Greek’, used allusively by S. and early 17th cent. writers=seductive women, harlot 2H4 II. iv. 172 , 188 (? with quibble on ‘iron’).

Hob.text: by-form of ‘Rob’=Robert, used as a generic name for a rustic Cor. II. iii. 123 “Hob and Dick.”

Hobbididance.text: name of a fiend taken, like FLIBBERTIGIBBET, from Harsnet, who spells it ‘Hoberdidance’ Lr. IV. i. 60 (Q1 “-dence”).

Hobgoblin.text: name for Puck or Robin Goodfellow Wiv. V. v. 47 , MND. II. i. 40 .

Holborn.text: formerly the place of residence of the bishops of Ely, R3 III. iv. 31 .

Hungarian.text: used, by association with ‘hunger’, =needy, beggarly Wiv. I. iii. 21 “O base wight!” ∥ A cant term of the Eliz. period.

Hydra.text: used attrib. = difficult to kill like the many-headed snake of Lerna (cf. Oth. II. iii. 310 ), whose heads grew as fast as they were cut off 2H4 IV. ii. 38 “this Hydra son of war” ; so Hydraheaded H5 I. i. 35 .

Hymen.text: Greek and Roman god of marriage, represented as a young man carrying a torch and veil Tp. IV. i. 23 “'s lamps,” 97 “'s torch,” AYL. V. iv. 136 “Hymen's bands” (=bonds of matrimony).

Hyperion.text: sun-god H5 IV. i. 295 , Ham. I. ii. 140 .

Hyrcania.text: ancient name of a country south of the Caspian Sea 3H6 I. iv. 155 ; the adjs. are Hyrcan Mac. III. iv. 101 “the tiger,” and Hyrcanian Mer.V. II. vii. 41 “ deserts,” Ham. II. ii. 481 [ 472 ] “the Hyrcanian beast.”

I1.text: used, as freq. in the late 16th c. and in the 17th c., for ‘me’ Mer.V. III. ii. 320 “all debts are cleared between you and I,” AYL. I. ii. 19 “my father hath no child but I,” Sonn. lxxii. 7 “And hang more praise upon deceased ”

I2.text: spelling of AY adv. in old edd.

Icarus.text: in Greek mythology, son of Dædalus, who flew so high that the sun melted the wax with which his artificial wings were fastened on, so that he fell into the ægean Sea, 1H6 IV. vi. 55 , 3H6 V. vi. 21 .

Ice2.text: reading of Ff in Lr. IV. vi. 247 (Qq “ile,” mod. edd. “ise, Ise”) = I shall. ∥ The form ‘-se’, ‘-s’ (=shall) is mainly northern.

Ides.text: fifteenth day of March according to the reckoning of the ancient Roman calendar Cæs. I. ii. 18 , &c.

India.text: used allusively for a country fabulously rich 1H4 III. i. 168 “as bountiful As mines of India,” H8 I. i. 21 , Troil. I. i. 105 .

Indies.text: the East Indies Tw.N. III. ii. 88 ; allusively for a place yielding great wealth or to which profitable voyages may be made Wiv. I. iii. 77 “they shall be my East and West , and I will trade to them both,” Err. III. ii. 137 , H8 IV. i. 45 .

Iniquity.text: comic character or buffoon in the old morality plays, also called VICE R3 III. i. 82 ; alluded to in Meas. II. i. 186 , 1H4 II. iv. 506 .

Ireland.text: 3 syll. in 2H6 I. i. 195 , III. i. 329 , H8 III. ii. 261 .

Iris.text: in Greek mythology, the goddess who acted as messenger of the gods and displayed as her sign, or appeared as, the rainbow; (hence, allusively) messenger 2H6 III. ii. 407 “I'll have an Iris that shall find thee out” ; used for ‘rainbow’ Troil. I. iii. 380 “blue Iris” ; an appearance likened to a rainbow All'sW. I. iii. 160 “That this distemper'd messenger of wet, The many-colour'd Iris, rounds thine eye” (cf. Lucr. 1586 ).

Janus.text: ancient Italian deity represented with two faces looking in opposite directions Mer.V. I. i. 50 .

Jew.text: phr. “a Jew's eye,” a proverbial expression for something valued highly Mer.V. II. v. 43 “There will come a Christian by, Will be worth a Jewes eye” (mod. edd. after Pope “Jewess'”†).

Jill.text: short for ‘Gillian,’ i.e. Julian, and used (in conjunction with “Jack”) generically = a lass LLL. V. ii. 883 , MND. III. ii. 461 , Shr. IV. I. 52

Joan.text: generic name for a female rustic LLL. III. i. 215 [ 207 ] “Some men must love my lady, and some ,” V. ii. 928 , John I. i. 184 “now can I make any Joan a lady.”

Jockey.text: pet form of ‘Jock,’=‘Jack’ R3 V. iii. 305 “Jockey of Norfolk.”

Jovial.text: of Jupiter Cym. V. iv. 105 “Our star” ; Jove-like, majestic IV. ii. 311 “his face.” ∥ The meaning ‘merry, jolly’ ( Mac. III. ii. 28 “Be bright and jovial among your guests” ) is derived from this through the astrological use, Jupiter as a natal planet being regarded as the source of joy and happiness.

Judean.text: Oth. V. ii. 346 (F1; others “Indian”; see comm.).

Jug.text: pet-form of, or familiar substitute for, the feminine name Joan, applied to a homely woman, a maidservant, or a mistress Lr. I. iv. 247 “Whoop, Jug! I love thee.”

Kad.text: Welshman's pronunciation of ‘God’ Wiv. I. i. 192 “So Kad vdge me” (Q; F1 “got-udge”).

Keisar.text: old form of ‘Kaiser’, emperor Wiv. I. iii. 9 .

Lapland.text: the fabled home of witches and magicians Err. IV. iii. 11 “Lapland sorcerers.”

Lethe.text: in Greek mythology, a river in Hades, the drinking of whose waters caused forgetfulness of the past; hence, ‘waters of oblivion’ Tw.N. IV. i. 66 , 2H4 V. ii. 72 “wash'd in , and forgotten,” R3 IV. iv. 251 , Ant. II. vii. 115 “steep'd our sense In soft and delicate ” ; attrib. Ham. I. v. 33 “ wharf.” ∥ In Cæs. III. i. 206 (F1 “Lethee”) used for ‘death’ app. through the influence of Latin “let(h)um”; cf. Blount ‘Glossographia’, 1670 , ‘Lethean’, deadly, mortal.

Lucina.text: goddess of childbirth Cym. V. iv. 43 , Per. I. i. 8 .

Lupercal.text: Roman festival of Lupercus (Pan), Cæs. III. ii. 101 .

Lycurgus.text: legislator of Sparta, Cor. II. i. 61 .

Machiavel.text: intriguer, unscrupulous schemer Wiv. III. i. 104 , 1H6 V. iv. 74 , 3H6 III. ii. 193 .

Mahu.text: name of a fiend taken from Harsnet (cf. FLIBBERTIGIBBET) Lr. III. iv. 148 , IV. i. 61 .

Mall.text: pet form of ‘Maud’ Tp. II. ii. 51 ; Tw.N. I. iii. 137 “Mistress ,” (?) the kitchen-maid (cf. MALKIN).

Marshalsea.text: prison in Southwark (abolished in 1842) under the control of the knight marshal of the royal household H8 V. iv. 92 (old edd. “-sey”).

Martial.text: like that of the war-god Mars, Cym. IV. ii. 310 “his Martial thigh.”

Martin.text: “Saint M-'s summer,” season of fine mild weather occurring about Martinmas, Nov. 11; fig. season of prosperity after adversity 1H6 I. ii. 131 .

Martlemas.text: old form of ‘Martinmas’; in 2H4 II. ii. 112 “how doth the , your master?” used derisively of Falstaff; perhaps short for ‘Martlemas beef’=meat of an ox slaughtered and salted at Martinmas; cf. 1H4 III. iii. 198 “O! my sweet beef.”

May1.text: prime Ado V. i. 76 “His May of youth” ; so Maymorn H5 I. ii. 120 “the very May-morn of his youth.”

Mercury.text: in Roman mythology, the messenger of the gods; (hence) messenger, newsbearer R3 II. i. 89 ; go-between Wiv. II. ii. 83 ; the god as patron of thieves and cheating Tw.N. I. v. 104 “ endue thee with leasing,” Troil. II. iii. 12 “, lose all the serpentine craft of thy caduceus.”

Minerva.text: Roman goddess of wisdom Cym. V. v. 165 .

Misanthropos.text: hater of mankind Tim. IV. iii. 53 .

Modo.text: name of a fiend taken from Harsnet (cf. FLIBBERTIGIBBET) Lr. III. iv. 148 , IV. i. 61 .

Monarcho.text: title assumed by an insane Italian who fancied himself emper or of the world; hence applied to one who is the object of ridicule for his absurd pretensions LLL. IV. i. 102 .

Moor.text: negro, negress Mer.V. III. v. 42 , Oth. I. i. 40 .

Moorditch.text: filthy stagnant ditch outside the city walls, draining the swampy ground of Moorfields 1H4 I. ii. 88 .

Moorfields.text: place outside Moorgate where the city trainbands were exercised H8 V. iv. 34 .

Myrmidon.text: one of a warlike race of Thessaly, whom Achilles led to the siege of Troy, Tw.N. II. iii. 30 , Troil. V. v. 33 , &c.; “the great ,” Achilles Troil. I. iii. 378 .

Naples.text: in Oth. III. i. 4 a ref. to the venereal disease; cf. NEAPOLITAN.

Nazarite.text: native of Nazareth Mer.V. I. iii. 35 .

Nemesis.text: goddess of retribution, (hence allusively) avenger 1H6 IV. vii. 78 .

Neptune.text: god of the sea, (hence) the sea Tp. V. i. 35 “the ebbing ,” MND. II. i. 126 “N-'s yellow sands,” Per. III. iii. 36 .

Nicholas.text: patron saint of scholars Gent. III. i. 303 ; “Saint Nicholas' clerks,” highwaymen 1H4 II. i. 68 .

Niobe.text: in Greek mythology, a woman changed into stone while weeping for the death of her children Troil. V. x. 19 , Ham. I. ii. 149 “Like , all tears.”

O1.text: sb. (plural written “Oes,” in mod. edd. “O's”) 1. cipher, mere nothing Lr. I. iv. 214 “thou art an O without a figure.”

O2.text: used as a sb.=lament Rom. III. iii. 89 “Why should you fall into so deep an O?.”

Obidicut.text: name of a fiend taken, like FLIBBERTIGIBBET, from Harsnet, where it is spelt ‘Haberdicut’, Lr. IV. i. 60 .

Od.text: minced form of ‘God’ used in oaths Wiv. I. i. 275 “Od's plessed will,” III. iv. 59 “Od's heartlings” (lit.= little heart), IV. i. 26 “Od's nouns,” Tw.N. V. i. 188 “Od's lifelings,” Oth. IV. iii. 76 “Od's pity,” Cym. IV. ii. 293 “Od's pittikins” ; by confusion Wiv. I. iv. 64 “Od's me,” AYL. III. v. 43 “Od's my little life,” IV. iii. 18 “Od's my will.”

Pantheon.text: temple in Rome dedicated to all the gods Tit. I. i. 242 , 333

Paracelsus.text: Swiss physician, chemist, and natural philosopher, whose true name was Philippus Theophrast von Hohen heim, in medical principles opposed to Galen, All'sW. II. iii. 12 .

Parca.text: goddess of Fate, H5 V. i. 21 .

Partlet.text: name used as the proper name of a hen Wint. II. iii. 75 , 1H4 III. iii. 60 .

Pelion.text: mountain in Thessaly, famous as that which the giants, in their war upon the gods, piled with Ossa on Olympus Wiv. II. i. 82 , Ham. V. i. 275 .

Pepin.text: founder of the Carlovingian dynasty of French kings; used, like CLOTHAIR, as a type of antiquity LLL. IV. i. 123 , All'sW. II. i. 79 , H8 I. iii. 10 .

Phebe.text: to treat cruelly, like Phebe AYL. IV. iii. 40 .

Pheezar.text: jocular derivative of PHEEZE invented to jingle with “Cæsar, Keisar” Wiv. I. iii. 10 .

Philip.text: name for the sparrow John I. i. 231 . ∥ Still dial.; cf. Skelton's ‘Boke of Philip Sparowe’.

Philippan.text: “sword ,” the sword that triumphed over Brutus and Cassius at Philippi, Ant. II. v. 23 ; taken by some as a noun, the proper name of the sword.

Phoebe.text: Diana, the moon-goddess MND. I. i. 209 .

Phoebus.text: sun-god Tp. IV. i. 30 , MND. I. ii. 38 .

Polack.text: Pole, Ham. II. ii. 63 , &c.;—adj. Polish V. ii. 390 . ∥ In Ham. I. i. 63 mod. edd. “Polacks”†, Qq Ff1 2 “pollax, Pollax,” F3 “Polax,” F4 “Pole-axe.”

Pomgarnet.text: pomegranate, the name of a room 1H4 II. iv. 42 .

Rhenish.text: Rhine wine Mer.V. I. ii. 102 , III. i. 45 , Ham. I. iv. 10 , V. i. 196 .

Roman.text: (of handwriting) applied in Eliz. times to a variety of the sloping Italian hand Tw.N. III. iv. 32 “the sweet hand” ; of the character of the ancient Roman alphabet Tit. V. i. 139 “ letters.”

Rome.text: rhymes with words in “-oom” Lucr, 715 , 1644 ; associated in word-play with “room” John III. i. 180 “let it be That I have room with Rome to curse awhile.”

Romish.text: of Rome, Roman, Cym. I. vi. 152 . ∥ This use was current from Eliz. times to 1800

Sackerson.text: famous bear of the Paris-Garden in Southwark, Wiv. I. i. 310 .

Sagittary.text: (2 cf. “Centaur” as the sign of an inn at Ephesus in Err. I. ii. 9 ) 1. the centaur who, according to mediaeval romance, fought in the Trojan army against the Greeks, Troil, V. v. 14 ,

Salique.text: “ law,” the alleged fundamental law of the French monarchy, by which females were excluded from the succession to the crown H5 I. ii. 91 ; “ land,” = Latin ‘terra Salica’ (a term of which the meaning is disputed), alleged to mean France, H5 I. ii. 40 “Which Salique land the French unjustly gloze To be the realm of France” (cf. Hall's Chronicle, ‘They say that Pharamond made the law for the land Salicque, which the glose calleth Fraunce’).

Saltier.text: blunder for ‘Satyr’ Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 336

Saturn.text: the most remote of the seven planets known to ancient astronomy, supposed to cause coldness, sluggishness and gloominess of temperament in those born under its influence Ado I. iii. 12 , Tit. II. iii. 31 ; the same qualities were attributed to the ancient Italic god after whom the planet was named Cym. II. v. 12 , Sonn. xcviii. 4 “heavy ”

Scogan.text: John Scoggin or Scogan, court fool to Edward IV, confused with Chaucer's friend Henry Scogan in 2H4 III. ii. 33 .

Seneca.text: Roman tragedian (died A.D. 65) Ham. II. ii. 428 [ 419 ].

Sibyl.text: in classical antiquity, inspired prophetess attached to the god Apollo, Shr. I. ii. 70 “As old as Sibyl,” 1H6 I. ii. 56 “the nine s-s of old Rome” ; hence gen. Oth. III. iv. 71 ; “Sibyls' leaves,” the Sibylline Books, the name for one or more collections of prophecies ascribed to the Sibyls Tit. IV. i. 105 “the angry northern wind Will blow these sands like Sibyl's leaves abroad.”

Sibylla.text: = Sibyl Mer.V. I. ii. 114 “as old as Sibylla.”

Sicil.text: Sicily 2H6 I. i. 6 ; “the S-s,” Sicily and Naples 3H6 I. iv. 122 , V. vii. 39 .

Tartar.text: Tartarus, the infernal regions, hell Err. IV. ii. 32 “in limbo, worse than hell” (see LIMBO), Tw.N. II. v. 227 “the gates of ,” H5 II. ii. 123 .

Taurus.text: (1 cf. Chaucer's Astrolabe, ‘Everiche of these 12 signes hath respecte to a certeyn parcel of the body of a man, and hath it in governaunce, as . . . Taurus thy nekke and thy throte’) 1. the second of the zodiacal constellations, the Bull, including the Pleiades and Hyades Tw.N. I. iii. 150 “! that's sides and heart.—No, sir, it is legs and thighs” (cf. note above) Tit. IV. iii. 68 .

Telamon.text: Ajax Telamonius (see AJAX), who went mad when the shield of Achilles was awarded to Ulysses and not to him Ant. IV. xi. [ xiii. ] 2 “more mad Than Telamon for his shield.”

Tellus.text: the earth personified Ham. III. ii. 168 “Tellus' orbed ground,” Per. IV. i. 13 .

Temple.text: name of two of the Inns of Court (see INN) 1H4 III. iii. 221 “the hall,” 1H6 II. iv. 3 , 125 “the Temple garden.”

Termagant.text: imaginary deity supposed in mediaeval Christendom to be worshipped by Mohamme dans, represented in mystery plays as a violent overbearing personage Ham. III. ii. 16 “for o'erdoing ” ; —as adj. violent 1H4 V. iv. 114 “that hot Scot.”

Tewkesbury.text: in 16th-17th cent. the chief seat of the mustard manufacture in England 2H4 II. iv. 262 “his wit is as thick as Tewkesbury mustard.”

Thessaly.text: Ant. IV. xi. [ xiii. ] 2 “the boar of ,” the Calydonian boar sent by Artemis to ravage Thessaly and killed by Meleager in the celebrated Calydonian hunt, to which allusion is made in MND. IV. i. 132 .

Thetis.text: sea-nymph, daughter of Nereus and mother of Achilles Troil. I. iii. 212 , III. iii. 94 ; used for ‘the sea’, prob. partly by confusion with Tethys, wife of Oceanus, Troil. I. iii. 39 , Per. IV. iv. 39 ; applied to Cleopatra app. as the partner in Antony's naval war Ant. III. vii. 60 .

Thracian.text: “the poet, singer,” Orpheus, who was torn to pieces by Thracian women under the excitement of the Bacchanalia MND. V. i. 49 ; his music charmed even Cerberus Tit. II. iv. 51 ; “the steeds,” the snow-white horses of Rhesus, king of Thrace, 3H6 IV. ii. 21 ; “the tyrant,” Polym(n)estor, king of the Thracian Chersonese, who murdered Priam's son Polydorus, Tit. I. i. 138 .

Tib.text: as a proper name typifying women of the lower class All'sW. II. ii. 25 “As fit . . . as Tib's rush for Tom's foRefinger” ; common woman Per. IV. vi. 181 “every Coystril that comes inquiring for his Tib.”

Titan.text: god of the sun 1H4 II. iv. 135 “Didst thou never see kiss a dish of butter?,” Rom. II. iii. 4 “T-'s fiery wheels,” Ven. 177 .

Tom.text: typical name of a servant or man of the lower class LLL. V. ii. 922 “Tom bears logs into the hall,” All'sW. II. ii. 25 “fit . . . as Tib's rush for Tom's foRefinger,” 1H4 II. i. 6 [an ostler's name], II. iv. 9 [a drawer's name], 2H6 II. iii. 77 .

Trojan.text: cant term for ‘boon companion, dissolute fellow’ LLL. V. ii. 636 , 679 , 1H4 II. i. 77 , H5 V. i. 20 , 32

Tully.text: Cicero 2H6 IV. i. 136 “sweet ,” Tit. IV. i. 14 “Tully's Orator” (=the treatise De Oratore).

Turk.text: (1 in this sense replacing the once common use of ‘Saracen’) 1. used generically=infidel AYL. IV. iii. 34 “she defies me, Like Turk to Christian,” R3 III. v. 40 “think you we are T-s or infidels?” ; phr. “turn ,” change completely (as from a Christian to an infidel) Ado III. iv. 56 , Ham. III. ii. 292 .

Tybalt.text: the fact that ‘Tybert’ or ‘Tybalt’ was the name of the cat in the History of Reynard the Fox is alluded to Rom. II. iv. 18 , III. i. 80 , 82

Tyburn.text: usual place of execution in London; only allusively LLL. IV. iii. 54 “the triumviry, the cornercap of society, The shape of love's Tyburn” (with ref. to the triangular form of the gallows).

Typhon.text: another name of Typhoeus, a fire-breathing giant, defeated in an attempt to dethrone Jove, and imprisoned in Tartarus under Aetna, Troil. I. iii. 160 “roaring ,” Tit. IV. ii. 95 “Enceladus” (son of Tartarus), “With all his threatening band of Typhon's brood.”

Ullorxa.text: Tim. III. iv. 114 (F1 “Sempronius Vllorxa: All,” Ff3 4 “Sempronius: all”); printed in italics in F1, like the names that precede it.

Volquessen.text: Vexin, ancient territorial division of France, John II. i. 527 .

Vulcan.text: “V-'s badge,” cuckold's horns Tit. II. i. 89 .

Wheeson.text: Whitsun 2H4 II. i. 99 (Q; Ff “Whitson”). ∥ ‘W(h)issun’ is a north-country and midland form.

Xanthippe.text: wife of Socrates, typical of a scold Shr. I. ii. 71 .

Yead.text: short for YEDWARD Wiv. I. i. 162 .

a1.text: for ‘ha’ = he, in mod. edd. usually “a',” or replaced by “he” Ham. II. i. 58 “There was a' gaming.”

a2.text: for ‘ha’ (q.v.) = have LLL. V. ii. 17 , Ham. IV. v. 65 .

abandoned.text: banished, kept away “from” Shr. Ind. ii. 117 .

abase.text: to lower (the eyes) 2H6 I. ii. 15 , R3 I. ii. 248 (Ff).

abate.text: (1 the usual sense; the corresponding intr. sense ‘decrease’ is rare; 2 is common Eliz.; 3-6 are rare) 1. to lessen, shorten MND. III. ii. 432 “ thy hours!”

abatement.text: (in sense 1 usu. legal metaphor) 1. reduction, diminution Ham. IV. vii. 120 “abatements and delays,” Lr. I. iv. 64 , Cym. V. iv. 21 .

abhor.text: (2 term of canon law = Latin ‘detestor’) 1. to horrify, disgust Ham. V. i. 205 (Ff) “how abhorred my imagination is,” Oth. IV. ii. 162 “It does me.”

abhorring.text: (rare; ‘abhorrence’ is post-S.) 1. abhorrence, loathing Cor. I. i. 174 “flatter Beneath ”

abide.text: (senses ‘remain’ and ‘endure’ are common) 1. “no more but ,” make only a brief stay Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 100

ability.text: wealth, means Tw.N. III. iv. 380 , 2H4 I. iii. 45 ; cf. Ado IV. i. 201 “Ability in means.”

abject.text: adj. “his abject object,” the object of his contempt H8 I. i. 127 .—sb. “the queen's abjects,” the most servile of her subjects R3 I. i. 106 .

abjectly.text: basely Tit. II. iii. 4 “thinks of me so abjectly.”

able1.text: adj. (1 occurs six times, 2 once) 1. strong, vigorous, active All'sW. IV. v, 87 , 2H4 I. i. 43 , Ham. V. ii. 211 .

able2.text: to warrant, vouch for Lr. IV. vi. 173 .

abode1.text: sb. (1 and 2 now obs.; 3 now chiefly in echoes of the Bible; cf. ‘We will . . . make our abode with him’ John xiv. 23 ) 1. waiting, delay Mer.V. II. vi. 21 “my long abode.”

abode2.text: to bode, forebode 3H6 V. vi. 45 , H8 I. i. 93 .

abomination.text: (sense of ‘detestation’ not S.) 1. abominable thing or act Ant. III. vi. 94 “most large In his abominations,” Lucr. 921 , 1832

abortive.text: adj. born prematurely; (hence) untimely, unnatural, monstrous, lit. and fig. LLL. I. i. 104 “an birth,” 2H6 IV. i. 60 “this thy pride,” R3 I. ii. 21 , I. iii. 228 .—sb. untimely or monstrous birth John III. iv. 158 “Abortives, presages.”

abound.text: to be rich H8 I. i. 83 ; cf. Philippians iv. 18 .

about1.text: used imperatively: get to work, bestir yourself! Wiv. V. v. 61 , 2H4 III. ii. 305 , Cæs. III. ii. 209 , Ham. II. ii. 625 .

about2.text: follows its noun in Per. III. Gower 2 “No din but snores the house about.”

above.text: upstairs Wiv. IV. ii. 80 , Err. II. ii. 211 , 1H4 II. iv. 558 .

abram.text: corruption of ‘abron’ = auburn Cor. II. iii. 21 .

abridge.text: to deprive of, debar from Mer.V. I. i. 127 “to be abridg'd From such a noble rate.”

abridgement.text: means of shortening or whiling away the time, pastime MND. V. i. 39 “what abridgement have you for this evening?,” Ham. II. ii. 448 “look where my abridgement comes” [i.e. the players].

abroach.text: “set abroach,” to set on foot 2H4 IV. ii. 14 , R3 I. iii. 325 , Rom. I. i. 110 .

abroad.headword: abroad (the following are the chief uses) 1. outside certain limits
abroad.text: (a) away or apart from one's own body or person 2H6 III. ii. 172 “His hands abroad display'd,” Cym. I. ii. 4 , III. iv. 180 , Compl. 137 , 183 “All my offences that abroad you see” ; (b) away from one's home, out of one's house, in foreign lands Tp. III. i. 52 , Cæs. V. iii. 95 , Ham. I. i. 161 “then . . . no spirit can walk abroad.”

abrook.text: to brook, endure, bear 2H6 II. iv. 10 .

abruption.text: breaking off in speech Troil. III. ii. 68 .

absent.text: “absent time,” time of absence R2 II. iii. 79 ; so “absent hours” Oth. III. iv. 173 .

absolute.text: (sense 3 is common in 17th cent.) 1. free from imperfection, complete, finished, per fect Meas. V. i. 54 , Ham. V. ii. 112 “an absolute gentleman,” Per. IV. Gower 31 .

abstract.text: (3 and 4 are peculiar to S.) 1. epitome (of something greater), compendium (of many qualities) John II. i. 101 , Ant. I. iv. 9 “the abstract of all faults.”

abuse1.text: sb. (1 and 2 were common Eliz., now obs.) 1. ill-usage, injury, wrong, insult, offence, crime Wiv. V. iii. 9 , Meas. V. i. 241 , 3H6 III. iii. 188 “the abuse done to my niece,” Rom. III. i. 199 , Sonn. cxxxiv. 12 “through my unkind abuse.”

abuse2.text: vb. (precise meaning often doubtful; in many examples two or more senses are blended) 1. to impose upon, cheat, deceive Ado V. ii. 104 , Ham. II. ii. 640 , Lr. IV. i. 22 “thy abused father's wrath,” IV. vii. 77 , Cym. I. iv. 129 .

abuser.text: corrupter Oth. I. ii. 78 “abuser of the world.”

aby.text: to pay the penalty for, atone for MND. III. ii. 175 (Q2 Ff “abide”), 335 (Ff “abide”).

abysm.text: (orig. form ‘abime’; rhymes with ‘time’ as late as 1616) 1. bottomless pit Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 147 “abysm of hell.”

academe.text: academy, philosophical school LLL. I. i. 13 , IV. iii. 303 .

accent.text: (1 first in S., as also the senses ‘peculiar mode of utterance’ AYL. III. ii. 363 , ‘metrical stress’ LLL. IV. ii. 125 ） 1. word, speech, language John V. vi. 14 “any accent breaking from thy tongue,” 1H4 I. i. 3 , Rom. II. iv. 31 , Cæs. III. i. 113 “In . . . accents yet unknown,” Lucr. 566 .

accidence.text: rudiments of (Latin) grammar Wiv. IV. i. 18 .

accident.text: occurrence, incident, event Tp. V. i. 305 “the particular accidents gone by,” Ado II. i. 190 , Ham. III. ii. 211 .

accite.text: (1 common 1500-1680; 2 used by Ben Jonson) 1. to summon, cite 2H4 V. ii. 141 , Tit. I. i. 27 .

accommodate.text: (rare; 1 first in S.) 1. to furnish, equip 2H4 III. ii. 73 , Lr. IV. vi. 82 .

accommodation.headword: accommodation (Ben Jonson in his ‘Discoveries’ speaks of
accommodation.text: the perfumed terms of the time, as ‘accommodation’, ‘complement’, ‘spirit’, &c.) 1. provision, entertainment Oth. I. iii. 239 “such and besort As levels with her breeding.”

accomplish.text: (not very freq.; sense 2 only S.) 1. to equip perfectly Mer.V. III. iv. 61 , R2 II. i. 178 “Accomplish'd with the number of thy hours” (= of the same age as thou), H5 IV. Chor. 12 “The armourers, accomplishing the knights.”

accord1.text: (‘at a.’ is Chaucerian; 2 not post-S.) 1. harmony, concord Shr. III. i. 74 , H5 V. ii. 381 ; AYL. I. i. 69 “at accord” (=in agreement).

accord2.text: to agree, assent AYL. V. iv. 140 , Rom. I. ii. 19 “my consent and fair according voice.”

accountant.text: liable to give an account, accountable Meas. II. iv. 87 , Oth. II. i. 305 “accountant for as great a sin.”

acerb.text: sour and bitter Oth. I. iii. 355 (Q1 only).

ache1.text: pronounced ‘aitch’ like the letter H (cf. Ado III. iv. 55 ); hence pl. “aches” is of two syllables ( Tp. I. ii. 370 ).

ache2.text: pronounced ‘ake’ and so spelt in orig. edd.

achieve.text: (freq. in sense 1; rare in 2 and 3) 1. to gain, obtain All'sW. I. i. 53 , Cor. I. ix. 33 , Sonn. lxvii. 3 .

achievement.text: acquisition 2H4 IV. v. 188 , Troil. I. ii. 317 , IV. ii. 72 .

acknown.text: “be on,” confess knowledge of Oth. III. iii. 320 .

aconitum.text: poisonous extract of the plant wolf's-bane or monk's-hood, Aconitum Napellus 2H4 IV. iv. 48 .

acquit.text: (the foll. are the rarer meanings in S.) 1. to atone for Lucr. 1071 “Till life to death acquit my forc'd offence.”

acquittance1.text: sb. (rare; a doubtful instance occurs in Oth. IV. ii. 193 ; Q1 only, the rest “acquaintance”) 1. writing in evidence of a discharge LLL. II. i. 160 “acquittances For such a sum,” Cym. V. iv. 174 .

acquittance2.text: to acquit, clear R3 III. vii. 231 .

across1.text: crossed, folded Cæs. II. i. 240 “with your arms across,” Lucr. 1662 .

act1.text: sb. (S. has several ordinary uses; earliest known example of ‘act’ of a play H8 Epil. 3 ). 1. performance, action, operation, execution Mer.V. I. iii. 84 , All'sW. I. ii. 30 , John III. i. 274 , H8 III. ii. 183 “the honour of it Does pay the act of it.”

act2.text: to put in action 2H6 V. i. 103 “to controlling laws,” Rom. III. ii. 16 , Ant. V. ii. 45 .

action.text: gesture, gesticulation Shr. Ind. i. 132 , Cæs. III. ii. 226 “, nor utterance, nor the power of speech,” Mac. V. i. 31 , Ham. III. ii. 20 , Lucr. 1403 .

actor.text: doer Meas. II. ii. 37 “Condemn the fault, and not the actor of it?,” All'sW. II. iii. 29 , Lucr. 608 .

actual.text: consisting in action, active Mac. V. i. 13 “her walking and other actual performances,” Oth. IV. ii. 153 “of thought or actual deed.”

adamant.text: stone or mineral of excessive hardness 1H6 I. iv. 52 ; identified with the loadstone or magnet MND. II. i. 195 , Troil. III. ii. 186 “as turtle to her mate, As iron to adamant.”

addiction.text: inclination, bent H5 I. i. 54 , Oth. II. ii. 6 .

addition.text: (the ordinary uses occur; 1 is freq.; 2 and 3 rare) 1. something added to a man's name to denote his rank, &c.; title, style of address; mark of distinction; Wiv. II. ii. 316 “devils' additions,” All'sW. II. iii. 134 , Cor. I. ix. 66 , Mac. III. i. 106 (cf. sense 3), Ham. I. iv. 20 , Lr. I. i. 138 “The name and all th' addition to a king,” II. ii. 26 , Oth. IV. i. 105 .

address.text: (most freq. in sense 2; 3 and 4 are rare) 1. to direct LLL. V. ii. 92 , MND. II. ii. 143 , Tw.N. I. iv. 15 “address thy gait unto her.”

adhere.text: to hang together, agree Wiv. II. i. 63 , Mac. I. vii. 52 “Nor time nor place Did then adhere.”

adjunct.text: (not pre-Eliz.) adj.. connected, annexed John III. iii. 57 , Sonn. xci. 5 “every humour hath his adjunct pleasure.”

admirable.text: to be wondered at, wonderful MND. V. i. 27 “strange and admirable.” [ x. 2 ].

admiral.text: flagship 1H4 III. iii. 28 , Ant. III. viii. 12

admiration.text: (the foll. are occasional uses) 1. quality of exciting wonder or approbation, admirableness Tp. III. i. 38 .

admire.text: to wonder (“at”) Tp. V. i. 154 , Tw.N. III. iv. 167 “nor admire not in thy mind, why I do call thee so.”

admired.text: (1 cf. UNAVOIDED = inevitable) 1. admirable Tp. III. i. 37 , Ant. II. ii. 125 .

admittance.text: acceptance, sanction; (hence) vogue, fashion Wiv. III. iii. 61 ; II. ii. 240 “of great admittance” (= in high favour).

adoptedly.text: by adoption Meas. I. iv. 47 “Adoptedly; as school-maids change their names.”

adoptious.text: christenings of adopted children All'sW. I. i. 190 * .

advance.text: to raise, lift up Tp. I. ii. 405 , H5 V. Prol. 44 , R3 I. ii. 40 “ thy halberd higher than my breast,” Rom. II. iii. 5 . ∥ The many passages in which flags and standards are said to be ‘advanced’ may bear this meaning.

advantage1.text: sb. (sense ‘profit, benefit’ is freq. with phr. “make” or “take of,” rarely “on” Ven. 405 ); also ‘advantageous or favourable position’) 1. favourable opportunity, chance Tp. III. iii. 13 “The next Will we take,” Oth. I. iii. 299 , II. i. 249 , Ven. 129 ; 3H6 III. ii. 192 “for advantages” (=as it serves my convenience; cf. Compl. 123 ); Oth. III. iii. 312 “to the advantage” (= opportunely).

advantage2.text: vb. (1 the trans. sense is more freq.) 1. to be of benefit Tp. I. i. 36 “our own doth little ”

advantageable.text: profitable, advantageous H5 V. ii. 88 “advantageable for our dignity.”

advantageous.text: anxiety to obtain a position of advantage Troil. V. iv. 23 .

adventure1.text: hazard, chance Wint. V. i. 156 , John V. v. 22 ; “at all adventures,” at all hazards, whatever may be the consequences Err. II. ii. 220 , H5 IV. i. 123 .

adventure2.text: to venture Wint. I. ii. 38 , R3 I. iii. 116 , Rom. II. ii. 84 , V. iii. 11 , Cym. III. iv. 156 .

adversity.text: perverse one, quibbler Troil. V. i. 14 .

advertisement.text: (stressed always on the second syllable) 1. information 1H4 III. ii. 172 “this is five days old.”

advice.text: consideration, deliberation, consultation Gent. II. iv. 208 , Mer.V. IV. ii. 6 , Shr. I. i. 116 , John III. iv. 11 , H5 II. ii. 43 “on his more advice” (= after maturer reflection).

advise.text: （‘to counsel’ is the commonest sense; cf. ADVISED 2) 1. refl. and intr. to bethink oneself, consider Tw.N. IV. ii. 104 , H5 III. vi. 171 , Rom. III. v. 192 , Lr. ii. i. 29 “Advise yourself.”

advised.text: (see also WELL-ADVISED) 1. considerate, deliberate, cautious, well-considered Mer.V. I. i. 143 “with more advised watch,” John IV. ii. 214 , R2 I. iii. 188 , H5 I. ii. 179 “The advised head defends itself.”

advocation.text: pleading of an advocate Oth. III. iv. 122 .

aerial.text: of the atmosphere Oth. II. i. 39 (Ff “eriall”).

aerie.text: nest, or (esp. in S.) brood of a bird of prey, and particularly of hawks John V. ii. 149 , R3 I. iii. 264 ; Ham. II. ii. 362 “aerie of children” (with reference to the young choristers of the Chapel Royal and St. Paul's, who acted plays).

affect.text: sb. (both senses were in common Eliz. use) 1. kind feeling, affection R2 I. iv. 30 .

affect1.text: vb. 1 (2 by far the commonest sense; 4 only once) 1. to aim at, aspire to Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 433, 2H6 IV. vii. 103 , Cor. III. iii. 1 “affects Tyrannical power,” IV. vi. 32 .

affect2.text: to act upon contagiously, as a disease Troil. II. ii. 59 “what infectiously itself affects.”

affected.text: (the mod. sense ‘full of affectation’ occurs once LLL. V. i. 15 ) 1. disposed, inclined Gent. I. iii. 60 , Shr. I. i. 26 “in all affected as yourself,” Lr. II. i. 100 “ill affected.”

affecting.text: using affectation, affected Wiv. II. i. 145 .

affection1.text: sb. (the usual S. sense is the ordinary one of ‘love’; 4 is rare) 1. emotion, feeling, esp. pl. LLL. I. i. 9 , Mer.V. I. i. 16 , Cæs. II. i. 20 “when his affections sway'd More than his reason.”

affection2.text: to have affection for Wiv. I. i. 234 .

affeer.text: to confirm Mac. IV. iii. 34 “The title is affeer'”

affiance.text: confidence H5 II. ii. 127 , Cym. I. vi. 163 .

affianced.text: betrothed Meas. III. i. 221 “affianced to her by oath.”

affined.text: (sense 2 is only S.) 1. related Troil. I. iii. 25 “The wise and fool . . . seem all affin'd and kin.”

affirm.text: to maintain (a statement) H5 V. ii. 117 , Lr. II. ii. 83 ,

affray.text: to frighten away Rom. III. v. 33 .

affront1.text: “gave th' ,” made the stand Cym. V. iii. 87 .

affront2.text: vb. (the precise sense in passages under 2 and 3 is doubtful) 1. to meet, accost Ham. III. i. 31 “That he . . . may here Affront Ophelia.”

affy.text: (both senses were in gen. use till 1650) 1. to trust “in” Tit. I. i. 47 “I do affy In thy uprightness.”

after.text: (unusual applications of common meanings) 1. according to Tp. II. ii. 79 “after the wisest” (=in the wisest fashion).

again.headword: again (sense 2 arose first with vbs. like ‘ring’
again.text: cf. Mac. V. iii. 54 “the very echo, That should applaud ” ) 1. back AYL. III. v. 132 “why I answer'd not again,” Shr. II. i. 217 “come again, Good Kate,” Cym. IV. iii. 1 , Sonn. lxxix. 8 “pays it thee again.”

against.text: (see also the aphetic form 'GAINST) 1. exposed to Sonn. lxxiii. 3 “those boughs which shake against the cold.”

agate.text: used fig. in allusion to the small figures cut in agates for seals Ado III. i. 65 , 2H4 I. ii. 18 “I was never manned with an agate till now” ; so agatestone Rom. I. iv. 56 .

aggravate.text: (S. has only two out of many contemporary uses) 1. to increase Sonn. cxlvi. 10 “to aggravate thy store.”

agnize.text: to acknowledge, confess Oth. I. iii. 232 .

agood.text: in good earnest Gent. IV. iv. 172 “I made her weep agood.”

ague.text: malarial fever Cæs. II. ii. 113 “that same ague which hath made you lean” ; fit of shivering Mer.V. I. i. 23 “My wind . . . Would blow me to an ague.”

aidance.text: assistance, aid 2H6 III. ii. 165 “for aidance 'gainst the enemy,” Ven. 330 .

aidant.text: helpful Lr. IV. iv. 17 “aidant.. In the good man's distress.”

aim1.text: sb. (3 meaning doubtful; some interpret ‘let me have space or scope’） 1. mark, butt Meas. I. iii. 5 , R3 IV. iv. 90 “To be the aim of every dangerous shot,” H8 V. iii. 118 ; “gave aim to,” was the object of Gent. V. iv. 101 “her that gave aim to all thy oaths.”

aim2.text: vb. (S. has also the ordinary sense ‘direct a weapon’ with its fig. derivatives) 1. to guess, conjecture 2H6 II. iv. 58 “thou aimest all awry,” R3 I. iii. 65 , Ham. IV. v. 9 “they aim at it.”

air1.text: sb. (senses 2, 3, and 4 become common after S., as also the sense of ‘tune’ MND. I. i. 183 ) 1. breath Wint. V. iii. 78 “There is an air comes from her,” 2H6 III. ii. 371 * “catch the air.”

air2.text: vb. (1 is now associated with ‘to put on airs’) 1. to wear openly, expose to public view Cym. II. iv. 96 “to air this jewel.”

alarum.text: to call to arms (fig.), rouse to action Mac. II. i. 53 , Lr. II. i. 55 .

alate.text: Lr. I. iv. 211 (Qq); Ff and mod edd. “of late.”

albeit.text: usu. disyllabic, is trisyllabic in John V. ii. 9 .

alderliefest.text: dearest of all 2H6 I. i. 28 “mine alderliefest sovereign.”

alien.text: adj. belonging to others Sonn. lxxviii. 3 “every alien pen” ; sb. stranger 1H4 III. ii. 34 “an alien to the hearts Of all the court.”

all.text: sb. “all our,” of us all John IV. ii. 102 , Cor. IV. vi. 34 .—adj. any whatever Mac. III. ii. 11 “Things without all remedy.” —adv. only, exclusively All'sW. III. ii. 71 , Lr. I. i. 102 , Sonn. lxxvi. 5 .—“all too,” altogether too 2H4 V. ii. 24 .—conj. although R3 IV. iv. 226 “Thy head, all indirectly, gave direction.”

allay.text: means of abatement Wint. IV. i. [ ii. ] 9 “to whose feeling sorrows I might be some allay”; so allayment Troil. IV. iv. 8 , Cym. I. v. 22 .

allaying.text: diluting Cor. II. i. 53 “not a drop of allaying Tiber.”

allegiant.text: giving allegiance, loyal H8 III. ii. 177 “allegiant thanks.”

alliance.text: marriage Ado II. i. 332 , Rom. II. iii. 91 .

allied.text: related, connected Gent. IV. i. 49 , Meas. III. ii. 111 “the vice is of a great kindred; it is well ”

allot.text: to appoint 1H6 V. iii. 55 “Thou art allotted to be ta'en by me.”

allottery.text: share, portion AYL. I. i. 78 “the poor allottery my father left me.”

allow.text: (the foll. are the less common S. uses) 1. to approve, sanction, license Tw.N. I. ii. 57 , I. v. 100 “an allowed fool,” Tim. V. i. 167 “Allow'd with absolute power,” Lr. II. iv. 194 .

allowance.text: admission or acknowledgement of a claim Troil. I. iii. 377 , Ham. III. ii. 32 “in your allowance,” Oth. II. i. 49 .

ally.text: kinsman, relative AYL. V. iv. 196 , Rom. III. i. 115 .

allycholly.text: corr. of ‘mallycholly’, old form of ‘melancholy’ Gent. IV. ii. 28 , Wiv. I. iv. 160 .

almost.text: used to intensify a rhetorical question John IV. iii. 43 . ∥ A 16th-18th cent. use.

alone.text: having no equal, unique Gent. II. iv. 168 “She is ,” Ant. IV. vi. 30 “ the villain of the earth.”

alter.text: to exchange Tw.N. II. v. 173 “She that would alter services with thee.”

amain.text: with full force or speed Tp. IV. i. 74 , “her peacocks fly amain,” Troil. V. viii. 13 “cry you all ”

amaze2.text: to bewilder, perplex John IV. iii. 140 “I am amaz'd . . . and lose my way,” Ven. 684 .

amazement.text: bewilderment, perplexity, distraction, frenzy Meas. IV. ii. 220 , John V. i. 35 , Troil. V. iii. 85 , Ham. III. iv. 111 “amazement on thy mother sits.” ∥ The mod. sense of ‘overwhelming wonder’ occurs, e.g. Ham. III. ii. 346 .

ambition.text: object of strong desire Ham. III. iii. 55 “My crown, mine own ambition, and my queen.”

amend.text: (cf. the much more freq. MEND) 1. to correct, reform, improve LLL. IV. iii. 76 “God amend us,” 1H4 III. i. 179 , 2H4 I. ii. 143 ; to repair, mend Cor. IV. vii. 12 “I must excuse What cannot be amended.”

amerce.text: to punish Rom. III. i. 196 “I'll amerce you with so strong a fine.”

amiable.text: (2 the common use in S.'s time; the mod. sense is later) 1. of love Wiv. II. ii. 248 “an amiable siege,” Ado III. iii. 160 “this amiable encounter.”

amiss.text: (thrice only in S., and somewhat rare otherwise; cf. MISS sb.) 1. misdeed, fault Sonn. xxxv. 7 “Myself corrupting, salving thy amiss,” cli. 3

among.text: “ever among,” all the while 2H4 V. iii. 22 “And ever among so merrily.”

ample.text: fully, completely All'sW. III. v. 43 , Tim. I. ii. 138 “how ample you're belov'”

an1.text: 1 (in old edd. often “and,” of which it is only a clipped form) 1. if (freq.); even if, though ( Mer.V. I. ii. 95 ); also “an if” Tp. II. ii. 125 , Mer.V. IV. i. 446 ; “what an if,” though Tit. IV. iv. 9 .

anatomize.text: (old edd. “anathomize”) 1. to dissect Lr. III. vi. 80 “let them anatomize Regan.”

anatomy.text: (popular word in sense 1; survives dialectally as ATOMY) 1. skeleton Err. V. i. 239 , John III. iv. 40 “that fell anatomy” [i.e. Death].

anchor2.text: vb. (literal phrases are used in 2H6 IV. i. 9 , Lr. IV. vi. 19 ) 1. to fix firmly R3 IV. iv. 232 , Ant. I. v. 33 “There would he anchor his aspect.”

ancient.text: (corruption of ‘ensign’, which in its early forms was confused with ‘ancyen’, &c., contemporary forms of ‘ancient’) 1. ensign, standard 1H4 IV. ii. 34 “an old faced ”

ancientry.text: (1 F1 “aunchentry”; 2 a 16th cent. use) 1. old-fashioned style Ado II. i. 81 “state and ”

and.text: 1. joins two nouns (forming the figure called hendiadys) one of which is logically in adjectival relation to the other; or two adjs. the first of which is adverbial to the second: “tediousness and process”=tedious process R2 II. iii. 12 , “flint and hardness”=flinty hardness Ant. IV. ix. 16 ; “slow and moving”=slowly moving Oth. IV. ii. 54 .

andirons.text: fire-dogs Cym. II. iv. 88 “her andirons . . . two winking Cupids Of silver.”

angel.text: (the sense of ‘ministering spirit, divine messenger’ is freq.; “angels of light” Err. IV. iii. 55 ) 1. genius, demon Mac. V. vii. 43 [ viii. 14 ] “the angel whom thou . . . hast serv'”

angerly.text: angrily Gent. I. ii. 60 , Mac. III. v. 1 “how now, Hecate! you look angerly.”

angle1.text: fishing-hook or line Ant. II. v. 10 ; fig. Wint. IV. i. 51 [ ii. 52 ], Ham. V. ii. 66 .

angle2.text: corner Tp. I. ii. 223 “an odd of the isle.”

angle3.text: to fish with a rod; fig. to use artful means to catch a person All'sW. V. iii. 214 “She . . . did angle for me,” Ant. II. v. 16 .

annexion.text: addition, adjunct Compl. 208 “With the annexions of fair gems enrich'”

annexment.text: adjunct, appendage Ham. III. iii. 21 “Each small annexment, petty consequence.”

annothanize.text: to explain, interpret LLL. IV. i. 70 .

anon.text: (like ‘presently’, ‘anon’ meant orig. ‘straightway’, ‘at once’） 1. soon, in a little while, presently; = a waiter's ‘coming’ 1H4 II. i. 5 ; “till anon,” for a while Ant. II. vii. 45 .

answer1.text: sb. (the foll. uses are somewhat technical) 1. reply made to a charge, defence, account 2H6 II. i. 201 “call these foul offenders to their answers,” Cor. III. i. 176 , Cæs. I. iii. 114 .

answer2.text: vb. (‘reply’, ‘correspond to’, ‘satisfy’, are freq. senses) 1. to return, requite Wiv. IV. vi. 10 “hath answer'd my affection.”

answerable.text: (only thrice in S.) 1. accountable 1H4 II. iv. 579 “if he have robb'd these men, He shall be answerable.”

anthem.text: song of grief or mourning Gent. III. i. 241 , Ven. 839 , Phœn. 21

antic.text: to make like buffoons Ant. II. vii. 132 .

antickly.text: fantastically Ado V. i. 96 “Go antickly, show outward hideousness.”

antipathy.text: contrariety of feeling or disposition Lr. II. ii. 92 .

antiquity.text: old age 2H4 I. ii. 211 “blasted with antiquity” Sonn. lxii. 10 .

antre.text: cavern Oth. I. iii. 140 “antres vast and desarts idle.”

ape.text: (allusion in Ham. III. iv. 194 “like the famous ape,” is obscure) 1. imitator Wint. V. ii. 112 , Cym. II. ii. 31 “O sleep! thou ape of death.”

apoplexed.text: paralysed Ham. III. iv. 73 “that sense Is apoplex'”

apostrophas.text: ?read ‘apostrophus’ (usu. 16th18th cent. form) = apostrophe LLL. IV. ii. 124 * “You find not the , and so miss the accent.”

apparent.text: adj. (most freq. in sense 1) 1. evident, plain Gent. III. i. 116 “Without apparent hazard of his life,” Cæs. II. i. 198 .

apparently.text: evidently, openly Err. IV. i. 79 “If he should scorn me so apparently.”

appeach.text: (2 peculiar to S.) 1. to inform against, impeach R2 V. ii. 79 , 102

appeal1.text: impeachment, accusation R2 I. i. 4 “to make good the . . . late appeal,” Ant. III. v. 12 .

appeal2.text: to accuse, impeach R2 I. i. 9 “If he appeal the duke,” I. iii. 21 .

appeared.text: made evident Cor. IV. iii. 9 “your favour is well (approved†) by your tongue.”

appellant.text: adj. accusing or impeaching another of treason R2 I. i. 34 “Come I appellant to this princely presence,” IV. i. 104 “Lords Appellants” (Fr. pl. of adj.).—sb. one who challenged another to single combat to prove upon his body the treason or felony of which he ‘appealed’ him R2 I. iii. 4 “the summons of the appellant's trumpet,” 2H6 II. iii. 49 .

appendix.text: adjunct (said of a bride) Shr. IV. iv. 105 .

apperil.text: peril, risk Tim. I. ii. 33 “Let me stay at thine apperil.”

appertainments.text: rights, prerogatives Troil. II. iii. 88 “We lay by Our appertainments.”

appertinent.text: (by-form of ‘appurtenant’ after Latin ‘pertinere’) adj.. belonging or becoming “to” LLL. I. ii. 17 , 2H4 I. ii. 196 “gifts appertinent to man.”

applaud.text: to approve of, praise Gent. I. iii. 48 “O! that our fathers would applaud our loves,” Mac. III. ii. 46 , Per. II. v. 58 .

applause.text: approbation, approval AYL. I. ii. 280 “High commendation, true applause.”

apple.text: the pupil of the eye, so called because it was supposed to be a solid globular body MND. III. ii. 104 ; LLL. V. ii. 476 * “laugh upon the apple of her eye” (‘laugh upon her in a very affectionate manner’).

appliance.text: (the medicinal sense colours most uses) 1. (a) willing service; (b) medicinal treatment All'sW. II. i. 116 * “I come to tender . . . my appliance.”

application.text: administration of a medicament, medicinal treatment All'sW. I. ii. 74 .

apply.text: (used freq. with ref. to the application of remedies; the foll. are rare uses) 1. “apply for,” interpret as Cæs. II. ii. 80 “these does she apply for warnings.”

appoint.text: (the more usual senses are ‘determine’, ‘designate’, ‘nominate’) 1. to arrange (e.g. a meeting) Tit. IV. iv. 101 .

appointment.text: (the sense ‘engagement, assignation’ and 3 are equally common) 1. resolution, purpose Ant. IV. x. 8 * .

apprehend.text: (1 the commonest meaning; mod. sense ‘anticipate with dread’ barely appears; cf. Troil. III. ii. 78 ) 1. to seize, arrest Oth. I. i. 178 , ii. 77 .

apprehension.text: (4 tends to pass into the mod. sense ‘anticipation with dread’) 1. seizure, arrest 3H6 III. ii. 122 , Lr. III. v. 20 “that he may be ready for our apprehension.”

apprehensive.text: possessed of intelligence or understanding, quick to perceive or learn All'sW. I. ii. 60 , 2H4 IV. iii. 107 , Cæs. III. i. 67 “men are flesh and blood, and apprehensive.”

approach.text: hostile advance, attack John V. ii. 131 “This apish and unmannerly approach,” Tim. V. i. 169 “Of Alcibiades the approaches wild” ; (of a river) H8 III. ii. 199 .

approbation.text: (non-technical sense of ‘approval, assent’ also occurs) 1. confirmation, attestation, proof Wint. II. i. 176 , H5 I. ii. 19 , Cym. I. iv. 139 “put . . . on the approbation of what I have spoke.”

approof.text: (not freq. outside S., who has 4 examples) 1. trial, proof All'sW. II. v. 3 “of valiant approof” (=of proved valour), Ant. III. ii. 27 “on thy approof” (=on the trial or proof of thy conduct).

appropriation.text: special attribute or excellence (added “to his own good parts”) Mer.V. I. ii. 45 .

approve.text: (1 and 3 are freq.; the ordinary mod. sense occurs) 1. to prove, demonstrate to be true, corroborate, confirm Mer.V. III. ii. 79 “approve it with a text,” All'sW. III. vii. 13 “which well approves You're great in fortune,” H8 II. iii. 74 , Mac. I. vi. 4 , Ham. I. i. 29 “He may approve our eyes,” Cym. V. v. 246 .

approver.text: one who makes a trial Cym. II. iv. 25 .

appurtenance.text: that which belongs to something Ham. II. ii. 397 .

apricock.text: apricot MND. III. i. 173 , R2 III. iv. 29 .

apt.text: (1 is freq., but hardly passes into the mod. ‘likely, calculated’; the sense ‘fit, suitable’ is also freq.) 1. ready, prepared, willing Ado II. i. 215 , H5 II. ii. 86 “how apt our love was to accord,” Cæs. III. i. 160 “so apt to die.”

araise.text: to raise from the dead All'sW. II. i. 79 .

arch1.text: “watery arch,” rainbow Tp. IV. i. 71 ; “vaulted arch,” heaven Cym. I. vi. 33 .

arch2.text: adj.. chief, prime, principal, pre-eminent R3 IV. iii. 2 “The most arch deed of piteous massacre,” H8 III. ii. 103 ; 3H6 II. ii. 2 (“arch-enemy”), Oth. IV. i. 71 (“archmock”), Meas. V. i. 57 (“arch-villain”).

argosy.headword: argosy [orig. form ‘ragusy’=a vessel of Ragusa in Sicily]
argosy.text: merchant vessel of the largest size and burden Mer.V. I. i. 9 , &c.

argue.text: to prove, evince, betoken LLL. IV. ii. 57 , 3H6 II. ii. 25 “Which argu'd thee a most unloving father,” Ham. V. i. 11 “it argues an act,” Lucr. 65 .

argument.text: (occurs 78 times in S., of which 18 have the sense ‘debate, discussion’) 1. proof, evidence, Ado II. iii. 254 [ 242 ] “no great argument of her folly.”

arithmetic.text: computation, calculation Cor. III. i. 244 “'tis odds beyond arithmetic.”

arm.text: to take in one's arms Cym. iv. ii. 400 .

armado.text: fleet of ships Err. III. ii. 141 “whole armadoes of carracks,” John III. iv. 2 .

armipotent.text: mighty in arms LLL. V. ii. 647 “armipotent Mars,” All'sW. IV. iii. 266 .

arms.text: military profession 1H6 II. i. 43 “since first I follow'd arms.”

aroint.text: avaunt, begone Mac. I. iii. 6 , Lr. III. iv. 127 . ∥ Cf. the north-country ‘roint’ or ‘rynt thee’=get out of the way.

arrant.text: thoroughgoing, out-and-out (freq.) H5 III. vi. 64 . ∥ The orig. application was to ‘thief’ (cf. Tim. IV. iii. 443 ); an arrant (=errant) thief was an outlawed robber roving about the country.

arras.text: hanging screen of tapestry placed round the walls of household apartments, often at such a distance from them as to allow of people being concealed in the space between Wiv. III. iii. 97 , Ham. II. ii. 163 .

arrearages.text: arrears Cym. II. iv. 13 “grant the tribute, send the arrearages.”

arrest1.text: sb. (always with legal or judicial reference) 1. “under (an) arrest,” under legal restraint, arrested Meas. I. ii. 141 , R2 IV. i. 158 .

arrest2.text: vb. (usu. in sense ‘to apprehend’ a person) 1. to seize (property) by legal warrant Wiv. V. v. 121 “his horses are arrested for it.”

arrive.text: (1 is close to the etymol. meaning, Latin ‘arripare’ to bring ashore; cf. ‘I aryve or come newly to a porte by sea’, Palsgr.) 1. to land at 3H6 V. iii. 8 “have arriv'd our coast,” Cæs. I. ii. 110 .

art.text: (4 short for ‘art magic’, Latin ‘ars magica’) 1. skill (esp. opposed to ‘nature’); skill in a particular science MND. I. i. 192 , Rom. II. iv. 97 “by art as well as by nature,” Mac. IV. i. 101 “if your art Can tell so much” (cf. sense 4), Ven. 291 .

article.text: (in 1 and 2 ‘matter, business, concern’ seems to be the underlying meaning) 1. “of great article” * , of great moment, of importance; of large scope Ham. V. ii. 123 .

articulate1.text: to come to terms Cor. I. ix. 77 “The best, with whom we may articulate.”

articulate2.text: set forth in articles, specified 1H4 V. i. 72 “These things . . . you have articulate.”

artificial.headword: artificial (the sense ‘produced by art (not nature)’ becomes common after S.
artificial.text: 3H6 III. ii. 184 ) 1. skilled in constructive art MND. III. ii. 203 “like two artificial gods.”

artist.text: (only 3 exx.; both senses are common Eliz.) 1. one learned in the ‘liberal arts’, scholar Troil. I. iii. 24 , Per. II. iii. 15 .

artless.text: unskilful Ham. IV. v. 19 “So full of artless jealousy is guilt.”

as.text: (the following are common old uses, now obs. in literary English) 1. =that R3 I. iv. 289 “coward as thou art.”

askance.text: to turn aside Lucr. 637 “askance their eyes.”

aslant.text: across, athwart Ham. IV. vii. 167 “aslant a brook.”

aspen.text: of the asp tree, Populus tremula Tit. II. iv. 45 .

aspersion.text: sprinkling (of dew) Tp. IV. i. 18 “No sweet aspersion shall the heavens let fall.”

aspic.text: asp, venomous serpent Oth. III. iii. 451 , Ant. V. ii. 295 .

aspire.text: (2 not common before the Eliz. period; 3 is Eliz., now obs.) 1. to be ambitious Gent. III. i. 154 , R2 V. ii. 9 .

ass.text: Lr. I. iv. 178 “thou borest thine ass” (allusion to æsop's fable of the man, his son, and the ass); Cor. II. i. 65 “the ass in compound with the major part of your syllables” (‘S. was thinking of the little Latin he learnt at school, and the “As in praesenti”, &c.’).

assail.text: to address with offers of love, woo Tw.N. I. iii. 61 , Rom. I. i. 219 , Cym. II. iii. 44 , Sonn. xli. 6 “Beauteous thou art, therefore to be assail'”

assault.text: love-proposal, wooing Meas. III. i. 187 , Ado II. iii. 129 .

assay1.text: sb. (cf. the vb.; 3 was in use down to 1700) 1. trial, test Meas. III. i. 162 , Tim. IV. iii. 408 , Ham. II. i. 65 “with assays of bias,” Oth. I. iii. 18 “By no assay of reason.”

assay2.text: vb. (now almost superseded by ‘essay’ except in the sense of testing metals) 1. to try, attempt Meas. I. iv. 76 “Assay the power you have,” Ham. IV. vii. 152 , Oth. II. iii. 209 “passion . . . Assays to lead the way.”

assemblance.text: semblance, appearance 2H4 III. ii. 280 * “the . . . big assemblance of a man.”

assign.text: appurtenance Ham. V. ii. 157 “six French rapiers . . . with their assigns.”

assist.text: to attend, accompany Tp. I. i. 59 , Wint. V. i. 113 “Yourself, assisted with your honour'd friends” ; absol. Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 156

assistance.text: body of associates Cor. IV. vi. 33 “affecting one sole throne, Without assistance.” ∥ In LLL. V. i. 131 Qq Ff have “assistants,” mod. edd. “assistance”: see the commentators.

associate.text: to accompany, escort, attend Cor. IV. vi. 77 , Tit. V. iii. 169 , Rom. V. ii. 6 “One of our order, to associate me.”

assubjugate.text: to reduce to subjection Troil. II. iii. 204 .

assume.text: to claim, lay claim to Mer.V. II. ix. 51 “I will assume desert,” Per. I. i. 61 .

assurance.text: (2 cf. ASSURE 1) 1. pledge, guarantee Tw.N. I. v. 193 , IV. iii. 26 , 3H6 IV. i. 141 “Give me assurance with some friendly vow.”

assure.text: (the following are special uses) 1. to convey (property) to a person Shr. II. i. 373 .

astonish.text: to stun, dismay H5 V. i. 40 , 2H6 V. i. 146 , Cæs. I. iii. 56 “Such dreadful heralds to astonish us,” Lucr. 1730 .

astronomer.text: one who professes a knowledge of the influence of the stars on human affairs, astrologer Troil. V. i. 103 , Cym. III. ii. 27 ; so astronomical Lr. I. ii. 170 , and astronomy Sonn. xiv. 2 .

athwart.text: from an unexpected quarter, perversely, awry Meas. I. iii. 30 “quite athwart Goes all decorum,” 1H4 I. i. 36 .

atomy1.text: 1 (common Eliz.; used archaically by Tennyson and Kingsley) 1. atom, mote AYL. III. ii. 246 “to count atomies.”

atone.text: (rare before S.; ‘atonement’ is earlier, in Sir T. More) 1. to set at one, reconcile R2 I. i. 202 “Since we cannot atone you,” Tim. V. iv. 58 , Oth. IV. i. 245 .

atonement.text: reconciliation 2H4 IV. i. 221 , R3 I. iii. 36 .

attach.text: (orig. a law-term = ‘arrest’, ‘indict’; the meaning ‘join’ is considerably post-S.) 1. to arrest or seize, as by authority of a writ (of attachment) Err. IV. i. 74 “I you by this officer,” 2H4 IV. ii. 110 “Of capital treason I attach you both,” H8 I. i. 217 ; fig. 2H4 II. ii. 3 ; hence “attached” = affected Tp. III. iii. 5 “attach'd with weariness,” Troil. V. ii. 158 .

attachment.text: arrest, confinement (fig.) Troil. IV. ii. 5 “soft attachment to thy senses.”

attainder.text: (the foll. senses are peculiar to S.) 1. condemnation, dishonouring accusation LLL. I. i. 156 , R2 IV. i. 24 “the of his slanderous lips.”

attaint.text: sb. (1 the orig. legal sense was ‘conviction of a jury for giving a false verdict’; 2 cf. ‘taint’) 1. impeachment Lr. V. iii. 83 (Ff “arrest”).

attaint1.text: vb. (2 cf. the aphetic form ‘taint’) 1. to convict; to condemn (one convicted of treason or felony) 1H6 II. iv. 96 * , 2H6 II. iv. 59 .

attaint2.text: 1. infected 1H6 V. v. 81 “never yet With any passion.”

attask.text: to take to task, blame Lr. I. iv. 368 .

attempt1.text: warlike enterprise, attack John V. ii. 111 , Mac. III. vi. 39 “some attempt at war” ; fig. Cym. III. iv. 185 “this attempt I'm soldier to.”

attempt2.text: vb. (ordinary sense of ‘endeavour’ freq.; 2 is 16th-17th c.) 1. to try to win, obtain, or subdue Wiv. IV. ii. 230 , Tim. I. i. 127 , Lr. II. ii. 129 “him attempting who was self-subdu'”

attemptable.text: open to attempts Cym. I. iv. 69 .

attend.text: (freq., and in various senses; 5 only once) 1. to listen to, heed Tp. I. ii. 78 “Dost thou attend me?,” 3H6 II. i. 168 , Cym. I. vi. 142 , Lucr. 818 .

attent.text: attentive Ham. I. ii. 193 , Per. III. Gower 11 .

attest1.text: evidence, testimony Troil. V. ii. 119 “the attest” (Ff “test) of eyes and ears.”

attest2.text: vb. (recorded first from S., who, however, does not use 1 with personal subject) 1. to certify, vouch for Tw.N. V. i. 162 “attested by the holy close of lips,” H5 Prol. 16

attired.text: enwrapped Ado IV. i. 146 “attir'd in wonder,” Lucr. 1601 “attir'd in discontent.”

attorney1.text: 1 (a different word from the next, this being from O Fr. ‘atorné’, that from ‘atornée’) 1. agent, deputy Err. V. i. 100 “I . . . will have no attorney but myself.”

attorney2.text: appointment of a legal representative, legal commission; hence “by attorney” = by proxy AYL. IV. i. 97 , R3 V. iii. 84 “I, by attorney, bless thee from thy mother.”

attorneyed.text: performed ‘by attorney’ or by proxy Wint. I. i. 30 ; employed as an attorney Meas. V. i. 386 “Attorney'd at your service.”

attorneyship.text: “by attorneyship”=‘by attorney’, by proxy 1H6 V. v. 56 .

attractive.text: drawing as by magnetic influence MND. II. ii. 91 “attractive eyes,” Ham. III. ii. 117 .

attribute.text: credit, reputation Troil. II. iii. 126 , Ham. I. iv. 22 , Per. IV. iii. 18 .

attribution.text: praise 1H4 IV. i. 3 “Such attribution should the Douglas have.”

attributive.text: that attributes qualities Troil. II. ii. 58 (Q “inclineable”).

audible.text: (in active sense) quick of hearing Cor. IV. v. 239 ; adv. = audibly Meas. V. i. 409 .

audience.text: (1 the commonest S. use; the sense ‘assembly of listeners’ occurs 7 times) 1. hearing, attention to what is said Cor. III. iii. 39 “audience; peace! I say,” Ham. I. iii. 93 , Ant. III. x. [ xii. ] 21; “have ,” to be heard LLL. V. i. 144 ; “give (lend, vouchsafe) audience,” listen Cæs. III. ii. 2 ; Compl. 278 ; LLL. V. ii. 314 .

audit.text: statement of account, chiefly fig. H8 III. ii. 142 , Cor. I. i. 150 “I can make my audit up,” Ham. III. iii. 82 “how his audit stands,” Sonn. iv. 12 .

auditor.text: (occurs only thrice in S.) 1. hearer, listener MND. III. i. 84 “What! a play toward? I'll be an auditor.”

auger.text: carpenter's tool for boring holes in wood Cor. IV. vi. 88 “confin'd Into an a-'s bore” ; augerhole Mac. II. iii. 129 “our fate, Hid in an -hole.”

augur1.text: prophet Sonn. cvii. 6 , Phœn. 7 “Augur of the fever's end.” ∥ In the technical sense S. uses AUGURER, q.v.

augur2.text: to prophesy Ant. II. i. 10 “my a-ing hope.”

augure.text: augury Mac. III. iv. 124 (Ff “augures,” mod. edd. “augurs”).

augurer.text: augur, religious official among the Romans whose duty it was to foretell future events from the observation of omens Cæs. II. ii. 37 “the augurers . . . Plucking the entrails of an offering forth,” Cor. II. i. 1 .

augury.text: art of the augur, divination by omens Ham. V. ii. 232 ; prophetic skill Gent. IV. iv. 74 “if my augury deceive me not.”

aunt.text: (1 peculiar to S.; 2 common 17th c. sense) 1. old woman, gossip MND. II. i. 51 “The wisest aunt, telling the saddest tale.”

auricular.text: perceived by the ear Lr. I. ii. 102 “an auricular assurance.”

auspicious.text: (not pre-S.; but ‘auspiciously’ is in Drayton, 1596 ) 1. favourable, propitious Tp. I. ii. 182 “A most auspicious star,” All'sW. III. iii. 8 .

authentic.text: of authority, authoritative Wiv. II. ii. 241 .

authority.text: those in office Cor. I. i. 16 “What authority surfeits on.”

authorize.text: (accented “autho'rize” in S.'s time) 1. to sanction Sonn. xxxv. 6 .

avail1.text: benefit, profit All'sW. I. iii. 192 , III. i. 22 “for your avails they fell.”

avail2.text: vb. (2 intr. use (=refl.) is peculiar to S.) 1. to be of use to 1H6 III. i. 178 , Lucr. 1273 “it small avails my mood.”

avaunt.text: order to be off H8 II. iii. 10 “To give her the ”

ave.text: shout of welcome Meas. I. i. 70 “A-s vehement.”

aver.text: to assert the existence of Cym. V. v. 204 .

avert.text: to turn away Lr. I. i. 214 “To avert your liking a more worthier way.”

avised.text: spelling in old edd. of ADVISED.

avoid.text: (1, 2, 3 common 16th-17th c.; 4 is a legal term) 1. to get rid of Wiv. III. v. 155 , AYL. I. i. 27 , Troil. II. ii. 65 “How may I avoid . . . The wife I chose?”

avouch.text: guarantee, assurance Ham. I. i. 57 “the . . . true avouch Of mine own eyes.”

await.text: (only two exx. in S.; 1 is an unusual sense) 1. to look out “for” 1H6 I. i. 48 “Posterity, await for wretched years.”

award.text: to adjudge, decree R3 II. i. 14 .

away.text: (1 arises from the ellipsis of some verb) 1. (cannot) get on “with” or tolerate 2H4 III. ii. 216 .

aweless.text: (rare, in senses not freq. in Eliz. period) 1. fearless John I. i. 266 “The aweless lion.”

awful.text: (sense 2 is common after S.) 1. commanding reverential fear or profound respect Gent. IV. i. 46 * (or sense 2), Shr. V. ii. 110 , 2H6 V. i. 98 “an awful princely sceptre.”

awkward.text: (root-meaning ‘turned in a wrong direction’; 2 not pre-S.) 1. perverse H5 II. iv. 85 “no sinister nor no claim.”

ay1.text: adv. (all old edd. have the spelling “I”) 1. yes Tp. I. ii. 268 ; introducing a more forcible statement than the preceding one Wint. II. i. 137 .

ay2.text: ah! alas! John III. i. 305 ; esp. “ay me!” (freq.) Ham. III. iv. 51 , Ven. 187 .

babe.text: rag doll John III. iv. 58 . ∥ ‘Babe that children play with,’ Palsgr.

baby.text: infant of a very young mother Mac. III. iv. 106 * .

back1.text: sb. (1 said orig. of a sword which is all steel from edge to back and not merely edged with steel; 3 was common 1560-1660) 1. “metal . . . steel to the very back,” sound all through Tit. IV. iii. 47 .

back2.text: vb. (S. is earliest authority for both uses) 1. to mount 1H4 II. iii. 76 , Cym. V. v. 428 , Ven. 419 .

backward.text: what lies behind, the past Tp. I. ii. 50 .

backwardly.text: perversely Tim. III. iii. 18 “And does he think so backwardly of me now?”

badge.text: device, emblem, or mark on a piece of cloth or of silver used to identify a knight or distinguish his followers 1H6 IV. i. 177 “he wears the badge of Somerset,” Lucr. 1054 ; (hence) token, symbol Mer.V. I. iii. 111 , 2H4 IV. iii. 114 “the badge of pusillanimity,” Sonn. xliv. 14 ; so badged (fig.) Mac. II. iii. 109 “badg'd with blood” (applied to Duncan's ‘grooms’).

baffle.text: to subject (a perjured knight) to public in famy by exhibiting the picture of him hanging by the heels 1H4 I. ii. 113 ; (hence) to disgrace, treat with contumely Tw.N. II. v. 177 , R2 I. i. 170 “disgrac'd, impeach'd, and baffled,” 2H4 V. iii. 106 “And shall good news be baffled?”

bag.text: (to retreat) with all belongings saved, without surrender of anything, and therefore honourably AYL. III. ii. 171 , Wint. I. ii. 206 .

bail.text: sb. (2 not recorded before S.) 1. security given for the release of a prisoner Meas. III. ii. 44 , All'sW. V. iii. 290 “I'll put in bail.”

bail1.text: to procure the liberation of (a person) from arrest or prison by becoming bail for him Tit. II. iii. 299 ; fig. Lucr. 1725 .

bailiff.text: officer of justice under a sheriff, who executes writs, distrains, and arrests Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 103

bait.text: (1 cf. “baiting-place” 2H6 V. i. 150 ; 3 first in S.) 1. to set on dogs to bite and worry (an animal, e.g. a bear, bull) 2H6 V. i. 148 ; (hence) to harass, worry Tw.N. III. i. 132 , R2 IV. i. 238 “my wretchedness doth bait myself,” Mac. V. vii. 58 [ viii. 29 ] “baited with the rabble's curse.”

baker.text: Ham. IV. v. 43 “the owl was a baker's daughter” ; the allusion is to a local legend to the effect that our Lord, being churlishly refused bread by a baker's daughter, turned her into an owl.

balance1.text: (1 cf. ‘a pair of ballance’, Fuller 1655; 2 and 3 are not pre-S.) 1. used as pl. Mer.V. IV. i. 255 “Are there here?”

balance2.text: to give due weight to 2H6 V. i. 9 .

bald.text: (1 nonce-use peculiar to S.) 1. bare-headed Cor. IV. v. 206 “stand bald before him.”

bale.text: injury; “have bale,” get the worst of it Cor. I. i. 169 .

balk.text: (2 cf. ‘in stryfful termes . . . to balke,’ Spenser) 1. to let slip, fail to use, &c. Tw.N. III. ii. 27 , Lucr. 696 “altogether balk The prey.”

ball.text: (also=‘round mass’, ‘eye-ball’, ‘the globe’) 1. the golden orb borne together with the sceptre as an emblem of sovereignty H5 IV. i. 280 .

ballad1.text: sb. (2 used contemptuously in H5 V. ii. 166 ) 1. light, simple song MND. IV. i. 222 “to write a ballad of this dream,” AYL. II. vii. 148 .

ballad2.text: to make (a person) the subject of a popular song Ant. V. ii. 215 “scald rimers Ballad us out o' tune.”

ballow.text: north-midland word for ‘cudgel’ Lr. IV. vi. 248 (Qq “battero, bat”).

balm.text: (only thrice in S.) 1. to anoint with fragrant oil or liquid Shr. Ind. i. 48 , Per. III. ii. 65 .

balmy.text: (only thrice in S.; 2 first in S.) 1. deliciously fragrant Oth. V. ii. 16 “balmy breath.”

band.text: (the foll. were all common uses in S.'s time) 1. pl. fetters, bonds Tp. Epil. 9 , 3H6 I. i. 186 .

bandy.text: (of obscure origin; 2 first in S.) 1. to strike or throw (a ball) to and fro as in the games of tennis and bandy; mostly fig. to give and take (blows, words) LLL. V. ii. 29 , Shr. V. ii. 173 , 3H6 I. iv. 49 “I will not bandy with thee word for word,” Rom. II. v. 14 , Lr. I. iv. 92 “Do you bandy looks with me?,” II. iv. 178 “To bandy hasty words.”

bane1.text: sb. (1 the orig. sense; 2 cf. ‘ratsbane’; 3 obs.) 1. cause of the death of another 2H6 V. i. 120 , Tit. V. iii. 73 “Lest Rome herself be bane unto herself.”

banished.text: “banished man,” outlaw, bandit Gent. V. iv. 152 ; “ years,” years of banishment R2 I. iii. 210 .

bank1.text: sb. (1 not later than S.; 2 not earlier than S.) 1. sea-shore 1H4 III. i. 45 , Troil. I. iii. 328 “as barren as banks of Libya,” Sonn. lvi. 11 .

bank2.text: to coast, skirt (S.) John V. ii. 104 * .

banner.text: little fringed flag on a trumpet (S.) H5 IV. ii. 61 .

banquet.text: (in ordinary sense freq.; 1 and 2 are obs.) 1. “running banquet,” slight repast between meals; fig. H8 I. iv. 12 , V. iv. 71 (=whipping).

bar.text: sb. (3 properly, the barrier marking off the precinct of the judge's seat, at which prisoners stand) 1. plea or objection of force sufficient to arrest entirely an action or claim at law Wiv. III. iv. 7 , Shr. I. i. 138 “this bar in law,” H5 I. ii. 35 , 42

barbed.text: having the breast and flanks armed R2 III. iii. 117 , R3 I. i. 10 .

bare1.text: napless, threadbare Gent. II. iv. 47 ; fig. All'sW. IV. v. 105 , H8 V. iii. 125 .

bare2.text: to shave (S.) Meas. IV. ii. 188 , All'sW. IV. i. 54 “the baring of my beard.”

barely.text: in a state of nakedness All'sW. IV. ii. 19 .

barful.text: hindering Tw.N. I. iv. 41 “a barful strife.”

bargain.text: “to sell” (a person) “a bargain,” to make a fool of him, to ‘sell’ him LLL. III. i. 107 . (Cf. BOOT sb 2 .)

barn.text: to store as in a barn Lucr. 859 .

barnacle.text: species of goose formerly supposed to be hatched from the fruit of a tree or from seashells growing on it Tp. IV. i. 251 .

baron.text: (2 first created under Richard III; 3 is obs.) 1. noble, peer (orig. one who held from the king) 1H4 IV. iii. 66 “the lords and barons of the realm.”

base.text: (2 a 16th cent. use, e.g. ‘colored high or base’) 1. low, low-lying R2 II. iv. 20 “the earth,” Lucr. 664 .

base1.text: reason Tw.N. V. i. 79 “on base and ground enough.”

base2.text: boys' game, in which a player who leaves his ‘base or ‘home’ is chased by another, and, if caught, made prisoner Cym. V. iii. 20 “to run The country base” ; phrase “bid a” or “the base,” to challenge as to a race Gent. I. ii. 94 , Ven. 303 .

bases.text: pleated skirt of cloth, velvet, or rich brocade, appended to the doublet and reaching from the waist to the knee Per. II. i. 173 .

basilisk.text: (2 cf. ‘serpentine’, ‘culverin’) 1. fabulous reptile, also called cockatrice, supposed to be hatched by a serpent from a cock's egg and said to kill by its breath and look Wint. I. ii. 388 .

basis.text: (S. is earliest for fig. sense of ‘foundation’) 1. base, foot Tp. II. i. 127 “o'er his wave-worn basis.”

bastard1.text: sweet Spanish wine, resembling muscadel Meas. III. ii. 4 “brown and white ,” 1H4 II. iv. 30 .
