bastard2.text: counterfeit, spurious Mer.V. III. v. 8 “a kind of bastard hope,” Sonn. lxviii. 3 .

baste1.text: to sew loosely Ado I. i. 289 .

bastinado.text: beating with a stick; AYL. V. i. 61 ; fig. John II. i. 463 “He gives the bastinado with his tongue: Our ears are cudgell'”

bat.text: stick, club Cor. I. i. 167 , Lr. IV. vi. 248 (Qq).

batch.text: quantity of bread produced at one baking; fig. Troil. V. i. 5 “Thou crusty batch of nature.”

bate1.text: to beat the wings impatiently and flutter away from the fist or perch Shr. IV. i. 199 “these kites That bate and beat,” 1H4 IV. i. 99 (old edd. “baited, bayted,” Malone “bated”); fig. H5 III. vii. 127 (with pun on BATE vb. 2 3), Rom. III. ii. 14 “Hood my unmann'd blood, bating in my cheeks.”

bate2.text: vb. 2 (for the meanings cf. the older ABATE) 1. to blunt LLL. I. i. 6 “bate his scythe's keen edge.”

bateless.text: not to be blunted, keen Lucr. 9 .

batlet.text: bat or club for beating clothes in the process of washing AYL. II. iv. 48 . ∥ Current until recently in Yorkshire and Warwickshire.

battalion.text: R3 V. iii. 11 , Ham. IV. v. 79 “not in single spies, but in battalions.”

batten.text: to grow fat “on” Cor. IV. v. 35 , Ham. III. iv. 67 .

battery.text: (2 not a common sense in or outside S.) 1. beating, assailing with blows, also fig. John II. i. 446 , Cym. I. iv. 23 ; in law, unlawful attack on another by beating or wounding Tw.N. IV. i. 38 “an action of battery,” Ham. V. i. 110 .

battle.text: (all the foll. are now obs. or archaic) 1. single combat R2 I. i. 92 “I . . .will in battle prove” . . .

battlement.text: used loosely for ‘embattled roof’ John II. i. 374 .

batty.text: bat-like MND. III. ii. 365 “leaden legs and batty wings.”

bauble.text: (orig. ‘babel’; the spelling ‘bauble’ appears first in English in S. F1; 1 is the orig. sense; 2 cf. ‘bable for a foole,’ Palsgr.; 3 and 4 are obs.) 1. showy trinket of little worth Shr. IV. iii. 82 .

bavin.text: brushwood, faggots; “ wits” 1H4 III. ii. 61 (‘soon ablaze’). ∥ Still current in the midlands.

bawbling.text: trifling Tw.N. V. i. 58 “A bawbling vessel.” ∥ Only S. and echoed by mod. writers.

bay.text: vb. (1 in mod. use an echo of S.; 2 not pre-S.) 1. to bark at Cæs IV. iii. 27 “bay the moon.”

bay1.text: division of a house included under one gable or between party-walls Meas. II. i. 261 .

bay2.text: sb. 2 (orig. ‘abay’=O Fr. ‘abai’, mod. Fr. ‘aboi’） 1. deep prolonged barking Tit. II. ii. 3 “Uncouple here and let us make a bay.”

bead.text: (1 not known earlier than S.) 1. pl. drops (of liquid), tears John II. i. 171 , 1H4 II. iii. 63 “beads of sweat” (most old edd. “beds”), Cæs. III. i. 284 “beads of sorrow.”

beaded.text: in the form of beads Compl. 37 “Of amber, crystal, and of beaded jet” (Q “bedded”).

beadle.text: inferior parish officer who might punish petty offences 2H6 II. i. 135 , &c., H8 V. iv. 72 ; fig. with reference to his punitive functions LLL. III. i. 185 [ 177 ], H5 IV. i. 180 “war is his ”

beadsman.text: man paid or endowed to pray for others, pensioner or almsman Gent. I. i. 18 , R2 III. ii. 116 .

beagle.text: small variety of hound, tracking by scent; fig. used contemptuously of a woman Tim. IV. iii. 176 * , but also approvingly(?) Tw.N. II. iii. 198 * .

beak.text: pointed and ornamented projection at the prow of ancient vessels Tp. I. ii. 196 .

beam.text: (1 cf. ‘the staff of [Goliath's] spear was like a weaver's beam’, 1 Samuel xvii. 7 ) 1. wooden roller in a loom, on which the warp is wound Wiv. V. i. 24 ; lance Troil. V. v. 9 .

bear1.text: the constellation Ursa major Oth. II. i. 14 .

bear2.text: vb. (besides the mod. senses we find the foll.) 1. to have as a member or part of itself Wint. I. ii. 309 , 3H6 V. i. 69 “the dearest blood your bodies bear,” Rom. I. iii. 29 “I do bear a brain.”

bearer.text: possessor, owner, holder 2H4 IV. v. 28 “O majesty! When thou dost pinch thy bearer,” H8 II. iii. 15 , Troil. III. iii. 104 .

bearing.text: carriage, deportment, behaviour, demeanour Ado II. i. 168 , H5 IV. vii. 186 “his blunt bearing,” Cor. II. iii. 257 .

beastly.text: in a beastly manner, like a beast Shr. IV. ii. 34 , Ant. I. v. 50 , Cym. V. iii. 27 .

beat.text: (1 intr. use peculiar to S.; cf. BATE vb. 1 ） 1. to flap the wings with force Shr. IV. i. 199 .

beaver.text: face-guard of a helmet 2H4 IV. i. 120 , H5 IV. ii. 44 “through a rusty beaver peeps,” Ham. I. ii. 229 ; sometimes, the whole helmet R3 V. iii. 50 “is my beaver easier than it was?”

become.text: (pa. t. “became,” pa. pple. “become” and “becomed”) 1. to agree with, befit Mer.V. V. i. 57 .

becoming.text: grace (S.) Ant. I. iii. 96 , Sonn. cl. 5 .

bed.text: (1 still to be seen at Rye House, Herts.) 1. “bed of Ware,” enormous bed 11 ft. square Tw.N. III. ii. 53 .

bedded.text: laid in a smooth layer Ham. III. iv. 120 .

beer.text: “small beer,” trifling matters Oth. II. i. 160 “chronicle small beer.”

beetle1.text: “three-man beetle,” mallet requiring three men to lift it, used in ramming paving stones 2H4 I. ii. 259 ; beetle-headed, thick-headed, stupid Shr. IV. i. 160 “beetle-headed, flap-ear'd knave!”

beetle2.text: to project like beetle brows, overhang threateningly Ham. I. iv. 71 “the dreadful summit of the cliff That beetles o'er his base into the sea.”

befall.text: to become “of” Err. I. i. 123 “to dilate What hath befall'n of them.”

before.text: rather than Meas. II. iv. 183 , Mer.V. III. ii. 302 , R3 III. ii. 44 .

before1.text: prep. (follows its sb. LLL. IV. i. 93 ) “before me!,” on my soul! Tw.N. II. iii. 197 , Oth. IV. i. 147 . (∥ Modelled on “before (my) God!”)

before2.text: 1. in front Shr. III. ii. 58 “near-legg'd before,” Mac. V. vii. 75 [ viii. 46 ] “Had he his hurts before?”

beforehand.text: “been beforehand with,” anticipated, forestalled John V. vii. 111 .

beg.text: to petition the Court of Wards, established by Henry VIII and suppressed under Charles II, for the custody of (a minor, an heiress, or an idiot), as feudal superior or as having interest in the matter LLL. V. ii. 491 (‘You cannot prove us idiots’).

beget.text: (1 this is a late example of the sense) 1. to obtain Ham. III. ii. 8 “You must acquire and beget a temperance.”

beggar1.text: one who begs a favour, suppliant All'sW. I. iii. 22 .

beggar2.text: vb. (3 freq. echoed by later writers) 1. to reduce to beggary Mer.V. II. vi. 19 , R3 I. iv. 145 [“Conscience”] “beggars any man that keeps it.”

beguile.text: (3 first in S.; 4 peculiar to S.) 1. to deprive or rob “of” LLL. I. i. 77 , Oth. I. iii. 156 , 210

behalf.text: “in (the) behalf of, on behalf of,” in the interest of, in favour of, for the benefit or advantage of AYL. Epil. 9 “in the behalf of a good play,” All'sW. IV. iii. 359 , IV. v. 77 , John I. i. 7 , 3H6 IV. i. 63 (F1), R3 IV. iv. 358 “Be eloquent in my to her,” Oth. III. iv. 19 (F1 “on”), Cym. III. ii. 74 ;—“in behalf of,” on the part of, in the name of 1H4 I. iii. 48 , R3 III. iv. 19 “in the duke's I'll give my voice,” Tim. III. i. 18 ;— “on behalf of,” concerning, with regard to Ado IV. i. 212 , Tw.N. III. i. 118 “your gentle thoughts On his ;—in that behalf,” in respect of that LLL. II. i. 27 , John II. i. 264 .

behave.text: (1 this constr. with pa. pple. not pre-S.) 1. “as he is behav'd,” according to his behaviour Ham. III. i. 35 .

behaviour.text: (1 in use 1540-1680; 2 only S.) 1. pl.=sing. Cæs. I. ii. 42 .

beholding1.text: 1. sight Cor. I. iii. 10 , Lr. III. vii. 9 “not fit for your ”

behowl.text: to bay (the moon) MND. V. ii. 2 [ i. 379 ] (F1 &c. “beholds”).

being.text: (2 is an application peculiar to S.) 1. life, existence Shr. I. i. 11 “Pisa . . . Gave me my being,” Mac. III. i. 55 , Ham. II. i. 96 “end his being,” Oth. I. ii. 21 “my life and ,” Cym. I. i. 38 “he quit ”

beldame.text: (1 cf. ‘belsire’=grandfather) 1. grandmother 1H4 III. i. 32 “the old beldame earth,” Lucr. 953 , 1458

belie.text: (often in sense 1; twice in sense 2) 1. to tell lies about, calumniate Oth. IV. i. 36 .

bell.text: (the ordinary sense occurs in various connexions) 1. with allusion to the little bells attached to hawks 3H6 I. i. 47 “if Warwick shake his bells.”

bellman.text: crier who announced deaths and called on the faithful to pray for the departed, and acted as night-watchman, calling the hours Mac. II. ii. 4 “the owl . . . the fatal bellman, Which gives the stern'st good-night.”

belonging.text: (recorded first from S.) 1. (?) caparison (of a horse) Cor. I. ix. 62 .

beloving.text: loving Ant. I. ii. 24 “more than belov'”

below.text: (not common as prep. or adv. before the Eliz. period) 1. downstairs Wiv. II. ii. 153 ;=“below stairs” Ado V. ii. 10 .

belt.text: Mac. V. ii. 16 “cannot buckle his distemper'd cause Within the belt of rule” (=cannot control his disorganized party); cf. Troil. II. ii. 30 .

bemoil.text: to befoul with mire Shr. IV. i. 77 .

bench2.text: vb. (the foll. senses are rare outside S.) 1. to raise to authority Wint. I. ii. 314 “whom I from meaner form Have bench'd and rear'd to worship.”

bend1.text: look, glance Cæs. I. ii. 123 , Ant. II. ii. 216 * (‘their adoring looks or obeisances added grace and beauty to her’).

bend2.text: vb. (3 properly, to bring a gun to bear) 1. “ up,” to strain, nerve H5 III. i. 16 , Mac. I. vii. 79 .

bending.text: submissive, courteous R3 IV. iv. 95 , Troil. I. iii. 236 ; H5 V. ii. 404 * [Chor. 2] (a) bending under the weight of the task, (b) stooping to the hearers' clemency.

beneath.text: “this beneath world,” this world below Tim. I. i. 45 . Cf. “this under globe” Lr. II. ii. 170 .

benediction.text: blessing Lr. II. ii. 168 (the usual form of the proverb is ‘out of God's blessing into the warm sun’).

beneficial.text: (thrice in S.; 1 ‘beneficent’ is post-S.) 1. beneficent Err. I. i. 151 , H8 I. i. 56 “the rays o' the beneficial sun.”

benefit.text: (1 ‘benefaction’ is post-S.; 2 is only S.) 1. bestowal of property or rights, benefaction 1H6 V. iv. 152 , R3 III. vii. 195 “This proferr'd of dignity.”

benetted.text: ensnared Ham. V. ii. 29 “benetted round with villains.”

benevolence.text: forced loan or aid levied by kings of England, first raised by Edward IV in 1473 as a token of his people's ‘goodwill’ R2 II. i. 251 . ∥ Its use here is an anachronism.

benign.text: stressed on the first syll. Per. II. Gower 3 .

benison.text: blessing Mac. II. iv. 40 “God's go with you.”

bent1.text: sb. (not earlier than 16th c. in any sense) 1. “at bent for” (so Ff; Qq and mod. edd. “is bent”), turned in the direction of Ham. IV. iii. 48 .

bent2.text: inclined (to), intent (upon) MND. III. ii. 145 , 2H6 II. i. 165 , Mac. III. iv. 134 “I am bent to know . . . the worst,” Per. II. Gower 23 * “full bent with sin” (=intent upon sin), Ven. 618 “bent to kill.”

berattle.text: to fill with din Ham. II. ii. 365 [ 357 ].

bereave.text: (the commonest use is ‘to deprive’ a person “of” a thing, chiefly in pa. pple. “bereft”) 1. to take away (a thing) “from” a person 2H6 III. i. 85 , Oth. I. iii. 259 , Lucr. 835 ; always passive.

beseech.text: entreaty Troil. I. ii. 317 (‘While men have still their object to gain, their attitude is one of entreaty’).

beseek.text: old northern and north-midland form of ‘beseech’ 2H4 II. iv. 174 .

beside.text: adv. by, past Ven. 981 “sometimes falls an orient drop beside.” —prep. out of (patience, one's senses) Ado V. i. 131 “ their wit,” 1H4 III. i. 178 “ his patience,” Cæs. III. i. 180 “ themselves with fear.”

beslubber.text: to daub, smear 1H4 II. iv. 344 “beslubber our garments.”

besort2.text: to befit Lr. I. iv. 274 “such men as may besort our age.”

bespeak.text: to speak to, address Tw.N. V. i. 193 “I bespake you fair,” R2 V. ii. 20 , Ham. II. ii. 140 “my young mistress thus I did ” ; with admixture of meaning ‘to engage’ Err. V. i. 233 .

bespice.text: to season with spice Wint. I. ii. 316 .

best.text: “to have the best,” to have the advantage 3H6 V. iii. 20 “having now the at Barnet field;—at the best,” (1) in the best possible way 3H6 III. i. 8 , Oth. I. iii. 173 “Take up this mangled matter at the best” ; (2) in the best or most advantageous condition Rom. I. v. 123 “the sport is at the ,” Tim. I. ii. 159 , III. vi. 30 ;—“in the best,” at best Ham. I. v. 27 “most foul, as in the best it is,” Pilgr. vii. 18 [ 102 ].

bestow.text: (3 not pre-S.; 4 with ‘of’ and ‘to’ only S.) 1. to give in marriage AYL. V. iv. 7 “You will bestow her on Orlando here?”

bestride.text: to stand over (a fallen man) in order to defend him, (hence) to protect Err. V. i. 192 , 2H4 I. i. 207 , Mac. IV. iii. 4 “Let us . . . Bestride our down-fall'n birthdom.”

beteem.text: to grant (perhaps with secondary ref. to ‘teem’=hour) MND. I. i. 131 ; to allow Ham. I. ii. 141 . ∥ Still in use in Gloucestershire.

bethink.text: (also used refl. = ‘reflect’; 1 and 2 became obs. in the 17th c.) 1. to think of, consider, devise 3H6 III. iii. 39 “bethink a means to break it off,” Ham. I. iii. 90 “well bethought.”

betide.text: to happen, befall R3 I. iii. 6 “what would betide on me?” (=happen to me, become of me).

betray.text: (1 is derivative of the sense ‘deliver up treacherously’, which is freq.; 2 is common with various objects) 1. to give over or expose “to” punishment, or some evil Wiv. III. iii. 207 “to betray him to another punishment,” Err. V. i. 90 , AYL. IV. i. 7 , H8 III. i. 55 “to betray you . . . to sorrow.”

better.text: “I were better,” it would be better for me AYL. III. iii. 97 , Oth. III. iii. 363 ;—adv. rather All'sW. III. vi. 95 , H8 III. ii. 254 “Surrey durst better Have burnt that tongue than said so.”

between.text: interval of time Wint. III. iii. 61 “in the ”

bevel.text: oblique, slant Sonn. cxxi. 11 “I may be straight though they themselves be bevel.”

bevy.text: company, properly, of ladies H8 I. iv. 4 , Ham. V. ii. 197 (F1 “Beauy,” Qq “breed”).

beware.text: take care of 1H6 I. iii. 47 “ your beard.”

beweep.text: (used now chiefly in imitation of S.) 1. to deplore Sonn. xxix. 2 “beweep my outcast state.”

bewray.text: to reveal 3H6 I. i. 211 , Cor. V. iii. 95 “would bewray what life We have led,” Tit. II. iv. 3 .

beyond.text: “beyond beyond,” (?) surpassing everything Cym. III. ii. 57 (but Ff rightly “beyond, beyond”).

bias.text: sb. (all the uses are derived from bowls) 1. one-sided form of the bowl which gives an oblique motion to it; in fig. phrase “against the bias” Shr. IV. v. 25 , R2 III. iv. 5 ; “assays of bias,” indirect attempts Ham. II. i. 65 .

bias1.text: protruding on one side like a bowl Troil. IV. v. 8 “thy sphered bias cheek.”

bias2.text: awry Troil. I. iii. 15 “draw Bias,” IV. v. 168 “bias-drawing” (= turning away from the truth).

bide.text: to dwell or insist “upon” Wint. I. ii. 242 .

biding.text: abode, dwelling Lr. IV. vi. 229 , Lucr. 550 .

bifold.text: double, twofold Troil. V. ii. 141 (Q “by-fould,” Ff “by foul(e).”

big.text: (1 orig. sense; the S. exx. are late instances) 1. strong, stout, mighty H5 IV. ii. 43 “Big Mars” ; fig. Oth. III. iii. 350 “big wars.”

bigamy.text: marriage with a widow (formerly an ecclesiastical offence) R3 III. vii. 188 .

bilberry.text: common midland name of the whortleberry, Vaccinium Myrtillus, Wiv. V. v. 51 .

bilbo.text: properly, sword of Bilbao, noted for the temper and elasticity of its blade Wiv. III. v. 115 “like a good bilbo . . . hilt to point.”

bilboes.text: shackles sliding on an iron bar which is locked to the floor, used for mutinous sailors Ham. V. ii. 6 “the mutines in the bilboes.”

bile.text: spellings in the old edd. of BOIL sb.

bill1.text: obsolete military weapon consisting of a long wooden handle having at one end a blade or axe-shaped head R2 III. ii. 118 ; in the 16th and 17th centuries painted or varnished in different colours, hence “brown bill” 2H6 IV. x. 14 , Lr. IV. vi. 93 ; a similar weapon used by constables (with play on BILL sb. 2 ) Ado III. iii. 189 “being taken up of these men's bills,” 2H6 IV. vii. 134 .

bill2.text: sb. 2 (3 late exx. of this sense; 5 is very rare) 1. note, memorandum Shr. IV. iii. 145 “Error i' the bill,” Cæs. V. ii. 1 .

billet1.text: thick stick used as a weapon Meas. IV. iii. 60 .

billet2.text: vb. (twice only in S.) 1. to enroll Cor. IV. iii. 48 “distinctly billeted.”

bird.text: (1 orig. sense, from which the mod. sense was developed; cf. Scotch proverb ‘Every craw thinks its ain bird the whitest’; 2 not pre-S.; 4 partly the old word ‘burd’=maiden, partly fig. use of 1 or the ordinary sense) 1. young of the feathered tribes 1H4 V. i. 60 “the cuckoo's bird,” 3H6 II. i. 91 , Tit. II. iii. 154 .

birding.text: hawking with a sparrow-hawk at small birds, which were driven into a bush and shot Wiv. III. iii. 245 ; so birding-piece IV. ii. 60 .

birth.text: (the sense of ‘act of bringing forth, being born’ is frequent) 1. that which is born 2H4 IV. iv. 122 “loathly births.”

bisson.text: (1 also in mod. edd. “ multitude”† Cor. III. i. 130 ). 1. purblind Cor. II. i. 72 (Ff “beesom(e).”

bite.text: “bite the” (or “one's) lip” for the purpose of restraining anger or agitation Shr. II. i. 243 , H8 III. ii. 114 , Troil. III. iii. 256 ; “bite the thumb at,” to defy ‘by putting the thumbe naile into the mouth, and with a ierke from the upper teeth make it to knack’ (Cotgr.) Rom. I. i. 56 ; “bite one's tongue,” to be silent or speechless 2H6 I. i. 231 , 3H6 I. iv. 47 , Tit. III. i. 132 ; “bite by the ear” as a sign of fondness Rom. II. iv. 84 ; “bite by the nose,” to treat with contempt Meas. III. i. 107 .

bitumed.text: pitched as with bitumen Per. III. i. 72 (Qq “bittumed”), III. ii. 56 (Qq “bottomed”).

blackberry.text: used as a type of what is of little worth 1H4 II. iv. 269 “as plenty as blackberries,” Troil. V. iv. 13 “is not proved worth a ” ∥ Cf. ‘He settethe not therby a blakberie’ (Hoccleve).

bladder.text: boil, pustule Troil. V. i. 24 “bladders full of imposthume.”

bladed.text: in the blade MND. I. i. 211 “the bladed grass,” Mac. IV. i. 55 * (‘not yet in the ear’).

blank1.text: sb. (etymol. meaning is ‘something white’) 1. white spot in the centre of a target; fig. anything aimed at, range of such aim Wint. II. iii. 5 “out of the blank And level of my brain,” Troil. III. iii. 232 , Ham. IV. i. 42 “As level as the cannon to his blank” . . ., Lr. I. i. 161 , Oth. III. iv. 127 “stood within the blank of his displeasure.”

blank2.text: to make pale, blanch Ham. III. ii. 232 .

blast.text: (3 metaphor from the testing of cannon) 1. to ‘split’ (the ears) with a din Ant. IV. viii. 36 .

blazon1.text: sb. (1, 2 proper terms of heraldry) 1. armorial bearings, coat of arms Wiv. V. v. 70 “With loyal blazon” ; fig. Tw.N. I. v. 314 .

blazon2.text: vb. (used partly with heraldic metaphor) 1. to describe fitly, set forth honourably in words, publish the praises of Rom. II. vi. 26 , Oth. II. i. 63 “the quirks of blazoning pens,” Compl. 217 “With wit well blazon'”

bleak.text: pale All'sW. I. i. 116 “Look in the cold wind.”

blear.text: to hoodwink, deceive Shr. V. i. 120 .

bleeding.text: running or suffused with blood, bloody John II. i. 304 “the ground,” Cæs. III. i. 168 , Mac. V. ii. 4 ; fig. unstanched, unhealed Cor. II. i. 87 “dismiss the controversy ” ; as adv. Tim. I. ii. 81 “-new.”

blench2.text: to start aside, ‘shy’ “at,” flinch “from” Meas. IV. v. 5 “blench from this to that,” Troil. I. i. 30 “ at sufferance,” Ham. II. ii. 634 [ 626 ] “if he but ”

blent.text: blended Mer.V. III. ii. 182 , Tw.N. I. v. 259 .

bless.text: (3 in Ado I. iii. 70 , with a pun on the sense ‘cross oneself, sign oneself with the cross’） 1. to guard, keep “from” R3 III. iii. 4 .

blest.text: endowed with healing virtues (cf. plantnames like ‘blessed thistle’) Per. III. ii. 35 “the blest infusions That dwell in vegetives” . . .

blind.text: (2 cf. L. ‘caeca nox’ Virgil, ‘caecum antrum’ Lucan) 1. heedless, regardless, reckless, indiscriminate Tw.N. V. i. 239 “the waves,” H5 III. iii. 34 “The and bloody soldier,” R3 I. iv. 262 “to thy own soul so ”

blindfold.text: (twice in S.; 1 is an exceptional use) 1. that destroys the sight R2 I. iii. 224 “ death.”

blindness.text: concealment Err. III. ii. 8 “Muffle your false love with some show of blindness.”

bloat.text: soft-bodied, puffed, bloated Ham. III. iv. 182 (Ff “blunt”). ∥ The proper form is “blowt” (Qq), for which Warburton substituted “bloat.” ‘Blowty’ in the same sense is used in Lincolnshire.

block.text: wooden mould for a hat, (hence) shape or fashion (of hat) Ado I. i. 78 , Lr. IV. vi. 188 .

blood.text: （“flesh and , let” (a person) “ ” are freq.; “man of blood” Mac. III. iv. 126 , 4 a hunting expression) 1. vital fluid, (hence) life Rom. III. i. 189 “the price of his dear blood.”

bloody.text: (2 first recorded from S.) 1. consisting of blood AYL. III. v. 7 “bloody drops” ; containing blood John IV. ii. 210 * “the bloody house of life” (=the body).

blossom.text: (much commoner than ‘bloom’) 1. one lovely and full of promise Wint. III. iii. 45 “Blossom, speed thee well,” 1H6 IV. vii. 16 , (ironically) Tit. IV. ii. 73 .

blot.text: (2 is common Eliz.; 3 not pre-S.) 1. to tarnish, stain, sully Shr. V. ii. 140 “It blots thy beauty” ; absol. LLL. IV. iii. 241 .

blow.text: (?) mixture of senses (a) stroke, (b) blasting noise Shr. I. ii. 212 . ∥ S. is the earliest authority for “fall to blows” 2H6 II. iii. 82 , “at a ” 3H6 V. i. 50 .

blow1.text: vb. 1 (2 not pre-S., but ‘blowing’=‘flies’ eggs' is earlier) 1. to inflate, swell, puff up Tw.N. II. v. 49 , Ant. IV. vi. 34 “This blows my heart.”

blow2.text: to blossom, bloom Gent. I. i. 46 , MND. II. i. 249 “a bank whereon† the wild thy me blows” ; fig. Troil. I. iii. 317 .

blown1.text: ppl. a. 1 (1 a very rare use) 1. whispered, hinted Oth. III. iii. 182 (Ff “blowed”).

blowse.text: ruddy-faced fat wench Tit. IV. ii. 73 .

blue.text: (first in S. as applied to mountains, flame, and veins) 1. formerly the distinctive colour of the dress of servants Shr. IV. i. 93 , 1H6 I. iii. 47 “Blue coats to tawny coats.”

blunt.text: (1 historically the earliest; ‘dull-edged,’ of a tool, is later; this occurs in S., as well as the meaning ‘abrupt, unceremonious’) 1. of dull perception, dull-witted Gent. II. vi. 41 , 2H4 Ind. 18 “the blunt monster with uncounted heads” (=‘the many-headed multitude’).

blurt.text: to pooh-pooh “at” Per. IV. iii. 34 “ours was blurted at.”

board.text: (1 and 2 are fig. uses of the hostile entering of a ship; the sense ‘provide meals for’ occurs) 1. to make advances to, address, accost Wiv. II. i. 91 , Shr. I. ii. 96 , All'sW. V. iii. 213 .

boast.text: (used both intr. and refl. in the usual sense) 1. to display proudly Lucr. 55 “When beauty boasted blushes.”

bob1.text: vb. 1 (of different origin from BOB vb. 2 and vb. 3 ) 1. to cheat “out of” Troil. III. i. 76 “You shall not bob us out of our melody.”

bob2.text: to bang, thump R3 V. iii. 335 “bobb'd, and thump'd,” Troil. II. i. 75 .

bob3.text: to move with a jerk MND. II. i. 49 “against her lips I bob.”

bodement.text: omen, augury Troil. V. iii. 80 , Mac. IV. i. 96 “Sweet bodements!”

bodkin.text: (1 the orig. sense, Chaucer onwards; the mod. use is post-S.) 1. dagger Ham. III. i. 76 “When he himself might his quietus make With a bare bodkin.”

body.text: to give mental shape to MND. V. i. 14 . ∥ Imitated by modern writers.

boggler.text: waverer Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 110 “You have been a boggler ever.”

boil.text: Cor. I. iv. 31 “Boils and plagues Plaster you o'er!”

boiled.text: “boiled brains” (Ff1 2 3 hyphened), hot-headed fellows Wint. III. iii. 63 (cf. Tp. V. i. 60 , and MND. V. i. 4 “Lovers and madmen have such seething brains” ); in “boil'd stuff” Cym. I. vi. 125 there is an allusion to the sweating-tub.

bold.text: (the ordinary senses are well represented in S.) 1. “be” or “make (so) bold,” to venture so far as to, presume to Wiv. II. ii. 164 , IV. v. 13 “I'll be so bold as stay,” H8 III. ii. 319 , Ven. 124 ; “be” or “make bold with” (or “upon”), to take liberties with, make free with Wiv. II. ii. 267 , Ado III. ii. 8 , Rom. III. i. 83 , Cæs. II. i. 86 “we are too bold upon your rest.”

boldness.text: confidence Meas. IV. ii. 164 “boldness of” (= confidence in).

bolin.text: early form of ‘bowline’ Per. III. i. 43 “Slack the bolins there.”

bollen.text: swollen Lucr. 1417 “all boll'n and red” ; Mer.V. IV. i. 56 “bollen† bagpipe” (old edd. “woollen”; many conj. “wauling,” &c.).

bolster.text: to lie on a bolster (i.e. together) Oth. III. iii. 400 .

bolt.text: sb. (the senses ‘door-fastening’ and ‘thunderbolt’ occur; 2 was common from 1480 to 1690) 1. arrow, esp. one of the stouter and shorter kind with blunt or thickened head MND. II. i. 165 “the bolt of Cupid,” Cym. IV. ii. 300 ; “A fool's bolt is soon shot” (proverb common from the 13th to 18th c.) H5 III. vii. 137 ; “I'll make a shaft or a bolt on't,” I'll risk making something or other out of it, I'll make the venture Wiv. III. iv. 24 .

bolt1.text: to sift (lit. and fig.) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 377 “the fanned snow That's b-ed by the northern blasts.”

bolt2.text: to fetter (fig.) Ant. V. ii. 6 “shackles accidents, and bolts up change.”

bolter.text: box or chest in which flour is sifted from bran 1H4 III. iii. 81 “I have given them away to bakers' wives, and they have made bolters of them” ; so bolting-hutch fig. 1H4 II. iv. 501 .

bombard.text: leather jug for liquor (probably resembling the cannons formerly so called) Tp. II. ii. 21 , 1H4 II. iv. 503 “that huge of sack,” H8 V. iv. 87 .

bombast1.text: cotton wool used for padding or stuffing 1H4 II. iv. 364 “my sweet creature of ” ; fig. LLL. V. ii. 789 “As and as lining to the time.”

bombast2.text: inflated, turgid Oth. I. i. 13 “bombast circumstance.”

bond.text: (2 and 4 are the most freq. uses) 1. chain, fetter, usu. pl. (often fig.) Err. V. i. 250 “gnawing . . . my b-s in sunder,” John III. iv. 70 “I tore them” (=hairs) “from their b-s,” Troil. I. iii. 66 , Cæs. I. i. 38 “captive b-s,” Cym. I. i. 117 “b-s of death.”

bondage.text: (1 with allusion to senses ‘captivity’, and ‘servitude’) 1. condition of being bound Cym. V. v. 307 “Let his arms alone; they were not born for bondage” Compl. 34 .

bone.text: (the usual senses are freq.; 2 used only in oaths; 4 cf. ‘The lace-makers still call their work getting their bread out of the bones’, Nares) 1. “young bones,” unborn child Lr. II. iv. 165 .

bonnet.text: to take off the bonnet in token of respect Cor. II. ii. 30 “those who, having been supple and courteous to the people, bonneted.”

bonny.text: (2 doubtful sense; 3 still dialectal) 1. pleasant to look upon, comely 2H6 V. ii. 12 “the bonny beast he lov'd so well,” Ham. IV. v. 186 “bonny sweet Robin” [line of an old ballad]

book1.text: (fig. and allusive uses of 2 are freq.) 1. writing, document 1H4 III. i. 224 “By that time will our book, I think, be drawn.”

bookful.text: Ado V. ii. 32 ; or read, “a whole book full.”

boorish.text: used as sb.=illiterate speech AYL. V. i. 54 .

boot1.text: sb. 1 (3 influenced by the word ‘booty’) 1. something given in addition or into the bargain Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 654, R3 IV. iv. 65 “Young York he is but boot,” Troil. IV. v. 40 “I'll give you boot; I'll give you three for one” ; esp. in phr. “to ” (freq.).

boot2.text: “to give” (a person) “the boots,” to fool him Gent. I. i. 27 * . ∥ Cf. ‘to give one the boots, to sell him a bargaine’ Cotgr. s.v. “Bailler.”

boot3.headword: boot vb. 1 (1 the usual sense; 2 once) 1. to avail
boot3.text: intr. R2 III. iv. 18 ; trans. Gent. I. i. 28 .

boot4.text: to put on one's boots 2H4 V. iii. 138 .

bootless.text: unavailing (freq.); adv. MND. II. i. 37 , Tit. III. i. 36 .

border.text: to keep within bounds Lr. IV. ii. 33 .

bore1.text: sb. (2 metaphor from a gun) 1. small hole Cor. IV. vi. 88 (see AUGER), Cym. III. ii. 58 “the bores of hearing” (=the ears).

bore2.text: vb. (2 used by Fletcher, ‘Spanish Curate’ IV. v.) 1. to perforate, trans. and intr. MND. III. ii. 53 , R2 III. ii. 170 .

borrow2.text: vb. (extensions of the common sense are) 1. to derive, receive Troil. IV. v. 132 “any drop” [of blood] “thou borrow'dst from thy mother,” Sonn. cliii. 5 “Which borrow'd from this holy fire of Love A dateless lively heat.”

bosky.text: shrubby Tp. IV. i. 81 “My bosky acres.”

bosom1.text: sb. (“bosom multiplied” Cor. III. i. 130 prob. =the bosom of the many-headed monster, i.e. the people; “bisson multitude”†） 1. “Abraham's ” ( Luke xvi. 22 )=Paradise R3 IV. iii. 38 .

bosom2.text: vb. (Cf. ‘I'll bosom what I think’, John Day, 1606 ) 1. lit. to take to the bosom, embrace; (hence) to admit to close companionship Lr. V. i. 13 “conjunct And bosom'd with her.”

botch.text: flaw resulting from unskilful workmanship Mac. III. i. 134 ; so botch vb. to patch, esp. unskilfully (chiefly fig. with “up”) Tw.N. IV. i. 60 “how many fruitless pranks This ruffian hath b-'d up” (=clumsily contrived), H5 II. ii. 115 , Ham. IV. v. 10 “ the words up to fit their own thoughts” ; botcher All'sW. IV. iii. 211 , Cor. II. i. 99 .

botchy.text: “core,” central hard mass of a boil or tumour Troil. II. i. 6 (? some pun on BOTCH vb.).

bottled.text: bottle-shaped, big-bellied R3 I. iii. 242 “that bottled spider,” IV. iv. 81 .

bottom1.text: sb. (freq. in the ordinary sense, and fig. = ‘depths’) 1. low-lying land, valley AYL. IV. iii. 80 “down in the neighbour bottom,” 1H4 III. i. 106 “so rich a ”

bottom2.text: to wind, as a skein of thread Gent. III. ii. 53 “as you unwind her love from him . . . You must provide to bottom it on me.”

bounce.text: bang John II. i. 462 “cannon fire, and smoke and bounce,” 2H4 III. ii. 307 “‘bounce,’ would a' say.”

bound.text: sb. (‘bound’=leap is a different word) 1. boundary, limit, barrier (lit. and fig.) Tp. I. ii. 97 “A confidence sans bound,” MND. III. ii. 65 , John III. i. 23 “Like a proud river peering o'er his bounds” ; Ham. IV. vii. 128 “Revenge should have no bounds.”

bound1.text: to enclose, confine, restrict John II. i. 431 , 442 “the banks that bound them in,” Troil. I. iii. 111 “the bounded waters,” IV. v. 128 .

bound2.text: vb. 2 (not pre-Eliz.; 1 and 2 are obs.) 1. to recoil, rebound All'sW. II. iii. 314 “these balls bound; there's noise in it,” R2 I. ii. 58 (‘She compares her reiterated complaints to the rebounding of a tennis-ball’).

bound3.text: ppl. a. 1 (older ‘boun’, ‘bun’ of Norse origin) 1. ready, prepared 3H6 II. iv. 3 , Ham. I. v. 6 “I am bound to hear,” III. iii. 41 “a man to double business bound,” Lr. III. vii. 11 .

bound4.text: ppl. a. 2 (pa. pple. of the vb. ‘bind’) 1. under obligation, obliged 1H6 II. i. 37 .

bounden.text: obliged “to” AYL. I. ii. 303 , John III. iii. 29 .

bourn1.text: brook Lr. III. vi. 28 “Come o'er the bourn.”

bourn2.text: boundary, confine, limit Wint. I. ii. 135 “No 'twixt his and mine,” Ant. I. i. 16 “I'll set a how far to be belov'd,” Lr. IV. vi. 58 “this chalky ” (=Dover cliffs). ∥ The meaning in Ham. III. i. 79 “country from whose No traveller returns” has been variously taken by modern writers to be ‘goal’ and ‘realm, domain’.

bout.text: round or turn (in fencing) Tw.N. III. iv. 341 , Ham. IV. vii. 158 , V. ii. 298 ; transf. to dancing Rom. I. v. 21 “ladies that have the toes Unplagued with corns will walk a bout† with you” (Q1 “have about=a bout,” Qq Ff “walke about”).

bow1.text: yoke for oxen AYL. III. iii. 85 “As the ox hath his bow.”

bow2.text: to cause to bend, make crooked Shr. II. i. 151 “bow'd her hand to teach her fingering,” H8 II. iii. 36 “a three-pence bow'd,” Per. IV. ii. 94 “you are a young foolish sapling, and must be bowed” ; fig. H5 I. ii. 14 “wrest, or bow your reading,” Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 25 “He bow'd his nature.”

bowels.text: used in the Eliz. period=offspring Meas. III. i. 29 “thine own bowels, which do call thee sire.”

bower.text: to embower, enclose Rom. III. ii. 81 .

bowl.text: (four times in S.; 1 rhymes with ‘owl’) 1. to play at bowls LLL. IV. i. 142 “challenge her to ”

bowsprit.text: Ff “bore-sprit(t,” common Eliz. form Tp. I. ii. 200 .

boy.text: Ant. V. ii. 219 ; allusion to the fact that boys or youths played female parts on the stage in S.'s time.

brabble.text: quarrel, brawl Tw.N. V. i. 69 “In private did we apprehend him,” Tit. II. i. 62 “This petty ”

brabbler.text: quarreller, brawler John V. ii. 162 ; cf. Troil. V. i. 102 “He will spend his mouth . . . like Brabbler the hound.”

brace1.text: sb. (etym. meaning ‘the two arms’, (hence) ‘armour covering the arms’; 3 orig. of dogs, perhaps because the leash was called a brace) 1. (?) coat of armour Per. II. i. 137 .

brace2.text: to tighten the skin of (a drum) John V. ii. 169 .

brach.text: kind of hound that hunts by scent Shr. Ind. i. 17 , Lr. III. vi. 72 “ or lym” ; esp. a bitch-hound 1H4 III. i. 240 “Lady, my brach,” Lr. I. iv. 125 .

brag.text: vb. (the foll. are rare uses; 2 peculiar to S.) 1. to boast of, vaunt Cor. I. viii. 13 , Cym. V. iii. 93 .

bragless.text: without vain boasting Troil. V. ix. 4 .

braid1.text: to plait Ven. 271 “braided . . . mane,” Compl. 35 “slackly braided. ”

braid2.text: to upbraid Per. I. i. 93 “'Twould braid yourself.”

brain1.text: “bear a brain,” to have remembrance Rom I. iii. 29 ; “beaten with brains,” satirized, mocked Ado V. iv. 104 ; for other phrases see BOILED, DRY, HOT, &c.

brain2.text: vb. (1 fig. from dashing out the brains) 1. to defeat Meas. V. i. 397 “That brain'd my purpose.”

brained.text: having brains Tp. III. ii. 7 “brained like us.”

brake.text: thicket Ven. 876 “her fawn hid in some ” ; fig. H8 I. ii. 75 “the rough That virtue must go through.”

branch.text: (1 peculiar to S.; in AYL. IV. ii. 5 there is a ref. to the palm-branch and to the division of a deer's horn called a ‘branch’) 1. pl. applied to the human hands Tit. II. iv. 18 “made thy body bare Of her two branches.”

branched.text: adorned with a figured pattern suggesting branches Tw.N. II. v. 55 “my branched velvet gown.” ∥ In use 1510-1700

brand.text: Cupid's torch Cym. II. iv. 91 , Sonn, cliii. 1

brass.text: used to symbolize (i) hardness, imperishableness Meas. V. i. 11 “characters of ,” H5 IV. iii. 97 “live in ,” Cæs. I. iii. 93 “walls of beaten ,” Sonn. lxiv. 4 ; (ii) insensibility Sonn. cxx. 4 “Unless my nerves were ” ; (iii) obduracy LLL. V. ii. 396 “any face of ”

brassy.text: hard as brass, pitiless Mer.V. IV. i. 31 “brassy bosoms and rough hearts of flint.”

brave.text: vb. (1 freq. in S.; 2 in common Eliz. use) 1. to challenge, defy (lit. and fig.) John IV. iii. 87 “dar'st thou brave a nobleman?,” R3 IV. iii. 57 “when traitors brave the field,” Lucr. 40 “so rich a thing, Braving compare” ; also intr. in pres. pple. All'sW. I. ii. 3 “A braving war,” R2 II. iii. 112 “braving arms.”

brave1.text: bravado, defiant threat Shr. III. i. 15 “I will not bear these braves of thine,” John V. ii. 159 “There end thy brave,” Tit. II. i. 30 .

brave2.text: adj. (neither sense is pre-Eliz.) 1. finely arrayed; (hence) showy, splendid Shr. Ind. i. 40 “brave attendants,” Sonn. xv. 8 “wear their brave state out of memory,” Pilgr. xii. 4 [ 160 ] “Youth like summer brave, age like winter bare.”

bravely.text: used in the senses of the adj., but the meanings ‘valiantly’ and ‘excellently, finely’ are often blended, e.g. Mac. V. vii. 26 “The noble thanes do bravely in the war.”

bravery.text: (sense ‘valour’ does not clearly emerge) 1. defiance, bravado Cæs. V. i. 10 , Cym. III. i. 18 .

brawl1.text: French dance resembling a cotillon LLL. III. i. 9 . ∥ A different word from ‘brawl’= quarrel, squabble (cf. next).

brawl2.text: vb. (1 freq. in lit. sense; 2, 3 not pre-S.) 1. to quarrel noisily; (hence) to be clamorous, or noisy, or discordant Meas. IV. i. 11 “my brawling discontent,” Shr. IV. i. 209 “I'll rail and brawl,” 2H4 I. iii. 70 “as the times do ,” Rom. I. i. 181 “O b-ing love!”

brawn.text: (2 in common use from 1400 and now dial.) 1. fleshy part of the body, esp. the arm, calf of the leg, or buttock Troil. I. iii. 297 “in my vantbrace put this wither'd brawn,” Cym. IV. ii. 311 “The brawns of Hercules” ; attrib.=fleshy All'sW. II. ii. 20 .

brazed.text: hardened Ham. III. iv. 37 (Ff Q6 “braz'd,” Qq2-5 “brasd,” mod. edd. “brass'd”†), Lr. I. i. 11 “I am brazed to it.”

brazen.text: in fig. senses following those of BRASS 2H6 III. ii. 89 “loos'd them” [the winds] “forth their brazen caves,” 3H6 II. iv. 4 “a brazen wall.”

brazier.text: worker in brass H8 V. iv. 43 “he should be a brazier by his face.”

breach.text: (1 is freq. and colours other uses, esp. 2) 1. gap in a fortification made by a battery H5 III. i. 1 “Once more unto the breach, dear friends.”

bread.text: “God's bread,” the sacramental bread, the Host (used in oaths) Rom. III. v. 177 ; “bread and cheese,” typical of simple fare Wiv. II. i. 139 “I love not the humour of bread and cheese.”

breadth.text: extent (S.) All'sW. III. ii. 26 (F1 “bredth,” Craig “breath”), John IV. ii. 99 (see BLOOD 5), Per. IV. i. 36 .

break.text: (see also BROKEN) 1. to cut open (a person's head) Wiv. I. i. 126 “I broke your head,” Err. I. ii. 79 “I shall that merry sconce of yours,” II. i. 78 “I will thy pate across” ; similarly Rom. I. iii. 38 “the day before she broke her brow.”

breast.text: pair of lungs, voice Tw.N. II. iii. 21 “the fool has an excellent breast.” ∥ Cf. ‘Lets heare him sing, h'as a fine breast,’ Fletcher.

breath.text: S. is an early authority for the senses: ‘power of breathing’ Err. IV. i. 57 “you run this humour out of ,” Ham. V. ii. 285 “drink to Hamlet's better ” ; and ‘breathing-space, short interval’ John III. iv. 134 “one quiet of rest,” H5 II. iv. 145 , R3 IV. ii. 24 “some little , some pause,” Troil. II. iii. 122 “An after-dinner's ” ; the sense ‘speech, utterance, language’ is freq. Ado V. i. 276 , MND. III. ii. 44 “ so bitter,” Lr. I. i. 62 .

breathe.text: (1 is imitated by later poets; 2 the opposite sense of ‘rest, pause’ is freq.) 1. to speak Wiv. IV. v. 2 “speak, breathe, discuss,” Ham. II. i. 44 “The youth you breathe of.”

breathed.text: (see also LUST-BREATHED) 1. exercised, trained LLL. V. ii. 656 “A man so breath'd,” AYL. I. ii. 234 , Shr. Ind. ii. 50 “as swift As breathed stags,” Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 177; (hence) inured Tim. I. i. 10 “breath'd, as it were, To an untirable and continuate goodness.”

breather.text: (not in general use before S.) 1. one who breathes, living creature AYL. III. ii. 298 , Sonn. lxxxi. 12 “all the breathers of this world.”

breathing.text: (1 cf. ‘Hide not thy ear at my breathing, at my cry’ Lamentations iii. 55 ) 1. utterance Ant. I. iii. 14 “to give to my purpose.”

breech.text: typifying ‘the authority of the husband’ 2H6 I. iii. 149 “wear no breeches,” 3H6 V. v. 24 “stol'n the breech from Lancaster.”

breed1.text: sb. (not pre-Eliz.; 2 now replaced by ‘brood’) 1. race, strain R2 II. i. 45 “This happy breed of men,” H8 II. ii. 4 , Cym. IV. ii. 25 “breed of greatness!” ; family Mac. IV. iii. 108 ; kind, species LLL. V. ii. 267 “the breed of wits so wonder'd at,” Ham. III. ii. 333 [ 327 ] “this courtesy is not of the right breed.”

breed2.text: vb. (sense 1 is peculiar to S.) 1. “bred out,” exhausted, degenerated H5 III. v. 29 “Our mettle is bred out,” Tim. I. i. 259 “The strain of man's bred out Into baboon and monkey.”

breeding.text: parentage, descent Wint. IV. iii. 744 [ iv. 741 ], 2H4 V. iii. 109 .

briber.text: something which wins indulgence Tim. III. v. 62 “a sufficient briber for his life.”

bride.text: to play the bride Shr. III. ii. 254 .

brief.text: (both senses were common Eliz.) 1. letter, dispatch 1H4 IV. iv. 1 “this sealed brief.”

briefly.text: in a short time, soon, quickly Cor. I. vi. 16 “'Tis not a mile; briefly we heard their drums,” Ant. IV. iv. 10 “Go put on thy defence.—Briefly, sir,” Cym. V. v. 107 , Per. III. Gower 12 , i. 53 ; so briefness, quickness Lr. II. i. 20 , Per. V. ii. 15 “In feather'd briefness sails are fill'”

bright.text: the sense ‘lively, cheerful’ is recorded first from S., Mac. III. ii. 28 “Be and jovial.”

brinded.text: marked with streaks of a different colour from the body-colour Mac. IV. i. 1 “the cat.”

brine.text: first applied to tears in S., Rom. II. iii. 69 , Lucr. 796 ; cf. brine-pit Tit. III. i. 130 “And made a brine-pit with our bitter tears,” and brinish Lucr. 1213 “the brinish pearl.”

bring.text: (the foll. are obs. or special uses; 1 is freq.; 2 peculiar to S.; 6 common in Eliz. dramatists) 1. to escort or accompany (a person) on his way Gent. I. i. 55 “thither will I bring thee,” H5 II. iii. 2 “let me bring thee to Staines,” Cæs. III. ii. 58 .

brisk.text: (not pre-Eliz.; rare before S.) 1. quick and active Rom. I. v. 18 ; (of the times) fast Tw.N. II. iv. 6 “these most and giddy-paced times.”

broach.text: (orig.=‘to pierce’; 3 now the usual sense) 1. to stick (a thing) on a sword's point as on a spit H5 V. Chor. 32 “Bringing rebellion broached on his sword,” Tit. IV. ii. 86 .

broad.text: (not very common in S.) 1. free, unrestrained Mac. III. vi. 21 “broad words,” Ham. III. iv. 2 “his pranks have been too broad” ; widely diffused Mac. III. iv. 23 “As broad and general” “as the casing air”; arrogant Troil. I. iii. 190 “in full as proud a place As broad Achilles.”

brock.text: badger; used contemptuously as if ‘a stinking fellow’ Tw.N. II. v. 115 .

brogue.text: rude kind of shoe, generally made of untanned hide, worn by the inhabitants of the wilder parts of Ireland and the Scotch Highlands Cym. IV. ii. 214 “My clouted brogues.”

broil.text: to suffer great heat H8 IV. i. 56 “Where have you been broiling?—Among the crowd i'the Abbey” ; to become heated or excited Troil. I. iii. 379 * “Who broils in loud applause.”

broke.text: to bargain, traffic All'sW. III. v. 71 .

broken.text: 1 cf. southmidland dial. ‘broken-mouthed’ = having lost teeth; R3 II. ii. 117 * “The broken rancour of your high-swoln hearts” (so Qq; Ff “hates”), ‘your quarrels (or spirits) which had risen high and broken out into rancour’) 1. fragmentary, incomplete; “broken meats,” remains of food, as eaten by servants Lr. II. ii. 15 “A knave, a rascal, an eater of broken meats” ; All'sW. II. iii. 66 “My mouth no more were broken” (=having gaps in the teeth), H5 V. ii. 264 “broken English.”

broker.text: agent or intermediary (freq. with implied censure), esp. go-between in love affairs John II. i. 568 “that sly devil, That broker, that still breaks the pate of faith,” 582, 3H6 IV. i. 63 “To play the broker on mine own behalf;” fig. Ham. I. iii. 127 , Compl. 173 “vows were ever brokers to defiling” ; so broker-between Troil. III. ii. 211 .

brooch.text: in S.'s time used to include any jewelornament, esp. one worn round the neck; hence fig. like ‘jewel’, ‘gem’ R2 V. v. 66 , Ham. IV. vii. 93 “the brooch indeed And gem of all the nation.”

brood.text: “sits on brood” (in earlier English ‘abrood’), sits brooding like a hen Ham. III. i. 174 .

brook1.text: “flying at the brook,” hawking at the river with a goshawk for waterfowl (contrast BIRDING), the royal sport of falconry 2H6 II. i. 1 .

broomstaff.text: broom-handle H8 V. iv. 59 “they came to the broomstaff to me.”

brother.headword: brother (pl. “brethren,” 3 syll. in Tit. I. i. 89 , 348 , 357 )
brother.text: often used for ‘brother-in-law’, e.g. Err. II. ii. 156 ; also ‘half-brother’ R3 V. iii. 96 .

brow.text: properly, the arch of hair over the eye 2H6 I. ii. 3 “Why doth the great Duke Humphrey knit his brows?” ; (hence) pl. the prominences of the forehead on either side above the eyes LLL. V. ii. 393 “Help! hold his brows!,” Cæs. V. iii. 82 ; sing. the forehead Ven. 59 “she kiss'd his brow” ; fig. aspect, appearance 1H4 IV. iii. 83 “by this face, This seeming brow of justice,” Mac. IV. iii. 23 , Ham. I. ii. 4 “our whole kingdom To be contracted in one brow of woe.”

bruit1.text: rumour, report 3H6 IV. vii. 64 , Tim. V. i. 198 .

bruit2.text: vb. (1 the ordinary sense; 2, 3 only in S.) 1. to noise abroad, report, rumour 1H6 II. iii. 68 “I find thou art no less than fame hath bruited.”

brush.text: forcible rush, hostile encounter Troil. V. iii. 34 “the b-es of the war” ; fig. Tim. IV. iii. 265 “with one winter's ” * ; app. associated with ‘bruise’ 2H6 V. iii. 3 “Aged contusions and all of time.”

bubble.text: fig. empty, unsubstantial thing AYL. II. vii. 152 “Seeking the bubble reputation,” All'sW. III. vi. 5 (said of a person).

bubukle.text: mixture of ‘bubo’ and ‘carbuncle’ H5 III. vi. 111 (Fluellen's speech).

buck.text: quantity of clothes put through the ‘buck’ or lye; hence, quantity washed 2H6 IV. ii. 52 “she washes bucks” ; so buck-basket, dirty-linen basket Wiv. III. iii. 2 , &c.; bucking, washing Wiv. III. iii. 140 .

bucket.text: “come off and on swifter than he that gibbets on the brewer's bucket” 2H4 III. ii. 286 : allusion of doubtful meaning.

buckle.text: (lit. sense ‘fasten with a buckle’ is freq.; also in fig. context Troil. II. ii. 30 , Mac. V. ii. 15 ) 1. “buckle in,” to limit AYL. III. ii. 141 “the stretching of a span Buckles in his sum of age.”

buckler2.text: vb. (thrice in S., not otherwise common) 1. to shield, defend Shr. III. ii. 242 “I'll buckler thee against a million,” 2H6 III. ii. 216 , 3H6 III. iii. 99 “buckler falsehood with a pedigree.”

buckram.text: coarse linen stiffened with gum or paste 1H4 II. iv. 217 “two rogues in buckram suits” ; attrib. prob. fig.=stiff, starched, stuck-up 2H6 IV. vii. 28 (with quibble: see SAY).

bud1.text: used for ingrafting under the bark of a different stock Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 95 “make conceive a bark of baser kind By bud of nobler race”; fig. John III. iv. 82 “now will canker-sorrow eat my bud” [i.e. Arthur].

bud2.text: fig. to develop Shr. IV. v. 37 “budding virgin,” H8 I. i. 94 “The sudden breach . . . is budded out.”

budge.text: spec. to flinch Cor. I. vi. 44 , Cæs. IV. iii. 44 ; hence budger (S.): one who flinches Cor. I. viii. 5 “the first budger.”

budget.text: pouch, wallet Wint. IV. ii. 20 (F1 “Bowget” rhyming with “avouch-it”).

buff.text: stout leather made of ox-hide, used for the attire of soldiers, and (in S.) sergeants and bumbailiffs Err. IV. ii. 36 , 1H4 I. ii. 48 “is not a buff jerkin a most sweet robe of durance?”

bug.text: hobgoblin, bogey, imaginary object of terror Shr. I. ii. 214 “fear boys with bugs,” Ham. V. ii. 22 “such bugs and goblins” ; fig. 3H6 V. ii. 2 , Cym. V. iii. 51 “The mortal bugs o' the field” ; so bugbear in lit. sense Troil. IV. ii. 34 .

bugle.text: tube-shaped glass bead, commonly black, used to ornament wearing apparel; only attrib. Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 224 “Bugle-bracelet”; = black AYL. III. v. 47 “bugle eyeballs.”

building.text: (2 cf. Err. III. ii. 4 “Shall love, in building, grow so ruinous?,” Sonn. cxix. 11 , cxxiv. 5 “[my dear love] was builded far from accident”) 1. “This jewel holds his building” (=keeps its place) Per. II. i. 168 (Malone and Steevens “biding”†).

bulk1.text: 1 (1 in use 1460-1720; 3 cf. ‘the bulke, bellie, or bodie of a ship’, Cotgr.) 1. trunk, body (of a person) R3 I. iv. 40 “my panting ,” Ham. II. i. 95 , Lucr. 467 “her heart . . . Beating her ”

bulk2.text: framework projecting from the front of a shop Cor. II. i. 229 , Oth. V. i. 1 “stand behind this ”

bull.text: the sign Taurus of the zodiac Tit. IV. iii. 70 .

bully.text: familiar endearing term=fine fellow; often prefixed to a proper name or a designation=gallant Tp. V. i. 258 “bully-monster,” Wiv. I. iii. 6 , &c., II. iii. 18 “bully doctor,” MND. IV. ii. 20 “O sweet bully Bottom!,” H5 IV. i. 48 “the lovely bully” ; so bullyrook Wiv. I. iii. 2 , &c. (not pre-S.; a common 17th cent. form was ‘bully-rock’).

buoy.text: to rise up Lr. III. vii. 60 .

burgher.text: citizen of a borough Meas. I. ii. 108 .

burgomaster.text: magistrate corresponding to an alderman 1H4 II. i. 84 “b-s and great oneyers.”

burgonet.text: light casque or steel cap 2H6 V. i. 200 ; fig. Ant. I. v. 24 “The demi-Atlas of this earth, the arm And of men” (F1 “burganet”).

burial.text: has the orig. sense of ‘burying-place, grave’ (like the older ‘buriels’, Anglo-Saxon ‘byrgels’) in Mer.V. I. i. 29 (fig. of a ship).

burn.text: (the ordinary physical senses are freq.) 1. “burn daylight,” burn candles in daytime, (hence) waste time Wiv. II. i. 54 , Rom. I. iv. 43 ; so Ant. IV. ii. 41 “To burn this night with torches.” to make (drink) hot Wiv. II. i. 222 “burnt sack,” Tw.N. II. iii. 209 “I'll go burn some sack.”

burr.text: rough seed-vessel or flower-head of a plant, esp. the burdock; (hence) something that clings like a burr and is difficult to get rid of Meas. IV. iii. 193 “I am a kind of burr; I shall stick,” MND. III. ii. 260 “Hang off, thou cat, thou burr!”

bury.text: often in fig. use (not pre-S.), to consign to oblivion, put out of sight, conceal 3H6 IV. i. 55 “in your bride you bury brotherhood,” Cæs. II. i. 74 “faces buried in their cloaks,” IV. iii. 158 “In this [bowl of wine] I bury all unkindness.”

bush.text: bush of ivy hung out as a vintner's sign AYL. Epil. 4 “good wine needs no bush” (cf. line 6).

busky.text: bosky, bushy 1H4 V. i. 2 “yon busky hill.”

buss.text: kiss John III. iv. 35 , 2H4 II. iv. 291 ; fig. Troil. IV. v. 219 “Yond towers, whose wanton tops do buss the clouds,” Cor. III. ii. 75 “Thy knee bussing the stones.”

busyless.text: Theobald's emendation of F1 “busie lest” in Tp. III. i. 15 ; others read with Singer “busiest”†.

but.text: (the foll. uses are now obs. or archaic) 1. after negative sentences containing a comparison: =than MND. I. ii. 84 “they would have no more discretion but to hang us,” Tw.N. I. iv. 13 “Thou know'st no less but all.”

butcher.text: man of blood, brutal murderer AYL. III. v. 14 “tyrants, b-s, murderers,” John IV. ii. 259 “ of an innocent child,” R3 V. iv. 39 [ v. 26 ] “ to the sire.”

butt1.text: cask for wine or ale containing two hogsheads Tp. II. ii. 130 ; fig. Troil. V. i. 32 * . ∥ In Tp. I. ii. 146 of doubtful meaning (mod. edd. “boat”†).

butt2.text: mark for archery practice, properly a mound or other erection on which the target is set up H5 I. ii. 186 “To which is fixed, as an aim or butt, Obedience,” 3H6 I. iv. 29 “I am your butt, and I abide your shot” ; (hence) goal, object Oth. V. ii. 266 “my journey's end . . . my butt.” See also BUTT-SHAFT.

butt3.text: butting of a horned animal Shr. V. ii. 41 .

by.text: prep. (the following uses are now obs.) 1. about, concerning Ado V. i. 316 “virtuous In anything that I do know by her,” 2H6 II. i. 16 , Oth. I. iii. 17 “How say you by this change?”

cabin1.text: sb. (1 in use 1400-1650; 2 was common Eliz.) 1. temporary shelter of slight materials Tw.N. I. v. 289 “a willow cabin,” Pilgr. xiv. 3 [ 183 ].

cabin2.text: vb. (1 cf. 2 of prec.; 2 echoed by mod. writers) 1. to lodge Tit. IV. ii. 181 “And cabin in a cave.”

cabinet.text: (1 common term in military writers of the 16th cent.; 2 cf. CABIN sb. 2) 1. tent Lucr. 442 “They, mustering to the quiet cabinet” [i.e. the heart].

cable.text: “give him cable,” allow him scope Oth. I. ii. 17 .

caddis.text: short for ‘caddis ribbon’, worsted tape or binding used for garters, &c. Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 208; so caddis-garter 1H4 II. iv. 80 .

caduceus.text: wand, having two serpents twined round it, fabled to have been carried by Hermes (Mercury), the messenger of the gods Troil. II. iii. 13 “the serpentine craft of thy caduceus.”

cage.text: prison for petty malefactors, lock-up 2H6 IV. ii. 59 .

caitiff.text: =wretch (2 thrice as freq. as 1) 1. expressing pity Oth. IV. i. 109 “Alas! poor caitiff!”

cake.text: (one's) “cake is dough,” one's project has failed Shr. I. i. 109 , V. i. 146 .

calendar.text: (1 not post-S.; 2 not pre-S.) 1. guide, directory Ham. V. ii. 115 “he is the card or calendar of gentry” (‘the general preceptor of elegance’, Johnson).

calf.text: term of endearment Wint. I. ii. 128 “Art thou my calf?” ; stupid fellow, dolt Ham. III. ii. 112 .

caliver.text: light kind of musket or harquebus, introduced during the 16th cent., which seems to have been the lightest portable fire-arm, excepting the pistol, and to have been fired without a ‘rest’ 1H4 IV. ii. 21 , 2H4 III. ii. 292 , 295

call1.text: decoy-bird John III. iv. 174 “they would be as a call To train ten thousand English to their side.”

call2.text: vb. (1 only S.; 2 a few uses only are given here) 1. =‘call upon,’ to visit (a person) at his house Meas. IV. iv. 18 “I'll call you at your house,” Tw.N. III. ii. 58 “We'll call thee at the cubiculo.”

calling.text: name, appellation AYL. I. ii. 250 “I am more proud to be Sir Rowland's son, . . . and would not change that ”

calm2.text: to becalm (a ship) 2H6 IV. ix. 33 (F4 “calm'd,” F1 “calme,” F2 “claimd,” F3 “claim'd”); Oth. I. i. 30 “be-lee'd and calm'd” (? for ‘becalm'd’).

camel.text: great awkward hulking fellow Troil. I. ii. 269 , II. i. 59 “do, rudeness; do, camel; do, do.”

camlet.text: a fabric which has varied considerably in material; in 16th and 17th cent. made of the hair of the Angora goat H8 V. iv. 95 (F1 “chamblet”).

camp.text: to serve as a lodging for Ant. IV. viii. 33 “Had our great palace the capacity To camp this host.”

can1.text: vb. 1 (1 instances with apparent pronominal object, as “all I can, such as I can, I can no more,” are probably to be regarded as due to ellipsis of the infinitive ‘do’) 1. trans. to know, be skilled in Phœn. 14 “the priest in surplice white That defunctive music can.”

can2.text: altered form of ‘gan’, past tense of ‘gin’ =to begin, used for ‘did’ LLL. IV. iii. 106 “the wind . . . can passage find,” Per. III. Gower 36 “And every one with claps can sound.”

canakin.text: small can or drinking-vessel Oth. II. iii. 72 “let me the canakin clink, clink.”

canary1.text: sb. (1 the idea of the dance is said to have been borrowed from the Canary Islands) 1. lively Spanish dance All'sW. II. i. 77 .

canary2.text: to dance a ‘canary’ LLL. III. i. 13 “canary to it with your feet.”

cancel.text: “ off” (Ff), strike off, annul Per. I. i. 113 “We might proceed to off your days” (Qq “counsel of,” Malone “cancel of”†, taking “ ” as sb.; but the sb. is not recorded in this sense till the 19th cent.).

candidatus1.text: candidate for office in Rome (properly = one clothed in white) Tit. I. i. 185 “Be candidatus then, and put it on” [viz. “This palliament of white and spotless hue,” line 182].

candied.text: (2 not common outside S.) 1. crystallized with frost Tim. IV. iii. 227 “the cold brook, with ice” ; (hence) congealed Tp. II. i. 287 * .

candle.text: (3 cf. CANDLE-HOLDER) 1. applied to the heavenly luminaries Rom. III. v. 9 “Night's candles are burnt out,” Mac. II. i. 5 .

candy.text: used as adj.=sugared 1H4 I. iii. 251 “candy deal of courtesy” : see CAUDIE.

canker.text: (1 fig. ? sometimes to be referred to 2) 1. eating, spreading sore or ulcer, usu. fig. John V. ii. 14 “the inveterate canker of one wound,” 2H6 I. ii. 18 “the canker of ambitious thoughts,” Tim. IV. iii. 49 .

cankered.text: (2 and 3 very freq. in the 16th cent.) 1. rusted, corroded, tarnished 2H4 IV. v. 70 The canker'd heaps of strange-achieved gold<*>

canon.text: properly, law or decree of the Church; “the canon”=canon law All'sW. I. i. 160 “self-love, which is the most inhibited sin in the canon” ; (hence) law or rule in general LLL. I. i. 260 , Ham. I. ii. 132 “fix'd His canon 'gainst self-slaughter.”

canopy.text: S. is earliest for the application of the sb. to ‘the firmament’ Cor. IV. v. 41 , Ham. II. ii. 318 , and for the use of canopy vb. Sonn. xii. 6 , and canopied Cym. II. ii. 21 , Lucr. 398 .

cantle.text: part, lit. corner-piece 1H4 III. i. 101 (Qq “scantle”); segment of a sphere Ant. III. viii. 16 [ x. 6 ] “The greater cantle of the world.”

canton.text: song Tw.N. I. v. 291 “Write loyal cantons.”

canvass.text: to toss in a canvas sheet as a sport or punishment, (hence) to deal with severely 2H4 II. iv. 242 , 1H6 I. iii. 36 .

cap.headword: cap (3 probably with allusion to the fool's cap) 1. phrases with ref. to
cap.text: i. throwing the cap into the air in token of joy R3 III. vii. 35 “hurl'd up their c-s,” Cor. II. i. 117 “Take my , Jupiter,” Ham. IV. v. 107 “C-s, hands, and tongues applaud it.”

capable.text: (1 and 2 now obs.; 3 archaic, the most freq. in S.; 4 and 5 (obs. legal) recorded first from S.) 1. able to take in much, comprehensive Oth. III. iii. 460 “a capable and wide revenge.”

capacity.text: (2 the general sense ‘ability’ is freq.) 1. power of receiving or containing Tw.N. I. i. 10 “thy Receiveth as the sea,” H8 II. iii. 31 , Ant. IV. viii. 32 .

capital.text: （‘punishable by death’ the most freq. use) 1. chief, principal 1H4 III. ii. 110 “military title capital,” H5 V. ii. 96 “She is our capital demand.”

capitulate.text: to draw up articles of agreement, propose terms 1H4 III. ii. 120 , Cor. V. iii. 82 .

capon.text: (in AYL. II. vii. 154 “the justice, In fair round belly with good capon lin'd,” there is a ref. to the ‘capon justices’, as they were called, i.e. corrupt magistrates who were bribed by gifts of capons) 1. like Fr. ‘poulet’=love-letter LLL. IV. i. 56 .

capricious.text: characterized by play of wit or fancy, fantastic, ‘conceited’ AYL. III. iii. 8 “the most capricious poet, honest Ovid” (with allusion to the Latin ‘capra’ goat, whence ‘capricious’).

captain1.text: sb. (the ordinary military senses are freq.; three syllables in 3H6 IV. vii. 30 , Mac. I. ii. 34 ） 1. chief, head (fig. from military senses) R2 IV. i. 99 “his Christ,” Lucr. 271 “Affection is my , and he leadeth” ; Rom. II. iv. 21 “the . . . of compliments” ; used of women 3H6 II. vi. 75 , Oth. II. i. 74 .

captivate1.text: to take prisoner, make captive LLL. III. i. 131 ; fig. to subjugate, subdue 3H6 I. iv. 115 ; to fascinate, charm Ven. 281 .

captivate2.text: made prisoner, captured 1H6 II. iii. 42 , V. iii. 107 “women have been ere now.”

captive.text: often used in the sense of ‘(one) vanquished’ LLL. IV. i. 76 , Troil. V. iii. 40 .

car.text: the chariot of the sun-god (freq.) MND. I. ii. 38 . ∥ With Tw.N. II. v. 72 “Though our silence be drawn from us with cars,” which has given rise to many conj.; cf. Gent. III. i. 266 “Yet I am in love; but a team of horse shall not pluck that from me.”

carat.text: (2 is confused with CHARACT) 1. measure of weight used for gold Err. IV. i. 28 “How much your chain weighs to the utmost ” (F1 “charect”).

caraway.text: sweetmeat containing caraway-seeds, caraway comfit 2H4 V. iii. 3 “a dish of caraways.”

carbonado1.text: meat scored across and broiled 1H4 V. iii. 61 , Cor. IV. v. 199 “scotched him and notched him like a carbonado.”

carbonado2.text: to make a carbonado of Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 267 “toads carbonadoed”; (hence) to cut, hack, slash All'sW. IV. v. 108 “your carbonadoed face,” Lr. II. ii. 42 “I'll so carbonado your shanks.”

carbuncled.text: adorned with carbuncles (red or fiery precious stones) Ant. IV. viii. 28 “carbuncled Like holy Phœbus' car” (cf. Cym. V. v. 190 “had it been a carbuncle Of Phœbus' wheel” ).

carcanet.text: collar or necklace of gold or set with jewels Err. III. i. 4 (F1 “-kanet”), Sonn. lii. 8 (Q “-conet”).

card1.text: sb. (1 always in fig. phrases; 2 cf. ‘That law . . . is the card to guide the world by’, Hooker) 1. playing-card John V. ii. 105 “the best cards for the game,” Tit. V. i. 100 “As sure a card as ever won the set;—card of ten,” card with ten pips, hence phr. “fac'd it with a card of ten,” put on a bold front Shr. II. i. 399 (cf. the use of ‘facing-card’ in the 17th cent.=imposing allegation or argument); —“cooling card,” app. term or some lost card-game, used fig.=something that cools one's ardour 1H6 V. iii. 84 ;—“Pack'd cards with,” made a fraudulent arrangement with Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 19

card2.text: to mix with something base 1H4 III. ii. 62 “he . . . carded his state, Mingled his royalty with capering fools.” ∥ The word was in use from 1590 to 1635 for mixing different kinds of drink.

carder.text: one who ‘cards’ wool, i.e. combs out its impurities H8 I. ii. 33 .

cardinal.text: the four ‘natural’ virtues, justice, prudence, temperance, fortitude, to which some add the three ‘theological’ virtues, faith, hope, and charity, making in all seven H8 III. i. 103 “I thought ye . . . two reverend virtues; But sins . . . I fear ye” (with pun on the title of ‘cardinal’).

cardinally.text: humorous perversion of ‘carnally’ Meas. II. i. 82 “a woman cardinally given.”

care.headword: care occurs in various proverbs and phrases
care.text: “care killed a cat” Ado V. i. 136 ; “past cure . . . past care” LLL. V. ii. 28 , Sonn. cxlvii. 9 ;—“have (a) care,” be attentive, pay attention, take care Tp. I. i. 10 , Wiv. IV. v. 77 , Ado I. ii. 30 , III. iii. 43 , MND. IV. i. 15 ; Tw.N. III. iv. 70 , Per. IV. i. 49 ;—“keep” or “make a care of,” care for Tp. II. i. 311 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 367

career.text: (old edd. also “careire, car(r)ier, carreer(e)” 1. short gallop at full speed Wiv. I. i. 185 * “and so conclusions passed the c-s” (referred by some to 2), Ado V. i. 138 “I shall meet your wit in the ”

careful.text: out of 25 instances, four, or at most five, have the sense ‘full of care or anxiety’ Err. V. i. 299 , R2 II. ii. 75 “careful business,” H5 IV. i. 251 “our careful wives,” R3 I. iii. 83 “him that rais'd me to this careful height” ; Tw.N. IV. ii. 11 “a careful man” (? =careworn from much study).

careless.text: (the sense ‘heedless’ is the most freq.) 1. free from care or anxiety Wiv. V. v. 58 “Sleep she as sound as careless infancy,” Troil. V. v. 40 , Ham. IV. vii. 79 .

carl.text: countryman, peasant, churl Cym. V. ii. 4 ; so carlot AYL. III. v. 108 .

carnation1.text: flesh-colour H5 II. iii. 35 “A' could never abide carnation” ; attrib. LLL. III. i. 153 “carnation riband.” ∥ By association with the next word the meaning has passed into ‘carnation-coloured’.

carnation2.text: any cultivated variety of the clovepink, Dianthus caryophyllus Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 82 ∥ An earlier form was ‘coronation’.

carol.text: (1) song AYL. V. iii. 28 ; (2) song of religious joy MND. II. i. 102 “with hymn or carol blest.”

carouse.text: cupful of liquor drunk ‘all out’ [German ‘gar aus’], full bumper, toast Shr. I. ii. 280 , Ant. IV. viii. 34 ; so carouse vb. (freq.).

carpet.text: “on carpet consideration,” as a mere carpetknight, whose achievements belong to the lady's boudoir or the drawing-room Tw.N. III. iv. 261 ; so carpet-monger Ado V. ii. 33 .

carriage.text: (5 and 6 not always distinguishable) 1. act of carrying, being carried, conveyance Cym. III. iv. 190 “suspected of Your from the court.”

carrier.text: messenger Wiv. II. ii. 143 , Tit. IV. iii. 85 .

carrion.text: (2 (i) is still in midland dialect use) 1. dead putrefying flesh Ham. II. ii. 184 “if the sun breed maggots in a dead dog, being a god kissing ” ; also attrib. “carrion men” Cæs. III. i. 275 ; esp.= feeding on carrion, e.g. “carrion flies” Rom. III. iii. 35 , “carrion kites” 2H6 V. ii. 11 .

carry.text: (the chief fig. uses are the foll.) 1. to win, obtain Cor. II. i. 257 “rather Than carry it” [i.e. the consulship] “by the suit o' the gentry”; so carry it, win the day Wiv. III. ii. 73 “he will carry't” All'sW. IV. i. 30 , Oth. I. i. 67 “What a full fortune does the thick-lips owe” (=possess), “If he can carry't thus!”

cart1.text: sb. (1 cf. CART vb.; 2 cf. CAR) 1. cart used for conveying criminals to the gallows, and for the public exposure and chastisement of offenders 1H4 II. iv. 554 .

cart2.text: to carry in a cart through the streets by way of punishment or public exposure Shr. I. i. 55 .

carve.text: (2 first in S.; 3 only S.; cf. MINCE) 1. to form, fashion Ado II. iii. 18 “c-ing the fashion of a new doublet,” Shr. IV. iii. 89 “c-'d like an apple-tart.”

carver.text: “Be his own carver,” take or choose at his own discretion R2 II. iii. 144 .

case1.text: sb. 1 (senses ‘contingency’ and ‘state of things’ are freq.; ‘grammatical case’ Wiv. IV. i. 47 ) 1. condition, circumstances; “in to,” in a position to Tp. III. ii. 30 ; “in good ,” well off 2H4 II. i. 119 .

case2.text: sb. 2 (2 perhaps ‘a pair’, like ‘a case of pistols’) 1. applied to (i) a mask LLL. V. ii. 388 “that superfluous case,” Rom. I. iv. 29 ; cf. Ado II. i. 99 , and CASE vb. 1; (ii) the body, as enclosing the soul Tw.N. V. i. 169 , Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 41, xiii. [ xv. ] 89 “This case of that huge spirit”; (iii) the sockets of the eyes Wint. V. ii. 14 , Lr. IV. vi. 148 “with the case of eyes,” Per. III. ii. 99 ; (iv) the skin Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 849; (v) clothes Meas. II. iv. 13 , 1H4 I. ii. 200 “cases of buckram,” Compl. 116 “Accomplish'd in himself, not in his case.”

case3.text: vb. (3 used in cookery parlance till about 1800) 1. to encase Err. II. i. 85 , R2 I. iii. 163 “like a cunning instrument cas'd up” ; in transferred uses akin to those of CASE sb. 2 1, 1H4 II. ii. 58 “Case ye, ye; on with your vizards,” Cym. V. iii. 22 , Per. V. i. 112 “her eyes as jewel-like, And c-'d as richly.”

casque.text: headpiece or helmet H5 Chor. 13, Troil. V. ii. 167 ; as a symbol of military life or authority Cor. IV. vii. 43 “not moving From the casque to the cushion.”

cast1.text: sb. (2 only S.; 3 not pre-S.) 1. throw of the dice 1H4 IV. i. 47 , R3 V. iv. 9 “I have set my life upon a cast.”

cast2.text: vb. (the more unusual senses are) 1. to throw in wrestling Mac. II. iii. 47 “though he took up my legs sometime, yet I made a shift to him.”

castigate.text: to chasten Tim. IV. iii. 241 “To castigate thy pride.” ∥ First in S., but castigation ( Oth. III. iv. 42 ) is in Chaucer.

castle.text: (1 cf. ‘some old Lads of the Castell’, ‘a lusty ladd of the Castell, that will binde Beares, and ride golden Asses to death,’ Gabriel Harvey) 1. “old lad of the ”: (?) roisterer 1H4 I. ii. 48 .

casual.text: (twice in S.) 1. accidental Ham. V. ii. 396 “casual slaughters.”

cat.text: (1 chiefly in allusions and proverbs) 1. domestic animal Tp. II. ii. 89 “here is that which will give language to you, cat” (very strong drink was said to make a cat speak), Ado V. i. 136 “care killed a cat” (i.e. for all its nine lives), MND. I. ii. 32 “a part to tear a cat in” (=to rant violently), Mac. I. vii. 45 “Like the poor cat i' the adage” (the cat that would eat fish, but would not wet her feet), Ham. V. i. 314 “The cat will mew.”

cataplasm.text: poultice, plaster Ham. IV. vii. 143 “ so rare, Collected from all simples that have virtue.”

catastrophe.text: (2 is recorded first from S.) 1. that which produces the conclusion or final event of a dramatic piece, dénouement LLL. IV. i. 78 , Lr. I. ii. 150 “pat he comes, like the of the old comedy.”

catch1.text: sb. (1 not pre-S.; 2 not pre-Eliz.) 1. that which is caught or is worth catching Shr. II. i. 325 “a quiet catch,” Troil. II. i. 110 “Hector shall have a great catch.”

catch2.text: vb. (“caught” occurs 31 times, “catched” 4 times; the senses ‘overtake, come up with’ ( Tp. V. i. 315 , MND. II. i. 233 , R3 II. ii. 44 ), ‘apprehend by the senses or intellect’ ( LLL. II. i. 70 , Ant. I. ii. 149 , Sonn. cxiii. 8 ), ‘apprehend so as to adopt or appropriate’ ( Mac. I. v. 19 ), and ‘catch a cold’ ( Gent. I. ii. 133 ) are recorded first from S.; there are many other uses; the foll. are occas.) 1. to attain, get possession of 3H6 III. ii. 179 “I . . . Torment myself to catch the English crown,” Mac. I. vii. 3 “if the assassination Could . . . catch With his surcease success,” Sonn. cxliii. 11 ; absol. John I. i. 173 “have is have, however men do catch.”

cates.text: dainties, delicacies Err. III. i. 28 , Shr. II. i. 190 .

catling.text: catgut Troil. III. iii. 309 “unless the fiddler Apollo get his sinews to make catlings on. ∥ Catling” is the name of a musician in Rom. IV. v. 133 .

caudie.text: 1H4 I. iii. 251 “what a caudie deal of courtesy” (F1 2 “caudie,” F3 4 “gaudie, -y,” mod. edd. “candy”†).

caudle.text: warm drink given to sick people, consisting of thin gruel, mixed with wine or ale sweetened and spiced LLL. IV. iii. 174 ; “hempen caudle,” halter 2H6 IV. vii. 94 .

cause.text: sb. (the foll. are obs. or archaic uses; 1 is a general application of the legal sense ‘subject of litigation’; 4 taken over from late Latin ‘causa’) 1. matter in dispute, affair to be decided Shr. IV. iv. 26 “a weighty cause Of love,” 2H6 III. i. 289 “What counsel give you in this weighty cause?”

cautel.text: crafty device, deceit, trickery Ham. I. iii. 15 “no soil nor doth besmirch” . . ., Compl. 303 .

cautelous.text: crafty, deceitful Cor. IV. i. 33 “caught With cautelous baits and practice,” Cæs. II. i. 129 .

caution.text: taking heed, precaution Mac. III. vi. 44 “that . . . might Advise him to a caution.”

cavaleiro.text: gentleman trained in arms; gay, sprightly military man, (hence) gallant 2H4 V. iii. 60 (Q “cabileros,” Ff “cavileros”); used as a title Wiv. II. i. 201 , iii. 76 ; also cavalery MND. IV. i. 25 .

caviare.headword: caviare (old edd. “Caviarie, -y,” the common 16th18th cent. forms)
caviare.text: roe of the sturgeon pressed and salted and eaten as a relish, generally unpalatable to those who have not acquired the taste for it Ham. II. ii. 466 “the play . . . pleased not the million; 'twas caviare to the general.”

cease1.text: cessation Ham. III. iii. 15 “The cease of majesty” (Ff “cease,” Qq “cesse”), Lr. V. iii. 266 “Fall and cease?.” ∥ Partly an aphetic form of ‘decease’.

cease2.text: “be not ceas'd,” do not allow yourself to be silenced Tim. II. i. 16 .

cellarage.text: “in the ,” underground Ham. I. v. 151 (old edd. “selleredge, selleridge, celleridge, sellerige”).

cement.headword: cement sb. and vb. (old edd. also “ciment, cyment, symant”)
cement.text: always stressed on the first syllable Cor. IV. vi. 86 , Ant. II. i. 48 , III. ii. 29 .

censer.text: perfuming-pan having an ornamented lid Shr. IV. iii. 91 “Here's snip and nip and cut and slish and slash, Like to a censer in a barber's shop,” 2H4 V. iv. 21 “thin man in a censer” (ref. probably to figures embossed on censer-lids).

censor.text: name of two magistrates in ancient Rome, who drew up the census of the citizens and had the supervision of public morals Cor. II. iii. 252 .

censure1.text: sb. (2 the prevailing S. use; 3 not pre-S.) 1. judicial sentence, esp. a condemnatory one Cor. III. iii. 45 , V. v. [ vi. ] 143 “Your heaviest censure,” Oth. V. ii. 367 “the censure of this hellish villain.”

censure2.text: vb. (1 the prevailing sense) 1. trans. to form or give an opinion of, estimate John II. i. 328 , Cor. II. i. 25 “how you are censured here in the city,” Cæs. III. ii. 16 , Lr. III. v. 3 .

center.text: girdle John IV. iii. 155 (Ff “center,” mod. edd. “cincture, ceinture”); by some taken = CENTRE 3

centre.text: (in Wint. II. i. 101 * the sense is perhaps architectural ‘temporary framework supporting a superstructure’) 1. middle point of the earth MND. III. ii. 54 , Ham. II. ii. 159 “I will find Where truth is hid, though it were hid indeed Within the centre.”

century.text: (sense of ‘100 years’ is post-S.) 1. division of the Roman army, probably consisting orig. of 100 men Cor. I. vii. 3 , Lr. IV. iv. 6 .

cerecloth.text: winding-sheet, properly one impregnated with wax Mer.V. II. vii. 51 .

cerements.text: waxed wrapping for the dead, (hence) graveclothes Ham. I. iv. 48 . ∥ A purely S. word, which has been caught up by modern writers.

ceremony.text: (1 common Eliz. use; 2 peculiar to S.) 1. external accessory or symbol of state Meas. II. ii. 59 “No ceremony that to great ones 'longs, Not the king's crown,” &c., H5 IV. i. 110 “his” [the king's] “ceremonies laid by”; applied to festal ornaments Cæs. I. i. 69 “Disrobe the images If you do find them deck'd with ceremonies.”

certes.text: (two syll. in Tp. III. iii. 30 and Err. IV. iv. 77 , one syll. in H8 I. i. 48 and Oth. I. i. 16 ): certainly LLL. IV. ii. 171 .

certify.text: to assure, inform with certainty Mer.V. II. viii. 10 , 1H6 II. iii. 32 , IV. i. 144 , R3 I. iv. 96 (Ff “signify”), III. ii. 10 .

cess.text: “out of all cess,” beyond all calculation 1H4 II. i. 8 .

cesse.headword: cesse [variant of ‘cease’ not generally current in S.'s time]
cesse.text: to cease All'sW. V. iii. 72 (F1): rhymes with “bless.”

chace.text: term of tennis for the second impact on the floor of a ball which the opponent has failed or declined to return; used vaguely in the pl.= tennis-play H5 I. ii. 266 “all the courts of France will be disturb'd With chaces.”

chafe1.text: rage, passion Ant. I. iii. 85 “How this Herculean Roman does become The carriage of his ”

chafe2.text: not pre-S. in the intr. sense ‘to fret, rage’ of the sea or a river against its banks Wint. III. iii. 89 , Cæs. I. ii. 101 “The troubled Tiber chafing with her shores,” Lr. IV. vi. 22 ,

chafed.text: John III. i. 259 ; see CASE vb. 2

chain.text: to surround as with a chain, embrace Ant. IV. viii. 14 “Chain mine arm'd neck.”

chair.text: (used as the symbol of old age, when rest is the natural condition, in 1H6 III. ii. 51 , IV. v. 5 ; cf CHAIR-DAYS) 1. seat of authority, as a throne, a judgement-seat, the Roman rostra Wiv. V. v. 67 “chairs of order” (in St. George's Chapel, Windsor), 3H6 I. iv. 97 “he that took King Henry's chair,” II. i. 90 “His dukedom and his chair,” H8 IV. i. 67 “chair of state,” Cor. III. iii. 34 “the chairs of justice,” IV. vii. 52 * , Cæs. III. ii. 69 “the public chair.”

challenge1.text: sb. (3 the usual sense in S.) 1. claim 1H6 V. iv. 153 “Of benefit proceeding from our king And not of any challenge of desert.”

challenge2.text: vb. (1 the orig. sense, the ultimate etym. of the word being Latin ‘calumniari’=to accuse falsely; 2, 3 the chief Eliz. uses) 1. to accuse, bring a charge against Tit. I. i. 340 “c-d of wrongs,” Mac. III. iv. 42 “ for unkindness.”

challenger.text: in senses 2 and 3 of the vb.; H5 II. iv. 95 , Ham. IV. vii. 28 ; AYL. I. ii. 172 , &c.

chamber.text: (2 London is called ‘Regum Angliae Camera’=Chamber of the Kings of England, by Camden in his ‘Britannia’; the orig. application was to cities or provinces directly subject and yielding immediate revenue to the king) 1. “of” (a person's) “chamber,” one of his attendants, chamberlain to him AYL. II. ii. 5 , Mac. I. vii. 76 , II. iii. 108 , Per. I. i. 152 .

chamberer.text: frequenter of ladies' chambers, gallant Oth. III. iii. 265 .

chamberlain.text: 1. one who waits on a king or lord in his bedchamber, fig. in Tim. IV. iii. 223 ; spec. officer having charge of the king's private apartments and household R3 I. i. 123 .

chameleon.text: formerly supposed to live on air; hence Gent. II. i. 181 “though the chameleon Love can feed on the air,” Ham. III. ii. 98 “Excellent, i' faith; of the 's dish; I eat the air, promise-crammed.”

champaign.text: flat open country Tw.N. II. v. 175 “Daylight and champaign” (Ff1 2 “champian,” Ff3 4 “champion,” mod. edd. “champai(g)n”), Lr. I. i. 66 “With shadowy forests and with champaigns riched” (F1 “champain,” Ff2 3 4 “Champion,” mod. edd. “champai(g)n”); attrib. Lucr. 1247 “a goodly champaign plain” (F1 “champaine”).

champion1.text: sb. (3 Wyclif has ‘strong schampions and pileris of holy chirche’) 1. fighting man, man of valour 1H6 III. iv. 19 “A stouter champion never handled sword,” Tit. I. i. 65 “Rome's best champion.”

champion2.text: to challenge Mac. III. i. 72 . ∥ Introduced by S. and imitated by mod. writers.

chance1.text: (2 is now archaic, 5 is obsolete) 1. fortuitous circumstance, accident Wint. II. iii. 182 “Where chance may nurse or end it,” Troil. III. iii. 131 , Cor. IV. iv. 20 , Lucr. 1596 ; so “by chance” LLL. V. ii. 219 , Ham. IV. vii. 161 .

chance2.text: vb. (now generally superseded by ‘happen’; the foll. are idiomatic uses, in which the word assumes the character of an adv.) 1. “may chance” with an infinitive=may possibly Ado II. iii. 255 [ 244 ], 2H4 II. i. 13 , Troil. I. i. 28 “you may chance burn your lips” (Ff “to burn”).

chancellor.text: secretary H8 I. i. 219 (Ff “counsellor”), II. i. 20 ; spec. the ‘King's Chancellor’ or Lord High Chancellor, the keeper of the Great Seal and highest judicial functionary in England 3H6 I. i. 238 “Warwick is chancellor,” H8 III. ii. 395 “Sir Thomas More is chosen Lord Chancellor.”

change1.text: sb. (the foll. are obs. or special uses) 1. exchange Ado IV. i. 185 “Maintain'd the change of words,” H5 IV. viii. 29 , Troil. III. iii. 27 “Give us a prince of blood, . . . In change of him,” Cæs. V. iii. 51 .

change2.text: vb. (in Cor. V. iii. 152 * , Ant. I. ii. 5 * Ff read “change,” mod. edd. “charge”†: see commentators) 1. to exchange Tp. I. ii. 438 , LLL. V. ii. 134 , AYL. I. iii. 94 “Wilt thou change fathers?” ; to exchange (a thing) “with” (a person) Sonn. xxix. 14 “I scorn to change my state with kings,” Oth. I. iii. 318 “change my humanity with a baboon” ; intr. with “for” before the thing taken in exchange Oth. I. iii. 356 “She must change for youth,” Per. IV. vi. 179 .

changeable.text: varying in colour in different lights, ‘shot’ Tw.N. II. iv. 75 “changeable taffeta.” ∥ In use 1480- 1815

changeling.text: (1 now obsolete or archaic) 1. fickle or inconstant person 1H4 V. i. 76 “fickle c-s,” Cor. IV. vii. 11 “his nature In that's no changeling.”

channel1.text: street gutter=KENNEL 2H4 II. i. 54 -5, 3H6 II. ii. 141 . ∥ Still in use locally in northern counties.

channel2.text: to furrow 1H4 I. i. 7 “No more shall trenching war channel her fields.”

chanson.text: song Ham. II. ii. 447 [ 438 ] “The first row of the pious chanson” (so Qq2-5; F1 “Pons Chanson,” Q6 Ff2 3 4 “Pans Chanson”).

chantry.text: chapel endowed for the maintenance of one or more priests to sing mass for the souls of the founders or others Tw.N. IV. iii. 24 , H5 IV. i. 321 .

chaos.text: (1 is a sense of the orig. Greek word; 4 is a rare use) 1. ‘black gulf’ or ‘deep abyss’ of night or darkness Oth. III. iii. 92 * “when I love thee not, Chaos is come again” (or ?=sense 2), Ven. 1020 “black chaos comes again,” Lucr. 767 “Vast sin-concealing ” (=night).

chape.text: metal plate or mounting of a scabbard, esp. that which covers the point All'sW. IV. iii. 165 “the chape of his dagger” ; so chapeless (S.) Shr. III. ii. 49 “with a broken hilt, and chapeless.”

chapless.text: lacking the lower jaw Rom. IV. i. 83 “yellow skulls” (Qq2 3 F1 “chap(p)els”), Ham. V. i. 95 .

chapman.text: (2 survived in dialect till the 19th cent.) 1. merchant, trader LLL. II. i. 16 “Not utter'd by base sale of chapmen's tongues.”

chaps1.text: cracks in the skin Tit. V. iii. 77 . See CHOPS.

chaps2.text: jaws Tp. II. ii. 93 , Mac. I. ii. 22 (Ff “chops”).

character1.text: sb. (in R3 III. i. 81 “chara'cter,” as often in 16th-17th cent.; the foll. uses are not pre-S.) 1. in collective sing. used=writing, printing Tim. V. iii. 6 “the character I'll take with wax,” Sonn. lix. 8 “Since mine at first in character was done.”

character2.headword: character vb. (thrice “chara'cter,” four times “cha'racter”; not pre-S.)
character2.text: to engrave, inscribe, also fig. Gent. II. vii. 4 , 2H6 III. i. 300 “one scar character'd on thy skin,” Ham. I. iii. 59 “these few precepts in thy memory Look thou character,” Sonn. cviii. 1 .

chare.text: turn of work, job, esp. of household work Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 75 “the meanest c-s,” V. ii. 230 .

charge1.text: sb. (the senses ‘accusation’ and ‘person or thing entrusted to one's care’ are also freq.) 1. load, burden (lit. and fig.) Wiv. I. iv. 103 , Ado I. i. 106 , Wint. I. ii. 26 “my stay To you a charge and trouble” ; (with quibble) Ham. V. ii. 43 “‘As’es of great charge.”

charge2.text: vb. (various senses occur; the foll. are the less freq.) 1. to load, burden (fig.) H5 I. ii. 15 , 283 , Cæs. III. iii. 2 “things unlucky charge my fantasy,” Mac. V. i. 59 “The heart is sorely charged” ; to saddle with expense Wiv. II. ii. 173 .

charity.text: in phrases of exhortation “for charity” R3 I. ii. 49 , “of charity” Tw.N. V. i. 240 ; “by Saint Charity” (F1 “ Charity”)=O Fr. ‘par seinte charite’, by holy charity Ham. IV. v. 59 . ∥ E. K. (Gloss. on Spenser) says that ‘deare Lord, and sweete Saint Charitee’ was ‘the Catholiques comen othe’.
