charm1.text: the orig. sense ‘incantation, enchantment, magic spell’ ( Tp. I. ii. 231 ) runs through the fig. applications Wiv. II. ii. 108 * “surely, I think you have charms, la,” Rom. II. Prol. 6 “bewitched by the charm of looks,” Lr. V. iii. 49 , Pilgr. xi. 8 [ 150 ]; occas. the sense approaches to ‘person or thing that charms’ Oth. V. i. 35 “those charms, thine eyes,” Ant. IV. x. 29 [ xii. 16 ], 38 [ 25 ] “this false soul of Egypt! this grave charm.”

charm2.text: vb. (as in the sb. the fig. uses retain a strong metaphor from the orig. sense ‘enchant’) 1. “charm the tongue,” keep it silent Shr. IV. ii. 58 , 2H6 IV. i. 64 , 3H6 V. v. 31 , Oth. V. ii. 182 .

charmed.text: (2 the phrase is echoed by mod. writers) 1. endowed with magic or occult power Mac. IV. i. 9 “the charmed pot,” Compl. 146 “in his charmed power.”

charter.text: publicly conceded right, privilege, immunity AYL. II. vii. 48 “as large a charter as the wind,” R2 II. i. 197 , R3 III. i. 54 , Cor. I. ix. 14 , Oth. I. iii. 247 “let me find a in your voice,” Sonn. lviii. 9 .

chartered.text: privileged, licensed H5 I. i. 48 “The air, a charter'd libertine.”

chary.text: adj. fastidious, shy, particular Ham. I. iii. 36 “The chariest maid” ;—adv. carefully Sonn. xxii. 11 “keep so chary As tender nurse her babe.”

chase1.text: sb. (2 the usual sense; 3 once) 1. hunting Oth. II. iii. 372 , Ven. 3 , &c.

chase2.text: vb. (in Tim. I. i. 25 Ff “chases,” mod. edd. “chafes,” Ven. 325 earlier Qq “chafing,” later “chasing”) 1. “chas'd your blood Out of appearance” (Ff1 2 “apparance”), driven the colour out of your face (i.e. rendered it invisible) H5 II. ii. 75 .

chaste.text: celibate, unmarried Mer.V. I. ii. 115 , Rom. I. i. 223 ; stainless Oth. V. ii. 2 “you chaste stars.”

chat.text: sb. and vb. are both used in the obs. sense of (1) frivolous talking, and the current one of (2) familiar conversation; in Cor. II. i. 227 “chats him” =gossips about him.

chattels.text: H8 III. ii. 344 (so mod. edd.; Ff “castles”).

che.text: form of south-western dial. ‘ch’ = I (as in ‘cham’=I am) used before consonants Lr. IV. vi. 247 “che vor ye.”

cheap.text: S. is the earliest authority for the senses ‘costing little labour or effort’ ( Meas. II. iv. 106 ), ‘accounted of small value, lightly esteemed’ ( 1H4 III. ii. 41 ), and the phrase ‘hold cheap’= despise ( Err. III. i. 21 ). See also GOOD CHEAP.

cheapen.text: to bargain or bid for Ado II. iii. 33 , Per. IV. vi. 10 “if he should cheapen a kiss of her.”

cheat.text: swindle, fraud Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 28, 130 ∥ The word passed through the senses (1) escheat, i.e. property which falls to the lord by forfeit or fine, (2) booty, (3) stolen thing (in the thieves' cant of the 16th cent. simply=thing), (4) fraud.

cheater.text: (the mod. sense occurs Err. I. ii. 101 , 2H4 II. iv. 150 ; S. plays on the other senses) 1. officer appointed to look after the king's escheats (see CHEAT), who would have opportunities of defrauding people of their estates; used fig. Wiv. I. iii. 75 (F2 “Cheator”), Tit. V. i. 111 , Sonn. cli. 3 .

check1.text: reproof, rebuke, censure Wiv. III. iv. 84 “against all checks, rebukes and manners,” Shr. I. i. 32 * “Aristotle's checks” (? restraints), 2H4 IV. iii. 34 , Oth. III. iii. 67 , Ant. IV. iv. 31 “Rebukeable And worthy shameful check.”

check2.text: vb. (gen. sense ‘restrain, repress’ is freq.) 1. to stop short “at” Ham. IV. vii. 62 “As checking at his voyage, and that he means No more to undertake it.”

cheek.text: side by side MND. III. ii. 338 .

cheer1.text: sb. (5 whence the sense ‘fare, provisions’ Wiv. III. ii. 55 ; Ham. III. ii. 231 where some read “chair,” comparing Hall's Satires ‘Sit seven yeres pining in an anchor's cheyre’) 1. face, complexion MND. III. ii. 96 “pale of cheer.”

cheer2.headword: cheer vb. (1 once in S.; common Eliz.
cheer2.text: ‘to comfort, gladden, console’ is the most freq. sense) 1. “How cheer'st thou?,” What cheer?, How is it with thee? Mer.V. III. v. 76 (Qq “farest”).

cheerly.text: blithely, cheerily AYL. II. vi. 15 ; as a cry of encouragement among sailors=heartily Tp. I. i. 6 “Heigh, my hearts! cheerly, cheerly, my hearts!”

chequin.text: sequin, gold coin of Italy and Turkey, worth from 7“ ” to 9“ ” 6“ ” Per. IV. ii. 28 (old edd. “checkins, chickens, -eens, -ins”).

cherish.text: (1 common in Eliz. use of rearing plants; 2 in use 1330-1740) 1. to foster 3H6 II. vi. 21 “what doth cherish weeds but gentle air?,” Lucr. 950 “To . . . cherish springs.”

cherubin.text: applied to an ‘angelic’ woman Tp. I. ii. 152 , Oth. IV. ii. 62 “thou young and rose-lipp'd cherubin” ; also attrib.=angelic Tim. IV. iii. 63 “For all her cherubin look.”

cheveril.text: kid-leather; always used allusively as a type of flexibility Tw.N. III. i. 13 , H8 II. iii. 32 “your soft conscience,” Rom. II. iv. 90 “a wit of ”

chew.text: to ruminate “upon” Cæs. I. ii. 170 ; to keep mumbling over Meas. II. iv. 5 “As if I did but only chew his name.”

chewet.text: chough, jackdaw [Fr. ‘chouette’]; applied to a chatterer 1H4 V. i. 29 * “Peace, chewet, peace!”

chick.text: used as a term of endearment (S.) Tp. V. i. 316 “My Ariel, chick.”

chicken.text: (2 cf. ‘chicken-hearted’) 1. applied to human offspring Mac. IV. iii. 218 .

chide.text: (pa. t. “chid,” pa. pple. “chid, chidden”) 1. intr. to scold, quarrel, speak loudly, brawl LLL. IV. iii. 132 “You chide at him,” Shr. I. ii. 96 “though she chide as loud As thunder,” Sonn. cxi. 1 “for my sake do you with Fortune chide.”

chiding1.text: brawling or angry noise MND. IV. i. 121 “never did I hear Such gallant chiding” [of hounds], AYL. II. i. 7 “chiding of the winter's wind.”

chiding2.text: brawling, noisy H8 III. ii. 198 “the chiding flood,” Troil. I. iii. 54 (of the tempest), Per. III. i. 32 .

chief.text: “in chief,” mainly, principally Meas. V. i. 214 , 2H4 IV. i. 31 . ∥ Ham. I. iii. 74 “Are most select and generous, chief in that” (old edd. “Are of a most,” Q1 “generall,” Ff “cheff,” Qq2-6 have a comma at “generous”; many conj.: see commentators).

child.text: (fig. uses of the ordinary senses are common) 1. female infant Wint. III. iii. 71 “A boy or a child, I wonder” ; so “my child” is always used by S. of a daughter Tp. V. i. 198 , Ado IV. i. 77 , Lr. IV. vii. 70 .

childed.text: having children Lr. III. vi. 119 “He childed as I father'”

childing.text: fertile, fruitful MND. II. i. 112 “ autumn.”

childishness.text: “second childishness,” second childhood AYL. II. vii. 165 .

chimney.text: fireplace Wiv. V. v. 49 , 1H4 II. i. 22 .

chip.text: (1 cf. ‘Chyp the vpper crust of your breade’ Andrew Borde's ‘Dyetary’, 1542 ; 2 not pre-S.) 1. to pare (bread) by cutting away the crust 2H4 II. iv. 258 .

chips.text: applied to the keys of a spinet or harpsichord Sonn. cxxviii. 10 “those dancing chips.”

chirurgeonly.text: like a skilled surgeon Tp. II. i. 147 .

chivalry.text: (orig. applied to the mounted and fully armed men-at-arms of the Middle Ages) 1. men-at-arms 2H4 II. iii. 20 “all the chivalry of England,” H5 I. ii. 157 .

choice1.text: sb. (1, 2, 3 not pre-S.; 4 only S.) 1. abundant and well-chosen supply John II. i. 72 , 1H6 V. v. 17 “So full replete with of all delights.”

choice2.text: “choice spirits” 1H6 V. iii. 3 , Cæs. III. i. 163 ; a S. expression taken up by modern writers.

choke.text: (the following are rare in S.; 3 cf. Matthew xiii. 22 in the Great Bible of 1539, ‘The care of the worlde, and the dissaytfulnes of riches, choke vp the worde’) 1. to prevent the free play of Mac. I. ii. 9 “As two spent swimmers, that do cling together And choke their art.”

choler.text: (orig.=bile, one of the ‘humours’; 1 cf. ‘These thynges folowyng do purge color: Fumytory, Centory, wormewod . . . Reuberbe’, Andrew Borde's ‘Dyetary’, (1542) 1. bilious disorder R2 I. i. 153 “Let's purge this choler,” Ham. III. ii. 320 : in both passages with quibble on sense 2

choleric.text: (3 the usual sense in S.) 1. causing bile Shr. IV. iii. 19 “too choleric a meat” (F1 Q “cholericke,” Ff2 3 4 “phlegmaticke”).

choose.text: (special idiomatic uses are) 1. to do as one likes, take one's own course Mer.V. I. ii. 50 “An you will not have me, choose.”

chop.text: to thrust with sudden force, ‘pop’ R3 I. iv. 161 “we will chop him in the malmsey butt” (so Qq; Ff “throw him into”). ∥ A word of the modern Shropshire dial.; in literary use 1560- 1650

chopine.text: kind of shoe raised by means of a cork sole or the like, worn in Spain and Italy, esp. at Venice, Ham. II. ii. 455 .

chops2.text: jaws Mac I. ii. 22 (Ff); person with fat or bloated cheeks 1H4 I. ii. 150 , 2H4 II. iv. 234 .

chorus.text: the chorus of Attic tragedy (consisting of a band of interested spectators) was imitated and adapted by English dramatists, and by S. and others reduced to a single person, who speaks the prologue and explains or comments upon the course of events Wint. IV. i. “Enter Time, the ,” H5 Prol. 32 “Admit me to this history,” Ham. III. ii. 259 , Phœn. 52 “As to their tragic scene”; choruslike Ven. 360 “And all this dumb play had his acts made plain With tears, which, , her eyes did rain.”

chough.text: applied to the small chattering species of the crow family, esp. the jackdaw MND. III. ii. 21 “russet-pated c-s,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 632, Mac. III. iv. 125 ; (hence) as the type of a chatterer Tp. II. i. 274 “A of as deep chat,” All'sW. IV. i. 22 “c-'s language, gabble enough.” ∥ In Lr. IV. vi. 14 per haps the Cornish chough or red-legged crow, which was abundant on the Sussex coast 150 years ago.

christen.text: Christian 1H4 II. i. 19 “ne'er a king christen” (Ff “in Christendom”), II. iv. 8 “their christen names” (so Qq; Ff omit).

christendom.text: (usu. sense ‘Christians, or Christian countries collectively’） 1. Christianity John IV. i. 16 , H8 I. iii. 15 .

chrysolite.text: name formerly given to several different gems of a green colour, as zircon, tourmaline, topaz, and apatite Oth. V. ii. 143 .

chuff.text: close, avaricious person, esp. one who does not know how to put his wealth to good use 1H4 II. ii. 98 .

church.text: “I am of the ,” I am a ‘churchman,’ i.e. clergyman Wiv. I. i. 32 ; cf. the familiar phrase ‘to enter the church’=to take holy orders; “to go to church,” to be married Ado II. i. 373 “when mean you to go to church?,” Mer.V. III. ii. 304 , Shr. III. ii. 129 , Rom. II. v. 74 , III. v. 162 ; so Ado III. iv. 97 “to fetch you to church.”

churl.text: (2 not earlier than the 16th cent.) 1. countryman, peasant, rustic, boor Err. III. i. 24 “Good meat . . . is common; that every churl affords” ; (hence) rude, low-bred fellow Rom. V. iii. 163 “O churl! drunk all . . .?,” Tim. I. ii. 26 .

churlish.text: (4 formerly said also of soil and metal) 1. rude, rough, brutal AYL. V. iv. 81 “the ‘reply churlish,’” Ham. V. i. 262 “churlish priest,” Ven. 134 .

cicatrice.text: properly=scar Cor. II. i. 166 ; used loosely = mark, impression AYL. III. v. 23 .

cinders.text: (1 still so used dialectally) 1. ashes (residue of combustion) Tit. II. iv. 37 “burn the heart to cinders,” Oth. IV. ii. 74 , Phœn. 55

cinquepace.text: kind of lively dance, the steps of which are supposed to be based on the number five Ado II. i. 78 , Tw.N. I. iii. 141 (F1 “Sinke-a-pace”).

cipher1.text: zero, usu. in fig. application=nonentity, a mere nothing Meas. II. ii. 39 , LLL. I. ii. 60 , AYL. III. ii. 310 ; with ref. to its increasing the value of figures preceding it Wint. I. ii. 6 “like a , Yet standing in rich place,” H5 Chor. 17 “let us, ciphers to this great accompt, On your imaginary forces work.”

cipher2.text: vb. (1 common Eliz.; 2 peculiar to S.) 1. to show forth, express Lucr. 207 “To me how fondly I did dote,” 1396 “The face of either c-'d either's heart.”

circle.text: (3 in use 1400-1670; 4 only S.) 1. ring used as a figure in magic AYL. II. v. 60 “a Greek invocation to call fools into a circle,” H5 V. ii. 318 , Rom. II. i. 24 .

circled.text: rounded, circular Rom. II. ii. 110 “the . . . moon, That monthly changes in her circled orb,” Lucr. 1229 * “'gan wet Her circled eyne.”

circuit.text: circlet, diadem (S.) 2H6 III. i. 352 “the golden circuit on my head” ; cf. 3H6 I. ii. 30 .

circumstance.text: (1, 4 the commoner S. senses) 1. attendant fact or ‘adjunct’ of an action: e.g. time, place, manner, &c. amid which it takes place Meas. IV. ii. 108 “neither in time, matter, or other ,” Tw.N. III. iv. 90 , V. i. 261 , 1H6 III. i. 152 , Ham. III. ii. 81 ; pl. R3 III. vii. 175 “All circumstances well considered,” Lucr. 1262 .

circumstantial.text: (1 cf. CIRCUMSTANCE 4, AYL. V. iv. 100 ) 1. indirect AYL. V. iv. 86 “the ‘lie circumstantial’.”

circumvention.text: means or power of circumventing Cor. I. ii. 6 * .

city.text: (2 after Greek ‘polis’, Latin ‘civitas’) 1. “the City” = London 3H6 I. i. 67 .

civet.text: perfume derived from the civet cat AYL. III. ii. 70 “civet . . . the very uncleanly flux of a cat,” Lr. IV. vi. 133 “an ounce of civet.”

civil.text: (freq. in collocations referring to civil war, e.g. “ arms” R2 III. iii. 102 , “ wounds” I. iii. 128 ; 1 rare in S.; 2 not pre-S.; the sense of ‘wellmannered, polite’ MND. iii. ii. 147 comes partly out of sense 2; in Ado II. i. 306 there is a pun on ‘Seville’) 1. of or belonging to citizens Rom. Prol. 4 “Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.”

claim.text: to demand the fulfilment of (a promise) Gent. IV. iv. 94 , R3 III. i. 197 .

clamour1.text: din (as of guns) 3H6 V. ii. 44 “like a clamour in a vault” (Ff “Cannon”).

clamour2.text: (?) to silence (the tongue) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 250 “ your tongues, and not a word more.” ∥ Said to be a metaphor from bell-ringing.

clangor.text: loud resonant ringing sound 3H6 II. iii. 18 “Like to a dismal clangor.”

clap1.text: “at a clap,” at one stroke Lr. I. iv. 318 .

clap2.text: (sense ‘to clap hands, applaud’ is not pre-S.; 3 is the usual S. sense; ‘to tap, pat’ also occurs) 1. “clap to,” shut smartly 1H4 II. iv. 309 , Cor. I. iv. 51 .

claw.text: (3 the fuller phrase was ‘to claw a person's ears, senses, humour,’ &c.) 1. to seize, grip Ham. V. i. 78 “age . . . Hath claw'd me in his clutch.”

clay.text: freq. applied to that of which men and mortal things are made or to which they will return.

cleanly.text: adv. (obsolete uses) 1. completely, quite Ven. 694 “till they have singled . . . the cold fault cleanly out.”

clear1.text: adj. (senses now obs. or archaic) 1. bright, fully light Meas. IV. ii. 227 “clear dawn,” H8 I. i. 226 “my clear sun,” Ven. 860 .

clear2.text: vb. (the less common senses are the foll.) 1. to get (any one) clear of a place Wint. I. ii. 439 “I will . . . Clear them o' the city.”

clearly.text: entirely, completely Tw.N. V. i. 292 ; John III. iv. 122 * “In this which he accounts so won” (or ? manifestly, evidently), V. v. 7 * “And wound our tottering colours clearly up” (or? stainlessly).

clearness.text: freedom from suspicion Mac. III. i. 133 * .

cleave.text: to split; pa. t. “cleft” Wint. III. ii. 197 , 3H6 I. i. 12 , “clove” Lr. I. iv. 176 ; pa. pple. “cleft” Gent. V. iv. 103 , “cloven” (always qualifying a sb., e.g. Tp. I. ii. 277 “a cloven pine” ).

clef.text: key in music Shr. III. i. 78 “‘D sol re,’ one clef, two notes have I” ; fig. Troil. V. ii. 11 “any man may sing her, if he can take her cliff” (Ff “find her . . . her life”).

clepe.text: to call LLL. V. i. 24 , Mac. III. i. 94 (Ff “clipt”), Ham. I. iv. 19 ; cf. YCLEPT.

clerestory.text: upper part of the nave, choir, and transepts of a large church lying above the triforium (or the nave arches) containing windows admitting light to the central parts of the building; also applied to similar features in other buildings Tw.N. IV. ii. 42 (F1 “cleere stores,” Ff2 3 4 “clear(e stones,” mod. edd. “clearstories”).

clerk.text: man of learning, scholar MND. V. i. 93 . H8 II. ii. 92 * , Per. v. Gower 5 “Deep clerks she dumbs.”

clerkly2.text: in a scholarly manner Gent. II. i. 119 , 2H6 III. i. 179 “ignominious words, though couch'”

clew.text: ball of thread All'sW. I. iii. 190 “you have wound a goodly clew” (fig.).

climate1.text: formerly used = region, country, ‘clime’, without ref. to climatic conditions R2 IV. i. 130 “in a Christian climate,” Cæs. I. iii. 32 .

climate2.text: to dwell in a particular region or ‘clime,’ reside Wint. V. i. 170 “whilst you Do here.”

climb.text: to reach by climbing, Gent. II. iv. 182 “ her window,” III. i. 115 , Rom. II. v. 76 “ a bird's nest” ; fig. Tim. I. i. 77 “To his happiness.”

cling.text: to pinch with hunger Mac. V. v. 40 .

clinquant.text: glittering H8 I. i. 19 “All , all in gold.”

clip.text: (3 is the prevailing use) 1. to cut Per. V. iii. 74 “clip to form.”

clipper.text: one who mutilates current coin by fraudulently paring the edges H5 IV. i. 249 (allusive passage).

clock1.text: “twixt and ,” between the striking of one hour and another; “tell the ,” count the strokes of the clock Tp. II. i. 297 , R3 V. iii. 277 .

clock2.text: to cluck Cor. V. iii. 163 . ∥ ‘To clucke, or clocke, as a Henne,’ Cotgr.

close1.text: enclosure Tim. V. i. 210 “a tree which grows here in my close.”

close2.text: sb. 2 (from the vb. CLOSE; 2 and 3 not pre-S.) 1. conclusion of a piece of music, cadence R2 II. i. 12 “music at the ” (Q1), H5 I. ii. 182 “Congreeing in a full and natural close, Like music.”

close3.text: adj. and adv. (uses not now general) 1. enclosed, shut up, shut in, confined Gent. III. i. 236 “ prison” (hence “ prisoner” Oth. V. ii. 334 ), MND. III. ii. 7 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 503, R3 IV. ii. 52 “I will take order for her keeping ,” H8 V. iv. 31 , Rom. III. ii. 5 “thy curtain,” Lucr. 367 .

close4.text: vb. (often used where ‘enclose’ would now be usual, e.g. Lucr. 761 “Some purer chest to close so pure a mind” ) 1. to join (hands) John II. i. 533 , Rom. II. vi. 6 .

closely.text: (obs. in both S. uses) 1. in close confinement Shr. I. i. 187 “closely mew'd her up,” R3 I. i. 38 .

closet.text: (1 is freq.; also fig. Lucr. 1659 , Sonn. xlvi. 6 ） 1. private room, spec. private apartment of a monarch or potentate John IV. ii. 267 , H5 V. ii. 210 , Cæs. II. i. 35 .

closure.text: (2 not recorded before S.) 1. enclosure, bound, limit R3 III. iii. 10 “Within the guilty closure of thy walls,” Ven. 782 “the quiet closure of my breast,” Sonn. xlviii. 11 .

cloth.text: (3 in use about 1450-1650) 1. handkerchief, napkin 3H6 I. iv. 157 , Cym. V. i. 1 , Per. III. ii. 87 .

cloud1.text: dark spot on the face of a horse (used punningly) Ant. III. ii. 51 .

cloud2.text: recorded first from S. in senses ‘to overspread with gloom or sorrow’ 3H6 IV. i. 74 , ‘cast a slur upon, asperse’ Wint. I. ii. 280 , ‘to become gloomy’ LLL. V. ii. 729 .

cloudy.text: chiefly fig.=gloomy, sullen Mac. III. vi. 41 .

clout.text: (1 see also BABE “of clouts”) 1. piece of cloth, rag R3 I. iii. 177 , Rom. II. iv. 221 “as pale as any ,” Ham. II. ii. 537 , Ant. IV. vii. 6 * ,

cloy.text: (?) to claw Cym. V. iv. 118 “cloys his beak.”

cloyless.text: that does not satiate Ant. II. i. 25 .

club.text: 1H6 I. iii. 85 “I'll call for clubs” (=I'll summon assistance), H8 V. iv. 54 , Tit. II. i. 37 , Rom. I. i. 79 . ∥ ‘Prentices and clubs’ was the rallying cry of the London apprentices.

cluck.text: in mod. edd. for CLOCK vb. Cor. V. iii. 163 .

clusters.text: crowds, mobs Cor. IV. vi. 123 , 129 “Here come the clusters” ; so clust'ring, thronged 1H6 IV. vii. 13 “the clust'ring battle of the French.”

clutch.text: to clench (the hand) Meas. III. ii. 51 , John II. i. 589 “I have the power to clutch my hand.”

coal.text: (the following are special uses) 1. “dead coal(s,” cinder(s, charred fuel Wint. V. i. 68 , fig. John V. ii. 83 “the dead coal of wars” ; (hence, sing.) ashes Cor. IV. vi. 138 .

coarsely.text: slightingly, meanly All'sW. III. v. 57 “Reports but coarsely of her.”

coast.text: (2 old edd. “cost,” which some take to be the verb ‘cost’=cause the loss of) 1. to go a roundabout way, travel circuitously Err. I. i. 134 “And, c-ing homeward, came to Ephesus,” H8 III. ii. 38 “how he c-s And hedges his own way” ; to make progress against obstacles Ven. 870 “all in haste she coasteth to the cry.”

coat.text: (the ordinary sense, with proverbial phrases pertaining to it, is common Wiv. III. v. 147 “there's a hole made in your best coat,” H5 III. vi. 92 , Oth. I. i. 53 “when they have lined their coats; be in” (a person's) “coat,” stand in his shoes Tw.N. IV. i. 33 ) 1. =coat of arms, or coat-armour Wiv. I. i. 17 , &c. MND. III. ii. 213 , R2 III. i. 24 , 1H4 IV. ii. 49 “a herald's coat” ; fig. Compl. 236 “spirits of richest coat.”

cobloaf.text: ‘little loafe made with a round head’ (Minsheu 1617) Troil. II. i. 41 .

cock1.text: 1 (the foll. senses occur each once) 1. weather-cock Lr. III. ii. 3 .

cock2.text: small ship's boat, cockboat Lr. IV. vi. 20 .

cock3.text: perversion of ‘God’ in oaths Shr. IV. i. 121 “Cock's passion,” Ham. IV. v. 62 “By Cock” ; also cock and pie Wiv. I. i. 319 , in which ‘pie’ is commonly taken to be the word meaning ‘directory of divine service’.

cockatrice.text: =BASILISK 1, Rom. III. ii. 47 “the deathdarting eye of cockatrice.”

cockle1.text: prob. darnel, Lolium temulentum (the ‘tares’ of Matthew xiii. 25 ) LLL. IV. iii. 383 “Sow'd cockle reap'd no corn” ; fig. Cor. III. i. 69 “The cockle of rebellion.”

cockle2.text: applied to any bivalve shell, esp. that of the scallop Shr. IV. iii. 66 , Per. IV. iv. 2 “Sail seas in c-s; cockle hat,” hat with a scallop-shell stuck in it, worn by pilgrims as a sign of their having been to the shrine of St. James of Compostella in Spain Ham. IV. v. 25 (quoting an old ballad).

cockled.text: having a shell (S.) LLL. IV. iii. 338 “cockled snails.”

cockney.text: effeminate or foppish fellow Tw.N. IV. i. 15 “I am afraid this great lubber, the world, will prove a cockney” ; squeamish woman Lr. II. iv. 123 .

cockpit.text: properly, enclosed place for fightingcocks, transf. applied to a theatre H5 Prol. 11

codling.text: immature or half-grown apple Tw.N. I. v. 168 “a when 'tis almost an apple.”

coffin.text: pie-crust Tit. V. ii. 189 “of the paste a I will rear.” Cf. CUSTARD-COFFIN.

cog.text: (1, 2 common Eliz.; 3 not pre-S.) 1. to employ fraud or deceit, cheat Ado V. i. 95 , LLL. V. ii. 236 , R3 I. iii. 48 , Tim. V. i. 100 , Oth. IV. ii. 132 .

cohere.text: to agree (“with”) Meas. II. i. 11 , Tw.N. V. i. 262 ; so coherence, agreement 2H4 V. i. 72 ; coherent, in accordance All'sW. III. vii. 39 .

cohort.text: band of soldiers Lr. I. ii. 167 (Qq).

coign.text: corner-stone Cor. V. iv. 1 (Ff “Coin”), Per. III. Prol. 17 ; “ of vantage,” position (properly, a projecting corner) affording facility for observation or action Mac. I. vi. 7 .

coil.text: （“kept a coil” * , in F2 “acoyle,” bustled about, pestered All'sW. II. i. 27 : see A 3 3) 1. noise, disturbance Err. III. i. 48 .

coistrel.text: knave, base fellow Tw.N. I. iii. 4 1 , (F1 “Coystrill”), Per. IV. vi. 181 (Qq1 2 3 “custerell”).

cold1.text: coldness H8 IV. ii. 98 “of an earthy cold.”

cold2.text: adj. (5 the meaning is somewhat doubtful) 1. deliberate, cool 2H4 III. ii. 136 “a soldier,” V. ii. 98 “ considerance,” Cym. II. iii. 2 “the most coldest” [man] “that ever turned up ace.”

coldly.text: calmly, tranquilly, coolly Err. V. i. 273 , Ado III. ii. 134 , John II. i. 53 “We coldly pause for thee,” Rom. III. i. 57 ; lightly, with indifference Ham. IV. iii. 65 .

collateral.text: indirect All'sW. I. i. 100 , Ham IV. v. 206 .

collect.text: to gather (information), deduce, infer 2H6 III. i. 35 , H8 I. ii. 130 , III. ii. 295 “the articles Collected from his life.”

collection.text: inference, deduction Ham. IV. v. 9 , V. ii. 199 , Cym. V. v. 433 “I can Make no of it.”

collied.text: blackened, darkened MND. I. i. 145 “the night,” Oth. II. iii. 208 “my best judgement ” (Qq “coold”).

collop.text: slice of meat; applied to offspring (16th c. use) Wint. I. ii. 138 , 1H6 V. iv. 18 .

coloquintida.text: the colocynth or bitter-apple, Citrullus Colocynthis, which furnishes a purgative drug Oth. I. iii. 356 .

colour1.text: sb. (after the literal sense and sense 1, 4 is the most freq. in S.; the word easily lends itself to quibbling; of doubtful place is All'sW. II. v. 65 “holds not colour with” =is not in keeping with) 1. pl. military ensigns (freq.); phr. “fear no c-s,” fear no enemy, have no fear Tw.N. I. v. 6 , 2H4 V. v. 94 ; “under her colours,” in her party, led by her Cym. I. iv. 21 .

colour2.text: vb. (2 cf. COLOUR sb. 4) 1. to dye Shr. I. i. 211 , IV. i. 137 , Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 49, Cym. V. i. 2 .

colt1.text: young inexperienced fellow Mer.V. I. ii. 43 .

colt2.text: to befool 1H4 II. ii. 43 . ∥ In use 1580- 1620

combat.text: always = fight between two, duel, e.g. Ham. I. i. 84 ; “single combat” 1H6 I. ii. 95 , 2H6 I. iii. 212 , “personal combat” Ant. IV. i. 3 .

combination.text: agreement, treaty, alliance (S.) Tw.N. V. i. 395 , H8 I. i. 169 “The articles o' the combination,” Ham. III. iv. 60 .

combined.text: tied, bound (S.) Meas. IV. iii. 153 “combined by a sacred vow” ; cf. AYL. V. iv. 157 “Thy faith my fancy to thee doth combine.”

come.text: (1 is frequent=come to be) 1. to become MND. II. ii. 92 , Ham. V. i. 170 “How came he mad?”

comeddle.text: to mix Ham. III. ii. 74 (Qq “com(m)edled,” Ff “co-mingled,” mod. edd. “commingled”).

comfort1.text: used as interj. (S.)=cheer up, take heart Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 854 “, good ,” John III. iv. 4 , R2 III. ii. 75 , R3 II. ii. 89 , Ant. III. vi. 89 “Best of !;—what ?” =what cheer? Meas. III. i. 53 , R2 II. i. 72 ;—“have , be of (good) ,” be of good cheer Tp. I. ii. 492 , Tw.N. III. iv. 375 , John V. iii. 9 , V. vii. 25 .

comfort2.text: vb. (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. to minister relief to, relieve LLL. IV. ii. 44 , Wint. II. iii. 56 “in c-ing your evils,” Tit. II. iii. 209 “comfort me, and help me out,” Lr. III. v. 21 .

comfortable.text: (2 was a common Eliz. sense) 1. affording comfort, consolation, or help All'sW. I. i. 87 “Be to my mother,” Rom. V. iii. 148 , Lr. I. iv. 330 “kind and ” ; of things Tw.N. I. v. 240 , R2 II. ii. 76 “ words,” Lr. II. ii. 171 , Lucr. 164 “No star.”

comfortless.text: (1 now rare of persons; 2 obs.) 1. unconsoled, inconsolable Err. V. i. 80 “grim and despair,” H8 II. iii. 105 “The queen is comfortless.”

comma.text: (1 term of rhetoric; 2 fig. for punctuation) 1. short member of a sentence (fig.) Tim. I. i. 49 * “no levell'd malice Infects one comma in the course I hold.”

command1.text: “upon command,” (1) at a given order R3 I. iv. 202 “;” (2) at pleasure AYL. II. vii. 125 .

command2.text: vb. (1 is freq.; 2 is rare) 1. to demand with authority 2H6 V. i. 49 , Cym. I. v. 8 .

commanded.text: entrusted with command Cor. I. i. 268 “to be Under Cominius.”

commandment.text: (old edd. usually “commandement” or “command'ment,” representing four-syll. pronunciation, which still survives dial.) 1. “at my, your ,” at my, your service Mer.V. II. ii. 32 , 2H4 V. iii. 141 ; “at ,” at pleasure 2H4 III. ii. 27 .

commence.text: 2H4 IV. iii. 126 “learning, a mere hoard of gold kept by a devil till sack c-s it and sets it in act and use” ; allusion probably to the commencement at Cambridge University, i.e. proceeding to the degree of Master or Doctor and so qualifying to teach.

commend1.text: sb. (1 late examples of this sense) 1. commendation Mer.V. II. ix. 90 * “commends and courteous breath,” Per. II. ii. 49 “speak in his just ”

commend2.text: vb. (senses 2, 3, and the sense ‘to praise’ are the most freq.) 1. to deliver, commit, entrust LLL. III. i. 177 “to her white hand see thou do This seal'd-up counsel,” R2 III. iii. 116 , H8 V. i. 17 , Mac. I. vii. 11 , Lr. II. iv. 28 , Lucr. 436 .

commendation.text: pl. greetings, remembrances Gent. I. iii. 53 .

comment1.text: mental observation, pondering John V. vii. 4 ; Ham. III. ii. 84 * “the very comment of thy soul,” thy most intense observation (Ff “my”).

comment2.text: vb. (2 cf. COMMENT sb.) 1. to discourse or expatiate “upon” Gent. II. i. 44 “a physician to on your malady,” Sonn. xv. 4 .

commerce.text: intercourse Tw.N. III. iv. 194 , Ham. III. i. 110 . ∥ The orig. stressing is “comme'rce,” e.g. Troil. III. iii. 206 .

commission.text: (2 the commonest use in S.) 1. order, mandate Meas. I. i. 13 , Lr. V. iii. 254 .

commit.text: to sin Gent. V. iv. 77 ; spec. to commit adultery Lr. III. iv. 80 .

commixture.text: (twice only; 2 peculiar to S.) 1. compound 3H6 II. vi. 6 “thy tough commixtures.”

commodity.text: (sense ‘wares, merchandise’ is freq.) 1. convenience Mer.V. III. iii. 27 , Wint. III. ii. 94 * .

common.text: vb. (early variant of COMMUNE) 1. to share, take part Ham. IV. v. 202 “I must with your grief” (F1 “common,” Qq Ff2 3 4 and mod. edd. “commune”).

common1.text: sb. (3 (i) not pre-S.; 3 (ii) only S.) 1. common people, commonalty Cor. I. i. 157 .

common2.text: adj. (all the foll. are common uses) 1. belonging equally to more than one, or to all mankind 1H4 II. i. 104 “homo is a name to all men” (cf. the grammatical term ‘common noun’), Mac. III. i. 69 “the common enemy of man.”

commoner.text: prostitute All'sW. V. iii. 196 , Oth. IV. ii. 72 .

commotion.text: (1 occurs four times, 2 thrice) 1. tumult, sedition 2H6 III. i. 358 .

commune.text: (cf. COMMON vb.) 1. to converse Wint. II. i. 161 (“commu'ne”).

compact1.text: ppl. a. 1 [Latin ‘compact-’ from ‘compingere’ to fasten together] 1. knit together Lr. I. ii. 7 .

compact2.headword: compact ppl. a. 2 [Latin ‘compact-’ from ‘compacisci’ to make a compact]
compact2.text: leagued Meas. V. i. 236 , Lr. II. ii. 125 (Ff; Qq “coniunct”).

compact3.text: vb. (2 peculiar to S.) 1. to combine, incorporate Lucr. 530 .

companion1.text: used as term of contempt=fellow Err. IV. iv. 63 , All'sW. V. iii. 252 , 2H4 II. iv. 130 “scurvy companion,” 2H6 IV. x. 33 , Cæs. IV. iii. 137 , Oth. IV. ii. 141 .

companion2.text: to make a companion Ant. I. ii. 31 .

companionship.text: Tim. I. i. 251 “All of companionship,” all belonging to one party.

company1.text: sb. (S. is earliest for the application to a ship's crew) 1. “from company,” alone, in solitude 1H6 V. v. 100 ; “for company,” by way of sociableness Shr. IV. i. 180 .

comparative.text: adj. 1. =‘full of comparisons’ (cf. COMPARISON 2) 1H4 I. ii. 90 “comparative, rascalliest, sweet young prince.”

compare1.text: comparison Tw.N. II. iv. 103 , Sonn. xxi. 5 .

compare2.text: vb. (2 cf. ‘Art stryving to compayre With Nature’, Spenser) 1. to draw comparisons R2 II. i. 186 .

comparison.text: (1 perhaps there is a suggestion of ‘caparison’ intended) 1. pl. Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 26 “his gay comparisons,” advantages which appear when we are compared.

compass.text: (sense ‘range of voice’ occurs Ham. III. ii. 391 ) 1. circle, circumference Gent. II. vii. 51 “What will you wear your farthingale?,” Wiv. V. v. 72 , R2 II. i. 101 , 3H6 IV. iii. 46 “the of her” [Fortune's] “wheel.”

compassed.text: round, arched Shr. IV. iii. 139 “a small cape,” Ven. 272 “his crest;— window,” semicircular bay-window Troil. I. ii. 118 .

compassionate.text: (a) feeling pity for oneself, (b) sorrowfully lamenting, (c) piteous R2 I. iii. 174 * .

compeer.text: to rival, equal Lr. V. iii. 70 “he compeers the best.”

compel.text: to take or get by force, extort All'sW. IV. iii. 361 “I'd compel it of you,” 2H4 IV. i. 147 , H5 III. vi. 119 , H8 I. ii. 57 .

compelled.text: enforced, unsought, involuntary Meas. II. iv. 58 “Our co'mpell'd sins,” H8 II. iii. 87 “This co'mpell'd fortune,” Ham. IV. vi. 18 “a valour,” Lucr. 1708 “this compe'lled stain.”

competent.text: sufficient, adequate Tw.N. III. iv. 273 , Ham. I. i. 90 .

competitor.text: associate, partner Gent. II. vi. 35 , R3 IV. iv. 505 “more competitors Flock to the rebels,” Ant. V. i. 42 . ∥ This is the commoner S. use.

compile.text: to compose as an original work LLL. IV. iii. 134 “Did never sonnet for her sake compile,” Sonn. lxxviii. 9 .

complain.text: = ‘complain of’, bewail R2 III. iv. 18 , Lucr. 1839 “that late complain'd Her wrongs to us.”

complement.text: that which goes to ‘complete’ the character of a gentleman in regard to external appearance or demeanour WIV. IV. ii. 5 , LLL. I. i. 167 “A man of c-s,” III. i, 24 , H5 II. ii. 134 “deck'd in modest ” (=unostentatious demeanour), Rom. II. iv. 21 “captain of c-s,” Oth. I. i. 63 “ extern.” ∥ Mod. edd. fluctuate between “complement” and “compliment” in some of these passages.

complete.text: (stressed “co'mplete” in the attributive and “comple'te” in the predicative position; Ham. I. iv. 52 “in co'mplete steel” =in full armour, Troil. IV. i. 27 “A thousand co'mplete courses of the sun,” 3H6 II. v. 26 “make the hour full comple'te” ) 1. perfect in nature or quality, perfectly constituted Meas. I. iii. 3 “a complete bosom.”

complexion.text: (3 orig. as showing the bodily temperament) 1. bodily habit or constitution, orig. supposed to be constituted by the four ‘humours’ Ham. V. ii. 103 “very sultry and hot for my complexion.”

complice.text: confederate, comrade R2 II. iii. 165 , 2H4 I. i. 163 . (Cf. ACCOMPLICE.)

daff.text: (2 “daff'd the world aside” 1H4 IV. i. 96 has been much imitated by modern writers) 1. to put off (clothes, armour) Ant. IV. iv. 13 “till we do please To daff't for our repose,” Compl. 297 “my white stole . . . I daff'”

dagger.text: (S. is earliest for fig. uses exemplified in Mer.V. III. i. 118 , Mac. II. iii. 147 , Ham. III. ii. 421 ) 1. “rapier” (or “sword) and ,” method of fighting introduced towards the end of the 16th cent. and taking the place of sword-and-buckler fighting Wiv. I. i. 297 , Ham. V. ii. 152 ; attrib. Meas. IV. iii. 16 “the rapier and dagger man.”

dainty1.text: sb. (2 common phrase 1550-1650) 1. daintiness, fastidiousness 2H4 IV. i. 198 “weary Of ”

dainty2.text: “ of,” scrupulous or particular about Troil. I. iii. 145 , Mac. II. iii. 151 “let us not be of leave-taking.”

daisied.text: full of daisies Cym. IV. ii. 398 .

dally.text: to trifle (“with”) Shr. IV. iv. 68 , Tw.N. II. iv. 47 , III. i. 16 .

damask.text: the colour of the “ rose” ( Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 222), = (1) blush-red colour Cor. II. i. 235 “the war of white and in Their . . . cheeks” ; (2) striped red and white AYL. III. v. 123 “mingled ” ;—adj. of such colour (in both applications) LLL. V. ii. 297 “their sweet commixture,” Tw.N. II. iv. 114 “her cheek,” Pilgr. vii. 5 [ 89 ] “A lily pale, with dye to grace her.”

dame.text: (3 by far the most freq. use) 1. mistress (of a household, &c.) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 57 “Both and servant,” Lucr. 1034 .

damnation.text: abusively addressed to a person Rom. III. v. 235 “Ancient ! O most wicked fiend!”

damp.text: vapour, fog, mist All'sW. II. i. 166 , Ant. IV. ix. 13 , Lucr. 778 “With rotten damps ravish the morning air.”

dance.text: “ bare-foot,” said of an elder sister when a younger one is married before her Shr. II. i. 33 .

danger.text: (2 these are late exx. of this sense) 1. power to harm; reach or range (as of a weapon): “within” (a person's) “,” John IV. iii. 84 “Nor tempt the of my true defence” ; in his power, at his mercy Mer.V. IV. i. 180 ; so “in, into” or “out of the of” Tw.N. V. i. 88 , Mac. III. ii. 15 , Ham. I. iii. 35 “Out of the shot and of desire.”

dangerous.text: threatening Ado V. i. 97 “ words,” 1H4 V. i. 69 “ countenance.”

dankish.text: dank, humid Err. V. i. 248 “ vault.”

dare.text: defiance Ant. I. ii. 197 “Pompeius Hath given the to Cæsar” ; daring, boldness 1H4 IV. i. 78 “It lends . . . A larger to our great enterprise.”

dare1.text: not pre-Eliz.) 1. to go so far as “to,” be willing “to” Mer.V. V. i. 251 “I be bound,” H8 V. i. 17 “I love you And durst commend a secret to your ear” ; phr. “dares” or “durst better”=would rather All'sW. III. vi. 95 , H8 III. ii. 254 .

dare2.headword: dare vb. 2 (of different origin from vb. 1 )
dare2.text: to daze, dazzle, or fascinate (larks) and so entrap them, e.g. by means of a piece of scarlet cloth and a looking-glass H8 III. ii. 283 “And us with his cap like larks” (ref. to the cardinal's biretta); so H5 IV. ii. 36 “dare the field” (=make the prey crouch).

dark1.text: S. is the earliest authority (in the mod. period) for the senses ‘iniquitous, evil’ ( R2 I. i. 169 ), ‘gloomy, dismal’ ( Mer.V. V. i. 87 , Rom. III. v. 36 ), ‘frowning, clouded’ ( Ven. 182 ), ‘indistinct, indiscernible’ ( Tp. I. ii. 50 , Ven. 760 ), ‘concealed, secret’ ( Lr. I. i. 38 ); also for “ house, room,” formerly considered a proper place of confinement for madmen Err. IV. iv. 96 , AYL. III. ii. 427 ; similarly “keep him ,” keep him confined in a dark room All'sW. IV. i. 101 .

dark2.text: to obscure, eclipse Per. IV. Gower 35 .

dark3.text: adv. = DARKLING AYL. III. v. 39 “go to bed.”

darken.text: to deprive of lustre or renown, eclipse Cor. II. i. 278 , Ant. III. i. 24 “gain which d-s him.”

darking.text: eclipse Troil. V. viii. 7 “ of the sun.”

darkling.text: in the dark MND. II. ii. 86 , Lr. I. iv. 240 .

darkly.text: S. is earliest for ‘secretly’ ( Meas. III. ii. 192 , All'sW. IV. iii. 14 ), ‘gloomily, frowningly’ ( Tw.N. II. i. 4 “My stars shine over me,” R3 I. iv. 178 “How darkly . . . dost thou speak!” ).

darkness.text: death Meas. III. i. 82 . ∥ Cf. the biblical phrase ‘darkness and the shadow of death’.

darnel.text: a grass, Lolium temulentum, a weed injurious to growing corn Lr. IV. iv. 5 . ∥ In 1H6 III. ii. 44 there is possibly a ref. to the belief that ‘Darnell hurteth the eies and maketh them dim, if it happen in corne’ (Gerarde).

darraign.text: to set in array 3H6 II. ii. 72 .

darting.text: shooting darts Ant. III. i. 1 “ Parthia” (ref. to the practice of Parthian horsemen, who retreated shooting flights of arrows backward upon the enemy).

dash1.text: sb. (1 common Eliz. and Caroline phr.) 1. “at first dash,” from the first 1H6 I. ii. 71 .

dash2.text: vb. (physical senses also occur) 1. to destroy, frustrate LLL. V. ii. 463 , 3H6 II. i. 118 .

date.text: (1 the prevailing S. meaning) 1. duration, term of existence Err. I. ii. 41 , MND. III. ii. 373 “whose till death shall never end,” John IV. iii. 106 , R3 IV. iv. 255 , Rom. I. iv. 3 , 109 , Sonn. cxxiii. 5 “Our dates are brief.”

dateless.text: without term, endless, limitless R2 I. iii. 151 “The limit,” Rom. V. iii. 115 , Sonn. xxx. 6 , cliii. 6

daub.text: to cover with a specious exterior R3 III. v. 28 “d-'d his vice with show of virtue” ; so “ it,” dissemble, pretend Lr. IV. i. 52 (Qq “dance it”).

daughter.text: rhymes with ‘after’ in Shr. I. i. 243 .

daw.text: type of foolishness 1H6 II. iv. 18 , Cor. IV. v. 48 .

dawning.text: morning Lr. II. ii. 1 “Good ” (Qq “euen); bird of dawning,” the cock Ham. I. i. 160 .

day.text: (3 the lit. sense of ‘daylight’ occurs in comparisons 2H4 IV. iv. 32 “Open as day,” 2H6 II. i. 107 “clear as day” ) 1. phrases: “How's the ?,” what time is it? Tp. V. i. 3 ; so “by the ” = o'clock 1H4 II. i. 2 ; “take no longer d-s,” be no longer about it Tit. IV. ii. 167 ; “The duty of the ,” morning salutation Cym. III. v. 32 , also “time of day” (freq.).

dazzle.text: (of the eyes) to lose distinctness of vision, esp. from gazing at too bright light LLL. I. i. 82 , 3H6 II. i. 25 “ mine eyes, or do I see three suns?,” Tit. III. ii. 85 , Ven. 1064 . ∥ In Gent. II. iv. 211 “d-d” is 3 syll. (F1 “dazel'd,” Ff2—4 “dazel'd so”).

dead.text: （“a dead man” = ‘a man marked out for death’ occurs once Wiv. IV. ii. 45 ） 1. “is dead” = has died Ado V. i. 254 , H5 V. i. 86 , Rom. V. iii. 210 “my wife is dead to-night,” Lr. V. iii. 294 .

deadly1.text: death-like, deathly Err. IV. iv. 95 “their pale and looks,” Tw.N. I. v. 286 “such a life,” Lr. V. iii. 292 “cheerless, dark, and deadly.”

deadly2.text: = mortally (in various uses) Ado V. i. 182 “hate him ,” R3 III. vii. 26 “ pale,” Troil. V. v. 12 “deadly hurt,” Cor. II. i. 68 “they lie deadly.”

deal1.text: “no ,” not at all Sonn. Music iii. 27

deal2.text: to act (freq.) John V. ii. 22 ; phr. “ upon,” Pilgr. set to work upon, proceed against R3 IV. ii. 73 ; “ in,” (1) proceed or act in (a matter) Ado IV. i. 249 , V. i. 101 ; (2) have to do with Tp. V. i. 271 , 1H6 V. v. 56 , 3H6 III. ii. 154 ; “dealt on lieutenantry,” fought by proxy Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 39

dealing.text: “in plain ,” putting it plainly Meas. II. i. 270 .

dear1.text: adj. 1 (2, 4, and 5 peculiar to S.; many instances of “ ” usu. referred to this word belong to the next) 1. precious, valuable, worthy Mer.V. I. i. 62 “Your worth is very in my regard,” R2 I. iii. 156 , 1H4 IV. iv. 31 “ men Of estimation,” Cor. I. vi. 72 , II. iii. 102 , Sonn. xxx. 4 “wail my times' waste.”

dear2.text: adj. 2 (of different origin from DEAR adj. 1 , but undoubtedly associated with it in use): hard, grievous, dire Tp. II. i. 142 , LLL. V. ii. 872 , All'sW. IV. v. 11 , Tw.N. V. i. 75 , John I. i. 257 “my offence,” R2 I. iii. 151 “thy exile,” R3 I. iv. 219 , Tim. IV. iii. 384 , V. i. 233 “In our peril,” Oth. I. iii. 261 , Sonn. xxxvii. 3 “fortune's d-est spite.” ∥ Cf. ‘turnd to disadvantage deare,’ Spenser.

dear3.text: = dearly (i) with the verbs ‘aby’, ‘buy’, ‘cost’, (ii) with ‘love’; occas. with ‘grieve’ Cæs. III. i. 196 “grieve thee dearer.”

dearly.text: (sense 3 is purely S.) 1. richly, finely Troil. III. iii. 96 “how ever parted” (= richly gifted), Cym. II. ii. 18 .

dearth.text: costliness, high value Ham. V. ii. 124 .

death.headword: death (first in S. as an exclamation H8 I. iii. 13 ) 1. “the death”
death.text: a common idiom in earlier English Err. I. i. 146 “adjudged to the ,” MND. I. i. 65 , R2 III. i. 29 , H5 IV. i. 184 , R3 I. ii. 179 “beg the ” ; also in phrases still current “die the , to the , be the death of.”

deathful.text: deadly, mortal 2H6 III. ii. 404 “a wound” ; so death-like Per. I. i. 29 “death-like dragons.”

debase.text: to degrade the dignity of R2 III. iii. 190 .

debate1.text: contention, quarrel MND. II. i. 116 , Sonn. lxxxix. 13 . ∥ Not used = argument, discussion.

debate2.text: to fight Lucr. 1421 “ with angry swords,” Sonn. xv. 11 ; with “it” All'sW. I. ii. 75 * “nature and sickness Debate it at their leisure.” ∥ The sense of ‘discuss’ occurs.

debatement.text: deliberation, consideration Meas. V. i. 100 , Ham. V. ii. 45 .

debile.text: weak All'sW. II. iii. 40 , Cor. I. ix. 48 “some debile wretch.”

debitor.text: statement of account, accountbook Oth. I. i. 31 , Cym. V. iv. 171 .

deboshed.text: (2 a 17th cent. sense) 1. corrupted, depraved Tp. III. ii. 31 , All'sW. II. iii. 145 , Lr. I. iv. 265 (Ff “debosh'd,” Qq “deboyst”).

decay1.text: sb. (1 a common 16th c. use) 1. downfall, destruction, ruin John IV. iii. 154 “The imminent of wrested pomp,” 2H6 III. i. 194 , R3 IV. iv. 410 , Lucr. 516 “thy life's ” ; also, cause of ruin Sonn. lxxx. 14 “my love was my decay.”

decay2.text: vb. (cf. prec. word) 1. to perish, be destroyed 1H6 I. i. 34 , Ant. II. i. 4 , Lucr. 23 , Sonn. lxxi. 12 .

deceivable.text: deceitful, deceptive Tw.N. IV. iii. 21 , R2 II. iii. 84 .

deceive.text: (rare and obs. uses) 1. to be false to, betray 1H4 V. i. 11 .

deceptious.text: delusive Troil. V. ii. 120 “As if those organs had deceptious functions.”

decimation.text: selection of every tenth man for punishment by death Tim. V. iv. 31 .

decipher.text: (both S. senses are obs.) 1. to reveal, detect 1H6 IV. i. 184 , Tit. IV. ii. 8 “both decipher'd . . . For villains, mark'd with rape.”

deck1.text: pack of cards 3H6 V. i. 44 . ∥ Since 17th c. dial. (chiefly midland).

declension.text: falling away from a high standard 2H4 II. ii. 193 (Q “descension”), R3 III. vii. 188 ; decline, deterioration Ham. II. ii. 149 “and by this Into the madness.”

decline.text: (the sense of ‘fall off in vigour, vitality, &c.’ occurs, cf. DECLINED) 1. to incline or lean “to” Err. III. ii. 44 .

declined.text: fallen, decayed, deteriorated, enfeebled Troil. III. iii. 76 , IV. v. 188 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 27 (‘decayed in fortune’); similarly declining (Qq) Lr. I. ii. 80 (Ff “declin'd”).

decoct.text: to warm up (S.) H5 III. v. 20 .

dedicate.text: dedicated Meas. II. ii. 154 “whose minds are To nothing temporal,” 2H6 V. ii. 37 “dedicate to war.”

dedicated.text: Tim. IV. ii. 13 “A beggar to the air” (= ‘a beggar devoted by fortune to a homeless life’); Sonn. lxxxii. 3 “The words” (=words of dedication, dedicatory epistle).

deed.text: performance (“of” what is promised) All'sW. III. vi. 101 , Tim. V. i. 29 , Ham. I. iii. 27 ; Lr. I. i. 73 “my very deed of love” (=what my love really is).

deem.text: thought Troil. IV. iv. 59 “what wicked is this?”

deep1.text: depths in “ of night” Wiv. IV. iv. 41 , Cæs. IV. iii. 225 .

deep2.text: adj. (besides the sense of ‘intense’ the following are the chief fig. uses) 1. grave, serious, weighty 1H4 I. iii. 190 “matter and dangerous,” R3 III. VII. 66 “ designs,” IV. ii. 118 “my service” (Qq “true”), Mac. I. iii. 126 “In d-est consequence,” Cym. II. iii. 96 ; grievous, heinous R3 II. ii. 28 “ vice,” Tim. III. iv. 31 , Mac. I. vii. 20 , Lucr. 701 .

deeply.text: (3 freq., with various applications) 1. profoundly, thoroughly Tw.N. ii. v. 48 ; with profound craft Shr. IV. iv. 42 “dissemble deeply.”

deer.text: in Lr. III. iv. 142 “mice and rats and such small deer,” a line from the old romance of Sir Bevis of Hampton is echoed, where ‘deer’ has the old sense of ‘beasts’, ‘animals’; but S. no doubt associated the word with the object of the chase.

deface.text: to efface, obliterate, cancel Mer.V. III. ii. 300 “deface the bond,” 2H6 I. i. 103 .

default.text: (1 phrase peculiar to S.) 1. lack All'sW. II. iii. 241 “in the ” (=at need).

defeat1.text: destruction, ruin Ado IV. i. 47 “defeat of her virginity,” Ham. II. ii. 606 [ 598 ].

defeat2.text: vb. (1 common 1435-1635; 2 rare sense) 1. to undo, destroy, ruin Tim. IV. iii. 164 , Ham. I. ii. 10 “a d-ed joy,” Oth. IV. ii. 160 “may my life.”

defect.text: defectiveness, faultiness Mac. II. i. 18 , Sonn. cxlix. 11 “all my best doth worship thy ”

defence.text: (2 a 17th cent. use, now rare) 1. capacity of defending itself 3H6 V. i. 64 * .

defend.text: (1 chiefly in “God defend!”) 1. to forbid Ado II. i. 99 , IV. ii. 22 , 1H4 IV. iii. 38 , Oth. I. iii. 268 , Ant. III. iii. 43 “Isis else defend!”

defensible.text: able to make a defence 2H4 II. iii. 38 , H5 III. iii. 50 .

defiance.text: (1 the usual S. sense; 2 only S.) 1. challenge to fight R2 III. iii. 130 , Cæs. V. i. 64 .

deficient.text: failing, fainting Lr. IV. vi. 24 “the deficient sight.” ∥ Not pre-Eliz. in any sense.

defile.text: used with a quibble on ‘pitch’ All'sW. IV. iv. 24 “D-s the pitchy night,” Tim. I. ii. 234 ; cf. Ado III. iii. 61 .

definite.text: resolute Cym. I. vi. 43 ; so definitive Meas. V. i. 428 .

defunct.text: dead H5 IV. i. 21 ; (?) discharged, laid aside Oth. I. iii. 266 “In my (me†) defunct and proper satisfaction.”

defy.text: (1, 2, and sense ‘set at defiance’ are about equally common in S.) 1. to challenge, esp. to a fight Err. V. i. 32 , John II. i. 406 , H5 II. i. 76 , Ant. II. ii. 164 .

deign.text: to condescend to take, accept without grudging Gent. I. i. 162 , Ant. I. iv. 63 .

deject.text: downcast, dejected Troil. II. ii. 50 “Make . . . lustihood ,” Ham. III. i. 164 “ and wretched.”

dejected.text: abased, humbled Wiv. V. v. 175 , Lr. IV. i. 3 (= thing most humbled by fortune), Per. II. ii. 46 “the state wherein he is.”

delation.text: accusation Oth. III. iii. 123 (Q1 “denotements,” Ff Qq2 3 “dilations”).

delicate2.text: (often more than one sense is implied) 1. delightful, pleasant Wint. III. i. 1 “The climate's ,” Mac. I. vi. 10 , Oth. I. iii. 360 , Ant. II. vii. 115 “delicate Lethe.”

delight.text: charm, delightfulness LLL. V. ii. 905 , Rom. I. iii. 82 , Ven. 78 , Sonn. xci. 11 , cii. 12 “sweets grown common lose their dear ” ∥ The senses ‘pleasure’ and ‘source of pleasure’ are the usual; “of ”=delightful, e.g. Sonn. xcviii. 11 .

delighted.text: endowed with or affording delight, delightful Meas. III. i. 119 , Oth. I. iii. 291 “ beauty,” Cym. V. iv. 102 “to make my gift, The more delay'd, delighted.”

deliver.text: (3 weakening of the legal use ‘hand over’) 1. to bring forth (offspring), lit. and fig., chiefly passive Err. V. i. 405 , LLL. IV. ii. 72 , Oth. I. iii. 378 , Per. V. i. 107 .

deliverance.text: (sense ‘release’ is used 5 times) 1. bringing forth of offspring Cym. V. v. 371 .

demand.text: sb. and vb. are often used simply = question, without any idea of authoritative or peremptory asking.

demean.text: refl. to behave oneself Err. IV. iii. 83 , V. i. 88 “he d-'d himself rough,” 2H6 I. i. 189 , 3H6 I. iv. 7 .

demerit.text: (1 the orig. sense in English) 1. pl. merits, deserts Cor. I. i. 278 , Oth. I. ii. 22 .

demesne.text: (old edd. “demeane”) 1. pl. lands, estates Rom. III. v. 182 “Of fair d-”

demise.text: to convey, transmit R3 IV. iv. 248 .

demon.text: (old edd. “Dæmon”) 1. attendant or ministering spirit Ant. II. iii. 19 “Thy demon—that's thy spirit which keeps thee.”

demonstrate.text: (stressed “de'monstrate, demo'nstrate”） 1. to exhibit, set forth, manifest, show AYL. III. ii. 405 , H5 IV. ii. 54 , Ham. I. i. 124 , Oth. I. i. 61 .

demure1.text: grave, sober H8 I. ii. 167 , Lucr. 1219 .

demure2.text: (?) to look demurely Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 29

demurely.text: gravely Mer.V. II. ii. 207 ; with subdued sound Ant. IV. ix. 31 .

denay2.text: old form of DENY, 2H6 I. iii. 107 .

denier.text: French coin, the twelfth of a sou; used as the type of a very small sum Shr. Ind. i. 9 , 1H4 III. iii. 90 , R3 I. ii. 253 “My dukedom to a beggarly denier.”

denote.text: (not pre-S.) is used in the ordinary mod. senses.

denotement.text: indication, token Oth. II. iii. 325 (Q2; see DEVOTEMENT), III. iii. 123 (Q1; others “delations, dilations”).

denounce.text: to proclaim, declare John III. i. 319 “ a curse,” III. iv. 159 “denouncing vengeance,” Ant. III. vii. 5 [war] “denounc'd against us.”

deny.text: (see also DENAY) 1. to refuse “to” do something Shr. II. i. 180 “If she deny to wed.”

depart1.text: departure Gent. V. iv. 97 , 2H6 I. i. 2 , 3H6 IV. i. 92 ; death 3H6 II. i. 110 .

depart2.text: vb. (2 this sense is now only used in ‘depart this life’) 1. to take leave of one another Tim. I. i. 263 “Ere we depart,” Cym. I. i. 108 “The loathness to depart.”

departing.text: separation 3H6 II. vi. 43 “life and death's departing.”

depend.text: （‘rest or hang “upon”’, and ‘rely “upon”’ are the commonest senses) 1. to lean Cym. II. iv. 91 “Cupids . . . D-ing on their brands.”

deplore.text: to tell with grief Tw.N. III. i. 176 .

depose.text: (the foll. are the rarer uses) 1. to deprive a person of (something) R2 IV. i. 192 “You may my glories and my state depose.”

depositary.text: one with whom anything is lodged in trust Lr. II. iv. 254 .

depravation.text: defamation, detraction Troil. V. ii. 129 “stubborn critics, apt . . . For ”

deprave.text: to vilify, detract Tim. I. ii. 147 ; intr. Ado V. i. 95 “deprave and slander.”

deprive.text: to take away (a possession) Ham. I. iv. 73 “ your sovereignty of reason,” Lucr. 1186 “to dishonour'd life,” 1752

deputation.text: appointment to act on behalf of another, office of deputy Meas. I. i. 20 , 1H4 IV. i. 32 , IV. iii. 87 “in ” (=as deputies, as vice-regents), Troil. I. iii. 152 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 74 (Ff “disputation”).

depute.text: to appoint Oth. IV. i. 249 , IV. ii. 226 .

deputed.text: sword delivered as an emblem of office or dignity Meas. II. ii. 60 .

deputy.text: Lord Lieutenant (of Ireland) H8 III. ii. 261 ; “ of the ward,” member of the Common Council of London, who acts instead of an alderman in his absence 1H4 III. iii. 129 , 2H4 II. iv. 91 .

deracinate.text: to uproot H5 V. ii. 47 , Troil. I. iii. 99 .

derision.text: 4 syll. at end of line MND. III. ii. 197 , 370

derive.text: the sense ‘gain, obtain’ is the most freq., of which somewhat exceptional uses are in 2H4 I. i. 23 “How is this derived?” = (‘Whence does thy information come?’, Lr. I. ii. 90 ) 1. refl. to pass by descent, be descended or inherited Ado IV. i. 137 “This shame d-s itself from unknown loins,” 2H4 IV. v. 42 “this imperial crown, Which . . . Derives itself to me.”

dern.text: dark, wild, drear Lr. III. vii. 63 “that dern time” (Ff “sterne”), Per. III. Gower 15 .

derogate1.text: to act in a way derogatory to one's position Cym. II. i. 50 ; in line 59 (quibblingly) degenerate.

descant1.text: melody sung extempore upon a plainsong, ground, or bass, to which it forms the air Gent. I. ii. 91 “you . . . mar the concord with too harsh a ” ; (hence) fig. comment R3 III. vii. 48 “on that ground I'll make a holy descant.”

descant2.text: to sing a descant or air, (hence) to ‘sing with a small, yet pleasant and shrill voice as birds doe’ (Minsheu), warble Lucr. 1134 ; (hence) to comment R3 I. i. 27 “ on mine own deformity,” Pilgr. xiv. 4 [ 184 ].

descend.text: to come down from 3H6 I. i. 74 “ my throne,” Compl. 31 “[hair] untuck'd, descended her sheav'd hat.”

descending.text: descent, lineage Per. V. i. 130 (Qq1 2 3 “discending,” Qq4 5 6 “discent,” Ff3 4 “descent”).

descent.text: (the foll. are rare S. uses) 1. that to which one descends, lowest part Lr. V. iii. 139 “To the and dust below thy foot.”

descry1.text: sight of a distant object Lr. IV. vi. 218 .

descry2.text: to reconnoitre R3 V. iii. 9 , Lr. IV. v. 13 .

desert.text: “without ,” undeservedly, without cause Gent. II. iv. 58 , Err. III. i. 112 , R3 II. i. 67 .

deserved.text: deserving, meritorious (S.) All'sW. II. i. 192 , Cor. III. i. 290 . ∥ Cf. Latin ‘meritus’.

deserving.text: (the two uses are equally freq.). 1. that which one deserves, desert, due reward Meas. V. i. 478 “[death] 'Tis my ,” Lr. V. iii. 306 , Sonn. lxxxvii. 6 .

design1.text: the sense of ‘plan, scheme’ is weakened to that of ‘purpose, aim, intention’; whence ‘thing in view, project, enterprise’ LLL. IV. i. 89 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 515 “not prepar'd For this ,” R2 I. i. 81 , Troil. II. ii. 194 , Mac. II. i. 55 “murder . . . toward his Moves like a ghost,” Ant. V. i. 43 .

design2.text: to point out, indicate R2 I. i. 203 (‘appoint which of the two combatants shall be victorious’), Ham. I. i. 94 (‘meaning borne by the article drawn up’).

designment.text: enterprise, undertaking Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 35, Oth. II. i. 22 “their designment halts.”

desire.text: (1 S. affords late exx. of this construction) 1. to request the boon or favour “of” something from (a person) MND. III. i. 189 , 197 (Qq “you of,” Ff “of you”), Mer.V. IV. i. 403 “ your Grace of pardon,” AYL. V. iv. 56 ; with “of” dropped MND. III. i. 204 “I desire you more acquaintance” (so Qq Ff1 2; Ff3 4 “your more”).

desired.text: sought after, beloved Oth. II. i. 207 .

despair.text: to be without hope of Mac. V. vii. 42 [ viii. 13 ] “Despair thy charm.”

desperate.text: reckless, utterly careless “of” Tw.N. V. i. 68 “desperate of shame and state.”

desperately.text: in despair, without hope, hopelessly Meas. IV. ii. 151 “ mortal” * (‘likely to die in a desperate state,’ J.), Lr. V. iii. 294 “And are dead.”

desperation.text: “of ,” involving thoughts of selfdestruction Tp. I. ii. 210 , Ham. I. iv. 75 .

despised.text: despicable (cf. ABHORRED) Rom. III. ii. 77 , Tim. IV. iii. 468 , Ven. 135 , Sonn. xxxvii. 9 . ∥ In Ham. III. i. 72 stressed “de'spis'd” (Ff “dispriz'd”).

despite1.text: sb. (3 the prepositional use is not pre-S.) 1. contempt, scorn, disdain Ado I. i. 245 “an obstinate heretic in the despite of beauty,” Oth. IV. ii. 116 .

despiteful.text: malicious, spiteful, cruel AYL. V. ii. 87 , All'sW. III. iv. 13 ; fig. of things Shr. IV. ii. 14 “ love!,” R3 IV. i. 36 .

detain.text: to withhold Err. II. i. 107 , R2 I. i. 90 , Lr. I. ii. 43 “I shall offend, either to or give it,” Sonn. cxxvi. 10 .

detect.text: to expose, lay bare, esp. in wrong-doing Wiv. II. ii. 329 , Meas. III. ii. 133 , AYL. III. ii. 324 , Ham. III. ii. 94 .

detention.text: withholding Tim. II. ii. 39 “the detention of . . . debts.”

determinate1.text: to fix the limits of R2 I. iii. 150 .

determinate2.text: pple. (1 legal metaphor; cf. next) 1. ended, expired Sonn. lxxxvii. 4 .

determination.text: (1 legal metaphor) 1. cessation, end Sonn. xiii. 6 .

determine.text: (the sense of ‘decide’ trans. and intr. is the usual one) 1. to put an end to 2H4 IV. v. 80 “Till his friend sickness hath d-'d me,” 1H6 IV. vi. 9 “To my d-'d time thou gav'st new date.”

detested.text: detestable (cf. ABHORRED) Tw.N. V. i. 143 , R2 II. iii. 109 , Lr. I. ii. 84 , II. iv. 220 .

device.text: （‘contrivance, plan’ is the usual sense) 1. ‘manner of thinking, cast of mind’ (Schmidt) AYL. I. i. 176 * “full of noble ,” Ven. 789 * “your in love.”

devise.text: to think Cor. I. i. 107 “the other instruments Did see and hear, , instruct, walk, feel” ; to decide “on” 1H6 I. ii. 124 * “what devise you on?.”

devoted.text: consecrated, holy R3 I. ii. 35 “ charitable deeds.”

devotement.text: devotion, worship Oth. II. iii. 325 (Q1, F1 “deuotement,” Q3 Ff2 3 4 “devotement”; Q2 “denotement”).

devotion.text: devout purpose or object R3 IV. i. 9 * “Upon the like as yourselves.”

devour.text: “ the way” (not pre-S.), to cover it with great rapidity 2H4 I. i. 47 ; Tp. V. i. 155 “they devour their reason” (= make their reason inoperative).

dew.text: first applied to tears by S. (cf. BRINE) LLL. IV. iii. 30 , R2 V. i. 9 , Lucr. 1829 ; other fig. uses are R3 IV. i. 83 “ of sleep,” Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 23 “d-s of flattery,” Cæs. II. i. 230 “dew of slumber.”

dewlap.text: applied to a woman's breast MND. II. i. 50 (old edd. “dewlop”).

dexter.text: right Troil. IV. v. 127 “the dexter cheek.”

dexteriously.text: 17th cent. variant of ‘dexterously’ Tw.N. I. v. 65 .

dial.text: clock, or watch AYL. II. vii. 20 , R2 V. v. 53 “like a d-'s point,” Rom. II. iv. 122 , Lucr. 327 ; so dial-hand Sonn. civ. 9 .

dialogue.text: vb. (not found before S.) 1. to hold a conversation Tim. II. ii. 51 .

diameter.text: extent from side to side Ham. IV. i. 41 “o'er the world's diameter.”

diapason.text: a bass sounding in exact concord, i.e. in octaves, with the air Lucr. 1132 “And with deep groans the diapason bear.”

dibble.text: instrument for making holes in the ground for seeds or young plants Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 100

dich.text: orig. contraction of ‘do it’ in ‘much good do it you’; hence in similar phrases Tim. I. ii. 74 “Much good dich thy good heart.”

dictator.text: chief magistrate with absolute power, elected in ancient Rome in times of emergency Cor. II. ii. 94 “our then dictator.”

diction.text: expression or description in words Ham. V. ii. 124 “to make true of him” (euphuistic).

die1.text: used with quibble on the verb ‘die’ MND. V. i. 314 , Tim. V. iv. 34 ; fig. =chance, luck R3 V. iv. 10 “I have set my life upon a cast, And I will stand the hazard of the die.”

die2.text: phr. “to die the death,” to be put to death, suffer the penalty of capital punishment MND. I. i. 65 , Cym. IV. ii. 96 ; S. is earliest for “die (with laughing)” Shr. III. ii. 244 , Troil. I. iii. 176 “at this sport Sir Valour dies.”

diet1.text: sb. (1 the orig. sense etymologically, but ‘daily food’ is the earliest sense in English) 1. course of life R3 I. i. 139 “an evil diet.”

diet2.text: vb. (2 exact meaning not always clear) 1. to feed (lit. and fig.) 1H6 I. ii. 10 “d-ed like mules,” Cor. I. ix. 52 , Oth. II. i. 306 “to my revenge,” Cym. III. iv. 183 “all the comfort The gods will me with.”

dieter.text: regulator of diet Cym. IV. ii. 51 .

difference.text: (the ordinary sense is freq.; in Sonn. cv. 8 app. a ref. to the use in logic=differentia, the attribute by which a species is distinguished from all other species of the same genus) 1. diversity of opinion, disagreement, dispute Mer.V. IV. i. 171 ; “at ,” at variance, in disagreement Cor. V. iii. 201 : “Vexed . . . with passions of some difference” (=conflicting emotions) Cæs. I. ii. 40 .

difficult.text: Oth. III. iii. 82 “full of poise and difficult weight” (=weighty and difficult to be estimated).

diffidence.text: distrust, suspicion John I. i. 65 , 1H6 III. iii. 10 , Lr. I. ii. 166 . ∥ The sense ‘distrust of oneself’ is post-S.

diffuse.text: (2 peculiar to S., but cf. next) 1. to pour, shed Tp. IV. i. 79 “D-st honey-drops.”

diffused.text: confused, disorderly Wiv. IV. iv. 56 “some song,” H5 V. ii. 61 “diffus'd attire” (old edd. “defus'd”), R3 I. ii. 78 “diffus'd infection of a man” (old edd. “defus'd”).

digest.text: (old edd. often “disgest”; 1 the oldest sense of the word) 1. to arrange R3 III. i. 200 “ our complots in some form,” Troil. Prol. 29, Ham. II. ii. 469 [ 460 ] “an excellent play, well d-ed in the scenes,” Ant. II. ii. 182 .

digestion.text: Troil. II. iii. 44 “my cheese, my ” ; cf. Jonson's Epigrams ci, ‘Digestiue cheese, and fruit there sure will bee.’

digress.text: (both senses are Eliz.) 1. to depart, deviate Shr. III. ii. 110 , Rom. III. iii. 126 “D-ing from the valour of a man.”

digression.text: moral going astray, transgression LLL. I. ii. 122 , Lucr. 202 “my is so vile.” ∥ Once also in the sense ‘deviation from the subject or purpose’ 2H4 IV. i. 140 .

dilate.text: to relate at length Err. I. i. 122 “ at full What hath befall'n,” Oth. I. iii. 153 “all my pilgrimage dilate.”

dilated.text: (in Ham. I. ii. 38 F1 perhaps a spelling of DELATED, perhaps=sense 2) 1. spread far and wide Troil. II. iii. 264 “Which, like . . . a shore, confines Thy spacious and dilated parts.”

dildo.text: word of obscure origin used in the refrains of ballads Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 195 “burthens of d-s and fadings.”

diligence.text: (2 is mainly contextual) 1. assiduity, esp. in service 1H6 V. iii. 9 “your accustom'd to me,” Ham. V. ii. 95 “all of spirit,” Cym. IV. iii. 20 .

diligent.text: 1. attentive, heedful Tp. III. i. 42 “diligent ear.”

dim.text: not bright, dull, lustreless Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 120 “violets dim,” John III. iv. 85 , Lucr. 403 “death's dim look.”

dimension.text: bodily frame; pl. bodily parts or, proportions Mer.V. III. i. 64 , Tw.N. I. v. 282 “in and the shape of nature,” Lr. I. ii. 7 “my d-s are as well compact.”

diminish.text: to impair Tp. III. iii. 64 , Ven. 417 “If springing things be any jot diminish'”

diminutive.text: very small thing Troil. V. i. 38 “d-s of nature,” Ant. IV. x. 50 [ xii. 37 ] “poor'st d-”

dint.text: force Cæs. III. ii. 199 “you feel The of pity.”

dire.text: dreadful, dismal, horrible Mac. II. iii. 64 “prophesying with accents terrible Of dire combustion.”

direct.text: to address (words) 1H6 V. iii. 178 . ∥ S. is the earliest authority for the senses ‘address (a letter)’, ‘inform (a person) as to whereabouts’ and ‘appoint, order’.

direction.text: capacity for directing R3 V. iii. 16 .

directive.text: subject to direction (S.) Troil. I. iii. 356 .

directly.text: (the sense ‘at once’, Ham. III. ii. 221 is not pre-S.) 1. straight John III. iv. 129 , Cæs. IV. i. 32 “to run on,” Oth. III. iii. 408 “lead to the door of truth.”

dirge.text: funeral song, song of mourning Rom. IV. v. 88 , Ham. I. ii. 12 , Lucr. 1612 .

dirty.text: as an epithet of disgust or aversion (not pre-S.) Cym. III. vi. 55 “those Who worship gods.”

disappointed.text: unprepared (cf. APPOINT 2) Ham. I. v. 77 “Unhousel'd, disappointed, unanel'”

disaster1.text: unfavourable aspect of a star Ham. I. i. 118 “D-s in the sun” ; (hence) ill-luck Mac. III. i. 112 “So weary with d-s, tugg'd with fortune.”

disaster2.text: to ruin Ant. II. vii. 18 “the holes where eyes should be, which pitifully disaster the cheeks.”

disbench.text: to cause (a person) to leave his seat (S.) Cor. II. ii. 76 “I hope My words d-'d you not.”

disbranch.text: fig. to sever Lr. IV. ii. 34 .

discandy.text: to dissolve or melt out of a solid condition Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 165, IV. x. 35 [ xii. 22 ].

discase.text: to undress Tp. V. i. 85 “I will me” ; to unmask Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 651 ∥ Cf. CASE sb. 2 1 (i) and 1 (v).

discerner.text: person of judgement, critic H8 I. i. 32 .

discernings.text: intellectual faculties Lr. I. iv. 250 “his discernings Are lethargied.”

discharge1.text: occurs 7 times in S., who is the earliest authority for the senses ‘letting off a firearm’ ( 1H4 I. i. 57 ), ‘emission’ ( AYL. II. i. 37 , Troil. IV. iv. 41 ), ‘payment’ ( Cym. V. iv. 173 ), ‘performance, execution’ ( Tp. II. i. 262 ).

discharge2.text: vb. (‘dismiss, disband’ and 4 are the most freq. meanings) 1. to unburden, disburden, deliver, free Ado V. i. 335 , 2H4 II. iv. 145 , Rom. V. i. 63 “d-'d of breath.”

discipline1.text: sb. (the earliest sense in English, ‘chastisement, correction,’ is not S.) 1. instruction, teaching Gent. III. ii. 88 , Shr. I. i. 30 “this moral ,” Troil. II. iii. 33 “heaven bless thee from a tutor, and discipline come not near thee.”

discipline2.text: vb. (2 this sense was orig. applied to the penitential use of the scourge) 1. to instruct, train Troil. II. iii. 258 “he that d-'d thy arms to fight,” Compl. 261 “d-'d, ay, dieted in grace.”

disclaim.text: (not in pre-Eliz. use) 1. to renounce or disavow all share “in” Lr. II. ii. 58 .

disclose1.text: vb. (the sense ‘reveal’ is the common one) 1. to unfold Ham. I. iii. 40 “before their buttons be d-'d,” Sonn. liv. 8 “their masked buds discloses.”

discolour.text: to bring a blush to 2H4 II. ii. 5 “it d-s the complexion of my greatness to acknowledge it.”

discomfited.text: discouraged Shr. II. i. 164 “be not so ”

discomfort1.text: sb. (sense ‘uneasiness’ is late) 1. discouragement R2 III. ii. 65 , Mac. I. ii. 28 . ∥ ‘Discourage’ and its compounds are not S.

discomfort2.text: vb. (thrice in S.; cf. the senses of prec.) 1. to discourage Troil. V. x. 10 , Cæs. V. iii. 106 .

discontented.text: full of discontent Oth. V. ii. 313 .

discontinue.text: to cease to frequent Ado V. i. 197 “I must your company,” Mer.V. III. iv. 75 “I have discontinu'd school.”

discourse1.text: sb. (“ of reason” dates from the 15th c.) 1. reasoning, thought, reflection Meas. I. ii. 196 “reason and ,” Tw.N. IV. iii. 12 , Troil. V. ii. 139 , Ham. IV. iv. 36 “with such large , Looking before and after; of reason,” process or faculty of reasoning Troil. II. ii. 116 , Ham. I. ii. 150 ; cf. “ of thought” Oth. IV. ii. 153 .

discourse2.text: vb. (5 now only as a reminiscence of the S. passage) 1. to hold discourse, talk, converse MND. V. i. 153 “Let” [them] “At large ,” Cæs. III. i. 295 “ . . . of the state of things.”

discover.text: (2 is the most freq. S. sense; the sense ‘find out’ is not common) 1. to uncover, expose to view Mer.V. II. vii. 1 “ The several caskets,” Tw.N. II. v. 175 , R3 IV. iv. 241 .

discovery.text: (obs. or arch. uses are the foll.; the word does not appear before mid-16th cent.) 1. revelation, disclosure (of a secret) Wint. I. ii. 441 , H5 II. ii. 162 “the of . . . treason,” Ham. II. ii. 312 .

discretion.text: “use thy , do your ,” act as you think fit AYL. I. i. 154 , Oth. III. iii. 34 .

discuss.text: to declare, tell Wiv. I. iii. 102 , IV. v. 2 , H5 III. ii. 67 , IV. i. 37 , IV. iv. 5 “What is thy name? discuss,” 30 “Discuss the same in French unto him.”

disease1.text: trouble, grievance, vexation AYL. V. iv. 68 , 1H6 II. v. 44 , Tim. III. i. 57 , Lr. I. i. 177 “To shield thee from d-s of the world” (Ff “disasters”).

disease2.text: to trouble, disturb Cor. I. iii. 117 , Mac. V. iii. 21 (Ff2 3 4; see DISSEAT).

disedge.text: to satisfy the appetite of Cym. III. iv. 96 .

disfurnish.text: to deprive Gent. IV. i. 14 , Tim. III. ii. 49 “to myself,” Per. IV. vi. 12 “she'll us of all our cavaliers.”

disgrace.text: disfigurement LLL. I. i. 3 “in the of death,” Sonn. xxxiii. 8 “[the sun] Stealing unseen to west with this disgrace.”

disgraceful.text: devoid of grace, unbecoming 1H6 I. i. 86 “these wailing robes.”

disgracious.text: out of favour, disliked R3 III. vii. 111 , IV. iv. 178 .

disguise.text: drunkenness, intoxication Ant. II. vii. 131 “the wild hath almost Antick'd us all.” ∥ Cf. the old use of ‘disguised’=drunk.

dishclout.text: used in contemptuous comparison Rom. III. v. 221 “Romeo's a dishclout to him.”

dishonest.text: unchaste Wiv. III. iii. 195 , Tw.N. I. v. 45 , H5 I. ii. 49 .

disjoint1.text: to fall to pieces Mac. III. ii. 16 “let the frame of things disjoint.”

disjoint2.text: ‘out of joint,’ distracted Ham. I. ii. 20 “thinking . . . Our state to be disjoint.”

dislike1.text: disagreement, discord 1H4 V. i. 26 , Troil. II. iii. 239 , Lr. I. iv. 350 .

dislike2.text: vb. (the current trans. use is commonest) 1. to displease Rom. II. ii. 61 “if either thee ” (Q1 “displease”), Oth. II. iii. 50 “I'll do 't; but it d-s me.”

disliken.text: to disguise Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 669 “ The truth.”

dislimn.text: to obliterate the outlines of, efface, blot out Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 10 (Ff “dislimes”). ∥ In mod. use only in reminiscences of S.

dismal.text: ill-boding, sinister 3H6 II. vi. 58 “Now death shall stop his” (i.e. the screech-owl's) “ threatening sound,” Ven. 889 ; disastrous, calamitous Rom. IV. iii. 19 “My scene I needs must act alone.” ∥ The orig. application of the word is to the unlucky days (“dies mali”) of the mediaeval calendar; the derived senses are none of them pre-Eliz.

dismantle.text: refl. to change one's outward covering Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 669 “muffle your face; you”; to divest, strip Ham. III. ii. 298 “This realm d-d was Of Jove himself” ; to remove (a covering) Lr. I. i. 220 “dismantle So many folds of favour.”

dismay.text: to be discouraged 1H6 III. iii. 1 “ not, princes.”

disme.text: tenth man sacrificed Troil. II. ii. 19 .

dismiss.text: S. is the earliest authority for the senses ‘discard, reject’ ( Tp. IV. i. 67 “the d-ed bachelor” ), ‘put out of the mind, cease to entertain’ ( Ven. 425 “ your vows” ), ‘to send out of court, refuse further hearing to’ ( Cor. II. i. 86 “ the controversy” ).

dismission.text: discharge from service or office Ant. I. i. 26 ; rejection Cym. II. iii. 57 .

dismount.text: (1 and 2 are not pre-S.; sense 2 is a metaphor from gunnery practice) 1. to unseat, unhorse (fig.) H5 III. vii. 89 “your horse . . . would trot as well were some of your brags d-ed.”

disorbed.text: removed from its sphere Troil. II. ii. 46 “Like a star disorb'” ∥ A S. coinage.

disorder.text: sb. (not earlier than the 16th c.; the verb occurs in S. only in the pa. pple.) 1. disorderly act or practice, misdemeanour Tw.N. II. iii. 107 , Lr. I. ii. 127 “machinations, hollowness, treachery, and all ruinous disorders,” II. iv. 202 .

dispark.text: to throw open (park land) for common use R2 III. i. 23 “D-'d my parks, and felled my forest woods.”

dispatch1.text: sb. (2 is the commonest S. sense) 1. dismissal, leave to go, congé LLL. IV. i. 5 , Cor. V. iii. 180 “give us our ,” Lr. II. i. 127 “the several messengers From hence attend dispatch.”

dispatch2.text: vb. (the most freq. meaning in S. is ‘to make haste’) 1. to make away with, kill R2 III. i. 35 ; absol. John IV. i. 27 , R3 I. ii. 182 , Lr. II. i. 60 ; also “to dispatch” a person's “life” Lr. IV. v. 12 .

dispensation.text: (2 cf. DISPENSE 4) 1. licence granted by ecclesiastical authority to do what is forbidden or omit what is enjoined by ecclesiastical law or by any solemn obligation LLL. II. i. 87 “seek a for his oath,” 1H6 V. iii. 86 “a dispensation may be had.”

dispense.text: always in the constr. “dispense with” = (1) to make an arrangement with, for an offence 2H6 V. i. 181 “Canst thou with heaven for such an oath?” ; (2) to give exemption or relief from LLL. I. i. 146 “ with this decree,” 1H6 V. v. 28 “ with that contract” ; (3) to set aside, disregard Wiv. II. i. 47 “ with trifles” ; (4) to forgo, do without Meas. III. i. 152 “ with your leisure,” Tim. III. ii. 94 “learn now with pity to ” ; (5) to condone by dispensation, pardon Meas. III. i. 133 “Nature d-s with the deed,” Err. II. i. 103 , Lucr. 1070 , 1279 , 1704

displace.text: to remove, banish Mac. III. iv. 109 , Lucr. 887 .

displant.text: to uproot (fig.) Rom. III. iii. 58 “ a town.”

displanting.text: deposition from office Oth. II. i. 286 .

display.text: to behave ostentatiously Lr. II. iv. 41 .

displeasure.text: (the foll. are special or obs. uses) 1. “your ,” the unpopularity you are in H8 III. ii. 393 , Oth. III. i. 45 .

disponge.text: reading in mod. edd. for DISPUNGE.

disport1.text: pastime, sport Oth. I. iii. 273 , Lucr. Arg. 11

disport2.text: refl. to amuse oneself 3H6 IV. v. 8 “Comes hunting this way to himself,” Tim. I. ii. 143 .

dispose1.text: sb. (not pre-S.) 1. disposal Gent. II. vii. 86 , IV. i. 76 “Which . . . all rest at thy dispose,” Err. I. i. 20 , John I. i. 263 .

dispose2.text: vb. (“dispose of” is common in sense 2) 1. to place or distribute, to manage, do with H5 IV. Chor. 51 , H8 I. ii. 116 “these so noble benefits . . . Not well d-'d,” Troil. IV. v. 115 “His blows are well d-'d: there, Ajax!.”

disposed.text: inclined to merriment, in a merry mood LLL. II. i. 248 , V. ii. 467 , Tw.N. II. iii. 91 .

disposition.text: (1 rare; 2 and 3 about equally freq.) 1. arrangement Oth. I. iii. 237 “fit for my wife.”

disprize.text: to hold in contempt Troil. IV. v. 74 (Q “misprising”), Ham. III. i. 72 “d-d love” (Qq “despiz'd”).

disproperty.text: to alienate (a possession) Cor. II. i. 267 “Dispropertied their freedoms.”

disproportion1.text: want of fitness Oth. III. iii. 233 “Foul , thoughts unnatural” (so Qq; Ff “d-s”).

disproportion2.text: to make out of proportion 3H6 III. ii. 160 “To me in every part, Like to a chaos.”

dispunge.text: to pour down as from a squeezed sponge Ant. IV. ix. 13 “The poisonous damp of night dispunge upon me.”

dispurse.text: to disburse 2H6 III. i. 117 . ∥ ‘Probably from some Scottish chronicle’ (H. C. Hart); the only other recorded examples of this word are from a Scottish Act of Parliament (1643), and Heslop's Northumberland glossary (1892).

disputable.text: inclined to dispute (S.) AYL. II. v. 35 .

disputation.text: conversation (S.) 1H4 III. i. 205 , H5 III. ii. 105 .

dispute.text: (1 an obs. sense; 2 not pre-S.) 1. to discuss Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 413; cf. Rom. III. iii. 62 .

disquietly.text: in a disturbing manner (S.) Lr. I. ii. 127 .

disseat.text: to unseat Mac. V. iii. 21 (F1 “dis-eate,” Ff2 3 4 “dis-ease”; many conj.).

dissemble.text: to disguise (once in S.) Tw.N. IV. ii. 5 .

dissembling.text: falseness, hypocrisy 3H6 III. iii. 119 ; so the ppl. adj.=false, hypocritical Err. IV. iv. 102 “ villain,” Troil. V. iv. 2 “That . . . varlet” ; fig. MND. II. ii. 98 “What . . . glass of mine.”

dissembly.text: Dogberry's perversion of ‘assembly’ Ado IV. ii. 1 .

dissolution.text: (5 times in S.; 1 not pre-S.) 1. liquefaction Wiv. III. v. 121 “a man of continual and thaw,” Lucr. 355 “Against love's fire fear's frost hath dissolution.”

dissolve.text: (sense 4 intr. is most freq.) 1. to loosen, undo R2 II. ii. 71 “ the bands of life,” Troil. V. ii. 153 “The bonds of heaven are . . . d-'d, and loos'”

distaff.text: cleft stick on which wool or flax was formerly wound; used as the type of woman's occupation Lr. IV. ii. 17 , Cym. V. iii. 34 ; so distaff-woman R2 III. ii. 118 .

distain.text: to defile, sully, dishonour R3 V. iii. 323 , Troil. I. iii. 241 , Per. IV. iii. 31 “She did distain† my child” (old edd. “disdain(e),” Lucr. 786 .

distance.text: (1 the orig. sense of the word; the usual S. sense is that of ‘intervening space’, of which 2 is a special use) 1. disagreement Mac. III. i. 116 “in such bloody ”

distaste.text: (not pre-Eliz.; 2, 3 not pre-S.) 1. to have no taste for, disrelish, dislike Troil. II. ii. 66 , Lr. I. iii. 15 (Qq “dislike”).

distasteful.text: expressing dislike or aversion Tim. II. ii. 221 “distasteful looks.”

distemper1.text: sb. (2 and 3 not pre-S.; 3 cf. DISTEMPERING) 1. ill humour, ill temper Wiv. III. iii. 230 , III. v. 80 “instigated by his ,” Wint. I. ii. 385 , Ham. III. ii. 358 “what is your cause of ?,” III. iv. 122 .

distemper2.text: to disturb, disorder Tw.N. II. i. 5 “the malignancy of my fate might, perhaps, yours,” Ven. 653 “disturbing Jealousy . . . Distempering gentle Love in his desire.” ∥ See also DISTEMPERED.

distemperature.text: (in MND. II. i. 106 , 1H4 V. i. 3 there is probably a glance at the old sense of ‘inclemency of weather’, but the direct ref. is to ‘ill humour, discomposure’) 1. physical disorder or derangement, ailment, illness Err. V. i. 82 “pale d-s,” 1H4 III. i. 34 “Our grandam earth, having this , In passion shook.”

distempered.text: (1 the orig. sense; cf. prec. word) 1. inclement John III. iv. 154 “no d-'d day” ; transf. All'sW. I. iii. 159 “this d-'d messenger of wet” (i.e. the rainbow).

distil.text: (3 is much the commonest S. use) 1. to fall in minute drops Tit. III. i. 17 .

distillation.text: product of distilling Wiv. III. v. 117 , Sonn. v. 9 ; so distilment Ham. I. v. 64 “The leperous distilment.”

distinct.text: stressed “disti'nct” Troil. IV. v. 244 ; “di'stinct” Mer.V. II. ix. 61 , Troil. IV. iv. 45 .

distinctively.text: (?) distinctly Oth. I. iii. 155 (so Ff2 3 4; F1 “instinctiuely,” Qq “intentively”).

distinctly.text: separately, individually Tp. I. ii. 200 , Cor. III. i. 205 , IV. iii. 48 , Oth. II. iii. 292 * .

distract2.text: 1. to separate, divide, scatter All'sW. V. iii. 35 “to the brightest beams D-ed clouds give way,” Oth. I. iii. 328 , Ant. III. vii. 43 “Distract your army.”

distraction.text: division, detachment Ant. III. vii. 76 “His power went out in such d-” ∥ The senses referring to mental derangement follow the vb.

distrain.text: to levy a distress upon R2 II. iii. 131 , (hence) to confiscate 1H6 I. iii. 61 “d-'d the Tower to his use.”

distraught.text: mentally deranged R3 III. v. 4 , Rom. IV. iii. 50 .

distressful.text: gained by hard toil H5 IV. i. 290 “distressful bread.”

disturb.text: disturbance R3 IV. ii. 72 “my sweet sleep's d-s” (Ff “disturbers”). ∥ Used by Samuel Daniel (1597) and Milton (1667).

divers.text: (1 now expressed by the form ‘diverse’; in H8 V. iii. 18 “new opinions, and dangerous,” the old meaning ‘wrong, perverse’ is perhaps represented) 1. different in kind AYL. III. ii. 329 , 2H4 III. i. 53 , H5 I. ii. 184 , Rom. II. iii. 11 .

divest.text: (spelling of the earlier ‘devest’, not recorded earlier than F1, i.e. 1623) 1. intr. to undress Oth. II. iii. 183 (Qq Ff “Devesting”).

divine1.text: applied to a priest of a heathen religion Wint. III. i. 19 “Apollo's great divine.”

divine2.text: immortal, blessèd R2 I. i. 38 “Or my soul answer it in heaven.”

divinely.text: piously, religiously, sacredly John II. i. 237 “most vow'd,” R3 III. vii. 61 “ bent to meditation.”

division.text: (the foll. are technical senses) 1. in music, execution of a rapid passage of melody, esp. one consisting of florid phrases or runs 1H4 III. i. 210 “ditties . . . Sung . . . With ravishing , to her lute,” Rom. III. v. 29 “the lark makes sweet ” ; (hence fig.) variation, modulation Mac. IV. iii. 96 “abound In the of each several crime, Acting it many ways.”

divorce.text: that which causes separation H8 II. i. 76 “the long of steel” (=executioner's axe), Tim. IV. iii. 384 “dear 'Twixt natural son and sire,” Ven. 932 “Hateful of love” (viz. Death).

divulge.text: to proclaim (a person) to be so-and-so Wiv. III. ii. 44 “ Page himself for a secure and wilful Actæon,” Tw.N. I. v. 281 “In voices well d-'d” (=of good repute).

dizzy.text: to make ‘dizzy’, confuse Troil. V. ii. 171 “ with more clamour Neptune's ear,” Ham. V. ii. 120 “ the arithmetic of memory” (Q2 “dosie,” Q3 “dazzie,” Qq4-6 “dizzie”).

do.text: (the chief obs. or archaic uses are the following; see also DOING, DONE) 1. to put “to death” Ado V. iii. 3 , 2H6 III. ii. 179 ; also “do him dead” 3H6 I. iv. 108 .

doctrine.text: (2 a late example of this sense) 1. instruction, lesson LLL. IV. iii. 302 , Rom. I. i. 244 , Ant. V. ii. 31 “learn A of obedience.”

dodge.text: to be shifty Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 62

dog.text: occurs in various proverbs and comparisons, e.g. Wiv. I. iv. 118 , Mer.V. I. i. 94 , Tw.N. II. iii. 156 , 1H4 II. i. 10 , Tit. V. i. 122 ; “dogs of war” Cæs. III. i. 273 (cf. H5 I. Chor. 7 ) is a S. expression much echoed by mod. writers;—“(a) dog at,” an adept at Gent. IV. iv. 14 , Tw.N.
