II. iii. 66 “I am dog at a catch;—the dog's name,” applied to the letter R, which Ben Jonson says ‘is the dog's letter, and burreth in the sound’ Rom. II. iv. 225 .

dogfish.text: name of a kind of small shark, applied opprobriously to a person 1H6 I. iv. 107 .

dogged.text: like a dog John IV. iii. 149 “Now . . . Doth war bristle his angry crest” ; (hence) cruel, malicious John IV. i. 129 “these spies,” 2H6 III. i. 158 “ York.”

doing.text: deed, action, performance R3 II. ii. 90 , H8 I. ii. 74 , Cor. I. ix. 40 ; also pl. Cor. I. ix. 23 .

doit.text: a former Dutch coin, equivalent to half a farthing, used as the type of a small sum Tp. II. ii. 34 , Mer.V. I. iii. 141 , 2H6 III. i. 112 , Cor. IV. iv. 17 .

dole1.text: 1 (in 2H4 I. i. 169 =distribution) 1. share, portion All'sW. II. iii. 176 “what of honour Flies where you bid it.”

dole2.text: grief, sorrow, mourning AYL. I. ii. 140 “making such pitiful dole,” Ham. I. ii. 13 “weighing delight and dole.”

dollar.text: in S.'s time applied both to the German thaler and the Spanish piece of eight (eight reals) Mac. I. ii. 64 ; also with play on ‘dolour’ Tp. II. i. 18 ; cf. Lr. II. iv. 54 .

dolphin.text: mammal of the whale family Tw.N. I. ii. 14 ; see also DAUPHIN, and cf. 1H6 V. iv. 107 .

domineer.text: to feast riotously Shr. III. ii. 227 .

dominical.text: for ‘d. letter,’ the letter, marked in red on old almanacs, used to denote the Sundays in a particular year LLL. V. ii. 44 . ∥ The seven letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G are used in succession to denote the first seven days of the year (January 1-7), and then in rotation the next seven days, so that, e.g. if the 3rd of January be a Sunday, the dominical letter for the year is C.

done.text: (1 is recorded first from S.) 1. agreed! Tp. II. i. 33 , Shr. V. ii. 74 , Cor. I. iv. 2 .

doom1.text: sb. (1 the usual S. sense) 1. judgement, sentence R2 I. iii. 148 .

doom2.text: to decide, judge Cym. V. v. 421 .

door.text: “Speak within door,” lower your tone, do not talk so loud Oth. IV. ii. 144 (Qq “dores”); in Warwickshire the phr. ‘Speak within the house’ was current till recently in the same sense; — “is the wind in that door?,” Is that the tendency of affairs? 1H4 III. iii. 101 .

dotage.text: feebleness of mind Lr. I. iv. 317 ; excessive fondness Oth. IV. i. 27 .

dotant.text: dotard Cor. V. ii. 47 “a decayed dotant.”

dote.text: to act or talk foolishly Err. IV. iv. 60 , Ven. 1059 ; to be excessively fond or in love Gent. IV. iv. 89 , Ham. V. ii. 197 . Ven. 837 ; hence doter, fond lover LLL. IV. iii. 260 , doting, fond R3 IV. iv. 301 , Lucr. 1064 .

double1.text: “as as,” having twice the power or influence of Oth. I. ii. 14 ; “ beer,” strong beer 2H6 II. iii. 64 .

double2.text: doubly, twice All'sW. II. iii. 252 , Wint. V. iii. 107 , Mac. IV. i. 83 “make assurance sure; double-fatal yew” R2 III. ii. 117 so called because it has poisonous leaves, and was used for instruments of death; with duplicity, deceitfully Rom. II. iv. 180 “deal double with her.”

doublet.text: close-fitting body-garment, with or without sleeves, worn by men from the 14th to the 18th cent. Tp. II. i. 108 ;—“ and hose,” typical male attire; also, a kind of undress, or dress for active pursuits, implying absence of the warm cloak, or the dignified gown or long coat Wiv. III. i. 46 “in your and hose! this raw rheumatic day?,” AYL. II. iv. 6 “ and hose ought to show itself courageous to petticoat.”

doubt.text: (1 remains in dial. use) 1. to suspect, apprehend Cor. III. i. 151 , Ham. I. ii. 255 “I doubt some foul play,” Oth. III. iii. 19 .

doubtful.text: inclined to suspect, suspicious, apprehensive Mer.V. III. ii. 109 , Tw.N. IV. iii. 27 , Mac. III. ii. 7 “dwell in joy,” Lr. V. i. 12 “I am that you have been . . . bosom'd with her.”

doubtless.text: without fear or suspicion John IV. i. 130 “pretty child, sleep ,” 1H4 III. ii. 20 “I am I can purge Myself.”

dout.text: to put out, extinguish (fig.) H5 IV. ii. 11 , Ham. IV. vii. 192 (Qq Ff2 3 4 “drown(e)s”).

dove.text: common type of gentleness and harmlessness MND. I. i. 171 “the simplicity of Venus' doves,” Ham. V. i. 308 ; hence, an innocent or simpleton Shr. III. ii. 160 “she's a lamb, a dove, a fool to him.”

dowlas.text: coarse kind of linen 1H4 III. iii. 79 .

down.text: used in ballad refrains without appreciable meaning Wiv. I. iv. 44 , Ham. IV. v. 169 .

downright1.text: 1. directed straight downwards, vertical 2H6 II. iii. 93 “a downright blow,” 3H6 I. i. 12 .

downright2.text: adv. (in Ven. 645 ?=‘straight down,’ or ‘straightway, forthwith’) 1. positively, absolutely, out and out LLL. V. ii. 390 , Rom. III. v. 129 “It rains downright.”

doxy.text: vagabond's cant for a beggar's mistress Wint. IV. ii. 2 .

drabbing.text: associating with bad women Ham. II. i. 26 .

draff.text: pig-wash, hog's-wash Wiv. IV. ii. 112 “Still swine eats all the draff” (Ff Q3 “draugh”), 1H4 IV. ii. 38 “eating draff and husks.”

dragon.text: a yoke of dragons is attributed by S. to the goddess of the night MND. III. ii. 379 , Troil. V. viii. 17 “The wing of night,” Cym. II. ii. 48 “you dragons of the night.”

drain.text: to let fall in drops 2H6 III. ii. 142 .

dram.text: 1/8 ounce apothecaries' weight, 1/16 ounce avoirdupois weight; (hence) very small quantity All'sW. II. iii. 232 ;—1/8 fluid ounce; (hence) spec. dose of poison Wint. I. ii. 320 , Rom. V. i. 60 “let me have A dram of poison.”

draught.text: cesspool, privy, sewer, Troil. V. i. 84 , Tim. V. i. 107 .

draw.text: (see also DRAWN; 8 is not pre-S.) 1. intr. to pull a vehicle, fig. applied to acting in concert Troil. V. v. 44 “we together,” Oth. IV. i. 68 “Think every bearded fellow that's but yok'd May with you.”

drawer.text: tapster Wiv. II. ii. 167 , Rom. III. i. 9 .

drawn.text: (the foll. are special uses) 1. “ fox,” a fox driven from cover and therefore wily in his attempts to get back again 1H4 III. iii. 128 (? also ref. to ‘fox’ = broadsword).

dread1.text: dreadful, terrible Tp. I. ii. 206 “his dread trident” ; held in awe, revered 2H6 V. i. 17 “our dread liege,” Ham. III. iv. 108 “your dread command.”

dread2.text: to be anxious about Pilgr. vii. 10 [ 94 ] “Dreading my love, the loss thereof still fearing.”

dreadful.text: full of dread R3 I. i. 8 , Ham. I. ii. 207 , Oth. II. iii. 177 ; so dreadfully, with dread Meas. IV. ii. 149 “apprehends death no more but as a drunken sleep” ; also colloquially used as a strong intensive, = exceedingly, ‘terribly’ Ham. II. ii. 281 “I am most attended.”

dregs.headword: dregs (once sing. dreg Troil. III. ii. 68 )
dregs.text: always fig. (1) worthless part “of” something, impurity, corrupt matter Troil. III. ii. 68 , 70 , Tim. I. ii. 242 “Friendship's full of ,” Sonn. lxxiv. 9 ; (2) residue, last remains Tp. II. ii. 43 “till the of the storm be past,” R3 I. iv. 125 , Cor. V. ii. 83 .

dress.text: (the sense ‘to prepare, equip’ is freq., often with more or less explicit ref. to putting on clothes) 1. to cultivate (a plot of ground) R2 III. iv. 56 .

dressing.text: trimming up, refashioning Sonn. cxxiii. 4 “They are but d-s of a former sight” ; pl. ornaments of office Meas. V. i. 56 .

drift.text: (1 once; 2 the usual S. sense) 1. shower (of bullets) John II. i. 412 .

drink1.text: carousal (S.) Tim. III. v. 75 , Ant. II. vii. 112 .

drink2.text: “to ” (a person) “dead drunk, to bed,” said of the seasoned toper who sees his companions succumb to the effects of their potations Oth. II. iii. 85 , Ant. II. v. 21 .

drive.text: (past tense “drove, drave”; pa. pple. “driven, droven, (?) drove” in 2H6 III. ii. 84 ) 1. to rush “at or upon” Tit. II. iii. 64 , Ham. II. ii. 502 .

driven.text: (of snow) drifted Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 220 “Lawn as white as snow”; (of down) separated from the heavier down by a current of air Oth. I. iii. 232 “My thrice- bed of down.”

drollery.text: puppet-show Tp. III. iii. 21 “A living ” ; comic picture 2H4 II. i. 160 “a pretty slight ”

eager.text: (most of the S. uses are obs.) 1. pungent, acrid Sonn. cxviii. 2 “With compounds we our palate urge” ; (of air) keen, biting Ham. I. iv. 2 ; (of speech) R2 I. i. 49 “two tongues,” 3H6 II. vi. 68 “eager words.”

eagle.text: referred to as (i) one of the emblems of Jupiter, (ii) an ensign in the Roman army Cym. IV. ii. 348 “Jove's bird, the Roman ,” V. v. 474 “our princely eagle, The imperial Cæsar.”

eale.text: Ham. I. iv. 36 “the dram of ” (Qq2 3 “eale,” Qq4 5 6 “ease,” passage not in Q1 F1); corrupt, many conj.

ean.text: to bring forth (lambs) 3H6 II. v. 36 ; “eaning time” Mer.V. I. iii. 88 , Per. III. iv. 6 .

ear1.text: “about” (a person's) “e-s,” in expressions denoting severe treatment or hard measure H5 III. vii. 96 , 3H6 V. i. 108 , Rom. III. i. 87 ;—“by the ,” by hearsay All'sW. III. v. 50 ;—“by the e-s,” quarrelling, at variance (said orig. of animals) All'sW. I. ii. 1 , Cor. I. i. 239 ;—“in and ,” in everybody's ears Ham. IV. v. 94 ;—“in the ,” within hearing Ham. III. i. 193 ;—“o'er e-s,” drowned Tp. IV. i. 215 ;—“shake” (one's) “e-s,” to make the best of things (? like a dog when wet) Tw.N. II. iii. 135 , Cæs. IV. i. 26 .

ear2.text: to plough, till All'sW. I. iii. 48 , R2 III. ii. 212 , Ant. I. ii. 120 , I. iv. 49 , Ven. Ded. 6

earl.text: order of nobility next below a marquis and next above a viscount (freq.); used for the foreign ‘count’ All'sW. III. v. 12 , H5 IV. viii. 103 .

earn1.text: to gain deservedly or as recompense, deserve Ado III. i. 99 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 175, IV. i. 16 .

earn2.text: to grieve H5 II. iii. 3 , 6 (F1 “erne”), Cæs. II. ii. 129 (F1 “earnes”).

earnest.text: money paid as an instalment to secure a bargain Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 659; quibblingly in Gent. II. i. 165 , Err. II. ii. 24 with the other word meaning ‘seriousness’.

earth.text: (the foll. are obs. or special uses; 1 was in use from Anglo-Saxon times down to the 17th c.) 1. country, land Wint. III. iii. 44 , John II. i. 344 “the this climate overlooks,” R2 II. i. 41 , H8 III. i. 142 “this English ” ; landed estate Rom. I. ii. 15 “She is the hopeful lady of my earth.”

earthly.text: (the ordinary sense is common; 2 peculiar to S.) 1. existing in the ground 3H6 I. iv. 17 .

earthy.text: grossly material Tp. I. ii. 273 “her . . . commands,” Err. III. ii. 34 “my earthy-gross conceit.”

ease.text: (the meanings ‘comfort’ and ‘leisure’, in a bad sense ‘idleness, sloth’, are the common ones) 1. “do” (a person) “ease,” give pleasure or assistance to Shr. V. ii. 180 , 3H6 V. v. 72 , Ham. I. i. 131 .

easily.text: (the usual sense is ‘without difficulty’) 1. comfortably, at ease AYL. III. ii. 342 “sleeps ,” Oth. V. i. 83 “To bear him easily hence.”

easiness.text: indifference Ham. V. i. 74 “Custom hath made it in him a property of ” ; facility Ham. III. iv. 166 “that shall lend a kind of To the next abstinence” ; indulgence H8 V. iii. 25 “Out of our easiness and childish pity.”

easy1.text: adj. (the sense ‘not difficult, requiring little effort’ is the most freq., often with some ellipsis or condensation of expression, e.g. Cor. V. ii. 45 “the groans of old women,” Ant. III. viii. [ x. ] 41 “'Tis to 't” (= It is not a difficult journey thither), Cym. I. iv. 23 “which . . . an battery might lay flat” ; S. is earliest for sense 1 and the sense ‘loosely fitting’ All'sW. V. iii. 282 , R3 V. iii. 50 ) 1. moved without difficulty to action or belief, yielding, compliant Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 518, H5 II. ii. 125 * , H8 III. ii. 357 “good man,” Cym. II. iv. 47 “Your lady being so easy.”

easy2.text: freq.=easily; also in comp. “-borrow'd” Lr. II. iv. 188 , “-melting” 3H6 II. i. 171 , “-yielding” 2H4 II. i. 130 .

eat.headword: eat (there are many exx. of the fig. sense ‘devour’) 1. phrases
eat.text: “ the air,” be ‘fed’ upon promises 2H4 I. iii. 28 , Ham. III. ii. 99 ; “ iron, a sword,” be stabbed Ado IV. i. 279 , 2H6 IV. x. 31 , Troil. II. iii. 231 .

ebb1.text: “at ,” (of the eyes) dry Tp. I. ii. 432 ; “his e-s, his flows,” his capriciousness Troil. II. iii. 140 .

ebb2.text: fig. to decline, decay Tp. II. i. 230 “to , Hereditary sloth instructs me,” 234, AYL. II. vii. 73 “the . . . means do ,” Wint. V. i. 102 , Oth. III. iii. 459 ; “ebb and flow” 1H4 I. ii. 36 , Lr. V. iii. 19 .

ebon.text: black (like ebony) LLL. I. i. 244 “the -coloured ink,” 2H4 V. v. 40 , Ven. 948 .

eche.text: to eke “out” Mer.V. III. ii. 23 “To eche it and to draw it out in length” (Ff1 2 3 “ich,” Q1 “eck,” Q2 “ech,” Qq3 4 “eech,” F4 “itch,” mod. edd. “eke”), Per. III. Gower 13 (rhymes with “speech”).

ecstasy.text: (1 the orig. meaning of the Greek word) 1. state of being beside oneself, in a frenzy or stupor, excitement, bewilderment, (sometimes) madness Tp. III. iii. 108 , Tit. IV. i. 125 “attend him in his ,” Mac. III. ii. 22 “In restless ,” Ham. II. i. 102 “the very ecstasy of love,” III. i. 169 , III. iv. 74 , 137

edge.text: (used in various fig. applications of literal phrases “take away, take off, turn, blunt, abate the edge”; cf. sense 2; humorously misused in Mer.V. II. ii. 180 “ of a feather-bed,” H5 III. vi. 50 “ of penny cord” ) 1. cutting weapon, sword Cor. V. v. 113 “Stain all your edges on me.”

edged.text: sharpened, sharp H5 III. v. 38 , 1H6 III. iii. 52 .

effect1.text: sb. (meaning ‘result, consequence’ is freq. and colours many exx. given below; quibbles are freq.) 1. contemplated result, purpose, end Gent. II. vii. 73 , 1H6 V. iv. 102 , Oth. I. iii. 105 ; “to ,” to the purpose Tit. IV. iii. 59 , Lr. III. i. 52 .

effect2.text: vb. (obs. uses are) 1. to produce (a state) Shr. I. i. 86 .

effectless.text: fruitless Tit. III. i. 77 , Per. V. i. 53 .

effectual.text: (2 is an obs. sense) 1. having due effect Gent. III. i. 224 “stands in force” (=must take effect).

effectually.text: with the due or intended result Tit. IV. iv. 106 “Your bidding shall I do ” ; in effect, in reality Sonn. cxiii. 4 “mine eye . . . Seems seeing, but effectually is out.”

effeminate.text: (2 rare use, found also in Nashe) 1. womanish, unmanly, feeble, self-indulgent AYL. III. ii. 436 , R2 V. iii. 10 , 1H6 I. i. 35 , V. iv. 107 , Troil. III. iii. 219 , Rom. III. i. 120 .

effuse.text: pouring out 3H6 II. vi. 28 “effuse of blood.”

effusion.text: shedding (“of blood, of tears”) John V. ii. 49 , H5 III. vi. 142 , 1H6 V. i. 9 ; concr. Meas. III. i. 30 “The mere of thy proper loins” (=thy children).

eftest.text: (?) most convenient Ado IV. ii. 39 . ∥ An unexplained blunder of Dogberry's.

egal.text: equal Mer.V. III. iv. 13 , Tit. IV. iv. 4 ; so egally R3 III. vii. 212 .

egg.text: (both uses appear to be only S.) 1. taken as a type of a worthless thing All'sW. IV. iii. 282 “He will steal, sir, an out of a cloister,” Wint. I. ii. 162 “Will you take e-s for money?.”

egma.text: rustic's blunder for ‘enigma’ LLL. III. i. 75 “No egma, no riddle.”

eight.text: “in and six,” in alternate verses of eight and six syllables each, the common ballad metre MND. III. i. 25 .

eisel.text: vinegar Ham. V. i. 298 , Sonn. cxi. 10 .

either.text: =‘each other’ Tp. I. ii. 447 , H5 II. ii. 106 , Rom. II. vi. 29 , Sonn. xxviii. 5 ; “ which,” either one or the other Ham. IV. vii. 13 . ∥ “Either” is one syll. in R3 I. ii. 64 , Cæs. IV. i. 23 , Mac. V. vii. 18 .

eke1.text: to increase, add to Mer.V. III. ii. 23 (cf. ECHE); “eke out,” to supplement AYL. I. ii. 211 , All'sW. II. v. 80 .

eke2.text: also Wiv. I. iii. 103 , MND. III. i. 100 .

elbow1.text: “rub the ,” show oneself pleased, chuckle LLL. V. ii. 109 , 1H4 V. i. 77 .

elbow2.text: to jog Lr. IV. iii. 44 ; cf. 2H4 I. ii. 80 “Go, pluck him by the elbow.”

eld.text: old age Meas. III. i. 36 “palsied ,” Troil. II. ii. 104 “wrinkled eld” † (Ff “old,” Q “elders”); people of olden times Wiv. IV. iv. 37 “The superstitious idleheaded eld.”

elder1.text: “heart of ,” jocular alteration of ‘heart of oak’, = faint heart Wiv. II. iii. 30 .

elder2.text: older (freq.) Mer.V. IV. i. 251 “How much more art thou than thy looks!” ; more advanced, belonging to a later period R2 II. iii. 43 “ days,” Cym. V. i. 14 ;—sb. aged person 2H4 II. iv. 281 , Cæs. I. ii. 7 ; senator Cor. I. i. 232 , II. ii. 47 .

eldest.text: oldest, earliest Tp. V. i. 186 , Err. I. i. 124 , Ham. III. iii. 37 .

elect.text: to pick out, select Meas. I. i. 18 , 1H6 IV. i. 4 .

element.text: (1 this sense colours the whole word) 1. general name for earth, water, air, and fire, which were held in ancient and mediaeval philosophy to be the simple substances of which all material bodies are compounded; hence, a constituent part of a whole, material or immaterial; pl. materials Tp. III. iii. 61 “the e-s Of whom your swords are temper'd,” Ado II. i. 359 “There's little of the melancholy in her,” Tw.N. I. v. 296 , II. iii. 10 “Does not our life consist of the four e-s?,” R2 III. iii. 55 , H5 III. vii. 23 , H8 I. i. 48 * “no ” (=no component part), Troil. I. iii. 41 “the two moist e-s,” Cæs. V. v. 73 “the e-s So mix'd in him,” Ham. IV. vii. 181 , Oth. II. iii. 60 , Ant. II. vii. 51 “the e-s once out of it” (=at its dissolution), V. ii. 291 , Sonn. xlv. 5 .

elf.text: to twist, tangle Lr. II. iii. 10 .

ell.text: 45 inches Err. III. ii. 113 , Rom. II. iv. 91 .

elm.text: with ref. to the practice of training vines on elms Err. II. ii. 178 “Thou art an , my husband, I a vine,” 2H4 II. iv. 363 “thou dead ” (? = poor support).

else.text: (in MND. V. i. 229 “nor ” = nor, as “or ” freq.=or) 1. anything besides, such like John II. i. 276 “Bastards, and else.”

elvish.text: Err. II. ii. 194 “owls, and † sprites” (F1 “Owles and Sprights,” F2 “and Elves Sprights”); elvishmark'd, marked at birth by malignant fairies R3 I. iii. 228 .

emballing.text: probably used in an indelicate sense; explained by comm. as ‘investing with the ball as the emblem of royalty’ H8 II. iii. 47 .

embarquement.text: laying under embargo, (hence) hindrance, impediment Cor. I. x. 22 “E-s all of fury.”

embassade.text: mission as ambassador 3H6 IV. iii. 31 “When you disgrac'd me in my embassade.”

embassador.text: freq. form of ‘ambassador’ in old edd.

embassage.text: errand Ado I. i. 290 , II. i. 280 “do you any to the Pigmies” ; message LLL. V. ii. 98 , R2 III. iv. 93 , R3 II. i. 3 , Sonn. xxvi. 3 “To thee I send this written embassage” (Q1 “ambassage”).

embassy.text: (3 not recorded outside S.) 1. mission of an ambassador LLL. I. i. 133 “comes in ,” John I. i. 99 , Troil. IV. v. 215 .

embattle.text: to draw up in battle array Wiv. II. ii. 265 , John IV. ii. 200 “e-d” (4 syll.) “and rank'd,” H5 IV. ii. 14 ; also intr. to be drawn up Ant. IV. ix. 3 “we shall embattle By the second hour.”

emblaze.text: to set forth, as with a heraldic device 2H6 IV. x. 75 “To emblaze the honour.”

embodied.text: united to another as if in one body All'sW. V. iii. 174 “I by vow am so embodied yours.”

emboss.text: to drive (a hunted animal) to extremity, close round (fig.) All'sW. III. vi. 106 .

embossed1.text: swollen, tumid AYL. II. vii. 67 “ sores,” 1H4 III. iii. 176 “ rascal,” Lr. II. iv. 227 “embossed carbuncle.”

embossed2.text: foaming at the mouth from exhaustion Shr. Ind. i. 17 “the poor cur is e-'d,” Ant. IV. xi. [ xiii. ] 3 “the boar of Thessaly Was never so e-'d”; cf. Tim. V. i. 222 “his embossed froth.”

embowel.text: to disembowel 1H4 V. iv. 109 , 111 , R3 V. ii. 10 ; fig. to empty All'sW. I. iii. 249 .

embrace.text: (1 is not recorded before S.) 1. to welcome as a friend, companion, or the like Cor. IV. vii. 10 , Tim. I. i. 45 , Cym. III. iv. 179 “With joy he will you” ; to welcome or receive (a thing) joyfully Ado I. i. 106 , Tw.N. II. v. 161 [ 150 ], R2 I. iii. 89 “ His golden uncontroll'd enfranchisement,” Troil. IV. i. 14 , Ham. V. ii. 266 ; (hence) to submit to with resignation Wiv. V. v. 263 [ 251 ] “What cannot be eschew'd must be e-'d,” Mac. III. i. 137 “embrace the fate Of that dark hour.”

eminence.text: (not pre-S. in any of its senses) 1. “the of,” the advantage of Troil. II. iii. 269 .

emperial.text: blunder for ‘imperial’ Tit. IV. iv. 40 , for ‘emperor’ Tit. IV. iii. 93 .

empery.text: (1 late exx. of this sense) 1. status of emperor Tit. I. i. 22 , 201

emphasis.text: intensity of feeling Ham. V. i. 277 “whose grief Bears such an ” ; emphatic expression (S.) Ant. I. v. 68 “Be chok'd with such another !.”

empiric.text: quack All'sW. II. i. 125 . ∥ The empirics were an ancient sect of physicians who drew their rules of practice entirely from experience.

empiricutic.headword: empiricutic (S.; coined word put in the mouth of Menenius)
empiricutic.text: empirical, quackish Cor. II. i. 130 “the most sovereign prescription in Galen is but ” (F1 2 “Emperickqutique”; F3 4 “Empericktique,” whence some mod. edd. “empirictic”).

employ.text: to send (a person) with a commission somewhere Ant. III. iii. 36 “I will thee back again,” V. ii. 70 “ me to him,” Cym. II. iii. 68 “To employ you towards this Roman.”

employment.text: （‘business, occupation’ is the usual sense) 1. (one's) service John I. i. 198 “At your employment.”

empoison.text: to destroy Ado III. i. 86 , Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 11

emulation.text: (2 is the most freq. S. use) 1. endeavour or ambition to equal or excel Cor. I. x. 12 , Lucr. 1808 .

emulous.text: (in a good sense) ambitious Troil. IV. i. 28 ; (in a bad sense) envious Troil. II. iii. 81 “ factions,” 245, III. iii. 189 .

enact2.text: vb. (2 echoed in mod. use from S.; 3 Crowley, 1616 , has ‘enact a murder’) 1. to ordain, decree Mer.V. IV. i. 349 , 1H6 V. iv. 123 , Lucr. 529 .

enacture.text: performance, fulfilment Ham. III. ii. 209 “Their own enactures” (Qq; Ff “en(n)actors”).

enchafed.text: excited, irritated Cym. IV. ii. 174 ; furious, angry Oth. II. i. 17 “the enchafed flood.”

enchant.text: to influence as if by a charm, hold spellbound, attract as if by magic 1H6 III. iii. 40 , Oth. I. ii. 63 , Cym. I. vi. 167 , Compl. 128 .

enchantment.text: applied to a person (cf. DREAD sb.) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 447

encompass.text: to outwit, take advantage of, ‘get round’ (S.) Wiv. II. ii. 161 .

encompassment.text: ‘talking round’ a subject (S.) Ham. II. i. 10 “this and drift of question.”

encounter1.text: sb. (the sense of ‘meeting, friendly or hostile’ is the common one; 1, 2, and 3 are only S.) 1. amatory meeting Wiv. III. v. 76 , Meas. III. i. 263 , Ado III. iii. 160 “this amiable ,” IV. i. 94 , All'sW. III. vii. 32 , Troil. III. ii. 217 .

encounter2.text: vb. (the foll. are peculiar to S.) 1. to go to meet Ado I. i. 100 “the fashion of the world is to avoid cost, and you it” ; used bombastically= to go towards Tw.N. III. i. 83 “Will you the house?.”

end1.text: sb. (some obs. or unusual phrases are given below; see also AN-END, LATTER END) 1. extremity, extreme part; “at the arm's end,” at arm's length AYL. II. vi. 10 ; “at the stave's end” Tw.N. V. i. 295 .

end2.text: to get (a crop) in Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 37 “I . . . holp to reap the fame Which he did end all his” (= garner as all his own). ∥ Current in Warwickshire, Worcestershire, and Herefordshire.

endart.text: to shoot as a dart Rom. I. iii. 98 .

endeared.text: (2 a common 17th c. sense) 1. enhanced in value, made more precious John IV. ii. 228 “to be endeared to a king,” Sonn. xxxi. 1 .

ender.text: “my origin and ,” my beginning and my end, source of my life and death Compl. 222 .

ending.text: vbl. sb. death John V. vii. 5 , H5 IV. i. 166 , Lucr. 1612 ; ppl. adj. dying 2H4 IV. v. 78 .

endurance.text: (occurs thrice; also “indurance in” old and mod. edd.; 2 the phrase is taken from Foxe's account of Cranmer's trial; 3 not pre-S.) 1. patience Ado II. i. 248 “past the of a block.”

endure.text: used with adverbial phrase or complement to denote continuance in a place or state Cor. I. vi. 58 “to friends,” Lucr. 1659 “my mind . . . still pure Doth in her poison'd closet yet endure.”

enemy.text: the devil Meas. II. ii. 180 , Tw.N. II. ii. 29 ; — as adj.=hostile Mer.V. IV. i. 448 “hold out for ever,” Cor. IV. iv. 24 “This town,” Lr. V. iii. 222 , Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 71

enew.text: to drive (a fowl) into the water Meas. III. i. 89 “Whose . . . deliberate word . . . follies doth As falcon doth the fowl” (Ff misprinted “emmew,” some mod. edd. “enmew”). ∥ An old hawking term.

enforce.text: (also “inforce”; the sense of compelling the observance of a law is post-S.) 1. to drive by force 2H4 IV. i. 71 “e-'d from our most quiet sphere By the rough torrent of occasion,” H5 IV. vii. 66 “as swift as stones E-d from the old Assyrian slings.”

enforced.text: (also “inforced” in old and mod. edd.) 1. ravished, violated MND. III. i. 209 “some chastity,” Tit. V. iii. 38 , Cym. IV. i. 19 , Lucr. 668 .

enforcement.text: compulsion, constraint 2H4 I. i. 120 , R3 III. vii. 231 ; violation R3 III. vii. 8 , Lucr. 1623 .

enfranchise.text: (2 is freq.) 1. to set free from political subjection Ant. I. i. 23 .

enfree.text: to set free Troil. IV. i. 38 ; so enfreedom LLL. III. i. 130 .

engage.text: (the S. uses are the foll.) 1. to pledge, pawn, mortgage Tim. II. ii. 156 “let all my land be sold.—'Tis all e-'d” ; to keep as a hostage 1H4 IV. iii. 95 , V. ii. 43 .

engagement.text: what one is pledged to do Cæs. II. i. 307 “All my engagements I will construe to thee.”

engild.text: to brighten with golden light MND. III. ii. 187 .

engine.text: (the following are the only S. senses) 1. artifice, contrivance, device, plot All'sW. III. v. 20 “all these e-s of lust,” Tit. II. i. 123 , Oth. IV. ii. 221 “engines for my life.”

enginer.text: (1 most mod. edd. “ingener”) 1. inventor Oth. II. i. 65 (F1 “Ingeniuer”).

engirt1.text: to surround, encircle 2H6 V. i. 99 “ these brows,” Ven. 364 “engirts so white a foe.”

engirt2.text: surrounded, beset (lit. and fig.) 2H6 III. i. 200 “My body round with misery,” Lucr. 221 , 1173 “Grossly engirt with daring infamy.”

englut.text: to swallow up H5 IV. iii. 83 , Oth. I. iii. 57 .

engraffed.text: implanted, firmly fixed Lr. I. i. 301 (Ff1 2 “ingraffed,” Qq1 2 “ingrafted”), Oth. II. iii. 146 (F1 “ingraft”); closely attached “to” 2H4 II. ii. 69 .

engrafted.text: firmly fixed or rooted Cæs. II. i. 184 “the love he bears to Cæsar,” Sonn. xxxvii. 8 “I make my love engrafted to this store.”

engrave.text: pa. pple. “engrav'd” Gent. II. vii. 4 , 1H6 II. ii. 15 ; “engraven” Lucr. 203 .

engross.text: (old and some mod. edd. also “ingross”) 1. to write out in a legal hand R3 III. vi. 2 .

enjoin.text: to bind (a person) as by an oath or obligation (“to” do something) Ado V. i. 291 “any heavy weight That he'll me to,” Mer.V. II. ix. 9 “e-'d by oath to observe three things,” All'sW. III. v. 94 “e-'d penitents,” Wint. III. iii. 52 .

enjoy.text: to have the possession or use of John II. i. 240 , Ant. II. vi. 78 (do not part with), Sonn. xxix. 8 ; absol. R2 II. iv. 14 “to by rage and war.”

enkindle.text: fig. to incite Mac. I. iii. 121 .

enlarge.text: (doubtful sense in Sonn. lxx. 12 ; ? 2) 1. to widen the limits or scope of, give free scope to, extend Wiv. II. ii. 236 “she e-th her mirth,” AYL. III. ii. 152 “fill'd With all graces wide e-'d,” 2H4 I. i. 204 , Troil. V. ii. 35 , Ham. V. i. 248 “Her obsequies have been as far e-'d” . . .; to give vent to Cæs. IV. ii. 46 “enlarge your griefs.”

enlargement.text: (1 is the usual S. use) 1. release from confinement LLL. III. i. 5 , 1H4 III. i. 31 , 1H6 II. v. 30 , 3H6 IV. vi. 5 .

enlighten.text: to shed lustre upon Sonn. clii. 11 .

enow.text: pl. form of ‘enough’ Mer.V. III. v. 23 , H5 IV. i. 243 “we have French quarrels ,” IV. ii. 28 , IV. iii. 20 , 1H6 V. iv. 56 , Mac. IV. ii. 55 , Ant. I. iv. 11 .

enpatron.text: to have under one's patronage Compl. 224 “Since I their altar, you enpatron me.”

enpierced.text: pierced Rom. I. iv. 19 (Qq F1 “enpearced,” Ff2 3 “impearced,” F4 “impierced”).

enraged.text: maddened with love or desire, ardent Ado II. iii. 112 “she loves him with an affection,” Ven. 29 , 317 ; violent 2H4 I. i. 144 “my limbs . . . being now enrag'd with grief.”

enrank.text: to draw up in battle array 1H6 I. i. 115 .

enridged.text: thrown into ridges Lr. IV. vi. 72 “wav'd like the enridged sea” (Qq1 2; F1 “enraged”).

enrolled.text: written, as a deed, on a roll or parchment LLL. I. i. 38 , &c.

enrooted.text: entangled as root with root (S.) 2H4 IV. i. 207 “His foes are so enrooted with his friends.”

ensconce.text: (old edd. also “insconce”; not pre-S.; in mod. use chiefly a revival from S.) 1. to shelter behind or within a ‘sconce’, earthwork, or fortification, (hence fig.) Wiv. II. ii. 28 , Err. II. ii. 38 , All'sW. II. iii. 4 , Lucr. 1515 “therein so e-'d his secret evil,” Sonn. xlix. 9 .

enseamed.text: (properly) loaded with grease, greased; (hence fig.) Ham. III. iv. 92 .

ensear.text: to dry up Tim. IV. iii. 188 .

enskied.text: placed in heaven Meas. I. iv. 34 .

ensue.text: (rare use in Wint. IV. Chor. [ i. ] 25 “what of her ensues”=what becomes of her) 1. to follow upon, succeed R2 II. i. 198 “Let not tomorrow then ensue to-day,” Lucr. 502 .

entail1.text: succession of estate; phrase “cut the ” All'sW. IV. iii. 316 .

entail2.text: to bestow as an inalienable possession 3H6 I. i. 194 “I here The crown to thee” ; to appoint (a person) heir 3H6 I. i. 235 “To him and his heirs unto the crown.”

enter1.text: entrance on the stage LLL. V. i. 145 .

enter2.text: vb. (the ordinary physical senses occur) 1. intr. and pass. to bind oneself by a bond, &c. Err. IV. iv. 127 “I am here e-ed in bond for you,” R2 V. ii. 65 “some bond he's e-ed into” : to engage “in” Ado II. iii. 214 [ 203 ] “ into a quarrel,” Oth. III. iii. 412 “enter'd in this cause.”

entertain2.text: vb. (4 the current mod. meaning of ‘amuse’ does not emerge) 1. to keep up, maintain (a state of things) Meas. III. i. 73 , Mer.V. I. i. 90 , Lucr. 1514 .

entertainer.text: one who cherishes a feeling Tp. II. i. 17 .

entertainment.text: (2 cf. note on ENTERTAIN) 1. maintaining a person in one's service, employ All'sW. III. vi. 12 , IV. i. 17 “i' the adversary's ,” Cor. IV. iii. 49 , Oth. III. iii. 250 , Ant. IV. vi. 17 “, but No honourable trust.”

entire.text: (stressed “e'ntire” when immediately preceding a monosyllabic sb. or one stressed on the first syll. LLL. II. i. 130 , 2H4 II. iv. 357 ; otherwise “enti're”) 1. unmixed, pure 2H4 II. iv. 357 “pure fear and cowardice,” Lr. I. i. 243 * “Aloof from the point.”

entirely.text: (2 a common sense 1340-1720) 1. without intermission Meas. IV. ii. 157 .

entitled.text: having a claim to or upon LLL. V. ii. 820 “Neither in the other's heart,” Sonn. xxxvii. 7 “Entitled in thy parts.” See also INTITULED.

entrance.text: (3 syll. in Rom. I. iv. 8 , Per. II. iii. 64 old edd. “enterance,” and Mac. I. v. 40 ): 1H4 I. i. 5 “the thirsty of this soil,” ‘the parched surface of the earth’; Shr. II. i. 54 “for an ,” as an entrance fee.

entreasured.text: stored up 2H4 III. i. 85 , Per. III. ii. 65 .

entreat1.text: entreaty R3 III. vii. 223 (F1 “entreaties”), Tit. I. i. 449 , 483 (F1 “intreats”).

entreat2.text: vb. (the sense ‘ask earnestly’ is the usual one, and occurs with various constructions) 1. to treat R2 III. i. 37 , 2H6 II. iv. 82 , 3H6 I. i. 271 , R3 IV. iv. 152 , Troil. IV. iv. 113 .

entrench.text: to cut All'sW. II. i. 45 “this very sword e-ed it.” ∥ A meaning recorded otherwise only from Spenser ‘A wide wound therein . . . Entrenched deep.’

envenom.text: to kill by poison, (hence) destroy AYL. II. iii. 15 , John III. i. 63 .

envious.text: malicious, spiteful (the more freq. S. sense) LLL. I. i. 100 “an sneaping frost,” R2 II. i. 62 “the siege,” 2H6 III. i. 157 “The load” (=load of malice), Ham. IV. vii. 174 .

envy1.text: sb.; ill-will, malice (freq.) Tp. I. ii. 258 , Mer.V. IV. i. 10 “carry me Out of his e-'s reach,” Tw.N. II. i. 31 , 3H6 III. iii. 127 “Exempt from ,” R3 IV. i. 99 “Whom envy hath immur'”

envy2.text: Cor. III. iii. 56 “Rather than you,” rather than such as show malice towards you; 93 “Envied against,” showed malice towards. ∥ The stressing varies “e'nvy, envy'.”

enwombed.text: born of (my) womb All'sW. I. iii. 152 .

epicure.text: luxurious person, sybarite Mac. V. iii. 8 “mingle with the English epicures,” Ant. II. vii. 59 .

epigram.text: short poem ending with a witty or ingenious turn of thought Ado V. iv. 103 .

epileptic.text: ‘distorted and pale like that of a man in a fit of epilepsy’ (Wright) Lr. II. ii. 86 .

epithet.text: term, phrase, expression (S.) Ado V. ii. 69 “‘Suffer love,’ a good !,” LLL. IV. ii. 8 , V. i. 17 , V. ii. 171 , Oth. I. i. 14 “epithets of war.”

epitheton.text: adjective indicating some characteristic quality or attribute LLL. I. ii. 15 (Q1 “apethaton,” F1 Q2 “apathaton”).

epitome.text: representation in miniature (not pre-S.) Cor. V. iii. 68 .

equal1.text: 1. forming a perfect balance or counterpoise Meas. II. iv. 69 “ poise” (=equipoise), Mer.V. I. iii. 150 “an pound” (=an exact pound), 2H4 IV. i. 67 “ balance,” 2H6 II. i. 202 “justice' scales,” Ham. I. ii. 13 ; fig. equally balanced AYL. I. ii. 190 “a more enterprise,” Lucr. 1791 .

equinox.text: equal length of days and nights (used fig.) Oth. II. iii. 130 .

equipage.text: “of better ,” more richly equipped Sonn. xxxii. 12 ; cf. “in ,” a military phrase meaning orig. ‘in military array’, used by Pistol app. fig. in Wiv. II. ii. 4 (Qq).

equivalent.text: equal in power Per. V. i. 92 .

equivocal.text: ambiguous Oth. I. iii. 217 ; expressing himself ambiguously All'sW. V. iii. 252 .

ergo1.text: therefore Err. IV. iii. 56 . ∥ Cf. ARGAL.

eringo.text: candied root of sea holly, Eryngium maritimum, formerly used as a sweetmeat and regarded as an aphrodisiac Wiv. V. v. 23 .

erroneous.text: deviating from the path of right, criminal 3H6 II. v. 90 ; misguided R3 I. iv. 204 .

error.text: transgression, wrongdoing Gent. V. iv. 111 , LLL. V. ii. 779 , Sonn. cxvii. 9 .

erst.text: once upon a time, formerly H5 V. ii. 48 .

escape.text: (both uses are peculiarly S.) 1. sally (of wit) Meas. IV. i. 64 .

eschew.text: to keep clear of, escape Wiv. V. v. 263 .

escot.text: to pay a reckoning for, maintain Ham. II. ii. 370 “how are they escoted?.”

esperance.text: hope Troil. V. ii. 118 , Lr. IV. i. 4 ; the motto of the Percy family used as a battle cry 1H4 II. iii. 76 , V. ii. 96 “Now, ! Percy! and set on.”

espial.text: spy 1H6 I. iv. 8 , IV. iii. 6 , Ham. III. i. 32 .

espouse.text: to unite in marriage 2H6 I. i. 9 ; fig. H5 IV. vi. 26 “e-'d to death,” Lucr. 20 “espoused to more fame.”

esquire.text: a man belonging to the higher order of English gentry, ranking immediately below a knight H5 I. i. 14 “Six thousand and two hundred good e-s,” IV. viii. 109 “Davy Gam, esquire.”

essence.text: (occurs 4 times in S.) 1. life, existence Phœn. 26

essentially.text: in one's essential nature 2H6 V. ii. 39 ; in fact, really (S.) 1H4 II. iv. 548 , Ham. III. iv. 187 “I am not in madness, But mad in craft.”

estate1.text: sb. (1 and 4 are the commonest uses) 1. state or condition Mer.V. III. ii. 317 “my is very low,” R2 III. iv. 42 , H5 IV. i. 100 “what thinks he of our ?,” Cor. II. i. 127 , Lr. V. iii. 211 “seen me in my worst ” ; Tw.N. V. i. 405 “man's ” (= manhood); spec. good or settled condition Mac. V. v. 50 .

estate2.text: to settle or bestow “upon” Tp. IV. i. 85 , MND. I. i. 98 , AYL. V. ii. 13 .

esteem1.text: 1. supposed or estimated value All'sW. V. iii. 1 .

esteem2.text: to estimate the value of, value Cym. I. iv. 90 “What do you it at?”

estimable.text: valuable Mer.V. I. iii. 167 ;— Tw.N. II. i. 28 “estimable wonder” (=admiring judgement).

estimate.text: (2 not pre-S., and rare) 1. valuation, value Troil. II. ii. 54 , Tim. I. i. 14 , Sonn. lxxxvii. 2 ; All'sW. II. i. 183 “in thee hath ” (has a claim to be considered in appraising thee).

estimation.text: (4 is purely S.) 1. value, worth Ado II. ii. 25 , Mer.V. II. vii. 26 , All'sW. V. iii. 4 (cf. ESTEEM sb. 1).

estridge.text: ostrich 1H4 IV. i. 98 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 196

eternal.text: Ham. I. v. 21 * “this blazon” (=revelation of eternity), Ant. V. i. 66 “Would be ” (=would be eternally recorded);—‘used to express extreme abhorrence’ (Schmidt) Cæs. I. ii. 159 “Th' devil,” Ham. V. ii. 379 “in thine cell,” Oth. IV. ii. 130 “some villain” ;—adv. Wint. I. ii. 65 “to be boy eternal.”

eterne.text: eternal Mac. III. ii. 38 , Ham. II. ii. 520 [ 512 ].

eunuch.text: in Cor. III. ii. 114 “a pipe Small as an ” usu. taken as=“eunuch's”†, but perhaps the ref. is to the ‘eunuch flute’, in playing which the performer hums through a hole.

even.text: vb. (occurs thrice, in senses only S.) 1. pass. to be even or quits “with” Oth. II. i. 311 .

even1.text: adj. (the foll. uses are now obs.) 1. uniform R2 III. iv. 36 .

even2.text: adv. (employed in the foll. obs. or archaic uses; often contracted “e'en”) 1. in exact agreement Tw.N. V. i. 249 “as the rest goes ,” Cym. I. iv. 50 “to go with what I heard.”

evenly.text: in a straight line, directly (S.) 1H4 III. i. 104 “run In a new channel, fair and ,” H5 II. iv. 91 “ deriv'd From his most fam'd of famous ancestors” ; in an even direction or position “with” Ado II. ii. 7 .

event.text: outcome, issue, consequence Tp. I. ii. 117 , Meas. III. ii. 258 * “leave we him to his e-s” (=the issue of his affairs), Shr. III. ii. 130 “after him, and see the of this,” R2 II. i. 215 , Cor. II. i. 289 * , Ham. IV. iv. 41 * , 50 ∥ The sense of ‘happening, occurrence’ is recorded first from S., Tit. V. iii. 204 .

ever.text: (often contracted E'ER; obs. or arch. senses are) 1. throughout all time, eternally, ‘for ever’ (freq.) Tp. IV. i. 122 “Let me live here ,” Mac. V. iii. 21 “Will cheer me ever or disseat me now.”

everlasting.text: (1 cf. Gent. V. iv. 81 ; 2 cf. ‘I would . . . get mee an euerlasting robe, . . . and turne Serieant,’ Fletcher ‘Woman Hater’ IV. ii.) 1. “the Everlasting,” God, Ham. I. ii. 131 .

evermore.text: with negative=at any time H8 II. iv. 129 “no, nor ,” Sonn. xxxvi. 9 “not evermore.”

every.text: adj.=either, each H8 II. iv. 50 “a wise council to them Of realm” ; with pl. sb.=all severally Tp. V. i. 249 “ These happen'd accidents” ;—sb.= every one AYL. V. iv. 179 “ of this happy number,” Ant. I. ii. 40 “every of your wishes.”

evidence.text: witness or witnesses Ado IV. i. 37 , 2H6 III. ii. 21 “true , of good esteem,” Lr. III. vi. 38 “Bring in their ,” Lucr. 1650 “came ” (=came as a witness); treated as a pl. R3 I. iv. 192 “Where are the ?” (Ff).

evident.text: indubitable, certain, conclusive Cor. IV. vii. 52 , V. iii. 112 “We must find An calamity,” Cym. II. iv. 120 “some corporal sign about her, More evident than this.” ∥ A 16th-17th cent. use.

evil1.text: sb. 1 (1 the commonest S. sense) 1. sin, crime Meas. II. ii. 91 “to do that ,” R3 I. ii. 76 “Of these supposed e-s” (Ff “Crimes) . . . to acquit myself,” Lucr. 972 “the dire thought of his committed evil.”

evil2.text: of uncertain meaning Meas. II. ii. 172 , H8 II. i. 67 ; interpreted by comm. as ‘jakes, privy’, but the meaning ‘hovel’ would suit equally well.

evil3.headword: evil adj. (about 20 instances; much less freq. than the adj. ILL)
evil3.text: occas. uses: ill-boding Troil. I. iii. 92 “planets ” ; unwholesome R3 I. i. 139 “an diet” ;— adv. 3H6 IV. vii. 84 , H8 I. ii. 207 , Lr. I. i. 169 .

evilly.text: with difficulty, reluctantly, impatiently John III. iv. 149 * “This act so borne” (some mod. edd. “born”); inappropriately, unproperly Tim. IV. iii. 470 “good deeds evilly bestow'”

exact.text: for stress cf. ENTIRE; 1H4 IV. i. 46 “the e'xact wealth of all our states,” Troil. IV. v. 231 “with e'xact view,” Ham. V. ii. 19 “an exa'ct command,” Lr. I. iv. 289 “the most exa'ct regard;—the exact,” the precise, the actual All'sW. III. vi. 64 .

exactly.text: perfectly, completely Ham. I. ii. 200 “Armed at points , cap-a-pe” ; in express terms R2 I. i. 140 “I . . . exactly begg'd Your Grace's pardon.”

exalt.text: refl. to be elated with pride Lr. V. iii. 68 .

exalted.text: raised, high Cæs. I. i. 64 “exalted shores.”

example1.text: parallel case in the past John III. iv. 13 .

example2.text: vb. (2 a late 16th cent. sense) 1. to give an example of LLL. III. i. 89 , Sonn. lxxxiv. 4 .

exceed.text: intr. to be greater or better (than something else), to be superior or pre-eminent Ado III. iv. 17 , Per. II. iii. 16 , Lucr. 229 “The guilt being great, the fear doth still exceed.”

excellent.text: surpassing, exceptionally great, exceeding (used in a bad sense) R3 IV. iv. 52 “That grand tyrant” Tit. II. iii. 7 , Lr. I. ii. 132 , Ant. I. i. 40 “ falsehood!” ;—adv. eminently, extremely Ado III. i. 98 “an good name,” Ham. II. ii. 174 .

excellently.text: exceedingly Ado III. iv. 13 “I like the new tire within ,” Troil. IV. i. 24 “love . . . more ”

except1.text: (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. intr. to make objection Gent. I. iii. 83 , II. iv. 155 , Tw.N. I. iii. 7 “let her before e-ed” (a legal phrase ‘exceptis excipiendis’ perverted).

except2.text: (without ‘that’) All'sW. IV. iii. 303 “more . . . I know not; . . . he had the honour” . . ., R2 I. iv. 6 .

exception.text: (the sense of ‘something excepted’ occurs in 1H4 I. iii. 78 “proviso and ” ) 1. objection (to a person's status or fitness) H5 IV. ii. 25 .

exceptless.text: making no exception Tim. IV. iii. 504 .

exchange1.text: (3 these are inaccurate uses) 1. reciprocal giving and receiving; phrase “make (an) ” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 650, Rom. II. iii. 62 ; “in of” (=for) Wiv. II. ii. 248 , 1H4 IV. ii. 14 ; “in right great ,” in exchange for persons of great importance Troil. III. iii. 21 ; of passes in fencing Ham. V. ii. 283 “in answer of the third exchange.”

exchange2.text: (1 cf. ‘She . . . death for life exchanged foolishlie,’ Spenser, Faerie Queene VII. vi. 6) 1. to obtain in exchange “for” LLL. IV. i. 84 .

excitement.text: incentive, encouragement Troil. I. iii. 182 “Excitements to the field,” Ham. IV. iv. 58 .

exclaim1.text: outcry R2 I. ii. 2 , Troil. V. iii. 91 .

exclaim2.text: “ against,” protest against, rail at Ham. II. ii. 375 , Oth. II. iii. 316 , Lucr. 757 , Compl. 313 ; “ on,” accuse loudly, blame Mer.V. III. ii. 175 , R3 III. iii. 15 , Ven. 930 “e-s on Death,” Lucr. 741 .

exclamation.text: loud complaint, ‘vociferous reproach’ (J.) John II. i. 558 , R3 IV. iv. 154 .

excrement.text: outgrowth (of hair) Err. II. ii. 81 , LLL. V. i. 112 “with my , with my mustachio,” Mer.V. III. ii. 87 “valour's ” (=a brave man's beard), Ham. III. iv. 120 “like life in excrements.”

excuse1.text: indulgence, pardon Shr. Ind. ii. 126 “I hope this reason stands for my ,” Cor. I. iii. 114 “Give me , good madam,” V. v. [ vi. ] 69, Lucr. 235 , 1715

excuse2.text: vb. (the foll. are uses now obs.) 1. to seek to extenuate (a fault); used with a clause Err. III. i. 92 “she will well Why at this time the doors are made against you” ; absol. MND. V. i. 364 “Never excuse.”

execute.text: (the commoner uses are to ‘carry into effect’, of which sense 1 is an extension, and ‘inflict capital punishment on’, of which sense 2 is an extension) 1. to give practical effect to (a passion, &c.), allow to operate Tp. I. ii. 104 “e-ing th' outward face of royalty” (=‘acting as a king to all appearance’), LLL. V. ii. 853 , R3 I. iv. 71 “ thy wrath,” Cym. III. v. 147 ; to bring (a weapon) into play Troil. V. vii. 6 “ your aims” ; absol. Oth. II. iii. 230 “To upon him.”

execution.text: giving practical effect to a passion, &c.; exercise (of powers) 3H6 II. ii. 111 “The of my big-swoln heart,” Troil. I. iii. 210 , Lr. I. i. 139 , Oth. III. iii. 467 “The of his wit, hands, heart.”

executioner.text: murderer 2H6 III. i. 276 , R3 I. ii. 186 .

executor.text: (the testamentary sense is used fig. in Sonn. iv. 14 ; stressed “e'xecutor” in sense 2) 1. performer, agent Tp. III. i. 13 .

exempt.text: cut off, debarred, excluded Err. II. ii. 175 “from me ,” AYL. II. i. 15 “ from public haunt,” 1H6 II. iv. 93 , Tim. IV. ii. 31 “from wealth ”

exempted.text: “ be from me,” far be it from me All'sW. II. i. 198 .

exercise.text: (the general meaning of ‘practice’ is the most usual; 4 cf. ‘Sermons, commonly termed by some Prophesies or Exercises,’ Canons of the Church, 1604 ; for Tp. I. ii. 328 * see the comm.) 1. habitual practice or employment Wint. I. ii. 166 “He's all my ,” 3H6 IV. vi. 85 “hunting was his daily ”

exhalation.text: meteor John III. iv. 153 , H8 III. ii. 227 “fall Like a bright in the evening,” Cæs. II. i. 44 .

exhale.text: to draw forth R3 I. ii. 58 , 166 ; esp. of the sun drawing up vapours and thereby producing meteors LLL. IV. iii. 70 “thou, fair sun, . . . E-'st this vapour-vow,” 1H4 V. i. 19 “an e-'d meteor,” Rom. III. v. 13 “some meteor that the sun e-s” ; in the language of Pistol, absol.=‘draw!’ H5 II. i. 66 .

exhaust.text: to draw forth Tim. IV. iii. 120 .

exhibit.text: to submit (a petition, bill) for inspection or consideration Wiv. II. i. 29 “ a bill in the parliament,” Meas. IV. iv. 11 , 1H6 III. i. 150 . ∥ Misused for ‘inhibit’ in Mer.V. II. iii. 10 * .

exhibiter.text: presenter of a bill H5 I. i. 74 .

exhibition.text: (1 in use from 15th c. to Swift's time) 1. allowance of money for a person's support Gent. I. iii. 69 “What maintenance he . . . receives, Like thou shalt have,” Lr. I. ii. 25 , Oth. I. iii. 238 .

exigent.text: state of pressing need, emergency, strait Cæs. V. i. 19 , Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 63; (spec.) end 1H6 II. v. 9 “These eyes . . . Wax dim, as drawing to their exigent.”

exile3.text: stressed “exi'le”; but in attrib. use the pa. pple. is “e'xiled” Mac. V. vii. 95 [ viii. 66 ], Lucr. 640 : cf. EXHALED.

exorcism.text: calling up spirits, conjuration 2H6 I. iv. 5 ; so exorcist All'sW. V. iii. 309 , Cæs. II. i. 323 , exorcizer (F1 “Exorcisor”) Cym. IV. ii. 276 .

expect2.headword: expect vb. (not pre-Eliz. in any sense)
expect2.text: to wait for, await Gent. I. i. 54 , Mer.V. V. i. 49 , 1H6 V. iii. 144 “here I will thy coming,” Ant. IV. iv. 23 , Per. I. iv. 94 .

expectance.text: state of waiting to know (something) Troil. IV. v. 145 “ . . . What further you will do.”

expectancy.text: expectation Oth. II. i. 41 ; source of hope Ham. III. i. 161 (Qq “expectation”).

expectation.text: waiting 2H4 V. ii. 31 “You stand in coldest ,” Cæs. I. i. 45 “with patient ,” Lr. IV. iv. 23 “our preparation stands In of them” ; phrase “full of ,” full of promise, hopeful, promising 1H4 II. iii. 22 ; cf. Ham. III. i. 161 (Qq).

expecter.text: one who waits Troil. IV. v. 155 .

expedience.text: (not pre-S.; both senses only S.) 1. speed, dispatch R2 II. i. 287 , H5 IV. iii. 70 .

expedient.text: speedy, expeditious John II. i. 60 , 223 , IV. ii. 268 * “with all haste” (cf. “with the speediest expedition” Gent. I. iii. 37 ), R2 I. iv. 39 , 2H6 III. i. 288 , R3 I. ii. 217 * . ∥ “Expeditious” occurs only once Tp. V. i. 315 .

expedition.text: hence “in ,” in motion, in progress H5 II. ii. 191 “Putting it straight in expedition.”

expense.text: （‘cost, charge’ is the most freq. sense) 1. spending (of money), esp. extravagant expenditure Wiv. II. ii. 149 , Lr. II. i. 102 “ and waste” (so Q2; Q1 “wast and spoyle”), Sonn. xciv. 6 .

experimental.text: “with seal,” ‘setting the stamp of experience upon the results of his reading’ Ado IV. i. 168 .

expert.text: (in passive sense) tried, proved by experience Oth. II. i. 49 “ and approv'd allowance.”

expiate1.text: (of an appointed time) fully come R3 III. iii. 23 “the hour of death is ” (Ff2 3 4 “now expir'd,” Qq “the limit of your liues is out”).

expiate2.text: (said of death) to end (one's days) Sonn. xxii. 4 “Then look I death my days should ”

expire.text: to bring to an end, conclude Rom. I. iv. 110 “Shall . . . the term Of a despised life.”

exploit.text: spec. military enterprise All'sW. I. ii. 17 “sick For breathing and ,” IV. i. 41 “in ” (=in action).

expostulate.text: to set forth one's views, discourse, discuss Gent. III. i. 252 , 3H6 II. v. 135 , R3 III. vii. 191 , Ham. II. ii. 86 “to What majesty should be,” Oth. IV. i. 216 .

exposture.text: exposure Cor. IV. i. 36 . ∥ “Exposure” (not pre-S.) occurs twice.

express1.text: (a) exact, fitted to its purpose, (b) well framed or modelled Ham. II. ii. 325 * “in form, in moving, how and admirable!” ∥ Stressed “expre'ss” and “e'xpress”; cf. ENTIRE.

express2.text: to manifest, reveal, betoken Shr. II. i. 77 , 2H6 I. i. 18 “I can no kinder sign of love Than this kind kiss,” Cor. I. iii. 1 , Tit. I. i. 422 “hath e-'d himself . . . A father and a friend to thee,” Ham. I. iii. 71 “Costly thy habit . . . But not e-'d in fancy,” Lr. IV. iii. 19 .

expressive.text: open and emphatic in expressing sentiments All'sW. II. i. 53 .

expressure.text: (not pre-S.; 2 peculiar to S.) 1. expression Tw.N. II. iii. 174 “the of his eye,” Troil. III. iii. 205 “more divine Than breath or pen can give expressure to.”

exquisite.text: sought out, in geniously devised Tw.N. I. v. 182 , II. iii. 159 “I have no exquisite reason for '”

exsufflicate.text: (?) puffed up, inflated, ‘windy’ Oth. III. iii. 182 .

extemporal.text: impromptu, extempore LLL. I. ii. 192 “some god of rime,” IV. ii. 50 , 1H6 III. i. 6 “ speech” ; so extemporally adv. Ant. V. ii. 216 , Ven. 836 . ∥ “Extempore” is also S.

extend.text: (3 an extension of the legal sense ‘to take possession of by a writ of extent’; cf. EXTENT 1) 1. to prolong in duration Mac. III. iv. 57 .

extent.text: (2 is a transferred use of 1) 1. seizure of lands in execution of a writ AYL. III. i. 17 “let my officers . . . Make an upon his . . . lands.”

extenuate.text: (both were freq. 16-17th cent. uses) 1. to mitigate (a law) MND. I. i. 120 .

extern.text: external, outward Oth. I. i. 63 ; only S. as sb.=outward appearance, exterior Sonn. cxxv. 2 .

extinct.text: extinguished, quenched R2 I. iii. 222 , Ham. I. iii. 118 “these blazes . . . in both.”

extincted.text: =prec. Oth. II. i. 81 “Give renew'd fire to our extincted spirits.”

extirp.text: to root out, extirpate Meas. III. ii. 112 “to extirp it” [a vice] “quite,” 1H6 III. iii. 24 .

extirpate.text: to drive completely “out of” Tp. I. ii. 125 .

extort.text: MND. III. ii. 160 “ A poor soul's patience,” ‘wrest it from her, make her impatient.’

extravagancy.text: vagrancy Tw.N. II. i. 12 “My determinate voyage is mere extravagancy.”

extravagant.text: straying, roaming, vagrant LLL. IV. ii. 68 , Ham. I. i. 154 “ and erring spirit,” Oth. I. i. 137 .

extreme.text: one third of the instances are in the superlative form “e-st”; for the stress cf. ENTIRE, LLL. V. ii. 748 “The e'xtreme part of time,” Sonn. cxxix. 4 “Savage, extre'me, rude, cruel” ;—sb. not preS. in the phrases “in the ” ( Oth. V. ii. 345 ), “in e-s” ( 3H6 III. ii. 115 ), “break into . . . e-s” ( Tit. III. i. 215 ).

extremity.text: (obs. or archaic senses, for most of which ‘extreme’ would be the modern equivalent) 1. extreme or utmost degree Err. I. i. 141 “the of dire mishap,” Lr. V. iii. 209 “another . . . would make much more, And top ,” Lucr. 969 “Devise extremes beyond ,” Sonn. li. 6 “swift ” (=the extreme of swiftness); phrase “in ,” in the highest degree MND. III. ii. 3 “Which she must dote on in ,” Ham. III. ii. 180 .

eyas.text: young hawk taken from the nest for the purpose of training, or one whose training is incomplete; fig. Ham. II. ii. 363 [ 355 ] “an aerie of children, little e-s” (F1 “Yases”); so eyas-musket, used jocularly of a sprightly child Wiv. III. iii. 22 . ∥ “ ” is literally a ‘nest-bird’ (‘an eyas’=‘a nyas’, which is ultimately from Latin ‘nidus’ nest); “musket” is the male of the sparrow-hawk.

eye1.text: sb. (archaic pl. “eyne” 11 times for rhyme, but not rhyming in Per. III. Gower 5 , Lucr. 1229 ) 1. the organ of sight; phr. “put the finger in the eye” (like a child weeping) Err. II. ii. 208 ; phr. referring to drunkenness Tp. III. ii. 10 “thy eyes are almost set in thy head” ; fig. MND. III. ii. 435 “sorrow's eye,” Tim. V. i. 26 “opens the eyes of expectation,” Lr. IV. iv. 15 “close the eye of anguish.”

eye2.text: to appear to the eye (S.) Ant. I. iii. 97 .

eyestrings.text: muscles, nerves, or tendons of the eye, supposed to crack at death or loss of sight Cym. I. iii. 17 .

fa.text: the fourth note of the scale LLL. IV. ii. 104 ; used jocularly as a vb. Rom. IV. v. 121 “I'll re you, I'll fa you.”

face1.text: there are various transf. and fig. uses; of the heavens Mer.V. II. vii. 45 , Rom. IV. v. 41 “to see this morning's ,” Sonn. xxxiii. 6 ; of the earth R2 III. iii. 97 “the flower of England's ,” R3 V. iii. 267 “the earth's cold ” ; of immaterial things (=appearance) John V. ii. 88 “to know the face of right,” Cæs. V. i. 10 , Lr. III. i. 20 ;—phr. “from to foot” Cor. II. ii. 113 , “full of ,” (? beautiful, or florid) Per. I. Gower 23 , John V. ii. 159 “turn thy ” (=depart).

face2.text: vb. (1 a 16th cent. use) 1. to show a false face, maintain a false appearance 1H6 V. iii. 141 “flatter, face, or feign.”

facinerious.text: infamous, vile All'sW. II. iii. 36 (mod. edd. “facinorous”†; but Latin ‘facinus’ had a byform ‘faciner-’ of the stem ‘facinor-’; cf. also Old Fr. ‘facinereux’).

facing.text: trimming Meas. III. ii. 11 “craft, being richer than innocency, stands for the facing.”

fact.text: (1 now used only in phrases such as ‘after the fact’, ‘before the fact’) 1. deed, esp. evil deed, crime 1H6 IV. i. 30 “this was infamous,” Mac. III. vi. 10 “damned fact!,” Lucr. 349 .

faction.text: （‘party’ is the most freq. sense) 1. class, set (of persons) Gent. IV. i. 37 , Troil. II. i. 130 “the faction of fools.”

factionary.text: active as a partisan (S.) Cor. V. ii. 30 .

factor.text: agent Ant. II. vi. 10 “factors for the gods.”

faculty.text: (1 an Eliz. sense) 1. personal quality, disposition H8 I. ii. 73 “neither know My faculties nor person.”

fadge.text: to fit, be suitable LLL. V. i. 158 , Tw.N. II. ii. 34 .

fading.text: ‘with a fading’ was the refrain of an indelicate song Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 195 “burthens of dildos and fadings.”

fail1.text: sb. (2 and 3 only S.) 1. failure, omission Wint. II. iii. 169 “the Of any point,” V. i. 27 “fail of issue,” H8 II. iv. 196 .

fail2.text: vb. (2 common down to the Eliz. period) 1. to die H8 I. ii. 184 “had the king in his last sickness f-'”

fain.text: glad, pleased 1H6 III. ii. 114 “ by flight to save themselves,” 2H6 II. i. 8 “man and birds are of climbing high” ; glad under the circumstances Gent. I. i. 128 , AYL. IV. i. 61 , 2H4 II. i. 157 “I must be to pawn . . . my plate” ; (hence) necessitated, obliged Lr. IV. vii. 38 ;—adv. gladly, willingly, always with “would” (freq.).

faint1.text: adj. (2 now only in the proverbial ‘faint heart’; “-hearted, f-ly” and “f-ness” follow the senses of the adj.) 1. inactive, inert, timid Tim. I. ii. 16 , III. i. 58 , III. iii. 25 , Lr. I. iv. 73 “a most faint neglect.”

faint2.text: to lose heart John V. vii. 78 , Ven. 569 “f-s not like a pale-fac'd coward” ; also impers. “it f-s me,” I am depressed H8 II. iii. 103 ; to become feeble MND. II. ii. 35 , AYL. II. iv. 76 “f-s for succour,” Lucr. 1543 ; so 1H6 II. v. 40 “f-ing kiss,” 95 “my f-ing words.”

fair1.text: that which is fair, a beautiful thing Rom. I. i. 237 “they hide the ,” I. iii. 90 , Cym. I. vi. 38 , Lucr. 780 “the supreme ” (viz. the sun); one of the fair sex, a woman, esp. a beloved woman LLL. V. ii. 37 , H5 V. ii. 176 “speak, my ,” Rom. II. Chor. 3 ; applied to a man Ven. 208 ; beauty Err. II. i. 98 “My decayed ,” LLL. IV. i. 17 , MND. I. i. 182 , Sonn. xviii. 7 “every fair from fair sometime declines.”

fair2.text: outside the physical senses of ‘beautiful, clear, bright, unsullied,’ and the immediate fig. uses, is employed very widely as an epithet of praise (cf. the adv. FAIR); uses no longer current are:—as a form of courteous address LLL. V. ii. 311 “Fair sir, God save you!;—Fair day-light” =broad daylight Lr. IV. vii. 52 .

fair3.text: adv. (4 now only in phr. ‘bid, promise fair’) 1. civilly, courteously, kindly (often with the vb. “speak”） Err. III. ii. 188 “so an offer'd chain,” R3 IV. iv. 152 “entreat me ” ; on good terms 2H4 II. i. 211 “tap for tap, and so part fair.”

fairly.text: (2 recorded only from S.) 1. beautifully, handsomely Shr. I. ii. 149 “I'll have them very bound,” Troil. I. iii. 84 , Rom. III. ii. 84 ; in beauty Sonn. v. 4 ; in a neat or elegant hand Shr. III. i. 71 , R3 III. vi. 2 .

fairness.text: “To the of my power,” as fairly as I can Cor. I. ix. 73 .

faith.text: (the commonest uses are) 1. loyalty, fidelity Gent. IV. iii. 26 , MND. III. ii. 127 “Bearing the badge of to prove them true,” 2H6 V. i. 166 “O! where is ? O! where is loyalty?,” H8 II. i. 143 , Cæs. III. i. 137 ; esp. faithfulness in love, true love (freq.).

faithful.text: (the meaning ‘loyal’ is the commonest; 2 cf. ‘This is a faithful saying’, 1 Timothy i. 15 ) 1. believing (in religion) R3 I. iv. 4 .

faithfully.text: (in Mer.V. V. i. 299 “answer all things ” is a formula used in the Court of King's Bench) 1. confidently Tim. III. ii. 46 “urge it half so ”

faithless.text: unbelieving Mer.V. II. iv. 38 “ Jew” ; disloyal John II. i. 230 , H8 II. i. 123 “ service” ; not to be trusted Meas. III. i. 135 “O faithless coward!.”

faitor.text: (properly) impostor, cheat: doubtful word in 2H4 II. iv. 171 (Q “faters,” Ff “Fates”).

falchion.text: (properly) sword more or less curved with the edge on the convex side R3 I. ii. 94 , Lucr. 176 , &c.

falcon.text: female hawk trained for the sport of hawking (contrast TERCEL) Mac. II. iv. 12 , Ven. 1027 .

fall1.text: sb. (of the following less frequent S. uses, 1 and 2 are only S., 3 and 4 are obs.) 1. shedding (of blood) H5 I. ii. 25 .

fall2.text: vb. (3 is used with various complements) 1. (of a river) to discharge itself, fig. Lucr. 653 .

fallacy.text: delusive notion, error Err. II. ii. 190 .

fallible.text: liable to be erroneous Meas. III. i. 169 “hopes that are ” ; blunderingly used in Ant. V. ii. 257 (old edd. “falliable”).

fallow1.text: adj. 1 uncultivated H5 V. ii. 44 “her leas The darnel, hemlock . . . Doth root upon” ;—sb. arable land H5 V. ii. 54 ; ground ploughed and harrowed but left uncropped for a time Meas. I. iv. 42 .

fallow2.text: of pale brownish or reddish yellow colour Wiv. I. i. 92 “your fallow greyhound.”

false.text: ?vb. or adj. in Cym. II. iii. 74 * ; if a vb. ?=betray their trust.

falsehood.text: (obs. meanings are) 1. falseness, faithlessness, perfidy Tp. I. ii. 95 , Gent. IV. ii. 8 “my to my friend,” Wint. III. ii. 142 “this is mere ,” John III. i. 95 , 277 , Troil. IV. ii. 107 “Make Cressid's name the very crown of falsehood.”

falsely.text: wrongly John IV. ii. 198 “ thrust upon contrary feet,” Oth. V. ii. 115 “O! , murder'd,” Sonn. cxlviii. 4 ; perfidiously, treacherously Tp. II. i. 71 , Meas. II. iv. 48 , Cor. III. i. 59 “laid I' the plain way of his merit,” Ham. II. ii. 67 “ borne in hand” ; improperly R3 V. iii. 252 * “England's chair, where he is falsely set.”

falsify.text: to prove (expectations) to be illfounded 1H4 I. ii. 233 “falsify men's hopes.”

fame1.text: common talk or report, rumour 1H6 II. iii. 68 “thou art no less than hath bruited,” H8 I. iv. 66 , Ant. II. ii. 169 ; personified Ado II. i. 223 “I have played the part of Lady Fame.”

fame2.text: to speak abroad the fame of, make renowned Troil. II. iii. 256 * , Sonn. lxxxiv. 11 .

familiar.text: adj. (‘intimate,’ ‘friendly’ is the most common meaning) 1. belonging to the household or family, domestic, household Wiv. I. i. 21 “a beast to man,” Oth. II. iii. 315 “good wine is a good familiar creature.”

famine.text: hunger, starvation 2H6 IV. x. 64 , Mac. V. v. 40 , Cym. III. vi. 19 .

famous.text: notorious Shr. I. ii. 257 , Wint. III. iii. 11 , 2H4 IV. iii. 70 , Ant. I. iv. 48 “famous pirates.”

famously.text: with renown R3 II. iii. 19 ; gloriously, splendidly Cor. I. i. 38 .

fan1.text: motion of the air such as is made by a fan Troil. V. iii. 41 “the and wind of your fair sword.”

fan2.text: fig. from the winnowing of corn Cym. I. vi. 177 “The love I bear him Made me to you thus.”

fancy1.text: sb. (2 the commonest S. sense) 1. fantasticalness LLL. I. i. 169 , Ham. I. iii. 71 “Costly thy habit . . . But not express'd in fancy.”

fancy2.text: to love, fall in love with Gent. III. i. 67 , Shr. II. i. 12 , 2H6 I. iii. 97 ; with a thing as object Shr. II. i. 16 ; intr. Tw.N. II. v. 30 “should she , it should be one of my complexion,” Troil. V. ii. 162 .

fane.text: temple Cor. I. x. 20 , Cym. IV. ii. 242 .

fang1.text: canine tooth, tusk; also fig. AYL. II. i. 6 “the icy fang . . . of the winter's wind,” Tw.N. I. v. 197 “the very fangs of malice.”

fang2.text: to seize Tim. IV. iii. 23 “Destruction fang mankind.”

fanged.text: having fangs Ham. III. iv. 203 “adders fang'”

fangled.text: fond of finery or foppery Cym. V. iv. 134 “our fangled world.”

fantasied.text: full of (strange) fancies John IV. ii. 144 .

fantastic.text: (cf. next word) 1. imaginary R2 I. iii. 299 .

fantastical.text: (3 the common S. sense) I. =FANTASTIC 1, Mac. I. iii. 53 , 139

fantastically.text: oddly, strangely 2H4 III. ii. 338 “a head fantastically carved,” H5 II. iv. 27 .

fantastico.text: absurd, irrational person Rom. II. iv. 31 (Q1 “-icoes”; other old edd. “phantacies, -asies”).

fantasy.text: (contrast FANCY sb.) 1. delusive imagination, hallucination 1H4 V. iv. 137 * “is it That plays upon our eyesight?,” Ham. I. i. 54 * “Is not this something more than fantasy?.”

far.text: (?) comparative in Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 444 “Far than Deucalion off” (F1 “Farre”).

farced.text: stuffed out with pompous phrases H5 IV. i. 283 “The farced title running 'fore the king.”

fare.text: state of things John V. vii. 35 “ill fare,” 3H6 II. i. 95 “What fare?” (=What cheer?).

farm1.text: “in farm,” on a lease R2 II. i. 257 .

farm2.text: to rent (land) Ham. IV. iv. 20 ; to let or lease (land) R2 I. iv. 45 .

farrow.text: properly, a litter of pigs; in Mac. IV. i. 65 “Her nine farrow” is used in sing. with numeral to indicate the number of young.

farthest.text: “at the ,” at latest Mer.V. II. ii. 125 (F1).

fashion1.text: sb. (the commoner S. meanings are ‘shape, make’, ‘manner, way’, ‘prevailing custom’, ‘conventional usage’) 1. kind, sort Gent. V. iv. 61 “Thou friend of an ill ,” Wint. III. ii. 105 , Per. IV. ii. 84 “gentlemen of all f-s” ; phr. “in to,” of a kind to Mer.V. I. ii. 23 .

fashion2.text: vb. (1 rare outside S.) 1. to contrive, manage MND. III. ii. 194 “To this false sport,” 1H4 I. iii. 298 “As I will it,” Oth. IV. ii. 242 “which I will to fall out between twelve and one.”

fashions.text: disease of horses closely allied to glanders Shr. III. ii. 54 .

fast.text: close (“by”) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 514, 2H6 III. ii. 189 .

fast1.text: fasting, abstinence Meas. I. ii. 135 “surfeit is the father of much fast.”

fast2.text: adj. (the sense ‘rapid, quick’ occurs) 1. (of sleep) deep, sound Mac. V. i. 9 ; also = fast asleep Rom. IV. v. 1 .

fasten.text: to induce to accept Oth. II. iii. 51 “ but one cup upon him.”

fat2.text: (1 a use app. peculiar to S., but ‘fat mist’ occurs in the 17th cent.) 1. close, stuffy 1H4 II. iv. 1 “that fat room.”

fatal.text: (1 the Parcae or Fates were called ‘the fatal dames’ or ‘ladies’) 1. concerned with or fraught with destiny H5 V. i. 21 “Parea's web,” 3H6 IV. ii. 21 .

fate1.text: what one is destined to achieve H5 II. iv. 64 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 169

fate2.text: to destine All'sW. IV. iv. 20 ; so fated, (1) destined “to” Tp. I. ii. 129 , Lr. III. iv. 67 , Oth. III. iii. 276 ; (2) invested with the power of destiny All'sW. I. i. 236 .

father1.text: the friend or relative that ‘gives away’ a bride at the altar Ado V. iv. 15 . ∥ Till recently termed ‘father-in-church’ in Warwickshire and Oxfordshire.

father2.text: Ado I. i. 116 “f-s herself,” shows who her father is.

fatherly.text: as a father Cym. II. iii. 39 .

fathom.text: (old edd. fadom, the orig. meaning is ‘the embracing arms’, hence ‘stretching the arms in a straight line’ (of which 1 is a fig. use), hence ‘measure of 6 feet’) 1. fig. grasp of intellect Oth. I. i. 153 “Another of his ”

fathomless.text: that cannot be embraced by the arms Troil. II. ii. 30 “a waist most fathomless.”

faucet.text: kind of tap for drawing liquor from a barrel; only in “faucet-seller” Cor. II. i. 80 (Ff1 2 3 “Forset,” F4 “Fauset,” mod. edd. “fosset”). ∥ ‘Faucet’ is the common spelling from the 14th cent. on wards.

fault.text: (2 and the sense ‘defect, imperfection’ are the most freq. S. meanings; 4? only S.) 1. lack, want, in phr. “for of,” in the absence of, for want of Wiv. I. iv. 17 , 2H4 II. ii. 47 , Rom. II. iv. 132 .

faulty.text: guilty 1H4 III. ii. 27 , 2H6 III. ii. 202 , H8 V. iii. 75 .

favour.text: (obs. or archaic senses are the foll.; 4 and 5 were very common in the 15th-16th cent.) 1. leave, permission, pardon LLL. III. i. 70 “By thy ,” John II. i. 422 “Speak on with ,” H8 I. i. 168 , Mac. I. iii. 149 , Ham. I. ii. 51 “Your leave and favour.”

favourable.text: gracious, kindly 2H4 IV. v. 2 “some dull and favourable hand.”

favoured.text: featured Cæs. I. iii. 129 ; see FAVOUR 4

fawn1.text: young fallow deer AYL. II. vii. 128 .

fawn3.text: to wag the tail with delight or fondness R3 I. iii. 290 , Cæs. V. i. 41 , Lucr. 421 “As the grim lion f-eth o'er his prey” ; fig. to wheedle, cringe (freq.).

fay.text: faith Ham. II. ii. 276 “by my fay.”

fealty.text: obligation of fidelity on the part of a feudal tenant or vassal to his lord R2 V. ii. 45 ; (hence gen.) fidelity, loyalty Gent. II. iv. 92 .

fear1.text: sb. (3 in some exx. ?=ground of alarm, as in Psalm liii. 6 (Prayer-book) ‘They were afraid where no fear was’) 1. dread, alarm, apprehension; phr. “give” or “put to,” make timid, intimidate Meas. I. iv. 62 , Ven. 1158 ; “for of trust” (= fearing to trust myself) Sonn. xxiii. 5 ; “Upon the foot of ,” in flight 1H4 V. v. 20 ; “out of ,” (i) for fear 1H4 IV. iii. 7 , (ii) without fear 1H4 IV. i. 135 “I am out of fear Of death” (cf. MND. III. i. 23 “this will put them out of fear” ).

fear2.text: vb. (1 was the orig. meaning of the vb. in Anglo-Saxon; 2 is now used only intr.) 1. to frighten, scare Meas. II. i. 2 “a scarecrow . . . to the birds of prey,” Shr. I. ii. 214 “ boys with bugs,” 3H6 V. ii. 2 “Warwick was a bug that f-'d us all,” Lr. III. v. 4 “How . . . I may be censured, . . . something fears me to think of.”

fearful.text: about equally freq. in (1) the objective sense ‘dreadful, terrible’ and (2) the subjective, ‘timorous, apprehensive’; “ of” occas. = concerned about 3H6 V. vi. 87 “ of his life.”

feast.text: to keep holiday, enjoy oneself (S.) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 359, 2H4 III. i. 59 , Per. I. iv. 107 .

feat1.text: adj. adroit, dexterous Cym. V. v. 88 “A page . . . So , so nurse-like” ; neat, trim Tp. II. i. 281 [ 273 ]; — adv. neatly Compl. 48 “With sleided silk and affectedly Enswath'”

feat2.text: (?) to constrain to propriety Cym. I. i. 49 * “A sample to the youngest, to the more mature A glass that feated them (featur'd†, fear'd).”

feather.text: (in Tw.N. III. i. 72 almost = bird) 1. kind of plumage 3H6 III. iii. 161 “birds of self-same ” ; fig. “of that ,” of such a kind Tim. I. i. 101 .

featly.text: with graceful agility, nimbly Tp. I. ii. 379 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 176

feature.text: shape or form of body Tp. III. i. 52 “how f-s are abroad,” Gent. II. iv. 74 “complete in and in mind,” H8 III. ii. 50 , Ham. III. i. 168 , Sonn. cxiii. 12 ; shapeliness, comeliness R3 I. i. 19 “Cheated of by dissembling nature.” ∥ The sense of ‘lineaments of the face’ is not S.

fedary.text: confederate, accomplice Meas. II. iv. 123 (F1 “fedarie,” Ff2 3 4 “feodary”), Cym. III. ii. 21 (Ff “Fœdarie”), Wint. II. i. 89 (F1 “Federarie,” ? a misprint or a scholarly correction).

fee1.text: sb. (1 phrases derived from the sense of inheritance in land) 1. “in fee,” (to be held) in absolute possession Ham. IV. iv. 22 “should it be sold in fee; — at a pin's fee,” at a pin's value Ham. I. iv. 65 .

fee2.text: to employ, make use of (an opportunity), as one would a servant Wiv. II. ii. 208 .

feed1.text: feeding-ground, pasture-land AYL. II. iv. 84 “bounds of feed” ; food-fodder Tit. IV. iv. 92 [sheep] “rotted with delicious feed.”

feed2.text: hired Tw.N. I. v. 305 “no feed post.”

feeder.text: one dependent on another for food, (hence) servant AYL. II. iv. 100 , Tim. II. ii. 169 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 109

feeding.text: food 2H4 I. i. 10 “a horse Full of high ,” Cor. V. i. 56 “wine and ,” Sonn. cxviii. 6 “To bitter sauces did I frame my ” ; pasture Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 169 ∥ Cf. FEED sb.

feel.text: to test, sound H5 IV. i. 132 “to other men's minds,” Lr. I. ii. 97 “to my affection to your honour.”

feeling1.text: vbl. sb. (the sense ‘sensibility, susceptibility’, e.g. LLL. IV. ii. 30 , is not pre-S.; the foll. are obs. or rare) 1. experience Meas. III. ii. 129 , LLL. III. i. 120 .

feeling2.text: (in passive sense) deeply felt, heartfelt Wint. IV. i. [ ii. ] 8 “ sorrows,” Rom. III. v. 75 “such a loss,” Lr. IV. vi. 227 “known and sorrows.”

feelingly.text: (1 arises from the meaning ‘with just perception, understandingly’; 2 not pre-S.) 1. appropriately, to the purpose Meas. I. ii. 37 , Tw.N. II. iii. 175 “most personated,” Ham. V. ii. 114 .

feign.text: to relate in fiction, fable Mer.V. V. i. 80 , 3H6 I. ii. 31 “all that poets feign of bliss and joy.”

feigning.text: (3 the sense ‘sing softly, hum’ was in use in the 15th-16th cent.) 1. inventive, imaginative AYL. III. iii. 22 “the truest poetry is the most feigning.”

fell1.text: skin Lr. V. iii. 24 “flesh and ” (used quasiadv.=entirely); covering of hair or wool, fleece AYL. III. ii. 56 , Mac. V. v. 11 .

fell2.text: fierce, cruel (freq.); hot, angry MND. II. i. 20 “Oberon is passing fell and wrath.”

fellow1.text: sb. (5 in 14th cent. implied polite condescension=‘comrade’, ‘my friend’; in S.'s time this notion had disappeared, but the word when addressed to a servant does not seem to have necessarily implied haughtiness or contempt, though its application to one not greatly inferior was a gross insult) 1. companion, associate (freq.) Tp. III. iii. 60 ; also attrib. AYL. III. ii. 378 , Ham. I. ii. 177 .

fellow2.text: to be a ‘fellow’ to Wint. I. ii. 143 .

fellowship.text: (see also GOOD-FELLOWSHIP) 1. partnership, membership MND. I. i. 85 “everlasting bond of ,” Ham. III. ii. 294 “a in a cry of players.”

felonious.text: wicked, criminal 2H6 III. i. 129 . ∥ The technical legal sense relating to felony is post-S.

female.text: womanish, effeminate R2 III. ii. 114 “their female joints.”

femetary.text: old spelling of FUMITORY H5 V. ii. 45 .

fence1.text: sb. (2 occurs only once) 1. art of fencing Ado V. i. 75 , John II. i. 290 .

fence2.text: to defend, shield, protect 3H6 II. vi. 75 , III. iii. 98 , Tim. IV. i. 3 , Lucr. 63 .

fennel.text: fragrant yellow-flowered perennial, Faeniculum vulgare, used in fish-sauces, and regarded as an emblem of flattery 2H4 II. iv. 267 “eats conger and fennel,” Ham. IV. v. 179 .

fere.text: spouse Tit. IV. i. 89 “the woeful fere. . . of that . . . dame,” Per. I. Gower 21 (Qq “Peere,” Ff3 4 “Peer”).

fertile.text: abundant Tw.N. I. v. 276 “ tears.” ∥ In 2H4 IV. iii. 132 * “ sherris” perhaps = promoting fertility (fig.).

festinate.text: hasty Lr. III. vii. 10 ; festinately LLL. III. i. 6 .

festival.text: like a feast-day John III. i. 76 “kept ” ; joyful Ado V. ii. 42 “woo in festival terms.”

fet.text: fetched H5 III. i. 18 , R3 II. ii. 121 (Qq “fetcht”). ∥ Cf. “deep-fet, far-fet.”

fetch1.text: dodge, trick Ham. II. i. 38 , Lr. II. iv. 90 .

fetch2.text: vb. (3 trans. from the phrase ‘fetch a blow’) 1. “ and carry,” said orig. of dogs, hence fig. to run backwards and forwards with news, tales, &c. Gent. III. i. 276 “her master's maid . . . hath more qualities than a water-spaniel . . . She can and carry.”

fettle.text: to make ready, prepare Rom. III. v. 154 .

fever.text: to throw into a fever Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 138 “The white hand of a lady thee.”

feverous.text: feverish Meas. III. i. 73 “a life,” Troil. III. ii. 36 “a fev'rous pulse,” Cor. I. iv. 61 , Mac. II. iii. 67 .

few.text: “in few,” in a few words, in short Tp. I. ii. 144 , Meas. III. i. 236 , H5 I. ii. 245 , Ham. I. iii. 126 .

fewness.text: only in “ and truth,” in few words and truly Meas. I. iv. 39 .

fico.text: Italian for ‘fig’ Wiv. I. iii. 31 . Cf. FIGO.

fiddlestick.text: “the devil rides upon a ,” here's a fine commotion! 1H4 ii. iv. 543 [ 535 ].

fidelity.text: “by my ,” upon my word Wiv. IV. ii. 164 .

fidiused.text: jocular formation on the name Aufidius Cor. II. i. 146 .

field.text: (1 a freq. sense, 4 common in lit. sense) 1. open country MND. II. i. 96 , Ven. 8 .

fielded.text: engaged in battle Cor. I. iv. 12 .

fierce.text: (2 cf. ‘fierce credulity,’ ‘fierce flattery,’ Ben Jonson) 1. proud, haughty 2H6 IV. ix. 45 “he is and cannot brook hard language.”

fife.text: in Mer.V. II. v. 30 * “the wry-neck'd ,” either the instrument or the player.

fift.text: old form of ‘fifth’ (Anglo-Saxon “fifta”), now confined to dial. use.

fifteen.text: =fifteenth; a tax of one fifteenth formerly imposed on personal property 2H6 IV. vii. 24 .

fig.text: contemptuous gesture consisting in thrusting the thumb between two of the closed fingers or into the mouth H5 III. vi. 62 ; hence fig vb., to insult (a person) by giving him the ‘fig’ 2H4 V. iii. 121 .

fight.text: to fight one after another Tp. III. iii. 103 “I'll fight their legions o'er.”

fights.text: kind of screen used during a naval engagement to conceal and protect the crew of the vessel Wiv. II. ii. 144 “up with your fights.”

figo.text: Spanish for ‘fig’ H5 III. vi. 60 “ for thy friendship,” IV. i. 60 “The figo for thee.”

figure1.text: sb. (3 referred by some to the sense ‘horoscope, diagram of the aspects of astrological houses’) 1. distinctive shape or appearance Ado I. i. 15 “doing in the figure of a lamb the feats of a lion.”

figure2.text: 1. to picture in the mind, imagine Meas. I. ii. 56 “Thou art always figuring diseases in me,” Sonn. cviii. 2 , Compl. 199 .

file.text: sb. (2 and 3 are not pre-Eliz.) 1. list, roll All'sW. IV. iii. 190 “the muster-,” 2H4 I. iii. 10 , H8 I. i. 75 “the Of all the gentry,” Mac. III. i. 95 “the valu'd file.”

file1.text: to rub smooth with a file Tw.N. III. iii. 5 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 626; (hence) to polish, refine neatly LLL. V. i. 12 “his tongue [is] f-d,” Tit. II. i. 123 “she shall our engines with advice,” Sonn. lxxxv. 4 “precious phrase by all the Muses f-d” (Q “fil'd”); in Sonn. lxxxvi. 13 some, after Malone, read “fil'd,” but Q has “fild=filled.”

file2.text: to defile Mac. III. i. 65 “For Banquo's issue have I fil'd my mind.”

file3.text: to march in line, keep pace “with” H8 III. ii. 172 (Ff “fill'd,” as also Ff1 2 in Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 626: see FILE vb. 1 ).

fill1.text: pl. thills or shafts of a cart Troil. III. ii. 46 ; cf. FILL-HORSE.

fill2.text: to satiate, satisfy H5 IV. i. 289 , Tim. I. i. 271 “to see meat fill knaves,” Sonn. lvi. 5 “fill Thy hungry eyes” ; also intr. to be satiated Ven. 548 “glutton-like she feeds, yet never filleth” ; fill up, (1) to come up to the measure of, equal LLL. V. ii. 194 “How many inches do fill up one mile” ; (2) to fulfil, satisfy Mer.V. IV. i. 160 “comes . . . to fill up your Grace's request in my stead.”

film1.text: fine thread, as of gossamer Rom. I. iv. 64 (F1 Qq “Philome,” others “filme”).

film2.text: to cover with a film Ham. III. iv. 147 .

filthy.text: (1 is peculiar to S.) 1. murky, thick H5 III. iii. 31 , Mac. I. i. 12 .

find.text: (obsolete uses are the foll.) 1. “ forth”=find out Err. I. ii. 37 , Mer.V. I. i. 144 .

fine.text: delicately, subtly Cym. I. i. 84 “How this tyrant Can tickle where she wounds” ; mincingly LLL. V. i. 22 “to speak dout, , when he should say, doubt.”

fine1.text: sb. (3 extension of the sense ‘pecuniary mulct’) 1. end Ado I. i. 255 [ 247 ] “the is, . . . I will live a bachelor,” All'sW. IV. iv. 35 , Ham. V. i. 113 “is this the of his f-s” ; esp. in the phrase “in ,” in the end, finally All'sW. III. vii. 19 , 1H6 I. iv. 34 , Ham. II. ii. 69 , Lr. II. i. 50 ;— All'sW. IV. iv. 35 “the f-'s the crown,” probably a translation of the Latin ‘Finis coronat opus’.

fine2.text: adj. (the ordinary material senses occur; 5 or 6 is often blended with the sense of ‘excellent, admirable’) 1. (of gold) containing a certain proportion of pure metal, specified in carats 2H4 IV. v. 160 “Other” [gold], “less fine in carat.”

finger.text: to pilfer, filch 3H6 V. i. 44 , Ham. V. ii. 15 “Finger'd their pocket.”

finical.text: excessively particular in dress Lr. II. ii. 19 “glass-gazing . . . finical rogue.”

finish.text: to die Ant. V. ii. 192 , Cym. V. v. 36 , 413

firago.text: meant for ‘virago’, which does not otherwise occur Tw.N. III. iv. 305 .

fire.text: phrases:—“give ,” discharge a volley Wiv. II. ii. 145 ; fig. Lucr. 1604 “Three times with sighs she gives her sorrow ;—give the ,” give the order to discharge a volley, fig. Gent. II. iv. 39 “A volley of words . . . you gave the ;—put” one's “finger in the ,” meddle with dangerous matter Wiv. I. iv. 91 .

firk.text: to beat, trounce H5 IV. iv. 29 , 33

first.text: (senses 3 (i) and 3 (ii), although really distinct, cannot always be separated) 1. in heraldry “the ”=the colour first mentioned in blazoning a coat of arms (fig.) MND. III. ii. 213 “Two of the †, like coats in heraldry” (old edd. “ life”).

firstlings.text: first-fruits Troil. Prol. 27, Mac. IV. i. 147 .

fist.text: to punch 2H4 II. i. 25 , Cor. IV. v. 131 , Per. IV. vi. 182 .

fit.text: vb. (obs. uses are as follows) 1. to be fitting or suitable Rom. I. v. 79 “It fits, when such a villain is a guest.”

fit1.text: paroxysm of lunacy, formerly regarded as a periodic disease Err. IV. iii. 91 , Tit. IV. i. 17 , Ham. IV. i. 8 ; “fit of the face,” grimace H8 I. iii. 7 ; applied to critical times Cor. III. ii. 33 “The violent fit o' the time,” Mac. IV. ii. 17 “The fits o' the season.”

fit2.text: adj. (2 now only dial. exc. with ‘for’ or ‘to’) 1. of the right measure or size, well fitting Gent. IV. iv. 169 , LLL. IV. i. 50 “One o' these maids' girdles for your waist should be fit,” All'sW. I. i. 114 , Cym. IV. i. 2 “How fit his garments serve me!” ; fig. All'sW. II. ii. 21 “Will your answer serve fit to all questions?,” Ham. IV. v. 10 , Lr. I. ii. 206 “All with me's meet that I can fashion fit.”

fitchew.text: polecat Troil. V. i. 67 , Lr. IV. vi. 125 ; used as a term of contempt Oth. IV. i. 148 .

fitful.text: marked by fits or paroxysms Mac. III. ii. 23 “life's fever.” ∥ Used once by S., the earliest authority for the word, and popularized in various applications by mod. writers.

fitly.text: at a fitting time Tim. III. iv. 113 , Lr. I. ii. 190 “I will fitly bring you to hear my lord speak.”

fitment.text: (not pre-S.; the S. exx. are the only instances till the 19th cent., when the word is used in the sense of ‘fittings’） 1. preparation Cym. V. v. 410 .

fitness.text: readiness, inclination (S.) Ham. V. ii. 209 * “if his fitness speaks, mine is ready” (Q2).

fitted.text: driven as by fits or paroxysms “out of” a place Sonn. cxix. 7 .

fives.text: disease of the parotid glands in young horses Shr. III. ii. 56 .

fixture.text: fixing Wiv. III. iii. 67 “the firm of thy foot” (Ff2 3 4 “fixure”); fixedness Troil. I. iii. 101 (Ff3 4).

fixure.text: fixedness, stability Wint. V. iii. 67 * , Troil. I. iii. 101 (Ff3 4 “fixture”).

flake.text: lock of hair Lr. IV. vii. 30 “these white flakes.”

flaky.text: broken into flakes of cloud R3 V. iii. 87 .

flamen.text: priest in ancient Rome devoted to the service of a particular deity Cor. II. i. 232 , Tim. IV. iii. 156 .

flannel.text: ludicrously used to designate a Welshman Wiv. V. v. 176 “to answer the Welsh flannel.”

flare.text: to stream in the wind Wiv. IV. vi. 42 .

flat1.text: level ground, plain Ham. V. i. 274 “Till of this a mountain you have made” ; swamp Tp. II. ii. 2 “bogs, fens, f-s” ; shallow, shoal Mer.V. I. i. 26 , John V. vi. 40 .

flat2.text: adj. (not very freq.; chiefly in fig. uses) 1. absolute, downright Meas.
