II. ii. 131 “ blasphemy,” Ado II. i. 231 “the transgression of a schoolboy,” IV. ii. 45 , John III. i. 298 ; “that's ” (not pre-S. =that's the absolute, undeniable truth LLL. III. i. 107 , 1H4 I. iii. 218 , IV. ii. 43 .

flatter1.text: 1. to try to please by obsequious speech or conduct AYL. IV. i. 194 “that f-ing tongue of yours,” R2 II. i. 87 “I mock my name, great king, to thee” ; also intr. “ with” R2 II. i. 88 “Should dying men with those that live?.”

flattery.text: gratifying deception, delusion (S.) Oth. IV. i. 131 “she is persuaded I will marry her, out of her own love and flattery,” Sonn. xlii. 14 .

flaw1.text: sb. 1 (1 by some referred to FLAW sb. 2 ) 1. flake of snow 2H4 IV. iv. 35 * “as sudden As f-s congealed in the spring of day.”

flaw2.text: 1. sudden burst or squall of wind 2H6 III. i. 354 , Cor. V. iii. 74 “a great seamark, standing every ,” Ham. V. i. 238 “winter's flaw,” Per. III. i. 39 .

flaw3.text: to make a flaw in, damage, mar H8 I. i. 95 “France hath f-'d the league,” I. ii. 21 , Lr. V. iii. 198 “his f-'d heart . . . 'Twixt two extremes of passion . . . Burst smilingly.”

flax.text: as the material of which a wick is made 2H6 V. ii. 55 “oil and flax.”

flay.text: to skin: (hence, jocularly) to strip (a person of his clothes) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 658 (old edd. “fled”).

fleckled.text: dappled Rom. II. iii. 3 “ darkness” (Q1 and mod. edd. “flecked”; also “flecker'd”†).

fledge.text: 1. to bring up (a young bird) till its feathers are grown and it can fly Mer.V. III. i. 32 “knew the bird was fledged.”

flee.text: used for ‘fly’ LLL. III. i. 68 , 2H4 I. i. 123 “arrows fled (fly†) not swifter,” Ven. 947 .

fleece.text: transf. head or mass of hair Tit. II. iii. 34 “My fleece of woolly hair,” Sonn. lxviii. 8 .

fleer2.text: to smile or grin contemptuously, gibe or sneer “at” Ado V. i. 58 , LLL. V. ii. 109 , Rom. I. v. 61 , Cæs. I. iii. 117 “no fleering tell-tale.”

fleet.text: (the sense ‘pass away, vanish’ is freq.) 1. to be afloat Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 171

flesh1.text: sb. (3 referred by some to 1) 1. “in ,” in good condition Rom. V. i. 84 “get thyself in ”

flesh2.text: vb. (the orig. meaning was ‘to reward a hawk or a hound with a piece of the flesh of the game killed to excite its eagerness in the chase’) 1. to initiate in or inure to bloodshed John V. i. 71 “ his spirit in a war-like soil,” Lr. II. ii. 50 “come, I'll flesh ye.”

fleshly.text: consisting of flesh John IV. ii. 245 .

fleshment.text: excitement resulting from a first success (cf. FLESH vb. 2) Lr. II. ii. 130 “in the of this dread exploit.”

flickering.text: shining with unsteady light Lr. II. ii. 114 “ Phoebus' front” (Qq1 2 printed “flitkering,” Q3 “fletkering,” Ff “flicking”).

flight.text: sb. (1 cf. ‘You must haue diuerse shaftes of one flight, fethered with diuerse winges, for diuerse windes,’ Ascham ‘Toxophilus’, 1545 ) 1. “of the self-same ,” having the same power of flight, applied to arrows of equal size and weight Mer.V. I. i. 142 .

fling.text: (2 used of animals from the 14th cent.) 1. to dash, rush Tim. IV. ii. 45 “He's flung in rage from this ingrateful sent Of monstrous friends.”

flood.text: (fig. uses are fairly numerous) 1. freq. used of large bodies of water, rivers, the sea ( Mer.V. IV. i. 72 “the main ” ), also for water as opposed to land ( MND. II. i. 5 “Through , through fire,” Oth. I. iii. 135 “by and field” ); hence, of streams of tears and blood.

floor.text: “ of heaven,” the sky Mer.V. V. i. 58 ; app. transf. from the meaning of ‘ceiling’, which is found in Holland's ‘Plutarch’, 1603

flote.text: sea (S.) Tp. I. ii. 234 “the Mediterranean ” ∥ The usu. meaning (1480-1660) is ‘wave, billow.’

flourish1.text: ostentatious embellishment, gloss, varnish LLL. II. i. 14 , IV. iii. 238 “Lend me the of all gentle tongues,” R3 I. iii. 241 , IV. iv. 82 , Ham. II. ii. 91 “since brevity is the soul of wit, And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes,” V. ii. 187 .

flout.text: to quote with sarcastic purpose Ado I. i. 298 “ere you flout old ends any further.”

flow1.text: 1. stream (fig.) H8 I. i. 152 “ of gall,” Tim. II. ii. 3 “cease his of riot,” V. iv. 76 “our brain's ” (=tears); phr. “set at flow,” cause to weep Tim. II. ii. 173 .

flow2.text: vb. (pa. pple. once “flown” All'sW. II. i. 142 ) 1. to circulate Meas. I. iii. 52 “Lord Angelo . . . scarce confesses That his blood f-s,” Cym. III. iii. 93 “The princely blood flows in his cheek.”

flowering.text: 1. blooming (fig.) H5 III. iii. 14 ; “ youth,” bloom of manhood 1H6 II. v. 56 .

flowery.text: full of or expressed in flowers of speech (not pre-S.) Meas. III. i. 81 * .

flush.text: (not pre-Eliz.; 1 and 2 not pre-S.) 1. full Tim. V. iv. 8 “Now the time is flush.”

fluster.text: to excite with drink Oth. II. iii. 61 .

flux.text: discharge AYL. III. ii. 71 “the very uncleanly of a cat” ; continuous stream (of people) II. i. 52 .

fly.text: (often used in the senses of ‘flee’) 1. trans. and intr. (of a falconer) to cause a hawk to fly at game 2H6 II. i. 1 “flying at the brook” (see BROOK sb.), Ham. II. ii. 459 [ 450 ] “We'll e'en to't like French falconers, fly at anything we see.”

fob2.text: to cheat, deceive, delude 1H4 I. ii. 68 , Oth. IV. ii. 197 (see FOP); “ off,” (1) put off deceitfully 2H4 II. i. 39 (old edd. “fub”); (2) set aside by a trick Cor. I. i. 99 “to fob off our disgrace with a tale.”

foil1.text: setting of a jewel, (hence fig.) that which sets something off to advantage R2 I. iii. 266 “as wherein thou art to set The precious jewel of thy home return,” 1H4 I. ii. 237 , R3 V. iii. 251 , Ham. V. ii. 269 “I'll be your , Laertes; in mine ignorance Your skill shall . . . Stick fiery off indeed,” Compl. 153 “the Of this false jewel” ; in Ant. I. iv. 24 Ff “foyl(e)s” is by some referred to this word, but see FOIL sb. 2 2

foil2.text: sb. 2 (1 orig. a term of wrestling=‘the fact of being almost thrown, a throw not resulting in a flat fall’) 1. defeat, repulse, check 1H6 III. iii. 11 ; phr. “give the , put to the ”=give a check to Tp. III. i. 46 , 1H6 V. iii. 23 .

foil3.text: light fencing weapon Ado V. ii. 14 , Ham. II. ii. 343 [ 334 ], V. ii. 182 , &c.

foil4.text: to throw in wrestling AYL. I. i. 138 , &c.; to overcome, defeat 3H6 V. iv. 42 , Troil. I. iii. 372 , Cor. I. ix. 48 , Ven. 114 , Sonn. xxv. 10 “After a thousand victories once f-'d” ; (hence) to frustrate, render nugatory or of no effect Oth. I. iii. 271 (Qq “foyles,” Ff “seel(e),” Cym. II. iii. 126 (mod. edd. “soil”†), Pilgr. vii. 15 [ 99 ].

foin.text: thrust in fencing Lr. IV. vi. 252 ; so foin vb. Wiv. II. iii. 24 , 2H4 II. i. 19 .

foison.text: plentiful crop or harvest Tp. IV. i. 110 “Earth's increase, plenty, Barns and garners never empty,” Meas. I. iv. 43 , Ant. II. vii. 23 “if dearth Or follow” ; pl. resources Mac. IV. iii. 88 .

follow.text: (4 used more widely than now) 1. to pursue as an enemy 2H4 IV. iii. 27 , Cor. III. iii. 137 , IV. v. 104 “I have ever f-'d thee with hate,” Ant. V. i. 36 “O Antony! I have follow'd thee to this.”

follower.text: pursuer 3H6 I. iv. 22 , Cor. I. iv. 44 .

folly.text: lewdness, wantonness Wiv. II. ii. 258 , III. ii. 36 , Meas. III. i. 89 , Troil. V. ii. 18 , Oth. II. i. 137 , V. ii. 130 .

fond1.text: adj. (the mod. sense ‘having a strong affection or liking for’ is first recorded from S., who construes it with “of” Wint. I. ii. 164 , John III. iv. 92 , 98 , Oth. V. ii. 155 , and “on” MND. II. i. 266 , Sonn. lxxxiv. 14 ; a contemporary sense, ‘foolishly affectionate, doting’, is doubtfully represented) 1. infatuated, foolish, silly (the commonest sense in S. and in the Eliz. period, since when the literary use has been narrowed to that of ‘foolishly credulous or sanguine’).

food.text: “in food,” while eating Err. V. i. 83 .

fool1.text: sb. 1 (the phrase “a to” = in every way inferior to Shr. III. ii. 160 is not pre-S.) 1. (with an adj. as “good, poor”） used as a term of endearment or pity Gent. IV. iv. 100 , Ado II. i. 328 , Tw.N. V. i. 381 , Wint. II. i. 117 , 3H6 II. v. 36 , Rom. I. iii. 31 , Lr. V. iii. 307 .

fool2.text: kind of custard or dish of whipped cream Troil. V. i. 10 (quibblingly) “thou full dish of fool.”

fool3.text: to make a fool of Lr. II. iv. 278 .

fooling.text: humour for jesting Tw.N. I. v. 35 .

foolish.text: used depreciatingly in speaking of one's own things Mer.V. I. ii. 128 “my eyes,” Rom. I. v. 126 “We have a trifling foolish banquet towards.”

foot1.text: phr. “at ,” close behind Ham. IV. iii. 57 , Ant. I. v. 44 ;—“on ” (i) standing Troil. I. iii. 135 “keeps Troy on ” ; (ii) moving, astir Cor. IV. iii. 49 , Ven. 679 “when thou hast on the purblind hare” ; (iii) in active employment or operation LLL. V. ii. 755 “since love's argument was first on ;— to ,” with one's foot against one's opponent's, in close combat Ant. III. vii. 66 ;—“ and hand,” putting the foot forward and dealing a blow at the same time 1H4 II. iv. 245 ;—“set on” (one's) “,” start on one's way Cæs. II. i. 331 ;—“Upon the of fear,” in flight 1H4 V. v. 20 (cf. Mac. II. iii. 132 “Upon the of motion” ).

foot2.text: vb. (the use of “ it”=‘dance’ Tp. I. ii. 379 “ it featly here and there,” has been much imitated by later writers; 4 said of birds of prey, esp. hawks, in 16-17th cent.) 1. intr. to go on foot, walk Wiv. II. i. 124 “thieves do by night” ; trans. to tread Lr. III. iv. 123 “Swithold f-ed thrice the old” (=wold).

footing.text: (2 only S.) 1. step, tread Mer.V. V. i. 24 , Troil. I. iii. 156 , Ven. 722 ; “set ” (i) set foot, enter 2H6 III. ii. 87 , H8 III. i. 182 ; (ii) gain a footing or firm position R2 II. ii. 48 , 1H6 III. iii. 64 , Troil. II. ii. 155 .

footman.text: (1 survives in Worcestershire dial.) 1. walker, pedestrian Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 69

fop1.text: fool Lr. I. ii. 14 . ∥ The mod. sense is post-S.

fop2.text: to fool, dupe Oth. IV. ii. 197 “to find myself fopt in it” (mod. edd. “fobbed”†).

foppery.text: (2 cf. FOP vb.) 1. folly Meas. I. ii. 143 , Mer.V. II. v. 35 “the sound of shallow foppery,” Lr. I. ii. 132 .

foppish.text: foolish Lr. I. iv. 183 “For wise men are grown foppish.”

for1.text: pref. (remarkable uses are the foll.) 1. before All'sW. IV. iv. 3 “for whose throne 'tis needful . . . to kneel” (mod. edd. “'fore”†).

for2.text: conj. (obs. uses are as follows) 1. introducing subordinate clauses with two meanings, (1) because Tp. I. ii. 272 “And, for thou wast a spirit too delicate . . . she did confine thee,” Oth. III. iv. 160 “They are . . . jealous for they are jealous” ; also “for that” (freq.) and “for because” Wint. II. i. 7 , John II. i. 588 , R2 V. v. 3 ; (2) in order that 3H6 III. i. 9 “And, for the time shall not seem tedious, I'll tell thee” . . ., III. ii. 154 .

forage2.text: to range abroad for food John V. i. 59 ; to glut oneself as a wild beast, raven H5 I. ii. 110 , fig. Ven. 554 .

forbear.text: to leave alone, withdraw from the presence of Lr. I. ii. 181 , Ant. I. ii. 130 , II. vii. 45 “ me till anon” ; (hence) intr. to withdraw, retire Wint. V. iii. 85 “, Quit presently the chapel,” Ant. V. ii. 174 , Cym. I. i. 68 .

forbid1.text: with personal object and negative clause Pilgr. ix. 8 [ 24] “She . . . Forbade the boy he should not pass those grounds.”

force.text: phrases:—“of force,” (1) of weight, weighty 1H6 III. i. 156 “those occasions . . . were of ,” 2H6 I. iii. 166 , 3H6 II. ii. 44 “arguments of mighty ” ; (2) necessarily LLL. I. i. 146 , MND. III. ii. 40 “That, when he wak'd, of force she must be eyed,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 436, 1H4 II. iii. 122 , Cæs. IV. iii. 202 “Good reasons must, of , give place to better;— perforce,” (1) by violent constraint, against one's will John III. i. 142 , 2H4 IV. i. 116 , 2H6 I. i. 259 ; (2) of necessity 2H4 IV. iv. 46 .

force1.text: vb. 1 (4 common 16th cent. sense; H5 II. Chor. 32 * “ a play,” by some referred to FORCE vb. 2 , is possibly corrupt) 1. to press home, urge Meas. III. i. 108 , H8 III. ii. 2 “If you will now unite in your complaints, And them with a constancy,” Cor. III. ii. 51 , Compl. 157 .

force2.text: to stuff, farce Troil. II. iii. 237 “ him with praises,” V. i. 64 “malice f-d with wit.”

fore.text: before Wint. V. i. 226 , John V. i. 7 .

fore1.text: before (of time) Sonn. vii. 11 “The eyes, duteous.”

fore2.text: prep. (in mod. edd. usually “'fore”; 1 and 2 late exx. of the senses) 1. in the presence of Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 403 “Contract us these witnesses”; in asseverations All'sW. II. iii. 51 “ God, I think so,” Cor. I. i. 126 “Fore me.”

forecast.text: forethought, prudence 3H6 V. i. 42 . ∥ Still common in the midlands.

foredoom.text: to condemn beforehand Lr. V. iii. 293 “Your eldest daughters have foredoom'd themselves” (Ff “fore-done”).

foregone.text: gone by, past All'sW. I. iii. 142 “days ,” Sonn. xxx. 9 “grievances ” ∥ Oth. III. iii. 429 “ conclusion,” a S. phrase, usually taken by the commentators = previous experience (cf. CONCLUSION 2), but used by mod. writers=(1) decision formed before the case is fully argued or the evidence known, or (2) result that might have been foreseen as inevitable.

forehand.text: “ shaft,” arrow used for shooting straight before one 2H4 III. ii. 52 ; done at an earlier time Ado IV. i. 50 “extenuate the sin;” —sb. “the ,” the upper hand or advantage H5 IV. i. 300 ; vanguard, mainstay (S.) Troil. I. iii. 143 “The sinew and the forehand of our host.”

forehorse.text: leader in a team; fig. All'sW. II. i. 30 .

foreign.text: not of one's household or family (S.) Oth. IV. iii. 91 “they . . . pour our treasures into foreign laps,” Per. IV. i. 33 “I love the king . . . With more than foreign heart.”

forespent.text: previously bestowed Cym. II. iii. 64 “his goodness on us” ; past H5 II. iv. 36 “his vanities ” ∥ Contrast FORSPENT.

forestall.text: 1. to deprive (a person) “of” something by previous action Cym. III. v. 69 “may This night him of the coming day.”

foretell.text: (2 in freq. use 1300-1680; once in S.) 1. to indicate beforehand Wint. II. iii. 198 , John V. vii. 5 , 3H6 II. i. 43 “thou, whose heavy looks Some dreadful story hanging on thy tongue.”

forethought.text: predestined John III. i. 312 “ by heaven.”

forfeit.text: lost by reason of breach of an obligation or the like, to be given up as a penalty Meas. II. ii. 73 , LLL. V. ii. 426 , Mer.V. IV. i. 366 ; “ to,” liable to All'sW. IV. iii. 216 , Sonn. cvii. 4 .

forfeit1.text: sb. (1 the orig. sense) 1. breach, violation (of an obligation) Mer.V. V. i. 252 * , Rom. I. i. 103 * “Your lives shall pay the forfeit of the peace.”

forfeit2.text: intr. to fail to keep an obligation Mer.V. III. i. 55 , 135

forget.text: to drop the practice of (a duty, &c.) Err. III. ii. 1 “you have quite forgot A husband's office,” 2H6 II. i. 192 “forgot Honour and virtue” ; with infin. to forget how to do something Gent. III. i. 85 , Meas. I. ii. 41 , 2H4 V. ii. 22 “like men that had forgot to speak,” 2H6 V. i. 161 , Ven. 1061 “Her voice is stopp'd, her joints forget to bow.”

forgetive.text: a S. word of uncertain formation, commonly taken to be a derivative of the vb. ‘forge’ and=inventive, creative 2H4 IV. iii. 107 “apprehensive, quick, forgetive.”

forgive.text: to remit (a debt), overlook the omission of (a duty, &c.) Wiv. V. v. 184 “ that sum,” LLL. IV. ii. 150 “I thy duty,” Mer.V. IV. i. 26 , Tw.N. I. v. 205 “I forgive you the praise.”

fork.text: only in transferred uses, of which 1 and 2 are only S.:—(1) forked tongue (popularly supposed to be the sting) of a snake Meas. III. i. 16 , Mac. IV. i. 16 ; (2) barbed head of an arrow Lr. I. i. 146 ; (3) pl. lower limbs of the body Lr. IV. vi. 122 .

forked.text: (2 and 4 are common Eliz.) 1. cleft at the summit Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 5

forlorn2.text: 2 adj. (“fo'rlorn” or “forlo'rn”; cf. ENTIRE) 1. (?) the same sense as in ‘forlorn hope’ Cym. V. v. 406 “The soldier, that so nobly fought.” ∥ ‘Forlorne boies,’ ‘forlorne sentinels,’ ‘forlorne fellowes’ are expressions found in the Eliz. period.

form.text: (the foll. are obs. uses; 1 is a peculiarly S. use of an old sense; 2, 3 are not pre-S.) 1. image, likeness, portrait Gent. IV. iv. 205 , Meas. II. iv. 127 , LLL. II. i. 235 , John V. vii. 32 “I am a scribbled form, drawn with a pen,” Sonn. ix. 6 .

formal.text: (the meaning is not always certain) 1. having regard to due form or propriety, ceremonious, precise Shr. III. i. 62 “Are you so ?,” IV. ii. 64 “ in apparel,” Ham. IV. v. 215 “ ostentation.”

forsake.text: (in H8 II. i. 89 * absol. app.=leave the body) 1. to decline, refuse All'sW. II. iii. 62 , 1H6 IV. ii. 14 “If you the offer of their love,” Oth. IV. ii. 125 “forsook so many noble matches.”

forsooth.text: in truth, certainly; used by low persons as a phrase of honest asseveration; implying some contempt when used by well-bred persons (Schmidt).

forspeak.text: to speak against Ant. III. vii. 3 .

forspent.text: worn out, exhausted 2H4 I. i. 37 “ with speed,” 3H6 II. iii. 1 “Forspent with toil.”

forswear.text: (also intr. and refl. ‘to swear falsely’) 1. to abandon or renounce on oath Tp. IV. i. 91 “Her and her blind boy's scandal'd company I have forsworn” ; construed with infin. (only S.) Tw.N. III. iv. 279 “ to wear iron about you,” Cor. V. iii. 80 “The things I have forsworn to grant,” Rom. I. i. 229 “She hath forsworn to love.”

forted.text: fortified Meas. V. i. 12 “A forted residence.”

forth1.text: adv. (used with “far” redundantly, in “thus far ” Tp. I. ii. 177 , “so far ” Wiv. IV. vi. 11 , “how far ” 2H4 IV. ii. 53 ) 1. forward (in movement or direction) Shr. IV. i. 149 “As he walked on his way,” H5 II. ii. 189 * “Then , dear countrymen,” Tim. I. i. 50 “flies an eagle flight, bold and on,” Cym. IV. ii. 149 “Did make my way long ” (=made it seem long).

forth2.text: out of MND. I. i. 164 “Steal thy father's house,” Cor. I. iv. 23 “issue their city,” Ant. IV. x. 7 “put the haven” ; similarly “from ” (freq.) Wiv. IV. iv. 55 “Let them from forth a sawpit rush.”

forthcoming.text: ready to appear or to be produced when required, e.g. in court Shr. V. i. 95 , 2H6 I. iv. 56 , II. i. 177 .

forthright.text: straight path Tp. III. iii. 3 , Troil. III. iii. 158 .

fortitude.text: physical or structural strength 1H6 II. i. 17 “his own arm's ,” Oth. I. iii. 222 “the of the place.”

fortress.text: 1H6 II. i. 26 “God is our ” ; cf. Psalm xxxi. 3 and Luther's ‘Ein feste burg ist unser Gott.’

fortressed.text: protected “from” Lucr. 28 ; cf. Compl. 9 “fortified her visage from the sun.”

fortune1.text: sb. (the chief obs. uses are the foll.) 1. “by ,” by chance Mer.V. II. i. 34 , AYL. I. ii. 48 , Oth. V. ii. 224 , Sonn. xxxii. 3 ; “at ,” at random Oth. III. iii. 263 .

fortune2.text: vb. (occurs twice; 1 late ex. of this sense) 1. to regulate the fortunes of Ant. I. ii. 79 .

forty.text: (1 very common in Eliz. dramatists) 1. used indefinitely to express a large number Err. IV. iii. 84 “worth ducats,” Cor. III. i. 242 “I could beat of them,” Sonn. ii. 1 “When winters shall besiege thy brow” ; so “ thousand” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 279, R2 III. ii. 85 (Ff Q5; others “twenty”), Ham. V. i. 291 , Oth. III. iii. 443 .

forward.text: (1 not pre-S.; the meanings ‘early’, ‘ready, prompt’, ‘precocious’, ‘pert, bold’ occur) 1. situated at the front Tp. II. ii. 98 “His voice,” All'sW. III. ii. 116 “Whoever charges on his breast,” V. iii. 39 “Let's take the instant by the forward top.”

foster.text: (gen. sense ‘cherish’ occurs four times) 1. to feed Cym. II. iii. 119 “f-'d with cold dishes.”

foul.text: (often merely a strong epithet of condemnation or disgust; 1 very freq., and in most midland and northern dials. the chief current sense; “ play”= unfair dealing Tp. I. ii. 60 , Ham. I. ii. 255 is not pre-Eliz.) 1. ugly LLL. IV. iii. 87 , H5 IV. Chor. 21 “ and ugly witch,” 2H6 V. i. 157 , Oth. II. i. 141 , Ven. 133 “hardfavour'd, foul.”

foully.text: shamefully, disgracefully, wickedly All'sW. V. iii. 155 , Mac. III. i. 3 ; impurely Meas. II. ii. 174 ; insultingly 1H4 I. iii. 154 .

foulness.text: moral impurity, wickedness Ado IV. i. 155 , H8 III. ii. 184 , Lr. I. i. 230 ; ugliness AYL. III. iii. 42 , III. v. 66 .

foundation.text: Ado V. i. 334 [ 327 ] “God save the !,” said to be a formula used on receiving alms at a house of charity.

founded.text: solid, steady Mac. III. iv. 22 “ as the rock.”

founder.text: (2 rare fig. use of the nautical sense) 1. to cause (a horse) to break down or go lame Tp. IV. i. 30 “Phoebus' steeds are f-'d,” 2H4 IV. iii. 39 .

four.text: used like the Fr. ‘quatre’ for an indefinite number, large or small according to the circumstances (cf. FORTY) Tw.N. I. iii. 115 “it's to one,” Wint. V. ii. 155 [ 148 ] “any time these hours,” 1H4 II. ii. 14 “If I travel but foot,” H5 V. i. 43 “I will peat his pate days,” Cor. I. ii. 6 “'Tis not days gone,” Ham. II. ii. 160 “he walks hours together” (mod. edd. incorrectly “for”†), Ant. II. vii. 109 “I had rather fast from all days.” ∥ Freq. in Eliz. writers.

fox1.text: type of ingratitude Lr. I. iv. 342 , III. vi. 25 , &c.; so foxship, ingratitude Cor. IV. ii. 18 .

fox2.text: kind of sword H5 IV. iv. 9 . ∥ The wolf on some makes of sword-blade is supposed to have been mistaken for a fox.

fracted.text: broken H5 II. i. 130 “His heart is ,” Tim. II. i. 22 “my reliances on his fracted dates.”

fraction.text: (2 not pre-S. in this gen. sense) 1. discord, dissension, rupture Troil. II. iii. 108 .

fragment.text: applied to a person as a term of contempt (S.) Troil. V. i. 9 , Cor. I. i. 228 .

frame1.text: sb. (the sense of ‘picture frame’ is not preS., used fig. in Sonn. xxiv. 3 ) 1. ‘framing’, contrivance Ado IV. i. 191 “toil in of villanies.”

frame2.text: vb. (1 survives in Yorkshire dial.) 1. to direct one's steps, go Per. I. Gower 32 .

franchise.text: pl. liberties, privileges Cor. IV. vi. 87 “Your f-s . . . confin'd Into an auger's bore” ; free exercise Cym. III. i. 57 “repair and franchise” [of the laws].

frank1.text: enclosure for hogs, sty 2H4 II. ii. 160 .

frank2.text: adj. (1 is obs.; 2 now somewhat archaic) 1. unrestrained All'sW. II. iii. 61 “thy election.”

franked.text: shut up in a sty R3 I. iii. 314 , &c.

franklin.text: freeholder; orig., in 14-15th cent., the name of a class of landowners, of free but not noble birth, and ranking next below the gentry Wint. V. ii. 181 [ 173 ] “boors and f-s,” 1H4 II. i. 60 , Cym. III. ii. 78 “no costlier than would fit A f-'s housewife.”

frankly.text: 1. freely, without restraint or constraint, unrestrictedly Troil. V. viii. 19 , Tim. II. ii. 189 “Men and men's fortunes could I use,” Ham. III. i. 34 “We may of their encounter judge,” V. ii. 267 .

fraud.text: faithlessness Gent. II. vii. 78 , Ado II. iii. 76 “The of men was ever so,” 1H6 IV. iv. 36 , Ven. 1141 .

fraught1.text: freight, cargo Tw.N. V. i. 65 , Tit. I. i. 71 ; fig. load Oth. III. iii. 450 “Swell, bosom, with thy ”

fraught3.text: laden, loaded, fig. stored, filled Gent. III. ii. 70 “full with serviceable vows,” Mer.V. II. viii. 30 “A vessel . . . richly ,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 527 “so with curious business,” H5 II. ii. 139 , Troil. Prol. 4, Lr. I. iv. 243 .

fraughting.text: forming the cargo Tp. I. ii. 13 .

freckled.text: spotted Tp. I. ii. 283 “A whelp,” H5 V. ii. 49 “The cowslip” (cf. MND. II. i. 13 ).

free1.text: adj. (the foll. are the chief obs. senses) 1. of noble or honourable character, generous, magnanimous Tw.N. I. v. 281 , H8 III. i. 59 “Like and honest men,” Troil. I. iii. 235 , IV. v. 138 , Oth. II. iii. 328 “of so , so kind . . . a disposition,” III. iii. 199 “your free and noble nature.”

free2.text: vb. (2 a rare sense; cf. Romans vi. 7) 1. to secure “from” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 446 “we thee From the dead blow of it.”

freedom.text: 1. “at ,” freely, at liberty Tp. IV. i. 268 “thou Shalt have the air at ,” Cym. III. iii. 71 “liv'd at honest ”

freely.text: in freedom, with absolute possession of one's privileges, &c. Mer.V. III. ii. 250 “I must have the half” . . . ., Tw.N. I. iv. 39 “thou shalt live as as thy lord, To call his fortunes thine.” ∥ The more usual meanings are ‘unreservedly, readily, willingly’, ‘frankly, openly’, ‘without hindrance’, ‘generously, liberally.’

frequent1.text: adj. (twice only in S.) 1. addicted “to” Wint. IV. i. [ ii. ] 36

frequent2.text: to resort to a place R2 V. iii. 6 .

fresh1.text: spring of fresh water Tp. III. ii. 77 .

fresh2.text: adj. (1 cf. ‘freshman’ at a university) 1. raw, inexperienced John III. iv. 145 .

freshly.text: newly, recently Tp. V. i. 236 * “ beheld Our . . . ship” (or ?=beheld our ship renovated); anew, afresh Meas. I. ii. 181 , Cym. V. iv. 143 ; with undiminished intensity H5 IV. iii. 55 “ remembered,” H8 V. iii. 31 “ pitied in our memories” ; healthily, bloomingly AYL. III. ii. 244 , H5 IV. Chor. 39 “freshly looks.”

fret.text: to adorn (a ceiling) with carved or embossed work in decorative patterns Cym. II. iv. 88 “The roof o' the chamber With golden cherubins is fretted” ; fig. Ham. II. ii. 320 [ 313 ]; to chequer Cæs. II. i. 104 “yon grey lines That fret the clouds.”

fret1.text: in instruments of the guitar kind, (formerly) a ring of gut (now a bar of wood) placed on the finger-board to regulate the fingering Lucr. 1140 .

fret2.text: to make or form by wearing away R2 III. iii. 167 , Lr. I. iv. 309 “fret channels in her cheeks.”

fretful.text: (not pre-S. in either sense) 1. eating away 2H6 III. ii. 403 “a fretful co'rrosive.”

friar.text: member of any of certain religious orders founded in the 13th cent. and afterwards, of which the chief were the Franciscans or Grey Friars, the Augustines or Austin Friars, the Dominicans or Black Friars, the Carmelites or White Friars; in Shr. IV. i. 148 “It was the of orders grey” is a fragment of a lost ballad.

friend1.headword: friend sb. (in the ordinary sense the foll. phrases occur
friend1.text: “at , to ”=as a friend, friendly, on one's side; “be” or “hold f-s with, make f-s to”) 1. pl. relatives, kinsfolk, ‘people’ Gent. I. i. 64 , III. i. 106 “she . . . is promis'd by her f-s Unto a youthful gentleman,” Meas. I. ii. 161 , AYL. I. iii. 65 , R2 I. iv. 22 , Tit. V. i. 136 ; occas. sing. 1H6 V. iv. 9 .

friend2.text: to befriend, assist Meas. IV. ii. 116 , H5 IV. v. 17 , H8 I. ii. 140 “Not f-ed by his wish,” Cym. II. iii. 52 ; absol. Troil. I. ii. 82 “time must or end.”

friending.text: friendliness Ham. I. v. 185 “his love and ”

friendship.text: friendly act, favour, friendly aid Mer.V. I. iii. 169 , Wint. IV. i. [ ii. ] 22 “the heaping f-s,” Tim. IV. iii. 70 “what may I do thee?,” Lr. III. ii. 62 “a hovel; Some will it lend you 'gainst the tempest,” Oth. III. iii. 21 .

frippery.text: place where cast-off clothes are sold Tp. IV. i. 228 .

fritters.text: “make fritters of,” hash up Wiv. V. v. 155 .

fro.text: =from Rom. IV. i. 75 , Cym. V. v. 262 .

frolic.text: merry MND. V. ii. 17 [ i. 394 ]; adv. Shr. iv. iii. 184 .

from1.text: prep. (the chief obs. uses are) 1. among, from among All'sW. II. i. 130 “entreating your royal thoughts A modest one,” Tim. I. ii. 96 “why have you that charitable title from thousands?.”

from2.text: away Tim. IV. iii. 404 “the falling- of his friends” (mod. edd. “falling-of”†).

front1.text: sb. (1 the usual S. sense) 1. forehead, (hence) face John II. i. 356 “these royal f-'s,” R3 I. i. 9 “smooth'd his wrinkled ,” Mac. IV. iii. 231 ; transf. 1H4 III. i. 14 “ of heaven” (cf. Lr. II. ii. 114 “flickering Phœbus' ” ), H5 I. Chor. 21 ; phr. Oth. I. iii. 80 “head and of my offending,” III. i. 52 “To take the saf'st occasion by the front.”

front2.text: to march in the front rank (S.) H8 I. ii. 42 “I . . . front but in that file” . . .

frontier.text: outwork in fortification 1H4 II. iii. 57 “palisadoes, f-s, parapets” ; fig. I. iii. 19 “The moody of a servant brow” (cf. H5 III. i. 10 ); frontier fortress or town Ham. IV. iv. 16 .

frontlet.text: band worn on the forehead; fig. with ref. to a frowning visage Lr. I. iv. 210 “what makes that frontlet on?.”

frosty.text: characteristic of old age 2H6 V. i. 167 “the head,” Tit. V. iii. 77 “my frosty signs.”

froth.text: to make drink frothy; fig. Wiv. I. iii. 14 “Let me see thee froth and lime.”

fruit.text: (1 not a common use in S. or elsewhere) 1. dessert Ham. II. ii. 52 “the fruit to that great feast.”

fruitful.text: (sense 1 is rare outside S.) 1. abundant, copious Meas. IV. iii. 165 “one meal,” Tim. V. i. 155 “a recompense more ,” Ham. I. ii. 80 .

fruitfully.text: copiously, fully All'sW. II. ii. 75 “you understand me?—Most ,” Lr. IV. vi. 271 “ offered.”

fruitless.text: barren, not producing offspring, unfertile MND. I. i. 73 “the cold moon,” Mac. III. i. 61 “a fruitless crown,” Ven. 751 “fruitless chastity.”

frush.text: to smash, batter Troil. V. vi. 29 .

frustrate1.text: to annul 3H6 II. i. 175 “To f . . . . his oath.”

frustrate2.text: frustrated Ant. V. i. 2 * ; vain Tp. III. iii. 10 “Our frustrate search.”

frutify.text: comic blunder for ‘notify’ Mer.V. II. ii. 146 .

fulfil.text: (1 the earliest sense) 1. to fill full, fill up LLL. IV. iii. 364 “charity itself f-s the law,” Lucr. 1258 [women] “so fulfill'd With men's abuses,” Sonn. cxxxvi. 5 “ the treasure of thy love.”

full1.text: —“at ,” (1) fully, completely Meas. I. i. 43 “be thou at ourself” ; (2) at length Err. I. i. 122 “dilate at ,” H5 II. iv. 140 “know our mind at ,” Ham. IV. iii. 66 ; (3) at the period or moment of fullness LLL. V. ii. 215 “look the moon at ,” Ant. III. ii. 49 “at of tide;—in the ,” with full complement Troil. IV. v. 271 ;—“to the ,” (1) fully All'sW. I. iii. 199 , 2H6 I. ii. 84 ; (2) to its full state Ant. II. i. 11 “it will come to the ,” Troil. III. iii. 242 “to my of view” (=to my eye's complete satisfaction).

full2.text: freq. in the senses (1) fully, quite; (2) very, exceedingly.

fullam.text: kind of false dice loaded at the corner Wiv. I. iii. 92 .

fuller.text: one who cleanses cloth H8 I. ii. 33 .

fullness.text: repletion, satiety Sonn. lvi. 6 ; abundance Cym. III. vi. 12 “To lapse in fullness.”

fully.text: to satiety Cor. I. ix. 11 , Lr. III. v. 22 .

fulsome.text: (1 a S. use; the rest are obs.) 1. (?) lustful Mer.V. I. iii. 87 “fulsome ewes.”

fumble.text: to wrap up clumsily Tit. IV. ii. 59 ; fig. Troil. IV. iv. 46 .

fume.text: to be clouded with fumes of liquor Ant. II. i. 24 “Keep his brain fuming.”

fumiter.text: the plant Fumaria Lr. IV. iv. 3 (Qq “femiter,” Ff incorrectly “Fenitar”); also fumitory (mod. edd.) H5 V. ii. 45 (most old edd. “femetary”).

function.text: (the usual meaning is ‘office, employment’, 2 not pre-S.) 1. activity, action (of the faculties) Mac. I. iii. 140 “ Is smother'd in surmise,” Ham. II. ii. 590 [ 582 ] “his whole ”

funeral.text: (1 a 16-17th cent. use) 1. pl. obsequies Tit. I. i. 381 , Cæs. V. iii. 105 .

furlong.text: “thousand f-s” opposed to “an acre” Tp. I. i. 70 , Wint. I. ii. 95 .

furnace.text: to exhale as from a furnace Cym. I. vi. 66 “f-s The thick sighs.” ∥ So used by Chapman.

furnish.text: (the construction “ with” also occurs) 1. to supply with what is necessary, equip, fit out Mer.V. II. iv. 9 “we have two hours To us,” 1H6 IV. i. 39 “He then that is not f-'d in this sort,” Ant. I. iv. 77 “I shall be furnish'd to inform you rightly.”

furnishings.text: unimportant appendages, mere externals Lr. III. i. 29 .

furniture.text: fitting out, equipping, provision 1H4 III. iii. 224 “Money and order for their ” ; equipment Shr. IV. iii. 182 “this poor and mean array,” 2H6 I. iii. 172 ; trappings, harness All'sW. II. iii. 65 .

fustilarian.text: (?) comic formation on the word ‘fustilugs’=fat frowzy woman 2H4 II. i. 68 .

gaberdine.text: loose upper garment Tp. II. ii. 41 .

gad.text: sharp spike; applied to a stylus Tit. IV. i. 103 “I . . . with a gad of steel will write these words” ; phrase “upon the gad,” suddenly Lr. I. ii. 26 “All this done Upon the !” (cf. ‘on the spur of the moment’).

gage1.text: sb. 1. pawn, pledge, security; in phr. “lay to ,” to put in pawn Lucr. 1351 .

gage2.text: vb. (3 a sense peculiar to S.) 1. to pledge, stake, risk Ham. I. i. 91 “a moiety competent Was g-d by our king,” Lucr. 144 “one for all, or all for one we gage.”

gain.text: (the foll. uses are app. only S.) 1. to acquire (a language) 2H4 IV. iv. 69 .

gait.text: walking, going forward Wiv. I. iv. 31 , MND. V. ii. 46 [ i. 423 ] “take his ” (=go his way), Tw.N. I. iv. 15 “address thy ” (=go), III. i. 94 “with and entrance,” H8 III. ii. 117 “fast ,” Lr. IV. vi. 243 “go your ” : fig. proceeding Ham. I. ii. 31 “to suppress His further gait herein.”

gall1.text: spirit to resent injury or insult Oth. IV. iii. 95 “we have galls.”

gall2.text: vb. (orig. sense ‘make sore by chafing’ and fig. ‘harass, annoy’ occur; 2 is only S.) 1. to graze with a weapon, to wound, hurt Shr. V. ii. 60 , John IV. iii. 94 , H8 III. ii. 208 , Tit. IV. iii. 70 , Ham. IV. vii. 147 .

gallant1.text: sb. (2 a courteous mode of address) 1. man of fashion and pleasure, fine gentleman Ado III. iv. 96 “all the gallants of the town,” Oth. II. iii. 31 .

gallant2.text: adj. (orig.=‘showy in appearance, smart’) 1. loosely used as a gen. epithet of praise=excellent, splendid, fine AYL. I. iii. 120 “A curtle-axe,” Wint. I. i. 42 “a child,” Cæs. IV. ii. 24 “ show” ; of a ship =noble, stately Tp. V. i. 237 .

gallantry.text: body of gallants Troil. III. i. 151 .

galled1.text: (a) irritated, (b) full of gall, rancorous Troil. V. x. 55 * “Some galled goose of Winchester.”

galled2.text: sore from chafing Ham. III. ii. 256 “the jade” ; fretted with salt water H5 III. i. 12 “a rock,” Lucr. 1440 “the shore” ; with tears R3 IV. iv. 53 , Ham. I. ii. 155 “her galled eyes.”

galley.text: low flat-built sea-going vessel with one deck, formerly used in the Mediterranean, Shr. II. i. 373 [ 381 ].

galliard.text: quick and lively dance in triple time Tw.N. I. iii. 129 , H5 I. ii. 252 .

galliass.text: heavy low-built vessel, larger than a galley, employed in war Shr. II. i. 372 [ 380 ].

gallop.text: “false ,” canter (fig.) Ado III. iv. 94 , AYL. III. ii. 120 “This is the very false gallop of verses.”

gallow.text: to frighten Lr. III. ii. 44 . ∥ Now dial. usually in the form ‘galley’, but ‘gallow’ is used in south-west midl.

gallowglasses.text: soldiers or retainers formerly maintained by Irish chiefs 2H6 IV. ix. 26 , Mac. I. ii. 13 .

gallows.headword: gallows (with additional pl. suffix “gallowses” Cym. V. iv. 213 )
gallows.text: one deserving to be hanged, gallowsbird Tp. I. i. 34 , LLL. V. ii. 12 .

gambol.text: as adj. sportive, playful 2H4 II. iv. 273 .

game.text: (the foll. are absolute meanings) 1. fun, sport LLL. V. ii. 155 , 361 “pleasant game,” MND. I. i. 240 “As waggish boys in game” . . .

gamester.text: (thrice in the sense ‘gambler’) 1. frolicsome person AYL. I. i. 173 , Shr. II. i. 394 [ 402 ], H8 I. iv. 45 “You are a merry gamester.”

gamut.text: musical scale Shr. III. i. 72 , &c. (old edd. “gamoth, gamouth”).

gape.text: to be eager “to” Rom. II. Chor. 2 .

gaping2.text: “ pig” * , pig's head served on the table with its mouth wide open Mer.V. IV. i. 47 , 54

garb.text: style, manner, fashion H5 V. i. 81 , Cor. IV. vii. 44 “austerity and ” (=austere behaviour), Ham. II. ii. 399 [ 390 ], Lr. II. ii. 103 “constrains the Quite from his nature,” Oth. II. i. 318 . ∥ The meaning ‘fashion of dress, costume’ is not S.

garboil.text: brawl, commotion Ant. I. iii. 61 , II. ii. 71 .

garland.text: (2 cf. ‘Bellay, first garland of free Poesie’ Spenser) 1. royal crown or diadem 2H4 IV. v. 200 (“garment”†), V. ii. 84 , R3 III. ii. 40 “Till Richard wear the of the realm.”

garnished.text: furnished (? with words or with brains) Mer.V. III. v. 75 .

gaskins.text: breeches Tw.N. I. v. 27 “if both break, your gaskins fall.”

gasted.text: terrified Lr. II. i. 57 “ by the noise I made.”

gastness.text: terror Oth. V. i. 106 “the of her eye.”

gate.text: in Ham. I. v. 67 “The natural g-s and alleys of the body” there is perhaps an allusion to the ‘vena porta’ (rendered ‘gate-vein’ by 17th cent. writers).

gather.text: to infer, deduce, conclude Err. I. i. 95 , IV. iii. 87 “The reason that I he is mad,” R3 I. iii. 68 ; absol. to draw inferences, get information All'sW. IV. i. 87 “To from thee,” Ham. II. ii. 108 “now, , and surmise.”

gay.text: in ballad style, conventional epithet of praise applied to women Sonn. Music 15 [ Pilgr. 225 ] “the lady gay.”

gaze.text: that which is gazed at Mac. V. vii. 53 [ viii. 24 ] “the show and o' the time,” Sonn. v. 2 “The lovely gaze.”

gear.text: (orig. sense is ‘apparel, dress’ LLL. V. ii. 304 ） 1. stuff, thing, article Mer.V. II. ii. 182 “a good wench for this gear,” Troil. III. ii. 220 , Rom. V. i. 60 .

geck.text: fool Tw.N. V. i. 355 , Cym. V. iv. 67 . ∥ Survives in midl. dial.; used by George Eliot in ‘Adam Bede’ ix.

geld.text: to deprive (“of” some essential part) LLL. II. i. 148 , R2 II. i. 238 “g-ed of his patrimony,” 1H4 III. i. 111 “Gelding the opposed continent.”

gemini.text: pair Wiv. II. ii. 9 “a gemini of baboons.”

gender.text: kind, sort, class Oth. I. iii. 327 “one of herbs,” Phoen. 18 ; “the general ,” the common sort Ham. IV. vii. 18 .

general1.text: sb. (the military sense is used fig. in Gent. IV. i. 61 , LLL. III. i. 195 [ 187 ], Rom. V. iii. 219 “ of your woes,” Sonn. cliv. 7 ) 1. “the general,” the whole Troil. I. iii. 342 .

general2.text: 1. all, all collectively, whole 1H4 III. ii. 178 “Our forces,” 1H6 IV. iv. 3 “all our force,” Troil. V. ii. 129 “the sex” (=all womenkind), Lr. I. iv. 65 , Oth. III. iii. 346 “the general camp.”

generally.text: (the sense ‘usually, commonly’ is post-S.) 1. in a body, as a whole AYL. III. ii. 372 , Shr. I. ii. 277 “To whom we all rest beholding,” H5 I. i. 88 .

generation.text: 1. offspring, progeny Wint. II. i. 147 , R2 V. v. 8 , Troil. III. i. 148 “is love a of vipers?,” Lr. I. i. 119 .

generative.text: capable of generation Meas. III. ii. 121 .

generous.text: of noble lineage, high-born Meas. IV. vi. 13 , LLL. V. i. 98 “most sir,” Ham. I. iii. 74 , Oth. III. iii. 280 .

genius.text: (3 not pre-S.) 1. in classical pagan belief, tutelary god or attendant spirit supposed to be allotted to every man at his birth Tw.N. III. iv. 144 , Troil. IV. iv. 50 “the so Cries ‘Come!’ to him,” Cæs. II. i. 66 , Mac. III. i. 56 “under him My genius is rebuk'”

gentle.text: to ennoble H5 IV. iii. 63 “ his condition.”

gentle1.text: pl. gentlefolk LLL. IV. ii. 174 ; chiefly used (sing. and pl.) in polite address Wiv. III. ii. 96 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 46 “Be merry, ,” H5 I. Chor. 8 “pardon, g-s all,” Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 47

gentle2.text: adj. (the senses ‘well born’, ‘kind’, ‘not violent, mild’ are well represented in S.) 1. used in polite address or as a complimentary epithet Gent. I. ii. 14 “What think'st thou of the Proteus?,” II. i. 118 “I thank you, servant,” III. i. 14 “your daughter,” Cæs. III. ii. 78 “You gentle Romans.”

gentleman.text: (1 in the 17th c. ‘something more than an ordinary Souldier, hath a little more pay, and doth not stand Centinel’） 1. officer of a company of soldiers 1H4 IV. ii. 26 , H5 IV. i. 39 .

gentry.text: (2 properly ‘what is proper to gentlemen’) 1. rank by birth, quality or rank of gentleman Wiv. II. i. 53 , Wint. I. ii. 393 “which no less adorns Our ,” 1H6 II. iv. 93 “ancient ,” Cor. III. i. 143 .

german.text: adj. and sb. (“cousin-german” = first cousin Troil. IV. v. 120 ) 1. closely related, akin Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 805 (Ff “Iermain(e),” Tim. IV. iii. 345 (Ff “Germa(i)ne”).

germen.text: germ Mac. IV. i. 59 “the treasure Of Nature's g-s,” Lr. III. ii. 8 .

gest1.text: pl. deeds Ant. IV. viii. 2 (old edd. “guests”).

gest2.text: time allotted for a halt (S.) Wint. I. ii. 41 .

gesture.text: carriage, bearing, demeanour AYL. V. ii. 70 “If you do love Rosalind so near the heart as your cries it out,” H5 IV. Chor. 25 “their gesture sad.”

get.text: (pa. t. “got,” in Per. II. ii. 6 “gat” to rhyme with “at,” pa. pple. “got,” also “gotten”) 1. intr. to gain 1H6 IV. iii. 32 “we lose, they . . . get.”

ghost1.text: sb. (the mod. use is the prevailing one) 1. incorporeal being, spirit Sonn. lxxxvi. 9 .

ghostly.text: spiritual Meas. IV. iii. 53 , Rom. III. iii. 48 “ghostly confessor.” [ i. 190 [ 182 ].

gibbet.text: to hang as on a gibbet (S.) 2H4 III. ii. 285 .

gig1.text: whipping-top LLL. IV. iii. 167 , V. i. 71 , 74

gig2.text: (?) to walk wantonly Ham. III. i. 152 (so Q 1604; F “gidge,” Q 1676 “jig”).

gild.text: (1 common in 16-17th cent.) 1. to smear with blood John II. i. 316 “all gilt with Frenchmen's blood,” Mac. II. ii. 57 (quibble).

gilded.text: of a golden colour Ant. I. iv. 62 “ puddle.”

gillyvor.text: clove-scented pink, Dianthus caryophyllus Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 82, 98

gimmaled.text: made with gimmals or joints, consisting of two similar parts hinged together H5 IV. ii. 49 “the bit” (Ff “Iymold,” mod. edd. “gimmal”).

gin.text: to begin Mac. I. ii. 25 “whence the sun gins his reflection” ; more usu. with an infin.; cf. CAN vb. 2 .

ging.text: gang, set Wiv. IV. ii. 126 (F1 Q3 “gin”).

gipsy.text: allusively identified with ‘Egyptian’ Ant. IV. x. 41 [ xii. 28 ].

gird.text: sharp or biting remark Shr. V. ii. 58 ; so gird vb. intr. 2H4 I. ii. 6 , trans. Cor. I. i. 262 .

girdle.text: Ado V. i. 146 “to turn his ,” said to refer to preparation for wrestling by turning the buckle to the back;— MND. II. i. 175 “put a round the earth,” make a circuit of the world.

girt.text: to gird 1H6 III. i. 170 , 2H6 I. i. 66 .

give.text: (pa. pple. once “gave” Ven. 571 ; 8 metaphor from the exuding of moisture, e.g. on a stone) 1. to ‘give away’ (the bride) at the marriage ceremony AYL. III. iii. 71 “Is there none here to the woman?.”

glad1.text: gladness Per. II. Gower 38 . ∥ An archaism; not in current use after 1450

glad2.text: to make glad 3H6 IV. vi. 93 , Tit. I. i. 166 .

glance1.text: satirical hit AYL. II. vii. 57 “g-s of the fool.”

glance2.text: 1. (of a weapon) to glide off an object struck Wiv. V. v. 261 [ 249 ] “your arrow hath g-d”; fig. Shr. V. ii. 61 “the jest did away from me,” Lr. V. iii. 150 ; “ on,” to strike obliquely upon and turn aside Per. III. iii. 7 .

glass.text: (the commonest S. sense is ‘mirror’) 1. sand-glass, hour-glass All'sW. II. i. 168 , Wint. I. ii. 306 “The running of one ,” IV. Chor. [ i. ] 16 “I turn my ,” 1H6 IV. ii. 35 , Sonn. cxxvi. 2 ; in nautical use, half-hour glass, hence=half-an-hour Tp. I. ii. 240 , V. i. 223 “three glasses since.”

glassed.text: enclosed or cased in glass LLL. II. i. 242 .

glassy.text: frail as glass Meas. II. ii. 120 “His essence.”

glaze.text: to stare Cæs. I. iii. 21 (mod. edd. “glar'd”†). ∥ In mod. use found only in Cornwall and Devon.

glean.text: to collect into one mass H8 III. ii. 285 .

gleaned.text: stripped of defenders H5 I. ii. 151 .

gleek.text: gibe, jest 1H6 III. ii. 123 , Rom. IV. v. 115 ; so gleek vb. MND. III. i. 154 , H5 V. i. 78 .

glib.text: to castrate, geld Wint. II. i. 148 .

glimpse.text: transient brightness, flash Meas. I. ii. 168 “ of newness” ; Ham. I. iv. 53 “g-s of the moon” (=the earth by night); fig. faint appearance, tinge, trace Troil. I. ii. 25 .

globe.text: Ham. I. v. 97 “this distracted ” =this confused head or brain.

glooming.text: dark (fig.) Rom. V. iii. 305 “A peace.” ∥ “Gloomy,” which occurs thrice in S., is not recorded before his date.

glorious.text: eager for glory Cym. I. vi. 7 “the desire that's ,” Per. I. Gower 9 .

gloss.text: “set a on,” to give a speciously fair appearance to 1H6 IV. i. 103 , Tim. I. ii. 16 .

glow.text: to make hot Ant. II. ii. 212 “To the delicate cheeks.”

gloze1.text: pl. ‘high falutin’ talk LLL. IV. iii. 370 .

gloze2.text: vb. (orig.=to make glosses upon) 1. to interpret (a thing) to be (so and so) H5 I. ii. 40 “Which Salique land the French unjustly To be the realm of France.”

glut.text: to swallow Tp. I. i. 65 “And gape . . . to him.”

glutted.text: satiated 1H4 III. ii. 84 “, gorg'd, and full.”

gnarl.text: to snarl R2 I. iii. 292 “y-ing sorrow,” 2H6 III. i. 192 “wolves are gnarling.”

gnarled.text: knotted Meas. II. ii. 116 “ oak.” ∥ First in S., app. as a variant of ‘knurled’, whence in mod. use only from the beginning of the 19th cent.

gnaw.text: pa. pple. “gnawn” Wiv. II. ii. 311 “my reputation gnawn at.”

go.text: (1 current till about 1800) 1. to walk, move on foot at an ordinary pace Tp. III. ii. 23 , Gent. III. i. 391 “going will scarce serve thy turn,” IV. ii. 20 “love Will creep . . . where it cannot go,” 1H4 II. iii. 88 , 2H4 II. iv. 178 , Lr. I. iv. 135 “Ride more than thou goest,” Sonn. cxxx. 11 .

goal.text: Ant. IV. viii. 22 “Get for of” =be even with.

gobbet.text: piece of raw flesh 2H6 IV. i. 85 , V. ii. 58 .

god1.text: prefixed, without the article, to the name of a deity, or a person likened to one Ado III. iii. 142 “like god Bel's priests,” Troil. I. iii. 169 “god Achilles” (Q F1; Ff2 3 “good);—God be wi' you,” in old edd. usually “God buy you or ye” (also “bu'y, buy'”), occas, “God be with you, God buy to you,” later Ff and Qq “God b' w' ye, b' wi' ye or you;—God dig-you-den, God (g)igoden”: see GOOD-DEN.

god2.text: to deify, idolize Cor. V. iii. 11 .

godfather.text: fig. sometimes with ref. to the godfather's naming the child at baptism LLL. I. i. 88 “These early g-s of heaven's lights That give a name to every fixed star,” Ven. Ded. 5:—jocularly, pl. jurymen whose verdict brings a man to the gallows Mer.V. IV. i. 399 (cf. ‘I will leaue you To your God-fathers in Law, Let twelve men worke,’ Jonson, ‘twelve God-vathers, good men and true’ Randolph).

goer.text: “-back,” one who retreats Cym. I. i. 169 ; “backward,” one who deteriorates All'sW. I. ii. 48 ; “-between,” go-between Troil. III. ii. 208 .

gold.text: the metal used in the ornamentation of fabrics, gold thread Shr. II. i. 348 [ 356 ] “Valance of Venice gold.”

golden.text: (the fig. sense ‘precious’ is freq.; 3 “ time” 2H4 V. iii. 98 is also used like “ age” Tp. II. i. 175 [ 168 ], Lucr. 60 , “ world” AYL. I. i. 127 ) 1. of gold (freq.); “ care,” the burden of the crown 2H4 IV. v. 22 ; “ sorrow,” (?) sorrow that comes from high rank H8 II. iii. 22 .

gondola.text: light flat-bottomed boat in use on the Venetian canals Mer.V. II. viii. 8 , AYL. IV. i. 40 ; hence gondolier Oth. I. i. 126 (Ff Qq2 3 “Gundelier”).

gone.text: not pre-S. in the senses (1) dead John III. iv. 163 , (2) “far” advanced R2 II. i. 185 , (3) lost, ruined Meas. V. i. 297 , Mer.V. III. v. 19 .

good1.text: “do to,” be of use or advantage to Mer.V. III. v. 7 , AYL. V. ii. 65 , Tit. IV. ii. 35 , Ven. 28 ;—“much do it” (cf. DICH) Wiv. I. i. 84 ; —“do on” or “upon,” prevail upon Meas. IV. ii. 71 , 1H4 III. i. 199 “one that no persuasion can do upon,” Rom. IV. ii. 13 ;—“do ,” be successful, make progress Wiv. I. iv. 148 “Shall I do any ?,” Wint. II. ii. 54 , 2H6 IV. iii. 15 “to thrive and do ”

good2.text: adj. (all the ordinary senses are freq.; 6 (ii) is the most freq. meaning of “make good”) 1. a conventional epithet to titles of high rank Wint. I. ii. 220 “At the queen's entreaty,” H8 III. i. 77 “ your Graces,” Cym. II. iii. 158 “She's my lady” ; hence freq., an epithet of courteous address or respectful reference Tp. I. i. 10 “ boatswain,” Gent. I. ii. 115 “Be calm, wind,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 200

goodman.text: (3 evolved from the use in 2 ii) 1. husband Shr. Ind. ii. 107 “I am your goodman.”

goodness.text: ‘good things’ Meas. III. ii. 234 “Bliss and on you!,” V. i. 6 “we hear Such of your justice,” 1H6 III. ii. 72 “Talbot means no ,” R3 I. iv. 198 (Ff), Lr. V. i. 7 , Oth. I. ii. 35 “The of the night” ; (hence occas.) success Mac. IV. iii. 136 “the chance of goodness.”

goodwife.text: formerly prefixed to surnames = Mrs. 2H4 II. i. 104 “goodwife Keech, the butcher's wife.”

goodwill.text: “by” or “of” one's “,” of one's own accord, voluntarily R2 IV. i. 177 , Ven. 479 .

goose.text: tailor's smoothing iron, of which the handle resembles a goose's neck Mac. II. iii. 17 .

gorge.text: what has been swallowed; “cast the ,” orig. a phrase of falconry Tim. IV. iii. 40 .

gorget.text: piece of armour for the throat Troil. I. iii. 174 .

gospel.text: used allusively with ref. to ‘the gospel for the day’ at mass Tw.N. V. i. 298 “a madman's epistles are no gospels.”

goss.text: gorse, furze, or whin, Ulex europaeus Tp. IV. i. 180 “pricking goss.” ∥ This form probably survives in the Warwickshire phrase ‘as rough as goss’.

gossip1.text: 1. a child's godfather or godmother, sponsor (always with ref. to their relation to the parents) Gent. III. i. 270 “'tis not a maid, for she hath had g-s” (i.e. for a child of hers), Wint. II. iii. 41 “About some g-s for your highness,” H8 V. v. 13 “My noble g-s” (=sponsors to Princess Elizabeth).

gossip2.text: vb. (cf. GOSSIP sb. sense 3) 1. to be sponsor to All'sW. I. i. 191 .

gossiping.text: merrymaking (orig. meeting of ‘gossips’, esp. at a birth) Err. V. i. 422 , John V. ii. 59 .

goujere.text: incorrect spelling of GOOD YEAR in mod. edd.

gourd.text: kind of false dice Wiv. I. iii. 92 .

gout.text: drop Mac. II. i. 46 “gouts of blood.”

govern.headword: govern (freq. in the gen. sense, once common)
govern.text: to direct, regulate, control Gent. II. vii. 74 “truer stars did Proteus' birth,” Wiv. V. i. 21 “the finest mad devil of jealousy . . . that ever g-ed frenzy,” Mer.V. IV. i. 134 , Cæs. I. iii. 83 , Ham. III. ii. 379 “ these ventages with your finger,” Lr. IV. vii. 19 “Be g-'d by your knowledge.”

governess.text: ruler, mistress MND. II. i. 103 “the moon, the of floods,” Lucr. 443 .

government.text: (the sense ‘rule, sway’ occurs) 1. control, management MND. V. i. 125 “a sound, but not in ” (i.e. without control of the stops of the ‘recorder’; cf. Ham. III. ii. 379 ), Rom. IV. i. 102 , Cym. II. iv. 150 “Quite besides The of patience.”

governor.text: (the obs. uses are as follows) 1. military commander Oth. II. i. 55 .

grace1.text: sb. (1 “do grace” occurs also in the sense ‘do a kindness, confer a favour’ cf. 3; 5 is only S. and is an extension of the religious sense ‘favour of God’) 1. “do” (a person or thing) “,” reflect credit on, set in a good light, embellish 1H4 II. i. 79 “to do the profession some ,” V. iv. 161 “if a lie may do thee ,” Ham. I. i. 131 , Sonn. xxviii. 10 , cxxxii. 11 “mourning doth thee ;—in of,” in honour of MND. IV. i. 140 .

grace2.text: to gratify, delight R3 IV. iv. 175 . ∥ The usual senses are ‘adorn, embellish’, and ‘confer honour on, do honour to’.

graceful.text: (1 otherwise only 15th cent.; 2 only S.) 1. full of divine grace Wint. V. i. 171 .

gracious.text: (only 3 is still current; 5 is not evidenced elsewhere in Eliz. literature) 1. finding favour, acceptable, popular AYL. I. ii. 202 * , 3H6 III. iii. 117 “ in the people's eye,” Tit. I. i. 11 , 170 , 429

graciously.text: through divine grace Per. IV. vi. 65 .

graff1.text: graft, scion Per. V. i. 60 “For every would send a caterpillar” ; fig. Lucr. 1062 “This bastard ”

graff2.text: to insert a graft in (a stock) AYL. III. ii. 126 “ it with a medlar,” 2H4 V. iii. 3 “pippin of my own g-ing,” 2H6 III. ii. 214 “stock Was graft with crab-tree slip,” R3 III. vii. 126 .

graft.text: vb. (‘graft’ as a sb. does not occur) 1. to fix, implant, or attach, as one does a graft or scion All'sW. I. ii. 54 , Wint. I. ii. 246 “A servant g-ed in my serious trust,” R2 III. iv. 101 “the plants thou g-'st,” 1H4 III. ii. 15 “Such . . . rude society, As thou art . . . grafted to,” Mac. IV. iii. 51 .

grafter.text: original tree from which a scion has been taken for grafting H5 III. v. 9 .

grain.text: (1 ‘grain’ is properly the red insect used in dyeing called ‘kermers’, ‘alkermes’, but also= ‘cochineal’) 1. “in ,” literally, dyed scarlet or crimson, fast dyed MND. I. ii. 98 “your purple in- beard” ; (hence) indelible, ineradicable, ingrained Err. III. ii. 109 “[a fault] 'tis in ,” Tw.N. I. v. 257 “'Tis in , sir; 'twill endure wind and weather.”

grained1.text: ingrained Ham. III. iv. 90 “such black and spots” ; furrowed, lined Err. V. i. 313 “this face of mine.”

gramercy.text: (2 the Qq read “God a mercy”) 1. = GOD-A-MERCY 2, Mer.V. II. ii. 131 “God bless your worship!—Gramercy!,” R3 III. ii. 105 , Tit. I. i. 495 , IV. ii. 7 , Tim. II. ii. 68 , 73 ; expressing thanks for advice Shr. I. i. 41 , 167

grand.text: (in Wiv. IV. v. 89 * , Lr. II. ii. 112 * the meaning is uncertain; in Ham. V. ii. 18 “ commission” is prob. modelled on technical terms like ‘grand assize’, ‘grand jury’) 1. pre-eminent, chief Tp. I. ii. 274 “her hests,” V. i. 280 “this liquor” (=the elixir), R2 V. vi. 19 “The conspirator,” R3 IV. iv. 52 .

grandsire.text: used for ‘old man’ Shr. IV. v. 50 ; adj. = ancient Rom. I. iv. 37 “I am proverb'd with a grandsire phrase” )

grange.text: farm-house, country house Meas. III. i. 279 “the moated ,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 309, Oth. I. i. 106 “My house is not a grange.”

grant.text: to assent “to” 3H6 I. i. 245 “g-ed to that act.”

grasp1.text: embrace Troil. IV. ii. 13 “the g-s of love.”

grasp2.text: vb. (2 not pre-S.) 1. to clutch 2H6 III. ii. 172 “g-'d And tugg'd for life.”

grate1.text: grating 1H6 I. iv. 10 , 60 ; barred place of confinement Wiv. II. ii. 9 “looked through the , like a geminy of baboons.”

grate2.text: vb. (the foll. are now obs. or rare uses) 1. to wear away Troil. III. ii. 195 “g-d To dusty nothing.”

gratify.text: (the sense ‘to please’ also occurs) 1. to reward, requite Cor. II. ii. 45 “To his noble service,” Oth. V. ii. 211 , Cym. II. iv. 7 “I barely your love.”

gratillity.text: clown's humorous perversion of ‘gratuity’ Tw.N. II. iii. 28 .

gratulate2.text: to greet, salute R3 IV. i. 10 “To the gentle princes,” Tim. I. ii. 133 ; to express joy at Tit. I. i. 221 “gratulate his safe return.”

grave.text: (pa. pple. “graved” and “graven”) 1. to bury, swallow up as in a grave R2 III. ii. 140 “g-'d in the hollow ground,” Tim. IV. iii. 167 “ditches grave you all!.”

gravelled.text: nonplussed AYL. IV. i. 76 “ for lack of matter.”

graymalkin.text: properly=grey cat, used in Mac. I. i. 8 as the name of a fiend.

graze1.text: (humorously of persons) to feed Rom. III. v. 190 “ where you will, you shall not house with me.”

graze2.text: to abrade in passing Oth. IV. i. 279 “neither nor pierce” ; to ricochet H5 IV. iii. 105 (F2 “grasing,” F1 Qq “crasing”).

grease.text: (?) to make gross or lewd (cf. GREASILY) Tim. IV. iii. 196 “greases his pure mind.”

greasy.text: contemptuous epithet Wiv. II. i. 110 “this knight,” AYL. II. i. 55 “you fat and citizens.”

great.text: (less usual or obs. senses are) 1. pregnant (fig.) Per. V. i. 107 “I am great with woe.”

greatness.text: often used with possessive pronoun as a title, e.g. LLL. V. i. 116 “it pleaseth his ”

gree.text: to agree (in various senses) Gent. II. iv. 184 “Plotted and g-d on,” Meas. IV. i. 44 “other tokens Between you g-d” (=agreed or determined upon), Mer.V. II. ii. 111 “How you now?,” Shr. II. i. 264 [ 272 ] “your dowry g-d on,” 291 [ 299 ] “we have g-d so well together,” Ant. II. vi. 37 “this g-d upon,” Sonn. cxiv. 11 “what with his gust is greeing.”

green1.text: verdure Sonn. xii. 7 , lxviii. 11; grassy turf or sod Per. IV. i. 16 (Ff3 4 “Grave”).

green2.text: adj. (“a eye” is regarded as a point of beauty MND. V. i. 343 , Rom. III. v. 222 ） 1. said of the sea, and hence of Neptune, Tp. V. i. 43 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 28, Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 58

greenly.text: unskilfully, foolishly H5 V. ii. 148 , Ham. IV. v. 83 .

greet.text: to gratify Per. IV. iii. 38 . ∥ A rare sense, found also in Greene's ‘James IV’.

grey1.text: cold sunless light of early morning Ado V. iii. 27 , Rom. III. v. 19 ; cf. grey-ey'd “morn” Rom. II. iii. 1 . ∥ These uses are not pre-S.

grey2.text: hoary, ancient 1H4 II. iv. 506 [ 499 ] “that iniquity.” ∥ In its application to the colour of eyes “grey” is supposed by some, e.g. Malone, to mean what we now call ‘blue’.

grief.text: (both the foll. are common Eliz.) 1. hardship, suffering, cause of pain or sorrow Ado I. i. 323 [ 315 ] “love's ,” LLL. IV. iii. 171 “Where lies thy ?,” Tw.N. II. iv. 117 * “smiling at ,” 1H4 V. i. 134 “the of a wound,” 2H4 I. i. 144 “my limbs, Weaken'd with grief.”

grievance.text: (the sense ‘cause of complaint’ occurs) 1. oppression, annoyance 2H4 IV. i. 198 “such picking grievances,” Oth. I. ii. 15 “restraint and grievance.”

grieve.text: (1 a rare use; 2 a freq. poetical use) 1. to be a grievance or cause of complaint Per. II. iv. 19 “It shall no longer grieve without reproof.”

grievous.text: used adv. (S.) R2 I. iv. 54 (Ff Q5 “very”), 1H4 IV. i. 16 “he's grievous sick.”

grievously.text: 1. with a heavy penalty, dearly Cæs. III. ii. 86 .

griffin.text: fabulous animal, half lion, half eagle.

grind.text: (2 metaphor from sharpening an axe) 1. to afflict, torment Tp. IV. i. 261 “ their joints.”

gripe.text: grasp H5 IV. vi. 22 , H8 V. iii. 100 , Mac. III. i. 62 .

gripe2.text: vb. (commonly said of grief in the 16th cent.) 1. to clutch or grasp “at” Per. I. i. 49 .

griping.text: painful, distressing Rom. IV. v. 129 “ grief.”

grisled.text: horrible, grisly Per. III. Gower 47 * “the north” (Q1; Qq2-6 “grislee,” Q5 “grieslee,” Ff3 4 “grisly”).

grisly.text: grim, ghastly MND. V. i. 141 “This beast,” 1H6 I. iv. 47 , Per. III. Gower 47 (see GRISLED).

grizzle.text: sprinkling of grey Tw.N. V. i. 169 .

grizzled.text: grey Ham. I. ii. 239 (Qq “grissl'd,” Ff “grisly”), Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 17 “this head” (F1 “grizled”).

grizzly.text: grey, grizzled Ham. I. ii. 239 (see prec.).

groat.text: coin equal to four pence All'sW. II. ii. 23 , H5 V. i. 62 .

groom.text: (the common sense is ‘servant’) 1. fellow Tit. IV. ii. 166 “you are gallant grooms.”

gross1.text: twelve dozen; only in phr. “by the ,” in large numbers Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 208

gross2.text: adj. (the senses ‘glaring, flagrant’ and ‘coarse’ are common) 1. big, bulky Wiv. III. iii. 42 “this watery pumpion,” Lr. IV. vi. 14 “The crows . . . Show scarce so as beetles” : with quibble in Ado V. i. 168 “a great one,” 1H4 II. iv. 254 “[lies] as a mountain.”

grossly.text: (3 now the only surviving use) 1. palpably, plainly, obviously Err. II. ii. 173 , All'sW. I. iii. 186 “so shown,” H5 II. ii. 107 , Sonn. xcix. 5 .

grossness.text: bulkiness Troil. I. iii. 325 “Whose little characters sum up” ; flagrant character, enormity Mer.V. III. ii. 80 “Hiding the with fair ornament” ; materiality MND. III. i. 167 “thy mortal ” ; coarseness, want of refinement Wiv. V. v. 133 , R3 III. i. 46 * ; stupidity Tw.N. III. ii. 80 “such impossible passages of grossness.”

ground1.text: sb. (2 is freq.; many quibbles occur between literal and figurative meanings) 1. the bottom of the sea or other water 1H4 I. iii. 204 “Where fathom-line could never touch the ” ; the bottom where the water becomes too shallow for a vessel to float 2H4 IV. i. 17 “touch And dash themselves to pieces,” IV. iv. 40 “on ” (=aground).

ground2.text: to fix, establish, found, base AYL. I. ii. 296 , R3 I. iii. 29 “g-ed malice,” H8 I. ii. 144 , Sonn. lxii. 4 , cxlii. 2

groundling.text: frequenter of the pit of a theatro Ham. III. ii. 12 “to split the ears of the groundlings.”

grow.text: (1 is common with adjs.) 1. to become Tw.N. V. i. 93 “grew a twenty years removed thing,” 1H4 III. ii. 68 , Cor. IV. iv. 21 “ dear friends,” Sonn. cliii. 7 “a cold valley-fountain . . . Which . . . grew a seething bath.”

growth.text: size, stature Wiv. IV. iv. 50 , AYL. I. ii. 131 , 2H4 I. ii. 182 .

grudge2.text: “ one thought,” have one envious thought 1H6 III. i. 175 .

grudging.text: =GRUDGE sb. Ado III. iv. 89 “he eats his meat without ” ; so grudging ppl. adj., unwilling, reluctant 1H6 IV. i. 141 “their stomachs.”

guard1.headword: guard sb. (other S. uses than those below are
guard1.text: ‘protection, defence,’ ‘posture of defence,’ ‘watch,’ ‘protector, defender’) 1. keeping, guardianship, custody Err. V. i. 149 “He broke from those that had the of him,” Mer.V. I. iii. 176 “in the fearful Of an unthrifty knave,” Cor. I. x. 25 (‘under the protection of my brother’), Lr. V. iii. 1 , 48 , Ant. V. ii. 67 “I'll take her to my ”

guard2.text: to ornament with ‘guards’ (see prec. 4), to trim Mer.V. II. ii. 170 , H8 Prol. 16 “a long motley coat g -ed with yellow”; fig. Ado I. i. 296 [ 288 ], John IV. ii. 10 “To a title that was rich before.” ∥ The only pre-Eliz. meaning of the word.

guardant.text: guardian, protector 1H6 IV. vii. 9 , Cor. V. ii. 67 .

guardsman.text: soldier of the guard Ant. V. ii. 232 stage dir. (F1).

gudgeon.text: one who will bite at any bait or swallow anything, credulous or gullible person Mer.V. I. i. 102 .

guerdon.text: reward, recompense Ado V. iii. 5 , LLL. III. i. 178 [ 170 ]; so guerdon'd, rewarded 2H6 I. iv. 49 , 3H6 III. iii. 191 .

guess.text: conjecture 2H4 III. i. 88 , H5 I. i. 96 “with a ready ,” Tit. II. iii. 207 , Cæs. II. i. 3 “Give ” ; rough estimate Mer.V. I. iii. 55 “by the near of my memory,” Lr. V. i. 52 , Sonn. lxix. 10 “in guess.”

guide.text: conduct, direction Tim. I. i. 252 “give them guide to us.”

guilder.text: properly, gold coin formerly current in the Netherlands and parts of Germany; also, Dutch silver coin; used in pl.=money Err. I. i. 8 , IV. i. 4 “I . . . want guilders for my voyage.”

guiltless.text: 2H6 IV. vii. 107 “guiltless blood-shedding” =shedding of innocent blood.

guilty.text: used with various implications; (1) Lucr. 1511 “ instance” =suggestion of guilt; (2) applied to the instrument, occasion, &c. of a crime Err. IV. iv. 65 “the doors,” Tit. V. ii. 184 “The bason that receives your blood” ; (3) playfully in a transf. sense LLL. I. ii. 117 “The world was very of such a ballet” ; (4) involving guilt, criminal 1H6 II. iv. 94 , R3 I. iv. 283 “ murder,” Rom. III. ii. 111 “damned deeds” ; (5) laden with guilt 3H6 V. vi. 11 “the mind” ; (6) prompted by sense of guilt Lucr. 1482 “ woe” ; the construction with “to” (=of) occurs twice Err. III. ii. 169 “ to self-wrong,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 551 “guilty To” (=to blame for).

guise.text: custom, habit, fashion 2H6 I. iii. 45 , Mac. V. i. 21 “This is her very ,” Cym. V. i. 32 , Ven. 1177 .

gules.text: heraldic name for ‘red’ Tim. IV. iii. 59 , Ham. II. ii. 488 [ 479 ].

gulf.text: voracious belly Mac. IV. i. 23 , Lucr. 557 .

gull.text: to dupe, cheat, take in Tw.N. II. iii. 147 , H5 II. ii. 121 , Sonn. lxxxvi. 10 .

gull1.text: unfledged bird 1H4 V. i. 60 “that ungentle , the cuckoo's bird,” Tim. II. i. 31 “a naked ” ∥ Now used in Worcestershire and Warwickshire dial. for a gosling.

gull2.text: sb. 2 (not pre-S.) 1. dupe, fool Tw.N. III. ii. 76 , V. i. 216 , 355 , H5 III. vi. 72 , R3 I. iii. 328 “simple gulls,” Oth. V. ii. 161 .

gum.text: used for ‘rheum’ H5 IV. ii. 48 ; cf. Ham. II. ii. 204 .

gummed.text: stiffened with gum 1H4 II. ii. 3 “a velvet.”

gurnet.text: fish of the genus Trigla; “soused ,” used as a term of opprobrium 1H4 IV. ii. 13 .

gust1.text: taste, liking, relish Tw.N. I. iii. 34 “the he-hath in quarrelling,” Tim. III. v. 55 * “sin's extremest ,” Sonn. cxiv. 11 .

gust2.text: app. to taste (fig.) Wint. I. ii. 219 * (? ‘when I am the last to hear of it’).

guts.text: gluttonous or corpulent person 1H4 II. iv. 255 “thou clay-brained ” ; still in use in Warwickshire for ‘a greedy person’; (?) offal, applied to a dead body Ham. III. iv. 212 * .

gyve.text: to fetter, shackle Oth. II. i. 171 (Ff1 3 4 “giue,” Qq “catch”).

gyves.text: fetters, shackles (also fig.); Ham. IV. vii. 21 “Convert his to graces” (? ‘regard his imprisonment as an ornament to him, and so calling for more devotion from them’).

ha.text: (2 is freq. and is chiefly S.) 1. exclamation expressing wonder or surprise, eagerness, indignation; often preceded by “ha” or “ah” ( Tp. V. i. 263 “Ha, ha! What things are these?,” Ham. I. v. 150 “Ah, ha, boy! sayst thou so?” ).

habit.text: the common mod. sense of ‘settled practice, custom’ occurs only three times ( Gent. V. iv. 1 , Mer.V. I. ii. 62 , Ham. I. iv. 29 ), the usual S. meanings being ‘dress, garb’ and ‘bearing, demeanour’, which are app. blended in some exx.

habited.text: not pre-S. in the sense ‘dressed, attired’ Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 559, Tit. II. iii. 57 “is it Dian, habited like her?.”

hack.text: of uncertain meaning in Wiv. II. i. 52 , IV. i. 69 ; the context suggests some indelicate ref. (cf. HACKNEY).

haggard.text: sb. wild female hawk caught when in her adult plumage Ado III. i. 36 “as coy and wild As h-s of the rock,” Shr. IV. i. 196 “to man my ” (fig.), Tw.N. III. i. 72 ; (hence) wild and intractable woman Shr. IV. ii. 39 ;—adj. wild, intractable Oth. III. iii. 260 “if I do prove her haggard.”

haggle.text: to hack, mangle H5 IV. vi. 11 “York, all haggled over.”

hair.text: (3 a common Eliz. sense; Ant. I. ii. 206 “like the courser's hair” refers to the popular notion that a horsehair placed in water will turn into an eel) 1. type of something small or slight, jot or tittle, iota Tp. I. ii. 217 “Not a perish'd,” 2H4 I. ii. 26 “it is not a amiss,” Troil. III. ii. 191 “If I . . . swerve a from truth” ; so “h-'s breadth” Wiv. IV. ii. 3 ; “to a ,” to a nicety, with the utmost exactness Troil. III. i. 159 .

halberd.text: military weapon, used chiefly in the 15th and 16th cent., consisting of a sharp-edged blade ending in a point and a spearhead mounted on a handle five to seven foot long Err. V. i. 185 , 3H6 IV. iii. 20 , R3 I. ii. 40 .

halcyon.text: a bird (identified with the kingfisher) of which the ancients fabled that it bred about the time of the winter solstice in a nest floating on the sea and produced a calm for the space of fourteen days; (hence) “ days” = period of calm 1H6 I. ii. 131 ; in Lr. II. ii. 83 “turn their beaks With every gale” there is a ref. to the belief that a dried specimen of the bird hung up so as to move freely would turn in the direction of the wind.

half.text: one of two partners LLL. V. ii. 250 “I'll not be your ,” Shr. V. ii. 78 “I will be your ” (=share the risk with you); (hence) wife Cæs. II. i. 274 “to me, your self, your ” ; cf. Ado II. iii. 188 [ 177 ] “half myself” (=my wife).

halidom.text: orig. the holy relics upon which oaths were sworn, the ancient formula being ‘as helpe me God and halidome’, altered later to ‘by my halidome’, which was subsequently used by itself as a weak asseveration Gent. IV. ii. 138 “By my , I was fast asleep,” Shr. V. ii. 100 , H8 V. i. 117 “Now, by my , What manner of man are you?,” Rom. I. iii. 43 . ∥ In old edd. “hallidome, hollidam, holydam(e”; the form “holydame” is due to association with ‘dame’, the phrase being popularly taken as=by our Lady.

hall.text: (3 not recorded before S.) 1. baronial or squire's residence Shr. II. i. 189 “Kate of Kate-Hall.”

halloo.text: in mod. edd. represents “a to, alow” of old edd. in Lr. III. iv. 76 .

hallow.text: to shout, (intr.) Gent. V. iv. 13 , Wint. III. iii. 78 , 2H4 I. ii. 216 ; once trans. Tw.N. I. v. 293 “Hallow your name to the reverberate hills.”

halt.text: halt or lame man Sonn. Music iv. 10 [ Pilgr. 308 ] “A cripple soon can find a ”: an alteration of the proverb ‘It is hard halting before a cripple’ (Heywood, 1562); cf. ‘It is ful hard to halten vnespied Byfore a crepul, for he kan the craft’ (Chaucer).

hammer.text: (the literal sense also occurs) 1. to devise, plan 2H6 I. ii. 47 “h-ing treachery” ; also intr. to deliberate earnestly “upon” or “of” Gent. I. iii. 18 “that Whereon this month I have been h-ing,” Wint. II. ii. 49 “hammer'd of this design.”

hand1.headword: hand sb. (the foll. obs. uses of phrases are found) 1. with preps.
hand1.text: “at ,” (i) at the beginning, at the start Cæs. IV. ii. 23 “like horses hot at ” ; (ii) by hand John V. ii. 75 “a lion foster'd up at ;—at” or “in any , of all h-s,” in any case LLL. IV. iii. 219 “Therefore, of all h-s must we be forsworn,” Shr. I. ii. 150 “see that at any ,” 229, All'sW. III. vi. 44 “in any ;—by this , by” one's own or another's “,” used freq. in asseverations Tp. III. ii. 57 “by this , I will supplant some of your teeth,” AYL. III. ii. 420 “by the white of Rosalind,” All'sW. III. vi. 75 , 2H6 V. iii. 29 “by my , lords, 'twas a glorious day,” Troil. IV. i. 22 “By Venus' I swear,” Cor. IV. v. 156 , Ven. 80 ; also “for my ” Shr. I. i. 193 ; “in” one's “,” led or held by one John II. i. 236 , R3 IV. i. 2 , H8 V. iii. 22 , Cor. V. iii. 23 , Tit. V. iii. 138 ; “brief in ,” shortly to be dispatched John IV. iii. 158 ; “in with,” occupied or engaged with Ven. 912 “In with all things, nought at all effecting;—of” one's “h-s,” in respect of one's actions or valour in fight Wiv. I. iv. 27 , Wint. V. ii. 186 [ 178 ] “a tall fellow of thy h-s,” &c., 2H4 II. ii. 74 ; “out of ,” (i) at once 1H6 III. ii. 102 , 3H6 IV. vii. 63 , Tit. V. ii. 77 ; (ii) done with 2H4 III. i. 107 “were these inward wars once out of ;—unto thy ,” ready for thee Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 29

hand2.text: to handle Tp. I. i. 26 “ a rope” ; to deal with Wint. II. iii. 63 , IV. iii. [ iv. ] 360

handfast.text: (1 the phrase is only S.) 1. firm hold; “in ,” held fast Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 798

handsaw.text: saw managed with one hand 1H4 II. iv. 190 “my sword hacked like a ” ∥ In Ham. II. ii. 407 [ 397 ] “when the wind is southerly, I know a hawk from a ” * , usually explained as a corruption of ‘her(o)nsew’, ‘her(o)nshaw’, but dial. variants of such a type, e.g. ‘ha(h)nser’, ‘ha(h)nsey’, are recorded only from East Anglia: see HAWK sb. and the comm.

handsome.text: proper, fitting, becoming, decent Ado IV. ii. 92 “one that hath two gowns, and everything about him,” V. iv. 105 ; ? also in Ham. II. ii. 475 [ 466 ] “more handsome than fine” * ; adv. 2H4 II. iv. 304 “that ever I dress myself handsome.”

handsomely.text: conveniently Tit. II. iii. 268 “if we miss to meet him ” ; elegantly, neatly Tp. V. i. 293 “trim it ,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 779 “he wears them not handsomely.”

hang.text: (pa. t. and pa. pple. “hung,” except in the sense ‘put to death by hanging’, in which “hanged” is usual; in MND. V. i. 367 Qq “hanged,” Ff “hung”; in AYL. III. ii. 183 , Cym. II. iv. 68 , Pilgr. xiv. 3 [ 183 ] “hanged” is used for “hung):—hang off,” leave go MND. III. ii. 260 ; “hang up,” hang on a gibbet LLL. IV. iii. 54 “love's Tyburn, that h-s up simplicity,” Rom. III. iii. 56 .

hanger.text: strap on a sword-belt from which the sword hung Ham. V. ii. 157 , &c.

hanging.text: gloomy Meas. IV. ii. 35 “a hanging look.”

hangings.text: fruit on a tree Cym. III. iii. 63 “my mellow hangings.”

hangman.text: playfully applied to Cupid, Ado III. ii. 11 “the little ” ; attrib. ?=fit for the hangman Gent. IV. iv. 61 hangman† boys * (Ff “Hangman's boyes” or “boy”).

hap.text: “dear hap,” good fortune Rom. II. ii. 189 ; “by haps,” by chance Ado III. i. 105 .

happiness.text: propriety, appropriateness, felicity Ado II. iii. 202 [ 191 ] He hath . . . a good outward * h. ; Ham. II. ii. 217 “a that often madness hits on.”

happy1.text: adj. 1. propitious, favourable; phr. “in time” Shr. Ind. i. 90 , All'sW. V. i. 6 , Cæs. II. ii. 60 , Ham. V. ii. 214 , Oth. III. i. 32 ; “in a hour” Ado IV. i. 288 ; “in very season” 2H4 IV. ii. 79 ; all meaning ‘at an appropriate moment, in time’; also Rom. III. v. 112 “in happy time” =a propos.

harbour1.text: shelter, lodging Meas. I. iii. 4 , LLL. II. i. 174 , 2H6 III. i. 336 , V. i. 168 , Tim. V. iv. 53 , Lucr. 768 .

harbour2.text: to lodge; trans. Err. I. i. 136 “any place that h-s men,” Tw.N. II. iii. 106 “she h-s you as her kinsman,” John II. i. 262 ; intr. Gent. III. i. 140 , R2 I. i. 195 , 3H6 IV. vii. 79 .

hard1.text: adj. (the ordinary lit. and fig. meanings occur) 1. hardened, obdurate Tim. IV. iii. 270 , Mac. III. iv. 143 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 111 “when we in our viciousness grow hard.”

hard2.text: adv. (1 cf. ‘a Trotting Horse, when he sets hard, and goes of an uneasy rate’, Holme's Armoury, 1688). 1. with an uneasy pace AYL. III. ii. 334 “trots hard.”

hardiment.text: boldness, bold exploit 1H4 I. iii. 101 “changing with great Glendower,” Troil. IV. v. 28 , Cym. V. iv. 75 .

hardiness.text: boldness, daring H5 I. ii. 220 , Cym. III. vi. 22 .

hardly.text: (the meaning ‘scarcely’, into which 2 imperceptibly passes, is the commonest) 1. severely, harshly H8 I. ii. 105 , Cym. III. iii. 8 .

hardness.text: difficulty Oth. III. iv. 35 “O! hardness to dissemble,” Cym. V. v. 432 ; hardship Oth. I. iii. 234 , Cym. III. vi. 21 .

hardock.text: (?) burdock Lr. IV. iv. 4 (Ff1 2 “Hardokes,” Qq “hor-docks,” mod. edd. “hoar-docks†, harlocks†, burdocks†”).

hark.text: used imperatively to start or urge on dogs in the chase Tp. IV. i. 260 “there, Tyrant, there! hark, hark!.”

harlock.text: see HARDOCK. ∥ Actually recorded once, from Drayton's Dowsabel.

harlot.text: lewd person Err. V. i. 205 “she with h-s feasted,” Cor. III. ii. 112 , Rom. II. iv. 46 , attrib. Wint. II. iii. 4 “the harlot king.”

harlotry.text: courtesan Oth. IV. ii. 239 (Q1 “harlot”); silly wench 1H4 III. i. 198 , Rom. IV. ii. 14 “A peevish self-will'd ” ; attrib. as a vague term of contempt=‘scurvy’, worthless 1H4 II. iv. 442 “these harlotry players.”

harmony.text: music, tuneful sound Tp. III. iii. 18 “What is this?,” Ham. III. ii. 385 [ 378 ]. ∥ The earliest meaning.

harness.text: body-armour Troil. V. iii. 31 , Mac. V. v. 52 ; used for men-at-arms 1H4 III. ii. 101 .

harp.text: to hit upon, guess Mac. IV. i. 74 .

harpy.text: fabulous monster, rapacious and filthy, having a woman's face and body and a bird's wings and claws, supposed to be a minister of divine vengeance Tp. III. iii. 83 , Ado II. i. 282 .

harrow.text: to lacerate (the feelings), distress Ham. I. i. 44 “it h-s me with fear and wonder,” I. v. 16 “a tale . . . whose lightest word Would up thy soul” ; with play on the lit. sense Cor. V. iii. 34 “Let the Volsces Plough Rome, and harrow Italy.”

harsh.text: （‘rough to the ear’ and ‘rude, roughly offensive’ are the commoner S. meanings) 1. unpleasantly rough (i) to the touch Troil. I. i. 60 , (ii) to the taste (fig.) Oth. V. ii. 114 .

harvest.text: season for reaping corn; fig. Ado I. iii. 27 , Tw.N. III. i. 146 “come to harvest” (=ripened), Cym. I. i. 46 . ∥ The fig. use of the sense ‘ripened fruit or produce’ is much commoner.

haste1.text: “in ,” (1) with speed, quickly, e.g. Mer.V. II. ii. 187 [ 180 ] “Return in ,” R2 I. i. 150 “In whereof” (=‘in order to expedite this proof’); Lr. II. i. 26 “i' the ” ; so “in all ,” with all possible speed R3 IV. i. 56 , Troil. I. i. 121 “In all swift ” ; (2) eager to get something done quickly, in a hurry, e.g. Gent. I. iii. 89 “He is in ; therefore I pray you, go;—make ” is freq.; in the same sense are used “take his ” Tim. V. i. 215 , “put it to the haste” Ant. V. ii. 195 .

haste2.text: to urge on, speed, accelerate Mer.V. II. ii. 124 , 1H4 III. i. 142 , Cor. V. i. 75 , Rom. IV. i. 11 ; Ham. I. v. 29 “ me to know't” = Let me know it quickly.

hastily.text: quickly, speedily Ado V. i. 45 , John I. i. 221 .

hasty.text: (the ordinary mod. sense is frequent) 1. quick, speedy 2H4 II. i. 143 , Rom. V. i. 64 “ powder,” Cæs. IV. iii. 111 , Ham. II. ii. 4 “Our sending.”

hat.text: used like CAP 1 (iii) Cor. II. iii. 104 “to have my hat” ; exclamation “by this hat!” Wiv. I. i. 175 (cf. HOOD).

hatch.text: (2 chiefly “under” or “beneath the h-es,” which is now associated with the mod. sense of ‘grated framework covering the hatchway’) 1. half-door, gate or wicket with an open space above Err. III. i. 33 , John I. i. 171 “In at the window, or else o'er the ” (=born irregularly), V. ii. 138 “take” (=jump over) “the hatch,” Lr. III. vi. 76 .

hatched1.text: closed with a hatch Per. IV. ii. 37 .

hatchment.text: square or diamond-shaped tablet displaying the armorial bearings of a deceased person Ham. IV. v. 214 “No trophy, sword, nor hatchment o'er his bones.”

hate.text: cause of hatred (not pre-S.) John III. iv. 28 , Cor. I. i. 189 .

haught.text: haughty R2 IV. i. 254 “thou insulting man,” 2H6 I. iii. 71 (F1 “haughtie”), R3 II. iii. 28 “ and proud.”

haughty.text: high-spirited, high-minded, exalted 1H6 II. v. 79 “this great attempt,” IV. i. 35 “ courage,” R3 IV. ii. 37 .

haul.text: to drag 2H4 V. v. 38 (Ff1 2 3 “Hall'd,” F4 “Hal'd,” Q “Halde”).

haunch.text: fig. latter end 2H4 IV. iv. 92 “the haunch of winter.”

haunt1.text: public resort, society of men AYL. II. i. 15 “our life exempt from public ,” Ham. IV. i. 18 “out of ” (= secluded), Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 54 “And all the haunt be ours” (=we alone shall be run after).

haunt2.text: trans. to frequent the company of, accompany or follow persistently Err. III. ii. 83 , MND. II. ii. 85 “do not me thus,” 1H4 II. iv. 498 , Troil. IV. i. 10 “how Diomed . . . Did you in the field” ; intr. to resort habitually, remain continually Mac. I. vi. 9 , Oth. I. i. 96 “to about my doors,” Compl. 130 “following where he haunted.”

hautboy.text: wooden double-reed instrument of high pitch 2H4 III. ii. 355 .

have.text: (often reduced to “ha',” in old edd. “ha, a”; in “me rather had” R2 III. iii. 192 there is confusion between the two idioms, ‘I had rather’ and ‘me were better’) 1. idiomatic uses with “it:—have it,” have the victory Shr. V. ii. 182 “thou shalt ha't” ; in phrases like “let me have it” = tell me it Wint. I. ii. 101 , II. i. 25 , H8 II. i. 145 , Ham. II. ii. 572 [ 565 ]; cf. Oth. I. iii. 379 “We will have more of this.”

haver.text: possessor Cor. II. ii. 90 “dignifies the haver.”

having.text: possession, property, wealth, estate Wiv. III. ii. 76 “The gentleman is of no ,” AYL. III. ii. 401 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 743, H8 II. iii. 23 “Our content Is our best ,” Cym. I. ii. 20 ; also pl. H8 III. ii. 160 ; in Oth. IV. iii. 94 “our ” * = our allowance of expense (J.); fig. endowments, ‘gifts’, accomplishments Troil. III. iii. 97 , Compl. 235 .

haviour.text: behaviour, bearing, manner Wiv. I. iii. 84 , Tw.N. III. iv. 229 , R2 I. iii. 77 , Ham. I. ii. 81 “the dejected of the visage,” II. ii. 12 (Ff “humour”), Cym. III. iv. 9 .

havoc.text: “cry ,” orig. to give an army the order ‘havoc!’ as the signal for pillaging John II. i. 357 , Cor. III. i. 273 , Cæs. III. i. 273 “Cry ‘!’ and let slip the dogs of war,” Ham. V. ii. 378 “This quarry cries on ” (=calls for merciless slaughter).

hawk1.text: in Ham. II. ii. 406 [ 397 ] commonly taken to be the bird (cf. HANDSAW), but perhaps a variant of ‘hack’, which was applied to various tools of the mattock, hoe, and pickaxe type.

hawk2.text: fly “at,” as a hawk Mac. II. iv. 13 .

hawking.text: ‘hawk-like, keen’ (Schmidt) All'sW. I. i. 106 “his hawking eye.”

hay1.text: country dance having a winding or serpentine movement LLL. V. i. 166 .

hazard1.text: (2 the prevailing sense; 4 cf. ‘Pelouse . . . the lower hazard in a tennis-court’ Cotgr.) 1. game at dice at which the chances are complicated by a number of arbitrary rules H5 III. vii. 98 ; hence fig. “come” or “go to ,” to run extreme risks Mer.V. II. ix. 18 , H5 III. vii. 98 .

hazard2.text: Ant. III. x. [ xii. ] 19 “h-ed to thy grace,” depending for its fate on thy favour.

he.text: “he . . . he”=one . . . another Mer.V. IV. i. 54 “Why he cannot abide a gaping pig; Why he, a harmless necessary cat; Why he, a woollen bagpipe,” Troil. IV. i. 66 “he as he” (=the one as well as the other), Sonn. xxix. 6 “Featur'd like him, like him with friends possess'd” ; cf. MND. III. ii. 25 -6, Cor. I. vi. 36 “Ransoming him . . ., threat'ning the other,” Mac. IV. iii. 80 “his jewels and this other's house.”

head1.text: sb. (the chief idiomatic, technical, and special uses are the foll.) 1. put for ‘ears’ LLL. IV. iii. 336 “When the suspicious of theft is stopp'd,” Troil. IV. v. 5 , Per. II. iii. 97 “Loud music is too harsh for ladies' heads” ; for ‘mouth’ Cym. V. v. 158 “Those” [viands] “which I heav'd to head”; = the mod. ‘face’ in the phr. “to” (one's) “head” Meas. IV. iii. 151 , Ado. V. i. 62 , MND. I. i. 106 .

headly.text: reading of F1 in H5 III. iii. 32 “headly murder” (other, Ff and mod. edd. “heady”). ∥ In early English the word was applied to the ‘capital’ or ‘deadly’ sins.
