headpiece.text: helmet H5 III. vii. 154 ; covering for the head Lr. III. ii. 26 “He that has a house to put his head in has a good ” ; head, brain Wint. I. ii. 227 .

heady.text: headlong, precipitate, impetuous Err. V. i. 216 “heady, rash,” 1H4 II. iii. 60 , Lr. II. iv. 111 “my more headier will” ; of a stream H5 I. i. 34 “With such a heady currance, scouring faults.”

health.text: welfare, well-being, prosperity Mer.V. V. i. 114 , 2H4 IV. iv. 81 “ to my sovereign,” Tim. II. ii. 207 “to the state's best ,” Cæs. IV. iii. 36 , Ham. I. iii. 21 , I. iv. 40 “Be thou a spirit of or goblin damn'” ∥ This sense survives in the phr. ‘drink “a health’,” recorded first from S., Shr. III. ii. 173 “He calls for wine: ‘A health!’ quoth he.”

healthful.text: healthy All'sW. II. iii. 54 , H8 I. i. 3 , Ham. III. iv. 141 ; fig. Cæs. II. i. 319 “Had you a healthful ear to hear it.”

heap1.text: sb. (3 a late ex. of this sense; cf. Coverdale, Ezekiel xxxviii. 22 ‘vpon him and all his heape’) 1. phr. “on heaps, on a heap,” in a fallen or prostrate mass, prostrate, in ruins H5 V. ii. 39 “all her husbandry doth lie on h-s,” Tit. II. iii. 223 “Lord Bassianus lies . . . All on a ,” Tim. IV. iii. 101 “laid proud Athens on a heap.”

heap2.text: Wint. IV. i. [ ii. ] 22 “the h-ing friendships,” increase of friendly relations.

hear.text: Mac. III. iv. 32 “We'll ourselves again” (=we will talk with one another again); Cæs. I. ii. 203 “he h-s no music” (=does not listen to, pays no attention to); Per. I. iv. 54 “hear these tears” (=hear of, be informed of), cf. Cym. II. iv. 17 “ The legions . . . sooner landed.”

hearing.text: 1. in the sense of ‘faculty or sense by which sounds are heard’ is used in contexts where ‘ear(s)’ would now be usual, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 265 “terrible To enter human ,” LLL. II. i. 75 “younger h-s are quite ravished,” Ant. V. ii. 95 “You lie, up to the of the gods,” Ven. 428 “would . . . I had no hearing.”

hearken.text: (2 peculiar to Eliz. and Caroline times) 1. to inquire or seek “after” LLL. I. i. 217 “to after the flesh” * , Ado V. i. 221 “ after their offence,” R3 I. i. 54 .

hearse.text: coffin 2H4 IV. v. 112 , 1H6 I. i. 104 , R3 I. ii. 2 , Cæs. III. ii. 170 . ∥ The only meaning in S.

hearsed.text: coffined, buried Mer.V. III. i. 96 , Ham. I. iv. 47 “hearsed in death;” fig. Lucr. 657 .

heart.text: (in 1H4 III. i. 251 “Heart!,” taken by some in sense 3, is the abbreviation of ‘God's heart!’, ‘sheart!’） 1. disposition, temperament Meas. V. i. 385 “Not changing with habit,” Ado II. i. 327 “a merry ”

hearted.text: fixed in the heart Oth. I. iii. 373 “I hate the Moor: my cause is ” ; III. iii. 449 “hearted throne.”

heartless.text: spiritless, disheartened Rom. I. i. 72 , Lucr. 471 , 1392 ∥ Usually taken =‘unfeeling’ in Sonn. Music iii. 35 [ Pilgr. 279 ] “ ground,” but this meaning is otherwise not recorded before the 19th cent.; perhaps=‘sterile’ (an Eliz. sense).

hearty.text: as a complimentary epithet Ant. IV. ii. 38 .

heat1.text: Tw.N. I. v. 139 “one draught above ” (?=beyond the point at which the body becomes warm with moderate drinking).

heat2.text: (?) to run swiftly over Wint. I. ii. 96 .

heat3.text: heated John IV. i. 61 “Theiron . . . red-hot” ; ? in Tw.N. I. i. 26 * “till seven years ” (?=heated for seven years by the sun's rays).

heave1.text: deep sigh Ham. IV. i. 1 ; thrust H8 II. ii. 85 “one heave at him” (Ff2 3 4; cf. HAVE-AT-HIM).

heave2.text: pa. t. and pa. pple always “heaved”; the meaning ‘utter’ (a groan, word) is not pre-S., AYL. II. i. 36 “h-'d forth such groans,” Lr. IV. iii. 27 “heav'd the name of ‘father’ Pantingly forth.”

heaven.text: (metrically treated as one or as two syll.; not pre-Eliz. in exclamations of surprise, etc.; often put for ‘God’ in old edd. in deference to the Act to restrain Abuses of Players, of 1605-6; sometimes in sing. with pl. concord R2 I. ii. 6 , Mac. II. i. 4 ; also in pl. with sing. concord John III. i. 108 , Mac. IV. iii. 230 ). 1. “floor of ,” the sky Mer.V. v. i. 58 .

heavily.text: sadly, sorrowfully Ado V. iii. 18 , R3 I. iv. 1 “Why looks your Grace so to-day?,” Ham. II. ii. 316 [ 309 ], Mac. IV. iii. 182 “the tidings, Which I have heavily borne.”

heaviness.text: drowsiness Tp. I. ii. 307 , 1H4 III. i. 218 . ∥ The commonest S. sense is ‘sadness’.

heaving1.text: deep groan or sigh Wint. II. iii. 35 .

heavy.text: (the literal sense of ‘weighty’, and the fig. senses of ‘oppressive, grievous, sore’, ‘sad, sorrowful’, ‘distressing, saddening’, and ‘sleepy, drowsy’ are freq.) 1. weighty, important, serious All'sW. II. v. 50 “matter of consequence,” 1H4 II. iii. 68 “ business,” H5 II. ii. 53 , Lr. V. i. 27 “Most just and causes.”

hebenon.text: (?) yew, which was notorious for its poisonous properties Ham. I. v. 62 “juice of cursed ” ∥ So ‘iouyce of Hebon’, Marlowe ‘Jew of Malta’ III.

hectic.text: hectic or wasting fever Ham. IV. iii. 69 .

hedge.text: (1 16-17th cent. use; 2 not pre-S.) 1. “hedge out,” shut out, debar Troil. III. i. 66 .

heed.text: that which one heeds or pays attention to (S.) LLL. I. i. 82 “that eye shall be his heed.”

heel1.text: in phr. referring to (1) flight or speed Err. I. ii. 94 “I'll take my h-s,” Mer.V. II. ii. 32 “my h-s are at your commandment,” AYL. III. ii. 295 “You have a nimble wit: I think 'twas made of Atalanta's h-s,” 1H4 II. iv. 52 “show it a fair pair of h-s,” Mac. I. ii. 30 “to trust their h-s” ; (2) punishment in the stocks All'sW. IV. iii. 119 “his h-s have deserved it,” 2H4 I. ii. 142 “To punish you by the h-s;—out at h-s,” in unfortunate or decayed circumstances, in trouble or distress Wiv. I. iii. 32 , Lr. II. ii. 164 .

heel2.text: to perform (a dance) Troil. IV. iv. 86 “I cannot . . . the high lavolt.” ∥ Only S. in this sense; cf. Ado III. iv. 46 “Ye light o' love with your h-s!,” V. iv. 122 , H5 III. v. 34 “our grace is only in our heels.”

heigh.text: cry of encouragement Tp. I. i. 6 , Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 2, 6 (Ff “hey”), 10 , 1H4 II. iv. 542 [ 534 ].

height.text: (old edd. also spelt “heighth, hight”） 1. high rank, degree, or position R2 I. i. 189 , R3 I. iii. 83 “this careful ,” Tit. IV. ii. 34 “to be advanced to this height,” Sonn. xxxii. 8 .

heighten.text: to exalt Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 22

heir.text: in transf. use (1) a person to whom something (e.g. fate, sorrow, &c.) is bound to fall due Wiv. V. v. 45 “h-s of fixed destiny,” R2 II. ii. 63 “my sorrow's dismal ,” Ham. III. i. 63 “That flesh is to” ; (2) offspring, product 2H4 IV. iv. 122 “Unfather'd h-s . . . of nature,” Ven. Ded. 5 “the first heir of my invention.”

hell.text: place of confinement for debtors Err. IV. ii. 40 “One that, before the judgement, carries poor souls to hell.”

helm.text: to steer, fig. Meas. III. ii. 155 .

help1.text: sb. (1 only S.; 2 a common S. sense) 1. “at help,” in our favour Ham. IV. iii. 47 .

help2.headword: help vb. (pa. t. and pa. pple. “helped,” but more often “holp”)
help2.text: to relieve, cure, remedy Tp. II. ii. 102 “I will his ague,” Gent. IV. ii. 48 “To him of his blindness,” Rom. I. ii. 49 “Turn giddy, and be holp by backward turning,” Lr. IV. iv. 10 , Lucr. 1822 “Do wounds help wounds?.”

helpless.text: affording no help, unavailing, unprofitable Err. II. i. 39 “urging patience,” R3 I. ii. 13 “the balm of my poor eyes,” Ven. 604 , Lucr. 1027 , 1056 “Poor help.” ∥ In Lucr. 756 * either this sense or ‘that cannot be helped, irremediable’, as in Spenser's ‘helpless hap’, helpless harms'.

hem.text: to clear “away” with a hem or cough AYL. I. iii. 19 .

hemp.text: the material of the hangman's halter H5 III. vi. 45 ; so hempen in jocular phr. 2H6 IV. vii. 94 “Ye shall have a caudle then.” ∥ Of such phrases there were many, e.g. ‘be not caute in an hempen snare’ (Skelton), ‘dauncing in a hempen circle’ (Nashe).

hence.text: (1 always with “here,” as in earlier English) 1. in the next world John IV. ii. 89 , Ham. III. ii. 234 .

henceforth.text: “for ,” for the future Ado V. i. 308 .

henchman.text: page of honour MND. II. i. 121 .

henloft.text: hen-house Wiv. III. iv. 41 (Qq1 2; Ff Q3 “pen”). ∥ Used by Nashe.

hent1.text: in Ham. III. iii. 88 * “Up, sword, and know thou a more horrid hent” it is doubtful whether we have the sense of ‘clutch, grasp’ or of ‘intention, design’, or whether “hent” is for HINT in its S. sense.

hent2.text: to take, seize Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 134 * “merrily the stile-a;” in pa. pple=reached, occupied Meas. IV. vi. 14 “The generous and gravest citizens Have hent the gates.”

her.text: old possessive pron. of the 3rd person pl.= their; app. surviving in 1H6 I. i. 83 “her flowing tides,” Troil. I. iii. 118 “right and wrong . . . Should lose her names” ; mod. edd. “their.”

herald1.text: sb. (in old edd. also “herauld, -ault, har(r)old”) 1. officer having the duty of (i) making proclamations 2H6 IV. ii. 190 , (ii) bearing messages between princes and hostile forces John. II. i. 325 , H5 III. v. 36 , Troil. I. iii. 218 , (iii) conveying challenges H8 I. i. 34 , Lr. V. i. 48 , (iv) arranging public processions, funerals, &c. 1H6 I. i. 45 , Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 145 “the most noble corse that ever Did follow to his urn,” (v) regulating the use of armorial bearings Shr. II. i. 223 “A , Kate? O! put me in thy books,” Lucr. 206 “Some loathsome dash the herald will contrive.”

herald2.text: to usher (“in”) Mac. I. iii. 102 , Per. III. i. 34 .

heraldry.text: (2 is only S.) 1. art or science of a herald, blazoning of armorial bearings MND. III. ii. 213 “like coats in ” ; fig. Oth. III. iv. 48 .

here.text: as sb.=the present life Lr. I. i. 264 ; as adj. “here-approach,” arrival Mac. IV. iii. 133 , “here-remain,” stay 148

hereafter.text: as adj. = future 1H6 II. ii. 10 “ ages,” R3 IV. iv. 391 “Hereafter time.”

hereby.text: close by LLL. IV. i. 9 ; in LLL. I. ii. 143 “That's hereby” is app. intended for a country expression, but the meaning is uncertain.

hermit.text: “begging ,” (?) mendicant friar Tit. III. ii. 41 ; beadsman (S.) Mac. I. vi. 20 “We rest your hermits.”

hest.text: bidding, command Tp. III. i. 37 , 1H4 II. iii. 67 * (Q1; others “hast(e).”

hew.text: Tim. V. iv. 46 “hew to 't,” cut thy way to it.

hewgh.text: imitation of a whistling sound Lr. IV. vi. 94 (Qq “hagh”).

hey.text: call to dogs Tp. IV. i. 258 ; cry expressing excitement, surprise, exultation, Qq “hagh” AYL. V. iii. 19 , 22 , Tw.N. IV. ii. 79 , Lr. III. ii. 75 ; with “nony, nonino” Ado II. iii. 73 , AYL. V. iii. 19 , Ham. IV. v. 164 . ∥ See also HEIGH.

heyday.text: state of excitement Ham. III. iv. 69 “The in the blood is tame.” ∥ As interj. put in mod. edd. for “high-day”（ Tp. II. ii. 199 [ 190 ]), HOYDAY, q.v.

hide.text: (pa. pple. usually “hid,” but “hidden” occurs in predicative use 9 times; 3 cp. ALL HID) 1. to sheath (a sword) AYL. II. vii. 119 , R3 I. ii. 176 .

hideous.text: detestable, odious Lr. I. i. 153 “check This rashness” ; shocking Tw.N. III. iv. 216 “a most hideous opinion of his rage.”

high1.text: All'sW. II. i. 12 * “higher Italy,” (?) the Italian nobility; Tim. IV. iii. 246 “at high wish,” at the height of one's desires; Cæs. II. i. 110 “the high east,” the exact east.

high2.text: adv. (in All'sW. IV. iii. 50 “higher” app.=further inland) 1. loudly Ant. I. v. 49 “neigh'd so high.”

hight.text: is named LLL. I. i. 169 , MND. V. i. 141 .

hild.text: form of the pa. pple. of HOLD used for rhyme's sake Lucr. 1257 . ∥ Found also in Golding (1587).

hilding.text: good-for-nothing fellow All'sW. III. vi. 4 ; attrib. 2H4 I. i. 57 “some hilding fellow” ; jade, baggage Rom. III. v. 169 .

hilt.text: pl.=sing. (formerly freq.) H5 II. i. 69 “I'll run him up to the hilts,” Cæs. V. iii. 43 .

hind1.text: female of the red deer MND. II. i. 232 .

hind2.text: 2 (2 occurs more frequently than 1) 1. servant Wiv. III. v. 101 , AYL. I. i. 20 .

hinge2.text: to bend Tim. IV. iii. 212 “ thy knee.”

hint.text: occasion, opportunity Tp. I. ii. 134 , II. i. 3 “Our of woe Is common,” Cor. III. iii. 23 “ready for this ,” Oth. I. iii. 142 , Ant. III. iv. 9 “When the best was given him, he not took't,” III. ix. [ xi. ] 18, Cym. V. v. 173 “took his hint.” ∥ The mod. sense of ‘suggestion’ is only in Oth. I. iii. 166 * “Upon this hint I spake.”

hip1.text: “on” or “upon the hip,” at a disadvantage Mer.V. I. iii. 47 , IV. i. 335 , Oth. II. i. 317 .

hip2.text: fruit of the wild rose Tim. IV. iii. 425 .

hipped.text: lamed in the hip Shr. III. ii. 50 “his horse , with an old mothy saddle.” ∥ ‘The horse is said to be hipt, when the hip-bone is remooued out of his right place’ (Topsell, 1607 ).

his.text: (3 “its” is S., but much less freq.) 1. =that one's 2H6 II. i. 131 “his” (Ff “it,” mod. edd. “that†) cunning . . . that could” . . ., Mac. IV. iii. 80 “Desire his jewels and this other's house.”

hist.text: ‘nota silentii’ (Minsheu, Ductor in Linguas, 1617 ) Rom. II. ii. 158 .

history1.text: sb. (in Per. V. i. 119 almost=life-story) 1. narrative, tale, story Tw.N. II. iv. 111 , 3H6 V. vi. 28 “that tragic ,” R3 III. v. 27 “The of all her secret thoughts,” Ham. III. ii. 314 , Oth. I. iii. 139 “in my travel's history,” Cym. III. v. 99 .

hit1.text: old form of IT, app. surviving in All'sW. V. iii. 197 (Ff), Mac. I. v. 48 (Ff1 2).

hit2.text: vb. (3, 4, 5 are not pre-S. as also the idiomatic “hit it” LLL. IV. i. 128 , and “hit or miss” Troil. I. iii. 384 ) 1. “hit of”=hit upon Err. III. ii. 30 .

hitherto.text: up to this point, thus far Ham. III. ii. 218 , Oth. I. iii. 185 ; to this place 1H4 III. i. 75 .

hive1.text: sb. (the ordinary sense occurs 5 times) 1. hived swarm 2H6 III. ii. 125 “an angry of bees.”

hive2.text: to lodge together (not pre-S.) Mer.V. II. v. 48 “drones hive not with me.”

ho.text: in old edd. also “hoa” and “how”; see also HEIGHHO, OHO, SOHO, WHAT HO, WHOA HO; repeated, it expresses derisive laughter, e.g. MND. III. ii. 421 .

hoar1.text: adj. (2 is only S.) 1. greyish-white Ham. IV. vii. 168 “a willow . . . That shows his hoar leaves.”

hoar2.text: to become mouldy Rom. II. iv. 147 “When it hoars ere it be spent” ; to smite with ‘hoar leprosy’ (S.) Tim. IV. iii. 156 .

hob.text: by-form of ‘Rob’=Robert, used as a generic name for a rustic Cor. II. iii. 123 “Hob and Dick.”

hoise.text: （“hoist” is also used by S.) 1. to hoist (sail) R3 IV. iv. 528 .

hold1.text: sb. (the sense of ‘grasp’, lit. and fig., is the most freq.; “hold”=place in a ship for cargo 2H4 II. iv. 69 is of different origin) 1. “in hold(s),” in custody, in prison Meas. IV. iii. 94 , Shr. I. ii. 121 , R3 IV. v. 3 .

hold2.text: vb. (pa. t. and pa. pple. usually “held”; pa. pple. once “holden” 2H6 II. iv. 71 , once HILD, q.v.) A.. Transitive meanings:— 1. to endure, bear Cor. III. ii. 80 “the ripest mulberry That will not the handling,” Tim. I. ii. 161 , Ham. V. i. 181 “many pocky corses . . . that will scarce the laying in.”

holdfast.text: adj. grasping firmly Lucr. 555 “in his foot the weak mouse panteth” ;—sb. as a name for a dog that holds tenaciously H5 II. iii. 55 “holdfast is the only dog.”

holding.text: (1 is S. only; 2 is an Eliz. use) 1. consistency All'sW IV. ii. 27 “this has no holding.”

hole.text: (1 Eliz. and still in some dial.) 1. phr. “find a in his coat,” find some fault in him H5 III. vi. 91 .

holiday.text: 1. “speak ,” use choice language Wiv. III. ii. 72 .

holla1.text: =stop! cease! AYL. III. ii. 259 “Cry ‘holla!’ to thy tongue,” Oth. I. ii. 56 “Holla! stand there!,” Ven 284; used to excite attention LLL. V. ii. 898 “Holla! approach,” Shr. IV. i. 12 “Holla, ho! Curtis,” Ham. I. i. 18 “Holla! Bernardo!” ; used to express surprise Tit. II. i. 25 “Holla, what storm is this?” (Qq F1 “Hollo”), Lr. V. iii. 72 “Holla, holla!.”

holla2.text: vb. (see also HOLLOW vb.) 1. to cry out loud, shout (trans. and intr.) Mer.V. V. i. 43 “Leave hollaing” † (old edd. “hollowing”), Tw.N. I. v. 293 “Holla† your name” (F1 “Hallow,” F2 “Hollaw,” Ff3 4 “Hollow”), R2 IV. i. 54 “as many lies As may be holla'd” † (old edd. “hollowed”), 1H4 I. iii. 222 “in his ear I'll holla ‘Mortimer’” (Qq1 2 “hollow”).

hollow1.text: =HOLLA vb. (which see for other instances) Cor. I. viii. 7 “Hollow me like a hare (Holla†),” Ven. 973 “she hears some huntsman hollow” (Qq1 2 3 “hallow,” the rest “hollow”).

hollow2.text: insincerely, falsely Tw.N. III. iv. 103 ; so hollowly Tp. III. i. 70 , Meas. II. iii. 23 , hollowness insincerity Lr. I. ii. 126 . ∥ The corresponding meaning of the adj. is common.

holy.text: devoted as a priest “to” Meas. V. i. 384 .

home.text: 1. “latest ,” the grave Tit. I. i. 83 “near at ” ; Meas. IV. iii. 103 “Petition us at ,” beg for me to come home Ant. I. ii. 196 ; “from ,” abroad John IV. iii. 151 ; “from” (one's) “,” not at (one's) home Err. II. i. 101 , Lr. II. i. 126 ; “not at home,” not prepared to receive visitors Tw.N. I. v. 116 .

home1.text: domestic Gent. II. iv. 120 , R2 I. i. 205 .

home2.text: 1. to its right or proper place, back to the person or place from which a thing issued MND. III. ii. 172 “now to Helen my heart is home return'd,” All'sW. V. iii. 225 “Send for your ring; I will return it home,” H8 III. ii. 159 “come home” (=accrue to you), Sonn. lxxxvii. 12 “Comes home again” (=returns to thee).

homely.text: not beautiful, plain, uncomely Gent. II. iv. 99 “Upon a homely object Love can wink,” Err. II. i. 89 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 439

honest.text: (the ordinary mod. sense is freq., as also are 1 and 3) 1. holding an honourable position, respectable Tp. III. iii. 34 “ lord,” Wiv. II. ii. 121 “Master Page is an man,” H8 IV. ii. 161 “ lord” ; hence (like ‘worthy’) a vague epithet of appreciation MND. III. i. 191 “Your name, gentleman?,” Cor. I. i. 65 “my good friends, mine honest neighbours.”

honesty.headword: honesty (the senses correspond to those of the prec. adj.)
honesty.text: honour, honourableness Gent. II. v. 1 “by mine !,” Err. V. i. 30 , Ado II. i. 398 , Cæs. IV. iii. 67 ; decency, decorum Tw.N. II. iii. 96 “no wit, manners, nor ,” H8 V. ii. 27 , Oth. IV. i. 288 ; womanly honour, chastity Wiv. I. iii. 53 , &c., Ham. III. i. 108 ; uprightness, integrity Cæs. II. i. 127 “what other oath Than to engag'd;—in ” =in truth Cym. III. vi. 69 ; occas. generosity Tim. III. i. 31 .

honey.text: to talk fondly or sweetly Ham. III. iv. 93 .

honeysuckle.text: the host's blunder for ‘homicidal’ 2H4 II. i. 58 .

honour.text: to do honour or homage to, pay worthy respect to 1H6 I. vi. 5 , V. iii. 50 , 3H6 I. i. 198 “To me as thy king,” Per. II. iii. 61 , Ven. Ded. 4 “till I have h-ed you with some graver labour,” Sonn. cxxv. 2 .

honourable.text: respectable, decent, be coming LLL. V. ii. 328 “chides the dice In terms,” Shr. Ind. i. 110 “bear himself with action.” ∥ The meaning ‘upright, honest’ is not pre-S. All'sW. V. iii. 241 , Rom. II. ii. 143 , Cæs. III. ii. 88 -9; also the advb. use=‘honourably’ 3H6 III. ii. 123 (so F1; Qq Ff2 3 4 “honourably”), Cæs. V. i. 60 .

hood1.text: Mer.V. II. vi. 51 “by my !” an asseveration as old as Chaucer, but of uncertain reference.

hood2.text: to blindfold (a hawk) when it is not pursuing game; always fig. H5 III. vii. 126 “'tis a h-ed valour; and when it appears, it will bate,” Rom. III. ii. 14 (see BATE vb. 1 ).

hoodman.text: blindfolded player in blind-man's-buff All'sW. IV. iii. 137 (allusively); hoodman-blind, blind-man's-buff Ham. III. iv. 77 .

hoodwink.text: to blindfold All'sW. III. vi. 25 “We will bind and him,” Rom. I. iv. 4 , Cym. V. ii. 16 ; fig. to cover up Tp. IV. i. 206 “the prize I'll bring thee Shall hoodwink this mischance.”

hoof.text: “i'” or “o' the hoof,” on foot Wiv. I. iii. 89 (Ff2 3 4 “oth',” F1 Q3 “ith'”).

hoop.text: vb. 2 (mod. edd. mostly “whoop”) 1. to shout with astonishment AYL. III. ii. 204 “and yet again wonderful! and after that, out of all h-ing,” H5 II. ii. 108 “admiration did not at them.”

hoop1.text: 1. “tumbler's ,” hoop decorated with ribbons of different colours twisted round it LLL. III. i. 198 [ 190 ].

hoop2.text: to encircle Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 452 (Ff “hope”).

hoot.text: to shout LLL. IV. ii. 61 “the people fall a h-ing,” Cæs. I. ii. 245 (F1 “howted,” Hanmer “shouted”†).

hop.text: 2H6 I. iii. 140 “ without thy head,” be beheaded.

hope1.text: 1. “out of ,” (i) without hope Tp. III. iii. 11 , Shr. V. i. 147 ; (ii) not merely hoping MND. III. ii. 279 ; (iii) past hope Ven. 567 “Things out of ” ; (iv) in hopes H8 Prol. 8, Cor. IV. v. 85 .

hope2.text: to expect, anticipate, suppose H5 III. vii. 82 , Ant. II. i. 38 .

hopeless.text: Cor. III. i. 16 “To restitution,” ‘in such a way that restitution should be hopeless’, Wright.

horn.text: (in Lr. III. vi. 79 “thy is dry” there is a ref. to the practice of beggars carrying a horn, by blowing which they announced their approach and in which they received liquor given to them) 1. attributed to cuckolds, who were fancifully said to wear horns on the brow Wiv. II. i. 123 , &c., Ado I. i. 274 [ 266 ], &c., LLL. IV. i. 115 , &c., John I. i. 219 , Ant. I. ii. 5 .

horse1.text: (the old pl. without “s” is freq. used) 1. proverbial phr. (of obscure meaning) Shr. I. ii. 82 “as many diseases as two-and-fifty h-s,” (cf. Lr. III. vi. 21 ); Tw.N. II. iii. 184 “a of that colour,” something of that kind; R3 I. i. 159 “I run before my to market,” I count my gains prematurely.

horse2.text: vb. (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. to set (one thing up “on” another) Wint. I. ii. 288 .

horseway.text: road for horse traffic Lr. IV. i. 56 “Both stile and gate, and footpath.” ∥ Cf. the modern Warwickshire use of ‘horse-road’ for the part of the roadway allotted to horse and wheeled traffic (opposed to ‘footpath’).

hose.text: two meanings were current in S.'s time,— (1) long stockings, e.g. Gent. II. i. 85 ; (2) article of clothing for the legs and loins, close-fitting breeches or drawers, e.g. 1H4 II. iv. 243 ; esp. in DOUBLET “and ;—French ,” large, wide breeches H5 III. vii. 60 , Mac. II. iii. 16 .

host1.text: “lie at ”=HOST vb. Err. V. i. 413 . ∥ A different word from “host”=landlord of an inn.

host2.text: to lodge, put up Err. I. ii. 9 “Go bear it to the Centaur, where we ,” All'sW. III. v. 94 .

hostage.text: 1. security or pledge given to enemies, &c., for the fulfilment of an undertaking Tit. IV. iv. 104 , Cym. IV. ii. 185 ; a person thus given and held in pledge Cor. I. x. 29 .

hot.text: eager, ardent Gent. II. v. 53 “a hot lover,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 702 “a hot brain,” R3 I. iii. 311 , Cæs. IV. ii. 19 “A hot friend cooling” ; angry, in a passion Err. I. ii. 47 “She is so hot because the meat is cold.”

hour.headword: hour (treated metrically as one or as two syll.)
hour.text: = moment Mer.V. IV. i. 19 “To the last hour of act.”

house1.text: “keep (the) ,” stay indoors, remain at home Meas. III. ii. 77 , Cym. III. iii. 1 “A goodly day not to keep ” ; so Tim. III. iii. 42 “Who cannot keep his wealth must keep his ” (=stay at home and look after it); cf. AYL. IV. iii. 83 “the doth keep itself,” Cym. III. vi. 36 “Poor , that keep'st thyself!” (i.e. that is empty).

house2.text: to drive or pursue into a house Err. V. i. 188 .

household.text: as adj. domestic, homely Shr. II. i. 272 [ 280 ] “a Kate Conformable as other Kates.”

housekeeper.text: 1. one who keeps at home Cor. I. iii. 56 * .

housekeeping.text: hospitality LLL. II. i. 104 , Shr. II. i. 350 [ 358 ], 2H6 I. i. 192 .

hovel.text: refl. to take shelter Lr. IV. vii. 39 .

how.text: (obs. or archaic uses are) 1. phr. “How's the day?,” What hour of the day is it? Tp. V. i. 3 ; “How say you?,” What is your opinion? What do you mean? Tp. II. i. 262 [ 254 ], Ham. II. ii. 190 ; “How so?,” How is that? Why? Wiv. III. v. 71 , Troil. III. iii. 247 .

howbeit.text: nevertheless H5 I. ii. 91 , Cor. I. ix. 70 ;—conj. although Oth. II. i. 300 .

hox.text: to hough, hamstring Wint. I. ii. 244 .

hoy.text: small coasting vessel Err. IV. iii. 39 .

hoyday.text: exclamation of surprise, &c. R3 IV. iv. 460 , Troil. V. i. 73 (Q “hey-day”), Tim. I. ii. 139 .

huddle.text: (not pre-Eliz.; neither 1 nor 2 is pre-S.) 1. to pile or heap up Ado II. i. 254 “huddling jest upon jest with such impossible conveyance upon me.”

hue.text: app. archaic in prose use about 1600, being included in contemporary dictionaries in the lists of ‘Hard Words’; not used by S. in prose.

hulk.text: large ship of burden or transport 2H4 II. iv. 69 “a better stuffed in the hold,” 1H6 V. v. 6 , Troil. II. iii. 280 (see BULK 1 3); (hence,) big, unwieldy person 2H4 I. i. 19 “the hulk Sir John.”

hull.text: to float or drift by the force of the wind or current acting on the hull alone, drift with sail furled (also fig.) Tw.N. I. v. 217 , R3 IV. iv. 439 , H8 II. iv. 197 .

hum.text: utterance of the interjection ‘hum!’ Wint. II. i. 70 “The shrug, the hum or ha,” 73 “these hums and ha's,” Cor. V. iv. 23 “his hum is a battery.”

humanity.text: nearly always = human nature; in 1H6 II. iii. 53 app. = mankind.

humble.text: the meaning ‘submissive, not self-assertive’ occas. passes almost into ‘gentle, kind’, e.g. LLL. V. ii. 629 , H5 I. Chor. 33 ; so humbleness Mer.V. iv. i. 373 , humbly Tit. III. i. 41 .

humorous.text: (not pre-Eliz. in any sense; 1, 2, and 3 are not pre-S.; 2 and 3 are rare; the meaning ‘full of drollery, facetious’ is post-S.) 1. moist, damp Rom. II. i. 31 “the humorous night.”

humour1.text: sb. (the excessive use of this word in fashion in S.'s time is often ridiculed by him, notably in Nym's jargon in Wiv. and H5) 1. moisture Cæs. II. i. 262 “suck up the humours Of the dank morning.”

humour2.text: vb. (not pre-S.; used nonsensically in Wiv. I. iii. 61 , II. i. 132 ; cf. note on prec. sb.) 1. to comply with the humour of, indulge; also, to influence (a person) by observing his humours or inclinations Err. IV. iv. 83 , Ado II. i. 399 , LLL. IV. ii. 52 , 2H4 V. i. 79 , Cæs. I. ii. 320 .

hundred.text: often used vaguely for a great number Gent. IV. iv. 152 , 1H6 I. i. 123 , Ham. I. ii. 237 ; “The Hundred Merry Tales,” a popular jest-book published in 1526, Ado II. i. 137 ; “ psalms,” (?) the psalter as a whole Wiv. II. i. 63 (mod. edd. “Hundredth Psalm”†).

hundredth.text: Wiv. II. i. 63 “the Hundredth Psalm” † (old edd. “the hundred Psalms”).

hungry.text: unfertile Cor. V. iii. 58 “the beach” ;— 1H6 I. ii. 28 “their prey” =prey of their hunger.

huntsman.text: two meanings were current in S.'s time,—(1) man who hunts, hunter, e.g. MND. IV. i. 144 ; (2) manager of a hunt, e.g. Shr. Ind. i. 16 .

hurling.text: impetuous, violent Ham. I. v. 133 “wild and hurling words” (Qq “whurling”).

hurricano.text: waterspout Troil. V. ii. 169 “the dreadful spout Which shipmen do the call,” Lr. III. ii. 2 “You cataracts and h-es.” ∥ In this sense otherwise only in Drayton (? copying S.) ‘downe the shower impetuously doth fall, Like that which men the Hurricano call’, Moon-Calfe, 1627

hurry2.text: is used trans. and intr.; in John V. i. 35 * trans. or intr. according as “up and down” is taken as adv. or as prep.; Per. IV. i. 20 “Hurrying me from my friends” (Qq1 2 3 “whirring”).

hurtle.text: (of weapons, battle) to clatter, crash AYL. IV. iii. 133 “in which hurtling . . . I awak'd,” Cæs. II. ii. 22 “The noise of battle hurtled in the air.”

husband1.text: sb. (cf. the senses of HUSBANDRY) 1. one who manages a household 2H4 V. iii. 11 (Ff3 4 “husbandman”).

husband2.text: vb. (3 not pre-S.) 1. to till, farm 2H4 IV. iii. 130 “land . . . husbanded, and tilled.”

husbandry.text: 1. management (of a household) Mer.V. III. iv. 25 “I commit into your hands The and manage of my house;—good ,” profitable, careful, or economical management H5 IV. i. 7 , Cor. IV. vii. 22 ; also “=good ,” economy, thrift Troil. I. ii. 7 “like as there were husbandry in war,” Per. III. ii. 20 (in both instances with ref. to early rising).

husht.text: hush! Shr. I. i. 68 (Ff12 Q “Husht” Ff34 “Hush'd”), Per. I. iii. 10 (Qq Ff3 4). ∥ A 16th-17th cent. form, which survives in dial.; mod. edd. substitute “hush”†, which occurs 9 times in S.

husks.text: fig. refuse H5 IV. ii. 18 , Troil. IV. v. 165 .

huswifery.text: (good) housekeeping H5 II. iii. 66 , Oth. II. i. 112 (Qq “hous(e)wifeny”).

hyen.headword: hyen (late instance of this form, otherwise only 14th cent.)

hyperbole.text: rhetorical figure of speech consisting in exaggerated or extravagant statement LLL. V. ii. 408 “Three-pil'd hyperboles.”

hyperbolical.text: exaggerated, extravagant Tw.N. IV. ii. 29 “ fiend!,” Cor. I. ix. 51 “acclamations ”

hyssop.text: aromatic herb, Hyssopus officinalis, formerly grown along with thyme Oth. I. iii. 326 .

ice1.text: symbolical of coldness or chastity AYL. III. iv. 17 “the very ice of chastity,” All'sW. II. iii. 99 “boys of ice,” R3 IV. ii. 22 “thou art all ice,” Ham. III. i. 142 “as chaste as ice.”

idea.text: (occurs thrice; 3 not pre-S.) 1. image, likeness R3 III. vii. 13 “your lineaments, Being the right idea of your father.”

idiot.text: ‘licensed’ fool, professional jester John III. iii. 45 (fig.) “Making that , laughter, . . . strain their cheeks to idle merriment,” Troil. II. i. 58 “Mars his ,” Tit. V. i. 79 “An holds his bauble for a god,” Lucr. 1812 “esteemed so As silly-jeering i-s are with kings.” ∥ Also in the sense ‘blockhead, simpleton, fool’.

idle1.text: 1. ineffective, worthless, vain, trifling LLL. V. ii. 873 “your scorns,” MND. III. ii. 168 “waste more breath,” Tw.N. III. iii. 46 “ markets” (= for articles of fancy or luxury), Tim. I. ii. 162 “an banquet,” IV. iii. 27 “I am no votarist,” Oth. I. ii. 95 “Mine's not an idle cause.”

idle2.text: to move lazily or uselessly Rom. II. vi. 19 “the gossamer That idles in the . . . air” ; cf. Meas. III. ii. 297 [ 289 ] “idle spiders' strings.”

idleness.text: trifling, frivolous occupation or pastime Tw.N. I. v. 69 , 1H4 I. ii. 218 , Ant I. iii. 92 - 3

idly.text: carelessly, lightly John IV. ii. 124 , R2 V. ii. 25 “the eyes of men . . . Are idly bent on him,” H5 I. ii. 59 , Tim. I. i. 20 “A thing slipp'd idly from me.”

ignoble.text: (the adv. “ignobly” occurs only in sense 2) 1. of low birth or base descent 1H6 III. i. 177 , V. iv. 7 , 3H6 IV. i. 70 , R3 III. vii. 126 .

ignorant.text: (obs. or peculiar uses are) 1. uninformed, unskilled “in” Wint. II. iii. 69 , Cym. III. ii. 23 “I am ignorant in what I am commanded.”

ill1.text: sb. (is used only in the foll. senses) 1. wrong-doing, wickedness, sin Tp. I. ii. 353 “capable of all ill,” R2 I. i. 86 “So much as of a thought of ill in him,” Oth. IV. iii. 106 “The ills we do,” Lucr. 91 “Whose inward ill no outward harm express'”

ill2.text: adj. (used in various applications of ‘bad’, ‘evil’; cf. EVIL) 1. morally evil, wicked Tp. I. ii. 454 , 455 , Wiv. V. v. 137 , Meas. II. i. 68 “a very ill house,” 2H4 I. ii. 188 “his ill angel,” H8 IV. ii. 43 , Mac. I. iii. 131 , Lucr. 579 .

illume.text: to light up Ham. I. i. 37 .

illustrate1.text: illustrious LLL. IV. i. 65 , V. i. 132 .

illustrate2.text: to make evident H8 III. ii. 182 .

illustrious.text: used as the negative of ‘lustrous’ Cym. I. vi. 109 “ as the smoky light That's fed with stinking tallow” (mod. edd. “illustrous†, inlustrous†, unlustrous†”).

image.text: (2 and 4 were 16-17th cent. senses) 1. appearance semblance, likeness Wint. V. i. 127 “Your father's is so hit in you,” John IV. ii. 71 “The of a wicked heinous fault,” Ham. V. ii. 77 “by the image of my cause I see The portraiture of his.”

imagery.text: hangings, tapestry R2 V. ii. 16 . ∥ An early 17th cent. inventory has ‘ij peeces of fyne tapestrie of silke Imagrie’.

imaginary.text: (1 the ordinary mod. sense; 2 and 3 obs. and somewhat rare, not pre-S.) 1. existing only in imagination, not real Err. IV. iii. 10 , R2 II. ii. 27 “Which for things true weeps things ,” 2H4 IV. iv. 59 “forms ,” Ven 597 “All is she doth prove.”

imagination.text: quasi-concr. in R3 I. iv. 80 “unfelt ” (Ff “I-s”), what they imagine but do not realize.

imbace.text: 16-17th cent. form of ‘embase’ in H5 I. ii. 94 (Qq1 2), of uncertain meaning: see next word. ∥ ‘Embase’ is known only in the sense ‘lower, debase, impair’.

imitate.text: to make (a thing) in imitation of something (S.) Sonn. liii. 6 “the counterfeit Is poorly imitated after you.”

immediacy.text: direct relation in a position of authority Lr. V. iii. 66 .

immediate.text: 1. next in succession (to a throne, &c.) All'sW. II. iii. 139 (fig.) “She is young, wise, fair; In these to nature she's heir,” 2H4 V. ii. 71 “The heir of England,” Ham. I. ii. 109 “the most to our throne.”

immediately.text: app. legal term = expressly MND. I. i. 45 “according to our law provided.”

immodest.text: immoderate, excessive Wint. III. ii. 103 ; arrogant 1H6 IV. i. 126 .

immoment.text: of no moment Ant. V. ii. 165 .

immure2.text: spelt “emure” in LLL. III. i. 131 , IV. iii. 328 (Qq F1).

imp1.text: used affectedly=child LLL. I. ii. 5 , V. ii. 589 ; fig. in “imp of fame” 2H4 V. v. 47 , H5 IV. i. 45 .

imp2.text: properly a term of falconry, to engraft feathers in the wing of a bird so as to make good losses and deficiencies and thus restore or improve the powers of flight R2 II. i. 292 “Imp out our drooping country's broken wing.”

impart.text: 1. to furnish, afford Lucr. 1039 “this no slaughterhouse no tool imparteth.”

impartial.headword: impartial (not pre-S.; the ordinary sense in R2 I. i. 115 , 2H4 V. ii. 36 )
impartial.text: indifferent Meas. V. i. 166 , Ven. 748 . ∥ In Rom. line 1856 (Q1） “Cruel, vniust, impartiall destinies” misused for ‘partial’, a use found also in Swetnam, ‘The Woman-hater,’ 1620

impasted.text: made into a paste Ham. II. ii. 490 [ 481 ].

impeach1.text: calling in question, challenge, accusation Err. V. i. 270 , 3H6 I. iv. 60 .

impeach2.text: to call in question, discredit, disparage MND. II. i. 214 “You do your modesty,” Mer.V. III. ii. 279 , III. iii. 29 , R2 I. i. 189 .

impeachment.text: (the orig. sense = Fr. ‘empêchement’; 2 a 16th-17th c. sense; 3 almost obs. in the gen. sense) 1. hindrance H5 III. vi. 154 “to march . . . Without ”

imperious.text: imperial Troil. IV. v. 171 “most Agamemnon,” Tit. I. i. 250 (Q2 Ff “imperiall”), IV. iv. 80 “be thy thoughts , like thy name,” Ham. V. i. 235 (Ff “Imperial(l),” Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 23, Ven. 996 . ∥ The prevailing mod. sense is equally freq.

imperseverant.text: undiscerning Cym. IV. i. 15 . ∥ ‘Perceiverant’ is instanced only once.

impertinent.text: irrelevant Tp. I. ii. 138 . ∥ Misused by Launcelot, Mer.V. II. ii. 151 .

impeticos.text: burlesque word put into the mouth of a fool, app. as a perversion of ‘impocket’, and perhaps intended to suggest ‘petticoat’ Tw.N. II. iii. 28 .

impiety.text: want of natural piety Tit. I. i. 355 * .

imply.text: to involve All'sW. I. iii. 224 , Per. IV. i. 81 .

impone.text: (?) intended to suggest an affected pronunciation of ‘impawn’ = to stake, wager Ham. V. ii. 155 (Qq “impawned, impaund”), 171

import.text: (comes into general use in the 16th cent. with many meanings; 5, 7 not pre-S.) 1. to bring about, carry with it or involve as a con sequence Meas. V. i. 109 , R3 III. vii. 67 , Lr. IV. iii. 5 “which i-s to the kingdom so much fear and danger,” Ant. II. ii. 139 .

importance.text: (? ‘consequence’ or sense 3 in Wint. II. i. 180 * ) 1. matter, affair (of slight importance) Cym. I. iv. 47 “upon importance of so slight . . . a nature.”

important.text: urgent, pressing, importunate Err. V. i. 138 “At your letters,” Ado II. i. 75 , All'sW. III. vii. 21 “his blood will nought deny,” Lr. IV. iv. 26 (Ff “importun'd”).

importing.text: significant, meaning All'sW. V. iii. 136 “her business looks in her With an visage.”

importune.text: (in the sense of ‘ask urgently and persistently’ usu. with a person as obj., but thrice with a thing) 1. to trouble, weary Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 19

impose2.text: vb. (2 not post-S.) 1. to lay (an imputation) “upon” H5 IV. i. 159 .

imposition.text: (1 only S.; the sense of ‘imposture’ is post-S., but is seen in germ in Oth. II. iii. 271 ) 1. imputation, accusation, charge Meas. I. ii. 200 [ 194 ] “stand under grievous ,” Wint. I. ii. 74 “the clear'”

impossible.text: extravagant, incredible, inconceivable Ado II. i. 145 “in devising slanders,” 254 * “huddling jest upon jest with . . . conveyance” (many conj.), Tw.N. III. ii. 79 “such passages of grossness.”

imposthume.text: purulent swelling, abscess Troil. V. i. 24 , Ham. IV. iv. 27 , Ven. 743 .

impress.text: variant of IMPRESE R2 III. i. 25 (Ff “impress(e,” Qq “impre(e)se”).

impress1.text: impression Gent. III. ii. 6 “weak. of love.”

impress2.text: enforced levy Troil. II. i. 107 , Ham. I. i. 75 , Ant. III. vii. 36 .

impressure.text: impression AYL. III. v. 23 , Tw.N. II. v. 104 , Troil. IV. v. 130 .

improvident.text: unwary, careless (not pre-S.) Wiv. II. ii. 306 , 1H6 II. i. 58 .

impure.text: stressed like ENTIRE R3 III. vii. 232 “all the i'mpure blots,” Ven. 736 “with impu're defeature,” Lucr. 1078 “pure streams to purge my i'mpure tale.”

imputation.text: reputation Troil. I. iii. 339 “Our shall be oddly pois'd In this wild action” ; opinion Oth. III. iii. 407 * “ and strong circumstances” (=‘opinion founded on strong circumstantial evidence,’ Schmidt).

impute.text: to reckon, regard Sonn. lxxxiii. 9 “This silence for my sin you did impute.”

in.text: prep. (1 extension of the normal use in which ‘in’ with a gerund is equivalent to a clause, e.g. Tp. II. i. 226 ） 1. used redundantly with gerunds R2 V. v. 54 , 1H6 V. iii. 41 “suddenly surpris'd By bloody hands, in sleeping on your beds,” H8 I. i. 145 , Troil. III. iii. 250 , Cor. IV. vi. 132 “cast Your . . . caps in hooting at Coriolanus' exile.”

in1.text: 1. within Troil. III. iii. 97 “or without or in.”

in2.text: to get (a crop) in All'sW. I. iii. 49 (F1 “Inne”).

incaged.text: caged, confined R2 II. i. 102 , 3H6 IV. vi. 12 , Ven. 582 .

incapable.text: (occurs 6 times; not pre-S. in active senses; 1, 2, 3, and 4 are construed with “of”) 1. unable to contain Sonn. cxiii. 13 “ of more.”

incarnadine.text: to tinge with red Mac. II. ii. 63 “will . . . The multitudinous seas ” (Ff printed “-ardine”).

incarnate.text: in human shape H5 II. iii. 34 , Tit. V. i. 40 . ∥ Always as an epithet of “devil,” as are also the corrupt forms above.

incense.text: to instigate or incite “to” Wiv. I. iii. 108 , Ado V. i. 247 , Cæs. I. iii. 13 , Lr. II. iv. 309 . ∥ For H8 V. i. 43 see INSENSE.

incertain.text: ‘not knowing what to think or do’ (Schmidt) Meas. III. i. 125 “lawless and thoughts,” Wint. V. i. 29 “What dangers . . . May . . . devour lookers-on.”

inch1.text: “the furthest inch,” the most distant part Ado II. i. 277 ; “the very extremest inch,” the very utmost 2H4 IV. iii. 39 ; “at an inch,” in immediate readiness 2H6 I. iv. 45 ; “even to his inches,” from top to toe Troil. IV. v. 111 . ∥ S. is the earliest authority for “inches”=stature Ant. I. iii. 40 , and the fig. phr. “by inches” Cor. V. iv. 43 .

inch2.text: small island Mac. I. ii. 63 “Saint Colme's Inch.”

inchmeal.text: “by inchmeal,” little by little Tp. II. ii. 3 .

incidency.text: happening, occurrence Wint. I. ii. 403 “what incidency of harm.”

incision.text: cutting for the purpose of letting blood LLL. IV. iii. 97 “A fever in your blood! why, then Would let her out in saucers,” Mer.V. II. i. 6 , AYL. III. ii. 76 “God make in thee!” (? to cure thee of thy simpleness), R2 I. i. 155 , H5 IV. ii. 9 ; (bombastically) 2H4 II. iv. 209 .

incivil.text: unmannerly, rude Cym. V. v. 293 ; so incivility Err. IV. iv. 48 .

inclination.text: natural disposition, nature, character John V. ii. 158 , Ant. II. v. 113 .

incline.text: intr. and refl. with “to,” to side with Cor. II. iii. 42 , Lr. III. iii. 14 , Ant. IV. vi. 14 .

inclining1.text: party, following (cf. prec.) Oth. I. ii. 82 .

inclip.text: to enclose, embrace Ant. II. vii. 75 .

include.text: to bring to a close, conclude Gent. V. iv. 160 “we will all jars With triumphs” ; refl. (?) to resolve itself (into) Troil. I. iii. 119 * .

inclusive.text: enclosing, encircling R3 IV. i. 58 “the verge Of golden metal” ; comprehensive All'sW. I. iii. 234 * .

incomprehensible.text: boundless, unlimited 1H4 I. ii. 208 “the lies that this same fat rogue will tell us.”

incontinent.text: forthwith, at once AYL. V. ii. 44 , R2 V. vi. 48 , Oth. IV. iii. 12 ; so “i-ly” Oth. I. iii. 307 .

inconvenience.text: mischief, harm H5 V. ii. 66 , 1H6 I. iv. 14 .

incony.text: (?) rare, fine, delicate LLL. III. i. 142 “my Jew,” IV. i. 146 “most vulgar wit.” ∥ A cant word, prevalent about 1600, of unascertained origin.

incorporate.text: 1. united in one body, closely united or combined, intimately bound up (with) MND. III. ii. 208 , Cor. I. i. 136 “my friends,” Tit. I. i. 462 “I am in Rome,” Cæs. I. iii. 135 “one To our attempts,” Ven. 540 .

incorpsed.text: incorporated, made into one body “with” Ham. IV. vii. 87 (Q “incorp'st,” Ff “encorp'st”).

increase.text: to cause to thrive Cor. IV. v. 236 * .

indeed.text: (the interrogative use=Is it so ? Really?, as in Wiv. IV. ii. 15 , Oth. III. iii. 101 , is not recorded before S.) 1. in reality, in truth Tp. I. ii. 103 , Wiv. I. i. 26 , MND. III. i. 20 “Pyramus is not killed ” ; placed after a word to emphasize it=really and truly Oth. II. i. 145 “a deserving woman indeed.”

indent.text: (2 this meaning arises from the fact that agreements between mutually contracting parties were written in duplicate on one sheet, the two copies being then severed by a zigzag line) 1. to move in a zigzag line, to double Ven. 704 “Turn, and return, i-ing with the way” ; cf. AYL. IV. iii. 114 “A green and gilded snake . . . with i-ed glides did slip away.”

indenture.text: contract, mutual agreement (lit. and fig.); “pair of i-s” (for the reason of the term see note on prec.) Ham. V. i. 117 .

index.text: table of contents prefixed to a book, (hence fig.) argument, preface, prologue R3 II. ii. 148 “As to the story we late talk'd of,” IV. iv. 85 “The flattering of a direful pageant,” Troil. I. iii. 343 “in such i-es, although small pricks To their subsequent volumes,” Ham. III. iv. 52 , Oth. II. i. 265 .

indifferency.text: (twice only; 2 only S.) 1. impartiality John II. i. 579 * .

indifferent1.text: 1. impartial R2 II. iii. 116 , H8 II. iv. 15 .

indifferent2.text: tolerably, fairly Shr. I. ii. 184 , Tw.N. I. iii. 145 , H5 IV. vii. 35 , Ham. III. i. 126 .

indifferently.text: unconcernedly Cæs. I. ii. 87 ; neutrally Cor. II. ii. 19 ; moderately, tolerably, fairly H5 II. i. 58 “to knock you well,” Ham. III. ii. 42 .

indigest.text: adj. shapeless, unformed Sonn. cxiv. 5 :—sb. (S.) shapeless mass John V. vii. 26 .

indigested.text: =INDIGEST adj. 2H6 V. i. 157 “foul lump,” 3H6 V. vi. 51 (Ff; Qq “undigest,” Malone “indigest”†).

indirect.text: wrong, unjust AYL. I. i. 161 , R3 I. iv. 227 “no or lawless course,” III. i. 31 , Oth. I. iii. 111 “indirect and forced courses.”

indirection.text: (not pre-S.) 1. devious course, roundabout means Ham. II. i. 66 .

indirectly.text: (2, 3 not pre-S.) 1. wrongly, unjustly John II. i. 49 , H5 II. iv. 94 .

indistinguishable.text: of indeterminate shape Troil. V. i. 33 “you whoreson cur” (? with ref. to Thersites' deformity).

indite.text: misused for ‘invite’ 2H4 II. i. 32 , Rom. II. iv. 138 .

indubitate.text: undoubted LLL. IV. i. 67 . ∥ Recorded from 1484 (Caxton) to 1678 (Cudworth).

inducement.text: (not pre-Eliz.; 1, 2 not pre-S.) 1. action of inducing All'sW. III. ii. 91 .

induction.text: initial step in an undertaking 1H4 III. i. 2 “our full of prosperous hope,” R3 I. i. 32 , IV. iv. 5 .

industriously.text: of set purpose Wint. I. ii. 256 .

inexecrable.text: not to be sufficiently execrated Mer.V. IV. i. 128 “damn'd, dog!.” ∥ Some regard it as a misprint for “inexorable,” which is the reading of Ff3 4.

infallible.text: undoubted, certain Meas. III. ii. 121 , All'sW. I. i. 152 “to accuse your mothers, which is most disobedience,” Wint. I. ii. 287 , 2H6 II. ii. 5 “my title, Which is infallible to England's crown.”

infant.text: fig. applied to a young plant Ham. I. iii. 39 . ∥ There are several attrib. uses LLL. IV. iii. 78 “an old play,” John II. i. 97 “ state” (=‘state that belongs to an infant’, Wright), H5 V. ii. 411 [Epil. 9] “ bands,” Rom. II. iii. 23 “the rind of this weak flower.”

infect1.text: to affect “with” some feeling Wint. I. ii. 262 “a fear Which oft i-s the wisest,” John IV. iii. 69 “Never to be i-ed with delight,” Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 72 “infected with my country's love.”

infected.text: affected, factitious Tim. IV. iii. 203 “This is in thee a nature but ,” Compl. 323 .

infection.text: misused for ‘affection’ Wiv. II. ii. 120 , Mer.V. II. ii. 137 .

infectious.text: infected with disease Wint. III. ii. 99 , Oth. IV. i. 21 (Qq “infected”).

infer.text: (1, 2 are 16th-17th cent. uses) 1. to bring about, cause R3 IV. iv. 344 * .

infest.text: to harass Tp. V. i. 246 “Do not your mind.”

infinite.text: infinity Gent. II. vii. 70 “ of love,” Ado II. iii. 112 “past the of thought,” Troil. II. ii. 29 .

infirmity.text: illness, disease All'sW. II. i. 71 , Cæs. I. ii. 274 , Mac. III. iv. 86 , Cym. I. vi. 124 .

inflict.text: to send an infliction or visitation upon, afflict Per. V. i. 61 . ∥ Mod. edd. “afflict”†, but this use of ‘inflict’ can be paralleled from 16th and 17th cent. writers.

infliction.text: fact of being inflicted Meas. I. iii. 28 “our decrees, Dead to ” (i.e. dead, as far as their execution goes).

influence.text: supposed flowing from the stars or heavens of an etherial fluid acting upon the character and destiny of men Tp. I. ii. 182 , Ham. I. i. 119 ; hence, exercise of personal power regarded as something akin to astral influence Gent. III. i. 183 “by her fair Foster'd, illumin'” ∥ In Sonn. lxxviii. 10 app.=inspiration.

inform.text: (the obs. uses are as follows) 1. to take shape Mac. II. i. 48 “It is the bloody business which informs Thus to mine eyes.”

informal.text: (?) disordered in mind, crazy (cf. FORMAL 5) Meas. V. i. 230 “These poor informal women.”

infuse.text: (the sense ‘instil’ also occurs) 1. to shed, diffuse 1H6 I. ii. 85 .

infusion.text: infused temperament, character imparted by nature (S.) Ham. V. ii. 123 .

ingenious.text: (5 cf. the misuse of INGENUOUS) 1. able, talented R3 III. i. 155 .

ingenuous.text: misused, as freq. in the 17th cent., for INGENIOUS (q.v. senses 3, 4) LLL. IV. ii. 80 “if their sons be ” (Q1 “ingenous,” Q2 Ff3 4 “ingenuous,” Ff1 2 “ingenuous”).

ingredience.text: ingredients Mac. I. vii. 11 “the of our poison'd chalice (ingredients†),” IV. i. 34 (“ingredients”†); in Oth. II. iii. 313 (Qq), see next word.

ingredient.text: chief component Oth. II. iii. 313 “Every inordinate cup is unblessed and the is a devil” (Ff; Qq “ingredience”).

inhabit.text: (?) to continue, (?) remain at home Mac. III. iv. 105 * “If trembling I inhabit then, protest mee The Baby of a Girle” (F1); many conj.

inhearse.text: to lay as in a coffin 1H6 IV. vii. 45 , Sonn. lxxxvi. 3 .

inherit.text: (1 the orig. sense ‘to make heir’) 1. to put (a person) in possession “of” R2 I. i. 85 “ us So much as of a thought of ill in him.”

inhibited.text: forbidden, as by ecclesiastical law All'sW. I. i. 160 (see CANON), Oth. I. ii. 79 “arts ”

initiate.text: of a novice (S.) Mac. III. iv. 143 .

injoint.text: to join, unite Oth. I. iii. 35 .

injurious.text: calumniating, contumelious, insulting 2H6 I. iv. 51 , Cor. III. iii. 68 “Call me their traitor! Thou tribune!,” Cym. IV. ii. 86 ; malicious or insolent in wrong-doing Gent. I. ii. 103 , R2 I. i. 91 “a false traitor and villain,” Cym. III. i. 48 .

injury.text: (1 common 16th-17th cent.; 2 only S.) 1. reviling, insult, calumny, affront Err. V. i. 200 , MND. II. i. 147 , III. ii. 148 “If you were civil and knew courtesy, You would not do me thus much ,” 3H6 IV. i. 107 “what said War wick to these injuries?.”

inkle.text: kind of tape LLL. III. i. 146 , Wint. IV. iii. [IV.] 208; linen or yarn from which it is made Per. V. Gower 8 .

inland.text: inlying districts of a country near the capital and centres of population and culture, as opposed to the remote or outlying wild parts H5 I. ii. 142 “to defend Our from the pilfering borderers” (Qq “your England”);—adj. cultured, refined AYL. III. ii. 367 “an man; one that knew courtship too well” ; cf. AYL. II. vii. 96 “yet I am inland bred, And know some nurture.”

inly.text: inward(ly) Tp. V. i. 200 “I have wept,” Gent. II. vii. 18 “the inly touch of love.”

inn.text: place of residence for law students, often named after the person from whom they were first rented or acquired 2H4 III. ii. 15 “Clement's Inn” (one of the Inns of Chancery, belonging to the Inner Temple), 36 “Gray's Inn;—inns o' court,” the four sets of buildings in London (the Inner Temple, the Middle Temple, Lincoln's Inn, and Gray's Inn) belonging to the four legal societies which have the exclusive right of admitting persons to practise at the bar 2H4 III. ii. 14 , 2H6 IV. vii. 2 . ∥ The original meaning of this word, ‘habitation, lodging’, is possibly glanced at in R2 V. i. 13 .

innocent.text: adj. silly Ado V. ii. 38 ;—sb. idiot, halfwit, simpleton All'sW. IV. iii. 214 “a dumb innocent,” Lr. III. vi. 9 , Per. IV. iii. 17 “play the pious ”

innovation.text: alteration for the worse Ham. II. ii. 356 [ 347 ]; disturbance, commotion Oth. II. iii. 42 ; revolution 1H4 V. i. 78 .

inoculate.text: to engraft Ham. III. i. 121 “ our old stock.”

inquire1.text: inquiry Ham. II. i. 4 (so Qq; Ff “inquiry”), Per. III. Gower 22 .

inquire2.text: in old edd. “enquire, enquier”; 3 syll. in Shr. I. ii. 169 “I pro'mis'd to' enqui're ca'refully'.”

insane.text: causing madness (S.) Mac. I. iii. 84 “the root, That takes the reason prisoner.”

insanie.text: madness LLL. V. i. 28 “it insinuateth me of ” (old edd. “infamie”). ∥ The word is otherwise known only from one other author.

inscroll.text: to describe on a scroll Mer.V. II. vii. 72 .

insculp.text: to carve, engrave Mer.V. II. vii. 57 .

insense.text: to make (a person) understand H8 V. i. 43 “I think I have I-'d the lords o' the council that he is . . . A most arch heretic” (F1 “Incenst”; referred by some to INCENSE and explained ‘provoked to believe’). ∥ In literary use from 15th to 17th cent., subsequently dial. and now in gen. use from Northumberland to Cornwall.

insensible.text: not perceptible by the senses 1H4 V. i. 139 .

insinuate.text: (in Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 763 perhaps an absol. use of a 15th-16th cent. sense ‘to win or attract subtly or covertly’) 1. intr. to wheedle oneself into a person's favour, ingratiate oneself “with” R2 IV. i. 165 “To , flatter, bow,” Cor. II. iii. 105 , Tit. IV. ii. 38 , Ven. 1012 “With Death she humbly doth insinuate.”

insinuation.text: 1. self-ingratiation John V. i. 68 ; ‘artful intrusion into the business’ (Clark and Wright) Ham. V. ii. 59 .

insisture.text: (a) steady continuance in their path, (b) persistency, (c) regularity Troil. I. iii. 87 .

insolence.text: pride, overbearing nature Cor. I. i. 268 .

insomuch.text: inasmuch as AYL. V. ii. 62 “insomuch I say I know you are.”

instalment.text: place or seat in which a person is installed Wiv. V. v. 69 .

instance.text: (the sense of ‘illustrative example’ passes almost into ‘sample, specimen’ in 2H4 I. i. 56 , Ham. IV. v. 161 ) 1. motive, cause All'sW. IV. i. 44 , R3 III. ii. 25 “shallow, without instance” (Ff), Ham. III. ii. 194 “The instances that second marriage move.”

instant1.text: “upon, on,” or, “o' the ,” immediately, at once LLL. III. i. 44 , Tim. II. ii. 208 , Oth. I. ii. 38 .

instant2.text: 1. now present, existing, happening All'sW. IV. iii. 128 , H8 I. i. 225 “this cloud,” Troil. III. iii. 153 “Take the way,” Cor. V. i. 37 “the army we can make.”

instate.text: to endow, to invest Meas. V. i. 425 .

instruct.text: to inform Meas. I. i. 80 , Shr. IV. ii. 120 , Cym. IV. ii. 360 “He'll, then, instruct us of this body.”

instruction.text: information Ant. V. i. 54 “Of thy intents desires instruction.”

instrument.text: (the sense of ‘tool’ is freq.) 1. fig. means agent Tw.N. V. i. 126 (with literal phraseology), 1H6 II. v. 58 , Oth. IV. ii. 44 .

insult.text: to exult proudly or contemptuously, triumph scornfully “over, on” AYL. III. v. 36 , 1H6 I. ii. 138 “that proud i-ing ship,” 3H6 I. iii. 14 “i-ing o'er his prey,” R3 II. iv. 51 “I-ing tyranny,” Tit. III. ii. 71 “I will insult on him.”

insuppressive.text: insuppressible Cæs. II. i. 134 “th' insuppressive mettle of our spirits.”

intelligence.text: 1. communication, intercourse AYL. I. iii. 50 “If with myself I hold ,” Cym. IV. ii. 347 , Sonn. lxxxvi. 10 “that . . . ghost Which nightly gulls him with intelligence.”

intelligencer.text: informer, spy, secret agent 2H4 IV. ii. 20 , R3 IV. iv. 71 .

intelligent.text: ‘bearing intelligence, giving information, communicative’ (Schmidt) Wint. I. ii. 378 , Lr. III. i. 25 , III. v. 12 , III. vii. 12 “Our posts shall be swift and intelligent betwixt us.”

intend.text: （‘purpose, design’ is the commonest sense) 1. to purpose making (a journey) Ant. V. ii. 200 “Cæsar through Syria I-s his journey,” Per. I. ii. 116 “I . . . to Tarsus Intend my travel,” Sonn. xxvii. 6 ; also intr. 1H4 IV. i. 92 “The king . . . is set forth, Or hitherwards intended speedily.”

intendment.text: purpose, intent, design AYL. I. i. 142 , H5 I. ii. 144 , Oth. IV. ii. 206 , Ven. 222 .

intenible.text: incapable of holding All'sW. I. iii. 210 .

intent.text: (the sense ‘purpose, design’, and its wider development ‘will, inclination, desire,’ are the commonest uses) 1. aim, bent Tw.N. II. iv. 78 , Lucr. 46 .

intention.text: =INTENT 1, Wiv. I. iii. 71 , Wint. I. ii. 139 .

intercept.text: to interrupt Tit. III. i. 40 “ my tale.”

interchained.text: linked one with another MND. II. ii. 49 (Qq; Ff “interchanged”).

interchangeably.text: mutually, reciprocally (in phr. based on the wording of legal agreements) R2 V. ii. 98 , 1H4 III. i. 82 “sealed ,” Troil. III. ii. 60 .

interdiction.text: restraint, exclusion Mac. IV. iii. 107 “By his own stands accurst” (so Ff2 3; F1 “accust”).

interest.text: (usu. 2 syll.; but sometimes 3 syll. at the end of line, e.g. 1H4 IV. iii. 49 “You shall have your desires with interest,” but not in Cym. IV. ii. 365 ) 1. legal concern (“in”), right or title (“to” possessions or the enjoyment of them) John IV. iii. 147 “unow'd of proud-swelling state,” 1H4 III. ii. 98 “ to the state,” 2H6 III. i. 84 “all your in those territories,” Lr. I. i. 52 “ of territory,” 87 “to be ” (=to constitute a claim; but see INTERESS'D); fig. AYL. V. i. 8 , Tit. III. i. 249 “Where life hath no more but to breathe,” Lucr. 1067 , 1619 , 1797

interim.text: “by i-s,” at intervals Cor. I. vi. 5 ; interlude LLL. I. i. 170 .

interjoin.text: to join mutually Cor. IV. iv. 22 .

interlude.text: (orig.) dramatic or mimic representation, of light or humorous character, such as was introduced between the acts of the long mystery or morality plays; (in 16th-17th cent.) stage-play, esp. of a popular kind, comedy, farco MND. I. ii. 6 , Lr. V. iii. 90 .

intermission.text: delay Mac. IV. iii. 231 , Lr. II. iv. 33 ; in Mer.V. III. ii. 200 “for ” (with stop at “ ”), ? to avoid loss of time, fill up the time.

interpret.text: used with ref. to the puppet-show (‘motion’) Gent. II. i. 105 “O excellent motion! O exceeding puppet! now will he to her,” Ham. III. ii. 260 “I could between you and your love, if I could see the puppets dallying,” Lucr. 1325 “the eye i-s to the ear The heavy motion that it doth lehold.”

intestate.text: not having made a will; fig. R3 IV. iv. 128 “Airy succeeders of joys” (Ff “intestine”), ‘mere words succeed as next of kin to an empty inheritance’ (Wright).

intitled.text: form in old edd. of ENTITLED.

into.text: unto, to (freq.) Tp. I. ii. 100 (Warburton “unto”†), All'sW. I. iii. 262 “pray God's blessing into thy attempt,” Tw.N. V. i. 88 , John III. iii. 39 , (?; “unto”†), H5 I. ii. 102 “Look back into your mighty ancestors,” Troil. III. iii. 12 , Cym. I. vi. 167 “he enchants societies into him.”

intolerable.text: excessive, exceedingly great Wiv. V. v. 165 “ entrails,” 1H4 II. iv. 599 [ 592 ] “ deal of sack”; also adv. exceedingly Shr. I. ii. 90 “she is intolerable curst.”

intrenchant.text: incapable of being cut Mac. V. vii. 38 [ viii. 9 ].

intrince.text: entangled Lr. II. ii. 80 “t'intrince t'unloose” (mod. edd. “too intrinse”†). ∥ (?) Abbreviated from next; cf. REVERB.

invention.text: 1. power of mental creation or construction, inventiveness, imagination Ado V. i. 296 “if your love Can labour aught in sad ,” LLL. IV. ii. 130 “the jerks of ,” H5 I. Chor. 2 , Oth. II. ii. 125 , Ven. Ded. 5 “the first heir of my invention.”

invest.text: to endow, furnish 2H4 IV. v. 71 “to Their sons with arts and martial exercises.” ∥ In H5 IV. Chor. 26 “their gesture sad I-ing lank-lean cheeks and war-worn coats” app. to accompany.

investment.text: pl. clothes 2H4 IV. i. 45 , Ham. I. iii. 128 .

invisible.text: (?) subtle Ant. II. ii. 220 “A strange perfume” ; (?) secret Cym. IV. ii. 177 “an instinct.”

inward.text: adj. familiar “with” R3 III. iv. 8 “Who is most with the noble duke” ; private, secret Ado IV. i. 12 “any impediment,” LLL. V. i. 10 5 “ between us”;— adv. inwardly, internally Mer.V. III. ii. 86 [Hercules and Mars] “ search'd, have livers white as milk,” Ham. IV. iv. 28 “the imposthume . . . That breaks,” Sonn. lxii. 4 , “so grounded in my heart”;—sb. intimate friend Meas. III. ii. 142 .

iron.text: (usu. two syll.; one syll. in John IV. i. 120 , IV. ii. 194 , R3 V. iii. 111 ) 1. the metal of which arms and armour are made; hence (i) offensive weapons Ado V. i. 257 , 1H6 IV. iii. 20 ; (ii) sword Tw.N. IV. i. 43 , R3 V. iii. 111 , Troil. II. iii. 18 ; (iii) armour 2H4 I. i. 150 , Ant. IV. iv. 3 .

irrecoverable.text: not to be recovered or redeemed 2H4 II. iv. 360 .

irregular.text: lawless John V. iv. 54 , 1H4 I. i. 40 , III. ii. 27 ; so irregulous (S.) Cym. IV. ii. 315 .

irreligious.text: believing in a false religion Tit. V. iii. 121 * .

issue1.text: sb. (the usual S. meanings are ‘offspring, progeny’ and ‘event, result, consequence’; 1 is not pre-S.; 2 is peculiar to S.) 1. outcome, product (“of” a practice or condition) All'sW. II. i. 109 , John III. iv. 21 “the of your peace,” Troil. II. ii. 89 , Lr. I. i. 18 .

issue2.text: to shed tears (S.) H5 IV. vi. 34 .

issued.text: born, descended Tp. I. ii. 59 “A princess,— no worse issued,” 1H6 V. iv. 38 .

issuing.text: pouring or gushing out 3H6 II. vi. 82 “the blood,” Tit. II. iv. 30 “three issuing spouts.”

it.text: (cf. HIT; 1 arose in the 16th cent.) 1. very freq. with intransitive verbs as a kind of vague object, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 379 “Foot it featly,” Shr. I. ii. 75 “to wive it,” III. ii. 254 “to bride it,” H5 V. ii. 130 “to mince it,” H8 II. iii. 37 “to queen it,” Mac. II. iii. 20 “devil-porter it,” Cym. III. iii. 85 “to prince it.”

iterance.text: iteration Oth. V. ii. 148 (Qq “iteration”). ∥ Not pre-S.; taken up by mod. writers.

its.text: not pre-Eliz.; in S. much less freq. than HIS (q.v.), but about as freq. as IT (see sense 3); used absol. (S.) once H8 I. i. 18 “till the last [day] Made former wonders its.”

itself.text: once in tmesis Cym. III. iv. 160 “Woman it pretty self.”

iwis.text: certainly, assuredly Shr. I. i. 62 , R3 I. iii. 102 , Per. II. Gower 2 . ∥ Often spelt “I wis” and erroneously understood as=I know.

jackanapes.text: (also “jackanape, jack'nape”) 1. ape H5 V. ii. 147 “sit like a , never off.”

jade1.text: 1. ‘sorry,’ ill-conditioned horse Meas. II. i. 276 [ 269 ] “let carman whip his jade,” H5 IV. ii. 46 , Ham. III. ii. 256 “let the galled jade wince” ; vicious horse (allusively) Ado I. i. 151 “You always end with a jade's trick,” Shr. I. ii. 252 “give him head: I know he'll prove a jade,” All'sW. IV. v. 64 , Troil. II. i. 21 .

jade2.text: vb. (not pre-S.; 2 a 17th cent. sense) 1. lit. to make a jade of (a horse), hence, to exhaust, weary Ant. III. i. 34 .

jangle.text: to dispute, wrangle LLL. II. i. 223 , MND. III. ii. 353 .

jar1.text: sb. (1 a 16th cent. use; 2 only S., cf. JAR vb. 2) 1. discord in music AYL. II. vii. 5 “If he, compact of jars, grow musical.”

jar2.text: vb. (2 cf. JAR sb. 2) 1. to make a musical discord, be out of tune Gent. IV. ii. 68 , Shr. III. i. 40 “the treble jars” ; in fig. context Shr. V. ii. 1 “our jarring notes agree,” All'sW. I. i. 188 “His jarring concord,” 2H6 II. i. 57 “When such strings jar,” Lr. IV. vii. 16 “The untun'd and jarring senses.”

jaunce1.text: =JAUNT sb. Rom. II. v. 26 (Qq23 “iaunce,” Ff Qq4 5 “iaunt, jaunt”). ∥ Perhaps only a misprint for “iaunte”; recorded otherwise only as in mod. Sussex dial.

jaunce2.text: vb. (in 2 Qq2 3 “iaunsing,” Ff Qq4 5 “jaunt-, iaunting”) 1. to fatigue a horse R2 V. v. 94 .

jaunt.text: running up and down or to and fro, ‘trotting’ or trudging about Rom. II. v. 26 ; so jaunt vb. Rom. II. v. 53 ; cf. JAUNCE sb. and vb.

jay.text: flashy or light woman Wiv. III. iii. 44 , Cym. III. iv. 51 “Some jay of Italy . . . hath betray'd him.”

jealous.text: (in old edd. often spelt “iealious,” a freq. 1617th cent. spelling, which does not, however, always denote 3 syll.; 1 survives extensively in mod. dial. use) 1. suspicious, careful or watchful H5 IV. i. 305 “ of your absence,” Rom. II. ii. 181 .

jealousy.text: suspicion, apprehension of evil, mistrust Ado II. ii. 50 “ shall be called assurance,” Tw.N. III. iii. 8 “ what might befall your travel,” 2H4 Ind. 16, H5 II. ii. 126 , Ham. II. i. 113 “beshrew my !,” IV. v. 19 (‘Guilt is so full of suspicion that it unskilfully betrays itself in fearing to be betrayed’).

jerk.text: short, sharp, witty speech, sally LLL. IV. ii. 130 “the jerks of invention.” ∥ A freq. 17th cent. use.

jerkin.text: close-fitting jacket often made of leather, worn by men in the 16th and 17th cent. Troil. III. iii. 269 “A plague of opinion! a man may wear it on both sides, like a leather jerkin.”

jesses.text: short straps of leather, silk, or other material fastened round the legs of a trained hawk Oth. III. iii. 261 .

jest1.text: sb. (the meaning ‘object of ridicule’ Wiv. III. iii. 161 is not pre-S.) 1. merriment, jocosity Ham. V. i. 203 .

jest2.text: (a) to amuse oneself, make merry, (b) to act in a masque or play R2 I. iii. 95 * .

jet1.text: to walk pompously, strut, stalk, swagger Tw.N. II. v. 36 “jets under his advanced plumes,” Cym. III. iii. 5 , Per. I. iv. 26 .

jet2.text: to encroach “upon” Err. II. ii. 28 “Your sauciness will jet† upon my love” (F1 “iest”), R3 II. iv. 51 “tyranny begins to jet” (Ff “Iutt, jut) Upon the . . . throne,” Tit. II. i. 64 “to jet” (Qq “iet,” Ff “set) upon a prince's right.”

jig1.text: sb. (3 cf. Cotgr. s.v. ‘Farce,’ ‘the Iyg at the end of an Enterlude, wherein some pretie knauerie is acted’） 1. lively, rapid kind of dance Ado II. i. 79 “hot and hasty, like a Scotch jig,” Tw.N. I. iii. 140 “My very walk should be a jig” ; music for such a dance, rapid, lively dance-tune LLL. IV. iii. 168 “to tune a jig.”

jig2.text: vb. (not pre-S.) 1. to sing as a jig LLL. III. i. 12 (F1 “Iigge”).

jigging.text: Cæs. IV. iii. 136 “these fools,” ‘these foolish writers of doggerel’ (Wright); cf. JIG sb. 2, 3

join.text: =‘join battle’, come together in conflict 1H4 V. i. 85 , 3H6 I. i. 15 , R3 V. iii. 313 ; pass. Ant. IV. x. 14 [ xii. 1 ].

joinder.text: joining, union Tw.N. V. i. 161 “Confirm'd by mutual of your hands.” ∥ Not pre-S. in the gen. sense; as a legal term it meant ‘the coupling of two in a suite or action against another’ (Cowell, 1607).

jointress.text: widow who holds a jointure, dowager Ham. I. ii. 9 .

journal.text: daily, diurnal Meas. IV. iii. 95 “Ere twice the sun hath made his greeting,” Cym. IV. ii. 10 “Stick to your journal course.”

journeyman.text: used depreciatively = one who is not a master of his trade Ham. III. ii. 38 .

joy1.text: 1. “take joy,” be pleased or glad AYL. IV. i. 92 , Wint. V. i. 80 .

joy2.text: 1. to gladden, delight R3 I. ii. 220 “it joys me,” Cym. V. v. 425 “Joy'd are we,” Per. I. ii. 9 .

judge.text: to think, suppose Gent. I. ii. 136 “although you I wink,” III. i. 25 “when they have j-d me fast asleep,” 2H6 III. ii. 67 “It may be judg'd I made the duke away.”

judgement.text: (2 was a 17th cent. use) 1. “in my 's place” Sonn. cxxxi. 12 = “in my ” Gent. IV. iv. 158 , R3 III. iv. 43 (Qq “in mine opinion), to my ” Lr. I. iv. 62 .

judicious.text: (?) judicial Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 128 “ hearing,” Lr. III. iv. 73 * “ punishment.” ∥ ‘Judicial’ is not S.

jump.text: exactly, precisely Ham. I. i. 65 “ at this dead hour” (Ff “just”), V. ii. 389 , Oth. II. iii. 395 “bring him jump when he may Cassio find.”

jump1.text: hazard, venture Ant. III. viii. 6 “our fortune lies Upon this jump.” ∥ Cf. JUMP vb. 2

jump2.text: vb. (unexplained in [ Wint IV. iii. iv. ] 195) 1. to agree, tally, coincide Mer.V. II. ix. 32 “ with common spirits,” Shr. I. i. 194 “meet and in one,” Tw.N. V. i. 262 “cohere and ,” 1H4 I. ii. 78 “it j-s with my humour,” R3 III. i. 11 .

jure.text: used contextually in connexion with “juror,” as if=make jurors of you 1H4 II. ii. 101 .

just.text: tilting match R2 V. ii. 52 “j-s and triumphs.”

just1.text: 1. honourable, faithful Cæs. III. ii. 91 “He was my friend, faithful and just to me.”

just2.text: in replies and expressions of assent= exactly so, just so, right! Meas. III. i. 66 , V. i. 196 [ 202 ], Ado II. i. 29 , AYL. III. ii. 282 “Rosalind is your love's name?—Yes, just,” All'sW. II. iii. 21 , H5 III. vii. 163 , Tit. IV. ii. 24 “O! 'tis a verse in Horace . . . —Ay just, a verse in Horace.”

justice.text: “do” (a person) “justice,” drink to his health Oth. II. iii. 91 .

justicer.text: judge, magistrate Lr. III. vi. 24 (Qq “iustice,” mod. edd. “justicer”†), 59 , IV. ii. 79 (corrected Q “Iustisers,” others “Justices”), Cym. V. v. 215 .

justify.text: 1. to show to be righteous, innocent, or in the right, vindicate Meas. V. i. 159 “To this worthy nobleman, So vulgarly . . . accus'd,” Wint. I. i. 10 , 2H6 II. iii. 16 ; with thing as object Sonn. cxxxix. 1 “call not me to justify the wrong.”

justle.text: spelling in old edd. of “jostle” Tp. III. ii. 30 , V. i. 158 .

justly.text: the senses ‘uprightly’, ‘rightfully, deservedly’, ‘with good reason, properly’, ‘correctly, truthfully’, ‘exactly, precisely’ are all represented.

jut1.text: to thrust out Tim. I. ii. 240 .

jutty1.text: projecting part of a wall or building Mac. I. vi. 6 “no jutty, frieze, Buttress.”

jutty2.text: to project beyond, overhang (S.) H5 III. i. 13 “O'erhang and jutty his confounded base.”

juvenal.text: youth LLL. I. ii. 8 , III. i. 69 , MND. III. i. 100 , 2H4 I. ii. 21 .

kam.text: “clean kam,” quite wrong Cor. III. i. 302 .

kecksy.text: local name for umbelliferous plants with hollow stems (e.g. Cow Parsnip) H5 V. ii. 52 .

keech.text: fat of a slaughtered animal rolled into a lump; applied to a butcher's wife 2H4 II. i. 104 , to Wolsey the butcher's son H8 I. i. 55 .

keel.text: to prevent (a pot) boiling over by stirring, skimming, or pouring in something cold LLL. V. ii. 928 “While greasy Joan doth keel the pot.”

keen.text: bitter, sharp, severe LLL. V. ii. 400 , MND. II. ii. 123 , V. i. 54 , John III. i. 182 , Ham. III. ii. 262 .

keep2.text: vb. (3 freq. in literary use c. 1580-1630) 1. refl. to restrain oneself Gent. IV. iv. 12 .

ken1.text: sb. (1 Bourne, 1574, says that a ken is 6 or 9 leagues; Leland, 1538, has ‘a Kenning, that is to say about a xx miles,’ Botoner, 15th cent., ‘quilibet kennyng continet 21 miliaria’) 1. the distance that bounds the range of ordinary vision, esp. at sea; about 20 miles 2H4 IV. i. 151 “within a ken our army lies,” Cym. III. vi. 6 “Thou wast with in a ken.”

ken2.text: vb. (occurs thrice; 3 an affected use) 1. to descry, see 2H6 III. ii. 101 .

kennel2.text: street gutter Shr. IV. iii. 98 , 2H6 IV. i. 71 .

kennelled.text: lodged as in a kennel Ven. 913 .

kerchief.text: cloth used to cover the head, formerly a female head-dress Wiv. III. iii. 62 , IV. ii. 76 ; phr. “wear a kerchief,” to be ill Cæs. II. i. 315 .

kernel.text: pip, seed Tp. II. i. 97 (of an apple), All'sW. II. iii. 276 (of a pomegranate); as the type of something insignificant Wint. I. ii. 160 .

kersey.text: kind of coarse cloth Meas. I. ii. 36 ; as adj. (fig.) plain, homely LLL. V. ii. 414 “honest noes.”

key.text: (not recorded before S. in the musical senses) 1. in phr. expressive of control or mastery All'sW. I. i. 77 , H5 II. ii. 96 “Thou that didst bear the key of all my counsels,” 2H6 I. i. 115 “These counties were the keys of Normandy,” Mac. III. vi. 18 , Oth. IV. ii. 21 .

kibe.text: chapped or ulcerated chilblain on the heel Tp. II. i. 284 [ 276 ], Ham. V. i. 152 “the toe of the peasant comes so near the heel of the courtier, he galls his ” (i.e. is in annoying proximity to him).

kickshaws.text: fancy dish 2H4 V. i. 29 “a joint of mutton, and any pretty little tiny kickshaws” ; fig. trifle Tw.N. I. iii. 124 “Art thou good at these kickshawses, knight?.” ∥ Florio, 1598, defines the Italian ‘Carabozzada’ as ‘a kinde of daintie dish or quelque chose vsed in Italie’; Cotgr., 1611, the French ‘Fricandeaux’ as ‘short skinlesse, and daintie puddings, or Quelkchoses’.

kill.text: “kill up” = ‘kill off’ exterminate AYL. II. i. 62 . ∥ Cf. Palsgr. ‘I kyll up, as one that kylleth the resyde we where many have been kylled a fore.’

killen.text: arch. infinitive of KILL Per. II. Gower 20 .

kin.text: not pre-S. in the predicative adj. use=related, akin All'sW. II. i. 41 “my sword and yours are ,” 2H4 II. ii. 122 “those that are to the king,” Troil. III. iii. 175 “One touch of nature makes the whole world ”

kind1.text: sb. (the foll. and the sense ‘sort, species’ are all the S. uses; 1 was common down to about 1600; 3 common in the 17th cent., freq. in S.) 1. natural disposition or character, nature AYL. IV. iii. 60 “thy youth and kind” (=thy youthful nature), Lucr. 1147 “to change their k-s;—of its own kind,” of itself, naturally Tp. II. i. 170 ; “do his kind,” act according to its nature Ant. V. ii. 263 .

kind2.text: 1. natural, appropriate, proper Ado I. i. 26 “A kind overflow of kindness,” Lucr. 1423 .

kindle1.text: to incite (cf. ENKINDLE) AYL. I. i. 182 .

kindle2.text: to bring forth AYL. III. ii. 362 .

kindly1.text: adj. ( AYL. II. iii. 53 * (a) natural, proper, (b) agreeable, pleasant; 2H4 IV. v. 82 k. * tears (a) natural, not forced, (b) naturally shed for a father; cf. sense 2) 1. innate, inherent Tim. II. ii. 227 “ warmth.”

kindly2.text: adv. (in Lr. I. v. 15 sense 1 with play on the more freq. sense of ‘affectionately’) 1. naturally (as of the same kin) Tp. V. i. 24 .

kindness.text: tenderness, affection, love Ado I. i. 26 , Shr. II. i. 77 , IV. i. 211 “to kill a wife with kindness,” Tw.N. II. i. 42 , R3 IV. ii. 22 “thy kindness freezes,” Sonn. clii. 9 .

kindred.text: attrib.=(1) of or belonging to relatives R2 II. i. 183 “guilty of no blood” (Qq1-4 “kin(d)red,” Ff “kindreds=kindred's”), R3 II. ii. 63 “our tears” ; (2) cognate John III. iv. 14 “any kindred action like to this” (Ff “kindred-action”).

kingdom.text: (2 cf. John IV. ii. 246 , 2H4 IV. iii. 118 ) 1. sovereignty R3 IV. ii. 61 .

kirtle.text: woman's gown, skirt, or petticoat 2H4 II. iv. 297 , [ Sonn. Music v. 11 = Pilgr. 363 ].

kiss.text: said of balls touching, at bowls Cym. II. i. 2 .

kitchen.text: to furnish with kitchen-fare (S.) Err. v. i. 418 .

kite.text: rapacious person, also indefinitely as a term of reproach H5 II. i. 80 , Lr. I. iv. 286 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 89 ∥ In H5 II. i. 80 “kite of Cressids kind, ?” read “kit” (=kitten), as in F4, the passage being app. an echo of Gascoigne's Dan Bartholomew ‘kits of Cressides kinde’.

knack.text: trifle, knick-knack MND. I. i. 34 , Shr. IV. iii. 67 .

knap.text: to bite noisily Mer.V. III. i. 10 ; to give a smart blow to Lr. II. iv. 118 .

knave.text: boy or lad employed as a servant; male servant or menial in general Wiv. III. v. 101 , 2H4 I. ii. 83 , Lr. I. iv. 88 , Oth. I. i. 126 “a of common hire,” Ant. V. ii. 3 ; opposed to “knight” Tw.N. II. iii. 72 [ 69 ], John I. i. 243 ; often used vocatively in addressing a servant with friendly familiarity LLL. III. i. 151 [ 144 ] “my good Costard,” Cæs. IV. iii. 240 “Poor knave.”

knavery.text: pl. roguish or waggish tricks MND. III. ii. 346 , All'sW. I. iii. 14 , H5 IV. vii. 53 . ∥ Used for the nonce, as a rhyme-word, = tricks of dress or ornament Shr. IV. iii. 58 .

knee1.text: part of the body used in kneeling or curtseying; hence, kneeliing, prostration, curtsey R2 II. iii. 83 , 1H4 IV. iii. 68 “with cap and knee,” Cor. V. iii. 57 “Your knees to me!,” Tim. III. vi. 108 “Cap and knee slaves,” IV. iii. 36 “give them title, knee, and approbation,” Oth. II. i. 84 .

knee2.text: to bend the knee before Lr. II. iv. 217 .

knit1.text: knitted work, texture Shr. IV. i. 94 .

knit2.text: to tie in or with a knot John IV. i. 42 “I my handkercher about your brows” ; usu. transf. or fig. to bind, pin, or unite firmly or closely MND. I. i. 172 “that which knitteth souls” ; also knit up (in various senses) Tp. III. iii. 89 “all up In their distractions,” MND. V. i. 194 “Thy stones with lime and hair up,” Rom. IV. ii. 25 “I'll have this knot up.”

knob.text: pimple H5 III. vi. 112 “bubukles, and whelks, and knobs” (Ff; Q3 “whelkes and knubs, And pumples”).

knock.text: the foll. uses are not recorded before S.:—to drive by striking Tp. III. ii. 71 “ a nail into his head;— off” Cym. V. iv. 198 ; “ out” 1H6 III. i. 83 ; “ it” (=strike up) H8 I. iv. 108 “Let the music knock it.”

knoll.text: to ring, toll AYL. II. vii. 114 “bells have k-'d to church,” 121, 2H4 I. i. 103 “k-ing a departed friend” (Q “tolling”), Mac. V. vii. 79 [ viii. 50 ].

knot1.text: sb. (said fig. of the marriage tie, e.g. R3 IV. iii. 42 ; 2 survives in midl. and south-west dial.) 1. folded arms Tp. I. ii. 224 , Tit. III. ii. 4 .

knot2.text: to gather into a knot, a cluster Oth. IV. ii. 61 .

knotted.text: laid out in intricate designs LLL. I. i. 248 “thy curious- garden” ; gnarled Troil. I. iii. 50 “knotted oaks.”

knotty.text: gnarled Tp. I. ii. 295 , Cæs. I. iii. 6 “ oaks.”

know1.text: knowledge Ham. V. ii. 44 “on the view and know of these contents” (Ff; Qq “knowing”).

know2.text: “have known (together),” have been acquainted (S.) Ant. II. vi. 83 , Cym. I. iv. 38 ; “more known,” better acquainted Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 66; “be not you known on't,” have no knowledge of it Oth. III. iii. 320 (Ff “acknown(e)”; know for, be aware of 2H4 I. ii. 5 ; know of, ascertain from Meas. I. iv. 8 , MND. I. i. 68 , Lr. V. i. 1 , Oth. V. i. 117 .

knowing.text: (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. knowledge Tim. III. ii. 75 “in My ,” Ham. V. ii. 44 (Qq) “on the view and of these contents,” Cym. I. iv. 31 “gentlemen of your ,” II. iii. 102 .

knowingly.text: from experience All'sW. I. iii. 258 , Cym. III. iii. 46 .

knowledge.text: 1. notice Ham. II. i. 13 “Take you . . . some distant of him.”

la1.text: sixth note of the scale LLL. IV. ii. 104 , Lr. I. ii. 154 .

la2.text: exclamation used to introduce or accompany a conventional phrase or an address, or to call attention to an emphatic statement Wiv. I. i. 87 “I thank you always with my heart, la! with my heart,” H5 IV. vii. 151 “in my conscience, la!” ; also “La you!” = look you Tw.N. III. iv. 113 , Wint. II. iii. 50 ; repeated, as an expression of derision Tim. III. i. 23 “La, la, la, la! ‘nothing doubting,’ says he?.”

label1.text: slip of paper Cym. V. v. 431 ; slip of paper or parchment for appending a seal to a document (fig.) Rom. IV. i. 57 . ∥ The sense ‘codicil’ is represented in S. in the vb.

label2.text: to add as a ‘label’ or codicil Tw.N. I. v. 267 “every particle and utensil labelled to my will.”

labour1.text: trouble or pains taken Gent. II. i. 143 “take it for your ,” R2 V. vi. 41 , H5 III. vi. 170 “There's for thy labour.”

labour2.text: vb. (the ordinary uses are freq.) 1. to endeavour to bring about, work for or with a view to Ado V. i. 296 , Shr. I. i. 119 “to and effect one thing,” R3 I. iv. 256 “he would my delivery.”

laboured.text: 1. oppressed with labour John II. i. 232 .

labouring.text: heaving, palpitating 2H6 III. ii. 163 “the heart” ; rolling or pitching heavily Oth. II. i. 190 “the labouring bark.”

laboursome.text: laborious, elaborate Ham. I. ii. 59 “laboursome petition,” Cym. III. iv. 167 .

lace1.text: cord for fastening up the bodice, &c. Wint. III. ii. 174 “cut my lace,” 2H6 IV. ii. 50 .

lace2.text: to trim with ornamental (gold or silver) braid Ado III. iv. 20 “l-d with silver” ; fig. to streak or stripe “with” golden (or other) colour Rom. III. v. 8 “envious streaks Do the severing clouds,” Mac. II. iii. 119 “His silver skin l-'d with his golden blood,” Cym. II. ii. 22 “white and azure l-'d with blue of heaven's own tinct” ; to trick out, adorn Sonn. lxvii. 4 “That sin . . . should . . . itself with his society.”

lack.text: (1 survives in the gerund ‘lacking’) 1. to be wanting Tit. IV. ii. 44 “Here l-s but your mother for to say amen,” Ham. I. v. 186 “what so poor a man . . . May do . . . shall not ” ; Ham. I. iv. 3 “it l-s of twelve” (=is not yet twelve o'clock).

lade.text: to empty as by baling 3H6 III. ii. 139 .

lading.text: cargo Mer.V. III. i. 3 , Tit. I. i. 72 .

lady.text: (the Virgin Mary is usually called “our Lady,” occas. “God's lady” Rom. II. v. 63 ; see also BY'R LADY and LAKIN) 1. wife Wiv. III. iii. 54 , MND. II. i. 64 , 2H6 II. i. 177 , Cym. I. vi. 160 “A to the worthiest sir.”

lag1.text: lowest class Tim. III. vi. 91 (old edd. “leg(ge,” conj. “tag”†). ∥ ‘Lag’ is not found elsewhere with this meaning.

lag2.text: late R3 II. i. 91 “came too lag to see him buried;—lag of,” behind, later than Lr. I. ii. 6 .

lagging.text: tardy R2 I. iii. 214 “Four lagging winters.”

lakin.text: “by'r ”=BY'R LADY Tp. III. iii. 1 , MND. III. i. 14 .

lamb.headword: lamb and lambkin are used as terms of endearment
lamb.text: Troil. IV. iv. 23 , Rom. I. iii. 3 ; 2H4 V. iii. 119 .

lamentable.text: of sorrow John III. i. 22 “that rheum.”

lamp.text: (2 now only a slang sense) 1. torch Tp. IV. i. 23 “Hymen's lamps.”

lampass.text: disease incident to horses, consisting in a swelling of the fleshy lining of the roof of the mouth behind the front teeth Shr. III. ii. 53 .

land.text: applied to the human body John IV. ii. 245 “this fleshly ,” Lucr. 439 “the heart of all her ” ∥ In Tp. IV. i. 130 , LLL. V. ii. 310 “land” is taken by some to be LAUND, but it is to be noticed that in both passages it is used for the sake of rhyme (“command, hand”).

language.text: power of speech Tp. II. ii. 89 “here is that which will give to you, cat” ; ability to speak a foreign tongue All'sW. IV. i. 75 “I shall lose my life for want of language.”

languishing.text: pl. lingering disease All'sW. I. iii. 237 ; so the ppl. adj.=lingering Cym. I. v. 9 .

lank.text: to become shrunken (S.) Ant. I. iv. 71 .

lap.text: to wrap R3 II. i. 116 , Mac. I. ii. 55 “lapp'd in proof,” Cym. V. v. 361 .

lapse1.text: fall from rectitude All'sW. II. iii. 170 .

lapse2.text: vb. (not pre-S.; 2 there was a 17th cent. sense ‘to let slip’ of which this may be an early instance with inverted construction) 1. to fall into sin (by lying) Cor. V. ii. 19 , Cym. III. vi. 12 .

lapwing.text: peewit; always with allusion to its habits, e.g. its wiliness in drawing away a visitor from its nest, its supposed habit of running about when newly hatched with its head in the shell Meas. I. iv. 32 , Err. IV. ii. 27 , Ado III. i. 24 , Ham. V. ii. 193 .

lard.text: (orig. a cookery term) 1. to fatten 1H4 II. ii. 120 “l-s the lean earth,” Tim. IV. iii. 12 .

large.text: (for S. uses other than those given below the mod. synonyms would for the most part be ‘extensive,’ ‘far-reaching,’ or ‘wide,’ rather than ‘great,’ ‘big’) 1. liberal, generous, bountiful, lavish 2H6 I. i. 112 “whose large style Agrees not with the leanness of his purse,” IV. vii. 76 , Lr. I. i. 54 “our largest bounty.”

largely.text: bountifully, copiously, abundantly Wiv. II. ii. 211 , 2H4 I. iii. 12 , Per. I. iv. 53 ; at length, in full Ado V. iv. 69 “I'll tell you of fair Hero's death.”
