largess.text: liberal bestowal of gifts, free gift of money Shr. I. ii. 154 , H5 IV. Chor. 43 , Mac. II. i. 14 ; lavish expenditure R2 I. iv. 44 .

laroone.text: robber Wiv. I. iv. 71 . ∥ The French ‘larron’, which is found in the anglicized forms ‘laroun’ (14th cent.), ‘larroon’ and ‘laron’ (17th cent.).

larum.text: 1. call to arms, battle cry Shr. I. ii. 210 “in a pitched battle heard Loud larums,” Cor. I. iv. 9 .

lash.text: to scourge, castigate Err. II. i. 15 * “headstrong liberty is lash'd with woe.”

last.text: “last morning,” yesterday morning Gent. II. i. 88 ; “the last,” (1) the conclusion, end Tp. I. ii. 170 “hear the last of our sea-sorrow,” Cæs. III. ii. 12 “Be patient till the last,” Ant. V. ii. 336 “Bravest at the last” ; Mac. V. vii. 61 [ viii. 32 ] “try the last” * , (?) go to the utmost lengths of venture; (2) the last time (S.) All'sW. V. iii. 79 ; “at the last” (e.g. Shr. V. i. 130 ) in the same senses as “at last,” but less freq.; “in the last” (S.), in the end, finally Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 42; (one's) “last”=last time, last breath Tp. III. iii. 50 “I will stand to and feed, Although my last,” R2 II. i. 1 “breathe my last,” Tim. III. vi. 101 “This is Timon's last,” Compl. 168 ‘“It is thy last.”’

lasting.text: contextually=everlasting (freq.) Tp. V. i. 208 “set it down With gold on lasting pillars.”

latch.text: to catch Lr. II. i. 54 “With his prepared sword he . . . latch'd mine arm” (Qq “la(u)ncht”); to catch or receive the sight or sound of Mac. IV. iii. 195 “Where hearing should not them,” Sonn. cxiii. 6 “For it no form delivers to the heart Of bird, of flower, or shape, which it doth ” ; to catch and hold fast as by a charm or spell MND. III. ii. 36 “hast thou yet l-'d the Athenian's eyes With the lovejuice?.”

late1.text: adj. (the superlative “latest” usu. = last LLL. V. ii. 795 “Now, at the l-st minute of the hour,” 2H4 IV. v. 181 “the very l-st counsel That ever I shall breathe,” Oth. I. iii. 28 “To leave that latest which concerns him first” ; absol. Tim. IV. ii. 23 “The l-st of my wealth” ) 1. performed at a late hour H8 V. i. 13 .

late2.text: recently, of late, lately Tp. V. i. 113 “to abuse me, As I have been,” MND. V. i. 53 “ deceas'd,” Tw.N. V. i. 225 “but so ago,” R3 III. i. 99 “Too he died that might have kept that title,” Ant. IV. i. 13 “those that serv'd Mark Antony but ” ; with ppl. adjs. 1H4 II. iii. 64 “Like bubbles in a -disturbed stream,” 1H6 III. ii. 82 “this -betray'd town,” Tit. I. i. 184 “our -deceased emperor's sons,” Ven. 818 “Gazing upon a -embarked friend,” Lucr. 1740 “a late-sack'd island.”

lated.text: belated Mac. III. iii. 6 , Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 3

lath.text: as the material of a counterfeit weapon (see also DAGGER 2) Rom. I. iv. 5 “no Cupid . . . Bearing a Tartar's painted bow of lath” ; contemptuously = sword Tit. II. i. 41 “have your lath glued within your sheath Till you know better how to handle it.”

latten.text: mixed metal of yellow colour, identical with or closely resembling brass Wiv. I. i. 167 “ bilbo.”

latter.text: last H5 IV. i. 144 “at the day,” 1H6 II. v. 38 “in his bosom spend my gasp” ; also “ days, times, age, end.”

lattice.text: “red ,” window of lattice-work painted red (the sign of an alehouse) 2H4 II. ii. 88 .

laud.text: hymn Ham. IV. vii. 178 “snatches of old lauds” (Q1 Ff “tunes”).

laughter.text: subject for merriment 1H4 II. ii. 105 , Cæs. IV. iii. 49 , 113

laurel.text: wreathed with laurel Ant. I. iii. 100 “Upon your sword Sit laurel victory” (Ff2 3 4 “Lawrell'd”).

lave.text: Mac. III. ii. 33 “Must lave our honours in these flattering streams” (=‘must keep our royal dignities unsullied by flattering Banquo and those who are formidable to us’).

lavish.text: unrestrained, wild, licentious 2H4 IV. iv. 64 , Mac. I. ii. 58 .

lavolt.headword: lavolt Troil. IV. iv. 86 , lavolta H5 III. v. 33

law1.text: sb. (special uses are the foll.) 1. what the law awards 2H6 I. iii. 214 .

law2.text: =LA, LLL. V. ii. 415 “so God help me, law.”

lay1.text: wager 2H6 V. ii. 27 “My soul and body on the action both!—A dreadful lay!,” Oth. II. iii. 332 , Cym. I. iv. 164 .

lay2.text: vb. (4 only once in S., but common in literature from the 14th cent. and app. not regarded as a solecism in the 17th and 18th) 1. to bury Tw.N. II. iv. 52 “in sad cypress let me be laid,” H8 IV. ii. 22 “to lay his weary bones among ye,” Cym. IV. ii. 233 “where shall's lay him?.”

lazar.text: poor and diseased person, esp. a leper H5 I. i. 15 , Troil. II. iii. 37 , V. i. 73 “the louse of a ,” Ham. I. v. 72 “Most -like, with vile and loathsome crust” ;—adj. H5 II. i. 80 “the kite of Cressid's kind.”

lazy.text: sluggish MND. V. i. 41 “The time” ; Rom. II. ii. 31 “the -puffing clouds” (Q1 “lasie pacing,” mod. edd. “lazy-pacing,” Collier “-passing”†).

lead1.text: bullets, shot LLL. III. i. 60 , 65 , 1H4 V. iii. 35 .

lead2.text: (1 the orig. sense of the verb) 1. to carry All'sW. IV. iii. 300 “h'as led the drum before the English tragedians” ; fig. Mer.V. IV. i. 18 “That thou but lead'st this fashion of thy malice To the last hour of act,” Tw.N. I. v. 262 “lead these graces to the grave.”

leaden.text: “ mace,” attributed to the powers of sleep Cæs. IV. iii. 267 ; so MND. III. ii. 365 “sleep With legs” ; inert, spiritless 1H6 IV. vi. 12 “ age,” Ven. 34 “ appetite” ; depressing Oth. III. iv. 176 “I have . . . with leaden thoughts been press'”

leading.text: command H5 IV. iii. 130 , R3 V. iii. 298 ; direction Lucr. 436 , Cor. IV. v. 143 “The of thine own revenges” ; generalship 1H4 IV. iii. 17 “men of such great leading.”

league.text: alliance, amity, friendship, truce Wiv. III. ii. 26 “a between my good man and he,” Err. II. ii. 149 , MND. III. ii. 373 , John II. i. 417 “peace and fair-fac'd ,” R3 I. iii. 281 “In sign of and amity,” Tit. V. iii. 23 “For peace, for love, for league.”

leagued.text: applied to the folded arms Cym. IV. ii. 213 . ∥ Oth. II. iii. 220 “If partially affin'd, or leagu'd† in office” (Qq “partiality,” Qq Ff “league”).

lean1.text: poor, meagre, mean Err. III. ii. 93 “I have but lean luck,” Tw.N. III. iv. 380 “my lean and low ability,” Ant. II. ii. 19 “A leaner action” ; unfertile, barren 1H4 II. ii. 120 , 2H4 IV. iii. 129 ; scantily furnished 1H4 I. ii. 82 “no lean wardrobe.”

lean2.text: vb. (physical senses, trans. and intr., occur) 1. to rely or depend “on” Meas. II. i. 49 (quibble), 2H4 I. i. 164 [their] “lives . . . Lean on your health,” Troil. III. iii. 85 , Ham. IV. iii. 60 “every thing . . . That else leans on the affair.”

leap1.text: place to be leaped H8 V. i. 140 “You take a precipice for no leap of danger.”

leap2.text: 1. to be eager “to” do a thing Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 51 “Will leap to be his friend,” Per. V. iii. 45 .

learn.text: to teach (always with two objects or accusative and infin.) Tp. I. ii. 365 “For l-ing me your language,” Gent. II. vi. 13 “To his wit to exchange the bad for better,” Ham. V. ii. 9 “that should us There's a divinity that shapes our ends” (Ff “teach”), Oth. I. iii. 183 “do me How to respect you” ; (hence) to inform of something Troil. II. i. 22 “ me the proclamation.”

learned.text: (so the customary ‘my learned friend’) 1. instructed, educated, experienced, wise AYL. I. i. 176 “never schooled and yet ,” Tw.N. I. v. 281 , Cor. III. i. 98 , Oth. III. iii. 259 “knows all qualities, with a learned spirit, Of human dealings.”

learning.text: what is learnt:—(1) lesson, instruction Cym. I. i. 43 , Sonn. lxxvii. 4 “of this book this mayst thou taste” ; (2) information Ant. II. ii. 51 “I . . . have my from some true reports” ; (3) acquirement (S.) Ham. V. ii. 35 “I . . . labour'd much How to forget that learning.”

lease.text: “in ”=on a lease Sonn. xiii. 5 “that beauty which you hold in ;— of nature,” the term of the natural life Mac. IV. i. 99 “Macbeth Shall live the of nature.”

leash.text: three (the usual number of hounds coupled in one leash) 1H4 II. iv. 7 “a leash of drawers . . . as Tom, Dick, and Francis.”

leasing.text: lying Tw.N. I. v. 104 , Cor. V. ii. 22 .

least.text: “in the ,” (1) at the lowest estimate Lr. I. i. 194 ; (2) in the smallest degree II. iv. 143 .

leave1.text: sb. (1 also in phr. “by , under of, by your , with your leave, have leave.”) 1. permission Gent. II. iv. 25 “Give him ” (=make allowances for him), Err. I. i. 35 “I'll utter what my sorrow gives me ” (=allows), 3H6 III. ii. 34 “you will have leave” (=you will be free to do as you please), Ven. 568 “love, whose exceeds commission.”

leave2.text: vb. (the usual mod. senses are freq.) 1. to abandon, forsake, give up Gent. V. iv. 138 , Mer.V. V. i. 196 “how unwillingly I left the ring,” Cor. II. iii. 180 “now you have left your voices,” Ham. III. iv. 91 “such . . . grained spots As will not their tinct.”

leaven.text: “lay the on,” taint Cym. III. iv. 64 .

leavy.text: abounding in foliage Ado II. iii. 77 .

lecture.text: (old edd. also “lector,” a 16th-17th cent. form) 1. discourse given before an audience for the purpose of instruction Cor. II. iii. 243 “Say we read l-s to you, How youngly he began . . .”

leer1.text: complexion, countenance AYL. IV. i. 69 “a Rosalind of a better leer than you,” Tit. IV. ii. 120 “Here's a young lad fram'd of another leer.”

leer2.text: (not pre-S.): amorous side-glance Wiv. I. iii. 48 .

lees.text: construed as a sing. Mac. II. iii. 102 .

leet.text: special court of record which the lords of certain manors were empowered to hold yearly or half-yearly Shr. Ind. ii. 89 “present her at the , Because she brought stone jugs and no seal'd quarts” ; used with tautology in Oth. III. iii. 140 “Keep leets and law days,” cf. ‘The Leete and Law day is al one’ (Sir T. Smith's Common wealth of England, 1589 ).

leg.text: obeisance made by drawing back one leg and bending the other All'sW. II. ii. 11 , 1H4 II. iv. 432 “here is my leg,” Cor. II. i. 78 “caps and legs,” Tim. I. ii. 241 .

lege.headword: lege [aphetic form of ‘allege’ in use 14th-16th cent.]
lege.text: to bring forward Shr. I. ii. 28 .

legend.text: misused for ‘legion’ Wiv. I. iii. 57 . (Ff Q3 “a legend,” Q1 “legians,” Q2 “legions”).

legion.text: host, military or otherwise, esp. of devils; in Tw.N. III. iv. 97 “If all the devils in hell be drawn in little, and Legion himself possess'd him,” the ref. is to Mark v. 9 ‘their name is Legion’.

leisure.text: (the now somewhat archaic sense of ‘opportunity’ is freq.; 3 cf. Greek σχολῇ ; in H8 III. ii. 141 “spiritual ” =‘time withdrawn from earthly business and devoted to religious duties’) 1. pl.=leisure moments Compl. 193 .

leman.text: sweetheart Tw.N. II. iii. 27 , 2H4 V. iii. 47 ; paramour Wiv. IV. ii. 175 .

lend.text: to hold out (a hand) to be taken Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 74 “ me thy hand, I'll help thee,” Tit. III. i. 187 .

lendings.text: (2 a 16th-17th cent. use; ‘Succors or lendings which they giue souldiers where there is no paie, and when the paie comes they take it off,’ Minsheu, 1599) 1. non-essential appurtenances Lr. III. iv. 112 .

length1.text: sb. (1 rare outside S.; 5 common Eliz.) 1. “of ,” long R2 IV. i. 11 “Is not my arm of ,” Troil. I. iii. 136 “To end a tale of length.”

lenten.text: meagre, scanty Tw.N. I. v. 9 “A good answer,” Ham. II. ii. 337 [ 329 ] “what entertainment; — pie,” pie containing no meat Rom. II. iv. 142 .

less.text: “less in,” inferior in point of R2 II. iii. 15 , R3 IV. iv. 300 , Ant. V. ii. 363 ; “nothing less than,” (1) the same thing as 1H6 II. v. 100 “my father's execution Was nothing less than bloody tyranny” ; (2) anything but R2 II. ii. 34 “'Tis nothing but conceit, my gracious lady.—'Tis nothing less.” ∥ Used peculiarly by S. with words expressing or implying a negative, where the sense requires ‘more’ Wint. III. ii. 57 , Cor. I. iv. 14 , Cym. I. iv. 24 ; similarly lesser in Troil. I. i. 30 .

lesson.text: musical piece or exercise Shr. III. i. 61 “My lessons make no music in three parts.”

let2.text: vb. (the other vb. “let” ‘to hinder’ occurs) 1. to allow to remain Wint. I. ii. 41 .

letter.text: (2 ‘hunt the letter’, ‘lick the letter’ were other Eliz. phrases) 1. “no letter,” not a word Cym. IV. iii. 36 .

level.text: vb. (2 is transf. from the sense of ‘aim’, which is the most freq. S. sense, lit. and fig.) 1. “level with,” be on a par with Oth. I. iii. 240 .

level1.text: sb. (2 only in fig. phrases) 1. “hold. . .level with,” be on an equality with 1H4 III. ii. 17 .

level2.text: adj. (used literally only once 2H4 III. i. 47 ) 1. “level to,” readily accessible to 2H4 IV. iv. 7 .

levy.text: app. misused for LEVEL = aim Per. II. v. 52 “Never did thought of mine levy offence.” ∥ There are other instances of this misuse in the 17th cent.

lewd.text: bad, vile, worthless (once a common sense) Ado V. i. 348 [ 341 ] “this fellow,” Shr. IV. iii. 65 “'tis and filthy,” 1H4 III. ii. 13 “such , such mean attempts,” R3 I. iii. 61 “ complaints” ; so lewdly, wickedly 2H6 II. i. 165 “naughty persons, bent” ; lewdness, wickedness H8 I. iii. 35 .

liable.text: 1. “ to,” (i) subject the influence or operation of Cæs. I. ii. 198 “if my name” (=I) “were to fear,” Per. IV. vi. 183 ; (ii) subject or subservient to John II. i. 490 , V. ii. 101 “such as to my claim are ,” Cæs. II. ii. 104 .

libbard.text: old form of ‘leopard’ LLL. V. ii. 549 “With l-'s head on knee.” ∥ Cf. ‘A Libbards head (on the knees or elbowes of old fashioned garments)’, Sherwood, 1632

libel1.text: defamatory bill or pamphlet R3 I. i. 33 .

libel2.text: to make libellous statements Tit. IV. iv. 17 .

liberal.text: (the most freq. sense is ‘bountiful, generous’) 1. the distinctive epithet of those arts and sciences which were deemed worthy of a free man Tp. I. ii. 73 .

libertine.text: one who follows his own inclinations H5 I. i. 48 “The air, a charter'd libertine.”

liberty.text: （“the ” in Ham. II. ii. 430 [ 421 ] is of doubtful meaning) 1. “the of,” unrestricted access to Meas. IV. ii. 155 .

licence1.text: leave, permission Meas. II. iv. 146 , H5 IV. vii. 75 , 2H6 IV. iii. 8 , Ham. IV. iv. 2 .

licentious.text: unrestrained by law or morality Tim. V. iv. 4 “you have . . . fill'd the time With all measure.”

lictor.text: official who attended upon a Roman magistrate, kind of beadle Ant. V. ii. 213 .

lie.text: (pa. pple. “lain” 5 times, “lien” twice; Ham. V. i. 189 Qq “lyen,” Ff “lain”; Per. III. ii. 85 Qq1-3 “lien,” Ff3 4 “been”) 1. to be or remain in bed asleep Troil. IV. i. 3 “to lie long,” Mac. II. iii. 26 “lie so late.”

lief.text: dear 2H6 III. i. 164 “My liefest liege” ; otherwise only in phr. “had as lief” (old edd. also “lieve”).

liege.text: only in the sense ‘sovereign lord, superior to whom allegiance is due’; fig. LLL. III. i. 193 [ 185 ].

liegeman.text: vassal, subject Wint. II. iii. 173 , 1H4 II. iv. 377 “that . . . swore the devil his true ,” Ham. I. i. 15 .

lieutenantry.text: lieutenancy Oth. II. i. 174 “If such tricks as these strip you out of your ;—on ,” by deputy Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 39

life.text: (for “o' life”† Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 263 see A-LIFE; 7 is recorded first from S.) 1. “of life,” living Sonn. xvi. 9 .

lifeless.text: obscure use in Err. I. i. 158 (“luckless†, life's last†”).

lifelings.text: in a trivial oath “Od's ” Tw.N. V. i. 188 .

light1.headword: light sb. (“put out” a person's “light” is not pre-S.) 1. in asseverations
light1.text: —“by this ” (freq.), “God's ” (cf. 'SLIGHT) Tp. II. ii. 155 [ 147 ], 162 [ 154 ], 1H4 III. iii. 71 , H5 IV. viii. 66 .

light2.text: adj. (quibbles are frequent) 1. unimportant, slight, trivial Tp. I. ii. 449 “Make the prize ,” MND. III. ii. 133 “as as tales,” H5 II. ii. 89 “for a few crowns;—hold, set ,” account of small value R2 I. iii. 293 , Oth. II. iii. 176 .

light3.text: to fall, descend (lit. and fig.); pa. pple. usu. “lighted,” once “light” Per. IV. ii. 77 .

light4.text: to grow light 1H4 III. ii. 138 “the day, whene'er it l-s” ; to shine Troil. I. i. 39 “as when the sun doth a-scorn” (mod. edd. “a storm”†).

lighten.text: to enlighten 2H4 II. i. 212 “the Lord thee.”

lightly.text: (5 current from 14th to 17th cent.) 1. to no great amount LLL. I. ii. 159 “but rewarded” ; in a slight degree R3 I. iii. 45 “they love his Grace but lightly.”

like.text: vb. 1 (1 the commonest S. sense) 1. to please Gent. IV. ii. 56 “the music l-s you not,” Troil. V. ii. 99 “that that l-s not you” (Q) “Pleases me best”; esp. in conventional phr. Tp. IV. i. 242 “an't like your grace,” H8 I. i. 100 “Like it your Grace,” Cym. II. iii. 59 “So like you, sir.”

like1.text: adj. (uses now mainly dial. are) 1. in accordance with appearances, probable, likely Meas. V. i. 105 “O, that it were as as it is true!,” Shr. III. ii. 216 “'Tis like you'll prove a jolly surly groom,” Rom. IV. iii. 46 “is it not like that I . . .?.”

like2.text: adv. (the use in “like as”=even as, e.g. Sonn. lx. 1 , gives rise by ellipsis to “like” conj., as in Per. I. i. 163 , where Ff read “as”) 1. equally, similarly, alike Tp. III. iii. 66 “my fellowministers Are invulnerable,” Err. I. i. 82 , H5 II. ii. 183 , Cym. III. iii. 41 “Like war-like as the wolf,” Sonn. cxxxii. 12 “suit thy pity like in every part.”

likelihood.text: (2 common 16th-17th cent.) 1. probability H5 v. Chor. 29, R3 I. iii. 33 ; “by all ” in all probability Shr. V. i. 14 , Cym. I. iv. 57 .

likely.text: comely, handsome Mer.V. II. ix. 92 , 2H4 III. ii. 188 “a likely fellow.”

liking.text: (good) bodily condition Wiv. II. i. 57 “men's liking,” 1H4 III. iii. 6 “while I am in some liking.”

limb.text: fig. member 2H4 V. ii. 135 , H8 I. i. 220 “the l-s o' the plot” ; H8 V. iv. 68 “Limbs of Limehouse,” used partly for alliteration, partly as a variation of ‘limb of Satan’.

limbeck.text: alembic, still Mac. I. vii. 67 , Sonn. cxix. 2 .

limbo.text: (properly) abode of the just who died before Christ's coming (‘Limbo patrum’) or of infants who have died unbaptized (‘Limbo infantum’); used vaguely=Hell, All'sW. V. iii. 264 , Tit. III. i. 150 “As far from help as is from bliss” ; transf. prison Err. IV. ii. 32 “in Tartar ,” H8 V. iv. 69 “I have some of 'em in Limbo Patrum.”

lime.text: (2 usually fig.) 1. to cement 3H6 V. i. 84 “to lime the stones together.”

limit1.text: 1. prescribed time or period Meas. III. i. 223 “the . . . of the solemnity,” R2 I. iii. 151 “The dateless of thy dear exile,” R3 III. iii. 7 “the of your lives is out;” period of rest after child-bearing Wint. III. ii. 107 “before I have got strength of limit.”

limit2.text: to appoint (a time) Meas. IV. ii. 175 , Err. I. i. 150 ; to appoint (a person) to an office R3 V. iii. 25 “Limit each leader to his several charge.”

limited.text: appointed Mac. II. iii. 58 “'tis my service” ; restricted Tim. IV. iii. 434 * “limited professions.”

limn.text: to paint AYL. II. vii. 197 , Ven. 290 .

line.text: to strengthen, reinforce, fortify John II. i. 352 , 1H4 II. iii. 88 “To line his enterprise,” H5 II. iv. 7 , Mac. I. iii. 112 “line the rebel With hidden help.”

line1.text: sb. 1 (1 metaphor from angling; 7 only S.) 1. “give ,” allow full play or scope Wint. I. ii. 181 , 2H4 IV. iv. 39 ; so “with full line” Meas. I. iv. 56 .

line2.text: (?) lime-tree Tp. IV. i. 193 * , 237 * . ∥ This form, a 16th-17th cent. variant of ‘lind’=linden, is older than ‘lime’ (first in the 17th cent.). Cf. LINE-GROVE.

lineal.text: lineally descended (from) H5 I. ii. 82 ; due by right of descent John II. i. 85 .

linen.text: used as adj.=white Mac. V. iii. 16 “ cheeks.”

ling1.text: fish of the cod kind; “old ling,” salted ling All'sW. III. ii. 14 .

ling2.text: heather Tp. I. i. 71 “ling†, heath, broom†, furze” (F1 “Long heath, Browne firrs”).

linger.text: to prolong, draw out R2 II. ii. 72 , Oth. IV. ii. 231 ; with “on, out” 2H4 I. ii. 270 , H5 II. Chor. 31 “ your patience on,” Troil. V. x. 9 , Sonn. xc. 8 ; to delay MND. I. i. 4 .

lingering.text: (of poison, &c.) slow Wint. I. ii. 320 “with a dram,” Ant. II. v. 66 “Smarting in pickle.”

link.text: torch 1H4 III. iii. 48 ; (?) material of ‘links’ used as blacking Shr. IV. i. 137 “no link to colour Peter's hat.”

lion.text: borne heraldically LLL. V. ii. 577 , 1H6 I. v. 28 .

lip1.text: “falling a lip of contempt,” expressing contempt by a movement of the lip Wint. I. ii. 373 ; “make a lip at,” make a contemptuous face at Cor. II. i. 129 .

lip2.text: to kiss Oth. IV. i. 72 , Ant. II. v. 30 .

liquor1.text: “grand ,” grand elixir of life Tp. V. i. 280 .

liquor2.text: to dress with oil or grease Wiv. IV. v. 101 “liquor fishermen's boots,” 1H4 II. i. 94 .

liquorish.text: pleasant, sweet Tim. IV. iii. 195 “ draughts” (Ff1 2 “Licourish,” Ff3 4 “Liquorish”).

list.text: spec. catalogue of the soldiers of a force Ham. I. i. 98 , I. ii. 32 “the levies, The lists,” Lr. V. iii. 112 “within the lists of the army,” Ant. III. vi. 76 (cf. line 67 “levying The kings o' the earth for war”); also gen. catalogue H8 IV. i. 14 “the list Of those that claim their offices this day.”

list1.text: 1. selvage of cloth Meas. I. ii. 32 , 35

list2.text: desire Oth. II. i. 104 (Q1; Qq23 Ff “leaue”).

listen.text: to endeavour to hear of 2H4 I. i. 29 “to after news,” 2H6 I. iii. 152 “ after Humphrey.”

lither.text: yielding 1H6 IV. vii. 21 “the sky.” ∥ ‘Lither air’ is used by Golding 1567

litter.text: to bring forth (contemptuously of human beings) Tp. I. ii. 282 , Cor. III. i. 238 .

little.text: （“littlest” once in Ham. III. ii. 183 ) 1. adj.=a little Tw.N. V. i. 175 , 2H4 III. i. 43 .

livelihood.text: animation, life All'sW. I. i. 59 “takes all from her cheek,” R3 III. iv. 55 (Ff “liuelyhood,” Qq “likelihood”), Ven. 26 “The precedent of pith and ”

lively1.text: 1. living, animate Tit. III. i. 106 “thy body,” V. iii. 44 , Sonn. lxvii. 10 “lively veins.”

lively2.text: ‘to the life’ Gent. IV. iv. 176 “Which I so acted,” Tim. V. i. 87 “Thou counterfeit'st most ”

liver.text: supposed seat of love and violent passion Ado IV. i. 233 “If ever love had interest in his ,” Tw.N. I. i. 37 “, brain, and heart, These sovereign thrones;—white” or “pale ,” symbolical of cowardice Mer.V. III. ii. 86 , Troil. II. ii. 50 ; cf. Tw.N. III. ii. 69 , and LILY-LIVER'D, MILK-LIVERED.

livery1.text: legal delivery of property into one's possession; only in “sue” one's “,” to institute a suit as heir to obtain possession of lands which are in the hands of the court of wards R2 II. i. 205 , II. iii. 129 , 1H4 IV. iii. 62 .

livery2.text: to array in a livery (fig.) Compl. 105 “Did livery falseness in a pride of truth.”

living2.text: 1. during one's life or lifetime, while one is or was alive Gent. III. i. 170 “death rather than torment,” R2 V. i. 39 “my last leave,” H8 IV. ii. 70 “my actions,” Sonn. lxvii. 6 “his hue” ; so “ death” R3 I. ii. 153 , Lucr. 726 .

lo.text: with 2nd personal pron. (cf. O. Fr. ‘es vos’) Wint. I. ii. 106 “lo you now,” Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 87 “Lo thee!.”

loathed.text: loathsome (cf. DESPISED) R3 I. iii. 232 , Rom. III. v. 31 .

loathly.text: with abhorrence Lr. II. i. 51 “ opposite.”

lob2.text: to hang heavily, droop H5 IV. ii. 47 .

lock.text: lovelock Ado III. iii. 181 “a' wears a lock.”

lockram.text: linen fabric Cor. II. i. 228 “Her richest ”

lodge.text: (1 Eliz. sense; 2 not pre-S.) 1. to harbour, entertain (feelings) Wint. II. i. 110 , 2H4 IV. v. 206 “lodge a fear,” R3 II. i. 65 .

lodging.text: (formerly of much wider use than now) 1. accommodation for rest at night or for residence LLL. V. ii. 809 “hard lodging,” H5 IV. i. 16 .

loffe.text: rare form of ‘laugh’ in old edd. of MND. II. i. 55 (rhyming with “coffe”).

long.text: phr. “before” or “ere it be long,” before long, shortly Meas. IV. ii. 79 , 1H6 III. ii. 75 , 3H6 III. iii. 232 ; “think ,” grow weary or impatient Rom. IV. v. 41 , Lucr. 1359 “ she thinks till he return again” :— adv. after a long time Shr. V. ii. 1 “At last, though ”

long1.text: “long of,” owing to, on account of LLL. II. i. 118 , 1H6 IV. iii. 33 , Cor. V. iv. 33 .

long2.text: to desire earnestly (with clause) Err. IV. iv. 152 “I long that we were safe and sound aboard” ;=‘thing long’ (see LONG adj. 1 ) 3H6 III. iii. 254 “I long till Edward fall by war's mischance.”

longing.text: prompted by strong desire Gent. II. vii. 85 “my journey,” Pilgr. vi. 4 [ 74 ] “A tarriance.”

longly.text: for a long while Shr. I. i. 169 .

loof.text: old form of ‘luff’, to bring the head of (a vessel) nearer to the wind Ant. III. viii. 27 [ x. 18 ].

look1.text: “have a of,” be looked at by Gent.II.IV. 109

look2.text: vb. (obs. and idiomatic uses are) 1. to take care, see Tp. IV. i. 51 “ thou be true,” R3 III. iv. 77 “ that it be done,” Oth. IV. iii. 9 “look it be done.”

loop1.text: (app.) part of a hinge Oth. III. iii. 366 “no hinge nor To hang a doubt on.” ∥ A north-country sense.

loop2.text: loop-hole, opening 1H4 IV. i. 71 “all sightholes, every loop.”

looped.text: having loop-holes Lr. III. iv. 31 “Your and window'd raggedness” (Qq “loopt”; Ff “lop'd”). ∥ A different word from ‘looped’=arranged or made up in loops, which is not S.

loose.text: lit. discharge of an arrow; hence fig. phr. “at his” [i.e. time's] “very ,” at the last moment LLL. V. ii. 750 .

loose1.text: adj. (1 cf. ‘Mosquettiers . . . are not be imployed as loose shot in skirmishes’, Sir J. Smyth, 1590) 1. “loose shot,” marksmen not attached to a company H8 V. iv. 60 .

loose2.text: 1. to unjoin hands Tit. II. iii. 243 “Thy hand once more; I will not loose again.”

loosen.text: to make a breach between (S.) Lr. V. i. 19 .

lop.text: smaller branches and twigs H8 I. ii. 96 .

lorded.text: raised to the position of a lord Tp. I. ii. 97 .

lording.text: 1. lord Sonn. Music 1 [ Pilgr. 211 ]; pl.=Sirs! 2H6 I. i. 146 .

lordliness.text: lordly state or office Ant. V. ii. 160 .

lordship.text: authority of a husband MND. I. i. 81 , All'sW. V. iii. 157 .

lose.text: (in old edd. freq. spelt “loose”) 1. to destroy, ruin 1H4 I. iii. 88 , H8 III. i. 106 , Ham. III. ii. 207 “What to ourselves in passion we propose, The passion ending, doth the purpose lose,” Cym. II. iv. 59 “gains or loses Your sword or mine” ; to ruin in estimation Lr. I. i. 236 “Hath lost me in your liking.” See also LOST.

losing.text: resulting in loss Mer.V. IV. i. 62 “A suit,” 2H4 I. i. 101 “a office,” Cæs. V. v. 36 “this day.”

loss.text: (2 cf. ‘vp peyne of los of lyf’, Chaucer; in Tw.N. V. i. 62 “the tongue of ” =‘the report of the losers’, Wright). 1. perdition, ruin, destruction All'sW. III. ii. 44 , Lr. III. vi. 104 “his life, With thine . . . Stand in assured loss,” Ant. IV. x. 42 [ xii. 29 ]; probably also in Wint. II. iii. 191 * , H8 II. ii. 31 * .

lost.text: 1. brought to destruction or death, perished All'sW. I. iii. 238 , Wint. V. iii. 135 , H8 IV. i. 96 “that title's lost” Mac. I. iii. 24 .

lot.text: prize in a lottery; allusive phr. “lots to blanks,” a thousand to one Cor. V. ii. 10 .

lottery.text: (2 is S. only) 1. decision by casting lots Troil. II. i. 140 ; “by ,” by chance Cæs. II. i. 119 .

loud.text: (2 and 3 are S. only) 1. full of noise John V. iv. 14 “this loud day.”

louse.text: to be infested with lice (S.) Lr. III. ii. 29 .

lousy.text: only fig.=‘scurvy’, contemptible; in 2H6 IV. i. 50 Ff “lowsie,” Qq “lowly.”

love1.text: sb. (3 an Eliz. sense) 1. act of kindness John IV. i. 49 , Per. II. iv. 49 .

love2.text: to love one another AYL. I. i. 120 , 2H6 IV. vii. 138 , Cæs. IV. iii. 130 “Love, and be friends,” Ant. I. iii. 88 .

lovely1.text: amorous, loving Shr. III. ii. 126 “a kiss,” Pilgr. iv. 3 [ 44 ] “many a lovely look.”

lovely2.text: lovably, beautifully 1H4 III. i. 124 , Oth. IV. ii. 67 “Who art so lovely fair.”

lover.text: (obs. or archaic uses are) 1. friend, well-wisher Mer.V. III. iv. 17 , H8 IV. i. 104 , Cor. V. ii. 14 “Thy general is my lover,” Cæs. III. ii. 13 .

loving.text: of love AYL. V. iv. 198 “thy voyage,” Lucr. 480 “my tale” ; H5 v. Chor. 29 “by a lower but likelihood” (‘one which the love of the people leads them to dwell on’, Wright). ∥ The usu. sense is ‘affectionate’, ‘friendly’.

low1.text: adj. (see also LOWER) 1. short, not tall Ado I. i. 179 , MND. III. ii. 295 “so dwarfish and so low,” AYL. IV. iii. 89 .

low2.text: poorly, on poor diet 1H4 I. iii. 167 .

lower.text: “ chair,” (?) easy chair Meas. II. i. 137 ; “the” or “this world” (not pre-S.), the earth Tp. III. iii. 54 , R2 III. ii. 38 .

lowliness.text: low or mean condition LLL. IV. i. 81 , H5 IV. viii. 55 .

lowness.text: abasement Lr. III. iv. 70 ; baseness Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 63

loyal.text: legitimate Lr. II. i. 86 “ and natural boy.”

lozel.text: worthless fellow, rascal Wint. II. iii. 108 .

lubber.text: clumsy stupid fellow, lout Gent. II. v. 47 , Lr. I. iv. 101 “If you will measure your l-'s length again.”

lubberly.text: loutish Wiv. V. v. 202 [ 195 ] “a great boy.”

luce.text: pike, as a heraldic bearing Wiv. I. i. 16 .

lucre.text: acquisition or gain (of something) 1H6 V. iv. 141 “for lucre of the rest unvanquish'”

luggage.text: heavy stuff to be carried, lumber Tp. IV. i. 233 , V. i. 298 , 1H4 V. iv. 160 ; baggage of an army H5 IV. iv. 80 , IV. vii. 1 .

lull.text: old form of ‘loll’ R3 III. vii. 71 .

lullaby.text: good-night, farewell Tw.N. V. i. 48 , Sonn. Music i. 15 [ Pilgr. 225 ].

lump.text: used with ref. to the piece of clay taken up by a potter or sculptor for one operation H8 II. ii. 49 “Lie like one before him, to be fashion'd” . . .

lunes.text: fits of frenzy or lunacy, mad freaks Wint. II. ii. 30 “These . . . unsafe lunes i' the king” ; in mod. edd. for “lines” (see LINE sb. 1 7) in Wiv. IV. ii. 22 , Troil. II. iii. 140 , and for “lunacies” (Qq “browes” ? misprint) in Ham. III. iii. 7 .

lurch.text: (both were common 16th-17th cent. uses) 1. to lurk about with evil design Wiv. II. ii. 27 “to shuffle, to hedge, and to lurch.”

lure1.text: apparatus used by falconers to recall their hawks, ‘being made of feathers and leather in such wise that in the motion it looks not vnlike a fowle’ (Latham, 1615) Shr. IV. i. 195 “she never looks upon her ,” Ven. 1027 “As falcon to the lure.”

lure2.text: to recall (a hawk) to the lure Rom. II. ii. 159 “To lure this tassel-gentle back again.”

lush.text: succulent and luxuriant Tp. II. i. 55 . ∥ The literary currency of this sense is due to S.

lust.text: (neither sense survived the 17th cent.) 1. pleasure, delight Tim. IV. iii. 494 , Lucr. 1384 “Gazing upon the Greeks with little lust.”

lustihood.text: bodily vigour Ado V. i. 76 , Troil. II. ii. 50 .

lusty.text: (the main sense is ‘vigorous’; often a vague epithet, so that it is difficult to say how far sense 1 and the common Eliz. meaning of ‘pleasing, pleasant’ are represented in S.; 2 was in use from Chaucer to Dryden) 1. merry AYL. IV. ii. 17 “the lusty horn,” John I. i. 108 “this same lusty gentleman.”

lute.text: stringed musical instrument, in vogue 14th17th cent.; “-case” H5 III.ii.47, “-string” Ado III.ii. 61

luxurious.text: lascivious, lustful Ado IV. i. 41 , H5 IV. iv. 20 ; so luxuriously Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 120

luxury.text: lasciviousness, lust Wiv. V. v. 100 , Ham. I. v. 83 .

lym.text: rare form of ‘lyam’ in the sense of ‘lyamhound’= bloodhound, proposed by Hanmer in Lr. III. vi. 72 (Qq “him,” Ff “Hym”).

mace.text: staff of office carried by a sergeant Err. IV. iii. 27 ; attributed to sleep Cæs. IV. iii. 267 “O murderous slumber! Lay'st thou thy leaden mace upon my boy?” (i.e. as if arresting him); sceptre of sovereignty H5 IV. i. 281 , 2H6 IV. vii. 143 .

machine.text: bodily frame (not pre-S.) Ham. II. ii. 123 .

maculation.text: stain of impurity Troil. IV. iv. 64 .

mad.text: to make mad, madden (freq.); to be mad 2H6 III. ii. 117 “madding Dido.”

madonna.text: Italian form of address=my lady, madam Tw.N. I. v. 46 , &c.

madrigal.text: properly, (1) short lyrical poem, (2) kind of part-song forming a musical setting to such poems; hence gen., song, ditty Wiv. III. i. 18 “Melodious birds sing madrigals.”

magnanimous.text: great in courage, nobly valiant All'sW. III. vi. 69 , 2H4 III. ii. 173 “most mouse,” H5 III. vi. 6 “as as Agamemnon,” Troil. II. ii. 200 “valiant and magnanimous deeds.”

magnifico.text: title given to the magnates of Venice Mer.V. III. ii. 281 , Oth. I. ii. 12 .

maiden.text: very freq. as adj.=(1) virgin 1H6 IV. vii. 38 “Thou youth” ; (2) belonging to or befitting a maiden Tw.N. V. i. 265 “my weeds,” 1H6 II. iv. 47 “this pale and blossom,” V. iv. 52 , H8 IV. ii. 170 “strew me over With flowers,” Rom. II. ii. 86 “a blush” ; (3) of a fortress, &c., that has never been taken Lucr. 408 ; (4) untried in warfare or bloodshed, (hence) innocent, bloodless John IV. ii. 252 “a maiden and an innocent hand,” 1H4 V. iv. 133 “flesh'd Thy sword,” Troil. IV. v. 87 “A battle.”

maidhood.text: maidenhood Tw.N. III. i. 164 , Oth. I. i. 173 .

mail.text: piece of mail-armour Troil. III. iii. 152 .

mailed.text: wrapped up, enveloped 2H6 II. iv. 31 “Mail'd up in shame, with papers on my back.”

maim.text: mutilation or mutilating wound, (hence fig.) grave defect or disablement R2 I. iii. 156 , 1H4 IV. i. 42 “Your father's sickness is a to us,” 2H6 II. iii. 41 , Cor. IV. v. 92 .

main.text: adj. (6 is the commonest S. sense) 1. exerted to the full, overpowering 2H6 I. i. 211 “by main force,” H8 II. ii. 7 “main power.”

main1.text: sb. 1 (the orig. sense of ‘strength’ is probably represented in Troil. II. iii. 276 “with all our main of power” ) 1. chief or main part, main body (“of” something) Mer.V. V. i. 97 “Empties itself, as doth an inland brook Into the main of waters,” Ham. IV. iv. 15 “against the main of Poland.”

main2.text: in the game of hazard, a number (from five to nine inclusive) called by the ‘caster’ before the dice are thrown; only fig. (cf. MAIN CHANCE) 1H4 IV. i. 47 “to set so rich a main On the nice hazard of one doubtful hour,” 2H6 I. i. 209 “look unto the main” (=the most important thing at stake).

mainly.text: forcibly, violently 1H4 II. iv. 226 “ thrust at me” ; greatly, very much Ham. IV. vii. 9 ; “so ,” so much Troil. IV. iv. 85 ; entirely, perfectly Lr. IV. vii. 65 “ ignorant What place this is.”

maintain.text: (the less freq. uses are the foll.) 1. to carry on (conversation) Ado IV. i. 185 , Tw.N. IV. ii. 109 “Maintain no words with him.”

major.text: adj. greater Cor. II. i. 66 “the part” ; paramount to all other claims Troil. V. i. 49 “My major vow lies here” ;—sb. major premiss of a syllogism 1H4 II. iv. 552 [ 544 ] “I deny your major.”

make1.text: mate, husband or wife Lr. IV. iii. 36 “one self mate and make” (Q1; the rest “mate”).

make2.text: vb. (6 always coupled with “meddle”) 1. to give (a dinner, &c.) H8 I. iii. 52 .

making.text: (2 not pre-S.) 1. form, shape, build, make Err. IV. ii. 22 , MND. II. i. 32 .

malapert.text: impudent, saucy Tw.N. IV. i. 48 , R3 I. iii. 255 .

malcontent.text: the usual 16th-17th cent. form is “malecontent” 3H6 IV. i. 10 , 60 (F1). [ 621 ].

malevolent.text: (of a star) exercising a baleful influence (fig.) 1H4 I. i. 97 (cf. ASPECT).

malice.text: (1 and 2 in use late 14th to late 17th c.) 1. power to harm John II. i. 251 “Our cannons' ”

malicious.text: violent John II. i. 314 “this hot day.”

maliciously.text: violently Wint. I. ii. 321 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 178 “fight maliciously.”

malign.text: to regard with hatred or envy Cor. I. i. 119 “you malign our senators,” Per. V. i. 90 .

malignant.text: (3 orig. astrological; the mod. sense occurs thrice Tp. I. ii. 257 , R3 II. ii. 52 , H8 I. ii. 141 ) 1. rebellious against God Oth. V. ii. 352 * .

malkin.text: untidy female servant, slut Cor. II. i. 227 , Per. IV. iii. 34 . ∥ A diminutive of ‘Malde’= Maud, Matilda; it occurs in GRAYMALKIN.

mammer.text: orig. to stammer, mutter, (hence) to waver Oth. III. iii. 70 (Q1 “muttering”).

mammet.text: doll, puppet 1H4 II. iii. 97 , Rom. III. v. 186 .

mammock.text: to break into fragments Cor. I. iii. 71 “O! I warrant, how he mammocked it.”

man1.text: “Since I was man,” since I was born Lr. III. ii. 45 ; “I write man,” I am entitled by my years to call myself a man All'sW. II. iii. 207 ; 2H6 IV. ii. 94 “I was never mine own man since” =what I used to be; Tp. V. i. 213 “no man was his own” =in his senses.

man2.text: vb. (in Oth. V. ii. 269 “Man but a rush against Othello's breast,” the metaphor may be from the manning of a gun) 1. to provide (one) with attendants 2H4 I. ii. 18 “I was never manned with an agate till now,” 59

manage1.text: sb. (1 used both lit. and fig.) 1. training of a horse in its paces R2 III. iii. 179 “the of unruly jades,” 1H4 II. iii. 54 “terms of ,” H8 V. iii. 24 “spur 'em, Till they obey the ,” Per. IV. vi. 70 , Compl. 112 .

manage2.text: vb. (in Ven. 598 there is probably a ref. to the technical sense of training a horse) 1. to handle, wield Gent. III. i. 248 , R2 III. ii. 118 “ rusty bills,” Rom. I. i. 75 ; fig. Lr. I. iii. 18 .

manager.text: wielder (of a weapon, &c.) LLL. I. ii. 191 “rust, rapier! be still, drum! for your is in love.”

mandrake.text: poisonous plant of the genus Mandragora, native to Southern Europe and the East, having emetic and narcotic properties; its forked root is thought to resemble the human form and was fabled to utter a shriek when pulled up 2H6 III. ii. 310 “the m-'s groan,” Rom. IV. iii. 48 “shrieks like m-s torn out of the earth” ; as a term of abuse 2H4 I. ii. 16 , III. ii. 342 .

mane.text: applied to the crests of waves Oth. II. i. 13 .

manhood.text: condition of being a man; as opposed to ‘childhood’ R3 IV. iv. 171 , Mac. V. ii. 11 ; as opposed to womanhood Cym. III. iv. 195 . ∥ The prevailing sense is ‘manliness, courage, valour’.

mankind.text: sb. stressed “ma'nkind” and “manki'nd” (6 out of 8 passages in Tim.) in both senses ‘human race’ and ‘male sex’;—adj. masculine, viragolike Wint. II. iii. 67 “A ma'nkind witch!,” Cor. IV. ii. 16 “Are you ma'nkind?.”

manly.text: gallantly, bravely (S.) Mac. IV. iii. 234 “This time” (Rowe “tune”†） “goes manly.”

manner1.text: 1. usage, custom, fashion, e.g. Meas. IV. ii. 138 “it was ever his to do so” ; Ham. I. iv. 15 “to the born” destined by birth to be subject to the custom in question.

manner2.text: “taken with the ,” taken with the thing stolen in one's possession, (hence) taken in the very act LLL. I. i. 203 , 1H4 II. iv. 350 ; Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 755 “if you had not taken yourself with the ” (=kept what you were going to give us). ∥ A term of Anglo-French law, orig. ‘mainoure’ (= Fr. ‘manœuvre’, lit. hand-work), which acquired the concrete sense of ‘thing stolen’.

mannerly1.text: seemly, decent Gent. II. vii. 58 , Wint. II. i. 85 , 1H6 II. iv. 19 , Rom. I. v. 102 .

mannerly2.text: decently, becomingly Ado II. i. 80 , “ modest,” Mer.V. II. ix. 100 , Cym. III. vi. 91 .

mansion.text: dwelling, ‘house’ Tim. V. i. 220 “his everlasting mansion” (i.e. grave); cf. HOME sb. 1

mansionry.text: (?) abode Mac. I. vi. 5 (Ff “mansonry,” ? misprint for “masonry”†).

mantle1.text: vegetable coating on the surface of stagnant water (S.) Lr. III. iv. 137 “the green of the standing pool” ; cf. Tp. IV. i. 182 “the filthymantled pool.”

mantle2.text: vb. (2 cf. MANTLE sb.) 1. to cover, envelope Tp. V. i. 67 “the ignorant fumes that mantle Their clearer reason,” Cor. I. vi. 29 .

manure.text: to till, cultivate Oth. I. iii. 329 .

many1.text: multitude 2H4 I. iii. 91 “thou fond ,” Cor. III. i. 65 “the mutable, rank-scented many” (so F4; Ff1 2 3 “Meyny, Meynie”).

many2.text: “ a day,” a long time ago H8 V. ii. 20 (contrast “for this a day”=all this long time Ham. III. i. 91 ); “ a ” = many and many a John I. i. 183 ; followed by a possessive pron. Tim. III. vi. 11 “ my near occasions” (= many urgent affairs of mine), Ant. I. ii. 195 “ our contriving friends” ; used once in the possessive form Sonn. xciii. 7 “In many's looks.”

map.text: fig. detailed representation in epitome, also embodiment, very picture or image (“of” something) R2 V. i. 12 “Thou map of honour,” 2H6 III. i. 203 , Cor. II. i. 69 “in the map of my microcosm,” Tit. III. ii. 12 “Thou map of woe,” Lucr. 402 , 1712 , Sonn. lxviii. 1 “Thus is his cheek the map of days outworn.” ∥ Freq. 17th cent. uses.

marble.text: (2 cf. Cym. V. iv. 87 “thy mansion,” 120) 1. hard-hearted Wint. V. ii. 100 “Who was most there changed colour,” 3H6 III. i. 38 “a heart” ; cf. “-breasted” Tw.N. V. i. 128 , “-hearted” Lr. I. iv. 283 .

marbled.text: =MARBLE 2, Tim. IV. iii. 192 “the marbled mansion all above” (=the heavens).

marcantant.text: corruption of Italian ‘mercatante’ =merchant Shr. IV. ii. 63 .

marches.text: the Scottish or Welsh border H5 I. ii. 140 , 3H6 II. i. 140 .

marchpane.text: confectionery made of almond paste, sugar, &c., marzipan Rom. I. v. 9 .

mare1.text: “The man shall have his again,” all will come right in the end MND. III. ii. 463 ; “ride the wild mare,” play at see-saw 2H4 II. iv. 268 ; “Whose mare is dead?” What is amiss? 2H4 II. i. 48 .

margent.text: （‘margin’ is not a S. word) 1. edge, border, brink MND. II. i. 85 “the beached of the sea,” Compl. 39 .

marish.text: marsh, swamp 1H6 I. i. 50 “a of salt tears” (old edd. “nourish”).

mark1.headword: mark 1 (1 freq. in the literal sense) 1. target, butt
mark1.text: fig. phr. “beyond the of,” beyond the reach of Cor. II. ii. 94 “he fought Beyond the of others,” Ant. III. vi. 87 “Beyond the of thought.”

market.text: LLL. III. i. 116 “he ended the ” is an allusion to the proverb ‘Three women and a goose make a market’); R3 I. i. 159 “I run before my horse to ,” I count the gain before the bargain is made; Ham. IV. iv. 34 “ of his time” * , (a) lit. marketing or selling of his time, i.e. the best use he makes of his time; (b) ‘that for which he sells his time’ (J.).

marl.text: clay, earth Ado II. i. 67 “a clod of wayward marl” (= a man).

marquess.text: (3 a common 16th-17th cent. use) 1. in Latin countries, grade of noble rank below those of duke and count Mer.V. I. ii. 123 “the Marquess of Montferrat.”

marry1.text: freq. fig.=to unite intimately, join closely, e.g. John III. i. 228 , Rom. I. iii. 83 , Sonn. viii. 6 .

marry2.text: orig. the name of the Virgin Mary used as an oath or invocation:=‘indeed, to be sure’ Err. II. ii. 105 “, and did, sir,” All'sW. II. iii. 64 , R3 I. iii. 261 , III. iv. 34 ; esp. (1) in answering a question, when it often implies surprise that it should have been asked = ‘why’ or ‘why, to be sure’ Tp. III. ii. 47 “Wilt thou be pleas'd? . . . —, will I,” Gent. II. i. 66 “How painted?—, sir, so painted,” R3 I. iii. 98 “What may she not? She may,—ay, , may she,” Cæs. I. ii. 228 “Was the crown offer'd him thrice?—Ay, , was't” ; (2) with asseverative words or invocations Tw.N. IV. ii. 111 “God be wi' you . . . , amen,” R2 IV. i. 114 “, God forbid!,” Rom. IV. v. 8 “God forgive me, , and amen!” ; (3) “marry come up!” (not pre-S.), used to express indignant or amused surprise or contempt Rom. II. v. 64 , Per. IV. vi. 164 ; “marry-trap” * (S.), ? be off with you Wiv. I. i. 172 .

marshal1.text: sb. (scanned as 2 or as 3 syll.) 1. high officer of state in England, now called ‘earl marshal’ 1H4 IV. iv. 2 “the lord ,” H8 IV. i. 19 “earl marshal.”

marshal2.text: to guide, lead, conduct Mac. II. i. 42 , Ham. III. iv. 205 , Oth. II. i. 270 , Per. II. iii. 19 .

mart1.text: sb. (not pre-S. in the sense ‘market-place or hall’ Err. I. ii. 74 , &c., Mer.V. III. i. 51 ) 1. meeting of people for buying and selling, time of holding a market Err. I. i. 17 “Syracusian m-s and fairs,” Per. IV. ii. 5 “this mart.”

mart2.text: to traffic Cym. I. vi. 151 ; trans. to traffic in, buy or sell Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 364, Cæs. IV. iii. 11 .

martlet.text: swallow or house-martin Mer.V. II. ix. 28 , Mac.I.vi.4 “temple-haunting martlet”† (Ff “Barlet”).

martyr.text: (2 a 17th cent. use) 1. to inflict grievous pain upon, torment, torture Rom. IV. v. 59 “hated, martyr'd, kill'”

marvel.text: 1. astonishment, wonder Wint. V. i. 188 , iii. 100 , Cym. III. i. 10 .

marvellous.text: wonderfully; only with adjs. and advs. (freq.) MND. IV. i. 26 “ hairy about the face.”

mash.text: (properly) to mix (malt) with water to form wort, (hence, gen.) to brew, used fig. in Tit. III. ii. 38 “no other drink but tears, Brew'd with her sorrow, mash'd upon her cheeks” (old edd. “mesh'd”).

mask.text: to take part in a masque or masquerade Rom. I. v. 41 .

mass.text: (1, 2 are 16th-17th cent. uses) 1. applied to the earth Ham. III. iv. 49 .

mast.text: fruit of the beech, oak, or chestnut, serving as food for swine Tim. IV. iii. 425 .

master1.text: sb. (old edd. sometimes “maister”) 1. leader, chief Tit. V. i. 15 “bees . . . Led by their ”

master2.text: vb. (neither sense is pre-S.) 1. to rule as a master, be the master of Cym. IV. ii. 383 , 395

masterly.text: Ham. IV. vii. 96 “a report,” ‘a report that describes Laertes as a master of fence’.

mastership.text: (the foll. are the only uses) 1. with possessive pron. (“your ”) used as a title Gent. III. i. 282 , Mer.V. II. ii. 63 .

mastick.text: (?) misprint for “mastice,” dial. form of ‘mastiff’, used as adj.=massive Troil. I. iii. 73 “When rank Thersites opes his jaws” (mod. edd. “mastiff†, massive†”).

match1.text: see SET vb.) 1. opponent, antagonist 2H6 V. ii. 10 “ to I have encounter'd him.”

match2.text: vb. (sense 7 is peculiar to S.) 1. to ally oneself in marriage Ado II. i. 69 “to in my kindred,” Tw.N. I. iii. 118 , 2H6 I. i. 132 , 3H6 III. iii. 210 .

mate.text: vb. 2 (the sense ‘match, marry’ also occurs) 1. to rival, vie with H8 III. ii. 275 .

mate1.text: sb. (2 sometimes contemptuous) 1. fellow, ‘chap’ Shr. I. i. 58 , 2H4 II. iv. 132 , 1H6 III. i. 99 “an inkhorn mate,” R3 i. iii. 340 .

mate2.text: to stupefy, confound Err. V. i. 282 “I think you are all m-d or stark mad,” 2H6 III. i. 265 , Mac. V. i. 85 “My mind she has m-d, and amaz'd my sight.”

material.text: (sense ‘important’ occurs thrice) 1. forming the substance of a thing Lr. IV. ii. 35 “She that herself will . . . disbranch From her sap.”

matter.text: (1 peculiar to S.) 1. sense, substance (as opposed to nonsense or trifling) Ado II. i. 346 “to speak all mirth and no ,” AYL. II. i. 68 “he's full of ,” Lr. IV. iv. 179 “O! matter and impertinency mix'”

mature.text: (stressed “ma'ture” in Lr. IV. vi. 283 ) 1. ripe or ready “for” Cor. IV. iii. 26 .

maugre.text: in spite of Tw.N. III. i. 165 , Lr. V. iii. 133 .

may2.text: the orig. sense ‘have power or ability, can’ is well represented, as are also the mod. uses; occas. with ellipsis of vb. of motion MND. III. ii. 433 “That I may back to Athens,” 1H4 III. i. 141 “you may away by night” ; the idiomatic “you may, you may” ( Troil. III. i. 120 , Cor. II. iii. 39 ) app. means go on, go on, divert yourself at my expense.

maypole.text: jocularly of a tall man MND. III. ii. 296 .

mazed.text: dazed, bewildered, confused MND. II. i. 113 “the mazed world,” H8 II. iv. 183 “maz'd considerings.”

meadow.text: low well-watered ground Tit. III. i. 126 .

meagre.text: poor, barren Mer.V. III. ii. 104 , John III. i. 80 .

mealy.text: covered with fine powder Troil. III. iii. 79 .

mean.text: the S. meanings are ‘of low degree, station, or position’ and ‘undignified, low, base’; “no mean,” no contemptible (an epithet of praise) Mer.V. I. ii. 7 (Q1) “no meane happinesse” (F1 “no smal”).

mean1.text: sb. (used in sing. and pl. with the sense ‘instrument, agency, method, &c. employed for doing something’ the pl. sometimes taking sing. concord; the meaning ‘pecuniary resources,’ e.g. Meas. II. ii. 24 , is not pre-S.) 1. middle position, medium Mer.V. I. ii. 48 “seated in the ,” Ant. II. vii. 22 “the height, the lowness, or the ” ; moderation 1H6 I. ii. 121 “since he keeps no ”

meaning.text: intention, purpose Shr. III. ii. 127 “He hath some meaning in his mad attire,” R2 II. iii. 74 , R3 III. v. 54 “Something against our ,” Lr. I. ii. 196 “if there be any good toward you,” V. iii. 4 “with best meaning.”

meanly1.text: poorly, badly LLL. V. ii. 329 “he can sing A mean most ” ; basely, lowlily R3 IV. iii. 37 , Cym. III. iii. 82 .

meanly2.text: in a slight degree Err. I. i. 58 “not proud.”

meantime.text: sb. usu. “in the ,” but once “the ” in the same sense Ant. III. iv. 25 “the . . . I'll raise the preparation of a war” ;—adv. (not pre-S.) used both in the temporal sense, and the adversative sense=still, nevertheless (Lucr. Ded. 5).

measle.text: loathsome disease Cor. III. i. 77 “those m-s, Which we disdain should tetter us” (old edd. “Meazels”). ∥ There is a ref. to the common 16th-17th cent. use of the word=scurvy wretch.

measure1.text: sb. (the sense ‘quantity (of drink),’ arising out of that of ‘unit of capacity’, develops into ‘carouse, toast’ in Mac. III. iv. 11 , Oth. II. iii. 32 ) 1. distance of a fencer from his opponent, fig.=reach Gent. V. iv. 127 “Come not with in the of my wrath.”

measure2.text: 1. “ ” one's “length,” fall or lie full length on the ground MND. III. ii. 429 “To out my length on this cold bed,” Lr. I. iv. 100 “If you will your lubber's length again” ; so Cym. I. ii. 26 “till you had measured how long a fool you were upon the ground.”

mechanic.text: adj. engaged in a manual occupation H5 I. ii. 200 “The poor porters,” Ant. V. ii. 208 “ slaves” ; (hence) vulgar, low Ant. IV. iv. 32 “to stand On more compliment” ;—sb. handicraftsman (contemptuous) Cor. V. iii. 83 “Do not bid me . . . capitulate Again with Rome's mechanics.”

mechanical.text: adj.=MECHANIC adj. Wiv. II. ii. 295 “ salt-butter rogue,” 2H4 V. v. 39 “ and dirty hand,” Cæs. I. i. 3 ;—sb.=MECHANIC sb. MND. III. ii. 9 “rude mechanicals,” 2H6 I. iii. 196 .

medal.text: metal disk used as trinket, locket Wint. I. ii. 307 “he that wears her like her medal, hanging About his neck.”

meddle.text: (1, 2 late exx. of these senses) 1. to mingle Tp. I. ii. 22 “More to know Did never with my thoughts.”

medicine1.text: applied, as commonly from 1400 to S.'s time, to drugs, &c., used for other than remedial purposes; e.g. the philosopher's stone or elixir All'sW. V. iii. 102 “multiplying ,” Ant. I. v. 36 “that good ” ; poison Lr. V. iii. 97 , Oth. IV. i. 46 “Work on, My , work!” ; a philtre 1H4 II. ii. 20 , 22 , Oth. I. iii. 61 .

medicine2.text: doctor, physician All'sW. II. i. 75 ; fig. Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 600, Mac. V. ii. 27 .

medicine3.text: to heal, cure Cym. IV. ii. 243 “Great griefs . . . the less” ; to bring by medicinal means “to” Oth. III. iii. 333 “ thee to that sweet sleep.”

medlar.text: the tree Mespilus germanica, or its fruit which is like a small brown-skinned apple and is eaten when decayed to a soft pulpy state; always with quibble on ‘meddler’ Meas. IV. iii. 188 , AYL. III. ii. 126 , 129 , Rom. II. i. 34 , Tim. IV. iii. 305 .

meed.text: （‘recompense, reward’ is the prevalent sense) 1. gift (S.) Tim. I. i. 288 * .

meek.text: (the moral sense also occurs) 1. mild, merciful, gentle Tim. III. vi. 106 “affable wolves, meek bears,” Cæs. III. i. 255 “That I am meek and gentle with these butchers.”

meet1.text: adj. “be meet with” (not pre-S.), be even or quits with Ado I. i. 47 ;—adv. fitly All'sW. V. iii. 338 “if it end so meet.”

meet2.text: vb. (1=mod. ‘meet with’; 2 now expressed by the simple ‘meet’) 1. to encounter, experience, receive, gain Gent. I. i. 15 “When thou dost meet good hap,” 1H4 V. v. 42 “Meeting the check of such another day,” 2H4 IV. v. 184 “By what by-paths I met this crown,” Lr. III. vii. 101 “If she live long, And . . . meet the old course of death.”

meetly.text: fairly good or well Ant. I. iii. 81 .

melancholy.text: ill-temper, sullenness John III. iii. 42 “that surly spirit, ” ∥ A late instance of a sense current from the 14th cent.

melt.text: to weaken, enervate Ado IV. i. 325 “manhood is m-ed into curtsies,” Tim. IV. iii. 257 “thou wouldst have . . . melted down thy youth.”

melting.text: yielding or softening to emotion, tender (hence of eyes, &c.) tearful 2H4 IV. iv. 32 “ charity,” 3H6 I. iv. 174 “thy tears,” II. ii. 41 “thy heart,” Cæs. II. i. 122 “The spirits of women,” Oth. V. ii. 348 “unused to the mood,” Ven. 315 “his melting buttock.”

member.text: (1 now Warwickshire and Worcestershire dial.) 1. person Meas. V. i. 231 [ 237 ] “instruments of some more mightier member That sets them on.”

memorable.text: (only in H5) 1. easily remembered H5 II. iv. 53 * .

memorial.text: of remembrance Troil. V. ii. 77 “memorial . . . kisses.”

memorize.text: to cause to be remembered, make memorable H8 III. ii. 52 , Mac. I. ii. 41 “Or another Golgotha.”

memory.text: (cf. ‘a perpetual memory of that his precious death’ Prayer Book, Communion) 1. phr. “of ,” remembered 1H6 IV. iii. 51 “That ever living man of ,” Ham. V. ii. 403 “rights of ;—of little ,” soon forgotten Tp. II. i. 241 [ 233 ]; “book of ,” memorandum-book 1H6 II. iv. 101 , 2H6 I. i. 101 .

mend.text: （‘make better, improve’ in various contexts is the most freq. sense) 1. to reform H8 III. i. 104 “hollow hearts I fear ye. 'em” ; refl. Tw.N. I. v. 49 “bid the dishonest man himself” ; intr.=refl. Meas. III. ii. 28 “go ,” Tw.N. I. v. 49 “if he ,” Lr. II. iv. 232 “ when thou canst.”

mends.text: means of reparation, remedy Troil. I. i. 70 . ∥ This meaning occurs in the 16th-17th cent. only in the phr. ‘have the m. in one's own hands.’

merchandise1.text: construed as a pl. Ant. II. v. 104 ; “make ,” trade, traffic Mer.V. III. i. 137 “make what merchandise I will.”

merchant.text: (1 and 2 common Eliz. uses) 1. fellow, ‘chap’ 1H6 II. iii. 57 , Rom. II. iv. 154 .

mercurial.text: fleet, like Mercury's, Cym. IV. ii. 310 “His foot Mercurial.”

mercy.text: (1 usu. in phr. “I cry you mercy”; 3 hence the general phr. “at, in,” or “within the mercy of”） 1. “cry ,” beg for pard on or forgiveness Gent. V. iv. 94 “O, cry you mercy, sir; I have mistook,” AYL. III. v. 61 “Cry the man ,” H8 V. iii. 78 “I cry your honour mercy,” Lr. III. vi. 55 .

mere1.text: absolute, sheer, perfect, downright Wiv. IV. v. 64 “cozenage, cozenage,” LLL. I. ii. 36 “the contrary,” H8 III. ii. 330 “the undoing Of all the kingdom,” Mac. IV. iii. 152 “The despair of surgery,” Oth. II. ii. 3 , Cym. IV. ii. 92 “to thy confusion.” ∥ A common sense for more than two centuries, surviving late in the 18th; but less freq. in S. than the ordinary mod. use (which is not pre-Eliz.).

mere2.text: absolutely All'sW. III. v. 55 “ the truth.”

merely.text: absolutely, entirely Tp. I. i. 61 “ cheated of our lives,” R2 II. i. 244 , Cor. III. i. 303 “clean kam.— awry,” Ham. I. ii. 137 “things rank and gross in nature Possess it merely.” ∥ About as freq. as the meaning ‘only’.

merit.text: due reward, recompense “A dearer , not so deep a maim,” LLL. II. i. 21 , R2 I. iii. 156 .

merry.text: (3 not pre-S.) 1. (of wind) favourable Err. IV. i. 91 .

mervilous.text: old form of ‘marvellous’ H5 II. i. 50 .

mess.text: 1. dish (of food), course of dishes Wiv. III. i. 63 “a of porridge,” Shr. IV. iv. 70 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 11 “our feasts In every have folly,” Tim. IV. iii. 427 , Lr. I. i. 119 .

message.text: “sent on a ,” sent to do an errand Gent. IV. iv. 119 , 1H6 IV. vii. 53 ; similarly “go of ” 2H6 IV. i. 113 .

mete.text: (occurs twice; old edd. also “meat”) 1. to measure, estimate 2H4 IV. iv. 77 .

meteor.text: luminous body or appearance of any kind in the sky R2 II. iv. 9 “And m-s fright the fixed stars of heaven,” Rom. III. v. 13 “some that the sun exhales” ; fig. Err. IV. ii. 6 “his heart's m-s tilting in his face.”

metheglin.text: spiced drink made from wort and honey, of Welsh origin Wiv. V. v. 171 , LLL. V. ii. 234 .

method.text: summary of the contents of a book, fig. Tw.N. I. v. 245 “In what chapter of his bosom?— To answer by the method, in the first of his heart.”

methoughts.text: past tense of “methinks”=it seemed to me Mer.V. I. iii. 70 (Qq1 3 4 “Methought”), Wint. I. ii. 154 , R3 I. iv. 9 , 24 ∥ Not recorded before S.; current till the middle of the 18th cent.

mew.text: to coop up, shut up MND. I. i. 71 , R3 I. i. 132 , Rom. III. iv. 11 .

mewl.text: to cry feebly AYL. II. vii. 144 .

mickle.text: great Err. III. i. 45 , H5 II. i. 70 “An oath of might,” Rom. II. iii. 15 . ∥ In S.'s time its use in literature was archaistic; in colloquial use it was northern and north-midl. dial.

microcosm.text: man viewed as the epitome of the universe Cor. II. i. 70 “in the map of my microcosm.”

midway.text: middle course, medium Ado II. i. 8 , Ant. III. iv. 19 ;—adj. “ air”=mid-air Lr. IV. vi. 14 ;— adv. half-way Troil. I. iii. 278 , Per. V. i. 48 .

might.text: (obs. or archaic senses are) 1. power to do a thing Troil. III. ii. 164 “to be wise, and love, Exceeds man's ” ; MND. V. i. 92 * “noble respect Takes it in , not merit” (=noble consideration accepts it as an act of ability without regard to its merit).

mightily.text: with great effort, vigorously Shr. I. ii. 282 “Strive ” ; greatly, very much (the usual S. sense) 3H6 III. ii. 74 “thou wrong'st thy children mightily.”

milch.text: giving milk Shr. II. i. 351 [ 359 ] “ kine,” Ven. 875 “a doe” ; transf. applied to the eyes when weeping Ham. II. ii. 548 [ 540 ] “Would have made the burning eyes of heaven.”

mild.text: calm Per. III. i. 27 “Now may be thy life! For a more blust'rous birth had never babe.”

militarist.text: soldier All'sW. IV. iii. 162 “Monsieur Parolles, the gallant militarist.”

milk.text: as a type of what is pleasant and ‘sweet’ Rom. III. iii. 54 “Adversity's sweet , philosophy,” Mac. IV. iii. 98 “the sweet of concord” ; S. phr. “milk of human kindness,” compassion characteristic of humane persons Mac. I. v. 18 .

milky.text: timorous, weak Tim. III. i. 58 “such a faint and heart,” Ham. II. ii. 508 [ 500 ], Lr. I. iv. 366 .

millstone.text: phr. “drop” or “weep m-s,” said of a hardhearted person R3 I. iii. 353 , I. iv. 249 ; so Troil. I. ii. 156 “Queen Hecuba laughed that her eyes ran o'er.—With millstones.”

mimic.text: burlesque actor MND. III. ii. 19 (F1 “Mimmick”; see MINNICK).

mince.text: (the mod. development sense 2 is illustrated in H5 V. ii. 130 ） 1. to extenuate, make light of Oth. II. iii. 249 “Thy honesty and love doth mince this matter.”

mind2.text: sb. (1, 2 now obs. exc. in phrases) 1. judgement, opinion; phr. “in my , to my ,” as I think Mer.V. IV. i. 408 , Ham. I. iv. 14 .

minded.text: disposed, inclined Tp. V. i. 126 , H8 III. i. 57 “to know How you stand minded,” Lr. III. i. 2 .

mindless.text: unmindful, careless Wint. I. ii. 301 , Tim. IV. iii. 93 .

mine1.text: subterranean cavity Oth. IV. ii. 78 “The bawdy wind . . . Is hush'd within the hollow mine of earth.” ∥ Cf. ‘When a wherilewind . . . tosseth . . . His fixt root from his hollow mines’ (Chapman).

mine2.text: my property Shr. II. i. 377 [ 385 ], Wint. I. ii. 135 , Sonn. cxxxiv. 3 ; my business Meas. II. ii. 12 “Go to; let that be mine.”

mineral.text: (1 an Eliz. use) 1. mine Ham. IV. i. 26 “Among a mineral of metals.”

mingle.text: (1 peculiar to S.) 1. to put together so as to make one, to ‘pool’ Cym. I. vi. 186 “have mingled sums To buy a present.”

minim.text: musical note (in ancient music, the shortest) Rom. II. iv. 23 “He . . . rests me his ” (Q1 and mod. edd. “rests me his rest,” Qq2 - 5 “rests(,) his minum rests”).

minion.text: saucy woman, hussy, jade Gent. I. ii. 89 , Err. III. i. 54 , 2H6 I. iii. 141 , Tit. II. iii. 124 “This stood upon her chastity,” Oth. V. i. 33 “, your dear lies dead.” ∥ The other S. sense is ‘darling, favourite’.

minister1.text: 1. one employed by another to carry something into effect, agent Tp. I. ii. 131 “The m-s for the purpose,” All'sW. II. i. 140 , Wint. III. ii. 161 “I chose Camillo for the minister to poison My friend,” 2H6 III. i. 355 “a of my intent,” Ham. III. iv. 175 “their” [i.e. heaven's] “scourge and minister.”

minister2.text: 1. to furnish, supply Ado II. i. 387 “ such assistance,” R2 II. iii. 105 “ correction to thy fault,” Oth. II. i. 279 “what other course you please, which the time shall . . . ” ; to prompt, suggest Meas. IV. v. 6 “As cause doth minister.”

minnow.text: as a type of smallness LLL. I. i. 249 “that base of thy mirth,” Cor. III. i. 88 “this Triton of the minnous.”

minstrel.text: one whose profession was to entertain with music and story-telling Shr. III. ii. 186 “I hear the m-s play,” Rom. III. i. 51 , Lucr. 817 “Feast-finding minstrels, tuning my defame.”

minstrelsy.text: company of minstrels LLL. I. i. 175 “I love to hear him lie, And I will use him for my ” ; music made by minstrels Tim. II. ii. 171 , Per. V. ii. 7 .

minute.text: “ while” 1H6 I. iv. 54 and “ of the hour” LLL. V. ii. 795 = simply ‘minute’; “by the ,” every moment Ant. III. i. 20 .

minutely.text: happening every minute Mac. V. ii. 18 “ revolts upbraid his faith-breach.”

minx.text: wanton woman Tw.N. III. iv. 135 , Oth. IV. i. 157 .

miracle.text: refl. (?) to be revealed by miracle (S.) Cym. IV. ii. 29 * .

mire.text: (2 not pre-S.) 1. to bespatter, defile Ado IV. i. 135 “m-'d with infamy.”

mirth.text: (obs. uses) 1. fun Wiv. IV. vi. 14 , Ado II. i. 345 “to speak all and no matter,” MND. V. i. 57 ; jest Ant. I. iv. 18 “for a mirth.”

miscarry.text: (1 the prevailing meaning in S. and from the 14th to the 18th cent.) 1. to come to harm or destruction, perish Mer.V. III. ii. 316 “my ships have all m-ied,” 2H4 IV. i. 129 “That by indictment and by dint of sword Hare since m-ied,” H5 IV. i. 157 , Lr. V. i. 5 “Our sister's man is . . . miscarried,” Oth. V. i. 6 .

mischief.text: (1 the orig. sense of the word) 1. misfortune, calamity Wiv. IV. ii. 78 , 1H4 V. i. 21 , 1H6 V. iii. 39 “A plaguing light on Charles,” Oth. I. iii. 204 “a that is past and gone,” Per. I. iv. 8 .

misconceived.text: having a wrong idea 1H6 V. iv. 49 .

misdoubt1.text: mistrust, suspicion 2H4 IV. i. 206 , 2H6 III. i. 332 “change misdoubt to resolution.”

misdoubt2.text: vb. (in common dial. use) 1. to have doubts as to All'sW. III. vii. 1 , Ant. III. vii. 62 ; absol. All'sW. I. iii. 132 .

misdread.text: dread of evil Per. I. ii. 12 .

misery.text: Cym. V. iii. 64 “noble ” * (a) miserable nobility, (b) wretchedness in noble estate.

misgraffed.text: fig. badly matched MND. I. i. 137 .

misorder.text: to confuse 2H4 IV. ii. 33 “The time m-'”

misplace.text: to use words in a wrong place (S.) Meas. II. i. 93 .

misprision1.text: mistake, misunderstanding Ado IV. i. 187 , 1H4 I. iii. 27 , Sonn. lxxxvii. 11 .

misreport.text: to speak ill of Meas. V. i. 148 .

miss1.text: sb. (1 ‘feel the miss of’ is now the usual expression in midland dialects) 1. disadvantage caused by the loss “of” (a person) 1H4 V. iv. 105 “I should have a heavy miss of thee.”

miss2.text: vb. (3 several times in pres. pple.) 1. to do without Tp. I. ii. 311 “We cannot miss him.”

missing.text: absence Cym. V. v. 276 “Upon my lady's ”

missingly.text: with a sense of loss Wint. IV. i. [ ii. ] 34

mission.text: sending of help Troil. III. iii. 189 .

missive.text: messenger Mac. I. v. 7 , Ant. II. ii. 78 .

mist1.text: state of uncertainty Err. II. ii. 220 .

mist2.text: to bedim Lr. V. iii. 264 “ or stain the stone.”

mistake.text: (pa. pple. “mistaken, mista'en, mistook”） 1. to take wrongly, falsely, or improperly Wiv. II. ii. 231 “I have lost my edifice by mistaking the place where I erected it,” John III. i. 274 “purposes mistook,” Ham. III. ii. 266 “So you your husbands” (Q1 and mod. edd. “must take”), V. ii. 398 ; to take to a wrong person or place LLL. IV. i. 57 “This letter is mistook,” 109

mistaking.text: mistake, error Tp. I. ii. 248 , Meas. III. ii. 154 , Shr. IV. v. 49 . ∥ A freq. sense about 1580-1650

mistempered.text: (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. disordered, deranged John V. i. 12 “ humour.”

mistership.text: old form of ‘mistress-ship’ Tit. IV. iv. 40 .

misthink.text: to think ill of 3H6 II. v. 108 , Ant. V. ii. 175 .

mistress.text: (3 is the commonest S. use) 1. woman having a protecting or guiding influence Lr. II. i. 42 “conjuring the moon To stand auspicious mistress.”

mistrust1.text: “ of,” doubt as to Cæs. V. iii. 66 .

mistrust2.text: to suspect the existence of or anticipate the occurrence of Ado II. i. 191 “an accident of hourly proof, Which I m-ed not,” Wint. II. i. 47 “All's true that is m-ed,” 3H6 V. vi. 38 “Which now no parcel of my fear,” R3 II. iii. 42 “ Ensuing danger” ; with clause Lucr. 1516 .

misuse1.text: sb. (1 is peculiar to S.) 1. ill-usage 1H4 I. i. 43 .

misuse2.text: vb. (‘use wrongly’ is the most freq. sense) 1. to abuse, revile Ado II. i. 248 , AYL. IV. i. 213 [ 205 ], Shr. II. i. 160 .

mixture.text: preparation of various ingredients Rom. IV. iii. 21 , Ham. III. ii. 272 , Oth. I. iii. 104 .

moan1.text: lamentation, grief Ado V. iii. 16 “assist our ,” 1H6 II. iii. 44 “thy mirth shall turn to ,” Cym. IV. ii. 273 “Thou hast finished joy and moan” ; also phr. “make moan.” ∥ The mod. sense is post-S.

mobled.text: muffled Ham. II. ii. 533 [ 525 ] “the queen” (Qq; F1 “inobled”). ∥ Survives in Warwickshire.

mock1.text: “in ,” derided Meas. V. i. 320 “As much in mock as mark” ; Oth. V. ii. 149 “made m-s with,” played or sported with.

mock2.text: vb. (3 is peculiar to S.) 1. to defy, set at nought Mer.V. II. i. 30 “mock the lion when he roars for prey,” Tw.N. III. iv. 228 “mocks reproof,” Mac. II. ii. 7 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 184

mocker.text: one who deceives or disappoints AYL. II. vi. 14 “thou art a mocker of my labour.”

mockery.text: 1. imitation, counterfeit representation, unreal appearance H5 IV. Chor. 53 “Minding true things by what their mockeries be,” R3 III. ii. 27 “the of unquiet slumbers,” Mac. III. iv. 107 “Unreal , hence!.”

mode.text: reading of Ff3 4 in 2H4 IV. v. 198 : see MOOD 2 .

model.text: (4 is peculiar to S.) 1. architect's design for a building 2H4 I. iii. 42 “We first survey the plot, then draw the ,” 46; fig. Ado I. iii. 48 “model to build mischief on.”

modern.text: everyday, ordinary, commonplace AYL. II. vii. 156 “Full of wise saws and instances,” John III. iv. 42 , Mac. IV. iii. 170 “A ecstasy.” ∥ The only S. sense; peculiarly Eliz.

modest.text: moderate, marked by moderation, becoming All'sW. II. i. 131 , Tw.N. I. iii. 9 “within the limits of order,” I. v. 193 “give me assurance if you be the lady of the house” (=sufficient to satisfy me), H8 V. iii. 69 “reverence to your calling makes me ” (=moderate in language), Cor. III. i. 274 “Do not cry havoc, where you should but hunt With warrant,” Lr. II. iv. 25 “with all haste,” IV. vii. 5 “All my reports go with the modest truth.”

modestly.text: without exaggeration, with due moderation Troil. IV. v. 221 , Cæs. I. ii. 69 .

modesty.text: moderation Shr. Ind. i. 68 “If it be husbanded with modesty,” Cæs. III. i. 213 “cold modesty.”

modicum.text: small quantity Troil. II. i. 73 “m-s of wit.”

module.text: mere image or counterfeit All'sW. IV. iii. 114 “this counterfeit (model†),” John V. vii. 58 “moduie of confounded royally.”

moiety.text: （‘half’ is the most freq. sense) 1. share, portion 1H4 III. i. 97 “my . . . equals not one of yours,” Ham. I. i. 90 “a competem,” Lr. I. i. 7 , Sonn. xlvi. 12 “The clear eye's and the dear heart's part.”

moist.text: (1 a 16th-17th cent. use) 1. rheumy 2H4 I. ii. 206 “a moist eye, a dry hand.”

moment.text: (2 a 17th cent. sense, not pre-S.) 1. “on” or “upon the ,” immediately Tim. I. i. 80 , Compl. 248 ; “in a ,” at one and the same time Mac. II. iii. 116 .

momentany.text: lasting but a moment MND. I. i. 143 “ as a sound” (Ff “momentarie”). ∥ Common 16th17th cent.; once in S.; “momentary” 7 times.

money.text: from S. on wards the use of the pl. for the sing. has been commonly attributed to Jews Mer.V. I. iii. 109 , &c. ∥ Cf. ‘monish’.

mongrel.text: abusive epithets for persons Troil. V. iv. 14 , Lr. II. ii. 24 .

monster.text: (1 peculiar to S.) 1. to make monstrous Lr. I. i. 223 “her offence Must be of such unnatural degree That monsters it.”

monstrous.text: as an exclamation=astounding MND. III. i. 110 , “O ! O strange! we are haunted,” 1H4 II. iv. 247 , Lr. V. iii. 161 ; as adv. exceedingly, wonderfully MND. I. ii. 55 “in a little voice,” All'sW. II. i. 187 “monstrous desperate.”

montant.text: ‘an upright blow, or thrust’ (Cotgr.) Wiv. II. iii. 27 “thy punto . . . thy distance, thy ” ; cf. “Signior Mountanto” applied to Benedick ( Ado I. i. 30 ) to imply that he is a professional fencer or bravo.

monument.text: (1 occurs freq., 2 once) 1. place of burial, grave, sepulchre Ado IV. i. 208 “your family's old ,” Tit. II. iii. 228 , Rom. III. v. 203 “In that dim where Tybalt lies,” Ant. IV. xi. [ xiii. ] 3, &c.

monumental.text: sepulchral Oth. V. ii. 5 “ alabaster” ; serving as a memento All'sW. IV. iii. 20 “his ring” ; like a monument Troil. III. iii. 153 “to hang . . . like a rusty mail In mockery.”

mood1.text: 1 (1 current from the 12th cent. to 1600) 1. anger, displeasure Gent. IV. i. 51 “Who, in my , I stabb'd,” All'sW. V. ii. 5 “muddied in Fortune's ,” H5 IV. vii. 38 , Rom. III. i. 13 , Oth. II. iii. 276 ; (?) angry cast of countenance Sonn. xciii. 8 “m-s and frowns.”

mood2.text: key in which music is written (fig. and associated with ‘mood’=state of mind) 2H4 IV. v. 198 “now my death Changes the ” (Q “mood,” Ff1 2 “moode,” Ff3 4 “mode”).

moon.text: (occurs six times in the sense ‘month’) 1. phr. “moon's men, minions of the moon,” ‘nightwalkers’, robbers by night 1H4 I. ii. 35 ; “go by the ,” be a ‘night-walker’ I. ii. 15 ; “under” or “beneath the ,” on earth Ham. IV. vii. 145 , Lr. IV. vi. 27 , Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 68; “below the ,” earthly H8 III. ii. 135 .

mooncalf.text: mis-shapen birth, monster Tp. II. ii. 115 .

moonish.text: changeable (as the moon) AYL. III. ii. 436 .

moonshine.text: (1 jocular nonce-use) 1. month Lr. I. ii. 5 .

mop.text: grimace Tp. IV. i. 47 “mop and mow” ; also vbl. sb. mopping Lr. IV. i. 62 “mopping and mowing.”

mope.text: to be in a state of bewilderment, go about or act aimlessly Tp. V. i. 240 “brought moping hither,” H5 III. vii. 148 (see KNOWLEDGE), Ham. III. iv. 81 . ∥ A sense now confined to northern dial.

moral1.text: sb. (both the foll. are rare) 1. hidden meaning Ado III. iv. 77 “you have some in this Benedictus,” Shr. IV. iv. 79 .

moral2.text: adj. (3 cf. MORAL sb. 1) 1. enunciating moral precepts, moralizing Ado V. i. 30 , Lr. IV. ii. 58 “a fool” ; so Ado I. iii. 13 “to apply a moral medicine to a mortifying mischief.”

moralize.text: to draw out the hidden meaning of, (gen.) interpret, explain AYL. II. i. 44 “Did he not this spectacle?,” Shr. IV. iv. 81 , R3 III. i. 83 “I two meanings in one word,” Lucr. 104 ; also intr. Ven. 712 “thou hear'st me moralize.”

more.text: 1. of higher class, only in “more and less”=persons of all ranks 1H4 IV. iii. 68 , Mac. V. iv. 13 , Sonn. xcvi. 3 .

morning.text: used as adj. connoting vaguely the attributes possessed in the morning, or the fact that morning is the time referred to MND. IV. i. 100 “I do hear the lark,” AYL. II. vii. 146 “the . . . schoolboy with his . . . shining face,” Ham. I. ii. 218 “the morning cock crew loud.”

morris2.text: “nine men's ,” game played on a board between two players, each with nine pebbles, disks, pegs, or ‘pins’ MND. II. i. 98 .

mort.text: note sounded on a horn at the death of the deer Wint. I. ii. 119 “The mort o' the deer.”

mortal.text: (the senses ‘deadly, fatal’ and ‘subject to death’ are the commonest in S.) 1. of or for death All'sW. III. vi. 81 “my preparation,” Mac. IV. i. 100 * “mortal custom.”

mortality.text: (2 not pre-Eliz.) 1. human or mortal life Meas. III. ii. 200 , John V. vii. 5 , H5 I. ii. 28 “brief ,” Mac. II. iii. 100 .

mortally.text: in the manner of mortals Per. V. i. 105 .

mortgage.text: pass. to be pledged Sonn. cxxxiv. 2 .

mortified.text: （ Mac. V. ii. 5 * is referred to 1 and 2) 1. destroyed, dead H5 I. i. 26 “his wildness, in him.”

mortifying.text: mortal, deadly Ado I. iii. 13 “a mischief” ; involving mortification of desire, selfdenying Mer.V. I. i. 82 “mortifying groans.”

mose.text: “ in the chine,” suffer from glanders Shr. III. ii. 52 .

most.text: （“the most of” = ‘the majority of’ Tp. I. ii. 477 ) 1. greatest in degree or extent Meas. III. i. 76 “The sense of death is in apprehension,” IV. i. 46 “my stay Can be but brief,” 1H6 IV. i. 38 “resolute in extremes,” Ham. I. v. 179 “at your need,” Ant. II. ii. 172 “With gladness.”

mote.text: (old edd. in 1 “mote, moat(e,” in 2 and 3 chiefly “moth, moath”) 1. particle of dust in a sunbeam Per. IV. iv. 21 .

moth.text: fig. parasite Cor. I. iii. 93 (pun), Oth. I. iii. 258 . ∥ As a proper name applied to small persons LLL. I. ii. 81 , &c. MND. III. i. 169 , but in this use perhaps a form of MOTE, q.v.

motion1.text: sb. (5, 6 still prevalent uses in 18th cent.) 1. power of movement Meas. III. i. 118 “This sensible warm ” (i.e. in the body), Rom. III. ii. 59 .

motion2.text: to propose 1H6 I. iii. 63 “One that . . . motions war.”

motive.text: (in the ordinary mod. sense construed with “of, for,” or clause; 2 only S.) 1. mover, promoter, instigator All'sW. IV. iv. 20 , Tim. V. iv. 27 , Oth. IV. ii. 42 “Am I the of these tears?,” Ant. II. ii. 100 ; that which promotes H5 II. ii. 156 .

motley.text: parti-coloured dress of a professional jester AYL. II. vii. 34 ; attrib. II. vii. 13 “A fool.” H8 Prol. 16 “a long coat”; (hence) fool AYL. III. iii. 84 , Sonn. cx. 2 “I have . . . made myself a to the view.”

mould.text: “ up,” go to form H8 V. v. 27 .

mould1.text: earth; “men of ,” mortal men H5 III. ii. 24 .

mould2.text: sb. 2 (2 cf. Fr. ‘moule’; 3 in poetical use since the Eliz. period) 1. model, pattern Ham. III. i. 162 .

mount1.text: “on ,” set up on high Ham. IV. vii. 28 .

mount2.text: 1. to cause to rise H8 I. i. 144 “The fire that m-s the liquor till it run o'er” ; to erect, set up Tp. II. ii. 11 “like hedge-hogs, which . . . Their pricks,” 2H6 I. iv. 40 “castles m-ed” ; to excite to a higher degree All'sW. I. i. 239 “which m-s my love so high.”

mountebank.text: to win over, with tricks like those of a mountebank Cor. III. ii. 132 .

mounting.text: phr. of Eliz. writers, used quibblingly in LLL. IV. i. 4 .

mouse1.text: playful term of endearment to a woman LLL. V. ii. 19 , Tw.N. I. v. 68 , Ham. III. iv. 183 .

mouse2.text: to tear, bite MND. V. i. 276 , John II. i. 354 .

mouth1.text: 1. phr.:—“a sweet mouth,” (?) a taste for sweet things Gent. III. i. 333 ; “in the mouth(s of,” spoken of by Mer.V. I. iii. 61 “Your worship was the last man in our m-s,” John IV. ii. 187 , 1H6 III. i. 196 , Oth. II. iii. 195 “m-s of wisest censure” (Q1 “men”), Sonn. lxxxi. 14 .

mouth2.text: vb. (2 used contemptuously) 1. to take into the mouth Ham. IV. ii. 20 .

mouthed.text: gaping, open-mouthed 1H4 I. iii. 97 “ wounds,” Sonn. lxxvii. 6 “mouthed graves.”

move.text: (the foll. are obs. fig. uses) 1. to make angry, exasperate Wiv. I. iv. 95 , Shr. V. ii. 143 , R3 I. iii. 248 “Lest . . . thou our patience,” Rom. I. i. 7 , Cæs. IV. iii. 58 “he durst not thus have m-d me,” Ven. 623 “Being mov'd, he strikes.”

mover.text: (1 so ‘first Mover’ in Milton) 1. applied to God as moving the universe 2H6 III. iii. 19 “eternal Mover of the heavens.”

moving1.text: vbl. sb. (common Eliz. uses) 1. motion (of a heavenly body) 1H6 I. ii. 1 .

moving2.text: exciting the feelings Meas. II. ii. 36 , R2 V. i. 47 ; as adv. “-delicate” Ado IV. i. 230 .

mow.text: (derisive) grimace Tp. IV. i. 47 “with mop and ,” Ham. II. ii. 390 [ 381 ], Cym. I. vi. 41 “Contemn with m-s the other” ; also as vb. Tp. II. ii. 9 “apes that mow and chatter,” Lr. IV. i. 63 “mopping and m-ing.”

moy.text: imaginary name of a coin evolved by ‘Ancient Pistol’ from a misunderstanding of the French “moy” (me) in his prisoner's speech H5 IV. iv. 14 .

much.text: (3 now only in phr. ‘much like’) 1. used ironically, where ‘no’ would be used in serious language AYL. IV. iii. 2 “Is it not past two o'clock? And here much Orlando!” ; also as adv. = not at all 2H4 II. iv. 141 “God's light! with two points on your shoulder? much!.”

mudded.text: buried in mud Tp. III. iii. 102 , V. i. 151 .

muddy.text: confused in mind Wint. I. ii. 325 .

muffled.text: blindfolded All'sW. IV. i. 95 , Rom. I. i. 176 .

muffler.text: bandage for blindfolding H5 III. vi. 32 .

mulled.text: dispirited, dull Cor. IV. v. 240 “, deaf.”

multitudinous.text: (occurs twice) 1. vast Mac. II. ii. 63 “The multitudinous seas.”

mum.text: Wiv. V. ii. 6 “I . . . cry ‘mum’; she cries ‘budget’” ; the two elements of the 16th-17th cent. ‘mumbudget’, which was used like ‘mum’ = silence, silent.

mummy.text: (2 a rare jocular use) 1. medicinal or magical preparation of the flesh of dead bodies Mac. IV. i. 23 “Witches' ,” Oth. III. iv. 75 “dy'd in which the skilful Conserv'd of maidens' hearts.”

munition.text: military stores John V. ii. 98 ; in the 16th-17th cent. often used = ammunition, as probably in 1H6 I. i. 168 .

mural.text: wall MND. V. i. 210 “Now is the down” (Ff “morall”; ? read ‘wall’).

murmur.text: rumour; “in ,” whispered about Tw.N. I. ii. 30 “'twas fresh in murmur . . . That” . . .

murrain.text: plague; in imprecations “a on” Tp. III. ii. 90 , Troil II. i. 21 ; used as adj.=diseased MND. II. i. 97 “the flock” (old edd. “murrion,” a 16th-17th cent. form).

muscadel.text: strong sweet wine made from the muscatel or similar grape Shr. III. ii. 175 .

muse.text: 2) this sense occurs in Sternhold & Hopkins, Psalm ii, ‘Why did the Jewish people muse?’) 1. to wonder, marvel All'sW. II. v. 71 , John III. i. 317 , R3 I. iii. 305 “I why she's at liberty,” Cor. III. ii. 7 , Mac. III. iv. 85 “Do not at me,” Ven. 866 ; also trans. to marvel at Tp. III. iii. 36 “I cannot too much muse Such shapes” . . .

muset.text: gap in a hedge or fence through which hares habitually pass, or run, when hunted, for relief Ven. 683 (Q “musits”).

music.text: band of musicians LLL. V. ii. 212 “Play, , then!,” 217, H8 IV. ii. 94 “Bid the leave,” Rom. IV. iv. 22 “The county will be here with ” ; as adj.= pleasing, delightful Ham. III. i. 165 “the honey of his music vows” (Qq2 3 4 musickt ).

musk.text: odoriferous substance secreted in a gland or sac by the male musk-deer Wiv. II. ii. 70 .

muss.text: game in which small objects are thrown down to be scrambled for Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 91 “Like boys unto a muss.” ∥ Survives=‘scramble’ in Leicestershire and Warwickshire.

must.text: very freq. with ellipsis of a vb. of motion Gent. II. iv. 177 “I must after,” R2 I. ii. 56 “I to Coventry,” Cæs. V. i. 22 “we out and talk.” ∥ As a past tense, used to express regret with regard to an untoward event Mac. IV. iii. 212 “And I must be from thence!.”

muster.text: (orig. sense is ‘show, display’; cf. 1) 1. (?) to set an example of All'sW. II. i. 55 .

musty.text: stale Ham. III. ii. 366 [ 359 ] “the proverb is” . . .

mute.text: silent spectator Ham. V. ii. 349 ; in oriental countries, dumb house-servant or janitor Tw.N. I. ii. 60 , H5 I. ii. 232 “our grave, Like Turkish , shall have a tongueless mouth,” Cym. III. v. 158 .

mutine.text: mutineer John II. i. 378 , Ham. V. ii. 6 ; also as vb. to rebel (fig.) Ham. III. iv. 83 .

mutiny1.text: discord, contention LLL. I. i. 168 , 1H6 IV. i. 131 , H8 III. ii. 121 “There is a in 's mind,” Rom. I. v. 84 , Lucr. 1153 “So with herself is she in ”

mutiny2.text: to contend, strive, quarrel R2 II. i. 28 , Oth. II. i. 284 , Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 13

mutton.text: (2 see also LACED MUTTON) 1. sheep Gent. I. i. 101 “a lost ,” AYL. III. ii. 58 .

mutual.text: (2 now regarded as incorrect, is the commonest S. sense) 1. intimate Meas. I. ii. 164 [ 158 ] “our most entertainment,” 2H6 I. i. 25 “The mutual conference.”

mutually.text: in return Wiv. IV. vi. 10 ; jointly, in common Wiv. V. v. 105 , Meas. II. iii. 27 .

my.text: in vocative phrases, often placed between an adj. and its noun, e.g. Wint. II. iii. 27 “good my lords,” R2 I. i. 184 “dear my liege,” Rom. III. v. 200 “sweet my mother,” Ham. I. ii. 50 “Dread my lord” (Ff).

mystery1.text: personal secret Ham. III. ii. 389 [ 382 ] “you would pluck out the heart of my mystery.”

mystery2.text: 2 (late Latin ‘misterium’=‘ministerium’) 1. craft, trade, profession Meas. IV. ii. 30 , &c., Tim. IV. i. 18 , iii. 461 “thrive in our mystery,” Oth. IV. ii. 29 .
