nag.text: applied to a wanton woman 2H4 II. iv. 204 , Ant. III. viii. 20 [ x. 10 ] “Yon ribaudred nag of Egypt.” ∥ Cf. HACKNEY, JADE.

nail.text: 1. “blow” one's “nail(s,” (i) lit. so as to keep one's hands warm LLL. V. ii. 921 “Dick the shepherd blows his nail,” 3H6 II. v. 3 ; (ii) fig. to exercise patience Shr. I. i. 108 .

naked.text: (the literal sense and derived fig. uses ‘destitute’, ‘unprovided’, ‘unfurnished’ are freq.) 1. “ bed,” used with ref. to the custom of sleeping entirely naked Ven. 397 “in her naked bed.”

nakedness.text: bareness, destitution H5 IV. i. 110 , Tim. IV. i. 33 .

name1.text: sb. (1 cf. the uses of Latin ‘nomine’) 1. “in (the) of,” under the title or designation of, in the character of Wiv. III. v. 102 “in the of foul clothes,” IV. iv. 78 , Ado II. i. 181 , Wint. III. ii. 61 “Which comes to me in of fault,” R2 I. i. 89 ; “by the of,” in the quality of, as Ado III. iii. 154 , H5 II. ii. 146 , &c., H8 II. i. 59 “by that name” (i.e. as a traitor), Mac. II. i. 16 .

name2.text: to utter, say (S.) LLL. V. ii. 240 , 3H6 V. v. 58 , Tit. III. ii. 33 “name the word of hands.”

nameless.text: (all senses are not pre-S.) 1. of unknown name Gent. II. i. 115 .

narrowly.text: carefully, closely Ado V. iv. 118 , Shr. III. ii. 142 .

native1.text: (?) origin, source Cor. III. i. 128 * “the Of our so frank donation” (Heath “motive”†).

native2.text: adj. (the gen. mod. sense ‘belonging to a certain country, or to one's birthplace’ is freq.) 1. natural LLL. IV. iii. 263 “ blood,” John III. iv. 83 “ beauty,” Rom. IV. i. 97 , Ham. III. i. 84 “the hue of resolution” ; with “to” Oth. II. i. 219 “a nobility . . . more than is native to them.”

natural1.text: idiot, half-wit Tp. III. ii. 38 , AYL. I. ii. 53 .

natural2.text: adj. (various ordinary uses occur) 1. that is so by birth 3H6 I. i. 82 “Whom should he follow but his king?,” Lr. IV. vi. 196 “The fool of fortune” (= born to be the sport of fortune).

naturally.text: in a life-like manner Shr. Ind. i. 87 .

nature.text: (2 not pre-S. and now dial.) 1. “of ” = natural (in various senses) Troil. V. i. 39 “diminutives of ,” Ham. I. iv. 54 “fools of ,” Lr. I. ii. 117 “wisdom of ” (=natural philosophy), 124 “bias of ” (=natural affection).

naught1.text: sb. (sometimes confused with “nought” =nothing) 1. “set at ,” slight, despise Gent. I. i. 68 , 2H4 V. ii. 85 , Cor. III. i. 269 ; “call all to ,” abuse or decry vehemently Ven. 993 (Qq1-4 “nought); be ,” efface yourself, withdraw AYL. I. i. 39 .

naught2.text: adj. (3 not pre-S.) 1. worthless, useless Ado V. i. 160 “my knife's naught” AYL. III. ii. 15 , H5 I. ii. 73 “[his title] was corrupt and naught.”

naughty.text: (of weather) bad, nasty Lr. III. iv. 114 “'tis a night to swim in.” ∥ The word is usu. applied to persons = bad, wicked, worthless.

nave.text: (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. hub (of a wheel) Ham. II. ii. 526 [ 518 ]; in 2H4 II. iv. 278 “this of a wheel” there is a ref. to Falstaff's rotundity and a quibble with ‘knave’.

nay.text: the commoner S. use is that of serving to correct, amplify, or emphasize something that precedes, or to express a mild protest, e.g. Tp. I. i. 17 “Nay, good, be patient,” Err. IV. ii. 36 “A wolf, nay, worse, a fellow all in buff.”

nayward.text: “to the ,” towards denial or disbelief Wint. II. i. 63 “lean to the nayward.”

nayword.text: (of obscure derivation) 1. watchword Wiv. II. ii. 132 , V. ii. 5 .

ne.text: and not, nor All'sW. II. i. 176 “ne worse of worst” (Ff; mod. edd. “nay, worse—if worst”†), Per. II. Gower 36 . ∥ Still current in the Eliz. period.

neaf.text: fist MND. IV. i. 20 (Qq F1 “neafe,” F2 “newfe,” F3 “newse,” F4 “news”), 2H4 II. iv. 199 (Q Ff “neaffe”).

near.text: 1. “come near the house, come or draw near,” enter Tp. V. i. 318 , Wiv. I. iv. 137 , III. iii. 159 , Mer.V. V. i. 223 .

near1.text: closely affecting or touching one Tim. III. vi. 11 “many my occasions” ; absol. in Mac. III. i. 118 “my near'st of life” (=my very inmost being).

near2.text: nearer R2 III. ii. 64 “Nor near nor further off . . . Than this weak arm,” Mac. II. iii. 147 “the near in blood, The nearer bloody;—ne'er the ,” no nearer the object in view R2 V. i. 88 .

neat1.text: animal of the ox-kind Tp. II. ii. 75 “neat'sleather,” Shr. IV. iii. 17 “a neat's foot,” 1H4 II. iv. 275 “you dried neat's tongue” ; cattle Wint. I. ii. 126 .

neat2.text: adj. (1 applied in both laudatory and depreciatory sense) 1. elegant Gent. I. ii. 10 “a knight . . . neat and fine,” Wint. I. ii. 124 “not neat, but cleanly,” 1H4 I. iii. 33 , Lr. II. ii. 46 “you neat slave.”

necessary.text: rendering useful service Cor. II. i. 93 “a necessary bencher in the Capitol.”

necessitied.text: “ to,” in need of All'sW. V. iii. 85 .

neck.text: phr. (1) with ref. to hanging or beheading 1H4 II. i. 68 “I'll give thee this neck,” H5 IV. viii. 44 “let his neck answer for it” ; (2) denoting the laying of a charge upon one Oth. V. ii. 168 “men must lay their murders on your neck” ; (3) “in” or “on the neck of,” immediately after 1H4 IV. iii. 92 “in the neck of that,” Sonn. cxxxi. 11 “One on another's neck” ; (4) “break” (one's) “neck,” destroy, kill Troil. III. iii. 262 , V. iv. 34 “a plague break thy neck!,” Cor. III. iii. 30 .

need1.text: “for a need,” in case of necessity, at a pinch 3H6 I. ii. 67 , R3 III. v. 84 , Ham. II. ii. 573 [ 566 ]; “had need,” would do well (to), ought (to) AYL. II. vii. 169 , Tw.N. II. iii. 202 , 2H4 II. iv. 161 , H8 II. ii. 45 .

need2.text: “it needs,” it is necessary, there is necessity Err. V. i. 393 “It shall not need,” 3H6 I. iv. 125 , Mac. V. ii. 29 ; “what need(s . . .?,” what necessity is there for . . .? Err. III. i. 60 “What needs all that?,” Tim. I. ii. 251 “what need these feasts?,” Ant. II. vii. 132 “What needs more words?,” Lucr. 31 “What needeth then apology be made?.”

needful.text: wanting supplies of men 3H6 II. i. 147 “this needful war.”

needle.text: one syll. in MND. III. ii. 204 , John V. ii. 157 (Ff1 2 “needl's”), Per. IV. Gower 23 , V. Gower 5, where mod. edd. substitute the once common spelling “neeld” for old edd. “needle”; in Per. V. Gower 5 Qq have “neele,” another old and still dial. form.

needless.text: not in need AYL. II. i. 46 “his weeping into the needless stream.”

needy.text: necessary Per. I. iv. 95 “your needy bread.”

neglect.text: to cause neglect of R3 III. iv. 24 .

neglection.text: negligence, neglect 1H6 IV. iii. 49 , Troil. I. iii. 127 , Per. III. iii. 20 .

negligence.text: disregard, contempt Ham. IV. v. 133 “both the worlds I give to negligence.”

negligent.text: due to negligence Ant. III. vi. 81 “And we in negligent danger.”

neighbour1.text: “the to,” privy to R3 IV. ii. 43 ; in attrib. use freq.=neighbouring.

neighbour2.text: to lie near Ven. 259 “a copse that n-s by.”

neighbourhood.text: friendly relations, neighbourly feeling H5 V. ii. 381 , Tim. IV. i. 17 .

neither.text: used to strengthen a negative = (i) nor that either Gent. II. v. 18 “shall she marry him?— No.—How then? Shall he marry her?—No, neither,” Err. V. i. 94 , 1H4 III. i. 244 ; (ii) either, e.g. Tp. III. ii. 23 “We'll not run . . . —Nor go neither,” Gent. II. iii. 18 “nay, that cannot be so neither” ; (iii) for all that, nevertheless Wint. II. iii. 157 “let it live: It shall not neither” ; also with “but” Ado I. i. 298 [ 290 ], Mer.V. III. v. 8 , All'sW. II. ii. 37 , Ham. V. ii. 121 “and yet but yaw neither, not so ,” by no means Ado III. iii. 152 , MND. III. i. 156 , Cor. IV. v. 176 .

nephew.text: (2 a common 17th cent. sense) 1. cousin 1H6 II. v. 64 , Troil. I. ii. 13 .

nerve.text: sinew, tendon; esp. pl.=the parts of the body in which the chief strength lies Tp. I. ii. 481 , Cor. I. i. 144 , Ham. I. iv. 83 , Cym. III. iii. 94 , Sonn. cxx. 4 ; fig. Meas. I. iv. 53 “the very n-s of state” ; sing. applied to a person Troil. I. iii. 55 “ and bone of Greece.” ∥ The mod. sense is probably represented in Ant. IV. viii. 21 “A brain that nourishes our nerves.”

nervy.text: vigorous, sinewy Cor. II. i. 179 “nervy arm.”

net.text: applied to sophistical argument H5 I. ii. 93 .

nether.text: committed here below Lr. IV. ii. 79 “our nether crimes.”

neuter.text: neutral R2 II. iii. 159 “remain as neuter.”

new.text: 1. newly, freshly, recently, lately John III. i. 233 “even before this truce, but new before,” Tim. I. ii. 81 “they were bleeding new,” Sonn. lvi. 10 “two contracted new.”

next.text: (1 “next way” survives in the midlands) 1. nearest in place Tp. III. ii. 42 “if you prove a mutineer, the next tree!,” Wint. I. ii. 195 “his next neighbour” ; phr. “the way” (lit. and fig.) All'sW. I. iii. 64 “I speak the truth the way,” Wint. III. iii. 129 , 1H4 III. i. 263 .

nice.text: (of somewhat vague use in the 16th-17th cent. and freq. variously explained by comm. on S.; the common mod. sense of ‘agreeable’ is post-S.) 1. wanton, lascivious LLL. III. i. 25 “nice wenches,” Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 179 * .

nicely.text: 1. elegantly, daintily Tw.N. III. i. 17 “they that dally nicely with words,” Cor. II. i. 236 .

nick1.text: sb. (1 developed from the sense of ‘notch used as a means of keeping a score’) 1. “out of all nick,” lit. beyond all reckoning, i.e. exceedingly Gent. IV. ii. 77 .

nick2.text: to cut in nicks or notches Err. V. i. 175 ; fig. to cut short Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 8

nickname.text: to name wrongly Ham. III. i. 153 ; to mention by mistake LLL. V. ii. 350 .

niece.text: grand-daughter R3 IV. i. 1 . ∥ Cf. NEPHEW.

niggard.text: to put off (“with” a small amount of something) Cæs. IV. iii. 227 .

night.text: “What is the ?,” what time of night is it? (cf. DAY 1) Mac. III. iv. 126 ; “good ,” farewell (“to”) Tp. IV. i. 54 “good your vow,” Meas. V. i. 296 “Good to your redress,” Shr. II. i. 295 [ 303 ], R3 IV. iii. 39 “bid the world good ,” Ant. III. viii. 39 [ x. 20 ]; “the ,” during the night, by night (S.) 2H4 IV. v. 124 , R3 IV. iv. 118 “to sleep the ;—on n-(s),” by night (habitually) 2H4 II. i. 85 , II. iv. 251 ; “of the ,” at night MND. II. i. 253 .

nighted.text: dark or black as night (S.) Ham. I. ii. 68 “cast thy colour off” (Qq; Ff “nightly”), Lr. IV. v. 13 “to dispatch His nighted life.”

nightly1.text: 1. belonging to the night, used by night, active at night Gent. II. iv. 133 “ tears,” MND. V. i. 379 “ revels,” Tit. II. iii. 97 “the owl,” Lucr. 680 “ linen,” 1080

nightly2.text: at night MND. II. ii. 6 , Rom. IV. i. 81 .

nill.text: will not; except in the phr. “will he, nill he” ( Ham. V. i. 18 ), “will you, nill you” ( Shr. II. i. 265 [ 273 ]) only archaically in Per. III. Gower 55 “I nill relate,” Pilgr. xiv. 8 [ 188 ] “nill I construe.”

nip.text: 1. “nips i' the head,” gives a decisive check to Meas. III. i. 89 .

nit.text: applied to persons in contempt LLL. IV. i. 152 “most pathetical nit,” Shr. IV. iii. 110 .

nobody.text: in old edd. mostly two words, sometimes hyphened: stressed “no'body” or “nobo'dy.”

nod2.text: to beckon (a person) Ant. III. vi. 66 .

noise1.text: sb. (2 Chaucer applies ‘make noyse’ to the nightingale) 1. rumour, report Troil. I. ii. 12 “The goes,” Lr. III. vi. 120 , Ant. I. ii. 150 “the least noise of this.”

noise2.text: vb. (chiefly in “noise abroad”) 1. to clamour Ant. III. vi. 96 “a trull, That noises it against us.”

nominate.text: to name, call LLL. I. ii. 16 , V. i. 8 , AYL. V. iv. 92 , 2H6 II. i. 129 ; to appoint, specify Mer.V. I. iii. 150 , IV. i. 260 .

nomination.text: naming, mention LLL. IV. ii. 140 , Ham. V. ii. 134 ; specifying, appointing R3 III. iv. 5 .

nonage.text: minority R3 II. iii. 13 “in his nonage.”

nonce.text: “for the ,” for the purpose in hand, on purpose, expressly 1H4 I. ii. 200 “I have cases of buckram for the ,” Ham. IV. vii. 160 “I'll have prepar'd him A chalice for the ” ; as a tag with no special meaning (after the fashion of Middle English poetry) 1H6 II. iii. 57 “This is a riddling merchant for the ”

noncome.text: usu. taken as a nonsensical abbreviation of ‘non compos (mentis)’, but perhaps intended as a substitute for ‘nonplus’ Ado III. v. 68 (Dogberry).

none.text: not any, no John III. iv. 151 “ so small advantage” (=no advantage however small), H8 IV. i. 33 “made of effect,” Ant. I. iii. 36 “ our parts” (= no parts of ours), Cym. I. iv. 108 “ so accomplished a courtier,” vi. 59 “none a stranger.”

nonpareil.text: one that has no equal Tp. III. ii. 111 , Tw.N. I. v. 275 “The of beauty,” Mac. III. iv. 19 , Ant. III. ii. 11 .

nonsuit.text: to reject the suit of Oth. I. i. 16 .

north.text: north wind Oth. V. ii. 218 “as liberal as the ” (Q1 “ayre”), Cym. I. iii. 36 “breathing of the ;—sailed into the of” =‘out of the sunshine of’ (Wright) Tw.N. III. ii. 29 .

nose.text: phr. “by” one's “nose,” under one's very eyes Tit. II. i. 94 ; so “to” one's “nose” Cor. IV. vi. 84 ; “bite, pluck, tweak by the ,” treat with contempt Meas. I. iii. 29 , III. i. 107 , V. i. 339 , Ham. II. ii. 609 [ 601 ]; “Speak i' the nose” Oth. III. i. 4 and “down with the nose” Tim. IV. iii. 158 refer to the effects of venereal disease.

not.text: (obsolete uses) 1. preceding the finite verb Tp. II. i. 128 [ 121 ] “I not doubt,” R3 I. ii. 251 “whose all not equals Edward's moiety,” Ant. II. i. 3 “what they do delay, they not deny.”

notary.text: clerk, secretary (fig.) Lucr. 765 “Dim register and notary of shame!.”

note1.text: sb. (3 occurs once; 5 phr. “of note” is not pre-S.) 1. sign, token, indication Ado III. ii. 54 , Wint. I. ii. 2 , 287 “a note infallible Of breaking honesty,” H5 IV. Chor. 35 “no note How” . . ., Tim. I. ii. 53 * “dangerous notes,” Cym. II. ii. 28 “natural notes about her body.”

note2.text: vb. (1 only in quibbles; 2 borrowed from North's Plutarch) 1. to set music to, provide with notes Troil. V. ii. 11 , Rom. IV. v. 123 .

nothing.text: nothingness Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 628 “admiring the nothing of it.”

notice.text: (the foll. meanings are now arch.) 1. information Gent. II. vi. 36 “I'll give her father Of their . . . flight,” H5 IV. vii. 123 “Bring me just of the numbers dead,” Cæs. III. ii. 275 “they had some ” (=they learned).

notify.text: (twice only) 1. to notice Wiv. II. ii. 86 “she gives you to that” . . .

notion.text: understanding, mind Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 107, Mac. III. i. 83 “a craz'd,” Lr. I. iv. 250 “his weakens.” ∥ The only S. meaning.

nouns.text: perversion of ‘wounds’ in the oath “od's nouns” Wiv. IV. i. 26 .

nourish1.text: nurse (fig.) 1H6 I. i. 50 “Our isle be made a nourish of salt tears (marish†).”

nourish2.text: to support, maintain 2H6 III. i. 348 “Whiles I in Ireland nourish a mighty band.”

novum.text: old game at dice played by five or six persons, the two principal throws being nine and five LLL. V. ii. 545 “Abate throw at novum.”

noyance.text: harm Ham. III. iii. 13 “To keep itself from ”

numb.text: causing chill R3 II. i. 118 “the cold night.”

number1.text: the multitude, the populace Cor. III. i. 71 “us, the honour'd number.”

number2.text: to celebrate in ‘numbers’ or verse (S.) Ant. III. ii. 17 * .

nuncle.text: variant of ‘uncle’ with ‘n’ carried on from ‘mine’, ‘the customary appellation of the licensed fool to his superiors’ (Nares) Lr. I. iv. 117 , &c.

nurse.text: fig. that which fosters or promotes something Gent. III. i. 244 “Time is the and breeder of all good,” H5 V. ii. 35 “Dear of arts,” Ant. V. ii. 8 , Ven. 446 ; so the vb. Meas. III. i. 15 “n-'d by baseness,” H8 V. v. 29 “truth shall nurse her,” Lucr. 141 .

nursery.text: nursing Lr. I. i. 126 . ∥ In Shr. I. i. 2 , Troil. I. iii. 319 the metaphor is taken from gardening; in All'sW. I. ii. 16 = school, sphere of training.

nurture.text: education, training Tp. IV. i. 189 , AYL. II. vii. 97 “I . . . know some nurture.”

nut.text: as a type of something of trifling value Err. IV. iii. 74 .

nuthook.text: beadle, constable Wiv. I. i. 173 , 2H4 V. iv. 8 .

nuzzle1.text: to push with the nose Ven. 1115 “nuzzling in his flank” (Qq “nousling”).

nuzzle2.text: to train “up” Per. I. iv. 42 “to up their babes” (old edd. “nouzle, nouzell,” mod. edd. “nousle†”).

nymph.text: young and beautiful woman Gent. V. iv. 12 , MND. II. i. 245 , &c., Ham. III. i. 89 .

oak.text: the wood of the tree Oth. III. iii. 210 “close as oak” ; the leaves used as a garland Cor. I. iii. 16 , II. ii. 103 ; cf. II. i. 140 “oaken garland.”

oathable.text: fit to take an oath Tim. IV. iii. 136 .

obedient.text: of obedience All'sW. II. iii. 167 “that right,” 1H4 V. i. 17 “move in that obedient orb.”

obey.text: twice construed with “to” Troil. III. i. 167 “his stubborn buckles . . . Shall more than to the edge of steel,” Phoen. 4 “To whose sound chaste wings obey.”

object.text: to urge 1H6 II. iv. 43 “it is well objected.”

object1.text: often somewhat specific=one that excites love or pity or their opposites MND. IV. i. 176 “The and the pleasure of mine eye, Is only Helena,” H8 I. i. 127 (see ABJECT), Troil. IV. v. 106 , Tim. IV. iii. 123 “Swear against objects” (i.e. be not moved to pity), Ven. 255 “her object will away.”

object2.text: presentation (of something) to the eye or the perception Troil. II. ii. 41 “reason flies the of all harm,” Cor. I. i. 21 “the object of our misery.”

objection.text: charge, accusation 1H6 IV. i. 129 , 2H6 I. iii. 158 , H8 III. ii. 308 “I dare your worst o-”

obligation.text: bond, contract Wiv. I. i. 11 “quittance, or ,” 2H6 IV. ii. 104 “he can make obligations.”

oblique.text: indirect Troil. V. i. 61 “ memorial of cuckolds,” Tim. IV. iii. 18 “all is ” † (old edd. “All's obliquie”).

obloquy.text: reproach, disgrace All'sW. IV. ii. 44 , Lucr. 523 “thou, the author of their obloquy.”

obscene.text: disgusting, repulsive LLL. I. i. 242 “that most and preposterous event,” R2 IV. i. 131 “so . . . a deed,” 1H4 II. iv. 256 “, greasy tallow-catch.”

obscenely.text: misused in LLL. IV. i. 147 , MND. I. ii. 112 .

obscure.text: adj. (stressed like ENTIRE) 1. dark, dim Mer.V. II. vii. 51 “the o'bscure grave,” Ven. 237 “brakes obscu're and rough” ; loving the darkness Mac. II. iii. 65 “The o'bscure bird.”

obscurely.text: in the dark Lucr. 1250 ; not openly Cæs. I. ii. 324 .

obsequies.text: dutiful acts performed in memory of one departed 3H6 I. iv. 147 , Rom. V. iii. 16 , 20

obsequious.text: (2 this sense is mainly S.) 1. dutiful, obedient Wiv. IV. ii. 2 “I see you are in your love,” Meas. II. iv. 29 “in fondness Crowd to his presence.”

observance.text: (obs. or arch. uses are) 1. respectful attention, dutiful service, reverence Wiv. II. ii. 207 “a doting ,” AYL. V. ii. 103 , 2H4 IV. iii. 16 “do ,” Troil. I. iii. 31 “With due of thy god-like seat,” Oth. III. iv. 148 (Qq “obseruances,” Ff2 3 4 “observance,” F1 “obseruancie”).

observation.text: (2 cf. OBSERVANCE 1, OBSERVANT, and OBSERVE) 1. observance (of rites) MND. IV. i. 110 .

observe.text: to show respectful attention to, pay court to, humour, gratify 2H4 IV. iv. 30 , Tim. IV. iii. 213 “his very breath, whom thou'lt ,” Ham. III. i. 163 “The observed of all observers.”

obstruct.text: impediment, bar Ant. III. vi. 61 “Being an 'tween his lust and him” (Ff “abstract”). ∥ A word not otherwise known.

obstruction.text: 1. shutting out of light Tw.N. IV. ii. 44 .

occasion.text: (3 only S.) 1. opportunity for attacking or fault-finding John IV. ii. 62 “To grace occasions” ; (?) AYL. IV. i. 184 * (see 3 below).

occupation.text: handicraft, trade, business Meas. IV. ii. 36 , &c., Cor. IV. i. 14 , vi. 98 “the voice of ” (=vote of working men), Cæs. I. ii. 269 , Ant. IV. iv. 17 “The royal occupation.”

occupy.text: to have to do with carnally Rom. II. iv. 108 (quibblingly). ∥ In consequence of its vulgar use in this sense, this vb. was little used in literature in the 17th and 18th cent.; cf. 2H4 II. iv. 159 “as odious as the word ‘occupy’.”

odd.text: (the sense ‘strange, peculiar’ is not pre-S.) 1. at variance “with” Troil. IV. v. 264 .

odds.text: (2 esp. in phr. “at ”; 3 the commonest S. sense; the betting sense in “lay odds” 2H4 V. v. 111 is not pre-S.) 1. “make all even,” level inequalities Meas. III. i. 41 “death . . . That makes these odds all even.”

oeillade.text: amorous glance, ogle Wiv. I. iii. 66 , Lr. IV. v. 25 .

of.text: (1 now represented by ‘off’; 4 a prevailing use of this prep. down to 1600) 1. from, away from Err. II. ii. 140 “tear the stain'd skin of my harlot-brow” (mod. edd. “off”), All'sW. III. iv. 1 “take the letter of her.”

off1.text: adv. (idiomatic uses with vbs. will be found under these vbs.; 3 not pre-S., still in dial. use) 1. beside the mark Cor. II. ii. 65 “that's off.”

off2.text: “off the matter,” irrelevantly (see MATTER 3) Ado III. v. 10 (old edd. “of”: see OF 1).

offcap.text: to doff the cap Oth. I. i. 10 .

offence.text: （‘transgression, fault’ is the most freq. sense, with phr. “do, make offence”) 1. hurt, harm, injury MND. II. ii. 23 , AYL. III. v. 117 , John II. i. 75 “To do and scathe,” Cæs. II. i. 268 “sick ” (=‘cause of harmful malady’, Aldis Wright), IV. iii. 200 “Doing himself ,” Oth. II. iii. 224 .

offend.text: (senses ‘annoy, vex physically or morally’ and ‘do amiss, transgress’ are common) 1. to sin against, wrong (a person), violate (a law) Meas. III. ii. 16 “he hath o-ed the law,” AYL. I. iii. 55 “Never . . . Did I your highness,” R3 I. iv. 228 , Lr. I. ii. 181 , Oth. V. ii. 59 , Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 49 “I have offended reputation.”

offender.text: one who wrongs another Sonn. xxxiv. 11 .

offer.text: (app. absol. for ‘offer battle’) 1. to act on the offensive, make an attack 1H4 IV. i. 69 “we of the o-ing side,” 2H4 IV. i. 219 “his power, like to a fangless lion, May offer, but not hold.”

office1.text: (the chief S. meanings are ‘service performed’, ‘duty’, ‘function’, ‘official position’) 1. proper function or action Oth. III. iv. 112 “with all the office of my heart.”

office2.text: 1. to perform as a service All'sW. III. ii. 129 “angels offic'd all.”

officer.text: 1. one who performs a service, agent Gent. I. ii. 43 , Shr. V. ii. 37 “Spoke like an officer,” All'sW. III. v. 17 “a filthy officer he is,” Cæs. IV. ii. 7 , Ant. III. i. 17 .

officious.text: zealous in one's duty Tit. V. ii. 202 .

oft.text: frequent Sonn. xiv. 8 “By oft predict” ; so often AYL. IV. i. 20 “by often rumination.”

oho.text: (also written “O ho, Oh ho”) 1. mockery Tp. I. ii. 349 , IV. i. 227 , Shr. V. ii. 57 .

old1.text: old age Troil. II. ii. 104 “mid-age and wrinkled old” (Ff1; Q “elders,” mod. edd. “eld”†). ∥ In Eliz. times used chiefly in phr. ‘old (=wane) of the moon’.

old2.text: early form of ‘wold’ Lr. III. iv. 123 .

old3.text: adj. (4 remains in midland dial.) 1. belonging to or characteristic of advanced age Tp. I. ii. 369 “old cramps,” Lr. I. i. 190 “his old course” ; Sonn. ii. 11 “my old excuse.”

omit.text: (the foll. are the rarer uses) 1. to take no notice of, disregard Meas. IV. iii. 80 , 2H4 IV. iv. 27 , 2H6 III. ii. 382 “Omitting Suffolk's exile, my soul's treasure,” Cor. III. i. 145 .

omittance.text: omission AYL. III. v. 133 “ is no quittance.”

omnipotent.text: ‘almighty’, arrant 1H4 I. ii. 121 “the most omnipotent villain.”

on.text: prep. (2 orig. often an actual difference of idiom, but from Eliz. times resulting from confusion of OF and ON, both of which were reduced to o') 1. =from Lr. V. iii. 167 * “what art thou That hast this fortune on me?”; often taken=against (cf. UPON).

once.text: (1 esp. with “an, if”=if even, if at all) 1. at any time, ever, at all Ado V. i. 218 “an you be a cursing hypocrite once,” 1H6 V. iii. 58 , Cym. V. iii. 78 , Sonn. lvii. 8 “When you have bid your servant once adieu” (“when . . . once”=whenever, every time).

onset.text: beginning, start Gent. III. ii. 94 “give the to thy good advice,” Sonn. xc. 11 .

onyx.text: variety of quartz allied to agate Ham. V. ii. 286 (Ff “union”).

open1.text: (2 chiefly in “lay open”; 3 chiefly in “open hand”) 1. public Meas. II. i. 140 “an room,” H8 II. i. 168 “We are too here to argue this,” Rom. V. iii. 193 “With outcry” ; so “in ,” in public H8 III. ii. 405 ; also adv.=publicly Tw.N. III. iii. 37 “Do not then walk too ”

open2.text: 1. to disclose, reveal (a matter) Gent. I. i. 137 , H5 I. I. 78, I. ii. 16 “o-ing titles miscreate,” Ham. II. ii. 18 , Cym. V. v. 42 “I would not Believe her lips in o-ing it.”

operant.text: active Ham. III. ii. 186 “My powers” ; potent Tim. IV. iii. 25 “thy most operant poison.”

operation.text: efficacy Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 26 “if knife, drugs, serpents, have Edge, sting, or operation.”

opinion.text: (4 app. peculiar to S.) 1. censure Oth. IV. ii. 108 .

opportunity.text: misused for ‘importunity’ Wiv. III. iv. 20 * . ∥ This use is found in other writers.

oppose.text: 1. to expose H8 IV. i. 67 “opposing freely The beauty of her person to the people,” Lr. IV. vii. 32 “To be o-'d against the warring winds” (Qq “exposd”).

opposed.text: 1. opposite, contrary Mer.V. II. ix. 62 “of natures,” 1H4 III. i. 111 “the opposed continent.”

opposite1.text: antagonist, adversary, opponent Tw.N. III. iv. 296 “the most skilful, bloody, and fatal ,” R3 V. iv. 3 “Daring an to every danger,” Lr. V. iii. 43 “the o-s of this day's strife.”

opposite2.text: hostile, antagonistic, adverse 2H6 III. ii. 251 , R3 IV. iv. 216 “at their births good stars were ,” Tim. I. i. 285 “ to humanity,” Lr. II. i. 51 , Oth. I. ii. 67 “ to marriage” ; const. “with” Tw.N. II. v. 164 “Be opposite with a kinsman,” R3 II. ii. 94 .

opposition.text: (not pre-S. in these senses; 1 is peculiar to S.) 1. offering for combat Ham. V. ii. 178 “the of your person in trial.”

oppress.text: (the lit. sense of ‘press’ is traceable in Lucr. 1242 ; cf. OPPRESSION 1) 1. to suppress Per. III. Gower 29 “The mutiny . . . t' ”

oppression.text: 1. pressure, burden R2 III. iv. 31 “ of their . . . weight,” Rom. I. iv. 24 “To great for a tender thing.”

or1.text: before Ham. V. ii. 30 (Ff “Ere”); esp. “or e'er” (in old edd. often spelt “ere”); once “or ever” Ham. I. ii. 183 “Or ever I had seen” (Ff “Ere I had euer seen”).

or2.text: conj. 2 (“or . . . or”=either . . . or, is very freq.) 1. “or . . . or” introduces alternative questions Mer.V. III. ii. 64 “Tell me where is fancy bred, Or in the heart or in the head?,” Cym. IV. ii. 356 “How! a page! Or dead or sleeping on him?” ; so “Or whether . . . Or whether” Sonn. cxiv. 1 , 3

orator.text: advocate Lucr. 30 “Beauty itself doth of itself persuade The eyes of men without an orator.”

orb.text: (6 is derived from 2) 1. circle MND. II. i. 9 “her orbs upon the green” (=fairy rings).

orbed.text: spherical; (of the sun) Tw.N. V. i. 281 ; (of the earth) Ham. III. ii. 168 , Compl. 25 .

ordain.text: (the most freq. sense is ‘decree’) 1. to establish, found, institute Shr. III. i. 10 “why music was o-'d,” 1H6 IV. i. 33 , Cym. III. i. 56 .

order1.text: sb. (1 a common 16th-17th cent. sense) 1. suitable measures for the accomplishment of a purpose Meas. II. ii. 25 “There shall be for't” ; esp. in phr. “take ,” take measures or steps, make necessary arrangements All'sW. IV. ii. 55 “I'll take my mother shall not hear,” R2 V. i. 53 “there is ta'en for you,” 1H6 III. ii. 126 “Now will we take some order in the town,” Oth. V. ii. 72 .

order2.text: ‘to regulate, direct, govern’, is the only S. sense; in R2 V. iii. 140 ‘to regulate the conveyance of (troops)’.

orderly.text: properly, duly, according to rule Mer.V. II. ii. 186 [ 179 ], Shr. IV. iii. 94 , Ham. III. ii. 222 .

ordinance.text: (in old edd. also “ord(e)nance, ord'nance”) 1. dispensation of providence, decree of destiny R3 IV. iv. 184 “God's just ,” Lr. IV. i. 69 , Cym. IV. ii. 145 “Let ordinance Come as the gods foresay it.”

ordinary.text: (1 not pre-Eliz.) 1. public meal regularly provided at a fixed price in an eating-house or tavern All'sW. II. iii. 210 ; used vaguely Ant. II. ii. 233 .

ordinate.text: (?) directing Ham. V. ii. 48 “even in that was heaven ” ∥ Perhaps a ref. to the phr. ‘ordinate power’ (of God) = the divine power as exhibited in the order of mundane things; but Qq read “ordinant.”

organ.text: (2 used sometimes absol., where mod. usage would require a qualifying phr. to be added) 1. musical instrument Ham. III. ii. 392 [ 385 ] “there is much music . . . in this little organ” (viz. a pipe).

orient.text: applied to pearls as coming anciently from the East MND. IV. i. 60 , Ant. I. v. 41 ; hence applied to a tear Ven. 981 “an orient drop.”

orifex.text: erron. form of ‘orifice’ Troil V. ii. 148 .

original.text: origin MND. II. i. 117 , 2H4 I. ii. 132 .

orison.text: prayer H5 II. ii. 53 , Ham. III. i. 89 .

ornament.text: pl. equipment, attire Shr. IV. iii. 61 , 1H6 V. i. 54 “For clothing me in these grave o-s,” Rom. I. i. 99 .

orphan.text: (?) = UNFATHERED, q.v. Wiv. V. v. 45 “You heirs of fixed destiny” (addressed to fairies).

ort.text: fragment of food, also fig. Troil. V. ii. 155 “The fractions of her faith, orts of her love,” Tim. IV. iii. 402 , Lucr. 985 “a beggar's orts to crave.”

orthography.text: app. an error for ‘orthographer’ in Ado II. iii. 21 (Rowe “orthographer”†, Capell “orthographist”†).

osprey.text: large diurnal bird of prey feeding on fish, Pandion Haliaëtus Cor. IV. vii. 34 (Ff “Aspray”).

ostent.text: manifestation, show, display Mer.V. II. ii. 211 “well studied in a sad ,” II. viii. 44 “such fair o-s of love,” H5 v. Chor. 21, Per. I. ii. 25 “th' ostent† of war” (old edd. “the stint”).

ostentation.text: (opprobrious sense once LLL. V. ii. 410 ) 1. show, exhibition, display Ado IV. i. 207 , R2 II. iii. 95 , Cor. I. vi. 86 , Ham. IV. v. 215 , Ant. III. vi. 52 .

other.text: adj., and sb. or pron. (“other” as a pl. is freq.) 1. each preceding (one) Meas. IV. iv. 2 “Every letter he hath writ has disvouched other,” R2 I. i. 22 “Each day still better other's happiness!,” Cæs. I. ii. 229 “every time gentler than other.”

othergates.text: in another way Tw.N. V. i. 199 . ∥ Survives in the north and Warwickshire.

ouch.text: brooch; pl. used vaguely=gems, jewels 2H4 II. iv. 52 “brooches, pearls, and ouches.”

ought.text: owed 1H4 III. iii. 151 “you him a thousand pound.”

ouph.text: elf, goblin Wiv. IV. iv. 51 , V. v. 63 (Ff). ∥ The synonymous forms ‘auf’, ‘oaf’, ‘ouph’ appear in literature about 1620- 5

ousel.text: blackbird MND. III. i. 131 “The -cock, so black of hue” ; applied to a person of dark hair or complexion (?) 2H4 III. ii. 9 “Alas! a black ousel.”

out.text: expressing abhorrence, reproach, or indignation Gent. II. vii. 54 “Out, out, Lucetta! that will be ill-favour'd,” MND. III. ii. 65 “Out, dog! out, cur!,” R3 I. iii. 118 “Out, devil!,” Lr. IV. vi. 250 “Out, dunghill!” ; so “out upon” (freq.) Wiv. I. iv. 174 “Out upon't! what have I forgot?” ; also with words of lamentation (“alack, alas”) Wiv. I. iv. 37 , Oth. V. ii. 117 , Sonn. xxxiii. 11 .

out1.text: adv. (obs. or peculiar uses; see also OUT OF) 1. without, outside Wiv. V. v. 62 “within and out.”

out2.text: prep. (2 cf. OUT adv. 1) 1. out of, from within 2H4 II. ii. 27 , Cor. V. ii. 41 “pushed out your gates” ; so “from out” Mer.V. III. iv. 21 , R2 III. iii. 64 .

outbrag.text: ‘to exceed in pride of beauty’ (Schmidt) Compl. 95 .

outbrave.text: (2 cf. BRAVERY 2) 1. to surpass in valour Mer.V. II. i. 28 .

outcrafty.text: to excel in craft Cym. III. iv. 15 .

outdare.text: 1. to brave, defy R2 I. i. 190 “this outdar'd dastard,” 1H4 V. i. 40 .

outdwell.text: to stay beyond Mer.V. II. vi. 3 .

outface.text: (1 the usual S. sense) 1. to stare down, (hence) put out of countenance Err. V. i. 245 , Mer.V. IV. ii. 17 “ them, and outswear them too,” Ham. V. i. 300 “To me with leaping in her grave” ; to browbeat, intimidate John II. i. 97 “hast . . . O-d infant state” ; to frighten away “from” 1H4 II. iv. 287 .

outjest.text: to dispel by means of jesting Lr. III. i. 16 “the fool, who labours to His heart-struck injuries.”

outlaw.text: used vaguely = exile 1H4 IV. iii. 58 ; so outlawed, banished Lr. III. iv. 171 .

outlive.text: intr. to survive Tit. II. iii. 132 .

outlook.text: to look or stare down John V. ii. 115 .

outnight.text: to outdo in mentioning nights Mer.V. V. i. 23 “I would outnight you.”

outprize.text: to exceed in value Cym. I. iv. 93 “she's outprized by a trifle.”

outrage.text: violent conduct or language, fury John III. iv. 106 , 1H6 IV. i. 126 “this immodest clamorous outrage,” R3 I. iii. 277 , II. iv. 64 , Rom. V. iii. 216 .

outsell.text: fig. to exceed in value Cym. II. iv. 102 , III. v. 74 .

outsleep.text: to sleep beyond MND. V. i. 374 .

outspeak.text: to describe what is more than (something) H8 III. ii. 128 .

outsport.text: to go beyond (limits) in revelling Oth. II. iii. 3 “Not to outsport discretion.”

outstretch.text: to stretch to its limit Tim. V. iii. 3 .

outstrike.text: to deal swifter blows than Ant. IV. vi. 36 “a swifter mean Shall outstrike thought.”

outward.text: outward appearance, exterior Troil. III. ii. 169 , Sonn. lxix. 5 , Compl. 80 .

outward1.text: not having an intimate knowledge of things All'sW. III. i. 11 .

outward2.text: externally Meas. III. i. 87 “This sainted deputy,” Ado I. ii. 9 , Ham. II. ii. 401 [ 392 ] (Ff).

outwards.text: externally Ham. II. ii. 401 [ 392 ] “must show fairly outwards” (Qq).

outwork.text: to excel in workmanship Ant. II. ii. 209 .

outworth.text: to be worth more than H8 I. i. 123 .

overblown.text: blown over Tp. II. ii. 119 “Is the storm ?” ; chiefly fig. past Shr. V. ii. 3 “perils ,” R2 III. ii. 190 , 2H6 I. iii. 155 “my choler being ,” R3 II. iv. 61 .

overbuy.text: to buy at a higher price Cym. I. i. 146 (‘I am worth but a small fraction of what, in giving himself, he has given for me,’ Dowden).

overcome.text: to take by surprise Mac. III. iv. 111 “ us like a summer's cloud.”

overflow.text: excess, superfluity R2 V. iii. 64 “Thy of good converts to bad.”

overglance.text: to cast the eye over LLL. IV. ii. 137 .

overgo.text: to go beyond, exceed R3 II. ii. 61 , Sonn. ciii. 7 ; to overcome, oppress 3H6 II. v. 123 .

overhear.text: to hear over again (S.) LLL. V. ii. 95 .

overlook.text: (cf. O'ERLOOK) 1. to overtop H5 III. v. 9 “Shall . . . Our scions . . . Spirt up . . . And over look their grafters?.”

overlusty.text: too lively H5 IV. Chor. 18 , Lr. II. iv. 9 .

overpeer.text: (1 cf. O'ERPEER) 1. to look over or down upon 1H6 I. iv. 11 “to the city, And thence discover how” . . .

overplus.text: sb. surplus Ant. III. vii. 50 “Our of shipping” ; phr. “in ,” in excess Sonn. cxxxv. 2 ;— adv. in addition Ant. IV. vi. 22 .

overscutched.text: “ huswife” (see HUSWIFE 2), app.= ‘overswitcht housewife, i.e. a whore; a ludicrous word’ (Ray's North Country Words, 1674 ). ∥ ‘Overscutched’ means literally ‘over-beaten’; ‘scutch’ and ‘switch’ were synonymous terms =rod, whip.

oversee.text: （‘o'ersee’ does not occur) 1. to see, attend to Lucr. 1205 .

overshot.text: wide of the mark, in error LLL. I. i. 141 “So study evermore is ,” H5 III. vii. 139 .

overslip.text: to pass unnoticed by Gent. II. ii. 9 , Lucr. 1576 .

overswear.text: to swear over again Tw.N. V. i. 279 .

overtake.text: Cor. I. ix. 19 “Hath overta'en my act,” hath done an act equal to my own.

overthrow.text: “have the ,” be defeated 1H6 III. ii. 106 ; “give the overthrow,” defeat Cæs. V. ii. 5 .

overture.text: disclosure Wint. II. i. 171 , Lr. III. vii. 89 “made the of thy treasons to us.” ∥ Occurs also in the sense ‘proposal’. In Cor. I. ix. 46 * not satisfactorily explained (Steevens “coverture”†).

overween.text: to be arrogant or presumptuous 2H4 IV. i. 149 , Tit. II. i. 29 ; chiefly in overweening, arrogant, presumptuous Tw.N. II. v. 34 , R3 V. iii. 329 .

overworn.text: stale Tw.N. III. i. 67 “the word is ”

owd.text: northern dial. form of ‘old’ Oth. II. iii. 100 “take thine owd cloak about thee” (Q1; Qq2 3 “auld,” Ff “awl'd”), a line of an old song.

owe.text: to possess, own, have Tp. I. ii. 451 “Thou dost here usurp The name thou ow'st not,” John IV. ii. 99 “That blood which ow'd the breadth of all this isle,” Mac. I. iii. 76 “Say from whence You owe this strange intelligence,” Oth. I. i. 66 “What a full fortune does the thick-lips owe” . . . ∥ The orig. meaning, and almost as freq. in S. as the mod. meaning of ‘be indebted or under obligation’.

own1.text: to have (a certain function) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 143

own2.text: Tp. V. i. 213 “When no man was his own” = master of his senses.

oxhead.text: used with ref. to cuckoldry (cf. HORN 1) John II. i. 292 .

oxlip.text: flowering herb uniting features of the cowslip and the primrose MND. II. i. 250 .

oyes.text: call of the public crier = hear (Fr. ‘oyez’) Wiv. V. v. 47 , Troil. IV. v. 142 .

pace1.text: phr. All'sW. IV. v. 71 “has no pace,” is under no restraint; “hold me pace,” keep pace with me 1H4 III. i. 49 .

pace2.text: to train (a horse) in its paces (e.g. to amble) H8 V. iii. 22 , Ant. II. ii. 68 ; fig. Meas. IV. iii. 141 “pace your wisdom In that good path that I would wish it go,” Per. IV. vi. 68 “she's not paced yet.”

pack.headword: pack vb. 2 (1 cf. PACK sb. and PACKING
pack.text: 3 now associated with the idea of packing up) 1. to conspire Tit. IV. ii. 157 “Go pack with him.”

pack1.text: confederacy, conspiring gang Wiv. IV. ii. 126 “a knot, a ging, a ,” Err. IV. iv. 104 , R3 III. iii. 4 , Lr. V. iii. 18 . ∥ Apparently a blending of “pack” =bundle, used fig., and the Eliz. “pack”=plot, conspiracy, intrigue.

pack2.text: 1. to load 1H4 II. i. 3 “our horse not packed,” 2H4 IV. v. 75 “Our thighs packed with wax.”

packhorse.text: fig. drudge R3 I. iii. 122 , Lucr. 928 .

packing.text: plotting Shr. V. i. 121 , Lr. III. i. 26 .

paction.text: compact H5 V. ii. 393 (Ff1 2 “pation,” Ff3 4 “passion,” not in Q).

paddle.text: to play fondly with the fingers Ham. III. iv. 185 , Oth. II. i. 261 ; trans. to finger fondly Wint. I. ii. 116 .

paddock.text: toad Ham. III. iv. 190 ; (?) ‘familiar spirit in the shape of a toad’ (Schmidt) Mac. I. i. 9 “Paddock calls.—Anon.”

page.text: to attend, follow Tim. IV. iii. 225 “ thy heels.”

pageant1.text: sb. (orig.=scene or act in a mediæval mystery play) 1. theatrical representation; hence, show, spectacle, sight Tp. IV. i. 155 “this insubstantial ,” Gent. IV. iv. 166 “When all our p-s of delight were play'd,” MND. III. ii. 114 “their fond ” (=the foolish spectacle they present), H8 IV. i. 11 “shows, P-s,” Troil. III. iii. 276 “the of Ajax” ; occas. false show Oth. I. iii. 18 “a pageant To keep us in false gaze.”

pain1.text: sb. (1 chiefly in phr. “on pain of,” also “in pain of” 2H6 III. ii. 257 ; 2 the pl. in this sense is freq.; “for thy pains” Wiv. III. iv. 104 has not its mod. ironical sense) 1. punishment, penalty Meas. II. iv. 86 “his offence is so, as it appears Accountant to the law upon that pain.”

pain2.text: to put to trouble Meas. V. i. 387 .

painful.text: laborious, toilsome (of actions, &c.) LLL. II. i. 23 “ study,” H5 IV. iii. 111 “marching in the field,” Cor. IV. v. 74 “the service” ; (rarely of persons) toiling Sonn. xxv. 9 “The painful warrior.”

painfully.text: laboriously LLL. I. i. 74 , John II. i. 223 .

paint.text: to flatter with specious words LLL. IV. i. 16 “Nay, never paint me now.”

painted.text: specious, feigned, unreal AYL. II. i. 3 “ pomp,” John. III. i. 105 “ peace,” Tit. II. iii. 126 “that hope,” Ham. III. i. 53 “my most painted word.”

painting.text: paint Wint. V. iii. 83 “You'll . . . stain your own” [lip] “With oily ,” Cor. I. vi. 68 ; H8 I. i. 26 “as a ” (=as good as using cosmetics for heightening the colour).

pajock.text: of unknown meaning, app. intended as an obscure substitute for ‘ass’ Ham. III. ii. 300 . ∥ Commonly taken to be a form of ‘peacock’; perhaps identical with ‘patchocke’, Spenser's name for the degenerate English in Ireland.

palate.text: vb. (not pre-S.) 1. to enjoy the taste of, relish Troil. IV. i. 59 , Ant. V. ii. 7 “never palates more the dung (dug†).”

pale.text: “ at mine heart”=PALE-HEARTED Meas. IV. iii. 161 .

pale1.text: sb. 1 (3 see PALE sb. 2 ). 1. pl. palings, palisade H8 V. iv. 96 .

pale2.text: paleness, pallor Ven. 589 “a sudden pale . . . Usurps her cheeks” ; also probably in Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 4 (see PALE sb. 1 3).

palfrey.text: saddle-horse H5 III. vii. 29 , 2H6 IV. ii. 78 , Tit. V. ii. 50 , Ven. 384 .

palisado.text: fence made of stakes 1H4 II. iii. 57 .

pall1.text: to fail Ham. V. ii. 9 “plots do pall.”

pall2.text: to cover as with a pall Mac. I. v. 52 .

pallet.text: mean bed 2H4 III. i. 10 (Ff “pallads,” a common 16th-18th cent. form).

palliament.text: white gown of a candidate for the Roman consulship Tit. I. i. 182 .

palm.text: used chiefly as an emblem of victory; also applied to a conspicuous person Tim. V. i. 14 .

palmer.text: pilgrim (properly one from the Holy Land, bearing a palm-leaf) Rom. I. v. 104 .

palsy.text: as adj.=palsied Troil. I. iii. 174 “ fumbling.”

palter.text: to shuffle, play fast and loose, use trickery Cor. III. i. 57 , Cæs. II. i. 126 , Mac. V. vii. 49 20] “ with us in a double sense,” Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 63 viii. “dodge And palter in the shifts of lowness.”

pamphlet.text: small composition in writing 1H6 III. i. 2 , Lucr. Ded. 1

pander.text: to minister to the gratification of Ham. III. iv. 88 “And reason panders will.”

pang.text: to cause pangs H8 II. iii. 15 .

pantaloon.text: enfeebled old man, old fool (S.) AYL. II. vii. 158 , Shr. III. i. 37 .

pantler.text: servant who had charge of the pantry Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 56, 2H4 II. iv. 258 , Cym. II. iii. 129 .

paper1.text: note fastened on the back of a criminal undergoing punishment, specifying his offence LLL. IV. iii. 48 , 2H6 II. iv. 31 .

paper2.text: to set down on paper H8 I. i. 80 “Must fetch him in he p-s” (Campbell “the papers”†, Staunton “he paupers”†).

paradox.text: statement or tenet contrary to received opinion Ham. III. i. 116 “this was sometime a , but now the time gives it proof.” ∥ The orig. sense; the ordinary meaning of ‘self-contradictory statement’ is commoner in S.

paragon.text: (2 and 3 are only S.) 1. to compare Ant. I. v. 71 “If thou with Cæsar again My man of men.”

parallel1.text: adj. coinciding with a person's wish or purpose Oth. II. iii. 358 ;—sb. pl. parallel lines Troil. I. iii. 168 “as near as the extremest ends Of p-s” ; transf. furrows, wrinkles Sonn. lx. 10 .

parallel2.text: vb. (1 and 3 not pre-S.; 2 only S.) 1. to bring into ‘line’ or conformity “with” Meas. IV. ii. 82 .

parcel1.text: sb. (1 cf. phr. ‘part and parcel of . . .’) 1. part, portion Wiv. I. i. 237 “that the lips is of the mouth,” Err. V. i. 106 “a branch and of my oath,” 1H4 II. iv. 115 , H8 III. ii. 126 , Cor. I. ii. 32 “Some p-s of their power,” Oth. I. iii. 154 “by parcels.”

parcel2.text: (a) to make up into a mass, (b) to specify Ant. V. ii. 162 * .

pard.text: panther or leopard Tp. IV. i. 264 “more pinchspotted . . . Than pard,” AYL. II. vii. 150 .

pardon1.text: leave, permission Ado II. i. 356 , LLL. IV. ii. 104 “Under ,” Ham. IV. vii. 46 “first asking your thereunto,” Ant. III. vi. 60 “I begg'd His for return.”

pardon2.text: vb. (2 cf. PARDON sb.) 1. to remit (a penalty) Mer.V. IV. i. 370 “I thee thy life,” Lr. IV. vi. 112 “I pardon that man's life.”

paritor.text: apparitor or summoning officer of an ecclesiastical court LLL. III. i. 196 [ 188 ] (Q1 Ff1 2 3 “Parretors,” Q2 “Parritors,” F4 “Parators”).

parkward.text: “the ” (S.), to ward the park Wiv. III. i. 5 .

parle.text: freq. in the same sense as “parley,” which is also common; e.g. 3H6 V. i. 16 .

parlous.text: [contracted from ‘perilous’] 1. perilous, dangerous AYL. III. ii. 46 “in a state.”

parmaceti.text: 16th cent. corruption of ‘spermaceti’ surviving dialectally 1H4 I. iii. 58 .

part1.text: sb. (6 “on the part of” occurs also in mod. sense) 1. “the better ,” the greater part Mer.V. I. i. 16 , AYL. III. i. 2 , 2H4 I. ii. 180 ; “a little ,” a little Tim. III. ii. 53 ; “no part,” not at all All'sW. II. i. 135 .

part2.text: vb. (the freq. S. senses ‘divide into parts’ and ‘share with others, take a share of’ are now rare; 3 is common) 1. “ from” = ‘part with’, give up Mer.V. III. ii. 173 “Which when you part from, lose, or give away.”

partake.text: (3 is peculiar to S.) 1. to take some of Wint. II. i. 40 “one may drink, depart, And yet partake no venom.”

partial.text: Meas. II. i. 31 “nothing . . . ,” no partiality; R2 I. iii. 241 “A slander,” an imputation of partiality.

partialize.text: to render partial R2 I. i. 120 .

partially.text: with undue favour Oth. II. iii. 220 , Lucr. 634 .

participate2.text: to share in common with others Tw.N. V. i. 248 * .

particular1.text: 1. detail All'sW. IV. iii. 207 “let me answer to the of the inter'gatories,” 1H4 II. iv. 419 , 2H4 IV. iv. 90 “With every course in his ,” Cor. II. iii. 48 * “by p-s” (=one by one, in detail), Ham. II. ii. 248 “question more in particular.”

particular2.text: private, personal Meas. IV. iv. 30 “no scandal,” 2H4 IV. iii. 52 , H5 III. ii. 88 “my knowledge,” H8 II. iii. 101 , Cor. IV. v. 92 , Lr. V. i. 30 “these domestic and particular broils.”

particularities.text: individual affairs or matters H5 III. ii. 145 , 2H6 V. ii. 44 .

particularly.text: individually Cor. IV. v. 72 “To thee ,” Tim. I. i. 47 “my free drift Halts not ” (= at any individual person).

partner.text: (2 cf. ‘partner with a thief’, Prov. xxix. 24 ) 1. fellow-sponsor H8 V. iii. 167 , V. v. 6 .

party.text: (1 cf. PART sb. 5) 1. side in a contest, (a particular) cause or interest John I. i. 34 “Upon the right and of her son,” &c., R2 III. ii. 203 , 1H6 II. iv. 32 “dare maintain the of the truth,” R3 IV. iv. 527 “they came . . . Upon his ,” Lr. II. i. 28 “have you nothing said Upon his party . . .?.”

pash1.text: head Wint. I. ii. 129 . ∥ Now chiefly a Scottish word, but surviving in Cheshire in the sense of ‘brains’.

pash2.text: to strike violently, smash Troil. II. iii. 217 “I'll pash him o'er the face” (Q “push”), V. v. 10 “the pashed corses of the kings.” ∥ Only in this play; common in Warwickshire in this sense.

pass1.text: sb. (8 only S. and in echoes) 1. passage H5 II. Chor. 39 “To give you gentle ,” Ham. II. ii. 77 “to give quiet pass.”

pass2.text: vb. (13 common 16th-17th cent.) 1. to die, ‘pass away’ 2H6 III. iii. 25 “let him peaceably,” Lr. IV. vi. 48 , V. iii. 315 .

passable.text: 1. current (like coin) Cor. V. ii. 13 “the virtue of your name Is not here passable.”

passado.text: forward thrust with the sword, one foot being advanced at the same time LLL. I. ii. 188 , Rom. II. iv. 27 , III. i. 90 .

passage.text: 1. passing of people, people passing by Err. III. i. 99 , Oth. V. i. 37 .

passing.text: adj. surpassing, extreme Gent. I. ii. 17 “a shame,” II. i. 83 , 3H6 V. i. 106 “O traitor” ;—adv. pre-eminently, exceedingly (freq.)

passion1.text: sb. (applied widely to all kinds of feeling by which the mind is powerfully moved, e.g. mirth John III. iii. 47 , H5 II. ii. 132 ; 2 is a special application; cf. the vb.) 1. painful affection or disorder of the body Err. V. i. 47 , 1H4 III. i. 35 , Mac. III. iv. 57 .

passion2.text: sorrow, grieve Tp. V. i. 24 , Gent. IV. iv. 174 , LLL. I. i. 261 , Ven. 1059 .

passionate1.text: adj. (1 cf. PASSION sb. 2, and vb.) 1. grieved, sorrowful Gent. I. ii. 121 , LLL. III. i. 1 , John II. i. 544 “She is sad and passionate.”

passionate2.text: to express with passion Tit. III. ii. 6 .

pastry.text: place where pastry is made Rom. IV. iv. 2 .

patch.text: fool, dolt Tp. III. ii. 73 , Err. III. i. 32 , 36 , LLL. IV. ii. 32 “a set on learning,” MND. III. ii. 9 “A crew of p-es, rude mechanicals,” Mer.V. II. v. 46 , Mac. V. iii. 15 .

patched.text: app. motley fool MND. IV. i. 216 ; cf. AYL. II. vii. 13 and Tp. III. ii. 73 .

patchery.text: roguery, knavery Troil. II. iii. 78 , Tim. V. i. 101 .

path.text: intr. to go about (S.) Cæs. II. i. 83 “if thou , thy native semblance on” (conj. “put†, hadst† thy native semblance on”).

pathetical.text: 1. moving, affecting LLL. I. ii. 104 “Sweet invocation of a child; most pretty and ,” IV. i. 152 “a most nit.”

patience.text: indulgence, leave, permission Ham. III. ii. 114 “they stay upon your ” ; chiefly in phr. “by your ,” e.g. Tp. III. iii. 3 ; also “with your ” 1H6 II. iii. 78 ; “under your patience” Tit. II. iii. 66 .

patronage.text: to uphold, defend 1H6 III. i. 48 , III. iv. 32 .

patten.text: thin plate (of metal) Mer.V. V. i. 59 “look, how the floor of heaven Is thick inlaid with p-s of bright gold” (Qq2 3 4 F1 “pattens,” Q1 “pattents,” later Ff “patterns”).

pattern1.text: sb. (1 16th-17th cent., not pre-S.) 1. precedent, instance appealed to John III. iv. 16 “find some pattern of our shame,” Tit. V. iii. 44 .

pattern2.text: vb. (1 cf. prec. sb.) 1. to be a pattern for, provide a precedent for Meas. II. i. 30 , Tit. IV. i. 57 , Lucr. 629 .

paunch.text: to stab in the belly Tp. III. ii. 101 .

pause1.text: hesitation, suspense Mer.V. II. ix. 53 , Troil IV. iv. 35 , Ham. IV. iii. 9 ; “give” (one) “pause,” cause one to hesitate, ‘pull up’ Ham. III. i. 68 ; “in pause,” hesitating Ham. III. iii. 42 “I stand in where I shall first begin.”

pause2.text: refl. to delay action 2H4 IV. iv. 9 .

pavement.text: “the marble ,” the sky Cym. V. iv. 120 .

pawn1.text: sb. (1, 2 only S.; in 2 there may be a ref. to the pawn in chess) 1. gage of battle R2 I. i. 74 “to take up mine honour's ,” V. i. 55 .

pawn2.text: vb. (2 and 3 app. peculiar to S.) 1. to stake, wager, risk Mer.V. III. v. 88 , Wint. II. iii. 165 , Lucr. 156 .

pax.text: tablet with a projecting handle behind, bearing a representation of the Crucifixion or other sacred subject, which was kissed by the priest and then by the people at mass H5 III. vi. 42 “he hath stol'n a pax.”

peace1.text: 1. “the ,” the king's peace, the general peace and order of the realm as provided for by law Wiv. II. iii. 47 , “I am of the ” (=an officer of the public peace), 55 “sworn of the peace” (=made a justice of the peace), 2H4 III. ii. 100 .

peace2.text: to be silent R2 V. ii. 80 “Peace, foolish woman.—I will not ,” Lr. IV. vi. 105 “when the thunder would not peace at my bidding.”

peach.text: 1. to denounce (one) as being (something) Meas. IV. iii. 12 “peaches him a beggar.”

peak.text: (3 survives in midland dial.) 1. to mope about Ham. II. ii. 602 [ 594 ].

peasant.text: low fellow, rascal (freq.) Wiv. II. ii. 299 ; attrib.=base Ham. II. ii. 584 [ 576 ].

peasantry.text: low birth, baseness Mer.V. II. ix. 46 .

peascod.text: season for peas 2H4 II. iv. 420 [ 413 ]. ∥ In old edd. also “pescod,” showing the shortened vowel, a pronunciation which has survived locally in the northern and east-Anglian area.

peat.text: pet, darling Shr. I. i. 78 “A pretty peat.” ∥ Common from about 1570 to 1640

peck.text: to pitch, fling H8 V. iv. 96 “get up o' the rail: I'll you o'er the pales else” (Ff “peck(e,” mod. edd. “pick”†).

peculiar.text: (the general sense is ‘appropriated to an individual’, ‘own particular’, ‘private’): “the single and life,” the private individual Ham. III. iii. 11 .

pedant.text: schoolmaster, tutor LLL. III. i. 187 [ 179 ], &c., Shr. III. i. 4 , &c., Tw.N. III. ii. 83 .

peep.text: early form of “pip” Shr. I. ii. 33 (Ff “peep(e).”

peer.text: (1 not pre-S.; 2 only S.) 1. to come in sight, be seen, appear Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 3 “Flora P-ing in April's front,” H5 IV. vii. 89 “a many of your horsemen ,” Ven. 86 “Like a dive-dapper peering through a wave.”

peevish.text: (the mod. sense occurs) 1. silly, senseless Wiv. I. iv. 14 , AYL. III. v. 110 “'Tis but a boy,” 1H6 V. iii. 185 “To send such tokens to a king,” Cæs. V. i. 61 “A peevish schoolboy.”

pelf.text: property, possessions Tim. I. ii. 64 “Immortal gods, I crave no pelf,” Per. II. Gower 35 .

pelican.text: used with reference to the fable that the pelican revives or feeds her young with her own blood R2 II. i. 126 , Ham. IV. v. 145 “the kind liferendering ” ; hence attrib. = feeding on their parent's blood Lr. III. iv. 74 “Those daughters.”

pellet.text: to form into small globules Compl. 18 “the brine That season'd woe had pelleted in tears.”

pelleted.text: falling in pellets Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 165

pelt.text: to throw out angry words Lucr. 1418 .

pelting.text: paltry, petty Meas. II. ii. 112 , MND. II. i. 91 “every river” (Ff “petty”), R2 II. i. 60 “ farm,” Troil. IV. v. 266 , Lr. II. iii. 18 .

pendant.text: hanging unsupported in space Meas. III. i. 124 “round about The world.” ∥ An Eliz. sense.

pendulous.text: hanging overhead Lr. III. iv. 66 “the pendulous air.”

penetrate.text: intr. to touch the heart (S.) Cym. II. iii. 14 .

penetrative.text: that sounds the depths of the feelings Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 75 “penetrative shame.”

pensioners.text: body of gentlemen instituted by Henry VIII to be a bodyguard to the sovereign within the royal palace Wiv. II. ii. 81 ; transf. MND. II. i. 10 “I serve the fairy queen . . . The cowslips tall her pensioners be.”

pepper.text: to give it (a person) hot; (hence) to punish decisively, make an end of, do for 1H4 II. iv. 216 , V. iii. 37 , Rom. III. i. 104 .

perceive.text: (obsolete uses) 1. to see through H8 III. ii. 38 “The king in this p-s him,” Troil. I. i. 38 “Lest Hector or my father should me,” IV. v. 87 “O! I perceive you.”

perch.text: measure of land Per. III. Gower 15 .

perchance.text: by chance, by accident Tw.N. I. ii. 5 “It is perchance that you yourself were sav'”

perdition.text: (2 only S., affected or rhetorical) 1. utter destruction Oth. II. ii. 3 .

perdu.text: soldier placed in a position of special danger Lr. IV. vii. 35 “to watch—poor perdu!—With this thin helm.”

perdurable.text: lasting H5 IV. v. 7 “O shame!” ; so perdurably Meas. III. i. 113 “perdurably fin'”

peregrinate.text: having the air of one who has travelled abroad LLL. V. i. 15 .

peremptory.text: 1. conclusive, final H5 V. ii. 82 “our . . . answer.”

perfect1.text: adj. (7 is peculiar to S.; the senses ‘entire, pure’ and ‘mere, sheer’ are not pre-S.) 1. full, mature Lr. I. ii. 79 “sons at perfect age.”

perfect2.text: vb. (2 app. peculiar to S.) 1. to carry through, accomplish All'sW. IV. iv. 4 , H5 I. i. 69 “the means How things are perfected.”

perfection.text: accomplishment, performance, execution Troil. III. ii. 92 “vowing more than the of ten and discharging less than the tenth part of one.”

perfit.text: one of the oldest forms of ‘perfect’, found in Qq of MND. I. ii. 99 , Lr. I. ii. 79 , and in Ff of H5 III. vi. 75 , R3 III. vii. 89 ; so perfitly H5 III. vi. 81 (Ff).

perforce.text: by violence or constraint, forcibly Err. IV. iii. 95 “He . . . took My ring away,” R2 II. iii. 121 “Pluck'd from my arms ,” Lr. I. iv. 322 “these hot tears, which break from me perforce.”

perform.text: intr. to do one's part H8 I. i. 35 “they did Beyond thought's compass,” Cor. I. i. 273 “though he perform To the utmost of a man.”

performer.text: doer, agent All'sW. III. vi. 64 , Tit. IV. i. 80 , Cym. V. iii. 30 .

perfumer.text: one employed to perfume rooms Ado I. iii. 60 .

peril.text: “in of,” (i) exposed to danger in regard to Mer.V. II. ii. 180 [ 173 ] “to be in of my life”; (ii) at the risk of, under the penalty of Cor. III. iii. 100 ; “in to,” at the risk of (doing something) Shr. Ind. ii. 124 ; “without the of,” beyond the dangerous reach of MND. IV. i. 159 .

perilous.text: =PARLOUS 2 and 3, R3 III. i. 154 , Rom. I. iii. 54 .

period1.text: sb. (‘extent of time’ is not a S. sense) 1. termination, conclusion 2H4 IV. v. 229 , 1H6 IV. ii. 17 “The of thy tyranny approacheth,” R3 I. iii. 238 , Oth. V. ii. 356 “O bloody period!.”

period2.text: to bring to an end Tim. I. i. 100 .

perjure1.text: one guilty of perjury LLL. IV. iii. 48 “like a perjure, wearing papers” (cf. PERJUR'D).

perjure2.text: to make perjured, corrupt Ant. III. x. [ xii. ] 30 “perjure The ne'er-touch'd vestal.”

pernicious.text: wicked, villainous Meas. II. iv. 151 “most purpose,” R2 I. iii. 82 “thy adverse enemy,” Ham. I. v. 105 “O most woman!,” Lr. III. ii. 22 “two pernicious daughters.”

perniciously.text: ‘so as to desire his death’ (Wright) H8 II. i. 50 “all the commons Hate him ”

perpend.text: to consider Wiv. II. i. 117 , Tw.N. V. i. 310 “ . . . and give ear,” H5 IV. iv. 8 “ my words.”

persecute.text: All'sW. I. i. 16 “p-d time with hope,” (?) tortured his present life in hope of future cure.

persisted.text: =persisted in Ant. V. i. 30 “Our most deeds.”

person.text: (the same word as that now written ‘parson’, which appears as “person” in old edd. of LLL. IV. ii. 85 , Rom. I. iv. 81 ) 1. bodily figure, personal appearance MND. IV. ii. 12 “he hath . . . the best too,” Ham. I. ii. 243 “If it assume my noble father's ,” Ant. II. ii. 205 “For her own person, It beggar'd all description.”

personage.text: personal appearance, figure MND. III. ii. 292 “her tall personage,” Tw.N. I. v. 165 .

personal.text: bodily, physical 2H4 IV. iv. 8 “a little strength” * , Cæs. I. iii. 77 “In personal action” * .

personate.text: to represent, typify Tw.N. II. iii. 176 , Cym. V. v. 455 “The lofty cedars . . . Personate thee.”

perspectively.text: as through a PERSPECTIVE (sense 1) H5 V. ii. 347 “you see them perspectively.”

persuade.text: 1. to urge (a person), plead with, advise strongly Wiv. I. i. 1 , R3 I. iv. 151 “persuading me not to kill the duke,” Lr. II. iv. 219 ; “ from,” dissuade from AYL. I. ii. 222 , 2H6 V. iii. 10 .

persuasion.text: (1 not pre-S.) 1. persuasiveness Tw.N. III. iv. 385 .

pert.text: lively, brisk LLL. V. ii. 273 , MND. I. i. 13 .

pertain.text: “pertain to life,” live Wint. V. iii. 113 .

perturbation.text: cause of agitation 2H4 IV. v. 22 “O polish'd perturbation! golden care!.”

perusal.text: (twice; not pre-S.) 1. scrutiny Ham. II. i. 90 “such perusal of my face.”

peruse.text: (2 the trans. use is freq.) 1. to survey, inspect Err. I. ii. 13 , H8 II. iii. 75 “I have p-'d her well,” Rom. V. iii. 74 “Let me this face,” Cym. I. iv. 7 “to peruse him by items.”

pervert.text: to turn, divert (S.) Cym. II. iv. 151 .

pester.text: to infest Cor. IV. vi. 7 “pestering streets.”

petar.text: small engine of war used to blow in a door or to make a breach Ham. III. iv. 207 “to have the enginer Hoist with his own petar.”

petition.text: clause of a prayer Meas. I. ii. 16 .

petitionary.text: suppliant, intreating AYL. III. ii. 200 “most petitionary vehemence,” Cor. V. ii. 82 .

petitioner.text: plaintiff in an action commenced by petition 2H6 I. iii. 26 .

pheere.text: Malone's reading in Per. I. Gower 21 (old edd. “Peer(e),” mod. edd. “fere”†).

pheeze.text: (properly) to drive or frighten away; (hence) to do for, settle the business of Shr. Ind. i. 1 “I'll you, in faith” (Q “fese”), Troil. II. iii. 219 “An a' be proud with me, I'll pheeze his pride” (Q Ff “phese”).

philosopher.text: “p-s' stone,” reputed substance supposed by the alchemists to have the property of changing other metals into gold; alluded to quibblingly in 2H4 III. ii. 358 , Tim. II. ii. 117 .

phoenix.text: fig. unique or matchless person All'sW. I. i. 184 ; attrib. = matchless Compl. 93 “His phoenix down.”

phrase.text: word Wiv. I. iii. 31 “‘Convey’, the wise it call. ‘Steal!’ foh! a fico for the phrase!,” 2H4 III. ii. 80 “Accommodated! . . . a good phrase,” Ham. II. ii. 111 “‘beautified’ is a vile phrase.”

phraseless.text: which there is no word to describe Compl. 225 “that phraseless hand.”

physic1.text: the healing art LLL. II. i. 186 , Per. III. ii. 32 ; transf. Rom. II. iii. 52 “thy help and holy ” ; the medical faculty, physicians Cym. IV. ii. 268 “The sceptre, learning, physic.”

physic2.text: to do (a thing) good, keep in health or vigour Wint. I. i. 43 “one that . . . p-s the subject,” Cym. III. ii. 34 “it doth physic love.”

physical.text: curative, remedial, beneficial Cor. I. v. 18 , Cæs. II. i. 261 .

physiognomy.text: art of judging character by the features of the face Lucr. 1395 .

pick.text: to pitch, throw Cor. I. i. 206 “as high As I could pick my lance” ; in H8 V. iv. 96 old edd. PECK.

picked.text: refined, exquisite, fastidious LLL. V. i. 14 , John I. i. 193 , Ham. V. i. 150 .

piece1.text: 1 cask of liquor; in fig. context Troil. IV. i. 62 “a flat tamed piece.” 2 applied to a woman or girl H8 V. v. 27 “such a mighty as this,” Tit. I. i. 309 , Per. IV. ii. 48 “I have gone through for this piece.”

piece2.text: to add to, eke out, augment, esp. “ out” Wiv. III. ii. 34 , H5 I. Chor. 23 , Troil. III. i. 55 , Cæs. II. i. 51 , Lr. III. vi. 2 ; “piece up” Wint. V. iii. 56 .

pight.text: (pa. pple. of ‘pitch’) 1. pitched Troil. V. x. 24 “tents . . . pight.”

pike.text: spike in the centre of a buckler Ado V. ii. 21 .

pilcher1.text: older form of ‘pilchard’ Tw.N. III. i. 40 .

pilcher2.text: scabbard Rom. III. i. 86 . ∥ App. transf. and contemptuous use of a word meaning ‘outer garment of skin or leather’.

pile.text: nap of velvet, etc.; applied to the down on the cheek All'sW. IV. v. 104 (“two pile,” pile of double the ordinary closeness).

piled.text: having a pile like velvet (used with a quibble) Meas. I. ii. 36 .

pill.text: (2 in mod. edd. “peel”) 1. to plunder, rob R2 II. i. 247 “The commons hath he pill'd with grievous taxes,” R3 I. iii. 159 “that which you have pill'd from me,” Tim. IV. i. 12 [you] “pill by law.”

pillage.text: booty, plunder H5 I. ii. 195 , 1H6 IV. vii. 41 , Lucr. 428 .

pillar.text: portable ensign of office in the form of a pillar borne before Wolsey as cardinal H8 II. iv. stage dir.

pillicock.text: penis Lr. III. iv. 75 (Qq1 2 “Pilicock . . . pelicocks hill”). ∥ Used also in Eliz. times as a term of endearment; cf. ‘Mistigowri’, my pillicocke, my prettie rogue (Cotgr.).

pin.text: (2 from the ordinary sense) 1. peg, nail, or stud fixed in the centre of a target LLL. IV. i. 140 “cleaving the pin,” Rom. II. iv. 15 .

pinch2.text: vb. (1 used by Chapman and Dryden) 1. to bite 3H6 II. i. 16 “a bear . . . having pinch'd a few.”

pinched.text: (a) made ridiculous, (b) galled Wint. II. i. 51 * “I Remain a pinch'd thing.”

pine.text: (the corresponding intr. senses are freq.) 1. to deprive of food, starve Ven. 602 “pine the maw.”

pinfold.text: pound for stray cattle Gent. I. i. 114 .

pinion.text: flight-feather of a wing Ant. III. x. [ xii. ] 4

pink.text: winking, half-shut Ant. II. vii. 121 “pink eyne.”

pinked.text: ornamented with perforations H8 V. iv. 51 “her pinked porringer.”

pioner.text: (in old edd. “pioner, pyoner,” even in Lucr. 1380 where it rhymes with “appear; pioneer” is only in later Ff): digger, miner Ham. I. v. 163 .

pip.text: phr. “two-and-thirty, a pip out,” not quite the thing Shr. I. ii. 33 ; ref. to the old card game of one-and-thirty or bone-ace.

pipe1.text: “put up” one's “p-s,” put one's instruments away, cease playing Rom. IV. v. 96 , Oth. III. i. 20 . ∥ This phr. was used fig. in the 16th cent. for ‘desist from action’.

pipe2.text: “ for,” look for in vain, ‘whistle for’ Tit. IV. iii. 24 “we may go pipe for justice.”

pit.text: applied to a dimple Ven. 247 “these round enchanting pits” ; phr. “beat to the pit,” driven to the last ditch Cæs. V. v. 23 .

pitch.text: vb. (1 the orig. sense from which that of setting up tents, &c., is derived) 1. to drive (stakes into the ground) 1H6 I. i. 118 .

pitch1.text: typifying something foul Oth. II. iii. 369 “So will I turn her virtue into pitch.”

pitch2.text: height (fig.) Tw.N. I. i. 12 “Of what validity and soe'er,” R3 III. vii. 187 , Ham. III. i. 86 “of great pitch and moment” (Ff “pith”).

piteous.text: full of pity, compassionate Tp. I. ii. 14 , R2 V. iii. 126 , Ven. 504 , Lucr. 1502 .

piteously.text: so as to excite pity Tit. V. i. 66 , Ant. IV. xi. [ xiii. ] 9 “word it, prithee, piteously.”

pith.text: 1. strength, vigour, mettle H5 III. Chor. 21 , Oth. I. iii. 83 , Ven. 26 .

pittikins.text: diminutive of ‘pity’ (like ‘bodikins’) in “'Ods pittikins” Cym. IV. ii. 293 .

pity.text: “of ,” (1) compassionate Mer.V. IV. i. 27 “an eye of ,” Wint. III. ii. 124 , (2) to excite pity Cym. V. iv. 47 “A thing of ;—it is of,” it is a sad thing for Meas. II. i. 78 , MND. III. i. 45 , Oth. II. iii. 131 .

pizzle.text: “bull's ,” as a type of something very thin 1H4 II. iv. 275 .

place.text: (2 so in “Crosby place,” &c.) 1. “in ,” present, at hand Meas. V. i. 500 , Shr. I. ii. 160 , IV. iii. 150 , 3H6 IV. i. 103 ; “keep ,” be in agreement or accord Wiv. II. i. 63 , Troil. III. iii. 200 ; “take ” (i) find acceptance All'sW. I. i. 115 ; (ii) seat oneself H8 I. ii. 10 ; (iii) be accomplished, take effect H8 III. ii. 34 .

placket.text: (not pre-Eliz.) 1. petticoat, or slit in a petticoat or skirt LLL. III. i. 194 [ 186 ] “Dan Cupid . . . Dread prince of p-s,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 245, 624 , Lr. III. iv. 97 .

plain.text: field of battle John II. i. 295 , H5 IV. vi. 8 , R3 V. iii. 292 .

plain1.text: to complain Err. I. i. 72 , R2 I. iii. 175 , Lr. III. i. 39 , Lucr. 559 .

planched.text: boarded Meas. IV. i. 32 “a planched gate.”

plant1.text: sole of the foot Ant. II. vii. 2 (with quibble on the other word “plant”).

plant2.text: to set up, establish LLL. I. i. 163 “A man in all the world's new fashion p-ed,” R2 IV. i. 127 , V. i. 63 “To unrightful kings,” 1H6 II. v. 80 “to the rightful heir.”

plantage.text: plants Troil. III. ii. 184 “As true as steel, as to the moon” (‘plants were supposed to improve as the moon increases’, Nares).

plantation.text: settlement Tp. II. i. 150 [ 143 ] “ of this isle.”

plash.text: pool Shr. I. i. 23 “A shallow plash.”

plate1.text: piece of money Ant. V. ii. 92 .

plate2.text: to clothe in armour R2 I. iii. 28 , Lr. IV. vi. 170 (fig.), Ant. I. i. 4 “plated Mars.”

platform.text: (1 common Eliz.) 1. plan 1H6 II. i. 77 “lay new platforms.”

plausible.text: laudable, acceptable Meas. III. i. 255 “answer his requiring with a plausible obedience.”

plausive.text: (1 only S.; 2 not pre-S.) 1. =PLAUSIBLE All'sW. I. ii. 53 “his words,” Ham. I. iv. 30 “plausive manners.”

plea.text: that which is claimed LLL. II. i. 7 “the of no less weight Than Aquitaine,” Mer.V. III. ii. 283 , IV. i. 198 , 203

pleached.text: (in early use only S. in both senses; 2 cf. IMPLEACHED) 1. (of the arms) folded Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 73

plead.text: to utter by way of plea or argument MND. I. i. 61 “In such a presence here to my thoughts,” 1H6 II. iv. 29 “If he suppose that I have p-ed truth.”

pleasant.text: jocular, facetious, ‘merry’ LLL. V. i. 4 “ without scurrility,” Shr. III. i. 59 “That I have been thus with you both,” H5 I. ii. 281 , Troil. III. i. 68 . ∥ ‘Pleasantry’ is post-S.

please.text: the impersonal, personal passive, and personal active constructions represented by (1) “if” or “an it please you, (so) please you, please it you, pleaseth your grace,” (2) “if you be p-d, be p-d to” . . ., (3) “if you please, if she p-d,” are all well represented, but the simple ‘please’ (=if you please) is post-S.

pleasing2.text: willing (scil. to listen) Lucr. 1126 * “Relish your nimble notes to pleasing ears.”

pleasure.text: (one's) will, desire, choice (freq.); “of ,” voluntarily 2H6 V. i. 16 “Art thou . . . come of ?; —you speak your ,” you give free expression to your thoughts H8 III. ii. 13 , Troil. III. i. 52 .

pleat.text: fold Lucr. 93 “Hiding base sin in p-s of majesty” (mod. edd. “plaits”†).

pleated.text: folded Lr. I. i. 283 “Time shall unfold what cunning hides” (Qq1 2; Ff “plighted,” mod. edd. “plaited”†).

pledge.text: (2 not pre-S.) 1. bail, surety Shr. I. ii. 45 “I am Grumio's ,” R2 V. ii. 44 , Tit. III. i. 291 .

plenty1.text: pl. necessaries and comforts of life H5 V. ii. 35 . ∥ A 16th-17th cent. use.

plenty2.text: abundant, plentiful Tp. IV. i. 110 “foison ,” 1H4 II. iv. 269 (Q1 “plentiful”).

pliant.text: suitable (S.) Oth. I. iii. 151 “Took . . . a hour.”

plot.text: piece of ground, spot (freq.); Cor. III. ii. 102 “this single plot” =my own person.

pluck.text: used much more widely than at present= draw in a particular direction, draw or bring “down,” take “away,” with an immaterial object, e.g. Meas. II. iv. 148 “To pluck on others,” All'sW. I. i. 79 “What . . . my prayers down” (=obtain from heaven), R2 V. ii. 92 “wilt thou my fair son from mine age?,” R3 IV. ii. 64 “sin will on sin,” Cor. III. iii. 94 “To away their power,” Lr. V. iii. 50 “To the common bosom on his side,” Sonn. xiv. 1 “Not from the stars do I my judgement ” (=desire); H8 II. iii. 40 “ off a little,” come down to a lower rank; “ up,” (intr.) rouse thyself, collect thyself Ado V. i. 212 .

plume1.text: (?) plumage Tp. III. iii. 65 “One dowle that's in my plume” (old edd. “plumb, plumbe”).

plume2.text: to trick out, glorify Oth. I. iii. 399 “to up my will In” (Q1 “make up my will, A) double knavery.”

plummet.text: Wiv. V. v. 177 * “is a o'er me,” has sounded me, got to the bottom of me.

pocket.text: (1) to put away out of sight, (hence) conceal or leave unheeded Tp. II. i. 71 , Ant. II. ii. 77 ; (2) to submit to, ‘swallow’ John III. i. 200 “I must pocket up these wrongs,” 1H4 III. iii. 182 .

point.text: aphetic form of APPOINT Shr. III. i. 19 “tied to . . . p-ed times,” &c., Lucr. 879 , Sonn. xiv. 6 “P-ing to each” [minute] “his thunder, rain, and wind.”

point1.text: sb. (in Cor. IV. vi. 125 “obeys his points” app. = obeys him in every point) 1. “ of war,” short phrase sounded on an instrument as a signal 2H4 IV. i. 52 .

point2.text: to indicate to, direct (a person) LLL. II. i. 243 (Q1), Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 539, Ham. I. v. 129 .

poise1.text: sb. (1 the literal sense does not occur) 1. weight (fig.) Meas. II. iv. 69 , 3H6 II. v. 13 “the equal of this fell war” (=equipoise, balance), Lr. II. i. 122 “Occasions . . . of some poise” (Qq2 3 Ff “prize”), Oth. III. iii. 82 .

poise2.text: vb. (2 not pre-Eliz.) 1. to weigh, estimate All'sW. II. iii. 161 , Troil. I. iii. 339 , Rom. I. ii. 100 .

poison.text: =EMPOISON LLL. IV. iii. 305 (“prisons”†), 1H6 V. iv. 121 “my p-'d voice,” Rom. III. ii. 46 , Oth. V. ii. 363 “the object poisons sight.”

pole.text: pole-star Ham. I. i. 36 , Oth. II. i. 15 “the guards of the ever-fixed ” ; fig. lodestar, guiding star Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 65

policy.text: (the most freq. meaning is ‘prudence in the management of affairs’） 1. form of government Lr. I. ii. 50 .

politic.text: dealing with political science Tw.N. II. v. 176 “politic authors.”

poll.text: (old spelling “pole”) 1. head 2H4 II. iv. 282 , Ham. IV. v. 195 .

polled.text: stripped (properly, of branches or foliage) Cor. IV. v. 216 .

pomander.text: perfumed ball Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 611

pomewater.text: large juicy kind of apple LLL. IV. ii. 4 “ripe as a pomewater.”

pomp.text: triumphal or ceremonial procession, pageant MND. I. i. 15 , John II. i. 560 , III. i. 304 , Tit. I. i. 176 “this funeral pomp,” Tim. I. ii. 252 “these feasts, pomps, and vain-glories.”

poop.text: to deceive, befool Per. IV. ii. 25 .

poorly.text: meanly, unworthily R2 III. iii. 128 “To look so and to speak so fair,” H5 IV. ii. 41 , Mac. II. ii. 72 “Be not lost So in your thoughts,” Lr. IV. i. 10 “My father, poorly led?.”

popular.text: plebeian, vulgar Tp. I. ii. 92 , H5 IV. i. 38 , Cor. II. i. 233 , &c.

popularity.text: keeping company with the common people 1H4 III. ii. 69 , H5 I. i. 59 .

poring.text: looking closely as if short-sighted, peering H5 IV. Chor. 2 “the poring dark.”

porpentine.text: porcupine Ham. I. v. 20 “Like quills upon the fretful ” ; applied allusively to a person Troil. II. i. 27 ; in Err. the name of an inn.

porridge.text: pottage, soup Tp. II. i. 10 , Lr. III. iv. 54 . ∥ The mod. sense is post-S.

porringer.text: basin from which soft or liquid food is eaten Shr. IV. iii. 64 “this [cap] was moulded on a ” ; applied humorously to a cap H8 V. iv. 51 “till her pinked porringer fell off her head.”

port1.text: gate All'sW. III. v. 37 , Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 6 “The city ports”: fig. 2H4 IV. v. 23 “the ports of slumber.”

port2.text: 2 (both senses are freq. 16th-17th cent.) 1. bearing, carriage, demeanour H5 I. Chor. 6 “Assume the port of Mars,” 2H6 IV. i. 19 , Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 52 “with our sprightly port.”

portable.text: bearable, endurable Mac. IV. iii. 89 , Lr. III. vi. 117 “light and portable.”

portage2.text: port-holes (fig.) H5 III. i. 10 “Let it pry through the portage of the head.”

portance.text: behaviour Cor. II. iii. 232 , Oth. I. iii. 139 .

portcullis.text: to enclose as with a portcullis R2 I. iii. 167 .

portend.text: to signify Tw.N. II. v. 133 “what should that . . . position portend?.”

portly.text: stately, dignified, majestic Mer.V. I. i. 9 “with sail,” 1H4 I. iii. 13 , Troil. IV. v. 161 “his large and size,” Rom. I. v. 70 “like a gentleman,” Per. I. iv. 61 . ∥ 1H4 II. iv. 470 “A goodly portly man, i' faith, and a corpulent,” shows the transition from this sense to that of ‘corpulent, stout’ Wiv. I. III. 67 “my portly belly.”

position.text: affirmation, affirmative assertion Troil. III. iii. 112 , Oth. II. i. 241 “a most pregnant and unforced ,” III. iii. 234 “I do not in Distinctly speak of her.”

positive.text: (neither use is pre-S.) 1. admitting no question, certain Wiv. III. ii. 50 “it is as positive as the earth is firm,” H5 IV. ii. 25 .

positively.text: with assurance or confidence R3 IV. ii. 25 , Ham. II. ii. 154 .

possess.text: (3 more commonly in the refl., and the pass. “possessed of” or “with”=possessing) 1. to be in occupation Cym. I. v. 48 “let instructions enter Where folly now possesses.”

possession.text: being possessed by a spirit Err. V. i. 44 .

posset1.text: drink composed of hot milk curdled with ale, wine, &c., formerly used as a delicacy and as a remedy Wiv. I. iv. 8 , Mac. II. ii. 7 .

posset2.text: to curdle like a posset (S.) Ham. I. v. 68 .

possibility.text: (2 an Eliz. sense; in Tit. III. i. 214 “speak with ” (Q1) =app. speak of things within the range of possibility; F1 has “possibilities”) 1. capability, capacity All'sW. III. vi. 87 “to the of thy soldiership,” 2H4 IV. iii. 39 “I have speeded hither with the very extremest inch of ” ; chance (of having something) 1H6 V. iv. 146 “cast from of all.”

post.text: vb. (the common meaning is ‘go with haste, speed, hasten’) 1. to convey swiftly Cym. II. iv. 27 .

post1.text: pole set up by the door of a sheriff Tw.N. I. v. 157 ; doorpost on which the reckoning at a tavern was kept Err. I. ii. 64 .

post2.text: 1. courier Mer.V. V. i. 46 “there's a come . . . with his horn full of good news,” 2H4 Ind. 37 “The p-s come tiring on,” Mac. I. iii. 98 “As thick as hail Came post with post.”

postern.text: small back or side door Gent. V. i. 9 “Out at the by the abbey-wall,” R2 V. v. 17 “as for a camel To thread the postern of a needle's eye.”

posy.text: motto inscribed on the inside of a finger-ring Mer.V. V. i. 151 , Ham. III. ii. 163 .

pot.text: “to the pot,” to destruction Cor. I. iv. 47 .

potato.text: the Spanish or sweet potato, Batatas edulis, in the 16th-17th cent. supposed to have aphrodisiac qualities Wiv. V. v. 21 , Troil. V. ii. 54 .

potch.text: to thrust “at” Cor. I. x. 15 (mod. edd. also “poach”). ∥ Survives in Warwickshire.

potent.text: potentate John II. i. 358 “You equal potents.”

pother.text: disturbance, commotion, turmoil Cor. II. I. 237 (Ff “poother”), Lr. III. ii. 50 (Ff “pudder,” Q1 “Powther,” Qq2 3 “Thundring”).

potting.text: tippling Oth. II. iii. 80 “potent in potting.”

pottle.text: measure of capacity for liquids = 2 quarts Wiv. II. i. 222 , Oth. II. iii. 88 ; so pottle-pot 2H4 II. ii. 86 .

pouch.text: purse Wiv. I. iii. 94 , AYL. II. vii. 159 .

pound.text: pound-weight Cor. III. i. 312 “Tie leaden pounds to's heels.”

pound1.text: public enclosure for stray cattle, pinfold Gent. I. i. 113 .

pound2.text: to shut up as in a pound Gent. I. i. 110 , Cor. I. iv. 17 .

poverty.text: poor stuff Sonn. xl. 10 “Although thou steal thee all my ,” ciii. 1 “what my Muse brings forth.”

powder.text: to salt 1H4 V. iv. 112 “to me and eat me too.”

powdered.text: lit. salted; (hence) subjected to the sweating-tub treatment (see next) Meas. III. ii. 64 “your powdered bawd.”

power.text: (2 a common S. sense) 1. person of rank or influence H8 II. iv. 111 .

practic.text: practical H5 I. i. 51 “the art and part of life.” ∥ ‘Practical’ is post-S.

practice.text: (2 the commonest S. sense) 1. execution Ado V. i. 260 “paid me richly for the of it” ; so in phr. “put in ” Gent. III. ii. 89 , LLL. I. i. 304 .

practisant.text: ? plotter, conspirator 1H6 III. ii. 20 “Pucelle and her practisants.”

practise.text: (2 cf. PRACTICE 2) 1. to perform, carry on 1H6 II. iii. 47 “to practise your severity,” Cæs. IV. iii. 87 .

practiser.text: practitioner All'sW. II. i. 188 “Sweet , thy physic I will try.”

praise1.text: that for which a person or thing deserves to be praised, desert, virtue Mer.V. V. i. 108 “To their right praise and true perfection,” H5 III. vii. 51 , Troil. II. ii. 145 , Per. I. i. 15 “Her face the book of p-s,” Sonn. lxxxiv. 14 “praise, which makes your p-s worse.” ∥ In Tp. III. iii. 39 the common Eliz. proverbial phr. ‘praise at parting’ (=praise given not too soon, not till the entertainment is over) appears as “Praise in departing.”

praise2.text: to appraise, value Tw.N. I. v. 270 “Were you sent hither to me?,” Troil. III. ii. 97 “ us as we are tasted.”

praiseful.text: laudable LLL. IV. ii. 58 (F2 “praysfull,” Ff3 4 “prais(e)full”; Qq F1 “prayful,” * see PREYFUL).

prank.text: malicious or mischievous deed or trick Err. II. ii. 212 , 1H6 III. i. 15 , Ham. III. iv. 2 “Tell him his p-s have been too broad to bear with,” Oth. II. i. 142 “foul pranks.”

pray.text: to invite Meas. II. i. 301 [ 292 ] “I pray you home to dinner with me.”

preambulate.text: walk in front LLL. V. i. 86 (mod. edd. “pre-, præambula”†).

precept.text: (in 1 “pre'cept,” in 2 “prece'pt”) 1. instruction, direction Tp. III. i. 58 “my father's p-s,” Ham. II. ii. 142 (Qq2-5 “prescripts”), Compl. 267 .

preceptial.text: consisting of precepts Ado V. i. 24 .

precious.text: egregious, arrant Oth. V. ii. 233 “ villain,” Cym. III. v. 81 , IV. ii. 83 ;—as adv. = preciously John IV. iii. 40 “too princely for a grave,” Troil. V. iii. 28 “more dear than life” (hyphened only in Ff2 3 4).

preciously.text: as a valuable thing Tp. I. ii. 241 .

precipit.text: precipice H8 V. i. 140 (F1 “Precepit,” mod. edd. “precipice”†).

precipitate.text: to fall headlong Lr. IV. vi. 51 .

precipitation.text: steepness of descent, precipitousness Cor. III. ii. 4 .

precisian.text: (?) rigid spiritual adviser Wiv. II. i. 5 (“physician”†). ∥ In 16th-17th cent. synonymous with ‘Puritan’.

predecessor.text: ancestor H5 I. ii. 248 , Cor. II. i. 102 , Mac. II. iv. 34 .

predicament.text: condition, situation Mer.V. IV. i. 358 , 1H4 I. iii. 168 “the line and the Wherein you range,” Rom. III. iii. 85 . ∥ Orig. a term of logic =category.

predominance.text: ascendancy of a planet Lr. I. ii. 138 “thieves and treachers by spherical predominance” ; so predominant, in the ascendant, ruling All'sW. I. i. 214 “born under Mars.—When he was predominant,” Wint. I. ii. 202 .

predominate.text: (twice; 2 not pre-S.) 1. to have ascendancy (like a planet) Wiv. II. ii. 299 .

prefer.text: (in MND. IV. ii. 40 * either 1 or the mod. sense) 1. to place or put before a person, put forward, present, offer 1H6 III. i. 10 , 33 , Cæs. III. i. 28 “ his suit to Cæsar,” Ham. IV. vii. 159 “I'll have preferred him” (Ff “prepar'd) A chalice,” Oth. I. iii. 109 .

preferment.text: preference Shr. II. i. 94 . ∥ The ordinary sense is ‘advancement, promotion’.

pregnant1.text: clear, obvious Meas. II. i. 23 , Wint. V. ii. 34 “Most true, if ever truth were by circumstance,” Oth. II. i. 241 , Ant. II. i. 45 , Cym. IV. ii. 325 . ∥ Old Fr. ‘preignant’, from ‘preindre’ to press; hence=pressing, cogent.

pregnant2.text: 2 [Latin ‘praegnans’] 1. resourceful, ready, apt Meas. I. i. 11 , Tw.N. II. ii. 29 , Ham. II. ii. 216 “How . . . his replies are.”

prejudicate.text: to pass judgement upon beforehand All'sW. I. ii. 8 .

prejudice.text: inquiry, detriment H8 I. i. 182 ; so the vb. 1H6 III. iii. 91 .

premises.text: (occurs thrice) 1. conditions, stipulations Tp. I. ii. 123 “in lieu o' the Of homage,” All'sW. II. i. 204 .
