prenominate.text: to name beforehand Troil. IV. v. 249 ; also ppl. adj. aforesaid Ham. II. i. 43 “the prenominate crimes.”

preparation.text: (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. force or fleet equipped for fight 1H4 IV. i. 93 , Cor. I. ii. 15 , Oth. I. iii. 14 “The Turkish makes for Rhodes,” Cym. IV. iii. 29 .

preposterous.text: inverting the natural order of things Shr. III. i. 9 “Preposterous ass.”

prerogative.text: precedence, pre-eminence Tp. I. ii. 105 , Shr. III. i. 6 , All'sW. II. iv. 43 “The great and rite of love,” Wint. II. i. 162 , 1H6 V. iv. 142 .

presage.text: sb. (the stress varies; the vb. is always “presa'ge” and is used in senses corresponding to those of the noun) 1. omen, portent John I. i. 28 “sullen pre'sage of your own decay,” III. iv. 158 “Abortives, pre'sages, and tongues of heaven,” Ven. 457 “This ill presa'ge.”

presence.text: (the senses ‘fact of being present’ and ‘demeanour, carriage, aspect’ are freq.) 1. “in ,” present R2 IV. i. 62 “you were in then; And you can witness with me this is true,” 2H4 IV. iv. 17 , H5 I. ii. 2 .

present.text: vb. (3 occurs only once) 1. to set forth, describe Oth. I. iii. 124 “So justly to your grave ears I'll present How” . . .

present1.text: sb. (“the ”=‘the present time’ not pre-S.; Tw.N. III. iv. 382 “my ” app.=my present store) 1. “the” or “this ,” the affair in hand, the present occasion or purpose Meas. IV. ii. 27 , Cor. I. vi. 60 , III. iii. 41 , Ant. II. vi. 30 .

present2.text: adj. (1 cf. ‘a very present help in trouble’ Psalm xlvi. 1; 2 very freq.) 1. (of money) immediately available, ‘ready’ Err. IV. i. 34 “I am not furnish'd with the money,” Mer.V. I. i. 179 “To raise a sum,” III. ii. 274 “The money to discharge the Jew.”

presentation.text: (1 some refer this to 2) 1. display, show AYL. V. iv. 113 * .

presently.text: immediately, instantly, directly Tp. IV. i. 42 “Presently?—Ay, with a twink.” ∥ Very freq. in S. and the usual Eliz. sense; the mod. sense of ‘in a little while, shortly’ is not evidenced with certainty before 1650, but there are possible instances in S., e.g. Wiv. IV. ii. 102 .

presentment.text: (not pre-S. in either sense) 1. dedication of a book Tim. I. i. 27 .

press.text: sb. 1 (in H8 IV. i. 78 F1 has “prease”) 1. crowd, throng H8 IV. i. 78 , Cæs. I. ii. 15 .

press1.text: warrant or commission giving authority to impress recruits 1H4 IV. ii. 13 * “I have misused the king's press damnably.”

press2.text: vb. (in 3H6 III. i. 19 F1 has “prease”) 1. “ to death,” (properly) subject to the ancient torture called the ‘peine forte et dure’ Meas. V. i. 524 “p-ing to death, whipping, and hanging” ; also in fig. use Ado III. i. 76 “she would . . . me to death with wit,” R2 III. iv. 72 , Troil. III. ii. 217 .

pressure.text: impressed character, impression, stamp Ham. I. v. 100 , III. ii. 28 .

prest.text: ready Mer.V. I. i. 161 , Per. IV. Gower 45 .

pretence.text: intention, purpose, or design Gent. III. i. 47 , Wint. III. ii. 18 “the whereof being . . . laid open,” Mac. II. iii. 138 , Lr. I. ii. 98 .

pretend.text: (only in obs. or arch. senses) 1. to hold out, offer Lucr. 576 .

prettily.text: ingeniously, skilfully, neatly MND. II. ii. 53 “Lysander riddles very ,” R3 III. i. 134 “He and aptly taunts himself.”

prevail.text: to avail, have effect H5 III. ii. 17 , Rom. III. iii. 59 “It” [sc. philosophy] “helps not, it p-s not.”

prevailment.text: superior power or influence MND. I. i. 35 .

prevent.text: (2 cf. PREVENTION 1) 1. to anticipate (an event) Cæs. V. i. 105 “so to The time of life,” Ham. II. ii. 312 [ 305 ] “so shall my anticipation prevent your discovery.”

prevention.text: 1. forestalling another in the execution of his designs Cæs. III. i. 19 “Be sudden, for we fear ”

preyful.text: killing much prey LLL. IV. ii. 58 .

pribbles.text: petty disputing, vain chatter Wiv. I. i. 56 .

price.text: (in sense 3 spelt “prize” in old edd.) 1. value, worth 2H4 V. iii. 98 “happy news of price” (=worth much), Troil. II. ii. 82 , iii. 143 , Lr. I. i. 200 “her price is fall'”

prick1.text: sb. (often with indelicate quibble) 1. each of the marks by which the circumference of a dial is divided 3H6 I. iv. 34 “Phaethon hath . . . made an evening at the noontide ,” Rom. II. iv. 122 , Lucr. 781 .

prick2.text: vb. (1 metaphor from spurring) 1. to urge, incite Gent. III. i. 8 “My duty p-s me on to utter that,” Shr. III. ii. 75 “some odd humour p-s him to this fashion,” 1H4 V. i. 131 “honour p-s me on,” Oth. III. iii. 413 .

pricket.text: buck in its second year LLL. IV. ii. 12 .

pricksong.text: descant or accompanying melody to a plainsong or simple theme ‘pricked’ or noted down Rom. II. iv. 22 .

pride.text: (the mod. uses are freq.) 1. magnificence, pomp Rom. I. ii. 10 “Let two more summers wither in their ,” Oth. III. iii. 355 “, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war,” Sonn. lxxx. 12 “of goodly ,” civ. 4 “three summers' ”

priest.text: 1. “be” a person's “priest,” kill him (in allusion to the priest's performing the last offices to the dying) 2H6 III. i. 272 .

priesthood.text: with possessive used as a mock title for a priest 2H6 II. i. 23 .

primal.text: primitive, primeval Ham. III. iii. 37 , Ant. I. iv. 41 .

primater.text: error for ‘pia mater’ LLL. IV. ii. 71 .

prime2.text: adj. (4 only S.) 1. first in time R3 IV. iii. 19 .

primero.text: gambling card-game very fashionable from about 1530 to 1640 Wiv. IV. v. 105 , H8 V. i. 7 .

pyramis.text: pyramid 1H6 I. vi. 21 ; pl. “pyramises” Ant. II. vii. 40 , “pyra'mides” V. ii. 61 .

quail2.text: to overpower Ant. V. ii. 85 “to and shake the orb” ; intr. MND. V. i. 294 “, crush, . . . and quell.”

quaint.text: (often difficult to determine exact meaning) 1. skilled, clever Shr. III. ii. 150 “The musician,” 2H6 III. ii. 274 “how quaint an orator.”

quaintly.text: 1. skilfully, cleverly, ingeniously Gent. III. i. 117 “a ladder made of cords,” 3H6 II. v. 24 , Ham. II. i. 31 .

qualification.text: (a) mitigation, appeasement, (b) condition Oth. II. i. 284 . *

qualified.text: “so ,” of such qualities Shr. IV. v. 66 , Wint. II. i. 112 ; “ in,” fit or competent for Lr. I. iv. 37 . ∥ See also CONSTANT-QUALIFIED.

qualify.text: (1 very common 16th-17th cent. sense, with a great variety of objects) 1. to moderate, mitigate Meas. I. i. 65 , John V. i. 13 , Lr. I. ii. 182 , Lucr. 424 .

quality.text: (the commonest sense is ‘character, disposition, nature’ of person or things) 1. good natural gifts Troil. IV. iv. 76 * “The Grecian youths are full of quality.”

quantity.text: (1 see HOLD vb. 2). 1. proportion MND. I. i. 232 “holding no ,” Ham. III. ii. 179 “women's fear and love hold quantity.”

quarrel1.text: sb. (2 used also by Bacon) 1. “have a to,” have a difference with Ado II. i. 245 , Cor. IV. v. 133 .

quarrel2.text: to be at variance “with” Tp. III. i. 45 , Mer.V. III. v. 61 (‘cavilling on every opportunity’).

quarry.text: heap made of the deer killed at a hunt Mac. IV. iii. 206 ; heap of dead men Cor. I. i. 204 , Ham. V. ii. 378 .

quarter.text: 1. part of an army or camp 1H6 II. i. 63 “Had all your q-s been so safely kept,” 68 “Within her ”; soldiers' lodging All'sW. III. vi. 69 , Tim. V. iv. 60 .

quartered.text: 1. slaughtered Cor. I. i. 205 , Cæs. III. i. 268 .

quat.text: pimple, pustule; applied contemptuously to a young person Oth. V. i. 11 .

quean.text: jade, hussy Wiv. IV. ii. 184 , 2H4 II. i. 53 .

queasy.text: (1 a rare use) 1. hazardous Lr. II. i. 19 “a queasy question.”

quench.text: (the chief use is ‘put out light or fire’) 1. to suppress a feeling in (a person) Cym. V. v. 196 “Being thus quench'd Of hope.”

quest.text: (2 occurs once; 3 only S.) 1. body of persons appointed to hold an inquiry R3 I. iv. 193 “What lawful have given their verdict up,” Ham. V. i. 23 “crowner's quest law,” Sonn. xlvi. 10 .

question1.text: sb. (2 cf. QUESTION vb. 2) 1. phr. “in ,” (i) under judicial examination, on trial Ado III. iii. 190 “A commodity in ” (? quibble on the meaning ‘in demand’), Wint. V. i. 198 , 2H4 I. ii. 67 “He that was in for the robbery” ; (ii) under consideration, to be considered Meas. I. i. 46 “Though first in question,” H5 I. i. 5 , Cym. I. i. 34 “besides this gentleman in question. call in ,” (i) inquire into, examine, consider AYL. V. ii. 6 “Neither call the giddiness of it in ,” Troil. III. ii. 58 , Rom. I. i. 235 , Cæs. IV. iii. 164 “call in our necessities,” Ham. IV. v. 217 ; (ii) raise doubts concerning Tw.N. I. iv. 6 “you call in the continuance of his love,” Troil. IV. iv. 84 . The foll. are all used=without doubt, no doubt:— “no ” Meas. III. ii. 150 , 2H6 IV. ii. 64 , Oth. IV. iii. 64 ; “out of ” Ado II. i. 348 , H5 V. i. 48 ; “past ” Tw.N. I. iii. 106 ; “sans ” LLL. V. i. 93 ; “in contempt of ” Tw.N. II. v. 99 .

question2.text: vb. (2 cf. QUESTION sb. 2) 1. to inquire into H5 II. iv. 142 .

questionable.text: inviting question or conversation Ham. I. iv. 43 “Thou com'st in such a shape.”

questrist.text: one who goes in quest Lr. III. vii. 17 .

quick.text: (obs. or arch. meanings are) 1. living, alive Wiv. III. iv. 90 , H5 II. ii. 79 “The mercy that was in us . . . is . . . kill'd,” Tim. IV. iii. 44 , Ham. V. i. 136 .

quicken.text: (arch. meanings are) 1. to make alive Tp. III. i. 6 , All'sW. II. i. 77 , Ant. I. iii. 69 ; to become living Meas. V. i. 496 , Oth. III. iii. 277 , Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 39

quiet.text: “out of quiet,” disquieted Tw.N. II. iii. 145 .

quietus.text: (2 not pre-S.) 1. discharge, acquittance Sonn. cxxvi. 12 .

quill.text: “in the ,” in a body 2H6 I. iii. 4 * . ∥ Of doubtful etymology, but at any rate distinct from the quill of a bird ( Lucr. 949 ) or of a porcupine ( Ham. I. v. 20 ).

quillet.text: verbal nicety or subtle distinction (always pl.) LLL. IV. iii. 288 , 1H6 II. iv. 17 “these nice sharp q-s of the law,” Ham. V. i. 106 “his quiddities . . ., his quillets.”

quilt.text: humorously applied to a fat person (Falstaff) 1H4 IV. ii. 55 .

quintain.text: stout post or plank or some object mounted on such a support, set up as a mark to be tilted at (used fig.) AYL. I. ii. 268 “a , a mere lifeless block.”

quip.text: sharp or sarcastic remark Gent. IV. ii. 12 , 1H4 I. ii. 51 . ∥ In common use circa 1530-1650; revived in the 19th cent.

quire2.text: to make music Mer.V. V. i. 62 , Cor. III. ii. 113 .

quirk.text: (4 peculiar to S.) 1. verbal subtlety, quibble Per. IV. vi. 8 * .

quit1.text: quits Shr. III. i. 93 “Hortensio will be with thee;— of,” revenged upon, Cor. IV. v. 89 “To be full of those my banishers.” ∥ ‘Quits’ is not S.

quit2.text: vb. (the sense ‘leave’ also occurs; the older form “quite” occurs in R2 V. i. 43 Qq1-4, Rom. II. iv. 206 Ff, Per. III. ii. 18 Qq) 1. to set free Tw.N. V. i. 333 “Your master quits you.”

quittance1.text: 1. discharge from debt Wiv. I. i. 10 , AYL. III. v. 133 .

quondam.text: “this day,” the other day LLL. V. i. 7 .

quote.text: (old edd. also “coat(e, cote)” 1. to give the reference to (a passage in a book); only fig. to indicate LLL. II. i. 244 “His face's own margent did quote such amazes.”

quoth.text: said; used with nouns, or pronouns of the 1st and 3rd persons, to indicate that the words of a speaker are being repeated (freq.); also with a pronoun of the 2nd person with the same force as QUOTHA LLL. IV. iii. 221 “‘Did they’, quoth you?.”

quotha.text: =said he? (see A 1 ), used with contemptuous or sarcastic force in repeating something said by another Wiv. II. i. 141 , Per. II. i. 83 . ∥ In Rom. II. iv. 127 old edd. “quatha”; in Per. II. i. 83 “ke-tha,” a dial. form current in the 17th cent.

quotidian.text: epithet of an intermittent fever recurring every day AYL. III. ii. 389 (fig.) “the of love”; nonsensically in H5 II. i. 124 “a burning tertian.”

race1.text: root (of ginger) Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 51, 1H4 II. i. 27 (old edd. “razes”).

race2.headword: race vb. [variant of RASE, RAZE in common use circa 1400-1650]
race2.text: to make away with Tit. I. i. 451 “to massacre them all, And their faction,” Cym. V. v. 70 “that [tribute] The Britons have r-'d out” ; mod. edd. “razed.”

raced.text: cut, slashed Ham. III. ii. 293 “on my shoes” (Ff “rac'd,” Qq “raz'd”).

rack1.text: mass of cloud driven before the wind in the upper air Ham. II. ii. 514 [ 505 ] “as we often see, against some storm . . . the rack stand still,” Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 10 ∥ In Tp. IV. i. 156 “Leave not a rack behind,” prob. blended with ‘wrack’.

rack2.text: 1. to stretch or strain beyond the normal extent Ado IV. i. 222 “we rack the value,” LLL. V. ii. 826 “your sins are rack'd” (=extended to their fullest), Mer.V. I. i. 182 “my credit . . . shall be rack'd . . . to the uttermost.”

racker.text: (app.) tormentor, ‘murderer’ LLL. V. i. 21 “such rackers of orthography.”

racking.text: driving 3H6 II. i. 27 “ clouds.” ∥ Cf. RACK sb.

rag.text: (1 in old cant=farthing) 1. ‘scrap’ (of money) Err. IV. iv. 88 .

ragamuffin.text: 1H4 V. iii. 37 . ∥ App. orig. the name of a demon.

rage1.text: sb. (the sense of ‘violent anger, furious passion’ is the commonest) 1. madness, insanity Err. IV. iii. 88 , V. i. 48 , Lr. IV. vii. 78 “the great rage, You see, is kill'd in him.”

rage2.text: vb. (2 cf. RAGE sb. 5) 1. to behave wantonly or riotously Ado IV. i. 61 “ in savage sensuality,” R3 III. v. 82 “his raging eye” (Qq “lustful”), Oth. I. iii. 335 , Compl. 160 .

rainy.text: done in the rain H5 IV. iii. 111 “ marching.”

raise.text: to originate (a rumour) Cor. IV. vi. 61 , 70

raised.text: roused up Oth. I. ii. 29 ; set on foot Oth. I. i. 159 “the raised search.” [ iii. ] 52

rake1.text: very lean person Cor. I. i. 24 .

rake2.text: to cover up Lr. IV. vi. 282 .

rampallian.text: ruffian, scoundrel; applied to a woman 2H4 II. i. 67 .

ramping.text: (2 cf. “rampant” 2H6 V. i. 203 ) 1. rearing on the hind legs and showing fierceness 1H4 III. i. 152 “A couching lion, and a cat” ; (hence) of fierce disposition 3H6 V.ii.13 “the lion.”

rampired.text: fortified against attack Tim. V. iv. 47 .

range2.text: vb. (1, 2, 3, 5 not pre-S.) 1. lit. to stretch out in a line; hence, to have a clearly recognized position Cor. III. i. 205 .

ranger.text: gamekeeper Cym. II. iii. 74 “Diana's r-s” (nymphs vowed to chastity).

rank.text: abundantly, excessively Wiv. IV. vi. 22 “While other jests are something rank on foot,” Troil. I. iii. 196 “How rank soever rounded in with danger.”

rank1.text: movement in line or file (S.) AYL. III. ii. 104 “it is the right butter-woman's rank to market” (conj. “rate†; rack†”=ambling pace).

rank2.text: adj. (a common meaning is ‘gross, coarse’ in various applications) 1. coarsely luxuriant H5 V. ii. 45 , 50 “Wanting the scythe, all uncorrected, rank,” Ham. III. iv. 152 ; fig. AYL II. vii. 46 , Troil. I. iii. 318 “the seeded pride That hath to this maturity blown up In rank Achilles” ; (hence) high or excessive in amount AYL. IV. i. 87 , Ham. IV. iv. 22 “A ranker rate.”

ranked.text: surrounded “with” ranks or rows Tim. I. i. 66 .

rankle.text: to cause a festering wound R2 I. iii. 302 , R3 I. iii. 291 “His venom tooth will to the death” (in Qq used transitively “rankle thee to death”).

rankness.text: 1. ‘fulness to overflowing’ (Wright) John V. iv. 54 ; fig. exuberance H8 IV. i. 59 “the mere of their joy.”

ransom1.text: sb. (the ordinary sense is freq.) 1. procuring of one's release from captivity 2H6 IV. i. 10 “Here shall they make their ransom.”

ransom2.text: to atone for Sonn. xxxiv. 14 , cxx. 14

rap.text: to affect with rapture, transport Cym. I. vi. 51 “What . . . Thus raps you?” ; cf. “rapt.”

rapture.text: 1. plundering Per. II. i. 167 “the † of the sea” (old edd. “rupture”).

rarely.text: finely, splendidly Ado III. i. 60 “ featur'd,” Ant. IV. iv. 11 “Is not this buckled well?—Rarely” ; exceptionally Ant. V. ii. 157 “O rarely base!.”

rarity.text: excellence Tp. II. i. 62 , All'sW. IV. iii. 309 .

rascal.text: young, lean, or inferior deer of a herd AYL. III. iii. 60 “the noblest deer hath them” (horns) “as huge as the ,” 1H6 IV. ii. 49 “If we be English deer, be then, in blood; Not -like, to fall down with a pinch,” Cor. I. i. 165 “Thou rascal, that art worst in blood to run.”

rase.text: to pull, pluck “off” R3 III. ii. 11 “had r-d off his helm” (mod. edd. “razed”†, Qq1-4 “raste,” Qq5-8 “cast(e,” Ff1 2 “rased off,” Ff3 4 “raised off”).

rash1.text: adj. (1 and 2 are peculiar to S.) 1. operating quickly Wint. I. ii. 319 “with no rash potion, But with a lingering dram,” 2H4 IV. iv. 48 “rash gunpowder.”

rash2.text: to dash Lr. III. vii. 58 “In his anointed flesh boarish fangs” (Ff “stick(e).” ∥ Mainly a Scottish word.

rate.text: to drive away by chiding or scolding Shr. I. i. 164 “Affection is not r-d from the heart,” 1H4 IV. iii. 99 “Rated my uncle from the council-board.”

rate1.text: sb. (4 common Eliz. sense) 1. (estimated) quantity 2H4 IV. i. 22 “I judge their number Upon . . . the rate of thirty thousand.”

rate2.text: 1. to allot Ant. III. vi. 25 “we had not r-d him His part o'the isle.”

rather.text: “the ,” the more quickly Mac. I. vii. 62 ; the confused idiom “me rather had” occurs once for the normal ‘I had rather’ R2 III. iii. 192 . ∥ “The ” ordinarily=the more readily (for some reason).

ratherest.text: most of all LLL. IV. ii. 19 . ∥ In use from 1420 to Eliz. times.

ratify.text: to bring into proper metrical ‘proportion’ or rhythm LLL. IV. ii. 126 “numbers ratified.”

rational.text: (occurs only twice) 1. endowed with reason, intelligent LLL. I. ii. 124 .

rattle.text: to assail with a rattling noise (S.) John V. ii. 172 .

ravel.text: 1. to become entangled Gent. III. ii. 52 “as you unwind her love from him, Lest it should ravel,” . . .; Mac. II. ii. 38 “the ravell'd sleave of care.”

raven.text: to devour voraciously Cym. I. vi. 49 “The cloyed will . . . ravening first the lamb” ; with “down, up” Meas. I. ii. 138 , Mac. II. iv. 28 .

ravin.text: ravenous All'sW. III. ii. 120 “the ravin lion.”

ravish.text: 1. to pollute, corrupt Lucr. 778 “With rotten damps ravish the morning air.”

ravishing.text: ravenous Mac. II. i. 55 * “With Tarquin's ravishing strides”† (Pope; Ff “sides”).

raw.text: unripe, immature R2 II. iii. 42 “my service . . . being tender, raw, and young, Which elder days shall ripen” ; inexperienced, unskilled, untrained Mer.V. III. iv. 77 “raw tricks,” AYL. III. ii. 77 , Ham. V. ii. 130 , Per. IV. ii. 60 .

rayed.text: dirtied, fouled Shr. III. ii. 55 , IV. i. 3 .

raze2.text: vb. 1 (see also RACE vb.) 1. to erase, blot out 2H6 I. i. 102 “Razing the characters of your renown,” Mac. V. iii. 42 “Raze out the written troubles of the brain,” Sonn. xxv. 11 “from the book of honour razed quite.”

razorable.text: fit to be shaved Tp. II. i. 258 [ 250 ].

razure.text: effacement Meas. V. i. 13 “ of oblivion.”

re.text: the second note of the scale LLL. IV. ii. 103 ; used jocularly as a vb. (see FA).

reach1.text: capacity, ability Ham. II. i. 64 “we of wisdom and of reach.”

reach2.text: vb. (pa. t. and pple. “raught”) 1. to lay hold of with the hand 2H6 II. iii. 43 “This staff of honour raught,” Ant. IV. ix. 30 “The hand of death hath raught him.”

reaching.text: able to reach far 2H6 IV. vii. 85 .

read.text: ellipt. for ‘read lessons (or lectures)’=give instruction 1H4 III. i. 46 .

readiness.text: Mac. II. iii. 140 “put on manly ” (=dress or arm ourselves).

ready.text: (2 cf. READINESS, UNREADY) 1. used in replying to a call or summons=here! MND. I. ii. 20 , Mer.V. IV. i. 2 “What, is Antonio here?—Ready, so please your Grace,” Rom. I. v. 12 .

reap.text: to acquire, get Tw.N. III. i. 147 “Your wife is like to reap a proper man,” H8 III. ii. 205 “What sudden anger's this? how have I reap'd it?” ; to get knowledge of Cym. II. iv. 86 .

rear1.text: “in” or “within the (of),” behind Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 594, Ham. I. iii. 34 .

rear2.text: used in various senses of ‘raise’, e.g. Tp. II. i. 303 [ 295 ] “ my hand,” R2 IV. i. 145 “ this house against this house.”

reason1.text: 1. observation, remark, account or explanation of something LLL. V. i. 2 “your r-s at dinner,” AYL. I. iii. 6 , R3 IV. iv. 362 “Your r-s are too shallow,” H8 V. i. 50 “those fell mischiefs Our r-s laid before him,” Cor. V. iii. 158 ; talk, discourse Meas. I. ii. 196 “ and discourse,” Sonn. cli. 8 “flesh stays no further ”

reason2.text: vb. (1 cf. REASON sb. 1) 1. to hold discussion, carry on conversation, discourse, talk LLL. I. i. 94 “How well he's read, to against reading!,” Mer.V. II. viii. 27 “I r-'d with a Frenchman yesterday, Who told me” . . ., H5 III. vii. 38 “my horse . . . 'Tis a subject for a sovereign to on,” R3 IV. iv. 536 “while we here,” Rom. III. i. 57 “Or coldly of your grievances.”

reasonable.text: requiring the exercise of reason Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 411 “incapable Of affairs.”

reave.text: (pa. t. and pa. pple. “reft”) 1. to rob, deprive Err. I. i. 115 , Ven. 766 .

rebate.text: =ABATE 2, Meas. I. iv. 60 “ . . . his natural edge.”

rebato.text: kind of stiff collar worn about 1590-1630 Ado III. iv. 6 .

rebuke.text: to check, repress John II. i. 9 “to the usurpation Of thy unnatural uncle,” H5 III. vi. 131 “we could have r-d him at Harfleur,” Mac. III. i. 56 “under him My genius is r-'d,” Per. III. i. 1 “ these surges.”

recant.text: to retract (a pardon) Mer.V. IV. i. 392 .

receipt.text: (2 not post-Eliz.) 1. that which is received (in money) R2 I. i. 126 ; (in food) Cor. I. i. 118 , Lucr. 703 .

receive.text: (freq. in the ordinary meanings) 1. to hear H5 IV. Chor. 6 , Lr. V. iii. 217 , Per. I. i. 1 .

receiving.text: reception Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 539 “you shall have such As shall become your highness”; understanding Tw.N. III. i. 133 “To one of your ” ∥ ‘Reception’ is not S.

recheat.text: series of notes sounded on the horn for calling the hounds together Ado I. i. 251 [ 242 ] (with ref. to the cuckhold's ‘horns’).

recite.text: to rehearse, tell, declare Sonn. lxxii. 1 .

reck.text: to care for, heed Gent. IV. iii. 40 , Ham. I. iii. 51 “Himself . . . r-s not his own rede,” Ven. 283 ; once with infin. AYL. II. iv. 82 ; once intr. Troil. V. vi. 26 .

reckon.text: to count among the number “of” Wint. III. ii. 191 “trespasses . . . whereof I The casting forth to crows thy baby daughter.”

reckoning.text: (3 Eliz. and Caroline sense) 1. way of looking at a thing Shr. IV. i. 87 “By this he is more shrew than she.”

reclaim.text: to reduce to obedience, subdue 1H6 III. iv. 5 , 2H6 V. ii. 54 , Rom. IV. ii. 48 .

recognizance.text: 1. ‘a Bond or Obligation of Record testifying the Recognisor to owe to the Recognisee a certain sum of money’ (Cowel, 1607 ) Ham. V. i. 111 .

recoil.text: (the foll. are rare 17th cent. uses) 1. to fall away, degenerate Mac. IV. iii. 19 “A good and virtuous nature may In an imperial charge,” Cym. I. vi. 128 “you Recoil from your great stock.”

recollect.text: to gather up Per. II. i. 55 .

recollected.text: (a) gathered with pains, not spontaneous, (b) picked, refined, studied, (c) recalled, repeated Tw.N. II. iv. 5 “recollected terms.”

recommend.text: (1 an Eliz. sense; 2 only S.) 1. to consign, commit Tw.N. V. i. 95 , Cor. II. ii. 156 .

reconcile.text: 1. to bring back (“to” a state of peace) R3 II. i. 59 .

reconciliation.text: (?) submission with a view to being restored to favour Oth. III. iii. 47 .

record1.text: sb. (chiefly “reco'rd”; also “re'cord”) 1. “in” or “upon ,” (properly) committed to writing as authentic evidence of a matter of legal importance; (hence) Meas. II. ii. 40 “whose fine stands in ,” Ado V. i. 252 , R2 IV. i. 230 .

record2.text: vb. (1 an Eliz. sense; 2 legal) 1. intr. to sing, warble Per. IV. Gower 27 “the nightbird . . . That still r-s with moan” ; trans. to sing about, render in song Gent. V. iv. 6 “Tune my distresses and record my woes.”

recordation.text: remembrance, recollection 2H4 II. iii. 61 , Troil. V. ii. 113 .

recorder.text: wind instrument of the flute or flageolet kind MND. V. i. 124 , Ham. III. ii. 308 , 367 ∥ ‘The Figure of Recorders, and Flutes, and Pipes are straight; But the Recorder hath a less Bore and a greater; Above, and below’ (Bacon).

recourse.text: (2 a 16th cent. meaning) 1. flowing Troil. V. iii. 55 “recourse of tears.”

recover1.text: 1 (2 an Eliz. use) 1. to bring back to friendship, reconcile Oth. II. iii. 275 .

recover2.text: to cover again, re-sole Cæs. I. i. 27 (with pun on RECOVER 1 , sense 4).

recoverable.text: capable of being retraced Tim. III. iv. 13 “a prodigal course Is like the sun's; but not, like his, recoverable.”

recovery.text: process by which entailed estate was commonly transferred from one party to another Ham. V. i. 113 , 114 ; see also FINE sb. 2

recreation.text: （‘diversion, amusement’ is the usual meaning) 1. refreshment by partaking of food LLL. IV. ii. 175 .

rectorship.text: rule Cor. II. iii. 213 “the of judgement.”

recure.text: to restore, make whole R3 III. vii. 129 , Sonn. xlv. 9 ; to remedy Ven. 465 .

red.text: specific name of one kind of the plague Tp. I. ii. 364 “the red plague rid you,” Troil. II. i. 20 “a red murrain o' thy jade's tricks,” Cor. IV. i. 13 “the red pestilence strike all trades in Rome.”

redbreast.text: “ teacher,” one who teaches robins to sing 1H4 III. i. 264 .

rede.text: counsel Ham. I. iii. 51 “Himself . . . recks not his own rede” (Ff “read(e,” Qq “reed”).

redeem.text: 1. to regain, recover 1H4 V. iv. 48 “Thou hast r-'d thy lost opinion.”

redoubted.text: feared, dreaded; common in 15th-17th cent. in addressing sovereigns (and in S. other high personages)=dread R2 III. iii. 198 , H5 II. iv. 14 “My most father,” 1H6 II. i. 8 , R3 IV. v. 14 “ Pembroke.”

redress.text: relief from trouble, assistance, aid John III. iv. 23 -4, R2 III. ii. 32 , Rom. IV. v. 147 “music with her silver sound . . . doth lend redress.”

reduce.text: (only in the foll. senses) 1. to bring R3 II. ii. 68 “All springs their currents to mine eyes.”

reechy.text: dirty, filthy Ado III. iii. 142 “like Pharaoh's soldiers in the painting” (old edd. “rechie”), Cor. II. i. 228 “pins Her richest lockram 'bout her neck.”

reek.text: to be exhaled, (hence) rise, emanate LLL. IV. iii. 140 “I . . . Saw sighs from you,” H5 IV. iii. 101 “the sun shall greet them, And draw their honours reeking up to heaven,” Sonn. cxxx. 8 “the breath that from my mistress reeks.”

reeky.text: full of rank moisture Rom. IV. i. 83 “reeky shanks.”

reel.text: to stagger along (a street) Ant. I. iv. 20 . ∥ A use peculiar to S.

reels.text: revels, revelry (S.) Ham. I. iv. 9 “Keeps wassail, and the swaggering up-spring reels,” Ant. II. vii. 101 “Drink thou; increase the reels.”

refer.text: 1. refl. to have recourse (“to”), rely (upon) Meas. III. i. 256 .

reference.text: (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. referring or submitting a matter to a person for consideration Ant. V. ii. 23 .

refigure.text: to reproduce the form of (a person) Sonn. vi. 10 .

reflect.text: (none of the S. uses are pre-S.) 1. to throw or cast back again Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 761 “reflect I not on thy baseness court-contempt?.”

reflection.text: (a) shining, (b) return Mac. I. ii. 25 “whence the sun gins his reflection.”

reflex.text: to throw or cast (beams) 1H6 V. iv. 87 .

reform.text: to put a stop to (an abuse or disorder) 1H4 IV. iii. 78 , H8 V. iii. 19 “heresies . . . not reform'd,” Ham. III. ii. 41 .

refuge1.text: 1. resource Cor. V. iii. 11 “Their latest refuge Was to send him.”

refuge2.text: to find protection for R2 V. v. 26 .

refuse.text: 1. to decline to meet (an opponent) Ant. III. vii. 39 ; to decline to bear (a name) Rom. II. ii. 34 .

regard1.text: sb. (exx. such as Tp. III. i. 40 , Gent. II. iv. 61 , by some referred to 6, probably have the sense ‘esteem, affection, kindly feeling’) 1. look, glance Tw.N. V. i. 222 “You throw a strange upon me,” Troil. III. iii. 257 “he . . . bites his lip with a politic regard.”

regard2.text: 1. to consider, take into account Gent. III. i. 257 “ thy danger” ; with clause Gent. III. i. 70 “Neither r-ing that she is my child.”

regent.text: ruler, governor R2 II. i. 109 “ of the world,” Per. V. i. 188 “the . . . of Mitylene” ; fig. LLL. III. i. 191 [ 183 ] “Regent of love-rimes.”

regiment.text: rule, government Ant. III. vi. 95 “Antony . . . gives his potent regiment to a trull.”

region.text: (1 current since the 14th cent.) 1. the air, heaven Rom. II. ii. 21 “her eyes in heaven Would through the airy stream so bright,” Ham. II. ii. 517 [ 509 ] “the dreadful thunder Doth rend the ”; attrib. Ham. II. ii. 615 [ 607 ] “the kites,” Sonn. xxxiii. 12 “The region cloud.”

register1.text: record Wiv. II. ii. 198 “turn another” eye] “into the of your own” [follies], Sonn. cxxiii. scil. 9 “Thy” [Time's] “r-s,” Compl. 52 ;—“in ,” on the list Ant. IV. ix. 21 .

register2.text: one who keeps a record Lucr. 765 “Night . . . Dim register and notary of shame.”

regreet1.text: greeting Mer.V. II. ix. 89 “From whom he bringeth sensible r-s,” John III. i. 241 “this seizure and this kind regreet.”

regreet2.text: vb. (not pre-Eliz.; in S. only in R2). 1. to greet again R2 I. iii. 142 , 186

regress.text: return, re-entry Wiv. II. i. 225 “thou shalt have egress and regress” (orig. a legal term).

reguerdon.text: reward 1H6 III. i. 169 ; also as vb. 1H6 III. iv. 23 .

rehearse.text: to give an account of, relate, narrate Mer.V. IV. i. 363 “The danger formerly by me r-'d,” Wint. V. ii. 68 “Like an old tale still, which will have matter to ,” Sonn. xxxviii. 4 “too excellent For every vulgar paper to rehearse.”

rein1.text: chiefly in fig. phr. “give the ,” allow full scope LLL. V. ii. 660 ; “take the ,” go on without restraint Wint. II. iii. 51 ; in phr. with the vb. “bear,” expressing the holding of the head up high or haughtily Troil. I. iii. 189 “Ajax . . . bears his head In such a rein . . . As broad Achilles,” Lr. III. i. 27 “the hard rein which both of them have borne.”

rein2.text: 1. to restrain (“from” something) Troil. V. iii. 48 “Spur them to ruthful work, rein them from ruth.”

reinforce.text: intr. to obtain reinforcements Cym. V. ii. 18 “Let's reinforce, or fly.”

rejoice.text: to feel joy at H5 II. ii. 159 , Cym. V. v. 371 “Ne'er mother Rejoic'd deliverance more.”

rejourn.text: to put off Cor. II. i. 80 “ the controversy.”

relapse.text: falling back into an illness Per. III. ii. 110 “he'r rela'pse is mo'rtal.” ∥ H5 IV. iii. 107 “Ki'lling in re'lapse of morta'lity” perh.=‘with renewed deadliness’; but some comm. explain ‘with a deadly rebound’.

relative.text: pertinent, relevant Ham. II. ii. 641 [ 633 ] “I'll have grounds More relative than this.”

release.text: to surrender, make over, give up R2 IV. i. 210 “With mine own breath all duty's rites,” 2H6 I. i. 52 “That the Duchy of Anjou . . . shall be released and delivered to the king her father.”

relent.text: (used also in the mod. sense) 1. to dissolve Meas. III. i. 239 “he, a marble to her tears, . . . relents not,” Ven. 200 “stone at rain relenteth.”

relenting.text: easily moved to pity, compassionate 2H6 III. i. 227 , R3 IV. iv. 432 “ fool,” Lucr. 1829 “such relenting dew of lamentations.”

relics.text: ancient remains Tw.N. III. iii. 19 “see the of this town.”

relieve.text: to lift up again Tp. II. i. 128 [ 121 ] “the shore, that . . . bow'd, As stoopiny to relieve him.”

religion.text: devotion to a principle, strict fidelity, conscientiousness AYL. IV. i. 208 [ 201 ] “keep your promise.—With no less than” . . ., Rom. I. ii. 93 “When the devout of mine eye Maintains such falsehood,” Cym. I. iv. 154 ; “make to,” make a point of Ant. V. ii. 198 .

religious.text: scrupulous, strict, conscientious All'sW. II. iii. 190 , Tw.N. III. iv. 426 “a most devout coward, in it,” H8 IV. ii. 74 “ truth and modesty,” Sonn. xxxi. 6 “religious love.”

religiously.text: solemnly John III. i. 140 “I . . . from Pope Innocent the legate here, Do in his name demand” ; faithfully, conscientiously John II. i. 246 , IV. iii. 73 , H5 I. ii. 10 .

relinquish.text: to give up as incurable (S.) All'sW. II. iii. 10 “relinquished of the artists.”

relish.text: to sing, warble Gent. II. i. 21 “to a love-song like a robin-redbreast,” Lucr. 1126 “ your nimble notes.”

relish1.text: sb. (old edd. “rellish, rallish”) 1. taste, flavour (of a thing), always fig. Tw.N. IV. i. 64 , Troil. III. ii. 18 “The imaginary is so sweet” ; hence=kind, quality H5 IV. i. 115 “his fears . . . be of the same relish as ours are.”

relish2.text: vb. 1 (the sense ‘enjoy’ is commonest) 1. to taste (a thing) AYL. III. ii. 248 “take a taste of my finding him, and it with good observance” ; fig. to appreciate Wint. II. i. 166 “if you . . . cannot . . . a (as†） truth like us” ; to feel Tp. V. i. 23 “One of their kind, that relish all as sharply.”

reliver.text: to give up again Meas. IV. iv. 6 “ our authorities” (Ff2 3 4 “deliver,” Capell “redeliver”†).

remain.text: vb. (1 not post-S.; 3 only S.) 1. to dwell Tp. I. ii. 420 , AYL. III. ii. 236 , Cym. IV. iii. 14 “for my mistress, I nothing know where she r-”

remain1.text: “the ,” what remains to be done Cym. III. i. 87 .

remain2.text: stay Cor. I. iv. 62 “make ” ; see also HERE-“remain.”

remainder.text: (2 used in 16th-17th cent.) 1. residual or further interest remaining over from an estate, coming into effect when this has determined, and created by the same conveyance by which the estate itself was granted All'sW. IV. iii. 316 “cut the entail from all remainders.”

remediate.text: remedial Lr. IV. iv. 17 “aidant and ” (Qq “remediat,” Ff-“ate”). ∥ (?) Error for ‘remedial’ or ‘remediant’.

remedy.text: reparation, redress; esp. in phr. “there's no ”=there's no help for it Wiv. I. iii. 34 , John IV. i. 91 , Oth. I. i. 35 ; “no ” often=inevitably, without a doubt Wiv. II. ii. 128 “You must send her your page; no ,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 673, V. i. 77 , Troil. IV. iv. 55 , Cym. III. iv. 165 ; “what ?,” what help is there for it? what can be done? Wiv. V. v. 262 [ 250 ] “Well, what ? . . . What cannot be eschew'd must be embrac'd,” Tw.N. I. v. 55 , 1H6 V. iii. 131 .

remember.text: (for “remember since” . . . see SINCE) 1. to maintain 2H4 V. ii. 142 “we will accite, As I before remember'd, all our state.”

remembered.text: “be ,” recollect, remember Meas. II. i. 113 , Shr. IV. iii. 96 , R3 II. iv. 23 , Lucr. 607 .

remembrance.text: (sometimes 4 syll., e.g. Tw.N. I. i. 32 , Mac. III. ii. 30 ） 1. faculty or power of remembering Tp. II. i. 240 [ 232 ] “this lord of weak ,” Cym. II. iv. 93 .

remembrancer.text: one who reminds another Mac. III. iv. 37 , Cym. I. v. 77 .

remission.text: inclination to pardon (S.) Meas. V. i. 499 “I find an apt remission in myself.”

remit.text: to give up, surrender LLL. V. ii. 460 .

remnant.text: surviving member of a family R3 I. ii. 7 .

remorse.text: (1 the commonest S. sense) 1. pity, compassion Tp. V. i. 76 “Expell'd and nature,” John IV. iii. 50 “the tears of soft ,” Tim. IV. iii. 123 “thy throat shall cut, And mince it sans ,” Mac. I. v. 45 .

remorseful.text: compassionate, full of pity Gent. IV. iii. 13 , R3 I. ii. 156 “remorseful tear.”

remorseless.text: pitiless 2H6 III. i. 213 , Ham. II. ii. 617 “Remorseless . . . villain,” Lucr. 562 .

remotion.text: keeping away or aloof Tim. IV. iii. 347 , Lr. II. iv. 115 .

remove1.text: sb. (2 and 5 are only S.; ‘removal’ is not S., although Eliz.) 1. removal or change from one place to another LLL. V. ii. 135 , Sonn. Music iii. 12 [ Pilgr. 256 ] “a may . . . without remove” (=irremovable).

remove2.text: to depart, go away, move to another place AYL. III. iv. 57 “let us ,” All'sW. V. i. 23 , John V. ii. 33 , V. vii. 62 , 1H6 II. v. 104 “is removing hence” (=dying), Mac. V. iii. 2 “Till Birnam wood to Dunsinane,” Ham. I. v. 163 “once more , good friends,” Ven. 81 “From his soft bosom never to ”

removed.text: 1. distant in relationship by a certain degree, properly of descent, but often vaguely of consanguinity in general Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 805 “those that are germane to him, though fifty times,” John II. i. 182 “the second generation ,” 186, Rom. III. iii. 95 ; fig. AYL. V. iv. 71 “a lie seven times removed.”

remover.text: one who constantly changes Sonn. cxvi. 4 .

render1.text: sb. (2 not pre-S.) 1. surrender Sonn. cxxv. 12 “knows no art, But mutual render, only me for thee.”

render2.text: (the commonest S. senses are ‘give back or in return’, ‘give, offer’, ‘give up, surrender’) 1. to give “back” (an image, &c.) by reflection, &c. Troil. III. iii. 122 “r-s back His” [the sun's] “figure and his heat”; fig. 1H4 III. ii. 82 .

renegue.text: intr. to deny Lr. II. ii. 83 “, affirm” (Ff2-4 “Renege,” Qq “Reneag”; F1 misprinted “Reuenge”); trans. to renounce Ant. I. i. 8 “r-s all temper” (Ff “rene(a)ges”).

renew.text: (1 rare poetical sense) 1. to repeat (an action) H5 I. ii. 116 “ their feats.”

renounce.text: to disown allegiance to (a person) 3H6 III. iii. 194 “I here renounce him.”

renown1.text: sb. (1, 2 not post-S.; 3 only S.) 1. report, rumour Tp. V. i. 193 “Of whom so often I have heard , But never saw before.”

renown2.text: to make famous Tw.N. III. iii. 24 , H5 I. ii. 118 “The blood and courage that renowned them.”

rent.text: to rend, tear MND. III. ii. 215 “ our . . . love asunder,” R3 I. ii. 127 (Qq “rend”), Mac. IV. iii. 168 .

renying.text: renunciation Sonn. Music iii. 7 [ Pilgr. 250 ] “Heart's renying.”

repair.text: to return LLL. V. ii. 293 , MND. IV. i. 73 “May all to Athens back again ,” Tim. III. iv. 70 “to some other hour.” ∥ The prevailing meaning is ‘go, betake oneself’.

repair1.text: going or coming to a place, resort Meas. IV. i. 45 , LLL. II. i. 238 “make their ,” 3H6 V. i. 20 , Ham. V. ii. 230 “their repair hither.”

repair2.text: sb. 2 (not pre-S.) 1. restoration Wint. V. i. 31 “for royalty's ,” John III. iv. 113 “repair and health,” Cym. III. i. 57 .

repast1.text: to feed Ham. IV. v. 146 “ them with my blood.”

repast2.text: in R3 IV. iv. 397 app. misprint for “orepast”: see “ill-used,” S.V. ILL-.

repeal1.text: recall from exile Gent. III. i. 235 , Cæs. III. i. 54 . ∥ The only S. use.

repeal2.text: vb. (1 see the prec. word) 1. to recall from exile R2 II. ii. 49 “The banish'd Bolingbroke r-s himself,” Cor. V. iv. 71 [ v. 5 ]; fig. All'sW. II. iii. 55 “whose banish'd sense Thou hast repeal'”

repent.text: to live “out” (a time) in repentance All'sW. IV. iii. 274 .

repetition.text: recital, mention All'sW. V. iii. 22 “kill All ” (=check any mention of what is past), John II. i. 197 “these ill-tuned repetitions,” Cor. I. i. 48 “he hath faults . . . to tire in repetition,” Lucr. 1285 .

replenish.text: to fill Lucr. 1357 “saw the blood his cheeks ”

replenished.text: complete, perfect LLL. IV. ii. 27 “his intellect is not ; he is only an animal,” Wint. II. i. 78 “The most replenish'd villain,” R3 IV. iii. 18 .

replication.text: (2 not pre-S.) 1. reply LLL. IV. ii. 15 , Ham. IV. ii. 13 , Compl. 122 .

report1.text: sb. (the sense ‘what is said about something’ is very freq. in various phrases: “give good ”= speak well (of a person) Wint. V. ii. 170 [ 162 ], “make r-s”=speak All'sW. IV. iii. 344 , “suffer the ” =be told Cym. I. iv. 63 ) 1. rumour, common talk AYL. I. i. 6 “ speaks goldenly of his profit,” 1H6 II. iii. 18 “I see is fabulous and false,” Ant. II. ii. 192 “if be square to her,” Per. I. i. 35 .

report2.text: vb. (2 cf. REPORT sb. 3) 1. to give an account of, describe Meas. III. ii. 176 , Cor. V. iv. 28 “if you him truly,” Ham. V. ii. 353 “ me and my cause aright” ; refl. Cym. II. iv. 83 “figures So likely to report themselves.”

reprieve.text: time during which one is reprieved Meas. II. iv. 40 “his reprieve, Longer or shorter.”

reproach.text: to bring disgrace upon Meas. V. i. 422 “reproach your life.”

reproachful.text: abusive Tit. I. i. 308 , II. i. 55 .

reprobance.text: reprobation, rejection by God Oth. V. ii. 207 “fall to reprobance” (Qq “reprobation”).

reprobate.text: depraved, morally degraded LLL. I. ii. 65 , Lucr. 300 “reprobate desire.”

reproof.text: (the ordinary sense is freq.) 1. shame, disgrace Err. V. i. 90 “She did betray me to my own reproof,” Tim. V. iv. 57 * “Those enemies . . . Whom you yourselves shall set out for reproof.”

reprove.text: to disprove, refute Ado II. iii. 252 [ 241 ] “'tis so, I cannot it,” 2H6 III. i. 40 “ my allegation,” Ven. 787 .

repugn.text: to oppose, resist 1H6 IV. i. 94 “ the truth.”

repure.text: to purify again Troil. III. ii. 21 .

repute.text: to think of, value Gent. II. vii. 59 “how will the world me?,” Cæs. II. i. 295 “A woman well r-d” ; to think highly “of” 2H6 III. i. 48 “by reputing of his high descent.”

request.text: to beg (a person) to come “off” (i.e. away) Ant. II. vii. 127 “Let me request you off.”

require.text: to ask, request (a person) Wiv. I. ii. 10 “to desire and her to” . . ., H8 II. iv. 142 “I your highness, That it shall please you” . . ., Cor. II. ii. 161 “He will require them, As if” . . .

required.text: requisite Wint. V. iii. 94 , Lr. IV. iii. 7 “most required and necessary.”

requiring.text: demand, request Tp. II. ii. 195 [ 186 ], Meas. III. i. 254 , H5 II. iv. 101 “if fail, he will compel.”

requit.headword: requit (variant of “requite,” which is more freq.)
requit.text: to repay Cor. IV. v. 76 “the drops of blood . . . are requitted,” Oth. IV. ii. 15 (F1 “requit,” Q1 “requite”), Per. III. ii. 75 (Q1 only); pa. pple. “requit” in Tp. III. iii. 71 .

rescue.text: forcible taking of a person out of legal custody Err. IV. iv. 113 “I am thy prisoner: wilt thou suffer them To make a ?,” Cor. III. i. 275 ; fig. Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 48 “death will seize her, but Your comfort makes the rescue.”

resemblance.text: likelihood, probability (S.) Meas. IV. ii. 202 “Not a resemblance, but a certainty.”

reservation.text: (the foll. are all the exx.) 1. reserving of something for oneself Lr. I. i. 135 “With of a hundred knights” ; reserved right II. iv. 255 “a to be follow'd With such a number.”

reserve.text: (uses now obs. are) 1. to keep safe, preserve All'sW. III. v. 63 “a r-d honesty,” Cym. I. i. 87 “Always r-'d my holy duty” (=‘so far as I may say it without breach of duty’ J.), I. iv. 148 , Per. IV. i. 39 , Sonn. lxxxv. 3 (‘preserve their style by labouring it precisely’, Wyndham).

reserved.text: with the reservation that 1H6 V. iv. 167 “Only reserv'd you claim no interest.” . . .

residence.text: remaining in a place or state All'sW. II. v. 43 , Ham. II. ii. 353 [ 343 ].

resign.text: to submit (fig.) Rom. III. ii. 59 “Vile earth, to earth resign.”

resist.text: to repel (S.) Per. II. iii. 29 “These cates me.”

resolve1.text: firmness of purpose 1H6 V. v. 75 “of so high resolve.”

resolve2.text: vb. (cf. RESOLVED; 4 common 17th cent.) 1. to dissolve, melt Tim. IV. iii. 445 “r-s The moon into salt tears,” Compl. 296 “his passion . . . r-'d my reason into tears” ; also refl. and intr. John V. iv. 25 “as a form of wax R-th from his figure 'gainst the fire,” Ham. I. ii. 130 “Thaw and thyself into a dew.”

resolved.text: (freq. in sense ‘determined’) 1. prepared in mind (esp. for some evil) Meas. III. ii. 269 “ to die,” Tit. I. i. 135 “stand r-'d; but hope withal” ; so “ for” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 521, 2H6 V. i. 194 .

resolvedly.text: so that doubt and uncertainty are removed All'sW. V. iii. 337 .

resort.text: recourse to or visiting of a place or person Gent. III. i. 108 “she . . . kept severely from resort of men,” Tim. I. i. 128 “to forbid him her ” (=visiting her by way of courtship), Ham. II. ii. 143 “lock herself from his resort” (=his going to see her).

respect1.text: sb. (the mod. sense of ‘deferential regard or esteem’ is one of the most freq.) 1. phr. “in of,” (i) in comparison with Ado III. iv. 19 , LLL. V. ii. 636 “Hector was but a Troyan in of this,” AYL. III. ii. 69 , Cæs. I. i. 10 ; (ii) in consideration of, on account of Gent. III. i. 330 “She is not to be kissed fasting, in of her breath,” 1H4 II. iii. 2 , Ham. V. ii. 121 ; (iii) in regard to MND. I. i. 137 “misgraffed in respect of years,” AYL. III. ii. 13 .

respect2.text: vb. (1 see RESPECTING) 1. to regard, consider, take into account Gent. V. iv. 54 “In love Who respects friend?,” Err. IV. iv. 43 “respice finem, respect your end,” Ven. 911 .

respecting.text: having regard to, considering 2H6 III. i. 24 , H8 II. iv. 178 ; in comparison with Wint. V. i. 35 .

respective.text: (3, 4 not pre-S.) 1. careful Mer.V. V. i. 156 * .

respite.text: (2 not post-S.) 1. date to which something is postponed R3 V. i. 19 “the determin'd respite of my wrongs.”

rest.text: vb. 1 (the ordinary senses are freq.) 1. “ in,” to lie in the power of Meas. I. iii. 31 “It r-ed in your Grace T' unloose this tied-up justice,” 3H6 III. ii. 45 , Tit. II. iii. 41 ; “ on,” to depend or rely upon Tit. I. i. 267 , Ham. III. iii. 14 ; cf. John V. i. 13 .

rest1.text: sb. 1 (of Anglo-Saxon origin; 2 only S.) 1. in phr. wishing one good repose Gent. IV. ii. 135 “And so, good rest,” Err. IV. iii. 32 “God give you good rest,” R3 I. iv. 75 , V. iii. 43 ; cf. Tit. IV. ii. 64 .

rest2.text: sb. 2 (of French origin) 1. “above the ,” above all, especially Gent. IV. i. 60 , Lr. IV. i. 48 , Sonn. xci. 6 .

resting.text: stationary Cæs. III. i. 61 “the northern star, Of whose true-fix'd and resting quality.”

restore.text: to make amends for (loss) Sonn. xxx. 14 . ∥ By extension=to make (amends) MND. V. ii. 69 [ i. 445 ] “And Robin shall restore amends.”

restrain.text: (2 once; rare outside S.) 1. to keep back, withhold (something “from” a person) R3 V. iii. 323 “They would the one” [viz. lands], Cor. V. iii. 167 “That thou r-'st from me the duty which To a mother's part belongs,” Tim. V. i. 153 “r-ing aid to Timon.”

restraint.text: (2 not pre-S.) 1. keeping back or out Err. III. i. 97 .

resty.text: inactive, inert, sluggish Troil. I. iii. 263 “Who in this . . . long-continu'd truce Is grown” (F1 “rusty”), Cym. III. vi. 34 “ sloth,” Sonn. c. 9 “Rise, Muse.”

retain.text: to have in one's service H8 I. ii. 192 .

retention.text: (2 only Eliz.) 1. power of retaining things in the mind, memory Sonn. cxxii. 9 “That poor ” ; capacity for holding Tw.N. II. iv. 98 “they lack retention.”

retentive.text: holding, confining Tim. III. iv. 83 “my enemy,” Cæs. I. iii. 95 .

retire1.text: sb. (2 common 1550-1600; 3 the commonest S. sense) 1. retirement, withdrawal LLL. II. i. 232 .

retire2.text: vb. (1 an Eliz. sense) 1. to return Troil. I. iii. 281 , Oth. III. iii. 456 “retiring ebb,” Ven. 906 “now she will no further, But back r-s,” Lucr. 962 .

retired.text: withdrawn into oneself Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 62; subsided John V. iv. 53 “a . . . retired flood.”

retort.text: (2 only S.; in Wiv. II. ii. 4 Qq “I will the sum in equipage” perhaps a humorous use of the sense ‘return a blow’) 1. to reflect (heat) Troil. III. iii. 101 .

retreat.text: recall of a pursuing force 2H4 IV. iii. 78 .

retrograde.text: (occurs twice) 1. (of planets) moving apparently in a direction contrary to the order of the signs, or from east to west All'sW. I. i. 215 “born under Mars . . . When he was retrograde.”

return2.text: vb. 1 1. refl. to turn away 1H6 III. iii. 56 “ thee therefore, with a flood of tears.”

revenge1.text: sb. (the pl. is freq. used=sing.) 1. pl. (one's) vindictive desires All'sW. V. iii. 10 “my revenges were high bent upon him.”

revenge2.text: vb. (in the trans. use the injury or the person injured is the object) 1. pass. “be r-d,” to take vengeance (freq.); const. “of” = on 2H4 II. iv. 165 (Q; Ff “on”); const. “on” = for Lucr. 1778 “to be revenged on her death.”

revengement.text: retribution, punishment 1H4 III. ii. 7 . ∥ Very common 1540- 1650

revengive.text: vindictive Lr. II. i. 47 “the gods” (Qq; Ff “revenging”).

reverb.headword: reverb (S. coinage, app. shortened from “reverberate,” which occurs twice)

reverberate.text: reverberating, resounding Tw.N. I. v. 293 “ hills.” ∥ Ben Jonson has ‘a reuerberate glasse’.

reverence.text: “save” or “saving your ,” an apologetic phr. introducing a remark that might offend the hearer Ado III. iv. 33 , 1H4 II. iv. 523 [ 515 ], Rom. I. iv. 42 , Cym. IV. i. 5 ; corrupted to SIR-REVERENCE, q.v.

reverse.text: back-handed stroke Wiv. II. iii. 27 ; cf. “punto reverso,” S.V. PUNTO.

reversion.text: prospect of possessing a thing at some future time 1H4 IV. i. 53 ; “in ,” destined to come into a person's possession, or to be realized in the future R2 I. iv. 35 “As were our England in his,” Troil. III. ii. 99 “No perfection in shall have a praise in present.”

revert.text: to return Ham. IV. vii. 23 “my arrows . . . Would have reverted to my bow again.”

reverted.text: (?)in opposition or rebellion Err. III. ii. 127 .

review.text: to see again Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 683; to survey Sonn. lxxiv. 5 .

revolt1.text: sb. 1 (the gen. sense of ‘casting off of allegiance, obedience, or faithfulness’ is freq.; 2 only S.) 1. “give” (one) “the revolt,” to rebel against Mac. V. iv. 13 .

revolt2.text: rebel John V. ii. 151 , V. iv. 7 , Cym. IV. iv. 6 “unnatural revolts.”

revolution.text: alteration, change (esp. as wrought by time) LLL. IV. ii. 70 “motions, r-s,” 2H4 III. i. 46 “the of the times,” Ham. V. i. 96 “Here's fine ,” Ant. I. ii. 134 , Sonn. lix. 12 “whether be the same.”

revolve.text: intr. to consider Tw.N. II. v. 157 “If this fall into thy hand, revolve.”

rheum.text: (see also SALT RHEUM) 1. watery matter secreted by glands, &c. (i) saliva Mer.V. I. iii. 118 , H5 III. v. 52 “spit and void his upon” ; (ii) mucus from the nose Err. III. ii. 132 ; (iii) tears Ado V. ii. 88 , John III. i. 22 “that lamentable ,” IV. i. 33 , iii. 108 , Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 46 “women's rheum,” Ham. II. ii. 537 [ 529 ] “bisson rheum.”

rheumy.text: inducing ‘rheum’ (sense 2) Cæs. II. i. 266 “the rheumy and unpurged air.”

rhyme.text: spelling of RIME in some mod. edd.

rib.text: to enclose with a strong protection Mer.V. II. vii. 51 , Cym. III. i. 19 .

ribald.text: (?) offensively noisy Troil. IV. ii. 9 “the busy day . . . hath rous'd the ribald crows.”

ribaudred.text: (?) lewd, wanton Ant. III. viii. 20 [ x. 10 ] “Yon nag of Egypt.” ∥ Perhaps an alteration of the Eliz. adj. ‘ribaudrous’; or (?) meant for ‘ribaudried’ (from ‘ribaudry’).

rich.text: (ordinary senses are freq.) 1. applied to eyes that have seen much AYL. IV. i. 25 , All'sW. V. iii. 17 .

rid.text: (2 the usual phr. was ‘rid ground’) 1. to make away with, kill, destroy Tp. I. ii. 364 “the red plague rid you,” R2 V. iv. 11 , 2H6 III. i. 233 “This Gloucester should be quickly rid the world,” 3H6 V. v. 67 , Sonn. cxxxix. 14 “rid my pain.”

ride.text: (pa. pple. “rode” 2H4 V. iii. 96 , H5 IV. iii. 2 in intr. senses, “ridden” Wiv. V. v. 148 , H8 II. ii. 3 in trans., “rid” MND. V. i. 119 , Cæs. III. ii. 274 in both) 1. to rest or turn as on a pivot or axle 1H4 V. ii. 83 “If life did ride upon a dial's point,” Troil. I. iii. 67 “the axle-tree On which heaven rides.”

rife.text: (?) current MND. V. i. 42 “how many sports are rife” (Q1 “ripe”).

rift.text: to split; intr. Wint. V. i. 66 ; trans. Tp. V. i. 45 .

right1.text: 1. just or equitable treatment; phr. “do” (one) “,” to do him justice, give him satisfaction Ado I. i. 254 [ 246 ] “I will do myself the right to trust none,” V. i. 152 “Do me , or I will protest your cowardice,” Tit. I. i. 203 “Romans, do me right: Patricians, draw your swords” ; with ref. to pledging a person by drinking to him 2H4 V. iii. 74 “Why, now you have done me right.”

right2.text: erroneous old spelling of ‘rite’ MND. IV. i. 139 .

right3.text: straight LLL. V. ii. 566 “it” [sc. your nose] “stands too right.”

right4.text: adv. (the sense ‘very’ is the most freq.) 1. in a straight course or line; “ on,” straight on Cæs. III. ii. 227 , Compl. 26 ; fig. “ out,” outright, completely Tp. IV. i. 101 “And be a boy right out.”

rightful.text: doing right, just Mer.V. IV. i. 302 “Most judge.”

rightly.text: directly, straight R2 II. ii. 18 “perspectives . . . rightly gaz'd upon.”

rim.text: short for ‘rim of the belly’, the lining membrane of the abdomen, the peritoneum H5 IV. iv. 15 “I will fetch thy rim out at thy throat.”

ring.text: “cracked within the ring,” (of a coin) having the circle broken that surrounds the sovereign's head Ham. II. ii. 457 [ 448 ].

rinsing.text: in old edd. “wrenching,” still a widespread dial. pronunciation H8 I. i. 167 .

riotous.text: dissolute Tim. II. ii. 169 , Lr. I. iv. 267 .

ripe.text: (of lips) red and full MND. III. ii. 139 , Lr. IV. iii. 22 ; ready for birth R2 II. ii. 10 ; grown-up AYL. IV. iii. 89 “a ripe sister” (F1); requiring immediate satisfaction Mer.V. I. iii. 64 “ripe wants” ; ready for use or possession MND. V. i. 42 “how many sports are ripe” (Q1), R3 III. vii. 157 “the ripe revenue.”

rival1.text: partner, associate Ham. I. i. 13 “The rivals of my watch.”

rive.text: (pa. pple. only “rived”) 1. to cleave, split; trans. Troil. I. iii. 316 , Cæs. I. iii. 6 ; intr. Troil. I. i. 37 .

rivo.text: exclamation (? of Spanish origin) used at drinking-bouts 1H4 II. iv. 126 .

road.text: (2 very common 1500-1650; 4 not pre-S.) 1. journey on horseback H8 IV. ii. 17 “At last, with easy roads, he came to Leicester.”

roar.text: (orig. a different word from the ‘roar’ of lions, cannon, &c., but associated with it in modern times, esp. in echoes of the Hamlet passage) 1. confusion, tumult Tp. I. ii. 2 “you have Put the wild waters in this roar.”

rob.text: to cut off “from” the possibility of doing something R2 I. iii. 173 “death, Which robs my tongue from breathing native breath.”

robustious.text: violent, boisterous H5 III. vii. 164 “ and rough coming on,” Ham. III. ii. 10 “a periwigpated fellow.”

rogue.text: (1 orig. a canting term of the 16th cent.; the Dict. of the Canting Crew, 1700 , defines ‘Rogues’ as ‘the fourth Order of Canters’; 3 common in the 17th cent. dramatists) 1. one of a class of idle vagrants or vagabonds Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 107, Lr. IV. vii. 39 “To hovel thee with swine and r-s forlorn.”

roll1.text: sb. (2 not pre-Eliz.) 1. list, register (fig.) 1H4 III. i. 43 “in the of common men,” Ant. V. ii. 180 “i' the roll of conquest.”

roll2.text: out of 13 exx. 9 refer to turning of the eyes in different directions.

romage.text: bustle, commotion Ham. I. i. 107 “post-haste and romage.”

ronyon.text: abusive term for a woman Wiv. IV. ii. 199 “you baggage . . . you ” (Ff “Runnion”), Mac. I. iii. 6 “the rump-fed ronyon.”

rook.text: to squat, crouch 3H6 V. vi. 47 “The raven rook'd her on the chimney's top.” ∥ In general literary use from 13th cent. to Eliz. times, afterwards dial. in the form of ‘ruck’ (as in Golding, Gabriel Harvey).

rooky.text: full of rooks Mac. III. ii. 51 “the wood.”

room.text: （“give room,” and simply “room,”=make way) 1. place assigned to one Shr. III. ii. 253 “let Bianca take her sister's ,” John III. iv. 93 , R2 V. v. 108 “Go thou and fill another in hell,” 3H6 II. vi. 54 , III. ii. 132 , Sonn. lv. 10 .

root.text: to dig up with the snout Tim. V. i. 170 “Who, like a boar . . . doth root up His country's peace,” Ven. 636 “as he roots the mead.” ∥ Later form of ‘wroot’, associated with ROOT vb. 1 =uproot.

root1.text: the ‘bottom’ “of” the heart Gent. V. iv. 103 “How oft hast thou with perjury cleft the root!,” Troil. IV. iv. 54 “my heart will be blown up by the root,” Cor. II. i. 204 “at very root on's heart,” Ant. V. ii. 105 “smites My very heart at root.”

root2.text: to fix firmly by the root, implant deeply Gent. II. iv. 163 “lest the base earth Should . . . Disdain to root the summer-swelling flower,” Sonn. cxlii. 11 “Root pity in thy heart.”

rope.text: halter Tp. I. i. 35 “the rope of his destiny” ; as a derisive cry (attributed to parrots) 1H6 I. iii. 53 “Winchester goose! I cry a rope! a rope!.”

ropery.text: trickery, knavery Rom. II. iv. 155 . ∥ Used also by the dramatist Fletcher.

roping.text: hanging or flowing down like a rope or thread H5 III. v. 23 “ icicles,” IV. ii. 48 “The gum down-roping from their pale-dead eyes.”

rose.text: “cake of roses,” preparation of rose-petals in the form of a cake, used as a perfume Rom. V. i. 47 .

rosed.text: rosy Tit. II. iv. 24 “thy rosed lips.”

rosemary.text: used as an emblem at funerals and weddings Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 74, Rom. II. iv. 221 , 228 , IV. v. 79 , Ham. IV. v. 174 “There's , that's for remembrance” ; in decorating dishes Per. IV. vi. 165 .

roted.text: learnt by rote Cor. III. ii. 55 (Ff “roated”).

rother.text: ox Tim. IV. iii. 12 “It is the pasture lards the rother's sides” (Ff “Brothers”).

rotten.text: applied to unwholesome vapour, &c. Cor. II. iii. 35 “ dews,” III. iii. 119 “reek of the fens,” Tim. IV. iii. 2 “ humidity,” Lucr. 778 “ damps,” Sonn. xxxiv. 4 “their” [clouds] “rotten smoke.”

round1.text: sb. (1 an Eliz. use) 1. “this mortal round,” the earth Ven. 368 .

round2.text: 1. (of a sum of money) large, considerable Mer.V. I. iii. 104 , H8 V. iv. 86 “round fines.”

roundure.text: circuit, enclosure John II. i. 259 “the of your old-fac'd walls” (Ff “rounder”; cf. “wafter= wafture”). ∥ Cf. RONDURE.

rouse1.text: sb. (prob. arose from phr. ‘drink carouse’, apprehended as ‘drink a rouse’) 1. full draught of liquor, bumper Ham. I. ii. 127 “the king's ,” I. iv. 8 “takes his ,” Oth. II. iii. 68 “they have given me a already—Good faith, a little one.”

rouse2.text: 1. to cause (an animal) to rise from his lair 1H4 I. iii. 198 “To a lion,” Tit. II. ii. 21 “I have dogs . . . Will the proudest panther,” Ven. 240 ; fig. R2 II. iii. 128 “To his wrongs and chase them to the bay,” 3H6 V. i. 65 .

rout.text: (the sense of ‘disorderly flight’ is not pre-Eliz.) 1. disorderly or disreputable crowd 2H4 IV. i. 33 , IV. ii. 9 “a rout of rebels,” 1H6 IV. i. 173 .

row.text: (?) stanza Ham. II. ii. 447 [ 438 ] “The first row of the pious chanson.”

royal.text: adj. (the senses of ‘belonging to, originating from, connected with, proceeding from a king or sovereign’, ‘of the rank of a sovereign’ are freq.; sometimes applied to dukes) 1. of or consisting of a sovereign or sovereigns John II. i. 347 “add a number to the dead,” H5 V. ii. 27 “this . . . interview” ; also H8 I. iv. 86 “My choice” (=choice of a king), Mac. I. iii. 56 “ hope” (=prospect of kingship).

royalty.text: (most of the foll. uses are obs.) 1. personality of a sovereign, royal person, (his, your) majesty Wint. I. ii. 15 , John V. ii. 129 , Ant. I. iii. 91 , Cym. V. v. 39 .

rub1.text: sb. (3 not pre-S.) 1. in bowls, an obstacle by which a bowl is hindered in or diverted from its proper course (fig.) R2 III. iv. 4 .

rub2.text: in bowls, to encounter an obstacle (allusively) LLL. IV. i. 143 “challenge her to bowl.—I fear too much rubbing,” Troil. III. ii. 50 “ on, and kiss the mistress.”

ruby.text: red pimple on the face Err. III. ii. 139 .

rude.text: the chief senses are ‘unlearned, ignorant’ LLL. V. i. 97 , ‘uncultured, unrefined’ Oth. I. iii. 81 , ‘uncivilized, barbarous’ Cym. III. vi. 65 , ‘unmannerly’ LLL. V. ii. 432 , MND. III. ii. 262 , ‘ungentle, violent, harsh, brutal’ Gent. V. iv. 60 , R2 V. v. 106 , (of sea, wind) ‘turbulent, rough’ 2H4 III. i. 20 , Lr. IV. ii. 30 , (of sounds) ‘discordant, harsh’ Troil. I. i. 94 , (of language) ‘lacking polish or elegance’ John IV. ii. 150 , Sonn. xxxii. 4 , (of natural objects) ‘rugged, rough’ Tit. II. iii. 199 (“rude-growing”), Ant. I. iv. 64 , ‘strong or big but rough in form’ John II. i. 262 ; with John V. vii. 27 “that indigest Which he hath left so shapeless and so rude” (= unformed) cf. Ovid's ‘rudis indigestaque moles’.

rudely.text: with violence Cor. IV. v. 148 , Lucr. 170 ; by violent or rough behaviour 1H4 III. ii. 32 “Thy place in council thou hast rudely lost” ; under rough or harsh conditions Per. III. i. 30 “thou art the rudeliest welcome to this world that” . . .

rudeness.text: violence Troil. I. iii. 207 “the great swing and of his poise,” Compl. 104 ; roughness, coarseness Troil. II. i. 58 , Cym. IV. ii. 214 “brogues . . . whose rudeness Answer'd my steps too loud.”

rudesby.text: unmannerly fellow Shr. III. ii. 10 , Tw.N. IV. i. 55 .

rue.text: to have pity for Tit. I. i. 105 “rue the tears I shed.”

ruffian.text: (of the wind) to bluster Oth. II. i. 7 .

ruffle1.text: ostentatious bustle or display Compl. 58 “the ruffle knew Of court, of city.”

ruffle2.text: vb. (1 a S. use) 1. to stir “up” to indignation Cæs. III. ii. 232 “ up your spirits.”

ruinous.text: brought to ruin or decay Tim. IV. iii. 468 “yond . . . ruinous man.”

rule.text: (3 cf. NIGHT-RULE) 1. law R3 I. ii. 68 “r-s of charity,” Troil. V. ii. 138 , Compl. 271 “gainst , gainst sense;— of (in) nature,” natural law All'sW. I. i. 150 , H5 I. ii. 188 , Oth. I. iii. 101 .

rumour.text: talk or report (“of” a person) 1H6 II. iii. 7 .

run.text: to ride on horseback rapidly 1H4 II. iv. 382 “that runs o' horseback up a hill perpendicular” ; transf. Tp. I. ii. 254 “To run upon the sharp wind of the north.”

runagate.text: (later form of ‘renegade’) 1. deserter Cym. I. vi. 137 “that runagate to your bed.”

runaway.text: vagabond, ‘runagate’ R3 V. iii. 317 “vagabonds, rascals, and runaways,” Rom. III. ii. 6 * .

rupture.text: (2 if genuine, only S.) 1. breach Meas. III. i. 244 .

rush1.text: sb. (1 the custom of ‘marrying’ with a rushring was formerly prevalent) 1. used for making a finger-ring All'sW. II. ii. 25 .

rush2.text: “rush aside,” to brush aside, or (?) elude Rom. III. iii. 26 .

rushle.text: early form of ‘rustle’ Wiv. II. ii. 70 .

russel.text: app. misprint for RUFFLE Lr. II. iv. 304 .

russet.text: homely, simple LLL. V. ii. 414 “russet years.” ∥ ‘Russet’ was a coarse homespun cloth.

ruth.text: pity R2 III. iv. 106 , Cor. I. i. 203 , Sonn. cxxxii. 4 .

ruthful.text: lamentable, piteous 3H6 II. v. 95 , R3 IV. iii. 5 (Ff “this piece of ruth full Butchery,” Qq1 2 “this ruthless piece of butchery”), Tit. V. i. 66 “villanies to hear.”

sa.text: repeated, accompanies or incites to sudden action Lr. IV. vi. 208 “Sa, sa, sa, sa.” [“Exit King running” (Qq). ∥ Not uncommon in Eliz. drama.

sable.text: adj. black Ham. II. ii. 483 [ 474 ] “whose arm, Black as his purpose,” Lucr. 117 “ Night,” Sonn. xii. 4 “ curls” ;—sb. black colour Ham. I. ii. 241 “It was . . . A sable silver'”

sables.text: fur of the sable, Mustela zibellina, worn on rich garments Ham.III.ii. 139 * “let the devil wear black, for I'll have a suit of ” (quibbling), IV. vii. 80 .

sack1.text: general name for a class of white wines formerly imported from Spain and the Canaries Tw.N. II. iii. 209 “I'll go burn some sack,” 1H4 II. iv. 524 [ 516 ] “If sack and sugar be a fault, God help the wicked!.” ∥ See also SHERRIS,

sack2.text: used loosely=to destroy Rom. III. iii. 106 .

sackbut.text: bass trumpet with a slide like that of a trombone for altering the pitch Cor. V. iv. 53 .

sacrament.text: “take or receive the ,” a formula used as a strong oath or pledge to perform or maintain something, (hence) to swear, bind oneself All'sW. IV. iii. 157 “I'll take the on't,” R3 I. iv. 212 “Thou didst receive the to fight” . . ., V. iv. 31 [ v. 18 ] “as we have ta'en the , We will unite the white rose and the red.”

sacred.text: (1 properly=consecrated by religious rite) 1. an epithet of royalty Err. V. i. 133 “most duke,” John III. i. 148 “a king,” Troil. IV. v. 133 “thy mother, My aunt” ; so Sonn. vii. 4 “his” [the sun's] “sacred majesty.”

sacrificial.text: having the character of sacrifice or worship offered to a god Tim. I. i. 82 “Rain whisperings in his ear.”

sad.text: (1 formerly a very common sense) 1. grave, serious Gent. I. iii. 1 “sad talk,” Ado I. i. 191 “a sad brow,” II. i. 360 , MND. IV. i. 101 “in silence sad,” Tw.N. III. iv. 21 “I sent for thee upon a sad occasion,” H5 IV. i. 321 “the sad and solemn priests,” Cæs. I. ii. 216 “That Cæsar looks so sad.”

sadly.text: gravely, seriously Ado II. iii. 240 [ 229 ], 2H4 V. ii. 125 , Rom. I. i. 207 “sadly tell me who.”

sadness.text: seriousness 3H6 III. ii. 77 “this merry inclination Accords not with the of my suit” ; usu. = phr. “in (good) ,” in all seriousness Wiv. III. v. 128 , Rom. I. i. 205 , Ven. 807 .

safe.text: “safe toward,” with a sure regard to Mac. I. iv. 27 .

safe1.text: adj. (1 not post-S.; 2 not pre-S.) 1. (mentally or morally) sound or sane Meas. I. i. 71 “the man of discretion,” Cor. II. iii. 226 “on a safer judgement,” Cæs. I. i. 14 “with a safe conscience,” Lr. IV. vi. 82 “The safer sense,” Oth. IV. i. 280 “Are his wits safe?,” Cym. IV. ii. 131 “in all safe reason.”

safe2.text: to make safe Ant. I. iii. 55 “should safe my going” ; to conduct safely IV. vi. 26 “best you saf'd the bringer Out of the host.”

safeguard.text: protection, safety Meas. V. i. 420 , Cor. III. ii. 68 ; “in of,” for the defence or protection of 3H6 II. ii. 18 , R3 V. iii. 260 ; “on ,” on the strength of a guarantee of safe-conduct Cor. III. i. 9 .

safely.text: in safe custody All'sW. IV. i. 99 .

safety.text: (3 syll. in Ham. I. iii. 21 Qq, where Ff read “sanctity”; cf. Spenser, ‘And of our sa'fetie' good hee'd to ta'ke’） 1. means of safety, safeguard John IV. iii. 12 , Mac. IV. iii. 30 .

saffron.text: orange-red product of the Autumnal Crocus, Crocus sativus; used to colour pastry All'sW. IV. v. 2 (with allusion to the fashionable wearing of yellow), Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 49

sag.text: to droop, decline Mac. V. iii. 10 .

sail1.text: collective sing.=ships, vessels John III. iv. 2 “A whole armado of convicted sail,” Oth. I. iii. 37 ; also pl. Ant. II. vi. 24 “Thou canst not fear us, Pompey, with thy sails,” III. vii. 49 .

sail2.text: number (of vessels) sailing Per. I. iv. 61 “A portly sail of ships.”

sain.text: old pa. pple. of ‘say’ used for rhyme in LLL. III. i. 88 .

sainted.text: 1. become a saint in heaven Meas. I. iv. 34 “a thing ensky'd and sainted.”

sake.text: Meas. iv. iii. 21 “are . . . for the Lord's sake” = are ‘doing time’. ∥ ‘For the Lord's sake’ was the cry used by Ludgate prisoners when asking for alms, &c. at the grated window.

salamander.text: applied to a fiery-red face 1H4 III. iii. 53 “I have maintained that of yours with fire” (ref. to the belief that the salamander lived in fire).

sale.text: “of ,” (1) that is to be sold, vendible, venal LLL. IV. iii. 240 “things of ,” Per. IV. vi. 86 “a creature of ” ; (2) for the sale of a commodity Ham. II. i. 60 “a house of , Videlicet, a brothel.”

sallet1.text: a prevalent Eliz. form of ‘salad’ 2H6 IV. x. 9 ; used as a type of (1) a mixture All'sW. IV. v. 18 “she was the sweet-marjoram of the ” ; (2) something tasty Ham. II. ii. 471 [ 462 ] “no s-s in the lines to make the matter savoury.”

sallet2.text: in mediaeval armour, a light round headpiece 2H6 IV. x. 13 .

salt.text: applied to tears from their bitter saline taste John V. vii. 45 , Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 93 “drops of salt,” Ham. I. ii. 154 , Lr. IV. vi. 200 “a man of salt” (i.e. melting to tears).

salt1.text: adj. 1 (freq. epithet of the sea and tears) 1. living in the sea Wiv. I. i. 22 “the salt fish.”

salt2.text: lecherous, wanton Meas. V. i. 402 “Whose imagination,” Tim. IV. iii. 85 “thy hours,” Oth. II. i. 246 “his and most hidden loose affection,” III. iii. 405 , Ant. II. i. 21 . ∥ Orig. ‘to go assaut’=to be in heat.

salutation.text: (2 only S.; cf. SALUTE) 1. used elliptically LLL. V. i. 38 “Most military sir, ,” AYL. V. iv. 39 .

salute.text: to come in contact with John II. i. 590 “When his fair angels would my palm” ; to affect or act upon H8 II. iii. 103 “If this salute my blood a jot,”

sample.text: example Cym. I. i. 48 “A to the youngest.”

sanctified.text: 1. consecrated, hallowed, holy All'sW. I. i. 154 “buried . . . out of all limit,” Oth. III. iv. 125 “every spirit sanctified,” Compl. 233 “a nun, Or sister sanctified.”

sanctify.text: (2 not post-S.) 1. to consecrate (a person) 2H4 IV. v. 113 “drops of balm to sanctify thy head.”

sanctimony.text: holiness, sanctity All'sW. IV. iii. 59 , Troil. V. ii. 137 “If be the gods' delight” ; pl. sacred things Troil. V. ii. 136 “if vows be sanctimonies” (Q).

sanctuarize.text: to afford sanctuary to Ham. IV. vii. 127 “No place . . . should murder ”

sanctuary.text: “break ,” to violate the right of a sanctuary R3 III. i. 47 “You break not in seizing him; — men, children,” those who have taken refuge in a privileged place of protection R3 III. i. 55 , 56

sanded.text: of a sandy colour MND. IV. i. 126 .

sandy.text: “ hour-glass,” sand-glass, hour-glass Mer.V. I. i. 25 ; so “sandy hour” 1H6 IV. ii. 36 .

sanguine.text: red 1H4 II. iv. 272 (red-faced), 1H6 IV. i. 92 , Tit. IV. ii. 98 , Cym. V. v. 365 .

sans.text: without LLL. V. ii. 416 “sans crack or flaw,” AYL. II. vii. 166 “Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything,” Ham. III. iv. 79 .

sap.text: juice, fluid (fig.) H8 I. i. 148 “If with the sap of reason you would quench . . . the fire of passion; —there's sap in” . . ., there is life or promise in . . . Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 578, Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 191

satire.text: satirist Sonn. c. 11 “[Muse] . . . be a to decay.”

satisfaction.text: “in heavy ,” in sorrowful acceptance of the truth All'sW. V. iii. 100 .

sauce.text: (1 ‘pay sauce’ was an old phr.=pay dearly.) 1. to make (a person) pay dearly Wiv. IV. iii. 10 “I'll make them pay; I'll sauce them.”

saucer.text: dish used to receive the blood in bloodletting LLL. IV. iii. 98 “A fever in your blood! why, then incision Would let her out in saucers.”

saucy.text: (in S.'s time often an epithet of more serious condemnation than at present with ref. to insolence or impertinence of behaviour) 1. highly-seasoned, piquant (fig.) Tw.N. III. iv. 161 “there's vinegar and pepper in't” [a letter].—“Is't so saucy?.”

savage.text: (not pre-S. in sense ‘uncivilized’) 1. wild, untamed Ado I. i. 271 [ 263 ] “the bull,” Mer.V. V. i. 78 “unhandled colts . . . Their eyes turn'd to a modest gaze,” AYL. II. vi. 7 “anything ” (=any wild animal).

save1.text: vb. (1 in old edd. often “'save”; 3 common 17th cent. phrase) 1. “,” short for “God ” (which is freq.) Gent. I. i. 70 , Lr. II. i. 1 “Save thee.”

save2.text: prep. and conj. (“ for”=‘but for’ not pre-S.) 1. followed by a pronoun in the nominative Tw.N. III. i. 174 “save I alone,” Cæs. III. ii. 67 , V. v. 69 “save only he” ; in the accusative Tim. IV. iii. 509 “all, save thee, I fell with curses.”

saving.text: prep. (2 see REVERENCE) 1. except John I. I. John I. I. 201

savour1.text: sb. (2 rare) 1. smell, perfume Tp. II. ii. 55 “the of tar,” Shr. Ind. ii. 73 “I smell sweet s-s,” John IV. iii. 112 “The uncleanly savours of a slaughter-house.”

savour2.text: vb. (2 “savour of” . . . occurs 5 times) 1. to have a particular smell Per. IV. vi. 121 “The very doors and windows savour vilely.”

say.text: vb. 1 (3 cf. the vulgar ‘Now you're talking’) 1. “I have said,” (i) I have finished speaking, I have spoken my mind John II. i. 235 “When I have said, make answer to us both,” Ant. III. ii. 34 ; (ii) I have spoken decisively H8 V. i. 86 “I have said. Begone” ; (iii) It is as I have said, That is so Mac. IV. iii. 213 “My wife kill'd too?—I have said,” Ant. I. ii. 60 ;— “You have said,” What you say is true Gent. II. iv. 29 , Tw.N. III. i. 12 , Oth. IV. ii. 204 , Ant. II. vi. 110 ;— “Say you?,” What is that you say? Meas. V. i. 270 , Ham. IV. v. 28 , Oth. III. iv. 82 , Cym. II. i. 28 (after an aside), IV. ii. 379 ;—“How say you by . . .?,” What do say about (see BY 1) Mer.V. I. ii. 57 , Oth. I. iii. 17 .

say1.text: cloth of fine texture resembling serge 2H6 IV. vii. 27 (punning).

say2.text: usu. taken as the aphetic form of ‘assay’, and=smack, flavour, or proof, sample Lr. V. iii. 145 “And that thy tongue some say of breeding breathes” ; but F1 has (“some say”) in brackets.

scab.text: ‘scurvy’ fellow Tw.N. II. v. 82 , Troil. II. i. 31 ; cf. Ado III. iii. 106 , Cor. I. i. 172 , in which literal phraseology is used allusively.

scald1.text: ‘scurvy’, mean H5 V. i. 5 “ . . . knave,” Ant. V. ii. 214 “scald rimers.”

scald2.text: vb. (1 cf. SCALDING) 1. intr. to get burning hot with the sun 2H4 IV. v. 30 “Like a rich armour worn in heat of day, That scalds with safety” [i.e. to the wearer].

scale.text: pl. graduations Ant. II. vii. 21 “By certain scales i' the pyramid.”

scale1.text: “equal ,” just balance Ham. I. ii. 13 “In equal weighing delight and dole.” ∥ The pl. takes sing. concord in Rom. I. ii. 101 “that crystal s-s” (fig. ‘eyes’).

scale2.text: to weigh as in scales, to compare, estimate Meas. III. i. 267 * “the corrupt deputy [is] scaled,” Cor. II. iii. 257 .

scaling.text: (?) scattering Troil. V. v. 22 “like scaling sculls” (Q; Ff “scaled”).

scalp.text: crown of the head, skull Gent. IV. i. 36 “the bare of Robin Hood's fat friar,” MND. IV. i. 70 “this transformed ,” R2 III. ii. 112 , Lucr. 1413 .

scamble.text: to struggle indecorously or rapaciously to obtain something, scramble John IV. iii. 146 “To tug and scamble,” H5 V. ii. 217 .

scambling.text: contentious, rapacious Ado V. i. 94 , H5 I. i. 4 .

scamels.text: not yet satisfactorily explained; (?) “seamels”† (Keightley)=sea-mews, i.e. sea-gulls Tp. II. ii. 185 [ 176 ] “I'll get thee Young s-s from the rock” (many conj.; Theobald “stannels”†, Dyce “staniels”†; see STANIEL).

scan.text: (3 an Eliz. sense) 1. to estimate, judge Per. II. ii. 56 “ The outward habit by the inward man.”

scandal1.text: disgraceful imputation Ham. II. i. 29 “You must not put another on him, That he is open to incontinency.”

scandal2.text: 1. to bring into disrepute Cym. III. iv. 62 .

scandalized.text: discredited, disgraced Gent. II. vii. 61 ; defamed 1H4 I. iii. 154 .

scant.text: chary Ham. I. iii. 121 “Be somewhat scanter of your maiden presence.”

scant2.text: 1. to put (a person) off “with” a scanty supply, to stint Troil. IV. iv. 47 “He . . . s-s us with a single famish'd kiss.”

scantle.text: piece 1H4 III. i. 101 “And cuts me . . . a monstrous scantle out” (Qq; Ff “cantle,” for which the Qq reading may be an error).

scantly.text: grudgingly Ant. III. iv. 6 “Spoke of me.”

scape1.text: sb. (some mod. edd. “'scape”) 1. escape Shr. V. ii. 3 “To smile at s-s and perils overblown,” Oth. I. iii. 136 “hair-breadth scapes.”

scarcity.text: penury Tp. IV. i. 116 “ and want shall shun you” ; phr. “in of,” badly off for, ill-provided with Tim. II. ii. 235 “he was . . . in scarcity of friends.”

scarf1.text: sb. (2 a 17th cent. sense; 3 cf. SCARFED) 1. military officer's sash Ado II. i. 200 .

scarf2.text: 1. to blindfold Mac. III. ii. 47 “Come, seeling night, up the tender eye of pitiful day.”

scarfed.text: decked with streamers Mer.V. II. vi. 15 * “The scarfed bark.”

scarlet.text: clothed in scarlet (the cardinal's colour) 1H6 I. iii. 56 “out, hypocrite!,” H8 III. ii. 256 “Thou scarlet sin” (cf. CARDINAL).

scarre.text: hitherto unexplained All'sW. IV. ii. 38 (many conj.).

scathe1.text: harm 2H6 II. iv. 62 ; phr. “do ” John II. i. 75 , R3 I. iii. 317 , Tit. V. i. 7 .

scene.text: representation of a piece on the stage, dramatic performance, play or drama Wiv. IV. vi. 17 “wherein fat Falstaff Hath a great ,” AYL. II. vii. 138 “the Wherein we play in,” H5 I. Chor. 4 “princes to act And monarchs to behold the swelling ,” Rom. IV. iii. 19 , Ham. II. ii. 427 [ 418 ] “scene individable,” 627 [ 619 ] “the very cunning of the ” ∥ The most freq. S. sense.

schedule.text: (2 a 16th-17th cent. sense). 1. slip or scroll of paper containing writing LLL. I. i. 18 “those statutes That are recorded in this here,” Mer.V. II. ix. 55 , 2H4 IV. i. 168 “this . . . contains our general grievances,” Cæs. III. i. 3 , Lucr. 1312 (a letter).

scholar.text: pupil Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 102 “Thy master dies thy ,” Per. II. iii. 17 “you're her labour'd ,” II. v. 31 , 39 , IV. vi. 203 .

scholarly.text: as befits a scholar Wiv. I. iii. 2 .

school.text: to reprimand, lecture MND I. i. 116 , 1H4 III. i. 189 ; to discipline, control Mac. IV. ii. 15 .

school1.text: sb. 1 (2 a sense once currentin certain phrases, e.g. ‘men of school’, ‘degree of school’, ‘art of school’) 1. “set to ,” to send to be taught, give instruction to 3H6 III. ii. 193 “And set the murd'rous Machiavel to ,” Lr. II. iv. 68 “We'll set thee to to an ant,” Lucr. 1820 “Now set thy long-experienc'd wit to school.”

school2.text: shoal (of fish) Troil V. v. 22 “they fly or die, like scaled schools” (Ff “sculs) Before the belching whale”; fig. large number, ‘crowd’ 2H4 IV. iii. 20 “I have a whole of tongues in this belly of mine.”

schoolmaster.text: private tutor Tp. I. ii. 172 , Shr. I. i. 94 , &c., Cor. I. iii. 61 , Lr. I. iv. 196 , Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 71 ∥ The mod. sense occurs only in LLL. IV. ii. 87 , V. ii. 529 .

science.text: knowledge Meas. I. i. 5 , All'sW. V. iii. 103 .

scion.text: (old edd. “sien, syen, seyen”) shoot, twig (fig.) Oth. I. iii. 337 “lusts, whereof I take this that you call love to be a set† or scion;” slip for grafting, graft Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 93 “we marry A gentler to the wildest stock,” H5 III. v. 7 .

scold.text: to quarrel noisily, brawl, rail (“against”), wrangle (“with”) Ado II. i. 251 , Tim. IV. iii. 157 , with phr. denoting the result H8 V. i. 175 “-it out of him.”

scolding.text: = CHIDING ppl. adj. Cæs. I. iii. 5 “ winds.”

sconce.text: refl. to entrench oneself (fig.) Ham. III. iv. 4 (old edd. “silence”).

sconce1.text: jocular term for the head Err. I. ii. 79 , Cor. III. ii. 99 “my unbarbed ,” Ham. V. i. 108 “knock him about the sconce.”

sconce2.text: small fort or earthwork H5 III. vi. 78 ; fig. defence Err. II. ii. 37 “I must get a for my head.”

scope.text: (phr. “give, have ” = give, have free play, liberty or opportunity) 1. end in view, object, aim R2 III. iii. 112 “His coming hither hath no further Than” . . ., 1H4 III. i. 170 “He . . . curbs himself even of his natural ,” Ham. III. ii. 231 , Sonn. lxi. 8 “me, The and tenour of thy jealousy” ; phr. “to ,” to the purpose Tim. I. i. 73 .

scorch.text: to slash with a knife Mac. III. ii. 13 “We have scorch'd the snake, not kill'd it” (Theobald “scotch'd”†).

score1.text: 1. notch cut in a stick or tally used in keeping accounts 2H6 IV. vii. 39 .

score2.text: Oth. IV. i. 128 * “scored me,” (a) made my reckoning, (b) branded me.

scorn1.text: 1. derisive utterance or gesture, taunt, insult LLL. V. ii. 873 “if sickly ears . . . Will hear your idle s-s,” 1H6 II. iv. 77 , Ham. III. i. 70 “bear the whips and s-s of time,” Oth. IV. i. 83 “the gibes, and notable scorns.”

scorn2.text: vb. (1 and 2 are the orig. senses) 1. intr. to mock or jeer (“at” a person) LLL. IV. iii. 147 “How will he scorn!,” AYL. III. v. 131 , John I. i. 228 “why s-'st thou at Sir Robert?,” Rom. I. v. 61 .

scornful.text: regarded with scorn Lucr. 520 “The mark of every open eye.”

scot.text: used fig. to express paying a person out thoroughly 1H4 V. iv. 115 “or that hot termagant Scot had paid me scot and lot too.”

scotch2.text: to cut, score, gash Cor. IV. v. 198 “he s-ed him and notched him like a carbonado.” ∥ See also SCORCH.

scour.text: to remove, get rid of 1H4 III. ii. 137 “Which, wash'd away, shall my shame with it,” H5 I. i. 34 “s-ing faults.” ∥ In H5 II. i. 60 “If you grow foul with me . . . I will you with my rapier” there is app. an allusion to a current sense of ‘beat, punish’.

scout1.text: to keep a look-out Tw.N. III. iv. 196 .

scrape.text: to erase (writing) with a knife Meas. I. ii. 9 “scraped one” [commandment] “out of the table”; fig. Wiv. IV. ii. 234 “to the figures out of your husband's brains.”

scribe.text: penman, writer Gent. II. i. 150 , Tit. II. iv. 4 .

scrip.text: piece of paper written upon MND. I. ii. 3 “according to the scrip.”

scrippage.text: contents of a scrip (or shepherd's pouch); only in “scrip and ,” modelled on “bag and baggage” in AYL. III. ii. 172 .

scrivener.text: 1. professional scribe R3 III. vi. stage dir.

scrowl.text: (?) a form of ‘scrawl’, to gesticulate, with a play on ‘scroll’, to write down Tit. II. iv. 5 “See, how with signs and tokens she can scrowl.”

scroyle.text: scoundrel, wretch John II. i. 373 “these scroyles of Angiers flout you.”
