scruple.text: “make of,” (1) to stick at Troil. IV. i. 56 “Not making any of her soilure” ; (2) to hesitate to believe or admit, to doubt 2H4 I. ii. 150 “the wise may make some dram of a , or . . . a itself,” Cym. V. v. 183 “I . . . Made scruple of his praise.”

scrupulous.text: cautious or hesitating in taking action Ant. I. iii. 48 .

scullion.text: domestic servant of the lowest rank who performed the menial duties of the kitchen 2H4 II. i. 67 , Ham. II. ii. 624 [ 616 ].

scuse.text: aphetic form of ‘excuse’, e.g. Mer.V. IV. i. 445 .

scut.text: tail of a deer Wiv. V. v. 20 .

sea.text: (the foll. are special uses) 1. used to typify water as one of the ‘elements’ Err. II. i. 17 , Ham. I. i. 153 “Whether in sea or fire, in earth or air,” Per. I. iv. 34 .

seal1.text: 1. something which authenticates, attests or confirms a covenant or undertaking, final addition which completes and secures Meas. IV. i. 7 “my kisses . . . S-s of love,” MND. III. ii. 144 , H5 IV. i. 174 , Troil. IV. iv. 122 ; pl. Ham. III. ii. 424 [ 417 ] “To give them seals” (=to confirm them by making words into deeds).

seal2.text: vb. (“ ” one's “lips, mouth” are not pre-S.; also “ ” one's “eyes,” for which see also SEEL) 1. intr. to set one's seal (to something) Mer.V. I. iii. 153 , Tw.N. II. v. 105 , 1H4 III. i. 269 , Ven. 512 ; “ under for,” to become surety for Mer.V. I. ii. 88 .

seam.text: fat, grease Troil. II. iii. 197 “bastes his arrogance with his own seam.” ∥ Cf. ENSEAMED.

seamy.text: “the side without,” the worst side outside Oth. IV. ii. 146 .

sear2.text: 1. to dry up, cause to wither, blight Cym. I. i. 116 .

search2.text: vb. (1 now only used with ‘out’) 1. to seek for Cym. V. v. 11 “He hath been search'd among the dead and living.”

searcher.text: official appointed to view dead bodies and report on the cause of death Rom. V. ii. 8 .

searching.text: (of words) cutting, trenchant 2H6 III. ii. 311 “bitter terms” ; (of wine) stirring or exciting the blood 2H4 II. iv. 30 .

seared.text: withered, blighted Meas. II. iv. 9 “sear'd† and tedious,” Cym. II. iv. 6 “sear'd hopes,” Compl. 14 “sear'd age.”

season1.text: sb. (the sense of ‘time’ is freq.) 1. “of (the) ,” in season Wiv. III. iii. 169 “buck; and of the too,” Meas. II. ii. 85 “kill the fowl of ;—of ,” befitting the time of year, seasonable All'sW. V. iii. 32 “a day of ;—to ,” when opportunity presents itself Err. IV. ii. 58 ;—“of such a ,” of such an age Cym. III. iv. 175 .

season2.text: vb. (5 a rare use) 1. to mature Tim. IV. iii. 85 , Ham. I. iii. 81 “my blessing this in thee,” III. ii. 221 , iii. 86 “fit and s-'d for his passage.”

seasoned.text: (a) matured, (b) made palatable Cor. III. iii. 63 * .

seat1.text: sb. (the sense of ‘throne’ is freq. in the historical plays, e.g. R2 III. ii. 119 ) 1. estate Mer.V. I. i. 172 , 1H4 V. i. 45 , H5 III. v. 47 , Cym. V. iv. 60 .

seated.text: (1 in the historical plays) 1. on the throne 3H6 III. i. 96 , R3 IV. ii. 4 .

second.text: to follow up Cym. V. i. 14 .

second1.text: 1. supporter Tp. III. iii. 103 , Cor. I. iv. 43 , viii. 16 , Lr. IV. vi. 199 “No s-s? All myself?,” Cym. V. iii. 90 ; (of a thing) Ham. IV. vii. 153 .

second2.text: adj. (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. secondary, subordinate 1H4 I. iii. 165 “base means,” 2H4 V. ii. 90 , Troil. II. iii. 150 .

secondary.text: subordinate Meas. I. i. 46 “thy ,” John V. ii. 80 “To be a secondary at control.”

secret1.text: “marks of ,” secret marks Cym. V. v. 207 .

secret2.text: adj. ( Lr. III. i. 32 “have feet In” = have landed secretly at) 1. belonging peculiarly to oneself, private Tw.N. I. iv. 14 “my soul,” R3 III. v. 27 “her thoughts,” Ham. II. ii. 243 “the secret parts.”

sect.headword: sect (in Oth. I. iii. 337 ? a misprint for “sett”
sect.text: see SET sb. 4) 1. party, faction Tim. III. v. 30 “sects and factions,” Lr. V. iii. 18 “packs and sects of great ones.”

sectary.text: “ astronomical,” student of astrology Lr. I. ii. 169 .

secure1.text: adj. (1 as freq. as the sense ‘safe’; “ of”= safe from Tit. II. i. 3 ; stressed like ENTIRE) 1. free from care or apprehension, confident, overconfident, unsuspicious Wiv. II. i. 240 “Though Page be a fool,” R2 V. iii. 43 “secu're, foolhardy king,” Ham. I. v. 61 “Upon my se'cure hour thy uncle stole,” Oth. III. iii. 198 “not jealous nor secu're,” IV. i. 72 “To lip a wanton in a se'cure couch.”

secure2.text: 1. to give confidence or a sense of safety to, make careless Tim. II. ii. 186 “ thy heart,” Lr. IV. i. 20 “Our means us” ; refl. Oth. I. iii. 10 “I do not so me in the error.”

securely.text: confidently, without apprehension or suspicion of evil Wiv. II. ii. 257 , John II. i. 374 “stand on their battlements,” Troil. IV. v. 73 “ done,” Tit. III. i. 3 “whilst you securely slept.”

security.text: consciousness of safety confidence, want of caution R2 III. ii. 34 , H5 II. ii. 44 , Cæs. II. iii. 8 “ gives way to conspiracy,” Mac. III. v. 32 “ Is mortals' chiefest enemy.”

see2.headword: see vb. (in sense 3 also with various constr.
see2.text: —object and adj. 1H6 II. v. 121 , 2H6 II. iii. 54 , object and pple. Mer.V. II. ii. 126 , 170 , clause Gent. I. ii. 44 , MND. III. ii. 98 ) 1. “see away,” spend in seeing H8 Prol. 12

seeded.text: arrived at maturity like a plant that has done flowering and is ready to sow itself Troil. I. iii. 316 “the pride That hath to this maturity blown up,” Lucr. 603 “How will thy shame be in thine age.”

seedness.text: sowing with seed Meas. I. iv. 42 .

seedsman.text: sower of seed Ant. II. vii. 24 .

seeing.text: 1. faculty of sight LLL. IV. iii. 333 “It adds a precious seeing to the eye.”

seek.text: “ through,” to seek out, follow up Cym. IV. ii. 160 ; “ to,” to approach in the way of appeal Lucr. 293 .

seeking.text: suit, petition Cor. I. i. 194 “What's their ?.”

seel.text: in falconry, to close up a hawk's eyes when it is taken by drawing the upper eyelids down with a needle and thread which is fastened under the beak; fig. to blind Mac. III. ii. 46 “s-ing night,” Oth. I. iii. 271 (Qq “foyles”), III. iii. 210 “To her father's eyes up close as oak” (Ff1 2 “seele,” Qq Ff3 4 “seale”), Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 112 ∥ Liable to confusion with SEAL vb.

seeming1.text: vbl. sb. (1 the commonest use) 1. outward form, appearance, or show Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 75 “these keep and savour all the winter long,” H8 II. iv. 106 “in full ” (=to all appearance), Troil. I. iii. 157 , Ham. III. ii. 92 , Cym. V. v. 65 “thought her like her seeming.”

seeming2.text: ppl. adj. (1 the commonest use) 1. that is so in appearance, apparent Mer.V. III. ii. 100 “The seeming truth,” 1H4 V. ii. 34 “There is no mercy in the king” (=no mercy even in appearance), Ant. II. ii. 217 “A seeming mermaid.”

seen.text: “well seen,” versed or skilled “in” Shr. I. ii. 136 .

seethe.text: (see also SOD, SODDEN) 1. to boil Tim. IV. iii. 436 .

seething.text: boiling hot Sonn. cliii. 7 “a bath” ; fig. MND. V. i. 4 “seething brains” (cf. BOILED).

seizure.text: grasp, clasp John III. i. 241 , Troil. I. i. 59 “her hand . . . to whose soft seizure.”

seld.text: seldom Troil. IV. v. 149 “As I have the chance,” Cor. II. i. 232 “seld-shown flamens.”

seldom.text: “ but” = it is seldom that . . . not, usually Per. IV. ii. 133 ; “ when” = seldom that Meas. IV. ii. 89 , 2H4 IV. iv. 79 .

self.text: (2 only with demonstratives “the, this, that”) 1. of or belonging to oneself, one's own Mac. V. vii. 99 [ viii. 70 ] “ and violent hands”; cf. R2 III. ii. 166 “ and vain conceit” (app.=vain self-conceit), and Mac. III. iv. 142 “My strange and self-abuse” (see SELF-2).

sell.text: (the orig. meaning is ‘to give’) 1. “ ” one's “life,” die Mer.V. II. vii. 67 , 3H6 V. i. 74 .

semblable.text: adj. similar 2H4 V. i. 72 , Ant. III. iv. 3 ; sb. (one's) like Tim. IV. iii. 22 , Ham. V. ii. 125 .

semblative.text: like, resembling Tw.N. I. iv. 34 “all is semblative a woman's part.”

send.text: to send acknowledgement of allegiance to Ant. V. ii. 29 “I send him The greatness he has got.”

sennet.text: set of notes played on a trumpet as a signal for the approach and departure of processions 2H6 III. i, H8 II. iv, Cor. II. i, Mac. III. i, Lr. I. i.

sennight.text: week AYL. III. ii. 337 , Mac. I. iii. 22 (Ff “Seu'nights”), Oth. II. i. 77 .

sense.text: (used as a pl. without inflexion in Mac. V. i. 28 Ff “their are shut,” Sonn. cxii. 10 ; the meanings ‘physical perception or feeling’, ‘mental perception, or apprehension’, ‘understanding’, ‘feeling, sensibility’, ‘reason, reasonableness’, ‘meaning, import’ are the chief; for “common ” see COMMON adj. 5) 1. mental faculty, mind Tw.N. IV. i. 66 , Oth. III. iii. 375 “have you a soul or ?,” Cym. II. ii. 11 “man's o'erlabour'd sense Repairs itself by rest.”

senseless.text: (2 the commonest sense) 1. having no sense (viz. of hearing), inattentive Cym. II. iii. 58 * ; “ of,” insensible to AYL. II. vii. 55 “ of the bob,” Cym. I. i. 135 “ of your wrath” ; (?) regardless Tim. II. ii. 1 “senseless of expense.”

sensible.text: (meaning ‘full of good sense’ occurs) 1. capable of physical feeling or perception, endowed with sensibility, sensitive Tp. II. i. 181 [ 174 ] “ and nimble lungs,” Meas. III. i. 118 , Err. IV. iv. 26 “ in nothing but blows,” LLL. IV. ii. 28 , MND. V. i. 184 “The wall, . . . being ,” Cor. I. iii. 95 “ as your finger” ; const. “of” 1H4 V. iv. 94 , Cæs. I. iii. 18 .

sensibly.text: 1. as a creature endowed with feeling Cor. I. iv. 53 , Tit. IV. ii. 123 .

sentence.text: sententious saying, maxim Ado II. iii. 260 “quips and s-s,” Mer.V. I. ii. 11 “Good s-s and well pronounced,” Oth. I. iii. 199 , Lucr. 244 “Who fears a , or an old man's saw.”

sententious.text: expressing much in few words, pithy LLL. V. i. 3 “your reasons . . . have been sharp and ,” AYL. V. iv. 66 “he is very swift and ” ∥ In Rom. II. iv. 227 app. a blunder for ‘sentences’.

sequel.text: “in ,” in due succession H5 V. ii. 361 “His daughter first, and then in sequel all.”

sequence.text: “in ,” one after the other Tit. IV. i. 37 “Why lifts she up her arms in thus?” ; Tim. V. i. 213 “in the of degree,” according to their status.

sequent2.text: 1. consequent Meas. V. i. 374 , Lr. I. ii. 118 ; “ to,” consequent upon All'sW. II. ii. 60 , Ham. V. ii. 54 .

sequester.text: to separate AYL. II. i. 33 “a poor s-'d stag,” Troil. III. iii. 8 , Tit. II. iii. 75 .

sequestration.text: separation, seclusion H5 I. i. 58 “ From open haunts,” 1H6 II. v. 25 , Oth. I. iii. 351 .

sere1.text: part of a gun-lock which keeps the hammer at full or half cock; only in fig. phr. “tickle o' the ,” ready to ‘go off’ at any time, yielding easily to any impulse Ham. II. ii. 347 [ 337 ].

sere2.text: dry, withered Err. IV. ii. 19 “crooked, old and ” ;—sb. withered state Mac. V. iii. 23 “fall'n into the , the yellow leaf” (mod. edd. “sear,” after F1 “Seare”).

sergeant.text: sheriff's officer Err. IV. ii. 56 , H8 I. i. 198 , Ham. V. ii. 350 “this fell , death, Is strict in his arrest.”

serpent.text: “s-'s tongue,” hissing MND. V. ii. 64 [ i. 430 ].

serpigo.text: skin eruption Meas. III. i. 31 , Troil. II. iii. 82 .

servanted.text: subject Cor. V. ii. 89 “My affairs Are to others.”

serve.text: (1 the corresponding trans. sense with a personal object is freq., esp. of the fitting of clothes, e.g. Gent. IV. iv. 169 , and in the phr. “serve” one's “turn”） 1. to be sufficient, avail, ‘do’ Ado I. i. 328 [ 320 ] “what will is fit,” 2H4 V. i. 7 “no excuse shall ,” R3 I. iv. 279 (Ff “do”), Rom. III. i. 102 “'tis enough, 'twill serve.”

service.text: all that was laid upon a table in preparation for a meal (cloth, bread, salt, &c.) Mac. I. vii. stage dir.; order of dishes at a meal Ham. IV. iii. 25 “variable service.”

serviceable.text: active or diligent in service Shr. I. i. 218 , Lr. IV. vi. 258 “a villain,” Cym. III. ii. 15 ; expressing readiness to serve Gent. III. ii. 70 “ vows.”

serving.text: “in their ,” using them Cym. III. iv. 173 .

sessa.text: interj. of doubtful import Shr. Ind. i. 6 “let the world slide, !,” Lr. III. iv. 101 “sessa†, let him trot by” (Ff “Ses(s)ey,” Qq2 3 “ceas(e),” III. vi. 77 (Ff “sese”).

session.text: sitting of a court of justice, judicial proceedings Wint. II. iii. 201 “Summon a ,” H8 II. iv. 64 “It's fit this royal do proceed,” Oth. I. ii. 86 “fit time Of law and course of direct ,” III. iii. 140 “in sit” (Ff “Sessions”); fig. Sonn. xxx. 1 “the s-s of sweet silent thought.”

set1.text: sb. (3 always in fig. context; 4 cf. mod. midl. dial.=‘bedding-out plant’) 1. sunset H5 IV. i. 292 “from the rise to set” ; cf. R3 V. iii. 19 , Mac. I. i. 5 .

set2.text: vb. (used in many connexions where ‘place’ or ‘put’ is now idiomatic) 1. pass. to sit Gent. II. i. 95 “I stand affected to her. —I would you were set,” H8 III. i. 73 “I was set at work,” Cor. IV. v. 204 , Ven. 18 “being set” ; also refl. LLL. IV. iii. 4 “set thee down” ; mixed constr. 3H6 IV. iii. 2 “The King . . . is set him down.”

setter.text: one who ‘sets matches’ (see SET vb. 10), one who decoys persons to be robbed 1H4 II. ii. 56 . ∥ Cf. ‘Setters’, or ‘Setting Dogs’, they that draw in Bubbles [=dupes] for old Gamesters to Rook (Dict. of Canting Crew).

setting.text: set expression Tp. II. i. 237 [ 229 ] “The setting of thine eye.”

settle.text: to become calm or clear Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 484 “till the fury of his highness ,” Lr. IV. vii. 82 “trouble him no more Till further settling” (=‘till his mind is more composed’).

settled.text: fixed, rooted Wint. IV. iii. [iv]. 537 “ponderous and project,” R2 I. i. 201 “your hate” ; congealed, stagnant 2H4 IV. iii. 113 “the blood . . . before cold and ,” Rom. IV. v. 26 “Her blood is , and her joints are stiff” ; resolved Mac. I. vii. 79 ; composed, calm Meas. III. i. 88 “ visage,” Ham. IV. vii. 80 “ age,” Sonn. xlix. 8 “settled gravity.”

seven.text: “ year(s),” typically for ‘a long period’ Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 591, 1H4 II. iv. 347 , 2H6 II. i. 2 “these years' day,” Lr. III. iv. 143 “for seven long year.”

sevennight.text: =SENNIGHT Ado II. i. 377 “a just sevennight” (=exactly a week), Wint. I. ii. 17 .

several.text: the main senses are (1) separate, distinct, different (e.g. Tp. III. i. 42 “for virtues Have I lik'd women” ; often “each , every ”=each or every particular), (2) particular, respective (e.g. Tp. III. iii. 88 “my meaner ministers Their kinds have done” ), (3) divers, various (e.g. Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 184 “He sings tunes,” H8 III. ii. 126 “The parcels of his plate” ). ∥ In Sonn. cxxxvii. 9 “a plot” = a private enclosed plot of ground (opposed to “common place” =common); hence allusively in LLL. II. i. 221 “My lips are no common, though they be” (quibble).

severally.text: each in a particular way or for a particular purpose Tim. II. ii. 197 , Cæs. III. ii. 10 , Cym. V. v. 398 ; separately, singly Troil. IV. v. 273 .

severals.text: (the sb. is not used in sing.) 1. individual persons Wint. I. ii. 226 .

sewer1.text: drain Troil. V. i. 85 , Per. IV. vi. 191 .

sewer2.text: servant who carried in and arranged dishes for a banquet Mac. I. vii. stage dir.

shackle.text: to fetter (only fig.) All'sW. II. iii. 159 , Ant. V. ii. 6 .

shade1.text: sb. (1 only in rhyme; 3 cf. SHADOW 6) 1. (a person's) shadow Sonn. liii. 3 .

shade2.text: 1. to dull the brightness of Pilgr. x. 3 [ 133 ].

shadow1.text: sb. (in 2H4 III. ii. 147 =mere name without a man to correspond to it) 1. shade Tp. IV. i. 67 “groves, Whose the dismissed bachelor loves,” R2 III. iv. 25 , Lr. V. ii. 1 “take the of this tree For your good host” ; shady place AYL. IV. i. 229 “I'll go find a ” ; obscurity, darkness Meas. III. i. 258 ; pl. Sonn. xliii. 5 .

shadow2.text: 1. to conceal Mac. V. iv. 6 “thereby shall we The numbers of our host.”

shadowy.text: shady Gent. V. iv. 2 “This desart,” Lr. I. i. 66 “shadowy forests” (Qq “shady”).

shady.text: Sonn. lxxvii. 7 “shady stealth,” slow progress of the shadow (on the dial).

shaft.text: arrow (freq.); see also BOLT sb. 1 ∥ ‘A shaft hath three principall partes, the stele, the fethers, and the head’ (Ascham, Toxophilus).

shag.text: shaggy Ven. 295 “fetlocks ” ; so shag-eared, hairy-eared Mac. IV. ii. 81 “thou villain” (mod. edd. “shag-haired”†), shag-haired 2H6 III. i. 367 “a crafty kern.”

shake.text: (pa. t. “shook,” twice “shaked”; pa. pple. “shook,” 5 times “shaken,” 3 times “shaked”): phr. “ ” a person's “beard,” defy, beard Ham. IV. vii. 32 , Lr. III. vii. 77 ; “ the ears,” see EAR sb.; “ the head,” (?) nod 2H6 IV. i. 55 ; “ off,” refuse to accept or entertain Tw.N. V. i. 77 “I off these names,” Ant. III. vii. 33 “these offers . . . he s-s off;— out,” (?) to blab All'sW. II. iv. 25 “many a man's tongue s-s out his master's undoing;— up,” use with violence AYL. I. i. 30 . ∥ The commonest S. meanings of “ off” are ‘lay aside, get rid of, discard’.

shale.text: shell H5 IV. ii. 18 “the s-s and husks of men.”

shall.text: (clipped to “s,” old edd. “se,” in Rom. I. iii. 9 ; cf. ISE and the monosyllabic scansion of “I shall” in John III. iv. 78 and elsewhere; the uses of SHOULD are given separately) 1. used where mod. idiom requires ‘will’ All'sW. V. iii. 27 “inform him So 'tis our will he should.—I , my liege,” Tit. IV. iv. 106 “Your bidding shall I do effectually,” Mac. III. iv. 57 “If much you note him You shall offend him,” Ant. II. i. 1 “If the great gods be just, they shall assist The deeds of justest men.”

shallow.text: “ in,” a superficial judge of All'sW. I. iii. 46 “shallow . . . in great friends.”

shallowly.text: without consideration 2H4 IV. ii. 119 “Most shallowly did you these arms commence.”

shame2.text: to be ashamed AYL. IV. iii. 137 “I do not To tell you what I was,” Cor. II. ii. 72 , Mac. II. ii. 65 “I To wear a heart so white,” Lucr. 1084 , 1143 “As shaming any eye should thee behold.”

shameless.text: as adv. Err. V. i. 202 , Cym. V. v. 58 .

shape1.text: used with considerable latitude and freq. in contexts where ‘form’ would now be preferred; almost=fashion in Ado III. ii. 34 “in the of two countries at once” ; 1H4 I. i. 58 “ of likelihood” =probability; Ham. IV. vii. 150 “to our ” = for the part we propose to act.

shape2.text: vb. (rare in material sense) 1. to conform, adjust, proportion (one thing “to” another) LLL. V. ii. 65 “make him . . . his service wholly to my hests,” Tw.N. I. ii. 59 “ thou thy silence to my wit,” Lucr. 1458 “shapes her sorrows to the beldam's woes” ; also intr. to suit, agree Cym. V. v. 347 .

shapeless.text: (2 cf. FEATURELESS, SIGHTLESS) 1. not shaped to any end, aimless, purposeless Gent. I. i. 8 * “shapeless idleness.”

shard.text: (twice; only in pl.) 1. fragment of pottery, potsherd Ham. V. i. 253 .

share.text: to take as one's share, receive or gain H5 IV. iii. 32 “so great an honour As one man more . . . would from me,” Troil. I. iii. 367 “What glory our Achilles s-s from Hector,” Rom. I. iii. 91 ; to experience Lucr. 1431 “sharing joy To see” . . .

sharp1.text: (?) shrill high note Rom. III. v. 28 .

sharp2.text: 1. hungry, famished (also used as epithet of “hunger” itself=keen) Shr. IV. i. 193 “My falcon now is and passing empty,” All'sW. III. ii. 121 “ constraint of hunger,” Ven. 55 “an empty eagle, by fast,” Lucr. 422 “Sharp hunger.”

sharply.text: keenly Tp. V. i. 23 “relish all as , Passion as they,” Cym. III. iv. 88 “those that are betrayed Do feel the treason sharply.”

sharpness.text: harshness, severity All'sW. I. ii. 37 , Ant. III. iii. 35 .

she.text: (1 occurs nine times, 2 four times) 1. woman Tw.N. I. v. 261 “the cruell'st she alive,” Wint. I. ii. 44 “lady she” (=titled lady), Cym. I. iii. 29 “The shes of Italy.”

sheaf.text: to make corn into sheaves AYL. III. ii. 114 .

shealed.text: shelled, with the peas taken out Lr. I. iv. 222 “That's a shealed peascod.”

shearman.text: one who shears woollen cloth 2H6 IV. ii. 145 .

sheathing.text: having a sheath made Shr. IV. i. 138 “Walter's dagger was not come from sheathing.”

shed.text: to be scattered Troil. I. iii. 319 .

sheep.text: used quibblingly with “ship” Gent. I. i. 73 , Err. IV. i. 94 , LLL. II. i. 219 . ∥ The two words are still pronounced alike in the midlands.

sheer.text: clear, pure R2 V. iii. 61 “Thou , immaculate, and silver fountain” ; Shr. Ind. ii. 25 “ ale” * , (?) ale and nothing else.

sheet.text: to cover as with a sheet Ant. I. iv. 65 .

sheeted.text: wrapped in a shroud Ham. I. i. 115 .

shelving.text: projecting Gent. III. i. 115 “Her chamber is . . . built so shelving.”

shelvy.text: made of sandbanks Wiv. III. v. 16 .

shent.text: blamed, reproved, rebuked, rated Wiv. I. iv. 38 , Tw.N. IV. ii. 115 “I am for speaking to you,” Cor. V. ii. 104 , Ham. III. ii. 423 [ 416 ]. ∥ Introduced as a pa. t. by Theobald in Troil. II. iii. 87 for Ff “sent.”

sherris.text: ‘sack’ (white wine) imported from Xeres in Spain, sherry 2H4 IV. iii. 111 , &c.; see SACK.

shield.text: “God ,” God forbid or foRefend Meas. III. i. 139 “Heaven my mother play'd my father fair,” All'sW. I. iii. 176 (with negative idea repeated in the second clause) “God you mean it not!,” Rom. IV. i. 41 “God shield I should disturb devotion.”

shift1.text: sb. (1 occurs once; 2 is freq.) 1. change Tim. I. i. 85 “Fortune in her and change of mood.”

shift2.text: vb. (freq. in the sense of ‘change’, trans. and intr.) 1. to exchange Ant. V. ii. 151 “mine will now be yours; And, should we shift estates, yours would be mine.”

shipman.text: mariner Troil. V. ii. 169 , Mac. I. iii. 17 , Per. I. iii. 24 .

shipping.text: “take ,” embark 1H6 V. v. 87 ; “good ,” good voyage Shr. V. i. 43 .

shive.text: slice Tit. II. i. 87 “easy it is Of a cut loaf to steal a shive.”

shiver.text: to be shattered into small pieces Lr. IV. vi. 52 “Thou'dst shiver'd like an egg.”

shivers.text: splinters, small fragments R2 IV. i. 289 “crack'd in a hundred shivers,” Troil. II. i. 42 .

shoal.text: shallow H8 III. ii. 437 “all the depths and s-s of honour,” Mac. I. vii. 6 “upon this bank and shoal† of time” (old edd. “school”).

shock.text: to ‘meet force with force’ (J.) John V. vii. 117 “we shall shock them.”

shoe.text: pl. “shoes; shoon” only in a ballad Ham. IV. v. 26 , and in the mouth of Jack Cade, 2H6 IV. ii. 199 .

shog.text: to move off, go away H5 II. i. 47 , II. iii. 48 . ∥ Remains in midl. dialects.

shoot.text: act of shooting, discharge of a missile, shot LLL. IV. i. 10 “A stand where you may make the fairest ,” 3H6 III. i. 7 “and so my is lost,” Ham. V. ii. 380 “at a shoot” (Qq “shot”).

shop.text: 1. fig. store Cym. V. v. 167 “A of all the qualities that man Loves woman for.”

shore1.text: H5 IV. i. 285 “the high of this world,” the exalted places of the earth; Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 11 “the varying of the world,” (?) the earth with its continual variations.

shore3.text: to put ashore Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 875

short1.text: adj. (1 see also COME “short”) 1. inadequate LLL. IV. iii. 241 “praise too doth blot,” Tim. I. i. 97 “five talents is his debt, His means most ”

short2.text: vb. (used only twice) 1. to cut short (fig.) Cym. I. vi. 200 “I shall my word By lengthening my return.”

shot1.text: what a person owes at an alehouse, tavernreckoning Gent. II. v. 7 , 10 , 1H4 V. iii. 31 (quibble on SHOT 2 ), Cym. V. iv. 158 .

shot2.text: marksman 2H4 III. ii. 298 “a little, lean, old, chopp'd, bald shot” ; as a collective=marksmen 1H6 I. iv. 53 “a guard of chosen ,” H8 V. iv. 60 “loose ” (see LOOSE adj. 1).

shotten.text: (of a herring) that has ‘shot’ or shed its roe and is worthless 1H4 II. iv. 145 .

shough.text: shaggy-haired kind of dog Mac. III. i. 94 .

should.text: (1 cf. SHALL 1; 3 common Eliz.) 1. used where the mod. idiom requires ‘would’ Mer.V. I. ii. 98 “you refuse to per form your father's will, if” . . ., Wint. I. ii. 57 “To be your prisoner import offending,” Troil. I. iii. 116 “Force be right,” Ham. III. ii. 321 “Your wisdom show itself more richer to signify this to his doctor.”

shoulder.text: “in the of,” behind Ham. I. iii. 56 “The wind sits in the shoulder of your sail.”

shout.text: in Cor. I. i. 220 , I. ix. 50 old edd. “shoot”; cf. HOOT (“howt”).

show1.text: sb. (the main senses are ‘act of exhibiting or demonstrating’, ‘display, ostentation’, ‘appearance, aspect’, ‘spectacular performance’） 1. thing seen, vision, sight Tp. II. ii. 5 “urchin s-s,” R2 III. iii. 71 “That any harm should stain so fair a ,” Lr. III. vi. 114 “Leaving free things and happy s-s behind,” Cym. V. v. 429 .

show2.text: vb. (1 very freq.; by ellipsis app.=seem to do in Sonn. xciv. 2 ） 1. to have (a certain) appearance, appear, seem AYL. I. iii. 84 “thou wilt more bright and seem more virtuous When she is gone,” H5 IV. i. 108 “the element shows to him as it doth to me,” Cor. IV. v. 68 “Thou show'st a noble vessel,” Mac. I. iii. 54 “Are ye fantastical, or that indeed Which outwardly ye show?,” Lr. I. iv. 267 “this our court . . . Shows like a riotous inn,” Ant. IV. viii. 7 “you have shown all Hectors,” Sonn. cv. 2 “Let not . . . my beloved as an idol show.”

shrew1.text: scold; often SHROW in old edd. and rhyming with “O, show, woe.”

shrew2.text: = the much commoner “beshrew” Wint. I. ii. 281 “ my heart,” Cym. II. iii. 147 “shrew me.”

shrewd.text: (3 often a mere intensive, cf. SHREWDLY 2) 1. malicious, mischievous, ill-natured; (of persons) LLL. V. ii. 12 “a unhappy gallows,” MND. II. i. 33 “that and knavish sprite,” 1H6 I. ii. 123 “ tempters,” Cæs. II. i. 158 “A contriver,” Ven. 500 “Thy eyes' tutor, that hard heart of thine” ; (of things) Wiv. II. ii. 237 “there is construction made of her,” All'sW. III. v. 68 “do her A shrewd turn,” H8 V. iii. 177 .

shrewdly.text: (2 cf. SHREWD 3) 1. sharply; (mentally) Ado II. i. 85 “you apprehend passing shrewdly” ; (physically) Ham. I. iv. 1 “The air bites shrewdly.”

shrieve.text: sheriff All'sW. IV. iii. 213 , 2H4 IV. iv. 99 (Q).

shrift.text: confession (and absolution) Meas. IV. ii. 224 , 3H6 III. ii. 107 , Rom. I. i. 164 , &c.; confessional Oth. III. iii. 24 “His bed shall seem a school, his board a shrift.”

shrill.text: to utter loudly Troil. V. iii. 84 “Andromache shrills her dolours forth.”

shrine.text: image (as of a saint) Mer.V. II. vii. 40 “To kiss this , this mortal-breathing saint,” Rom. I. v. 78 , Cym. V. v. 165 “laming The of Venus,” Lucr. 194 .

shrink.text: to shiver AYL. II. i. 9 “till I with cold,” Cym. IV. iv. 30 “The shrinking slaves of winter.”

shrive.text: to hear a person's confession and give him absolution Err. II. ii. 212 “I'll . . . you of a thousand idle pranks,” Mer.V. I. ii. 142 , Rom. II. iv. 196 “s-'d and married” ; gerund used attrib. R3 III. ii. 113 “shriving work,” Ham. V. ii. 47 “Not shriving-time allow'”

shroud1.text: shelter, protection Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 71

shroud2.text: to shelter, conceal LLL. IV. iii. 137 , 3H6 III. i. 1 , IV. iii. 39 ; intr. to take shelter Tp. II. ii. 43 “I will here shroud.”

shrouds.text: sail-ropes John V. vii. 53 , 3H6 V. iv. 18 .

shrow.text: shrew LLL. V. ii. 46 , Shr. IV. i. 213 , V. ii. 28 , 189

shuffle.text: 1. to practise trickery Wiv. II. ii. 26 , Ham. IV. vii. 137 “with a little shuffling you may choose A sword unbated.”

shut.text: “ up in,” confine to All'sW. I. i. 199 , Troil. I. iii. 58 , Mac. II. i. 16 * , Oth. III. iv. 120 * .

sick1.text: adj. (freq. in fig. context and expressive of a disordered, distempered, or corrupt condition) 1. oppressed with sorrow, weakness, or faintness Gent. I. i. 69 “heart sick with thought,” John V. iii. 4 , 3H6 V. ii. 8 “my sick heart,” Ham. I. i. 9 .

sick2.text: to sicken 2H4 IV. iv. 128 “sick'd and died.”

sicken.text: to be nauseated (i) with surfeit Tw.N. I. i. 3 , Mac. IV. i. 60 , (ii) with revulsion All'sW. V. iii. 209 .

sickly.text: of sickness All'sW. II. iii. 118 “my bed,” Ham. III. iii. 96 “thy sickly days.”

side2.text: vb. (2 perhaps aphetic form of ‘decide’, still in use in northern dial.) 1. to take sides with Cor. I. i. 199 [they] “side factions.”

siege.text: 1. seat Meas. IV. ii. 101 “siege of justice.”

sieve.text: used by witches to sail in Mac. I. iii. 8 ; fig. of a person All'sW. I. iii. 210 . ∥In Troil. II. ii. 71 Q has “the remainder viands We do not throw in vnrespect[i]ue siue,” F1 “same,” Ff2 3 4 “place,” mod. edd. “sew†, sure†.”

sigh.text: to lament Sonn. xxx. 3 “I the lack of many a thing I sought.”

sight.text: (1 still a Warwickshire use) 1. pupil of the eye Compl. 282 “his . . . eyes . . ., Whose sights till then were levell'd on my face.”

sighted.text: having eyes Wint. I. ii. 388 “sighted like the basilisk.”

sightless.text: (3 not pre-S.) 1. not seeing, blind Sonn. xxvii. 10 “my view,” xliii. 12 “ eyes”; not lit by the sun or ‘eye of day’ Lucr. 1013 “sightless night.”

sign1.text: sb. (the sense ‘omen, portent’ is freq.) 1. signal 1H6 II. i. 3 , III. ii. 8 , Cæs. V. i. 23 “shall we give sign of battle?.”

sign2.text: vb. (2 cf. note on SIGN sb.) 1. to mark H8 II. iv. 106 “You your place and calling . . . With meekness,” Cæs. III. i. 206 “S-'d in thy spoil” (=bearing the bloody tokens of thy slaughter); to mark out John IV. ii. 222 “s-'d to do a deed of shame” (? if not aphetic form of ‘assigned’).

signal.text: sign, token H5 V. Chor. 21 , 1H6 II. iv. 121 , R3 V. iii. 21 (Qq).

significant.text: token, sign LLL. III. i. 137 (applied bombastically to a letter), 1H6 II. iv. 26 “In dumb significants.” ∥ The adj. is not S.

signior.text: gentleman, nobleman Mer.V. I. i. 10 “s-s and rich burghers.”

signory.text: (old edd. also “seignory”) 1. pl. domains, estates R2 III. i. 22 , 2H4 IV. i. 111 .

silence2.text: euphemistically for ‘to keep under restraint’ 2H4 V. ii. 97 , H8 I. i. 97 ; cf. “put to silence,” Cæs. I. ii. 291 .

silent.text: silence 2H6 I. iv. 19 “the silent of the night.”

silly.text: (see the earlier form SEELY; senses 2, 3, 4, 6 and that of ‘foolish, senseless’ are not pre-Eliz.) 1. deserving of pity, ‘poor’ R2 V. v. 25 “ beggars Who sitting in the stocks” . . ., 2H6 I. i. 226 , Lr. II. ii. 109 “ ducking observants,” Lucr. 1812 * “ jeering idiots.”

silverly.text: with silvery brightness John V. ii. 46 .

simple1.text: sb. (common 1580-1750) 1. medicinal herb Wiv. I. iv. 65 , III. iii. 79 “like Bucklersbury in -time” (=midsummer, the time at which apothecaries were supplied with simples), Rom. V. i. 40 “Culling of s-s,” Lr. IV. iv. 14 .

simple2.text: adj. (the chief meanings are ‘humble, unpretentious’, ‘artless, unaffected’, ‘ordinary, undistinguished’, ‘plain, homely’, ‘insignificant, feeble’, ‘plain, mere’, ‘of weak intellect’, ‘foolish, silly’) 1. of poor or humble condition Shr. Ind. i. 135 “this peasant,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 774, Ant. V. ii. 340 “A countryman” [cf. line 232 “a rural fellow”]; phr. “simple though I stand here” Wiv. I. i. 226 .

simpleness.text: 1. simplicity, innocence MND. V. i. 83 , Oth. I. iii. 248 .

simplicity.text: folly, silliness LLL. IV. ii. 23 , V. ii. 52 “profound ,” Mer.V. I. iii. 44 , Sonn. lxvi. 11 “simple truth miscall'd simplicity.”

simply.text: without addition, by itself Wiv. III. ii. 81 “let him take her ,” All'sW. IV. iii. 373 “ the thing I am,” Troil. III. iii. 80 .

simular.text: sb. counterfeiter Lr. III. ii. 54 “ of virtue,” (Ff; Qq “ man of virtue”);—adj. counterfeited, pretended Lr. III. ii. 54 (Qq), Cym. V. v. 201 “with simular proof enough.”

since.text: (with verbs of recollection) when, the time when MND. II. i. 149 “Thou remember'st Since once” . . ., Wint. V. i. 219 , 2H4 III. ii. 208 , 2H6 III. i. 9 “We know the time since he was mild and affable.”

sinew1.text: 1. pl. nerves Lr. III. vi. 107 , Ven. 903 .

syrup.text: medicinal decoction Err. V. i. 104 “wholesome s-s, drugs,” Oth. III. iii. 332 “drowsy s-” ∥ Cf. ‘Diacodion’, is a syrup made with heads of the herbe called popy, and water, . . . to cause one to sleape (Elyot's Dict.).

ta.text: dial. form of ‘thou’ (after a dental, in interrogative sentences) 2H4 II. i. 65 “Thou wot, wot ta?” (Q; Ff “Thou wilt not?”).

table.text: (2 chiefly, and 3 only, in fig. context) 1. one or both of the stone tablets containing the ten commandments Meas. I. ii. 9 “scraped one” [commandment] “out of the ,” R3 I. iv. 205 “in the table of his law” (Ff “Table”).

tabled.text: set down in a list Cym. I. iv. 7 “though the catalogue of his endowments had been tabled.”

tables.text: backgammon LLL. V. ii. 327 . ∥ The ordinary name for the game circa 1300- 1650

tabor.text: small drum used on festive occasions LLL. V. i. 165 ; used by professional clowns and jesters Tw.N. III. i. 2 ; coupled with “pipe” as symbolical of peaceful rejoicing Ado II. iii. 15 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 183; so taborer, drummer Tp. III. ii. 164 .

tackled.text: “tackled stair,” rope ladder Rom. II. iv. 203 .

taffeta.text: lustrous kind of silk LLL. V. ii. 159 , 1H4 I. ii. 11 “in flame-colour'd ” ; used as adj. fig. LLL. V. ii. 407 “Taffeta phrases, silken terms precise.”

tag.text: rabble Cor. III. i. 247 ; so tag-rag “people” Cæs. I. ii. 259 .

tailor.text: MND. II. i. 54 * “down topples she, And ‘tailor’ cries”; obscure allusion.

taint1.text: sb. (not pre-Eliz. in these senses) 1. corruption, decay H8 V. iii. 28 , Lr. I. i. 224 .

taint2.text: vb. (not pre-Eliz. in these senses) 1. to affect or imbue slightly with an undesirable quality 1H6 V. iii. 182 “Never yet taint” [pa. pple.] “with love,” 3H6 III. i. 40 “Nero will be tainted with remorse” ; also intr. to become so affected Mac. V. iii. 3 “I cannot taint with fear.”

taintingly.text: (F1) Cor. I. i. 116 , app. misprint for “tantingly” (Ff2 3), “tauntingly” (F4), which last is the reading of mod. edd.

take.text: (2 see also TAKING vbl. sb. and ppl. adj.) 1. to strike R3 I. iv. 160 “ him over the costard with the hilts” ; with double obj. to give (a person a blow) Meas. II. i. 194 , Shr. III. ii. 166 , Tw.N. II. v. 76 , H5 IV. i. 234 “I will take thee a box on the ear.”

taking1.text: vbl. sb. (1 cf. TAKE 2) 1. blasting, malignant influence Lr. III. iv. 60 .

taking2.text: blasting, pernicious Lr. II. iv. 166 “You taking airs.”

tale.text: (1 the earliest sense; 2 Skelton 1523 has ‘Therby lyeth a tale’, Holland 1600 ‘Hereto longeth a tale’; the sense ‘number’ is not S.) 1. talk Rom. II. iv. 102 “to stop in my ,” Ven. 74 “to a pretty ear she tunes her tale.”

talent1.text: 1 (1 an Eliz. sense) 1. pl. riches, treasure Compl. 204 “these t-s of their hair.”

talent2.text: common old form of ‘talon’; hence the pun in LLL. IV. ii. 65 “If a talent be a claw, look how he claws him with a talent.”

talk.text: 1. (emphatically) to talk idly, talk nonsense Wint. III. ii. 42 , Mac. IV. ii. 62 “Poor prattler, how thou talkest,” Oth. IV. iii. 25 “Come, come, you talk.”

tall.text: (the ordinary sense is freq.; 2 common Eliz. prose use; 3 cf. HAND sb. 1) 1. goodly, fine, ‘proper’ MND. V. i. 146 “sweet youth and tall,” Shr. IV. i. 11 , IV. iv. 17 “Thou'rt a fellow.”

tallow.text: fat of an animal Wiv. V. v. 16 (=grow thin as a stag in rutting time). ∥ Cf. ‘All beestis that beere talow’, Book of St. Albans, 1486

tally.text: stick of wood, marked with transverse notches or scores representing the amount of a debt; it being cleft lengthwise across the notches, the debtor and creditor each retained one of the halves 2H6 IV. vii. 39 “the score and the ,” Sonn. cxxii. 10 “Nor need I tallies thy dear love to score.”

tame.text: “make to,” (i) subject or subjugate to John IV. ii. 262 , Lr. IV. vi. 226 (Qq “made tame by fortune's blows”); (ii) familiarize with Troil. III. iii. 10 . ∥ The fig. senses ‘submissive, meek’, ‘lacking animation, force, or effectiveness, spiritless’ are freq.

tamed.text: broached Troil. IV. i. 62 “He . . . would drink up The lees and dregs of a flat piece” (=broached cask).

tang1.text: ‘something that leaves a sting or pain behind it’ (J.) Tp. II. ii. 53 * “she had a tongue with a ” ∥ Perhaps ‘tang’=tongue of a snake (supposed to sting), sting of an insect, is here associated with ‘tang’=sharp ringing sound.

tang2.text: trans. to sound loud with Tw.N. II. v. 165 “let thy tongue tang arguments of state” ; intr. III. iv. 79 “let thy tongue tang with arguments” (Ff2 3 4; F1 “langer?” misprint).

tangle.text: to entrap, snare Gent. III. ii. 68 “lay lime to her desires,” 1H6 IV. ii. 22 , Ven. 67 “Look how a bird lies tangled in a net” . . .

tanling.text: one tanned by the sun's rays Cym. IV. iv. 29 “summer's tanlings.”

tap.text: to act as tapster Wiv. I. iii. 11 ; to draw “out” as liquor from a cask R2 II. i. 127 .

tardy1.text: “ta'en ,” taken unawares, surprised R3 IV. i. 51 ; “come off,” fallen short, inadequately done Ham. III. ii. 29 .

tardy2.text: to delay Wint. III. ii. 163 “tardied My swift command.”

tarre.text: to provoke, incite, hound “on” John IV. i. 117 , Troil. I. iii. 392 “ the mastiffs on,” Ham. II. ii. 379 [ 370 ] “ them to controversy.” ∥ Survives in midl. dial. (Worcestershire).

tarriance.text: delay Gent. II. vii. 90 ; waiting in expectation Pilgr. vi. 4 [ 74 ].

tarry.text: (1 common down to about 1800) 1. to lodge (in a place) Mer.V. IV. ii. 18 .

tart.text: only fig.; painful, grievous Lr. IV. ii. 87 “another way, This news is not so tart” ; (of aspect) sour Ant. II. v. 38 “so tart a favour.”

tartness.text: sourness (fig.) All'sW. IV. iii. 96 , Cor. V. iv. 19 .

task1.text: “at ” (S.), blamed Lr. I. iv. 368 “at task for want of wisdom” (Qq “attask'd”).

task2.text: vb. (cf. TAX vb.) 1. to lay a tax upon, tax 1H4 IV. iii. 92 .

tasking.text: challenge (see TASK vb. 3) 1H4 V. ii. 50 (Q1; the rest “talking”).

taste1.text: sb. (sense ‘savour’ is freq., lit. and fig.) 1. trial, test 2H4 II. iii. 52 “Have of their puissance made a little ,” Lr. I. ii. 48 “as an essay or of my virtue.”

taste2.text: vb. (2 the commonest sense) 1. to put to the proof, try, test Tw.N. III. iv. 270 “ their valour,” 1H4 IV. i. 119 “let me my horse,” Troil. III. ii. 97 “Praise us as we are t-d” (= prove to be); used affectedly Tw.N. III. i. 88 “ your legs, sir” ; also intr. const. “of” with same meaning 2H4 IV. i. 192 “every idle . . . reason Shall to the king of this action.”

tattering.text: in rags John V. v. 7 (old edd. “tott'ring”).

tawny.text: yellowish-brown Tp. II. i. 57 , Tit. V. i. 27 ; cf. “orange-tawny” MND. I. ii. 97 .

tax1.text: charge, accusation All'sW. II. i. 173 “Tax of impudence.”

tax2.text: vb. (2 the prevailing sense) 1. to censure, blame, accuse Ado I. i. 46 “you tax Signior Benedick too much,” Ham. I. iv. 18 “traduc'd and t-'d of other nations” ; with “of” for the more freq. “with” All'sW. V. iii. 122 “Shall tax my fears of little vanity.”

taxation.text: (2 cf. TASK vb. 3, TAX vb. 2) 1. demand, claim Tw.N. I. v. 226 “no of homage.”

teach.text: to show how LLL. IV. i. 111 “who is the suitor? —Shall I you to know?” (i.e. tell you), Rom. I. v. 48 “she doth teach the torches to burn bright” (i.e. by shining so brightly herself).

tear.text: “ a cat,” rant MND. I. ii. 32 “a part to a cat in.” ∥ This phr., and ‘tear-cat’=swaggerer, were specifically associated with ranting on the stage.

tedious.text: irksome, annoying, laborious, painful AYL. III. ii. 346 “heavy penury,” R2 II. i. 75 , 1H4 III. i. 48 “in the ways of art,” Tit. II. iv. 39 [she] “in a sampler sew'd her mind,” Mac. III. iv. 138 , Oth. III. iii. 398 “a difficulty.” ∥ Affectedly for ‘long’ in All'sW. II. iii. 35 “that is the brief and the tedious of it.”

tediously.text: tardily H5 IV. Chor. 22 “limp So away.”

teem.text: 1. to bring forth H5 V. ii. 51 , Tim. IV. iii. 180 “Whose womb . . . and . . . breast T-s, and feeds all,” Mac. IV. iii. 176 “Each minute teems a new one.”

teen.text: affliction, grief, woe LLL. IV. iii. 164 , R3 IV. i. 96 , Ven. 808 .

tell.text: (the foll. are obs. or special uses) 1. to count, reckon the number of LLL. I. ii. 42 “How many is one thrice told?,” R3 I. iv. 122 “while one t-s twenty,” Ham. I. ii. 237 , Ven. 277 “trots, as if he told the steps.”

temper1.text: sb. (the main sense is ‘disposition, temperament, constitution’） 1. good condition (of mind) Lr. I. v. 52 “Keep me in ; I would not be mad.”

temper2.text: vb. (used twice of tempering swords Tp. III. iii. 62 , Ven. 111 “Strong-t-'d steel” ; cf. MISTEMPERED 2; 4 cf. the Warwickshire expression of ‘humouring’ butter, e.g. before a fire) 1. to compound (a poison) Ado II. ii. 22 , Rom. III. v. 98 , Ham. V. ii. 342 , Cym. V. v. 251 .

temperality.text: Mistress Quickly's blunder (?) for ‘temperature’ (which is not S.)=temper 2H4 II. iv. 25 .

temperance.text: (its use by Puritans as a female name referred to in Tp. II. i. 44 ） 1. climate, temperature Tp. II. i. 43 .

temperate.text: 1. (of weather) mild, of genial temperature H5 III. iii. 30 “the cool and wind of grace,” Sonn, xviii. 2 .

temporary.text: (?) devoted to secular affairs Meas. V. i. 145 .

tempt.text: (the foll. are now rare or obs.) 1. to put to the test, try H8 I. ii. 55 “In t-ing of your” “patience,” Troil. IV. iv. 96 “When we will the frailty of our powers.”

ten.text: 3“ ” 4“,” amount of a lawyer's fee All'sW. II. ii. 23 .

tenable.text: that may be kept Ham. I. ii. 247 “Let it be in your silence still” (Ff “treb(b)le”).

tenant.text: one who holds land of a lord, vassal R3 IV. iv. 481 , H8 I. ii. 173 , Lucr. 1260 “those proud lords . . . Make weak-made women t-s to their shame,” Sonn. xlvi. 10 “A quest of thoughts, all t-s to the heart.”

tend.text: (1 is peculiar to S.; “tend”=have a tendency, is freq.; it has a different origin from this word) 1. to be in waiting or attendance Ham. I. iii. 83 “your servants tend,” IV. iii. 48 .

tendance.text: attention, care H8 III. ii. 150 , Tim. I. i. 58 , Cym. V. v. 53 ; concr. people in attendance Tim. I. i. 81 “his lobbies fill with tendance.”

tender.text: adj. (1 cf. TENDER-DYING; “ years” Ven. 1091 ) 1. young, youthful, immature R2 II. iii. 42 “, raw, and young,” 3H6 II. ii. 28 [birds] “in protection of their tender ones . . . Make war” . . .

tender1.text: (1) offer, (2) thing offered LLL. II. i. 170 “such welcome . . . As honour . . . may Make of,” John V. vii. 106 “the like of our love,” Rom. III. iv. 12 “I will make a desperate Of my child's love,” Ham. I. iii. 99 , 106 “you have ta'en these t-s for true pay,” Sonn. lxxxiii. 4 .

tender2.text: tender consideration, regard, care (S.) 1H4 V. iv. 49 “thou mak'st some of my life,” Lr. I. iv. 233 “in the tender of a wholesome weal.”

tenderness.text: LLL. III. i. 4 “ of years” =youth of tender years.

tending.text: attendance Mac. I. v. 38 “Give him tending.”

tennis.text: game in which a ball is struck to and fro with a racket by two players in a specially-constructed enclosed oblong court H8 I. iii. 30 , Ham. II. i. 59 ; also “-ball” Ado III. ii. 47 , H5 I. ii. 258 , “tennis-court” 2H4 II. ii. 22 , Per. II. i. 65 .

tenour.text: (in law) copy of an instrument not fully set out but containing only the substance or purport of it; fig. Lucr. 1310 “Here folds she up the of her woe, Her certain sorrow writ uncertainly.”

tent1.text: pl. (?) bed hangings Shr. II. i. 346 [ 354 ].

tent2.text: roll of lint used to search and cleanse a wound Troil. II. ii. 16 .

tent3.text: fig. to lodge Cor. III. ii. 116 .

tent4.text: to apply a tent to (a wound); only fig. to probe Ham. II. ii. 634 [ 626 ] “I'll tent him to the quick,” Cym. III. iv. 118 ; to cure Cor. I. ix. 31 “tent themselves with death,” III. i. 235 “a sore .. You cannot tent.”

tenth.text: (1 cf. ‘decimation’) 1. one out of ten Troil. II. ii. 21 “If we have lost so many tenths of ours,” Tim. V. iv. 33 “the destin'd ”

tercel.text: male of the falcon-gentle or peregrine falcon Troil. III. ii. 54 . ∥ Cf. TASSEL-GENTEL.

term.text: (1 freq.; the legal phr. “for of life” occurs Sonn. xcii. 2 ; Meas. I. i. 10 * “terms for common justice,” (a) conditions of the ordinary administration of justice, (b) ‘technical terms of the courts’, Blackstone) 1. (long) period of time Sonn. cxlvi. 11 “Buy t-s divine in selling hours of dross.”

termination.text: term, expression (S.) Ado II. i. 258 “if her breath were as terrible as her terminations.”

terrestrial.text: as sb. jocularly applied to a doctor (opposed to “celestial” = physician of the soul) Wiv. III. i. 108 (cf. line 100 “soul-curer and body-curer”).

terrible.text: usu. taken in a passive sense=frightened, but perhaps intensive=terribly rapid Lr. I. ii. 33 * “that dispatch of it” [a paper] “into your pocket.”

terribly.text: in a manner to excite terror Tp. II. i. 321 [ 313 ] “It struck mine ear most ,” MND. I. ii. 77 , Tim. IV. iii. 137 “you'll . . . swear Into . . . shudders . . . The immortal gods.”

tertian.text: fever of which the paroxysm occurs every third (i.e. every other) day H5 II. i. 124 “a burning quotidian tertian.”

test.text: witness, testimony Troil. V. ii. 119 “that test of eyes and ears” (so Ff14, but prob. misprint for “th'attest” of Q1), Oth. I. iii. 107 “Without more wider” (Ff) “and more overt test” (Qq12; Q3 F1 “over test”).

testament.text: will disposing of one's property after death AYL. I. i. 79 “the poor allottery my father left me by ” ; fig. R2 III. iii. 94 “to open The purple” (=blood-stained) “ of bleeding war,” H5 IV. vi. 27 “with blood he seal'd A of noble-ending love.” ∥ The only S. sense.

tester.text: sixpence Wiv. I. iii. 94 “ I'll have in pouch when thou shalt lack,” 2H4 III. ii. 299 “there's a for thee.” ∥ A corruption of ‘teston’, through the form ‘testern’ (cf. next), the shilling of Henry VII, Henry VIII, and Edward VI, which was gradually debased.

testern.text: to give a ‘tester’ or sixpence to, tip Gent. I. i. 155 “you have testerned me.”

testimony.text: to test, prove (S.) Meas. III. ii. 157 .

testril.text: fanciful form of ‘tester’=sixpence Tw.N. II. iii. 36 .

tetchy.text: fretful, peevish R3 IV. iv. 169 , Troil. I. i. 101 (old edd. “teachy”), Rom. I. iii. 32 (Qq “teachie”).

tetter1.text: skin eruption Troil. V. i. 27 , Ham. I. v. 71 .

tetter2.text: to affect with tetter Cor. III. i. 78 .

text.text: (3 cf. Cotgr. ‘Lettres cadelées’, great, capitall, or text letters) 1. legend Ado V. i. 190 “and underneath, ‘Here dwells Benedick . . .’”

than1.text: 1 (commonly spelt “then” in old edd.) 1. =as LLL. III. i. 188 [ 180 ] “Than whom no mortal so magnificent.”

than2.text: old form of THEN, retained in mod. edd. of Lucr. 1440 for the sake of the rhyme.

thane.text: Scottish title nearly equivalent to ‘earl’ Mac. I. ii. 46 “The worthy Thane of Ross,” &c.

thankful.text: worthy of thanks Per. V. ii. 20 .

thankings.text: thanks Meas. V. i. 4 “Many and hearty thankings,” Cym. V. v. 408 ,

that1.headword: that, pl. those demonstrative adj. and pron.
that1.text: 1. =such; adj. All'sW. V. iii. 86 “Had you that craft to reave her Of what should stead her most?,” R3 I. iv. 260 , H8 II. i. 85 , Mac. IV. iii. 74 “there cannot be That vulture in you, to devour so many,” Ham. I. v. 48 “whose love was of that dignity That” . . .; pron. Wiv. V. v. 59 “those as sleep,” H8 III. i. 166 “think us Those” (=such as) “we profess, peace-makers.”

that2.text: chiefly used to introduce characterizing clauses, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 6 “I have suffer'd With those that I saw suffer,” Err. I. ii. 36 “like a drop of water That in the ocean seeks another drop” ; but freely employed also in descriptive clauses, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 160 “Some food . . . and some fresh water that A noble Neapolitan, Gonzalo, . . . did give us” ; correlated with “so” and “such” it forms constructions now obs. Tp. V. i. 270 “a witch . . . so strong That could control the moon,” Cæs. I. iii. 116 “such a man That is no fleering tell-tale,” Cym. III. iv. 80 “a prohibition so divine That cravens my weak hand.”

that3.text: conj. (2 most freq. followed by “may”) 1. =in that, for the reason that, because Gent. IV. iv. 70 “I have entertained thee Partly, that I have need of such a youth,” Tw.N. I. i. 10 , Rom. I. i. 222 “only poor That, when she dies, with beauty dies her store,” Lr. I. i. 74 “Only she comes too short: that I profess” . . .; esp. after a comparative Ado I. iii. 74 , 3H6 III. iii. 118 .

theft.text: thing stolen Ham. III. ii. 94 “I will pay the ” ∥ In All'sW. II. i. 34 , Mac. II. iii. 152 it gets the meaning of ‘stealing away’ by virtue of a quibble.

theme.text: (on Ant. II. ii. 48 see the comm.) 1. what is said, discourse Err. V. i. 65 “the subject of my ,” Wint. V. i. 100 .

then2.text: old form of THAN 1 , as prob. in John IV. ii. 42 “more” [reason], “more strong, than” (F1 “then) lesser is my fear” (=‘more strong in proportion as my fear is less’, Aldis Wright); conj. “when†, the†.”

thence.text: away, absent Wint. V. ii. 123 , 3H6 II. v. 18 “They prosper best . . . when I am ,” Troil. I. i. 33 “‘when she comes’!—When is she ?” ; similarly “from thence”=away from home Mac. III. iv. 36 .

theoric.text: theory All'sW. IV. iii. 164 “the whole of war,” H5 I. i. 52 , Oth. I. i. 24 “the bookish ” ∥ ‘Theory’, although Eliz., is not S.

there.text: (5 cf. WHERE) 1. qualifying a noun or pron., e.g. Err. V. i. 219 “That goldsmith there,” R3 I. i. 67 “her brother there” (=that brother of hers), IV. iv. 502 ; sometimes separated from the pron. Err. II. i. 74 “he did beat me there” (i.e. ‘he there’).

thereabouts.text: meaning that, pointing at that Wint. I. ii. 378 , Ant. III. viii. 38 [ x. 29 ].

therefore.text: for that, for that purpose or reason, in respect of that Tp. III. iii. 100 , MND. III. ii. 78 “what should I get ?,” 1H4 I. i. 30 , 2H4 V. iii. 110 , 2H6 I. iv. 3 “we are provided,” IV. viii. 25 , R3 IV. iv. 479 “ mistrust me not,” Troil. III. iii. 20 , Cor. II. iii. 225 “dogs that are as often beat for barking As kept to do so,” Oth. I. iii. 263 (referring to the infin. foll.).

thereto.text: in addition, besides Wint. I. ii. 391 , Oth. II. i. 132 , Cym. IV. iv. 33 .

thereunto.text: =prec. Oth. II. i. 141 “There's none so foul and foolish thereunto” . . .

therewithal.text: (2 only after “and, but, when”） 1. by means of that Gent. IV. iv. 177 “moved ,” LLL. V. ii. 856 .

thews.text: sinews, bodily strength 2H4 III. ii. 279 , Cæs. I. iii. 81 , Ham. I. iii. 12 .

thick.text: (of slumber) heavy Per. V. i. 235 ; (of sight) dim 2H4 III. ii. 340 “his dimensions to any sight were invincible,” Cæs. V. iii. 21 ; (of words, &c.), quick, rapidly uttered Cym. I. vi. 67 “The thick sighs,” Lucr. 1784 ;—adv. fast, quickly All'sW. II. ii. 49 “, , spare not me,” 2H4 II. iii. 24 “speaking ,” Troil. III. ii. 36 “My heart beats t-er” . . ., Ant. I. v. 63 “Why do you send so thick?,” Cym. III. ii. 57 .

thicken.text: to become dim Mac. III. ii. 50 “Light t-s,” Ant. II. iii. 27 “thy lustre thickens.”

thief.text: term of reproach=wretch Meas. V. i. 40 “an adulterous ,” Ado III. iii. 130 ; used affectionately 1H4 III. i. 238 “Lie still, ye ,” 2H4 V. iii. 58 “my little tiny thief.”

thievish.text: 1. infested with robbers Rom. IV. i. 79 “thievish ways.”

thing.text: 1. applied to human beings=being, creature Gent. IV. ii. 52 “each mortal ,” H8 I. i. 91 “Every man . . . was A inspir'd,” Mac. V. iv. 14 “none serve with him but constrained t-s,” Cym. I. i. 125 “Thou basest thing.”

think1.text: 1 (for phr. see LONG adj. 1 , MUCH 2, SCORN) 1. to have despondent or melancholy thoughts Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 1 “Think, and die.”

think2.text: “it t-s,” it seems (impers., as in ‘methinks’) R3 III. i. 63 “Where it t-s† best unto your royal self” (Ff “think'st,” Qq12 “seems”), Ham. V. ii. 63 “Does it not, thinks't thee,” . . . (F1 “thinkst,” Qq “think(e)”; with the Ff readings cf. “methink'st” in All'sW. II. iii. 269 . ∥ In Compl. 91 “thinks” app.=methinks.

thinkings.text: thoughts All'sW. V. iii. 128 , H8 III. ii. 135 “His t-s are below the moon,” Oth. III. iii. 131 .

third.text: Eliz. form of THREAD Tp. IV. i. 3 “a of my life” (some mod. edd. “thrid”†, another 16th cent. form).

thirst.text: to desire to drink (“to” a person) Mac. III. iv. 91 “to all, and him, we thirst.”

thisne.text: (?) in this way MND. I. ii. 56 . ∥ ‘Thissen(s)’ belongs to northern and midl. dialects.

thitherward.text: on his way thither All'sW. III. ii. 55 .

thorough.text: through R2 V. vi. 43 “With Cain go wander thorough† shades of night” (Q1 “through,” Ff “through the”), 2H6 IV. i. 87 , Cæs. V. i. 110 “to be led. . . the streets of Rome,” Per. IV. iii. 35 “It pierc'd me ,” Lucr. 1851 “To show her bleeding body thorough Rome.”

thou.text: the pron. used (1) in addressing relatives or friends affectionately, (2) by masters when speaking good-humouredly or confidentially to servants; but “thou” is replaced by “you” when the tone of speech becomes cold, serious, or angry, or when “thou” with its pertaining inflexions would produce a heavy effect (cf. Tp. V. i. 75 -79, Gent. I. i. 9 -20, 25 , 28 , 36 -39, II. i. 16 , 46 , II. iv. 120 , IV. iv. 48 , 1H4 II. iii. 42 -62, 101 -117, III. ii., 1H6 IV. vi. 6 -9, Cæs. V. v. 31 -33, Lr. IV. vi. 33 , 42 ; it is used (3) in contemptuous or angry speech to strangers (cf. Tw.N. III. ii. 50 “if thou thou'st him some thrice it shall not be amiss” ), and (4) in solemn style generally. For details see Abbott's Shakespearian Grammar §§231 foll.

though.text: “what though” (1) with clause=even though Ado V. i. 135 “What care killed a cat, thou hast mettle enough in thee to kill care,” R3 I. i. 153 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 4, Ven. 574 “What the rose hath prickles, yet 'tis pluck'd” ; (2) with ellipsis of clause =What does it matter? What then? Wiv. I. i. 288 , AYL. III. iii. 53 , John I. i. 169 , H5 II. i. 9 .

thought.text: (1 cf. THOUGHT-SICK and THINK 1 2) 1. care, anxiety, sorrow, melancholy AYL. IV. i. 224 [ 217 ], Troil. IV. ii. 6 “infants' [sleep] empty of all ,” Cæs. II. i. 187 “take ” (=give way to sorrow or melancholy), Ham. III. i. 85 “the pale cast of ,” IV. v. 187 “ and affliction,” Ant. IV. vi. 36 .

thoughtful.text: careful 2H4 IV. v. 71 “they have been thoughtful to invest Their sons” . . .

thrasonical.text: boastful LLL V. i. 14 , AYL. V. ii. 35 “Cæsar's brag.” ∥ Thraso is a boasting character in Terence's Eunuchus.

thread.text: in allusion to the thread of life spun and cut by the Parcae or Fates, MND. V. i. 293 “O Fates, come, come, Cut thread and thrum” (cf. THRUM), 349 , H5 III. vi. 49 “Bardolph's vital ,” Oth. V. ii. 204 “grief Shore his old in twain.” ∥ See also THIRD.

threaden.text: made of woven threads H5 III. Chor. 10 “ sails,” Compl. 33 “threaden fillet.”

thrift.text: (the mod. sense is rare Ham. I. ii. 180 ) 1. gain, profit Wiv. I. iii. 45 , 91 , Mer.V. I. iii. 51 “my well-won ,” 91, Wint. I. ii. 311 “their profits, Their own particular t-s,” Ham. III. ii. 67 “Where may follow fawning,” 195

thriftless.text: unprofitable Tw.N. II. ii. 40 “What sighs,” Sonn. ii. 8 “thriftless praise.”

thrifty.text: (cf. THRIFT 2) 1. intent on gain Mer.V. II. v. 55 , Troil. V. i. 61 .

thrilling.text: causing one to shiver with cold Meas. III. i. 121 “thrilling region of thick-ribbed ice.”

thrive.text: “to ”=help me to succeed R2 I. iii. 84 “Mine innocency and Saint George to thrive!.”

throat.text: voice AYL. II. v. 4 , Cor. III. ii. 112 “My of war be turn'd . . . into a pipe” . . ., Oth. III. iii. 356 .

throe.text: to pain Tp. II. i. 239 [ 231 ] “a birth . . . Which t-s thee much to yield”; to bring “forth” Ant. III. vii. 80 * .

throne.text: to be enthroned Cor. V. iv. 27 .

throng.text: to oppress, overwhelm Per. I. i. 101 “to tell the earth is t-'d By man's oppression,” II. i. 78 “A man throng'd up with cold.”

through.text: thoroughly Troil. II. iii. 236 “ warm,” Cym. IV. ii. 160 “seek us ” (=follow us up with determination).

throughly.text: Tp. III. iii. 14 , H8 V. i. 111 , Ham. IV. v. 135 .

throw1.text: cast of the dice LLL. V. ii. 545 , Mer.V. II. i. 33 ; fig. venture Tw.N. V. i. 45 “at this ” ; of a bowl Cor. V. ii. 21 “Like to a bowl upon a subtle ground, I have tumbled past the ” (i.e. gone beyond the mark).

throw2.text: 1. to cast (a look), direct (the eye) AYL. IV. iii. 104 “he threw his eye aside,” Tw.N. V. i. 222 , 3H6 II. v. 85 “ up thine eye,” Cym. V. v. 395 , Lucr. 1499 “She t-s her eyes about the painting round.”

thrum.text: tufted end of a weaver's warp; only in phr. MND. V. i. 293 “thread and thrum,” fig. good and bad together, everything; cf. THREAD.

thrummed.text: made of coarse yarn Wiv. IV. ii. 82 “her thrummed hat.”

thwart2.text: to cross Per. IV. iv. 10 “thwarting the wayward seas.”

thwart3.text: crosswise, the wrong way Troil. I. iii. 15 * “every action . . . trial did draw Bias and thwart” (taken by some as a vb.).

tickle1.text: easily shifted, unstable, insecure Meas. I. ii. 183 “thy head stands so on thy shoulders,” 2H6 I. i. 217 “the state of Normandy Stands on a point,” Ham. II. ii. 346 [ 337 ] (see SERE). ∥ Cf. Tickyll nat stedy, ‘inconstant’ (Palsgr.).

tickle2.text: 1. to disturb by tickling Cym. IV. ii. 210 “as some fly had tickled slumber.”

tickled.text: app. error for TICKLE adj. Ham. II. ii. 346 [ 337 ].

tide1.text: sb. (most freq. applied to the ebb and flow of the sea, also fig.) 1. time, season John III. i. 86 “the high t-s in the calendar” (i.e. the great festivals), Rom. III. v. 178 (?), Tim. I. ii. 58 “Flow this way! . . . he keeps his tides well” (with a pun); perhaps=right time Troil. V. i. 92 “I have important business, The tide whereof is now” (or? short for ‘flood-tide’ used fig.).

tide2.text: to betide, befall MND. V. i. 207 “ life, death.”

tidings.text: equally common with sing. ( R2 III. iv. 80 ) and pl. ( Rom. III. v. 105 ) concord.

tidy.text: (?) in seasonable or prime condition, fit for killing; or delicate, tender (ironically) 2H4 II. iv. 249 “Thou whoreson little tidy Bartholomew boar-pig.” ∥ Cf. Tidie, fatte, or tender, ‘Cereus’ (Rider's Dict., 1589 ).

tie.text: to bring into bondage, restrict the liberties of H8 IV. ii. 36 “one, that by suggestion Tied all the kingdom.” ∥ In fig. meanings, used where we should now prefer to say ‘bind’ or ‘confine’.

tied.text: (of the eyes) fixed Compl. 24 ; obliged Shr. I. i. 216 , R2 I. i. 63 .

tight.text: (1 formerly said also of casks) 1. (of ships) not leaking, sound Tp. V. i. 224 “ and yare,” Shr. II. i. 373 [ 381 ] “tight galleys.”

tightly.text: 1. like a ‘tight’ ship, safely Wiv. I. iii. 86 * “bear you these letters : Sail like my pinnace to these golden shores.”

tike.text: small dog, cur Lr. III. vi. 73 “bobtail ” ; as a term of contempt to a person H5 II. i. 31 “Base tike.”

tilt.text: to thrust “at” Rom. III. i. 164 , Oth. II. iii. 185 “tilting one at other's breast” ; to fight, contend Err. IV. ii. 6 “his heart's meteors tilting in his face,” 1H4 II. iii. 97 “to tilt with lips.”

tilter.text: properly, one who runs a ‘tilt’ in a tournament AYL. III. iv. 44 ; transf. fighter, fencer Meas. IV. iii. 17 .

tilth.text: tillage, cultivation Tp. II. i. 159 , Meas. I. iv. 44 .

time.text: (often personified as masculine) 1. age, duration of life Gent. II. vii. 48 “a youth Of greater ,” LLL. I. ii. 18 “your old ,” H8 II. i. 93 , Cym. I. i. 43 “all the learnings that his Could make him the receiver of.”

timeless.text: (1 chiefly with “death”) 1. untimely, premature Gent. III. i. 21 “your grave,” 1H6 V. iv. 5 “thy cruel death,” Tit. II. iii. 265 “this tragedy,” Rom. V. iii. 162 .

timely1.text: early, speedy Err. I. i. 138 “my death” ; opportune, welcome Mac. III. iii. 7 “To gain the inn” (or?=to reach the inn betimes).

timely2.text: early, betimes Mac. II. iii. 52 , Cym. I. vi. 97 .

tinct.text: (2 cf. LIQUOR, MEDICINE) 1. colour Ham. III. iv. 91 , Cym. II. ii. 23 ; in Ant.I. v. 37 “that great medicine hath With his gilded thee,” there is allusion to sense 2

tincture.text: =TINCT 1, Gent. IV. iv. 162 , Wint. III. ii. 206 “bring or lustre in her lip, her eye,” Sonn. liv. 6 ; in Cæs. II. ii. 89 “t-s, stains, relics, and cognizance,” there is allusion to the heraldic use of the word, and to the practice of dipping handkerchiefs in the blood of martyrs.

tinker.text: proverbial type of tipplers and talkers Tw.N. II. iii. 97 “to gabble like t-s,” 1H4 II. iv. 21 “I can drink with any tinker in his own language.”

tinsel.text: cloth of gold or silver Ado III. iv. 22 “underborne with a bluish tinsel.”

tiny.text: always joined with “little,” Tw.N. V. i. 401 , 2H4 V. i. 29 , Lr. III. ii. 74 .

tipstaves.text: ‘[so called from their Staves being tipt with Silver] Officers who take into Custody such Persons as are committed by the Court’ (Bailey) H8 II. i. stage dir.

tire1.text: head-dress Gent. IV. iv. 192 , Ant. II. v. 22 , Sonn. liii. 8 . ∥ In Per. III. ii. 22 app.=bed furniture.

tire2.text: vb. (cf. ‘Tiring [in Falconry], giving a Hawk a Leg or Wing of a Pullet to Pluck at’, Bailey) 1. to prey or feed ravenously “upon” 3H6 I. i. 269 “Will . . . like an empty eagle on the flesh of me,” Ven. 56 ; fig. Tim. III. vi. 5 “Upon that were my thoughts tiring” (=busily engaged), Cym. III. iv. 97 “her That now thou tir'st on.”

tired.text: clothed, dressed (fig.) Ven. 177 * “Titan, in the mid-day heat”; adorned with trappings LLL. IV. ii. 132 “the tired horse.”

tiring.text: dressing the hair Err. II. ii. 101 (Ff “trying,” Pope “tyring”†, Collier “'tiring”†).

tisick.text: consumptive cough Troil. V. iii. 101 . ∥ Used as a proper name in 2H4 II. iv. 91 .

tissue.text: “cloth of gold of ,” stuff made of gold thread and silk woven together Ant. II. ii. 207 . ∥ Phr. borrowed from North's Plutarch, rendering Amyot's ‘or tissu’.

tithe1.text: tenth All'sW. I. iii. 90 “One good woman in ten . . . we'd find no fault with the tithe-woman if I were the parson” (quibblingly,=tenth woman and woman paying tithe), Troil. II. ii. 19 “Every tithe soul.”

tithe2.text: to levy a tenth, take tithe John III. i. 154 “tithe or toll.”

tithed.text: involving the slaughter of a tenth Tim. V. iv. 31 “a tithed death” (=decimation).

tithing.text: district, being orig. the tenth part of a hundred Lr. III. iv. 138 “whipped from to ” (i.e. as a vagabond).

title.text: (2 very freq.; phr. “make ”=lay claim All'sW. I. iii. 108 , H5 I. ii. 68 ) 1. inscription, motto Mer.V. II. ix. 35 .

titled.text: having a (certain) name All'sW. IV. ii. 2 “ goddess” (=having the name of a goddess), Troil. II. iii. 205 “As amply titled as Achilles is.”

tittle.text: point or dot; spec. applied to the dots commonly printed at the end of the alphabet in hornbooks LLL. IV. i. 85 “exchange . . . for t-s? titles.”

to1.text: used interjectionally=go on! Troil. II. i. 119 “to, Achilles! to, Ajax! to!;—to and back” = the commoner “to and fro” Ant. I. iv. 46 .

to2.text: prep. (obsolete or archaic uses are) 1. in addition to, besides, to accompany John I. i. 144 , R3 III. i. 116 “that's the sword to it,” Troil. I. i. 7 “strong, and skilful to their strength,” Rom. I. iii. 106 “seek happy nights to happy days,” Mac. III. i. 52 , Lucr. 1589 “new storms to those already spent.”

toast.text: piece of toast put into liquor Wiv. III. v. 4 ; fig. Troil. I. iii. 45 “made a toast for Neptune” (=swallowed up by the sea); allusive phr. 1H4 IV. ii. 22 “toasts-and-butter” (=eaters of buttered toast, i.e. delicate fellows).

toaze.text: to tear (fig.) Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 763 “ from thee thy business.” ∥ Cf. TOUSE.

tod.text: 28lb. weight of wool; as vb. to yield this quantity Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 33, 34 “Every 'leven wether t-s; every tod yields pound and odd shilling.”

todpole.text: old form of “tadpole” Lr. III. iv. 133 .

tofore.text: previously LLL. III. i. 88 ; formerly Tit. III. i. 293 “as thou tofore hast been.”

toge.text: Roman toga Gor. II. iii. 122 “in this wolvish toge” (F1 “tongue,” Ff2-4 “gowne”).

toged.text: wearing a toga, gowned Oth. I. i. 25 (Q1) “the toged consuls” (Ff Qq2 3 “tongued”; cf. prec.).

toil1.text: net, snare LLL. IV. iii. 2 “they have pitched a toil,” Ham. III. ii. 369 “drive me into a toil.”

toil2.text: to put to exertion, tax the strength of MND. V. i. 74 “t-'d their . . . memories,” R2 IV. i. 96 “toil'd with works of war,” 2H6 I. i. 84 , Ham. I. i. 72 .

token.text: mark on the body of disease or infection, esp. of the plague LLL. V. ii. 424 “the Lord's t-s” (=plague-spots), Troil. II. iii. 189 (see DEATHTOKEN), Lucr. 1748 “Corrupted blood some watery token shows.” ∥ Cf. ‘Tokens’, the plague (Dict. of Canting Crew).

tolerable.text: (app.) passable All'sW. II. iii. 212 “thou didst make vent of thy travel.” ∥ Otherwise only as misused by Dogberry for ‘intolerable’ Ado III. iii. 37 .

toll1.text: vb. 1 (each sense only once) 1. to take toll, levy a tax John III. i. 154 .

toll2.text: vb. 2 (each sense only once) 1. (of a clock) to strike H5 IV. Chor. 15 .

tongs.text: some rude musical instrument MND. IV. i. 33 “let us have the and the bones.” (In F1 follows stage dir. “Musicke Tongs, Rurall Musicke”).

tongue1.text: sb. (2 freq. in gen. sense) 1. “the common” or “general ,” common report, general opinion Tim. I. i. 175 , Ant. I. ii. 114 .

tongue2.text: to speak, utter Cym. V. iv. 147 “such stuff as madmen ” ; to speak against, scold, abuse Meas. IV. iv. 28 “How might she tongue me.”

tongueless.text: not spoken of Wint. I. ii. 92 .

too.text: “and too,” and at the same time Err. III. i. 110 “wild and yet, too, gentle,” Cæs. II. i. 244 , Ven. 1147 , 1155 “It shall be merciful, and too severe.”

tool.text: weapon Rom. I. i. 36 , Cym. V. iii. 9 , Lucr. 1039 .

tooth.text: “colt's ,” symbol of youthful inexperience H8 I. iii. 48 “Your colt's is not cast yet;—in, into,” or “to” one's “teeth,” in or to one's face Err. II. ii. 22 “flout me in the teeth,” 1H4 V. ii. 42 , Cæs. V. i. 64 “Defiance .. hurl we in your teeth,” Ham. IV. vii. 56 “tell him” “to his teeth;—in despite of the teeth of,” in defiance of Wiv. V. v. 135 ;—“from his teeth,” not from the heart Ant. III. iv. 10 .

top1.text: sb. (3 Lodge has ‘in top of all thy pride’) 1. head All'sW. I. ii. 43 , Lr. II. iv. 165 “fail On her ungrateful top,” Cym. IV. ii. 354 .

top2.text: to surpass Cor. II. i. 23 “topping all others in boasting,” Ham. IV. vii. 88 “so far he topp'd my thought” (Ff “past”).

torcher.text: torch-bearer; fig. light-bearer (the sun) All'sW. II. i. 165 .

torn.text: (of faith) broken LLL. IV. iii. 285 “our faith not torn,” Sonn. clii. 3 .

toss.text: to carry aloft on the point of a pike 1H4 IV. ii. 72 “good enough to toss” ; cf. 3H6 I. i. 244 ; transf. 2H6 V. i. 11 “A sceptre . . . On which I'll toss the flower-de-luce of France.”

tother.text: the other 2H4 II. iv. 91 , 2H6 I. iii. 87 (F1 “t'other”), Ham. II. i. 56 (Ff3 4 “'tother”), Lr. III. vii. 71 (Ff “Th'other,” Qq “tother”).

tottered.text: ragged R2 III. iii. 52 “ battlements” (Ff “tatter'd”), 1H4 IV. ii. 37 (mod. edd. “tattered”†); so tott'ring John V. v. 7 (see TATTERING†).

totters.text: rags Ham. III. ii. 11 “tear a passion to totters” (Qq; Ff “tatters”).

touch1.text: sb. (the physical sense of ‘act of touching, contact’ is the most freq.; cf. also the application to unlawful commerce in Meas. III. ii. 25 , V. i. 141 , Sonn. cxli. 6 ） 1. fingering or playing of a musical instrument Gent. III. ii. 79 “Orpheus' lute . . . Whose golden ” . . .; phr. “know no ,” have no skill in playing R2 I. iii. 165 , Ham. III. ii. 378 [ 371 ]; transf. in pl. notes, strains Mer.V. V. i. 57 “the touches of sweet harmony,” 67

touch2.text: vb. (obs. or special uses are) 1. to land at Wint. V. i. 139 , R2 II. i. 288 “to touch our northern shore,” Troil. II. ii. 76 ; intr. Wint. III. iii. 1 .

touchstone.text: stone used for testing gold Per. II. ii. 37 . ∥ The clown's name in AYL.

tourney.text: to tilt in a tournament Per. II. i. 120 , 154 “wilt thou tourney for the lady?.”

touse.text: to tear Meas. V. i. 309 “ you joint by joint.”

toward1.text: adj. (1 opposed to ‘froward’; 2 Eliz.) 1. docile, tractable, willing Shr. V. ii. 183 , Ven. 1157 .

toward2.text: in preparation, about to take place, forthcoming MND. III. i. 84 “What! a play toward,” 2H4 II. iv. 213 , Ham. V. ii. 379 “What feast is . . .?.”

toward3.text: prep. (freq.=simple ‘to’, e.g. Mac. I. iii. 152 ） 1. with a view to, tending to, aiming at Shr. II. i. 99 , Tim. II. ii. 202 “to use them a supply of money,” Cæs. I. ii. 85 , Mac. I. iv. 27 .

towards2.text: prep. (the uses correspond precisely with those of TOWARD prep., except that “towards” is used also in relation to time R3 III. v. 100 ） 1. =TOWARD 1, R2 II. i. 161 , 235 , Mac. V. iv. 22 .

tower.text: (of a falcon) to rise in circles of flight till she reaches her ‘place’ 2H6 II. i. 10 “My Lord Protector's hawks do so well,” Mac. II. iv. 12 “A falcon, t-ing in her pride of place” ; (hence) to soar, lit. and fig. John II. i. 350 , V. ii. 149 .

toy1.text: sb. (not in the sense of ‘plaything’) 1. trifle, trifling ornament Tw.N. III. iii. 44 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 328 “Any toys for your head.”

trace.text: vb. (reading of Ff Qq2 3 in Oth. II. i. 315 , but difficult to explain; see TRASH vb.) 1. to follow 1H4 III. i. 48 “ me in the tedious ways of art,” H8 III. ii. 45 , Mac. IV. i. 153 “his babes, and all . . . souls That him in his line,” Ham. V. ii. 126 .

tract.text: （“trace, track,” and “tract” were largely interchangeable in the Eliz. period; cf. Cotgr., ‘Trac’, a tracke, tract, or trace) 1. track of a path Tim. I. i. 51 “Leaving no behind.”

trade.text: (1 in this sense a variant of ‘tread’) 1. passing to and fro as over a path, resort R2 III. iii. 156 “Some way of common ,” 2H4 I. i. 174 “where most of danger rang'd” ; beaten path H8 V. i. 36 “Stands in the gap and trade of moe preferments” (i.e. where more preferments are to be found).

traded.text: practised John IV. iii. 109 “long in it,” Troil. II. ii. 64 “traded pilots.”

tradition.text: old custom R2 III. ii. 173 “, form, and ceremonious duty” ; so traditional, old-fashioned R3 III. i. 45 “Too ceremonious and traditional.”

traffic.text: business, occupation Rom. I. Chor. 12 “the two hours' traffic of our stage.”

trail.text: track, scent Wiv. IV. ii. 212 “cry out . . . upon no ,” Ham. II. ii. 47 “Hunts not the of policy,” IV. v. 109 ; traces (of an animal) Ant. V. ii. 352 .

train1.text: sb. (1 applied to the tails of birds in heraldry) 1. tail of (i) a peacock 1H6 III. iii. 7 , (ii) a comet Ham. I. i. 117 .

train2.text: to lure, allure, entice Err. III. ii. 45 “ me not . . . with thy note, To drown me,” John III. iv. 175 , 1H4 V. ii. 21 “train him on,” Tit. V. i. 104 .

trance.text: ecstasy, transport Shr. I. i. 181 , Lucr. 974 , 1595

tranced.text: in a trance, insensible Lr. V. iii. 220 .

tranect.text: (?) ferry Mer.V. III. iv. 53 (Qq Ff). ∥ Of uncertain origin.

tranquillity.text: concr. people who live at ease 1H4 II. i. 84 .

transfix.text: to remove Sonn. lx. 9 “Time doth the flourish set on youth.”

transform.text: to change (a person into something) 2H4 II. ii. 79 “if the fat villain have not t-ed him ape.”

transformation.text: shape into which one is changed Wiv. IV. v. 99 , Troil. V. i. 59 .

transformed.text: effecting a transformation MND. IV. i. 70 “this transformed scalp.”

translate.text: (the only S. uses are) 1. to transform, change, convert MND. III. i. 125 “Bottom! . . . thou art t-d,” AYL. V. i. 59 “ thy life into death,” Tim. I. i. 73 , Ham. III. i. 113 ; with allusion to translation from one language to another Wiv. I. iii. 52 , AYL. II. i. 19 , 2H4 IV. i. 47 “translate yourself Out of the speech of peace.”

transport.text: (the orig. sense of ‘carry from one place to another’ is the prevalent one) 1. to remove from this world to the next Meas. IV. iii. 75 .

transpose.text: to change, transform MND. I. i. 233 ; Mac. IV. iii. 21 .

trash1.text: worthless creature Oth. II. i. 315 , V. i. 85 .

trash2.text: to check (a dog) that is too fast by attaching a weight to its neck Shr. Ind. i. 17 “Trash† Merriman, the poor cur is emboss'd” (old edd. “Brach”); fig. Tp. I. ii. 81 “who t'advance, and who To for over-topping,” Oth. II. i. 315 “this poor trash of Venice, whom I † For his quick hunting” (Ff Qq2 3 “trace,” Q1 “crush”). ∥ The meaning ‘lop’ assigned by some to Tp. I. ii. 81 is not supported elsewhere.

traverse1.text: to march, esp. backwards and forwards Wiv. II. iii. 25 “To see thee fight . . . to see thee ,” 2H4 III. ii. 294 “Hold, Wart, ” ; transf. Oth. I. iii. 378 (spoken by Iago, the ancient') “Traverse; go.” ∥ The full phr. was ‘traverse one's ground’.

traverse2.text: across AYL. III. iv. 43 “swears brave oaths, and breaks them bravely, quite ” (with allusion to the disgrace of breaking one's lance across one's opponent's body, instead of length ways; cf. CROSS adv.).

traversed.text: (of the arms) folded Tim. V. iv. 7 . ∥ Cf. ACROSS.

treacherous.text: (?) cowardly 1H6 I. v. 30 “Sheep run not half so treacherous from the wolf.”

treasure1.text: treasury Sonn. cxxxvi. 5 “Will will fulfil the treasure of thy love.”

treasure2.text: to enrich Sonn. vi. 3 “ thou some place With beauty's treasure.”

treasury.text: treasure Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 362, H5 I. ii. 165 , Lr. IV. vi. 44 . ∥ Only once=storehouse (fig.) 2H6 II. i. 18 .

treatise.text: discourse, talk Ado I. i. 325 [ 317 ], Mac. V. v. 12 “my felt of hair Would at a dismal rouse and stir,” Ven. 774 . ∥ The only S. sense.

treaty.text: proposal of agreement, negotiation, discussion John II. i. 481 , H8 I. i. 165 , Cor. II. ii. 60 “convented Upon a pleasing ,” Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 62 “send humble treaties.”

treble.text: Tp. II. i. 229 [ 221 ] “T-s thee o'er,” makes thee three times as great.

tree.text: “Jove's tree,” oak AYL. III. ii. 251 , 3H6 V. ii. 14 . ∥ See also ARABIAN TREE.

trembling1.text: tremor denoting possession by a devil Tp. II. ii. 86 .

trembling2.text: contribution given with trembling H8 I. ii. 95 .

trench1.text: pl. furrows, wrinkles Tit. V. ii. 23 ; cf. Sonn. ii. 2 .

trench2.text: 1. to cut Gent. III. ii. 7 “a figure T-ed in ice,” Mac. III. iv. 27 “t-ed gashes,” Ven. 1052 “the wide wound that the boar had trench'”

trenchant.text: cutting, sharp Tim. IV. iii. 116 “ sword.”

trencher.text: (wooden) plate Tp. II. ii. 196 [ 187 ], Rom. I. v. 2 “he shift a trencher! he scrape a trencher!.”

trenchering.text: trenchers collectively Tp. II. ii. 196 “Nor scrape trenchering (trencher†).”

trey.text: throw of three with the dice LLL. V. ii. 233 . ∥ Cf. TRAY-TRIP.

tribulation.text: H8 V. iv. 67 “the Tribulation of Towerhill” ; allusion unexplained.

tribunal.text: seat of eminence Ant. III. vi. 3 “on a silver'”

tribune.text: in ancient Rome, title of representatives of the plebs or common people, orig. granted to them as a protection against the patricians and consuls Cor. I. i. 221 , &c.

trice.text: moment (of time); once gen. Lr. I. i. 219 “in this of time” ; twice in phr. “in a ” Tw.N. IV. ii. 137 , Cym. V. iv. 171 ; once “on a ” Tp. V. i. 238 .

trick1.text: sb. (‘device, artifice’, ‘deception’, ‘freakish practice or act’, ‘prank, joke’ are freq. senses) 1. custom, habit, way Meas. III. ii. 56 “Which is the way? Is it sad, and few words, or how? The of it?,” V. i. 506 “I spoke it but according to the ,” All'sW. III. ii. 9 , 1H4 V. ii. 11 , 2H4 I. ii. 244 , Ham. IV. vii. 188 .

trick2.text: 1. “ up,” deck out, adorn H5 III. vi. 82 “the phrase of war, which they trick up with new tuned oaths.”

tricksy.text: sportive Tp. V. i. 226 * “My spirit” (or perhaps ‘full of devices, resourceful’), Mer.V. III. v. 75 “for a word” (=‘for the sake of playing upon a word’ Clark and Wright).

trifle1.text: (a) phantom, (b) trick of magic Tp. V. i. 112 * .

trifle2.text: vb. (2 occurs only once) 1. to spend to no purpose Mer.V. IV. i. 299 “We time,” H8 V. iii. 178 “we trifle time away.”

trigon.text: triangle; in astrology, conjunction of three planets in a certain sign 2H4 II. iv. 288 “the fiery ” (=the three superior planets meeting in Aries, Leo, or Sagittarius).

trim1.text: sb. (2 Bailey defines ‘Trim of a Ship’, as ‘her best Posture, Proportion of Ballast, hanging of her Masts, &c. which conduce most to her good sailing’) 1. fine attire, apparel, trappings 1H4 IV. i. 113 “sacrifices in their trim” (i.e. decorated), Cor. I. ix. 62 “My noble steed . . . With all his belonging,” Ant. IV. iv. 22 “their riveted ,” Cym. III. iv. 167 “dainty t-s” ; fig. H5 IV. iii. 115 “our hearts are in the trim.”

trim2.text: often ironically=pretty!, fine! MND. III. ii. 157 “A exploit,” 1H4 V. i. 137 “A reckoning!,” Troil. IV. v. 33 ;—adv. neatly Rom. II. i. 13 “he that shot so trim.”

trim3.text: fig. 2H4 I. iii. 94 “trimm'd in thine own desires” =furnished with what thou desirest.

triple.text: one of three, third All'sW. II. i. 111 “a eye, Safer than mine own two,” Ant. I. i. 12 “The pillar of the world.” ∥ For “ Hecate” MND. V. ii. 14 391] see THRICE-CROWNED. [ 13 ]. i.

triplex.text: triple time (in music) Tw.N. V. i. 41 “the . . . is a good tripping measure.”

tristful.text: sad 1H4 II. iv. 439 “my † queen” (old edd. “trustfull”), Ham. III. iv. 50 “With visage” (Qq “heated”).

triumph.text: sb. (mod. senses also occur) 1. public festivity or rejoicing, festive show or entertainment Gent. V. iv. 161 , MND. I. i. 19 “with , and with revelling,” 1H4 III. iii. 47 “a perpetual , an everlasting bonfire-light,” 3H6 V. vii. 43 , Per. V. i. 17 ; spec. tournament R2 V. ii. 52 “justs and t-s,” 1H6 V. v. 31 “at a having vow'd To try his strength,” Per. II. ii. 1 ; so “triumph day” R2 V. ii. 66 .

triumphant.text: triumphal, celebrating a triumph 1H6 I. i. 22 “a car,” Cor. V. iv. 69 [ v. 3 ] “ fires”; transf. Sonn. cli. 10 “his triumphant prize.”

triumpherate.text: （ Ant. III. vi. 28 ), triumphery ( LLL. IV. iii. 53 ), readings of old edd. replaced by “triumvirate†, triumviry†” in mod. edd. ∥ The forms are due to association with ‘triumph’.

troll.text: to run over (a song) Tp. III. ii. 129 “will you troll the catch” . . .?

troop.text: to march Wiv. I. iii. 112 , 2H4 IV. i. 62 ; “ with,” follow in the train of Lr. I. i. 134 “all the large effects That troop with majesty.”

troops.text: retinue, followers 2H6 I. iii. 80 “with of ladies,” R3 IV. iv. 96 , Tit. II. iii. 56 “Unfurnish'd of her well-beseeming ,” Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 53 “Dido and her Aeneas shall want troops.”

trophy.text: (not S. in the definite sense of ‘spoil taken from the enemy’） 1. token H5 V. Chor. 21 “Giving full , signal and ostent, Quite from himself, to God” (cf. line 18 “His bruised helmet and his bended sword”), V. i. 76 “a memorable of predeceased valour,” Compl. 218 “all these trophies of affections hot.”

trot.text: “an old trot,” ‘a sorry old Woman’ (Bailey) Shr. I. ii. 80 ; applied to a man Meas. III. ii. 54 .

troth.text: (pronounced “trot” by Dr. Caius, Wiv. IV. v. 90 ) 1. truth MND. II. ii. 36 , Cor. IV. v. 198 , Cym. V. v. 275 “I'll speak troth.”

trouble.text: to agitate, disturb (water, the sky); chiefly in pa. pple. Shr. V. ii. 143 “like a fountain t-d,” 1H4 I. i. 10 “the meteors of a t-d heaven,” 2H6 IV. i. 72 “T-s the silver spring,” Cæs. I. ii. 101 , Lucr. 589 .

trow.text: (always in 1st or 2nd person present indicative) 1. to believe Lr. I. iv. 136 “Learn more than thou trowest.”

truant.text: “ with,” be unfaithful to Err. III. ii. 17 .

truce.text: peace Err. II. ii. 149 , 1H6 V. iv. 117 “peaceful shall be proclaim'd” ; phr. “take (a) truce,” make peace John III. i. 17 , Rom. III. i. 163 , Ven. 82 .

true.text: (1 “true man” often opposed to “thief” as in legal language, e.g. in Coke's Institutes) 1. honest Tp. V. i. 268 , Wiv. II. i. 149 “the priest . . . commended him for a true man,” 1H4 II. ii. 25 “to turn true man and leave these rogues,” Cym. II. iii. 76 .

trump.text: trumpet 1H6 I. iv. 80 , Oth. III. iii. 352 .

trumpet.text: trumpeter H5 IV. ii. 61 “I will the banner from a trumpet take,” Troil. IV. v. 6 .

truncheon1.text: staff or mace borne by kings and military officers Meas. II. ii. 61 “The marshal's ,” Troil. V. iii. 53 “the hand of Mars Beckoning with fiery truncheon,” Ham. I. ii. 204 , Oth. II. i. 282 (Qq).

truncheon2.text: (?) to beat “out” of the ranks with a truncheon (see prec.) 2H4 II. iv. 152 “An captains were of my mind, they would you out for taking their names upon you.”

truncheoner.text: one armed with a cudgel H8 V. iv. 55 (Ff3 4 “Truncheons”).
