trunk.text: in allusion to the carved chests in great vogue in S.'s time Tw.N. III. iv. 406 “the beauteous evil Are empty” human “trunks o'erflourish'd by the devil.” ∥ ‘Chest’, not ‘human body’, is app. the sense (fig.) in 1H4 II. iv. 501 “that of humours, that bolting-hutch of beastliness.”

truss.text: to pack 2H4 III. ii. 353 “you might have t-'d him . . . into an eel-skin” (Q “thrust”).

trust1.text: 1. belief, conviction Tw.N. IV. iii. 15 “persuades me To any other trust but that I am mad.”

trust2.text: 1. to believe, be sure of Shr. IV. ii. 67 “If he be credu-” “lous and trust my tale,” Wint. II. iii. 49 “ it, He shall not rule me,” Mac. I. iii. 120 “That, t-ed home, Might yet enkindle you unto the crown.”

truth.text: (the foll. senses are freq.) 1. honesty, righteousness Ado IV. i. 35 , John IV. iii. 144 , Lucr. 1532 .

try1.text: test Tim. V. i. 12 “a try for his friends.”

try2.text: vb. (3 cf. ‘a Ship is said to try, when she has no more Sails abroad but her Main or Missen Sail only, [and] is let alone to lie in the Sea’, Bailey) 1. to refine (gold) Mer.V. II. vii. 53 “tried gold” ; fig. ix. 63 , 64

tub.text: with ref. to the use of the sweating cure (cf. POWDERING-TUB) Meas. III. ii. 61 , H5 II. i. 79 , Tim. IV. iii. 86 ; so tub-fast Tim. IV. iii. 87 .

tuck.text: rapier Tw.N. III. iv. 247 “Dismount thy tuck.” ∥ See also STANDING ppl. adj. 4

tucket.text: preliminary signal given on a trumpet H5 IV. ii. 35 “let the trumpets sound The sonance and the note to mount” ; otherwise only in stage directions as a personal trumpet call Mer.V. V. i., All'sW. III. v., H5 III. vi., Lr. II. i.

tuft.text: clump (of trees) AYL. III. v. 75 , Wint. II. i. 33 , R2 II. iii. 53 .

tug.text: to buffet Mac. III. i. 112 “tugg'd with fortune.”

tuition.text: protection Ado I. i. 291 [ 283 ] “and so I commit you—To the of God” (a freq. concluding formula in 16th cent. letters).

tumble.text: the orig. sense ‘to roll’ (trans. and intr.) is prominent:— Tp. II. ii. 11 “hedge-hogs, which Lie tumbling in my bare-foot way,” John III. iv. 176 “a little snow, t-d about, Anon becomes a mountain,” Per. II. i. 34 [the whale] “plays and t-s”; in indelicate sense Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 12, Ham. IV. v. 63 , Ant. I. iv. 17 ; in nautical use “t-d,” ‘rolled’ about the trough of the sea Per. V. Gower 13 “t-d and tost” (Qq1-3 “wee there him left”).

tune.text: (1 common Eliz.) 1. tone, accent (of the voice) Cor. II. iii. 91 “the of your voices,” Cym. V. v. 239 “The of Imogen,” Sonn. cxli. 5 “thy tongue's tune.”

tuneable.text: tuneful, musical MND. I. i. 184 , IV. i. 130 .

turf.text: clod LLL. IV. ii. 90 . ∥ An Eliz. sense.

turlygod.text: app. a name (? cant) for a ‘bedlam-beggar’ Lr. II. iii. 20 . ∥ For the form cf. ‘grinagod’ (16th cent.), which was app. a name for a profane person.

turn.text: vb. (5 cf. TURNING and TRIPLE-TURNED) 1. to shape on a lathe 1H4 III. i. 130 “I had rather hear a brazen canstick turn'”

turning.text: fickle H5 III. vi. 35 “she is , and inconstant.”

turtle.text: turtle-dove, symbolical of faithful love Wiv. II. i. 83 , LLL. IV. iii. 212 , V. ii. 913 .

twain.text: 1. “both twain,” redundantly=both LLL. V. ii. 460 , Sonn. xlii. 11 .

tway.text: Scottish form of “two” H5 III. ii. 132 .

twelfe.text: old form of “twelfth”† (which is not found in old edd.) Tw.N. II. iii. 93 , and in the title of the play itself.

twenty.text: used indefinitely to express a large number Wiv. I. i. 3 “if he were Sir John Falstaffs,” Lr. II. iv. 71 “there's not a nose among ” (Qq “a hundred) but can smell him that's stinking,” Ven. 522 “ hundred kisses” ;— Wiv. II. i. 203 “Good even and ” (app.=twenty times good);— Shr. IV. ii. 57 “eleven and ” perhaps contains an allusion to the game of one-and thirty (see PIP); see also SWEET-ANDTWENTY.

twiggen.text: cased in wicker work Oth. II. iii. 153 * “I'll beat the knave into a bottle” (Qq “wicker bottle”).

twin.text: to be like twins in resemblance or close companionship Cor. IV. iv. 15 “who , as 'twere, in love Unseparable” (Ff2-4 “Twine”), Per. V. Gower 8 * “Her inkle, silk, twin with the rubied cherry” (=are as red as the red cherry; unless “twin” is adj.; old edd. “twine”).

twink.text: “in” or “with a ,” in a twinkling Tp. IV. i. 43 , Shr. II. i. 304 [ 312 ].

twire.text: to twinkle Sonn. xxviii. 12 “When sparkling stars twire not.”

twist1.text: skein Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 96 “A of rotten silk.”

twist2.text: to draw out (a thread) John IV. iii. 128 “the smallest thread That ever spider t-ed from her womb” ; fig. Ado I. i. 321 [ 313 ] “to so fine a story.”

type.text: (the only S. senses are) 1. distinguishing mark or sign, badge 3H6 I. iv. 121 * “Thy father bears the of King of Naples” (i.e. the crown; or ?=title, sense 2), R3 IV. iv. 245 , H8 I. iii. 31 “those types of travel.”

tyrannically.text: vehemently, outrageously Ham. II. ii. 364 [ 356 ] “most tyrannically clapped.”

tyrannize.text: to inflict pain or torment “on” John V. vii. 47 , Tit. III. ii. 8 “This poor right hand of mine Is left to tyrannize upon my breast.”

tyrannous.text: cruel, pitiless R3 IV. iii. 1 “The and bloody act is done,” Ham. II. ii. 491 [ 482 ], Lr. III. iv. 155 “this night,” Sonn. cxxxi. 1 . ∥ More freq. than the meaning ‘tyrannical, despotic’.

tyranny.text: (the sense ‘despotic rule’ is freq.) 1. usurpation Mac. IV. iii. 67 “intemperance In nature is a tyranny.”

tyrant.text: (1 cf. AYL. II. i. 61 ) 1. usurper 3H6 III. iii. 69 , 71 “To prove him this reason may suffice, That Henry liveth still,” Mac. III. vi. 22 “His presence at the tyrant's feast.”

umber.text: brown pigment, used to disguise the face AYL. I. iii. 115 “with a kind of smirch my face.”

umpire.text: applied to Death as ‘the friendly compounder of differences’ (Cotgr. s.v. Arbitrateur) 1H6 II. v. 29 , Rom. IV. i. 63 .

unable.text: weak, impotent Shr. V. ii. 170 “froward and worms,” H5 V. ii. 403 [Epil. 1] “rough and all- pen,” Lr. I. i. 62 .

unaccommodated.text: unfurnished with necessaries, e.g. dress Lr. III. iv. 109 “ man . . . a poor, bare, forked animal.”

unacquainted.text: (in active sense) having no intimate knowledge of things Troil. III. iii. 12 “As new into the world, strange, ” ; (in passive sense) unfamiliar, strange John III. iv. 166 “ change,” V. ii. 32 .

unadvised.text: by inadvertence Gent. IV. iv. 129 “I have u-'d Deliver'd you a paper that I should not” ; done in ignorance Lucr. 1488 “friend to friend gives wounds” ; inconsiderate(ly) John II. i. 45 “Lest u-'d you stain your swords with blood,” 191, V. ii. 132 , Rom. II. ii. 118 “too rash, too u-'d, too sudden” ; so unadvisedly R3 IV. iv. 293 .

unapt.text: unfit Shr. V. ii. 167 “ to toil,” Lucr. 695 ; not prepared or inclined 1H6 V. iii. 132 “a soldier, and to weep,” Cor. V. i. 53 , Ven. 34 ; so unaptness, disinclination Tim. II. ii. 141 .

unarm.text: to take off a person's armour; trans. Troil. III. i. 165 “To help our Hector” ; refl. I. ii. 298 , V. iii. 35 “ thee” ; intr. I. i. 1 “I'll again,” V. iii. 3 , 25 ; Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 35 “, Eros” (i.e. take off my armour).

unavoided.text: (2 cf. UNVALUED 2) 1. (if) not avoided R3 IV. i. 55 “A cockatrice . . . Whose unavoided eye is murderous.”

unbanded.text: having no hatband AYL. III. ii. 404 “your bonnet unbanded.”

unbated.text: unabated Mer.V. II. vi. 11 “with the fire” ; not blunted (with a button; cf. ABATE 2) Ham. IV. vii. 138 .

unbend.text: to make slack, relax Mac. II. ii. 46 .

unbent.text: “to be ,” not to have one's bow bent, (hence) to be unprepared Cym. III. iv. 111 ; (of a brow) not wrinkled or knit Lucr. 1509 .

unbless.text: not to make happy Sonn. iii. 4 .

unbolted.text: lit. unsifted, (hence) coarse Lr. II. ii. 70 .

unbonneted.text: ‘uncovered’, (hence) on equal terms Oth. I. ii. 23 “speak unbonneted with” . . .

unbraced.text: unbuttoned, unfastened Cæs. I. iii. 48 , II. i. 262 , Ham. II. i. 78 .

unbuckle.text: to tear off (a helmet) in a close fight Cor. IV. v. 131 , Ant. IV. iv. 12 .

uncase.text: refl. and intr. to undress LLL. V. ii. 706 , Shr. I. i. 211 .

uncharge.text: to acquit of guilt Ham. IV. vii. 67 .

unclasp.text: to disclose Ado I. i. 333 [ 325 ], Wint. III. ii. 168 “he . . . to my kingly guest U-'d my practice.”

uncleanly.text: improper, indelicate AYL. III. ii. 52 , John IV. i. 7 “Uncleanly scruples,” Oth. III. iii. 139 .

unclew.text: lit. to unwind (see CLEW); fig. to ruin Tim. I. i. 169 “It would unclew me quite.”

uncolted.text: deprived of one's horse 1H4 II. ii. 45 (pun).

unconfirmed.text: inexperienced Ado III. iii. 123 , LLL. IV. ii. 19 “untrained . . . unlettered . . . unconfirmed fashion.”

unconstant.text: uncertain, abrupt, irregular Lr. I. i. 304 “ starts.”

unconstrained.text: imposing no constraint Compl. 242 “in unconstrained gyves.”

uncovered.text: bare-headed 2H6 IV. i. 128 ; open, unconcealed Ado IV. i. 310 “uncovered slander.”

unction.text: salve, lit. and fig. Ham. III. iv. 145 , IV. vii. 141 .

uncurrent.text: fig. not allowable or passable, (hence) objectionable or extraordinary Wint. III. ii. 50 * “With what encounter so uncurrent.”

uncurse.text: to remove a curse from R2 III. ii. 137 .

undeeded.text: having accomplished nothing Mac. V. vii. 20 “my sword . . . I sheathe . . . undeeded.”

under.text: (follows its noun in Lucr. 386 ) 1. under the pretence of Tim. III. iii. 33 ; under the auspices of Sonn. lxxviii. 4 .

underbear.text: to endure John III. i. 65 “woes . . . which I . . . Am bound to ,” R2 I. iv. 29 “patient u-ing.”

underborne.text: with a lining or undergarment of Ado III. iv. 21 “underborne with a bluish tinsel.”

undercrest.text: to wear as if a crest Cor. I. ix. 72 * “I mean . . . To undercrest your good addition.”

undergo.text: (3 some explain ‘partake of, enjoy’) 1. to be liable or subject to, run the risk of Ado V. ii. 59 “Claudio u-es my challenge,” John IV. i. 134 , 1H4 I. iii. 164 .

underhonest.text: wanting in straightforwardness Troil. II. iii. 134 .

understand.text: used quibblingly=stand under Gent. II. v. 28 , Err. II. i. 49 , Tw.N. III. i. 90 .

undertake.text: (the mod. sense is most freq.) 1. to take charge of H8 II. i. 97 .

undertaker.text: one who takes upon himself a task or business Tw.N. III. iv. 353 (almost=meddler), Oth. IV. i. 223 “let me be his ” (=I will settle him).

underwrite.text: to subscribe to, (hence) submit to Troil. II. iii. 138 .

undeserving.text: ‘want of merit, unworthiness’ (Schmidt) LLL. V. ii. 367 “My lady . . . gives undeserving praise.”

undistinguished.text: indefinable Lr. IV. vi. 279 “O undistinguish'd” (Q1 Ff “in-) space of woman's will!” (Qq “wit”); intimately mingled Compl. 20 “shrieking u-'d woe In clamours of all size.”

undo.text: (2, 3 occur each only once) 1. to hinder, be a bar to Tim. III. ii. 53 , Lr. IV. i. 71 “So distribution should undo excess,” Per. IV. vi. 4 .

undone.text: ruined; once preceding the sb. Tim. IV. iii. 490 “his undone lord.”

undoubted.text: 1. beyond a doubt, unquestioned John II. i. 369 .

unearned.text: unmerited MND. V. ii. 63 [ i. 439 ] “ luck.”

uneffectual.text: losing its effect Ham. I. v. 90 .

unequal.text: unfair, unjust 2H4 IV. i. 102 “a heavy and unequal hand,” Ant. II. v. 101 .

uneven.text: 1. not straightforward Rom. IV. i. 5 “ is the course.”

unexpressive.text: inexpressible AYL. III. ii. 10 “the . . . unexpressive she.”

unfair.text: to rob of beauty Sonn. v. 4 .

unfashionable.text: with no comeliness R3 I. i. 22 .

unfeeling.text: without sensation 2H6 III. ii. 145 “his hand unfeeling.”

unfellowed.text: without an equal Ham. V. ii. 150 .

unfelt.text: (for the stress cf. ENTIRE) 1. not felt inwardly R3 I. iv. 80 “for unfe'lt ima'gina'tions” (=‘instead of what they dream of but never realize’, Wright), Mac. II. iii. 143 “an u'nfelt so'rrow.”

unfirm.text: unstable, fickle Tw.N. II. iv. 33 “giddy and unfirm” ; weak 2H4 I. iii. 73 “the u'nfirm king.”

unfold.text: (the prevailing meanings are ‘display, disclose, reveal, bring a thing to light’) 1. to open (a letter) Ham. V. ii. 17 (Ff “unseal”); fig. to expand Cym. I. i. 26 .

unfolding2.text: the star that by its rising tells the shepherd the time to release the sheep from the fold Meas. IV. ii. 219 .

unfool.text: to take from (a person) the reproach of folly Wiv. IV. ii. 123 .

ungalled.text: uninjured Err. III. i. 102 “your yet estimation,” Ham. III. ii. 288 “let . . . The hart play.”

ungird.text: to relax Tw.N. IV. i. 16 “ thy strangeness.”

ungracious.text: graceless, profane R2 II. iii. 89 , 1H4 II. iv. 496 , R3 II. i. 128 , Ham. I. iii. 47 .

unhair.text: to denude of hair Ant. II. v. 64 .

unhandled.text: not broken in Mer.V. V. i. 72 “ colts.”

unhandsome.text: improper, unbecoming, indecent AYL. Epil. 2 , 1H4 I. iii. 44 “a slovenly corse” ; unfair Oth. III. iv. 150 “unhandsome warrior as I am.”

unhappily.text: unfavourably, ill H8 I. iv. 89 “I should judge now ,” Ham. IV. v. 13 “there might be thought, Though nothing sure, yet much ,” Lr. I. ii. 162 “succeed ” ; mischievously Sonn. lxvi. 4 “purest faith unhappily forsworn.”

unhappiness.text: evil nature R3 I. ii. 25 “heir to his ”

unhappy.text: 1. fatal, pernicious Cym. V. v. 154 “ was the clock That struck the hour,” Lucr. 1565 “that guest” ; hence used as a term of depreciation=miserable Err. IV. iv. 126 “O most strumpet!,” Mer.V. V. i. 238 “the subject of these quarrels,” Lr. IV. vi. 233 “Thou old traitor,” Oth. II. iii. 35 “I have very poor and unhappy brains for drinking.”

unhatched1.text: fig. not brought to maturity Ham. I. iii. 65 “each u-'d . . . comrade” (Qq “new hatcht”), Oth. III. iv. 140 “some u-'d practice Made demonstrable.”

unhatched2.text: not hacked or blunted Tw.N. III. iv. 260 .

unheard.text: unheard-of, unexampled John V. ii. 133 (see UNHAIR'D).

unheedful.text: rash Gent. II. vi. 11 , 1H6 IV. iv. 7 .

unhouseled.text: not having received the holy sacrament Ham. I. v. 77 .

unintelligent.text: unaware Wint. I. i. 15 “ of our insufficience.”

union.text: pearl Ham. V. ii. 286 (Ff “union,” Q2 “Vnice,” Qq3-5 “Onix(e),” 340 (Ff “union,” Qq2-5 “Onixe”).

united.text: “ ceremony,” union of the marriage rite Wiv. IV. vi. 52 .

unity.text: oneness Troil. V. ii. 138 “If there be rule in itself” (=‘if there be a rule that one is one’, J.).

universal.text: “ earth, world,” the whole world H5 IV. i. 67 , viii. 10 , Rom. III. ii. 94 ; clipped to “versal” Rom. II. iv. 221 (nurse's speech).

unjust.text: (1 and the sense ‘inequitable, unlawful’ are the most frequent) 1. unfaithful, false Gent. IV. ii. 2 , iv. 175 , All'sW. V. iii. 63 , 3H6 V. i. 106 “perjur'd, and ,” Troil. V. i. 99 “a most knave,” Sonn. Music iv. 33 [ Pilgr. 331 ] “Unless thy lady prove unjust.”

unjustly.text: perfidiously Lucr. 1836 “this chaste blood so stain'd” ; dishonestly All'sW. IV. ii. 76 .

unkennel.text: fig. to reveal Ham. III. ii. 86 .

unkind.text: (prob.) unnatural AYL. II. vii. 175 , 1H6 IV. i. 193 , Tit. I. i. 86 “ and careless of thine own,” Lr. III. iv. 70 “his unkind daughters,” Ven. 204 (? with play on the sense ‘unfeeling, cruel’).

unkindness.text: ill-feeling, want of kindly feeling Wiv. I. i. 204 , Shr. IV. iii. 169 “Take no ,” All'sW. II. v. 36 “Is there any between my lord and you?,” Cæs. IV. iii. 158 .

unkiss.text: to undo by a kiss R2 V. i. 74 “Let me the oath 'twixt thee and me.”

unknown.text: (?) that may not be expressed or mentioned R3 I. ii. 218 “For divers reasons,” Sonn. cxvii. 5 “That I have frequent been with minds” ; All'sW. II. iii. 6 “an fear” (=a fear of what is unknown); Troil. III. iii. 125 * “The Ajax” (‘who has abilities which were never brought into view or use’, J.).

unlace.text: (app.) to undo (fig.) Oth. II. iii. 196 “That you unlace your reputation thus.”

unless.text: except, if it be not, if there be not All'sW. IV. i. 6 , R2 V. iii. 32 “My tongue cleave to my roof . . . a pardon ere I rise or speak,” R3 IV. iv. 475 -6, Cor. V. i. 72 “all hope is vain his noble mother and his wife” (i.e. there is no hope except in them), Oth. I. i. 24 “Nor the division of a battle knows . . . unless the bookish theoric.”

unlike.text: unlikely, improbable Meas. V. i. 52 , Cor. III. i. 47 , Cym. V. v. 355 .

unlimited.text: not limited by the ‘unities of time and place’ Ham. II. ii. 428 [ 419 ] “poem unlimited.”

unloved.text: Ant. III. vi. 53 * “our love, which, left unshown, Is often left unlov'd” (=often ceases to be love).

unluckily.text: with ill omen Cæs. III. iii. 2 “things charge my fantasy.”

unmastered.text: unrestrained Ham. I. iii. 32 “his unmaster'd importunity.”

unmeritable.text: undeserving, without merit R3 III. vii. 154 “my desert Unmeritable,” Cæs. IV. i. 12 .

unmoving.text: in Qq of Oth. IV. ii. 54 “slow finger,” prob. an error, which is corrected by F1 “slow, and mouing finger” (see AND 1).

unmuzzle.text: only fig. to set free AYL. I. ii. 76 “ your wisdom” ; ppl. adj. unrestrained Tw.N. III. i. 132 “unmuzzled thoughts.”

unnoted.text: (2 see NOTE 1) 1. unnoticed, unregarded All'sW. I. ii. 34 , Lucr. 1014 .

unowed.text: having no owner John IV. iii. 147 .

unparagoned.text: matchless Cym. I. iv. 92 , II. ii. 17 .

unpay.text: to undo 2H4 II. i. 134 “ the villany you have done her.”

unpeeled.text: stripped LLL. II. i. 88 “his house” (Q1; the rest “unpeopled”).

unperfect.text: not knowing one's part Sonn. xxiii. 1 “an actor.” ∥ Cf. “perfectness” LLL. V. ii. 174 .

unpregnant.text: (see PREGNANT 2 ) 1. unapt Meas. IV. iv. 23 “ And dull to all proceedings.”

unprevailing.text: unavailing Ham. I. ii. 107 . ∥ ‘Prevail’ =avail is a 16th cent. use.

unprizable.text: to which no value can be attached; hence in two opposite senses, (1) worthless Tw.N. V. i. 59 , (2) invaluable Cym. I. iv. 104 .

unproper.text: not belonging exclusively to an individual, common Oth. IV. i. 69 “lie in those beds Which they dare swear peculiar.” ∥ There is prob. no allusion to a sense ‘indecent’, since corresponding uses of the words ‘proper’ and ‘improper’ are post-S.

unprovide.text: to make unprepared, weaken the resolution of Oth. IV. i. 217 “lest her body and beauty unprovide my mind again.”

unprovided.text: unprepared H5 IV. i. 186 “if they die ,” 3H6 V. iv. 63 ; unarmed R3 III. ii. 73 , Lr. II. i. 54 “he charges home My unprovided body.”

unqualitied.text: divested of his (manly) qualities Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 44

unquestionable.text: unwilling to talk AYL. III. ii. 399 . ∥ Cf. QUESTIONABLE.

unraised.text: not aspiring H5 I. Chor. 9 “ spirits.”

unreasonable.text: not endowed with reason 3H6 II. ii. 26 “Unreasonable creatures.”

unrecalling.text: not to be recalled, past recall Lucr. 993 “his unrecalling crime.”

unreclaimed.text: untamed Ham. II. i. 34 “ blood.” ∥ Properly used of hawks.

unrecuring.text: incurable, past cure Tit. III. i. 91 “some unrecuring wound.”

unreprievable.text: without possibility of a reprieve John V. vii. 48 .

unrespected.text: unnoticed, not regarded Sonn. xliii. 2 “they view things ,” liv. 10 “They live unwoo'd, and unrespected fade.”

unrespective.text: unobservant, heedless R3 IV. ii. 29 “ boys” ; fig. Troil. II. ii. 71 * “throw in sieve” (app. =that cares not what is put into it).

unrightful.text: having no rightful claim R2 V. i. 63 “To plant unrightful kings.”

unrolled.text: struck off the roll (of thieves) Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 131

unroosted.text: ousted from one's place Wint. II. iii. 74 .

unsalted.text: not salted Troil. II. i. 15 “thou leaven” (Ff “whinid'st,” mod. edd. “vinewed'st”†).

unsanctified.text: wicked Mac. IV. ii. 79 , Lr. IV. vi. 282 .

unsealed.text: not ratified (as by a seal) All'sW. IV. ii. 30 .

unseam.text: to rip up Mac. I. ii. 22 “he unseam'd him from the nave to the chaps.”

unseasonable.text: not in season for hunting Lucr. 581 “To strike a poor unseasonable doe.”

unseasoned.text: 1. unseasonable, ill-timed Wiv. II. ii. 176 “this intrusion,” 2H4 III. i. 105 .

unsecret.text: “ to ourselves,” not keeping our own counsel Troil. III. ii. 133 .

unseeming.text: not seeming (to be willing “to”) LLL. II. i. 155 .

unset.text: not planted or sown Sonn. xvi. 6 “many maiden gardens, yet unset.”

unsettled.text: undecided All'sW. II. v. 69 , H8 II. iv. 62 .

unshape.text: to put out, upset Meas. IV. iv. 23 .

unshaped.text: unformed, artless Ham. IV. v. 8 “her speech is nothing, Yet the unshaped use of it” . . .

unshorn.text: having the nap unclipped Compl. 94 “ velvet.”

unshout.text: to reverse by shouting the effect of (former shouting) Cor. V. iv. 70 [ v. 4 ] “ the noise that banish'd Marcius.”

unsisting.text: (?) misprint in Ff1 2 3 for “insisting” (F4) =persistent Meas. IV. ii. 92 (many conj., e.g. “unresisting†, unassisting†”).

unsorted.text: ill-chosen (cf. SORT vb. 2) 1H4 II. iii. 15 “the time itself unsorted.”

unsphere.text: to remove (a star) from its sphere (see SPHERE) Wint. I. ii. 48 .

unsquare.text: not adapted to the purpose, inapt Troil. I. iii. 159 .

unstate.text: to strip of state and dignity Lr. I. ii. 111 “I would myself” (=lose my rank), Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 30 “Cæsar will Unstate his happiness.”

unsure.text: 1. unsafe 2H4 I. iii. 89 “A habitation giddy and unsure.”

untainted.text: (2 cf. TAINT vb. 3) 1. unaccused R3 III. vi. 9 .

untaught.text: uncultured, unmannerly Meas. II. iv. 30 “their love Must needs appear offence,” 1H4 I. iii. 43 “ knaves,” Rom. V. iii. 214 “O thou ! what manners is in this” . . .?.

untempering.text: not having a softening influence H5 V. ii. 239 “the poor and effect of my visage.”

unthread.text: John V. iv. 11 “ the rude eye of rebellion” =retrace the rough path of rebellion. ∥ Cf. the uses of “thread” in R2 V. v. 17 , Cor. III. i. 123 , Lr. II. i. 121 .

unthrift.text: prodigal, (hence) good-for-nothing; adj. Mer.V. V. i. 16 “an love,” Tim. IV. iii. 311 “What man didst thou ever know that was beloved after his means?” ;—sb. R2 II. iii. 122 “upstart u-s,” Sonn. ix. 9 , xiii. 13 . ∥ Marked as an ‘old word’ by Bailey.

unthrifty.text: (with 1 and 2 cf. UNTHRIFT) 1. not thrifty, not eager for increase or profit Wint. V. ii. 126 “ to our knowledge” (=not increasing in knowledge), Sonn. iv. 1 “Unthrifty loveliness.”

unto.text: =to, in various senses;=in addition to AYL. I. ii. 255 “I should have given him tears unto entreaties,” R2 V. iii. 97 “Unto my mother's prayers I bend my knee” ; in regard or relation to Ant. II. ii. 150 “His power unto Octavia” ; in accordance with Per. II. i. 169 “Unto thy value.” ∥ Usually placed so that the second syll. bears the verse-accent, e.g. Ven. 263 “The stro'ng-neck'd stee'd, being tie'd unto' a tree'” ; contrast 2H6 II. ii. 50 “Sole da'ughter u'nto Li'onel, Du'ke of Cla'rence.”

untold.text: unreckoned Sonn. cxxxvi. 9 “in the number let me pass untold.”

untoward.text: unmannerly Shr. IV. v. 79 , John I. i. 243 .

untowardly.text: perversely Ado III. ii. 136 “O day turned.”

untraded.text: unhackneyed Troil. IV. v. 177 “that I affect the untraded oath.”

untread.text: to retrace (a path, steps) Mer.V. II. vi. 10 , John V. iv. 52 , Ven. 908 .

untreasured.text: stripped of the treasure of AYL. II. ii. 7 .

untrimmed.text: with her hair hanging loose, after the fashion of brides John III. i. 209 “a new bride.” ∥ Cf. Untrimmed, ‘incomptus’, ‘impexus’ (Rider's Dict.).

untrue1.text: untruth Sonn. cxiii. 14 * “maketh mine ” (=is the cause of my not seeing things truly); Capell, Malone “makes mine eye† untrue.”

untrue2.text: untruly, in defiance of the truth Sonn. lxxii. 10 .

untrussing.text: untying the points (see POINT sb. 5) Meas. III. ii. 194 .

untruth.text: unfaithfulness, disloyalty R2 II. ii. 101 , Troil. V. ii. 176 .

untuneable.text: discordant Gent. III. i. 209 “harsh, ,” AYL. V. iii. 38 “the note was very untuneable” (Theobald “untimeable”†).

unwares.text: unawares 3H6 II. v. 62 ; in Troil. III. ii. 38 (Q) “at unwares,” misprint for “at unawares” (F1). ∥ Used by Golding, and freq. in Spenser.

unwashed.text: 1H4 III. iii. 205 “with hands,” without waiting to wash your hands, i.e. at once.

unwedgeable.text: not splittable into wedges Meas. II. ii. 116 “the unwedgeable and gnarled oak.”

unwish.text: to wish (persons) out of existence H5 IV. iii. 76 “thou hast unwish'd five thousand men.”

unwit.text: to deprive of understanding Oth. II. iii. 184 .

unworthy.text: undeserved, unfitting R3 I. ii. 88 “didst unworthy slaughter upon others.”

unwrung.text: not wrenched or galled, as by a bad saddle Ham. III. ii. 257 “our withers are unwrung.”

unyoke.text: 1. to free cattle from the yoke; fig. to finish one's work Ham. V. i. 57 “Ay, tell me that, and unyoke.”

up.text: 1. on foot, in motion, going on Tit. II. ii. 1 “The hunt is up,” Cæs. V. i. 68 “The storm is up,” Cym. III. iii. 107 “The game is up” (cf. supra “the game is roused”).

upbraid.text: to find fault with (a person's action) Tp. II. i. 295 [ 287 ] “who Should not our course,” 2H4 IV. v. 191 , Troil. III. ii. 198 “let memory . . . my falsehood,” Mac. V. ii. 18 “upbraid his faith-breach.”

upcast.text: a throw at the game of bowls Cym. II. i. 2 “when I kissed the jack, upon an to be hit away!.”

upmost.text: topmost Cæs. II. i. 24 “the upmost round.”

upon1.text: adv. (see also LOOK UPON) 1. on the surface Mer.V. II. vii. 57 “A coin . . . that's insculp'd upon.”

upon2.text: prep. (follows its noun in All'sW. III. iv. 6 “the cold ground upon,” R2 II. iii. 138 ; 6 developed from the use with words like ‘attack’; for idiomatic uses with vbs. and adjs. see the latter) 1. on the side or party of John II. i. 237 “whose protection Is most divinely vow'd upon the right Of him it holds,” Mac. III. vi. 30 “upon his aid To wake Northumberland.”

uproar.text: to disturb Mac. IV. iii. 99 “Uproar the universal peace.”

upshot.text: conclusion Tw.N. IV. ii. 77 , Ham. V. ii. 398 .

upspring.text: the wildest dance at the old German merrymakings Ham. I. iv. 9 “Keeps wassail, and the swaggering upspring reels.”

upstaring.text: standing on end Tp. I. ii. 213 “With hair ” ∥ Spenser has ‘upstaring crests’ and ‘upstart haire’.

upswarm.text: to raise in swarms 2H4 IV. ii. 30 .

uptill.text: against, on Sonn. Music vi. 10 [ Pilgr. 382 ].

upward1.text: top Lr. V. iii. 138 “from the extremest upward of thy head To the” . . .

upward2.text: upturned Tim. IV. iii. 191 “thy upward face,” Cæs. V. iii. 93 .

urge.text: (rare uses) 1. intr. to put forward a strong plea or argument (“for, against”) H8 II. i. 16 “The king's attorney . . . U-'d on the examinations . . . Of divers witnesses” (=pleaded on the evidence of . . .), V. iii. 48 “That . . . my accusers . . . may . . . freely against me,” Tim. III. ii. 14 “urged extremely for'”

urinal.text: glass vessel to receive urine Gent. II. i. 43 , Wiv. III. i. 14 , 91

urn.text: (2 as sense not elsewhere in S.) 1. (properly) vessel to hold the ashes of the dead 1H6 I. vi. 24 ; (transf.) grave H5 I. ii. 228 , Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 146

usage.text: habit Oth. IV. iii. 107 (Q1 only; the rest “uses”).

usance.text: interest on money, usury Mer.V. I. iii. 46 , &c.

use1.text: sb. (obsolete or archaic uses) 1. habitual practice, custom Meas. I. iv. 62 “use and liberty” (=licentious practice), Mer.V. IV. i. 269 “it is still her” (viz. Fortune's) “use To let the wretched man outlive his wealth,” All'sW. V. i. 24 “with more haste Than is his use,” Tim. I. i. 292 “a return exceeding All use of quittance,” Oth. IV. i. 285 “Is it his use?” ; pl. usages, ways Ham. I. ii. 134 “all the uses of this world,” Oth. IV. iii. 107 (Q1 “vsage”).

use2.text: vb. (obsolete or archaic uses) 1. to be in the habit of doing (a thing), make a practice of Mer.V. I. iii. 71 “I do never use it,” Cor. III. i. 113 “as 'twas us'd,” Lr. I. iv. 188 ; with infin. Troil. II. i. 52 “If thou use to beat me.”

usurer.text: “u-'s chain,” chain such as was worn by wealthy citizens of the merchant or banker class Ado II. i. 199 .

usuring.text: usurious, grasping, stingy Tim. III. v. 112 , IV. iii. 518 “a usuring kindness.”

usurp.text: intr. to encroach or exercise unlawful influence “upon” Tit. III. i. 268 “this sorrow . . . would upon my watery eyes,” Ham. III. ii. 275 , Per. III. ii. 82 “Death may usurp on nature many hours.”

usurped.text: false Oth. I. iii. 346 “an beard” ; so usurping LLL. IV. iii. 259 “usurping hair.”

ut.text: lowest note of the musical scale LLL. IV. ii. 103 , Shr. III. i. 77 .

utis.text: [variant form of ‘utas’=octave of a festival, i.e. the eighth day after the feast-day, or the period of eight days beginning with it]: in transf. sense, merrymaking 2H4 II. iv. 22 “old utis” (=rare fun).

utmost.text: furthest John II. i. 29 “that corner of the west,” Oth. V. ii. 267 “my butt, And very sea-mark of my sail” ; absol. furthest point Meas. II. i. 36 “that's the utmost of his pilgrimage.”

utter.text: (cf. 2 ‘utter false coin’) 1. to emit MND. IV. ii. 45 “eat no onions nor garlic, for we are to sweet breath,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 185, Cæs. I. ii. 246 .

utterance.text: “to the , at ,” to the uttermost, to the last extremity Mac. III. i. 72 “champion me to the ,” Cym. III. i. 73 “keep at utterance.”

uttermost.text: Mer.V. I. i. 157 “of my ,” of my doing my utmost; Cæs. II. i. 213 “the ,” the latest.

vacancy.text: 1. empty space, vacuity Ham. III. iv. 116 “bend your eye on vacancy,” Ant. II. ii. 224 .

vade.text: to fade R2 I. ii. 20 “his summer leaves all vaded,” Sonn. liv. 14 .

vagabond.text: moving to and fro Ant. I. iv. 45 “a flag upon the stream.”

vail1.text: going down Troil. V. viii. 7 “the vail and darking of the sun.”

vail2.text: vb. [aphetic form of ‘avail, avale’, Fr. ‘avaler’] 1. to let fall, lower LLL. V. ii. 298 “angels v-ing clouds” (=letting fall the clouds that hide them), Mer.V. I. i. 28 “Vailing her high-top,” 1H6 V. iii. 25 “ her lofty-plumed crest,” Ham. I. ii. 70 “thy vailed lids,” Per. II. iii. 42 .

vailful.text: advantageous Meas. IV. vi. 4 “to purpose” (Ff “vail(e full,” Malone “veil full”†).

vails.text: perquisites, tips Per. II. i. 163 . ∥ Remains in some midland dialects.

vain.text: (sense 1, and ‘empty, worthless’, ‘ineffectual’ are the chief meanings) 1. empty-headed, foolish, silly Err. III. ii. 187 “no man is so vain That would refuse so fair an offer'd chain,” LLL. V. ii. 769 “wanton . . . skipping and vain,” 1H4 III. ii. 67 “every beardless vain comparative,” Lr. IV. ii. 61 “O vain fool.”

vainness.text: boastfulness, vanity Tw.N. III. iv. 391 * , H5 V. Chor. 20 . [451 [ 442 ].

valanced.text: ‘curtained’ with a beard Ham. II. ii.

vale.text: fig. 2H6 II. i. 70 “this earthly vale,” Oth. III. iii. 266 “the vale of years.”

validity.text: 1. strength Ham. III. ii. 201 “Of . . . poor validity.”

value1.text: estimation H8 V. iii. 108 “How much more is his life in value with him” ; estimate Cor. II. ii. 64 “A kinder value of the people.”

value2.text: vb. (1 freq. in the gen. sense) 1. to rate, estimate; 1H4 III. ii. 177 “Our business v-d,” taking into consideration how long our business will take us; V. ii. 59 “valu'd with you,” compared with you in respect of worth.

vanish.text: to escape “from” Rom. III. iii. 10 “A gentler judgement vanish'd from his lips.”

vanity.text: (1 cf. INIQUITY) 1. character in the old morality plays Lr. II. ii. 40 “Vanity the puppet's part.”

vantage.text: (2 by far the most freq. sense) 1. superior position, superiority MND. I. i. 102 “as fairly rank'd If not with ,” H5 III. vi. 156 “an enemy of craft and ,” Lucr. 249 “Urging . . . for ” (=putting in the most favourable light); phr. 2H4 II. iii. 53 “get ground and of the king,” H5 IV. i. 300 “Had the fore-hand and vantage of a king.”

vantbrace.text: armour for the front part of the arm Troil. I. iii. 297 (Q “vambrace”).

vaporous.text: “ drop,” ‘a foam which the moon was supposed to shed on particular herbs, or other objects, when strongly solicited by enchantment’ (Steevens) Mac. III. v. 24 .

vara.text: dial. pronunciation of ‘very’ LLL. V. ii. 488 (Costard). ∥ Now confined to northern dial.

variable.text: various Cor. II. i. 231 “ridges hors'd With complexions,” Ham. III. i. 181 “the seas and countries different With variable objects,” Cym. I. vi. 134 .

varlet.text: gentleman's son in the service of a knight or prince H5 IV. ii. 2 (intended for French; F1 “Verlot”), Troil. I. i. 1 “Call here my , I'll unarm again.” ∥ The sense ‘rascal, knave’ is freq.

vary2.text: to express in different terms H5 III. vii. 35 “vary deserved praise on my palfrey.”

vassal.text: base wretch, slavish fellow LLL. I. i. 253 “that shallow (vessel†),” 2H6 IV. i. 111 “a lowly ,” Lr. I. i. 163 “O ! miscreant!.” —adj. slavish, base 1H4 III. ii. 124 “ fear,” H5 III. v. 51 “the valleys, whose low vassal seat The Alps doth spit . . . upon.”

vast.text: the senses ‘boundless, immense’ and ‘waste, desolate’ are app. sometimes blended R3 I. iv. 39 “the empty, , and wandering air,” Tit. IV. i. 53 “the ruthless, , and gloomy woods,” V. ii. 36 “No obscurity or misty vale” ; extending far and wide John IV. iii. 152 “ confusion” ;—sb. (1) desolate period (of the night) Tp. I. ii. 327 , Ham. I. ii. 198 “the dead vast and middle of the night” (Qq1 5 6; others “wast(e)”; (2) boundless desolate sea Wint. I. i. 33 , Per. III. i. 1 “The god of this great vast.”

vastidity.text: immensity Meas. III. i. 67 “all the world's ”

vasty.text: usu.=vast, as in 1H4 III. i. 53 “I can call spirits from the deep” ; but prob. with mixture of sense ‘waste’ in Mer.V. II. vii. 41 “the wilds Of wide Arabia.”

vaultage.text: app. cavern H5 II. iv. 124 “womby vaultages.”

vaulty.text: arched, hollow, cavernous John III. iv. 30 [death's] “ brows” (perhaps with a ref. to burial vaults), Rom. III. v. 22 “The vaulty heaven,” Lucr. 119 [night's] “vaulty prison.”

vaunt.text: beginning, rise Troil. Prol. 27 “the vaunt and firstlings of those broils.”

vaward.text: vanguard H5 IV. iii. 130 , Cor. I. vi. 53 ; fig. early part MND. IV. i. 111 “the of the day,” 2H4 I. ii. 202 “the vaward of our youth.”

vein.text: (1 the literal sense is freq.) 1. fig. John V. ii. 38 “combine The blood of malice in a of league,” Troil. I. iii. 6 , Per. I. iv. 94 “the Trojan horse was stuff'd within With bloody veins.”

velvet.text: adj. ‘sleek and prosperous’ (Aldis Wright) AYL. II. i. 50 “his velvet friends.”

vengeance.text: (3 cf. phr. ‘with a vengeance’) 1. mischief, harm AYL. IV. iii. 49 “That could do no vengeance to me,” Tit. II. iii. 113 .

venison.text: wild animals hunted for food AYL II. i. 21 “kill . . . ,” Cym. III. iii. 75 “He that strikes The ”

venom.text: poisonous (lit. and fig.) Err. V. i. 69 “The clamours of a jealous woman,” R2 II. i. 19 , 3H6 II. ii. 138 “venom toads,” Lucr. 850 “venom mud.”

venomed.text: (2 cf. “venom'd-mouth'd” H8 I. i. 120 , altered in mod. edd. to “venom-mouth'd”†） 1. poisoned R2 I. i. 171 “slander's v-'d spear,” Ham. IV. vii. 161 , Ven. 916 “venom'd sores.”

venomous.text: fig. injurious, pernicious Troil. IV. ii. 12 * “ wights,” Cor. IV. i. 23 “Thy tears are . . . to thine eyes,” Tit. V. iii. 13 “venomous malice.”

vent1.text: sb. 1 [? orig. a variant of ‘fent’=slit] 1. opening, aperture 2H4 Ind. 2 “The of hearing” (=the ear), Troil. V. iii. 82 “how thy wounds do bleed at many v-s,” Lucr. 310 “little v-s and crannies,” 1040

vent2.text: scent; Cor. IV. v. 239 * “full of ,” (?)full of excitement or activity, as a dog on a good scent.

vent3.text: to emit Tp. II. ii. 115 , Cym. I. ii. 5 ; esp. to utter, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 280 ; to void, get rid of Cor. I. i. 231 “to vent Our musty superfluity.”

ventage.text: vent-hole; applied to the stops of a flute Ham. III. ii. 380 [ 373 ].

ventricle.text: “the of memory,” that one of the three divisions of the brain which was held to be the seat of memory LLL. IV. ii. 70 .

venture.text: concr. venturous person Cym. I. vi. 123 .

verbal.text: (a) plain-spoken, (b) verbose, (c) playing with words Cym. II. iii. 111 * .

verbatim1.text: by word of mouth 1H6 III. i. 13 .

verge.text: compass R2 II. i. 102 ; circle R3 IV. i. 58 “the inclusive Of golden metal” ; (magic) circle 2H6 I. iv. 25 “within a hallow'd ” ∥ In R2 II. i. 102 there is allusion to the sense ‘Compass, or extent of the King's Court, formerly of twelve Miles extent, within the Jurisdiction of the Lord High Steward of the King's Household’.

verify.text: 1. to affirm, maintain Ado V. i. 228 “they have verified unjust things,” H5 III. ii. 79 , 1H6 I. ii. 32 .

verity.text: truthfulness AYL. III. iv. 23 “his in love,” Mac. IV. iii. 92 “justice, verity, temperance.”

versing.text: telling in verse MND. II. i. 67 “ love.”

very1.text: （“same ”=very same John IV. i. 125 , R3 III. ii. 49 ) 1. veritable, real, true, that is indeed so Ado IV. i. 188 “Two of them have the very bent of honour,” Ham. II. ii. 49 “The very cause of Hamlet's lunacy” ; esp. in “very friend” Gent. III. ii. 41 , Mer.V. III. ii. 224 , Rom. III. i. 116 ;— Cym. IV. ii. 107 “very Cloten” (=Cloten himself).

very2.text: quite, exactly, just Meas. IV. iii. 41 , Lr. V. iii. 296 , Oth. I. i. 88 .

vessel.text: freq. in the sense of (i) ‘ship’, less common in the sense (ii) ‘cask, &c., for holding liquids’; both are used fig. (i) All'sW. II. iii. 215 “believing thee a of too great a burden,” Cor. IV. v. 68 , (ii) 2H4 IV. iv. 44 , H5 IV. Chor. 3 “When creeping murmur and the poring dark Fills the wide of the universe,” Tim. II. ii. 187 “If I would broach the v-s of my love” (i.e. my friends); esp. applied to the human body (i) Tim. V. i. 206 “nature's fragile ,” Per. IV. iv. 30 “A tempest, which his mortal tears,” (ii) Oth. IV. ii. 82 “to preserve this for my lord” ; hence=person (ii) Wint. III. iii. 20 “I never saw a of like sorrow, So fill'd,” Cæs. V. v. 13 “Now is that noble full of grief” ; similarly “weaker ”=woman LLL. I. i. 271 , Rom. I. i. 20 .

vestal.text: sb. priestess of Vesta, vowed to chastity, and having the charge of keeping alight the vestal fire Ven. 752 ; transf. virgin MND. II. i. 158 “a fair throned by the west” (ref. to Queen Elizabeth); “kitchen ” (jocular), kitchen maid, ‘her charge being, like the vestal virgins, to keep the fire burning’ (J.) Err. IV. iv. 77 ;—adj. Per. III. iv. 10 “A livery will I take me to” (=I will embrace the life of a vestal); chaste Rom. II. ii. 8 , III. iii. 38 “pure and vestal modesty.”

vesture.text: applied to the human body Mer.V. V. i. 64 “this muddy of decay,” Oth. II. i. 64 “in th' essential of creation” (=‘the real qualities with which creation has invested her’, J.).

vex.text: (2 freq., as also the current mod. sense of ‘irritate, annoy’） 1. to disturb, agitate (physically) Tp. I. ii. 229 (see STILL adv. ∥), Lr. IV. iv. 2 “As mad as the vex'd sea.”

vexation.text: agitation; affliction, torment, uneasiness, anguish MND. IV. i. 75 “the fierce of a dream,” R3 IV. iv. 306 “Your children were to your youth,” Oth. I. i. 72 “changes of ,” Lucr. 1779 “The deep vexation of his inward soul.”

vial.text: bottle or flask Rom. IV. i. 93 ; spec. bottle such as those found in ancient Roman tombs, commonly supposed to have been made to receive tears Ant. I. iii. 63 “the sacred vials thou shouldst fill With sorrowful water.”

vice1.text: sb. 1 (2 cf. Cotgr., ‘Badiner’, to play the foole, or Vice) 1. sinful act, offence, transgression Meas. II. iv. 117 “You . . . rather prov'd the sliding of your brother A merriment than a vice,” Oth. IV. i. 179 “how he laughed at his vice,” IV. iii. 71 “'tis a great price For a small vice.”

vice2.text: screw Ado V. ii. 21 “you must put in the pikes with a vice” ; instrument for gripping things that are being worked upon; fig. grip 2H4 II. i. 26 “an a' come but within my vice” (Q “view”).

vice3.text: to screw Wint. I. ii. 416 “an instrument To vice you to '”

vicious.text: 1. faulty, wrong Oth. III. iii. 145 “Though I perchance am in my guess,” Cym. V. v. 65 “it had been To have mistrusted her.”

vie.text: (orig. a term at cards; cf. To Vie, as they do at cardes, ‘Augere, Admittere, Accipere Sponsionem’, Rider's Dict. 1589 ) 1. to stake; fig. Shr. II. i. 303 [ 311 ] “kiss on kiss She vied so fast” (i.e. as if to outdo me).

view.text: (1 freq. in the gen. sense of ‘sight’ with subjective and objective genitive, e.g. Gent. I. ii. 52 “force the letter to my view,” Ant. II. ii. 173 “to my sister's view” = to see my sister) 1. phr. “at ample view,” so as to be fully seen Tw.N. I. i. 27 ; “on more view,” on closer inspection Rom. I. ii. 32 ; “from view o',” out of sight of Cym. III. iii. 28 ; “full of view” * , having many opportunities of observation Cym. III. iv. 150 ; “to the view,” so as to be seen by all, to the public view Ham. V. ii. 392 , Ant. V. ii. 210 , Sonn. cx. 2 ; H8 I. i. 44 “gave each thing view,” showed everything to full advantage; “in (the) view” is freq.

vigil.text: eve of a festival H5 IV. iii. 45 .

vigour.text: power or efficacy (of a poison) Ham. I. v. 68 , Cym. I. v. 21 ; fig. Meas. II. ii. 184 “the strumpet, With all her double vigour, art and nature.”

vile.text: (very often spelt “vild, vil'd, vilde” in old edd.) 1. low or mean in rank or condition Mer.V. II. iv. 6 , 2H4 I. ii. 19 “in apparel,” H5 IV. iii. 62 , 2H6 IV. i. 134 “Great men oft die by vile bezonians.”

vilely.text: (twice so spelt in old edd. 1H4 III. iii. 1 , 121 ; elsewhere “vildly, vildely”).

villain.text: (most freq. in the mod. sense) 1. serf, bondman, servant AYL. I. i. 60 “I am no ” (with play on the sense ‘rascal’), Tit. IV. iii. 72 “the empress' ,” Lr. III. vii. 78 , Lucr. 1338 “The homely villain curtsies to her low.”

vinewed.text: most mouldy Troil. II. i. 15 “thou leaven” (Ff “whinid'st,” Q “vnsalted”).

viol.text: six-stringed instrument played with a bow R2 I. iii. 162 , Per. I. i. 81 .

violence.text: ‘bold action’ (Rolfe) Oth. I. iii. 251 “My downright violence.”

violent.text: to be violent Troil. IV. iv. 4 “The grief . . . violenteth in a sense as strong” . . .

viperous.text: venomous Cor. III. i. 285 “The traitor,” Cym. III. iv. 41 “This viperous slander.”

virgin1.text: of a virgin Mer.V. III. ii. 56 “The virgin tribute” (viz. Hesione) “paid by howling Troy To the sea-monster”; of virginity MND. I. i. 80 “my virgin patent” (=my privilege of virginity).

virgin2.text: (with “it”) to play the virgin, be chaste Cor. V. iii. 48 .

virginal.text: virgin, maidenly 2H6 V. ii. 52 “tears ,” Cor. V. ii. 45 , Per. IV. vi. 62 .

virginalling.text: lit. playing on the virginals, a keyed instrument of the harpsichord class; fig. fingering Wint. I. ii. 126 “Still Upon his palm!.”

virtue.text: (2 cf. Latin ‘virtus’ and Cor. II. ii. 89 “valour is the chiefest virtue” ) 1. concr. use of the moral sense 2H4 II. iv. 50 “my poor ,” Tim. III. v. 7 “a humble suitor to your v-s” (viz. the senate).

virtuous.text: (most freq. in the moral sense) 1. of efficacious or powerful properties MND. III. ii. 367 “Whose liquor hath this property,” Oth. III. iv. 110 “by your means” ; (?) beneficial Meas. II. ii. 168 * (see SEASON sb. 3).

virtuously.text: app. used affectedly=preciously, dearly Tim. I. ii. 235 .

visit.text: (2 cf. ‘visit their offences with the rod’ Psalm lxxxix. 32) 1. to afflict with disease LLL. V. ii. 423 “These lords are v-ed” (viz. with the plague), 1H4 IV. i. 26 , Mac. IV. iii. 150 “strangely-visited people.”

visitation.text: (1 spec. applied to attacks of the plague, cf. VISIT vb. 1; 2 the sb. ‘visit’ is not S.) 1. affliction Tp. III. i. 32 .

visitor.text: one who takes spiritual consolation to others Tp. II. i. 11 .

vizarded.text: masked Wiv. IV. vi. 40 , Troil. I. iii. 83 .

voice1.text: sb. (the usual medium of expressing one's meaning, intention, or opinion; hence the foll. senses) 1. what one says, speech, words Wiv. I. iii. 49 , I. iv. 163 “let me have thy in my behalf” (=speak for me), H5 V. ii. 93 “Haply a woman's may do some good,” Ham. I. ii. 45 “lose your voice” (=speak in vain).

voice2.text: vb. (twice) 1. to acclaim Tim. IV. iii. 82 “Is this the Athenian minion, whom the world Voic'd so regardfully?.”

void1.text: empty Cæs. II. iv. 37 “a place more void.”

void2.text: vb. [aphetic form of AVOID, q.v.] 1. to emit Mer.V. I. iii. 118 “ your rheum,” H5 III. v. 52 ; “void up,” vomit Tim. I. ii. 145 .

volable.text: quick-witted LLL. III. i. 69 (Q1; Ff Q2 “voluble”).

volume.text: Cor. III. iii. 33 “Will bear the knave by the ” =will endure whole volumes of contemptuous epithets.

voluntary.text: volunteer John II. i. 67 “Rash, inconsiderate, fiery voluntaries,” Troil. II. i. 106 “Ajax was here the voluntary.”

votaress.text: woman that is under a vow MND. II. i. 123 , 163 , Per. IV. Gower 4 .

votarist.text: =VOTARY Meas. I. iv. 5 , Tim. IV. iii. 27 .

votary.text: one who has taken a vow Gent. I. i. 52 , Sonn. cliv. 5 .

vouch1.text: testimony, witness Meas. II. iv. 157 , H8 I. i. 157 , Oth. II. i. 147 .

vouch2.text: to bear witness Oth. I. iii. 263 “ with me, heaven.” ∥ The common senses are (1) warrant, answer for, (2) assert, maintain, where mod.idiom prefers ‘vouch for’ (which is not S.).

voucher.text: person who is called upon to warrant a tenant's title Ham. V. i. 112 “double v-s,” 115; transf. Cym. II. ii. 39 .

vouchsafe.text: (the prevalent senses are ‘deign, condescend’ and ‘deign to grant’) 1. to allow (a person to do something) Err. V. i. 283 “ me speak a word” ; with infin. suppressed Ado III. ii. 4 “I'll bring you thither, . . . if you'll me.”

vulgar1.text: 1. common people LLL. I. ii. 52 “the base ,” Cæs. I. i. 74 ; pl. Wint. II. i. 93 “those That v-s give bold'st titles” ; common soldiers H5 IV. vii. 81 “our vulgar.”

vulgar2.text: adj. (the sense ‘low, mean’ occurs) 1. of the common people, plebeian 2H4 I. iii. 90 “the heart,” Cor. I. i. 221 “Five tribunes to defend their wisdoms,” II. i. 234 “ station” (=among the crowd), IV. vii. 21 .

waft.text: (pa. t. and pa. pple. “waft”) 1. to convey by water John II. i. 73 , 2H6 IV. i. 116 “I must waft thee to thy death,” 3H6 III. iii. 253 .

waftage.text: conveyance by water Err. IV. i. 96 “to hire waftage,” Troil. III. ii. 10 .

wafture.text: wave Cæs. II. i. 246 “ of your hand.”

wag.text: to go forward, go on one's way Wiv. I. iii. 7 “let them wag; trot, trot,” &c., Ado V. i. 16 “Bid sorrow wag,” AYL. II. vii. 23 “how the world wags” ; to go or move about Tit. V. ii. 87 “the empress never wags But in her company there is a Moor.”

wage.text: (the foll. are all the S. uses) 1. to lay as a wager, to stake Ham. V. ii. 154 (Qq “wagered”), Lr. I. i. 158 , Cym. I. iv. 149 .

waggish.text: frolicsome, roguish MND. I. i. 240 “waggish boys,” Cym. III. iv. 160 .

waggon.text: chariot, carriage All'sW. IV. iv. 34 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 118 “Dis's waggon,” Tit. V. ii. 51 “Provide two proper palfreys . . . To hale thy vengeful waggon swift away.”

waggoner.text: charioteer Tit. V. ii. 48 , Rom. I. iv. 65 .

wagtail.text: opprobrious term for a ‘bobbing’, ‘ducking’, or obsequious person Lr. II. ii. 72 .

waid.text: Shr. III. ii. 57 [a horse] “waid in the back” (Ff; mod. edd. “weighed†, swayed†”).

waist.text: 1. girdle Meas. III. ii. 42 “His neck will come to your ” (=he will be hanged), John II. i. 217 , 1H6 IV. iii. 20 “girdled with a waist of iron.”

wait.text: (the prevalent use is “wait on” = be at the service of, follow, accompany) 1. to remain expecting (something), await LLL. V. ii. 63 “And wait the season, and observe the times,” John IV. iii. 152 , Per. I. i. 55 “I the sharpest blow.”

wake1.text: feast of the dedication (or title) of a church and the merrymaking connected with it LLL. V. ii. 319 “At w-s and wassails,” Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 110, Lr. III. vi. 77 “wakes and fairs.”

wake2.text: 1. fig. to arouse, excite Ado V. i. 102 “ your patience,” Mac. III. vi. 31 , R2 I. iii. 132 , Oth. I. iii. 30 , III. iii. 364 “my wak'd wrath,” Lucr. 759 .

walk1.text: sb. (obsolete senses) 1. pl. (a person's) way or course MND. III. i. 172 “Hop in his walks, and gambol in his eyes,” V. i. 31 “in your royal walks,” Tit. II. iv. 8 “let's leave her to her silent walks,” Sonn. lxxxix. 9 “I will . . . Be absent from thy walks.”

walk2.text: (1 also “walk aside” Ado III. ii. 73 ) 1. to go aside, withdraw Wint. I. ii. 172 , Lr. IV. vii. 82 “Will't please your highness walk?,” Oth. IV. iii. 4 , Cym. I. i. 176 .

wan.text: to turn pale Ham. II. ii. 588 [ 580 ] “all his visage wann'd” (Qq “wand,” Ff “warm'd”).

wandering.text: “ knight,” knight errant MND. I. ii. 48 ; “ star,” planet Ham. V. i. 278 .

want.text: (1 the commonest S. sense; 3 cf. LESS ∥) 1. to be without, lack Tp. III. iii. 38 “they want the use of tongue,” John IV. i. 99 “the utterance of a brace of tongues Must needs want pleading for a pair of eyes” (=be insufficient to plead), R3 V. iii. 13 , Cor. I. iii. 90 “'Tis not . . . that I want love,” Lucr. 389 “to want” (=at missing), Sonn. xxiv. 13 “eyes this cunning want to grace their art” ; also intr. with “of” Rom. II. ii. 78 “wanting of thy love.”

wanton1.text: 1. person of unrestrained, sportive, or roguish behaviour, trifler Wiv. II. ii. 59 “your worship's a ,” MND. II. i. 63 “Tarry, rash ,” Rom. I. iv. 35 “w-s, light of heart” ; phr. “play the w-s,” dally, trifle R2 III. iii. 164 .

wanton2.text: adj. (‘lascivious’ the most freq. sense) 1. unrestrained, sportive, frolicsome LLL. IV. iii. 104 “the air,” V. ii. 769 “All as a child,” Mer.V. V. i. 71 “a wild and herd,” H8 III. ii. 360 “little boys,” Ham. II. i. 22 “wanton, wild, and usual slips.”

wantonness.text: playful or frolicsome behaviour, sportiveness John IV. i. 16 “as sad as night, Only for ,” 1H4 V. ii. 68 ; (?) wanton self-satisfaction Troil. III. iii. 137 * .

ward1.text: sb. (4 the commonest sense in S.) 1. guard, protection LLL. III. i. 139 .

ward2.text: to guard, protect R3 V. iii. 255 , Tit. III. i. 194 .

warden.text: ‘a large sort of delicious baking pear’ (Bailey) Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 49

warder.text: staff or mace held by one presiding over a combat R2 I. iii. 118 “the king hath thrown his down” (i.e. to stop the fight), 2H4 IV. i. 125 .

ware1.text: aware (“of”) AYL. II. iv. 57 “Thou speakest wiser than thou art ware of,” Rom. I. i. 130 , II. ii. 103 ; in AYL. II. iv. 59 the meaning ‘cautious’ is played upon.

ware2.text: beware of LLL. V. ii. 43 , Troil. V. vii. 12 .

warm.text: well off, comfortable 1H4 IV. ii. 19 * . ∥ Cf. ‘Warm’, well-lined or flush in the Pocket (Dict. of Canting Crew).

warn.text: (1 cf. WARRANT vb. 2, of which ‘warn’ is a widespread dial. pronunciation) 1. “God warn us!”=God keep us!, Mercy on us! MND. V. i. 328 (old edd. “warnd,” mod. edd. “warrant”†), AYL. IV. i. 79 .

warp.text: (1 here belongs app. AYL. II. vii. 187 “Though thou the waters warp,” viz. by freezing or ruffling them) 1. to change the aspect of, distort All'sW. V. iii. 49 “his scornful perspective . . . Which warp'd the line of every other favour” ; also intr. Wint. I. ii. 365 “My favour here begins to warp.”

warped.text: perverse, malignant,=CROOKED 2, Meas. III. i. 140 , Lr. III. vi. 56 .

warrant1.text: sb. (the legal senses colour the use of the word to a large extent) 1. deed by which a person authorizes another to do something in his name Wiv. I. i. 10 .

warrant2.text: vb. (2 cf. WARN 1) 1. to give (a person) security Meas. IV. ii. 179 “By the vow of mine order I you,” Err. IV. iv. 3 “I'll give thee . . . so much money, To thee, as I am rested for.”

warranted.text: justified Mac. IV. iii. 137 “our quarrel” ; requiring a warrant or guarantee Meas. III. ii. 155 “upon a warranted need.”

warrantise.text: 1. surety, guarantee 1H6 I. iii. 13 “I'll be your , Sonn. cl. 7 .”

warranty.text: authorization, permission Mer.V. I. i. 133 , Ham. V. i. 249 (F1 “warrantis”), Oth. V. ii. 60 “with such general warranty of heaven.”

warren.text: ‘a Franchise or privileged Place by Prescription or Grant to keep Beasts and Fowl of Warren, as Conies, Hares, Partridges, and Pheasants’ (Bailey) Ado II. i. 224 “as melancholy as a lodge in a warren.”

warrener.text: keeper of a warren Wiv. I. iv. 28 .

warrior.text: used playfully in ref. to Desdemona having followed Othello to the wars Oth. II. i. 185 ; prob. alluded to in III. iv. 150 “unhandsome ,” which J. glosses ‘unfair assailant’.

wash1.text: “Neptune's salt ,” the sea Ham. III. ii. 168 .

wash2.text: “wash” oneself “of,” get rid of Wiv. III. iii. 167 “I would I could wash myself of the buck!” (pun on BUCK-WASHING); “wash” one's “brain” (Eliz. phr.), drink copiously Ant. II. vii. 106 .

washing.text: =SWASHING (q.v.) Rom. I. i. 69 “thy blow.” ∥ Nashe uses this expression.

wassail.text: carousal, revelry LLL. V. ii. 319 , 2H4 I. ii. 181 “ candle” (=candle lighted up at a feast), Mac. I. vii. 64 , Ham. I. iv. 9 .

waste.text: vb. (see also WASTED) 1. to spend (time, money, &c.), consume (food) AYL. II. vii. 134 “we will nothing ” (=eat), R2 II. i. 253 , 2H4 IV. i. 215 “hath w-d all his rods On late offenders,” Ven. 583 “this night I'll waste in sorrow.”

waste1.text: sb. (in R2 II. i. 103 a ref. to the legal sense ‘destruction of houses, woods, lands, &c., done by the tenant to the prejudice of the heir’; 2 is also perhaps a legal metaphor) 1. wasting, squandering, devastation (often in phr. “make ”) Mer.V. I. i. 158 , H5 I. ii. 28 , III. iii. 18 , Lr. II. i. 102 “the waste and spoil of all revenues.”

wasted.text: consumed by fire MND. V. ii. 5 [ i. 382 ] “the brands”; (of time) past Oth. I. iii. 84 “Till now some nine moons ,” Sonn. cvi. 1 “the chronicle of wasted time.”

wasteful.text: devastating, consuming, destructive AYL. III. ii. 344 “ learning,” H5 III. i. 14 “ ocean,” Sonn. lv. 5 “wasteful war.”

watch1.text: 1. condition of being awake Cym. III. iv. 43 “in watch” (=awake); “keeps watch,” is awake H5 IV. i. 303 , Rom. II. iii. 35 ; state of sleeplessness Ham. II. ii. 148 “then into a fast, Thence to a watch.”

watch2.text: vb. (1 the commonest sense) 1. to be or lie awake, have no sleep, sit up at night LLL. III. i. 210 [ 202 ] “to sigh for her! to for her!,” Shr. IV. i. 208 , Lr. II. ii. 162 , Lucr. 1575 “they that see time how slow it creeps” ; to remain awake for a specified purpose John IV. i. 30 , Mac. V. i. 1 .

watcher.text: one who remains awake Gent. II. iv. 136 , Mac. II. ii. 72 .

watchful.text: （ John IV. i. 46 * “the minutes to the hour” =the minutes that watch the progress of the hour) 1. marked by or causing loss of sleep Gent. I. i. 31 “ . . . nights,” 2H4 IV. v. 24 , Cæs. II. i. 98 “ cares.”

water.text: (freq.=tears, e.g. 1H4 III. i. 95 , Cor. V. ii. 77 , Oth. IV. ii. 103 ) 1. phr. “raise the w-s,” call forth tears Mer.V. II. ii. 52 ; “for all w-s,” ready for anything Tw.N. IV. ii. 69 .

watering.text: drinking 1H4 II. iv. 17 “breathe in your watering” (=take breath when you drink).

waterish.text: well-watered, abounding in rivers Lr. I. i. 261 “ Burgundy” (with play on the sense ‘poor, thin’ exemplified in Oth. III. iii. 15 “ diet” ).

watery.text: 1. epithet of the moon as controlling the tides MND. II. i. 162 , R3 II. ii. 69 .

wawl.text: to wail Lr. IV. vi. 185 (Ff “wawle,” Q1 “wayle,” Qq2 3 “waile”).

wax1.text: with pun on WAX vb. 2H4 I. ii. 182 ; Rom. I. iii. 76 * “a man of wax,” like a model in wax for beauty; Tim. I. i. 48 * “In a wide sea of wax” (not satisfactorily explained; many conj.).

wax2.text: vb. (pa. pple. “waxed, waxen”; 2 freq.) 1. to grow, increase LLL. V. ii. 10 (with quibble on “wax” sb.), Cor. II. ii. 104 “he waxed like a sea,” Tit. III. i. 96 “the waxing tide,” Ham. I. iii. 12 .

waxen1.text: fig. uses:—easily impressed Tw.N. II. ii. 31 “women's hearts,” Lucr. 1240 “women” [have] “ minds”; easily effaced H5 I. ii. 233 * “a epitaph”; easily penetrable R2 I. iii. 75 “Mowbray's coat.”

way.text: (senses 3 and 4 are rare) 1. passage, course Err. IV. iii. 92 “Belike his wife . . . shut the doors against his way” ; chiefly in phr. “hold” or “keep” one's “way” Wiv. III. ii. 1 , H8 II. iv. 126 “pray you, keep your way,” Ant. III. vi. 85 “let determin'd things to destiny Hold unbewail'd their way.”

ways.text: old genitive of ‘way’ used in adverbial expressions “come your ways, go your ways”; and (dial.) “this ways” Wiv. II. ii. 48 , 52 “come . . . this ways.” ∥ Cf. German ‘geht Eures Weges!’.

we.text: used, like “I,” for the objective ‘us’ Cor. V. iii. 103 “to poor we,” Ham. I. iv. 54 “Making night hideous; and we fools of nature . . . to shake our disposition.”

weak.text: foolish, stupid Tp. II. ii. 156 [ 148 ], Ado III. i. 54 , Rom. II. iv. 181 .

weal.text: (1 survives in “weal and woe”) 1. welfare John IV. ii. 65 , 66 , Tim. IV. iii. 161 “the general weal,” Ham. III. iii. 14 .

wealth.text: welfare, prosperity Mer.V. V. i. 249 , Ham. IV. iv. 27 . ∥ Cf. Prayer Book, ‘Grant him in health and wealth long to live’.

wean.text: fig. to turn away, alienate 3H6 IV. iv. 17 “I the rather wean me from despair” (Ff “wain(e),” Tit. I. i. 211 “I will restore to thee The people's hearts, and wean them from themselves.”

wear1.text: fashion Meas. III. ii. 81 “it is not the wear,” AYL. II. vii. 34 “Motley's the only wear,” All'sW. I. i. 223 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 329

wear2.text: vb. (freq. used where ‘bear’ would now be idiomatic; Ado V. i. 82 “Win me and wear me,” a common Eliz. proverb; see also WORN) 1. to weary, ‘wear out’ AYL. II. iv. 38 “Wearing thy hearer” (Ff2-4 “Wearying”), All'sW. V. i. 4 “To wear your gentle limbs in my affairs.”

wearing.text: clothes Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 9 “a swain's ,” Oth. IV. iii. 16 “my nightly wearing.”

weary.text: tiresome, irksome Meas. I. iv. 25 “Not to be with you,” Ham. I. ii. 133 , Oth. III. iv. 175 ; AYL. II. vii. 73 * “the very means,” emended by Singer to “the wearer's”†.

weather.text: (2 nautical metaphor) 1. storm, tempest Tp. I. i. 42 “louder than the ,” Mer.V. II. ix. 29 , Wint. V. ii. 134 “extremity of continuing,” John IV. ii. 109 , Cym. III. iii. 64 .

weaver.text: ref. to as fond of singing Tw.N. II. iii. 63 “a catch that will draw three souls out of one ,” 1H4 II. iv. 149 “I would I were a ; I could sing psalms or anything.”

wedded.text: nuptial Rom. I. v. 139 “my bed” (F1; Qq “wedding”).

weed.text: to uproot (lit. and fig.) Gent. III. ii. 49 , Meas. III. ii. 292 [ 284 ] “To weed my vice and let his grow,” R2 II. iii. 167 “The caterpillars of the commonwealth, Which I have sworn to and pluck away,” Cor. IV. v. 108 , Oth. I. iii. 327 “set hyssop and up thyme.”

weed1.text: dress, garment Lucr. 196 “love's modest snowwhite weed” ; very freq. in pl. Gent. II. vii. 42 , Cor. II. iii. 162 , Ham. IV. vii. 80 .

weed2.text: (?) ill-conditioned horse Meas. I. iii. 20 “The needful bits and curbs to headstrong weeds” (Theobald “steeds”†).

weeding.text: what is weeded out, weeds LLL. I. i. 96 .

week.text: “in by the week,” trapped, caught LLL. V. ii. 61 ; “too late a week,” used like the phr. ‘too late in the day’ AYL. II. iii. 74 .

ween.text: to think, imagine 1H6 II. v. 88 , H8 V. i. 136 “Ween you of better luck.”

weet.text: to know Ant. I. i. 39 “I bind . . . the world to weet We stand up peerless.”

weigh.text: (rare in literal senses) 1. to consider, take into consideration Cæs. II. i. 108 “Weighing the youthful season of the year,” Sonn. cxx. 8 “To weigh how once I suffer'”

weight.text: “by weight, in weight, with weight,” with full measure, fully Meas. I. ii. 130 “Make us pay down for our offence by The words of heaven,” H5 III. vi. 139 “which, in to reanswer, his pettiness would bow under,” Troil. V. ii. 165 , Ham. IV. v. 155 “thy madness shall be paid by weight” (Qq “with weight”).

weird.text: (only in Mac.; one syll. in III. i. 2 ; 2 syll. in II. i. 20 , IV. i. 136 ; old edd. “weyard, weyward”): having to do with fate or destiny Mac. I. iii. 32 “The sisters,” &c., III. i. 2 “the women.” ∥ “The sisters,” taken from Holinshed's Chronicle of Scotland, is a Scottish expression, being used by Gawin Douglas for the Parcae or Fates.

welfare.text: health Mer.V. V. i. 114 “our husbands' ” (Q1 “health”), Lucr. 263 , Sonn. cxviii. 7 .

welkin.text: sky Tp. I. ii. 4 , John V. ii. 172 , Tit. III. i. 211 , Ven. 921 ; used ludicrously in Tw.N. III. i. 66 ; attrib. = heavenly, or blue Wint. I. ii. 137 “your welkin eye.”

well1.text: spring of water Troil. V. x. 19 , Compl. 255 , Sonn. Music iii. 37 [ Pilgr. 281 ] “Clear wells spring not.”

well2.text: (of the dead) happy, at rest Wint. V. i. 30 , Rom. V. i. 17 , Ant. II. v. 33 ; “well to live,” well to do, prosperous Mer.V. II. ii. 55 , Wint. III. iii. 125 . ∥ ‘Well-to-live’ is now only Scottish in this sense.

wen.text: tumour, swelling (fig.) 2H4 II. ii. 117 “this wen” (ref. to Falstaff).

wench.text: term of affectionate address to an inferior Tp. I. ii. 139 [Prospero to Miranda] “Well demanded, wench,” 409, 476 , H8 III. i. 1 [Queen Katherine to one of her women] “Take thy lute, wench,” Lucr. 1273 [Lucrece to her maid] “Know, gentle wench, it small avails my mood.”

wharf.text: bank (of a river) Ham. I. v. 33 “on Lethe wharf,” Ant. II. ii. 221 .

what.text: pron. and adj. (1, 7, 8 are all freq.) A.. Interrogative uses. 1. (in predicative use) Of what name?, Who? Meas. V. i. 468 “one in the prison . . . I have reserv'd alive. —What's he?—His name is Barnardine,” H5 III. vii. 120 , Mac. V. vii. 2 “What's he That was not born of woman?,” Oth. I. i. 94 “what are you?—My name is Roderigo.”

wheel1.text: sb. (2 freq.; 3 in Warwickshire, a clock that goes fast is said to go on wheels) 1. spinning-wheel AYL. I. ii. 36 “mock the good housewife Fortune from her wheel” (with ref. to sense 2), Ham. IV. v. 171 “how the wheel becomes it” (viz. as an accompaniment to the song).

wheel2.text: 1. to turn round R3 IV. iv. 105 “Thus hath the course of justice wheel'd about” (Ff “whirl'd”).

when.text: (1 for phr. “when? can you tell?,” see TELL) 1. as an exclamation of impatience Tp. I. ii. 316 “Come, thou tortoise! when?,” R2 I. i. 162 , Cæs. II. i. 5 “When, Lucius, when! Awake, I say!.”

whence.text: from the place where All'sW. III. ii. 124 “come thou home . . . honour but of danger wins a scar,” Mac. I. ii. 25 “As whence the sun gins his reflection . . . So from that spring . . .” ; also “from ” in the same sense Tit. I. i. 68 “is return'd From ” . . . (Qq “From where”), Tim. I. i. 22 .

where.text: (freq. in “look where, lo where, see where,” phrases directing attention to some action, without emphasis on locality) 1. in which condition or action Tw.N. V. i. 90 “I . . . Drew to defend him, . . . Where being apprehended” ; in a case in which, in circumstances in which, Gent. I. i. 29 “To be in love, where scorn is bought with groans,” Troil. IV. iv. 33 ; (hence=) when Tp. V. i. 236 , Cæs. I. ii. 59 “I have heard, Where many . . . Have wish'd” . . .

whereabout.text: on what errand or purpose 1H4 II. iii. 109 “question me Whither I go, nor reason ” ;— sb. what one is about Mac. II. i. 58 .

whereas.text: where 2H6 I. ii. 58 “unto Saint Alban's, the king and queen do mean to hawk,” Per. I. iv. 70 , Pilgr. vi. 13 [ 83 ].

wherefore.text: 1. to what end? R2 II. iii. 122 .

wherein.text: 1. in what clothes? AYL. III. ii. 235 “Wherein went he?.”

whereof.text: wherewith All'sW. I. iii. 237 “the desperate languishings The king is render'd lost,” Tim. IV. iii. 195 “Whereof ingrateful man . . . greases his pure mind.”

whereuntil.text: to what LLL. V. ii. 493 “we know it doth amount,” 500

whereupon.text: on what, on what grounds, for what reason John IV. ii. 65 , 1H4 IV. iii. 42 “to know The nature of your griefs, and You conjure” . . .

whet.text: to incite, instigate John III. iv. 181 “I will on the king,” Cæs. II. i. 61 “Cassius first did whet me against Cæsar.”

whether.headword: whether (freq. scanned as one syll., cf. WHE'R)
whether.text: which of the two All'sW. IV. v. 23 “ dost thou profess thyself, a knave, or a fool?,” Ven. 304 “whe'r he run or fly they know not ” ; hence, introducing the first of alternative questions Wiv. III. ii. 3 , John I. i. 134 “ hadst thou rather be a Faulconbridge . . . Or the reputed son of Cæur-de-Lion” ; occas. “or ” (i) introduces the second question Mer.V. III. ii. 117 “Move these eyes? Or . . . Seem they in motion?” ; (ii) introduces the first question Cor. I. iii. 69 “or his fall enraged him, or how 'twas,” Sonn. cxiv. 1 “Or doth my mind . . . Or shall I say” . . .?.

which.text: 1. refers freq. to persons=who, whom, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 32 , 1H4 III. i. 46 , Mac. V. i. 65 , Lucr. 1392 ; “the which” is very common, e.g. Ado II. i. 30 , V. i. 159 , H5 IV. viii. 90 , Cæs. III. i. 295 , Ven. 683 .

whiffler.text: officer who clears the way for a procession H5 v. Chor. 12 “the deep-mouth'd sea, Which, like a mighty 'fore the king, Seems to prepare his way.”

while1.text: “the while” in exclamations=(at) the present time Mer.V. II. i. 31 “alas the !,” John IV. ii. 100 “bad world the !,” R3 III. vi. 10 “Here's a good world the while!.”

while2.text: till R2 I. iii. 122 “let the trumpets sound we return these dukes what we decree,” Mac. III. i. 44 “while then, God be with you!.”

whiles.text: till Tw.N. IV. iii. 29 “He shall conceal it you are willing it shall come to note.”

whip.text: intr. and refl. to move quickly Ado I. iii. 63 “I whipt” (Q “whipt me) behind the arras,” LLL. V. ii. 310 “Whip to your tents.”

whipster.text: contemptible fellow Oth. V. ii. 242 “every puny whipster.”

whirligig.text: whipping-top; fig. Tw.N. V. i. 389 “thus the of time brings in his revenges” ; old edd. have only the old forms “whirl(e)gigg(”

whirling.text: impetuous, violent Ham. I. v. 133 “ words” (Q1 “wherling,” Q2 “whurling”; Ff “hurling”).

whissing.text: old form of ‘wheezing’ Troil. V. i. 24 (Q).

whist.text: silent Tp. I. ii. 378 “The wild waves whist!.”

whistle1.text: Lr. IV. ii. 29 “I have been worth the ” = Once I was worthy of some notice; ref. to proverb ‘It is a poor dog that is not worth the whistling.’

whistle2.text: phr. 2H4 III. ii. 345 “tunes . . . that he heard the carmen ” (ref. to a popular Eliz. tune named ‘The Carman's Whistle’); Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 716 “let the law go whistle” (=go hang); whistle off, (in falconry) to send (a hawk) from the fist Oth. III. iii. 262 “if I do prove her haggard . . . I'd her off and let her down the wind” (i.e. so that she may not return) “To prey at fortune”; fig. Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 247 “to whistle off these secrets.”

white1.text: sb. (in Oth. II. i. 133 with pun on WIGHT) 1. =BLANK sb. 1, Shr. V. ii. 187 “'Twas I won the wager though you hit the ” (with allusion to “Bianca”= white).

white2.text: typical of cowardice Mer.V. III. ii. 86 “livers as milk” (cf. MILK-LIVER'D), 2H4 IV. iii. 113 , Mac. II. ii. 66 “I shame To wear a heart so ;— herring,” fresh herring or pickled herring (opposed to ‘red herring’) Lr. III. vi. 34 .

whitely.text: pale LLL. III. i. 206 [ 198 ] “A wanton” (Qq Ff1 2 “whitl(e)y”; Aldis Wright “wightly”†).

whither.text: whithersoever 1H4 V. iii. 22 , Cor. I. ii. 16 . ∥ A freq. spelling in old edd. is “whether.”

whitster.text: bleacher of linen Wiv. III. iii. 15 .

whittle.text: small clasp-knife Tim. V. i. 185 “There's not a in the unruly camp But I do prize it” . . . ∥ Wright in his Provincial Dictionary quotes as a Warwickshire saying, ‘A penny whittle, That will neither cut stick nor vittle’.

who1.text: freq. used for ‘whom’ Mer.V. II. vi. 30 “For who love I so much?,” H5 IV. vii. 155 “Who servest thou under?,” 2H6 III. ii. 127 “And care not who they sting,” Ven. 847 .

who2.text: relative pron. (1 cf. prec.; see WHOM) 1. used for ‘whom’, e.g. Mer.V. I. ii. 25 (Qq “who,” Ff “whom”), R3 I. iii. 327 “who I, indeed, have cast in darkness” (F1 “who,” Qq “whom”), Oth. II. iii. 15 .

whole.text: in a healthy state, restored to health, well 2H6 IV. vii. 11 “he was thrust in the mouth . . . and 'tis not whole yet,” Cæs. II. i. 327 “make sick men ,” Ant. IV. viii. 11 “kiss The honour'd gashes ” ; fig. All'sW. V. iii. 37 , John I. i. 35 .

wholesome.text: 1. sound, healthy Mac. IV. iii. 105 “thy days” (= days of health), Ham. I. v. 70 “curd . . . The thin and blood,” III. ii. 275 , iv. 65 .

whom.text: 1. = which, e.g. 2H6 III. ii. 345 “the seal, Through whom a thousand sighs are breath'd for thee,” Troil. III. iii. 202 “a mystery—with whom” . . .

whoop1.text: a coarse exclamation Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 199 “he makes the maid to answer, ‘Whoop, do me no harm, good man’,” Lr. I. iv. 247 “Whoop, Jug! I love thee.”

whoreson.text: used in coarse playfulness = fellow, ‘dog’ H8 I. iii. 39 “the sly w-s,” Rom. IV. iv. 20 “a merry ” ; as adj. chiefly as an epithet of contempt, e.g. Tp. I. i. 48 “Hang, cur, hang! you , insolent noisemaker!,” 2H4 II. ii. 93 “Away, you upright rabbit, away!” ; also as a coarse term of endearment 2H4 II. iv. 224 “you little valiant villain, you!” ; or a mere intensive of little meaning 2H4 III. ii. 195 “What disease hast thou?—A cold, sir,” Ham. V. i. 188 “your dead body,” 192 “A whoreson mad fellow.”

whosoever1.text: no matter who it be Troil. I. ii. 206 “he's one o' the soundest judgements in Troy, ”

whosoever2.text: for ‘whomsoever’ Troil. II. i. 69 (Ff1 2 Q “who some euer”).

why.text: (obsolete idiomatic uses) 1. used, like WHAT, in calling to a person Mer.V. II. v. 6 “What, Jessica! . . . What, Jessica! . . . Why, Jessica, I say!,” 2H4 V. i. 8 “Why, Davy!—Here, sir.”

wicked.text: 1. mischievous, baneful Tp. I. ii. 321 “ dew,” Lr. II. i. 41 “wicked charms.”

wide.text: indifferent to Wiv. III. i. 58 “so wide of his own respect.”

widen.text: to open wide Cor. I. iv. 44 .

widow.text: (the sense ‘make a widow of’ occurs) 1. to settle a jointure upon Meas. V. i. 425 “We do instate and widow you withal.”

widowhood.text: estate settled on a widow Shr. II. i. 125 “I'll assure her of Her widowhood.”

wield.text: fig. to express Lr. I. i. 57 “I love you more than words can wield the matter.”

wife.text: the orig. sense of ‘woman’ (as in GOODWIFE, HOUSEWIFE) is traceable more or less clearly in the foll. passages:— Wiv. II. ii. 102 “she's . . . a civil modest wife,” Tw.N. V. i. 140 “him I love . . . More . . . than e'er I shall love wife,” H5 V. Chor. 10 “with men, with wives, and boys,” Cor. IV. iv. 5 “thy wives with spits and boys with stones.”

wight.text: man, person Wiv. I. iii. 21 , LLL. I. i. 176 , H5 II. i. 64 , Oth. II. i. 158 , Sonn. cvi. 2 .

wild1.text: Weald of Kent 1H4 II. i. 60 “a franklin in the wild of Kent.”

wild2.text: inconsiderate, rash Wint. II. i. 181 , Cor. IV. i. 36 “a wild exposture to each chance” . . .

wilderness.text: wildness, barrenness Meas. III. i. 140 “of wilderness” (=barren, worthless).

wildfire.text: gunpowder rolled up wet and set on fire 1H4 III. iii. 45 “a ball of ,” Lucr. 1523 “Whose words, like , burnt the shining glory Of rich-built Ilion.”

wildness.text: madness Ham. III. i. 40 “Hamlet's ,” Cym. III. iv. 9 “ere Vanquish my staider senses.”

wilful.text: 1. willing, eager Wiv. III. ii. 45 , MND. V. i. 213 “when walls are so to hear without warning,” Rom. I. v. 93 , Ven. 365 “wilful and unwilling.”

will1.text: sb. (“good will” is freq. in the senses of ‘favourable regard, favour’, ‘acquiescence, consent’, and ‘willingness, readiness’) 1. phr. “by my will,” (i) of my own accord, voluntarily Ado III. iii. 67 “I would not hang a dog by my will,” Tw.N. III. iii. 1 ; (ii) with my consent 2H4 IV. i. 159 “by my will we shall admit no parley,” Troil. II. iii. 204 , Ven. 639 ;—“by” or “of” one's “(own) good will,” of one's own accord R2 IV. i. 177 “To do that office of thine own good will Which tired majesty did make thee offer,” Ven. 479 “she, by her good will, Will never rise, so he will kiss her still” ; so “on my free will” Ant. III. vi. 57 .

will2.text: vb. (apparent instances of “I will”=I shall, are dealt with in Abbott's Shakespearian Grammar § 319; see separate article for the uses of WOULD) 1. to wish to have All'sW. I. i. 180 “Will you anything with it?” (idiomatic 16th cent. phr.=Is there anything else you'd like to know, So now you know), II. i. 74 “you will my noble grapes,” ; esp. with negative, to refuse to have, have nothing to do with 2H4 II. iv. 80 “I'll no swaggerers,” Ham. V. ii. 261 “I . . . will no reconcilement.”

willing.text: as adv. willingly R2 III. iii. 206 “What you will have, I'll give, and too,” 2H6 V. i. 51 , Tim. III. vi. 33 “The swallow follows not summer more than we your lordship.”

willingly.text: intentionally MND. III. ii. 346 “commit'st thy knaveries willingly” (Qq “wilfully”).

willow.text: “ garland,” emblem of disappointed love 3H6 IV. i. 100 ; cf. Oth. IV. iii. 51 “a green must be my garland” (part of a song), and Ado II. i. 196 .

wimpled.text: blindfolded LLL. III. i. 189 [ 181 ] (applied to Cupid).

win.text: “win of,” get the better of John II. i. 569 “he that wins of all,” H8 V. i. 58 , Cym. I. i. 121 , Sonn. lxiv. 7 “I have seen . . . the firm soil win of the watery main” ; similarly “win upon” Cor. I. i. 226 “it” [sc. the rabble] “will in time Win upon power” (=get the better of authority); cf. Ant. II. iv. 9 “You'll win two days upon me” (=get the advantage of me by two days).

wind.text: vb. 2 (pa. pple. “winded”) 1. to blow Ado I. i. 251 [ 243 ], MND. IV. i. stage dir.

wind1.text: sb. (see also BREAK, DOOR) 1. phr. “down the wind,” (to fly) in the direction of the wind, as a hawk was made to do when dismissed Oth. III. iii. 262 ; “sits in the wind against,” is in opposition to Ant. III. viii. 46 [ x. 37 ]; “on the wind,” speedily and without impediment, as if on the ‘wings of the wind’ Ant, III. vi. 63 ; cf. Cym. III. iv. 38 ; “have i' the wind,” get scent of All'sW. III. vi. 123 ; “keeps the wind,” keep to windward of the game so as to force it into the toils 3H6 III. ii. 14 ; so “recover the wind of” Ham. III. ii. 369 [ 362 ] “why do you go about to recover the wind of me, as if you would drive me into a toil?;—have the wind of,” keep watch upon (as upon the game, when following it down the wind) Tit. IV. ii. 134 .

wind2.text: vb. 1 (pa. t. and pa. pple. “wound”) 1. to turn or wheel (a horse) round 1H4 IV. i. 109 “To turn and wind a fiery Pegasus” ; also intr. Cæs. IV. i. 32 “a creature that I teach to fight, To wind, to stop.”

windgalls.text: disease attacking the fetlock in horses Shr. III. ii. 54 .

windlass.text: pl. roundabout ways Ham. II. i. 65 “With w-es, and with assays of bias.” ∥ The common Eliz. phr. was ‘fetch a windlass’ (cf. FETCH vb. 4).

window.text: often applied to the eyelids R3 V. iii. 117 , Rom. IV. i. 100 , Ant. V. ii. 318 “Downy w-s, close,” Ven. 482 ;—phr. “in at the ,” said of illegitimate children John I. i. 171 .

windowed.text: 1. placed in a window Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 72

windring.text: Tp. IV. i. 128 “ brooks” (mod. edd. “winding†, wand'ring†”).

windy.text: (2 following WIND sb. 2) 1. windward; “the side,” (fig.) the safe or advantageous side Ado II. i. 329 , Tw.N. III. iv. 183 .

wing.text: with defining adj. or in phr.=flight Tw.N. II. v. 126 “with what wing the staniel† checks at it,” 1H4 III. ii. 30 “thy affections, which do hold a wing” (=take a course) “Quite from the flight of all thy ancestors,” H5 IV. i. 113 , Mac. III. ii. 51 “the crow Makes wing.”

winged.text: 1. flying 1H6 IV. vii. 21 , Cym. IV. ii. 348 .

wink1.text: sb. (2 transferred from the sense ‘brief space of time’, cf. Wint. V. ii. 124 ) 1. closing of the eyes; only in phr. referring to death Tp. II. i. 293 [ 285 ] “[put] To the perpetual ,” Wint. I. ii. 317 “To give mine enemy a lasting wink.”

wink2.text: vb. (1 the commonest S. sense) 1. to shut one's eyes, have the eyes closed; said also of the eyes themselves Tp. II. i. 224 [ 216 ] “Thou . . . wink'st Whiles thou art waking,” H5 II. i. 8 “I dare not fight; but I will and hold out mine iron,” Cym. V. iv. 193 “such as wink and will not use them” [viz. their eyes], Ven. 90 “He winks, and turns his lips another way,” Sonn. xliii. 1 ;—in some exx. =blink LLL. I. ii. 55 “ere you'll thrice wink,” R2 IV. i. 284 “the face That like the sun did make beholders wink,” Lucr. 375 “his eyes begun To wink, being blinded with a greater light.”

winking1.text: closing of the eyes Ham. II. ii. 137 * “given my heart a ” (=closed the eyes of my heart; Qq2-5 “working”).

winking2.text: with eyes shut H5 III. vii. 158 “that run into the mouth of a Russian bear” ; blind Cym. II. iv. 89 “ Cupids” ; (of flowers, &c.) closed John II. i. 215 “your gates,” Cym. II. iii. 26 “winking Mary-buds.”

wintered.text: worn in winter AYL. III. ii. 112 “ garments must be lin'd” (Ff1 2).

winterly.text: cheerless Cym. III. iv. 13 “winterly [news].” ∥ Cf. SUMMER.

wiry.text: John III. iv. 64 “wiry friends” =hairs (cf. Sonn. cxxx. 4 ); Sonn. cxxviii. 4 “The wiry concord” =the harmony of the strings.

wisdom.text: “ of nature,” natural science Lr. I. ii. 116 .

wise.text: manner Per. V. ii. 11 (Gower) “in no wise” (=not at all), Pilgr. iii. 33 [ 277 ].

wish.text: to invite or commend (one) “to” another Shr. I. i. 112 “I will wish him to her father,” I. ii. 60 “shall I . . . wish thee to a shrewd ill-favour'd wife?.”

wishtly.text: with longing looks R2 V. iv. 7 “he looked on me, As who should say, ‘I would thou wert the man’” (Qq1 2; the rest “wistly”).

wist.text: knew 1H6 IV. i. 180 “An if I wist he did,—But let it rest” (old edd. “wish”; Theobald “I wis”†). ∥ See note S.V. WOT.

wistly.text: (of looking) steadfastly, attentively Ven. 343 , Lucr. 1355 “and, blushing with him, on him gaz'd,” Pilgr. vi. 12 [ 82 ]. ∥ Cf. ‘Robin behelde our comly kynge Wystly in the face’ (Robyn Hode, vii. fytte).

wit1.text: sb. (the foll. senses are characteristic of the Eliz. period) 1. the mental powers or faculties, the mind; usu. pl. e.g. Gent. I. i. 44 “love Inhabits in the finest wits,” Cor. II. iii. 21 , &c.; “five wits,” common sense, imagination, fancy, estimation, memory Ado I. i. 67 , Rom. I. iv. 47 , Lr. III. iv. 57 , Sonn. cxli. 9 “my five wits nor my five senses” ; occas. sing. Gent. I. i. 47 “the young and tender wit,” 1H6 I. ii. 73 “My wit untrain'd in any kind of art.”

wit2.text: to know 1H6 II. v. 16 “As witting I no other comfort have,” Per. IV. iv. 31 “Now please you wit The epitaph is for Marina writ.”

witch.text: to bewitch 1H4 IV. i. 110 , 3H6 III. ii. 150 (Ff “'witch”), Tim. V. i. 160 , Ham. III. ii. 413 [ 406 ] “the very witching time of night, When churchyards yawn.” ∥ Cf. WOT.

with.text: (1 one of the commonest S. senses) 1. expressing agency=by Ado II. i. 65 “to be overmastered with a piece of valiant dust,” John II. i. 567 “rounded in the ear With that same purpose-changer,” Ant. V. ii. 170 “must I be unfolded With one that I have bred?.”

withal.text: the common meanings are (1) with this, with it, therewith, (2) at the same time, besides, (3) with; phr. “I could not do withal,” I could not help it Mer.V. III. iv. 72 .

withdraw.text: Ham. III. ii. 367 [360 * ] “To with you,” let me speak privately with you.

wither.text: “ out,” cause to dwindle MND. I. i. 6 “w-ing out a young man's revenue.”

withers.text: in a horse, the part where the shoulderbones join the neck 1H4 II. i. 8 “wrung in the ,” Ham. III. ii. 256 “our withers are unwrung.”

within.text: to close quarters with Err. V. i. 34 “Some get him, take his sword away. ∥ Within” once follows its object, which is in the nominative Mac. III. iv. 14 “'Tis better thee without than he within.”

without1.text: beyond the reach of Tp. V. i. 271 “ her power,” MND. IV. i. 159 “Without the peril of the Athenian law,” Mac. III. ii. 11 “Things all remedy.”

without2.text: unless Gent. II. i. 40 , Err. III. ii. 92 , Ado III. iii. 85 .

witness1.text: “with a ,” with a vengeance Shr. V. i. 121 “Here's packing, with a witness.”

witness2.text: to give or show evidence of Meas. IV. iii. 103 “letters . . . whose contents Shall to him I am near at home,” R2 II. iv. 22 “W-ing storms to come,” Sonn. xxvi. 4 “I send this written ambassage, To duty.”

wittily.text: wisely Tw.N. IV. ii. 16 “as the old hermit of Prague . . . very said . . . ‘That that is is’” ; cleverly Ven. 471 .

witty.text: (obs. uses; cf. WIT sb.) 1. wise, prudent MND. V. i. 169 , Tw.N. I. v. 38 “Better a witty fool than a foolish wit,” 3H6 I. ii. 43 “Witty, courteous, liberal,” Troil. III. ii. 30 , Oth. II. i. 131 .
