woe1.text: lament Ado V. iii. 33 “this for whom we render'd up this woe!” ; grievous thing H5 I. ii. 26 “whose guiltless drops Are every one a woe . . . 'Gainst” . . .; in exclamations=alas for Tp. I. ii. 15 “woe the day!,” H5 IV. vii. 79 “woe the while!.”

woe2.text: sorry Tp. V. i. 139 “I am woe for't,” 2H6 III. ii. 73 , Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 133 “woe are we,” Sonn. lxxi. 8 “If thinking on me then should make you woe.” ∥ ‘I am woe’ was developed from the old ‘Woe is me’; Chaucer blends the old and the new in ‘me is as wo For him as ever I was for any man’.

wolvish.text: the form current in old edd.; mod. edd. often wolfish †.

woman1.text: sb. (1 contrast WIFE) 1. wife Wiv. II. ii. 309 “the hell of having a false ,” 1H4 II. iii. 44 .

woman2.text: to bend or subdue (like a woman) All'sW. III. ii. 53 .

womb1.text: transf. applied to anything hollow or conceived as hollow (e.g. the earth, night) R2 II. i. 83 “a grave, Whose hollow womb” . . ., 1H4 III. i. 31 , H5 IV. Chor. 4 “the foul womb of night,” Rom. V. i. 65 “the fatal cannon's womb,” Compl. 1 “a hill Whose concave womb” . . .

womb2.text: to enclose Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 503

wonder1.text: sb. (obsolete uses) 1. admiration Tw.N. II. i. 29 “such estimable wonder,” Wint. V. i. 133 , Lucr. 84 “In silent wonder of stillgazing eyes.”

wonder2.text: to admire Sonn. cvi. 14 “we . . . Have eyes to , but lack tongues to praise” ; const. “at” LLL. V. ii. 267 “Are these the breed of wits so wonder'd at?.”

wont.text: =the much commoner “is” or “are wont, was” or “were wont” Err. IV. iv. 38 “I bear it on my shoulders, as a beggar wont her brat” (=is accustomed to bear), 1H6 I. ii. 14 , I. iv. 10 .

wood.text: mad Gent. II. iii. 31 “O, that she could speak now like a wood† woman” (Ff “would-woman”), MND. II. i. 192 “here am I, and wood” (Q1 “wodde) within this wood,” 1H6 IV. vii. 35 “raging wood.”

woodbine.text: honeysuckle Ado III. i. 30 , MND. II. i. 251 ; (?) bindweed, Convolvulus sepium MND. IV. i. 48 “So doth the the sweet honeysuckle Gently entwist.”

woodcock.text: type of stupidity; hence=fool Ado V. i. 161 , Ham. I. iii. 115 .

wooden.text: fig. 1H6 V. iii. 89 * “a wooden thing,” (a) ‘awkward business’ (Steevens), (b) ‘expressionless, insensible thing—referring to the king’ (H. C. Hart).

woodman.text: hunter Wiv. V. v. 30 , Cym. III. vi. 28 “You, Polydore, have prov'd best ,” Lucr. 580 ; fig. woman-hunter Meas. IV. iii. 174 .

woollen.text: covered with woollen cloth Mer.V. IV. i. 56 “a bagpipe” (so Qq Ff1 2 3; Capell “wauling”†); coarsely clad, homely Cor. III. ii. 9 “woollen vassals” ;—sb. Ado II. i. 33 “lie in the ,” sleep between the blankets with no sheets.

woolward.text: with woollen clothing next the skin LLL. V. ii. 716 “I go for penance.” ∥ Cf. Palsgr., Wolwarde, without any lynnen nexte ones body, ‘sans chemyse’.

woot.text: wilt (thou) Ham. V. i. 297 “Woot weep? woot fight?,” Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 59 “Noblest of men, woot die?.” ∥ Remains in west-midland dial. Cf. WOT.

word1.text: sb. (4 is freq. in ordinary phrases) 1. “at a word,” to be brief, in short Wiv. I. i. 109 , Ado II. i. 120 , Cor. I. iii. 122 “go along with us.—No, at a , madam” ; so “with a word” 1H4 II. iv. 287 ; in phr. expressing prompt decision or action Wiv. I. iii. 14 “I am at a word; follow,” 2H4 III. ii. 322 “Go to; I have spoke at a word” (=you may depend upon me), Cæs. I. ii. 270 “if I would not have taken him at a word” ; cf. Cæs. I. ii. 104 “Upon the word . . . I plunged in.”

word2.text: vb. (only in Ant. and Cym.) 1. to say (as opposed to ‘sing’) Cym. IV. ii. 240 .

work1.text: fortification H8 V. iv. 63 , Oth. III. ii. 3 .

work2.text: vb. (pa. t. and pa. pple. always “wrought”; 1 cf. WORKING vbl. sb. and ppl. adj.; 5 said esp. of seething waters in Eliz. period) 1. to act upon or affect, powerfully move Tp. IV. i. 144 “your father's in some passion That works him strongly,” V. i. 17 “your charm so strongly works them,” Mac. I. iii. 149 “my dull brain was wrought With things forgotten,” Oth. V. ii. 344 .

working2.text: exciting the emotions, full of pathos H8 Prol. 3

workman.text: skilled worker Tim. IV. iii. 441 “Do villany . . . Like workmen,” Ant. IV. iv. 18 “thou shouldst see A workman in't,” Cym. IV. i. 7 .

world.text: 1. “matter of the ,” anything at all Troil. II. iii. 198 ; “it is a ,” it is wonderful (“to see”） Ado III. v. 38 , Shr. II. i. 305 [ 313 ].

worldlings.text: (?) men of this world, mortals AYL. II. i. 48 , 2H4 V. iii. 100 .

worldly.text: (the sense ‘devoted to the world and its pursuits’ is not S.) 1. belonging to this world or this life 2H4 IV. v. 229 “My business” (=my life), 2H6 I. ii. 45 “ pleasure,” III. ii. 151 “my solace,” Cæs. I. iii. 96 “life, being weary of those bars,” Cym. IV. ii. 260 “thy task.”

worm.text: (in early use applied widely to all small creeping things) 1. supposed to cause pain and decay in teeth Ado III. ii. 27 ; humorously supposed to infest the fingers of a lazy person (and hence sometimes called ‘idle worms’) Rom. I. iv. 66 “a . . . worm Prick'd from the lazy finger of a maid.”

worn.text: 1. (of time) spent, past Wint. V. i. 142 “infirmity, —Which waits upon worn times” (=attends old age), Lucr. 1350 “worn-out age.”

worry.text: to ‘pull to pieces’ Wint. V. ii. 59 “then again worries he his daughter with clipping her.”

worship1.text: honour, dignity Wint. I. ii. 314 “bench'd and rear'd to worship,” John IV. iii. 72 , 3H6 IV. iii. 16 “ and quietness” (=‘otium cum dignitate’), R3 I. i. 66 “that good man of ,” Cor. III. i. 141 (‘this divided authority of the senate and the people’), Lr. I. iv. 290 ; H8 I. i. 39 “belong to ” (=are of noble rank).

worship2.text: to honour, dignify H5 I. ii. 233 “our grave . . . Not worshipp'd with a waxen epitaph.”

wort1.text: plant, wegetable Wiv. I. i. 125 “Good worts! good cabbage.”

wort2.text: infusion of malt before it is fermented, sweet unfermented beer LLL. V. ii. 234 .

worth1.text: sb. (Malone explains “his ” in Cor. III. iii. 26 * ‘his full quota or proportion’) 1. wealth, riches MND. II. i. 219 “the rich of your virginity,” Tw.N. III. iii. 17 , Rom. II. vi. 32 “They are but beggars that can count their ,” Lr. IV. iv. 10 , Oth. I. ii. 28 “not . . . For the sea's worth.”

worth2.text: of value, valuable 1H4 IV. i. 27 , Troil. II. ii. 22 .

worthiness.text: deservedness Troil. I. iii. 241 “The of praise.”

worthless.text: unworthy 1H6 IV. iv. 21 “ emulation; —worthless of,” not deserving Cæs. V. i. 61 .

worthy.text: to give (a person) a reputation for excellence Lr. II. ii. 128 “he . . . put upon him such a deal of man, That worthied him.”

worthy1.text: pl. excellences Gent. II. iv. 167 , LLL. IV. iii. 236 .

worthy2.text: adj. (the senses ‘excellent’ and ‘deserving’ are the most freq., the latter with various constructions) 1. valuable Tp. I. ii. 247 “I have done thee service,” AYL. III. iii. 62 , Cæs. III. i. 116 “No worthier than the dust,” Sonn. xlviii. 6 .

wot1.text: know(s) Wiv. II. ii. 91 “the picture . . . that you wot of,” Wint. III. ii. 77 “the gods themselves, Wotting no more than I,” H5 IV. i. 302 “The slave . . . little wots What watch the king keeps,” R3 II. iii. 18 “no, no, good friends, God wot,” III. ii. 89 “Wot you what, my lord?” (=let me tell you), Tit. II. i. 48 , Ant. I. v. 22 “wot'st thou whom thou mov'st?.” ∥ The present tense of WIT vb.; the past tense ‘wist’ occurs in the 1611 Bible (e.g. Luke ii. 49 ), but is not S.

wot2.text: wilt 2H4 II. i. 65 “thou wot, wot ta,” (Q; Ff “thou wilt not?”), Ant. IV. ii. 7 . ∥ Cf. WOOT.

would.text: (obs. or archaic uses of the past subjunctive) 1. =wish, desire Gent. II. iv. 117 “my lord your father speak with you,” Tit. III. i. 209 “would thou kneel with me” (Ff “wilt”), Cæs. II. i. 12 “He be crown'd” Mac. I. v. 19 “thou wouldst be great” ; with sb. or pron. as obj. Mer.V. II. ii. 132 “wouldst thou aught with me?,” H5 IV. i. 32 “I no other company,” V. ii. 68 “If . . . you the peace” ; with clause Ham. I. ii. 234 “I I had been there” ; with accus. and infin. H5 II. Prol. 18 “What mightst thou do that honour would thee do.”

wound.text: entwined Tp. II. ii. 13 “wound with adders.”

woundless.text: invulnerable Ham. IV. i. 44 “the woundless air.”

wrack1.text: sb. (always so spelt in old edd., not ‘wreck’) 1. destruction, ruin All'sW. III. v. 23 “the of maidenhood,” 2H6 I. ii. 105 “Hume's knavery will be the duchess' ,” Mac. I. iii. 114 “He labour'd in his country's wrack,” Ven. 558 “honour's wrack.”

wrack2.text: to destroy, ruin R3 IV. i. 96 , Ham. II. i. 113 “meant to wrack thee.”

wrangler.text: adversary H5 I. ii. 264 , Troil. II. ii. 75 “The seas and winds—old wranglers.”

wrath1.text: sb. (1 freq.; 2 once) 1. warlike ardour=RAGE sb. 5 Tw.N. III. iv. 257 “your opposite hath in him what youth, strength, skill, and wrath can furnish withal,” 2H4 I. i. 109 , Cor. I. ix. 86 , Ham. II. ii. 492 [ 483 ].

wrath2.text: wrathful MND. II. i. 20 “fell and ” (rhyme “hath”). ∥ ‘Wroth’ adj. does not occur.

wrathful.text: ‘raging, furious, impetuous’ (Schmidt) R2 I. iii. 136 “ iron arms,” 2H4 III. ii. 173 “valiant as the dove,” 2H6 II. iv. 3 “Barren winter, with his wrathful nipping cold,” V. ii. 70 .

wreak1.text: vengeance, revenge Cor. IV. v. 91 “A heart of ,” Tit. IV. iii. 33 “Take ,” IV. iv. 11 “in his wreaks” (=vindictive acts).

wreak2.text: to revenge Tit. IV. iii. 51 “to wreak our wrongs,” Rom. III. v. 102 .

wreakful.text: revengeful Tit. V. ii. 32 , Tim. IV. iii. 230 .

wreathed.text: (of the arms) folded LLL. IV. iii. 135 .

wrest1.text: key for tuning a harp; fig. Troil. III. iii. 23 “Antenor . . . is such a wrest in their affairs That their negotiations all must slack, Wanting his manage.”

wrest2.text: vb. (2 cf. O'ER-WRESTED) 1. to get as if by main force Tit. III. ii. 44 “I of these” [signs] “will wrest an alphabet.”

wretch.text: as a term of endearment Rom. I. iii. 44 , Oth. III. iii. 90 , Ant. V. ii. 305 .

wretched.text: hateful, loathsome R3 V. ii. 7 “The , bloody, and usurping boar,” Lucr. 999 “Such wretched hands such wretched blood should spill.”

wring.text: (see also WRINGING, WRUNG) 1. to wrench, wrest (lit. and fig.) Meas. V. i. 32 “ redress from you,” 3H6 III. i. 16 “thy sceptre wrung from thee,” Ham. I. ii. 58 “He hath . . . wrung from me my slow leave,” Oth. V. ii. 287 (Ff “Wrench”).

wringing.text: torture, suffering H5 IV. i. 256 , H8 II. ii. 28 “wringing of the conscience.”

wrinkle.text: to give wrinkles to, make to appear old Troil. II. ii. 79 .

writ1.text: sb. (2 “holy writ” is the usu. phrase) 1. that which is written, writing, document 2H6 I. iv. 60 “the devil's writ,” Tit. II. iii. 264 “this fatal writ,” Ham. II. ii. 430 [421 * ] “For the law of writ and the liberty” (?=‘for repeating correctly what is written, and for freedom of improvisation’, Clark and Wright; Q 1676 “wit”), V. ii. 51 [I] “folded the writ up”; ‘penned or premeditated oration’ (J.) Cæs. III. ii. 225 “I have neither writ, nor words, nor worth” (Ff2-4 “wit”).

writ2.text: specified, stipulated Ham. I. ii. 222 “we did think it down in our duty To” . . ., IV. v. 140 “is't writ in your revenge, That . . .?.”

write.text: (pa. t. “writ,” rarely “wrote”; pa. pple. “writ, written,” rarely “wrote”) 1. to sign or subscribe one's name (“for”) 2H6 IV. i. 63 “This hand of mine hath writ in thy behalf,” Sonn. cxxxiv. 7 “He learn'd . . . to write for me, Under that bond.”

writing.text: words of a song LLL. I. ii. 120 .

wroath.text: irregular spellings of ‘ruth’=calamity, ruin Mer.V. II. ix. 78 “Patiently to bear my ” ∥ ‘Roth’ is a 15th cent. form, and ‘routh’ occurs as late as the 17th cent.

wrong.text: (very freq. in the ordinary senses) 1. phr. “have wrong,” suffer injury, injustice, or loss 2H4 II. ii. 107 , V. i. 58 , 3H6 IV. i. 102 , Cæs. III. ii. 116 ; “do” oneself “wrong,” put oneself in the wrong, be mistaken Tp. I. ii. 440 , Wiv. III. iii. 220 , Meas. I. ii. 43 .

wrung.text: wrenched or galled 1H4 II. i. 8 “ in the withers.” ∥ Cf. UNWRUNG.

wrying.text: swerving from the right path Cym. V. i. 5 .

yard.text: yard measure Shr. IV. iii. 113 ; “clothier's ,” ‘cloth-yard shaft’, an arrow used with the long bow Lr. IV. vi. 90 .

yare.text: ready, (hence) nimble, brisk Meas. IV. ii. 61 “if you have occasion to use me . . ., you shall find me ,” Tw.N. III. iv. 248 “be in thy preparation,” Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 131; (of a ship) easily managed Tp. V. i. 224 , Ant. III. vii. 38 ; adv. Tp. I. i. 7 “cheerly, my hearts! yare, yare!,” &c., Ant. V. ii. 285 ; so yarely Tp. I. i. 4 , Ant. II. ii. 219 .

yaw.text: (of a ship) to move unsteadily, fig. in Ham. V. ii. 121 ; but the passage is difficult.

yawn.text: to gape in surprise or wonder Cor. III. ii. 11 , Ham. IV. v. 9 (Ff “ayme, aim”), Oth. V. ii. 100 .

yawning.text: lulling to sleep Mac. III. ii. 43 “ peal.”

ycleped.text: called (see CLEPE) LLL. I. i. 240 , V. ii. 599 .

yea.text: freq. used, like NAY, to corrcct or amplify Tp. I. ii. 206 “make his bold waves tremble, Yea, his dread trident shake” ; prefixed to a question of reproof or surprise MND. III. ii. 411 “Yea, art thou there?,” R3 I. iv. 88 “Yea, are you” (Ff “What) so brief?.”

yean.text: form in mod. edd. of EAN.

year.text: pl.=mature age R2 II. iii. 66 “comes to y-s,” 2H6 II. iii. 28 “a king of y-s;—in y-s,” old 1H4 II. iv. 507 [ 500 ], Rom. III. v. 46 ; LLL. V. ii. 466 “smiles his cheek in years” (see SMILE 2).

yearn.text: to vex, grieve Wiv. III. v. 45 “it would your heart” ; impers. R2 V. v. 76 “it y-'d my heart” (Qq1-4 “ernd,” Ff1-3 Q5 “yern'd”), H5 IV. iii. 26 “It y-s me not.” ∥ Cf. EARN 2 .

yellows.text: jaundice in horses Shr. III. ii. 55 . ∥ Cf. ‘The Jandis, called in a Horse, the Yellowes’ (Blundeville, 1580 ).

yeoman.text: 1. one of the class of small freeholders (who formed a large part of the infantry of English armies) 1H4 IV. ii. 16 “good householders, yeomen's sons,” H5 III. i. 25 , 3H6 I. iv. 123 , R3 V. iii. 339 “Fight, gentlemen of England! fight, bold yeomen!,” Ham. V. ii. 36 “y-'s service,” (=good and faithful service); contrasted with “gentleman” 1H6 II. iv. 81 , Lr. III. vi. 12 .

yerk.text: to thrust or push smartly H5 IV. vii. 84 , Oth. I. ii. 5 “yerk'd him . . . under the ribs.”

yes.text: used to correct a negative statement=on the contrary, but it is or was 2H4 I. iii. 36 , Cor. IV. vi. 62 , V. iv. 28 , Cym. I. iv. 55 ;=YEA H8 I. ii. 176 “I say, take heed; Yes, heartily beseech you.”

yest.text: foam Wint. III. iii. 95 “yest and froth.”

yesty.text: foamy, frothy Mac. IV. i. 53 “the waves” ; fig. Ham. V. ii. 199 “ collection” (=superficial knowledge; Qq2 3 “histy,” Q4-6 “misty”).

yet.text: one of the most freq. senses is ‘still, now as before, now as always’ Wiv. II. ii. 148 “Will they yet look after thee?,” R3 I. iv. 126 “Some . . . dregs of conscience are yet within me,” Ham. I. iii. 55 “Yet here, Laertes!” ; also “as yet” Compl. 75 “I might as yet have been a spreading flower.”

yield.text: (the chief S. meanings are ‘afford, give, grant, allow’, ‘deliver, give up, surrender, resign’, and intr. ‘give way, submit, surrender, assent’） 1. to bring forth, bear Tp. II. i. 239 [ 231 ] “a birth . . . Which throes thee much to ,” Per. V. iii. 48 “she was yielded there.”

yielded.text: given up for lost John V. ii. 107 .

yielding.text: compliance LLL. I. i. 118 , John II. i. 474 , Rom. II. ii. 105 , Lucr. 1658 .

yoke1.text: pair of oxen 2H4 III. ii. 42 ; of servants Wiv. II. i. 180 “a yoke of his discarded men.”

yoke2.text: to be joined or coupled 3H6 IV. i. 23 , IV. vi. 49 “We'll yoke together,” Cor. III. i. 56 .

yore.text: “of ,” once upon a time Sonn. lxviii. 14 .

young.text: 1. raw, inexperienced AYL. I. i. 58 “you are too young in this,” Mac. III. iv. 144 “We are yet but young in deed.”

younger1.text: younger son (cf. Luke xv. 12 ) Mer.V. II. vi. 14 “like a or a prodigal (younker†).”

younger2.text: ago Per. I. iv. 39 “not yet two summers younger” † (=not two years ago; old edd. “yet”).

youngling.text: stripling, novice Shr. II. i. 331 [ 339 ], Tit. II. i. 73 , IV. ii. 94 .

youngly.text: early in life Cor. II. iii. 244 , Sonn. xi. 3 .

youthful.text: belonging to the period of youth, of or in youth Gent. IV. i. 34 “My travel,” AYL. II. iii. 67 “thy wages,” II. vii. 160 “His hose,” R2 I. iii. 70 “Whose youthful spirit,” Compl. 79 .

yslaked.text: reduced to inactivity Per. III. Gower 1 .

zany.text: buffoon who imitated the tricks of a professional clown or fool LLL. V. ii. 464 “some slight zany,” Tw.N. I. v. 95 “the fools' zanies.”

zeal.text: once construed with “of” (instead of the usual “to”) 2H4 IV. ii. 27 “Under the counterfeited of God.”

zed.text: the letter z Lr. II. ii. 68 “Thou whoreson zed! thou unnecessary letter.”

zenith.text: highest point of one's fortune Tp. I. ii. 181 .

zodiac.text: used for ‘year’ Meas. I. ii. 178 “nineteen zodiacs have gone round.”

zone.text: “the burning zone,” the path of the sun Ham. V. i. 304 .
